title: Celebrating 100 years of Delmarva chicken
content:
Celebrating 100 years of Delmarva chicken

 September 27, 2023 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Page: 20 | Section: News 
 
 1048
 Words 

 Read News Document

 The Delmarva Chicken Festival returns on Oct. 7 to Salisbury at the Arthur W. Perdue Stadium beginning at 1 p.m. with no admission charged.This year celebrates the 100th year anniversary of the first dedicated broiler chicken farm on Delmarva. This year's festival will include food trucks, live music, vendors, historical and educational exhibits, and children's activities. The fireworks display will conclude the activities at about 7 p.m.The first chicken festival was held in 1948 and the last one was held in 2014.Due to the 100th anniversary of the Delmarva Poultry Industry it was decided to hold a final festival to mark this milestone. The Delmarva Poultry Industry continues to operate without festivals - the last one held in 2014.Now let's cook some old-fashioned pan-fried chicken.FRIED CHICKEN1½ cups milk, 2 large eggs, 2½ cups all-purpose flour, 2 tablespoons salt, plus additional for sprinkling, 2 teaspoons black pepper, 4 pounds bone-in skin-on chicken pieces, vegetable oil for frying.Preheat the oven to 200 F and place a rack in a large baking pan. In a medium bowl, combine the milk and eggs. Whisk to blend well. In a large heavy-duty resealable plastic food storage bag, combine the flour, 2 tablespoons salt, and pepper. We used to use a wax lined hard paper bag.Seal and shake to combine.Dip the chicken pieces in the milk and egg mixture and let the excess drip off into the bowl. Set already dipped pieces aside on a plate until you have three or four. Add the dipped chicken pieces to the bag of seasoned flour. Seal the bag and shake well to coat the chicken pieces thoroughly.Remove to a plate and repeat with the remaining chicken pieces. Heat the oil in a deep, heavy skillet to 350 F. While it's heating up, set aside a large serving plate lined with paper towels. With a slotted spoon, move the done chicken pieces onto the paper towel-lined plate to drain. Sprinkle immediately with salt.Transfer the drained and seasoned chicken to the prepared pan with a rack. Keep warm in the preheated oven while frying subsequent batches. Depending on the size of your pan and number of guests on Sunday, this recipe will require about 3 to 4 batches.Leftover fried chicken can be reheated with good results. Take the chicken out of the refrigerator and bring it to room temperature.Heat the oven to 400 F. Put the chicken pieces on a rack on top of a rimmed baking sheet and bake for about 15 to 20 minutes until heated through and crisp.I gave you the mashed potato recipe earlier, but here is what makes that dish so special.COUNTRY CHICKEN POT PIE4 cups of diced cooked chicken, 2 cooked, cooled, diced potatoes, 3/4 cup diced celery, ½ cup onion, 2 Tablespoons butter, melted, 3 cups frozen mixed vegetables or 1 cup of fresh corn, 1 cup of fresh snapped green beans, 1 cup diced carrots,1 can cream of chicken soup,1 18 oz. value sized Heinz chicken gravy, 1 tsp salt, ½ tsp coarse black pepper, 1 tsp dried oregano, ½ tsp dried thyme, ¼ tsp dried ground sage, ½ tsp garlic salt, 1 Tablespoon chopped fresh parsley, 1 double pie crust, 1 egg, beaten, 2 tsp water. In a small skillet melt 2 Tablespoons butter. Add in 3/4 cup chopped celery and ½ cup diced onion. Sauté till translucent.In a large bowl add 4 cups chopped chicken, sauteed celery and onions, diced cold potatoes, 3 cups of frozen mixed vegetables, salt, pepper, thyme, oregano, sage, garlic salt and fresh parsley.Mix. Add in 1 can cream of chicken soup and the 18 oz. jar of chicken gravy. Mix till well blended.Roll bottom pie crust out.Place in a deep pie plate. Fill with meat and vegetable filling. Spread out evenly with a slightly mounded center. Roll out the top pie crust. Gently place it on top of the filling. Trim around the outside edge of the pie plate.Fold excess crust under. Flute crust edges with fingers. Cut small slits for vents in the top of the crust. Beat egg with water. Using a pastry brush, brush the top of the crust with egg wash. Place pot pie on top of foil lined baking sheet. Place in a preheated 325-degree oven and bake for 45-55 minutes.Pie is done when the crust is golden brown and the filling is bubbly. (If the crust begins to brown too soon, cover it with a foil tent.) Allow to cool for 10 minutes.Slice and serve.CHICKEN AND DUMPLINGS3 cups chicken (about 2-3 chicken breasts), 2 quarts chicken broth, 2 cups all-purpose flour, ½ teaspoon baking powder, 2 tablespoon cold salted butter, cubed, 1 cup milk, 2 tablespoon olive oil, salt and pepper, to taste.Preheat the oven to 350 F degrees.Spray a baking sheet with nonstick cooking spray. Place chicken breast on the baking sheet and Drizzle a little olive oil on the chicken and season with salt and pepper.Bake chicken for about 45 minutes. Once the chicken is cooked, shred it with two forks. Pour 2 quarts of chicken stock or broth into a large pot and start warming it up on the stove top while you make the dumplings. In a medium bowl, combine flour and baking powder.Then add in cubed butter.Combine using your fingers, fork or pastry cutter. Pour in the milk. Mix it all together.Dust your counter with a generous amount of flour.Place dumpling dough on the counter and dust it with more flour. With a rolling pin, roll the dough out to about ¼-inch thickness. Be sure to add flour as necessary to keep it from sticking underneath or to your rolling pin. Using a knife or a pizza cutter, start cutting out your dumplings into squares. Dust dumplings with a bit more flour. The extra flour is all going to help keep them from sticking but will also thicken your chicken broth some as well when you add them to the pot.Bring chicken broth up to a boil. Add in shredded chicken and stir. Begin adding dumplings one at a time so they don't all stick together. Stir frequently while adding them. Allow dumplings to cook for about 15-20 minutes. You should notice your broth starting to thicken (from the extra flour) and your dumplings may start to sink a little to the bottom because they are soaking up the broth.Take one out and taste test it. It shouldn't have a doughy taste anymore. 
 
 Caption: Fried chicken is an extremely popular food worldwide, but certainly on the Delmarva Peninsula.

title: Winter Festival to be 'bigger and better'
author: Connie Connolly; cconnolly@chespub.com
content:
Winter Festival to be 'bigger and better'

 September 27, 2023 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Connie Connolly; cconnolly@chespub.com | Page: 19 | Section: News 
 
 251
 Words 

 Read News Document

 DENTON - Based on Ridgely's successful Winter Festival last year, the town's Board of Public Works Director David Crist asked the Caroline County Commissioners for help managing public safety this year.The commissioners agreed to lend the needed assistance for this year's festival scheduled for 4 to 9 p.m. Saturday, Dec. 9. The rain date is Dec. 16.Crist said the town's first Winter Festival in 2022 was anticipated to be "a very small event - 1,000 to 2,000 people maybe."However, "going off the drone footage, we had 10,000 to 12,000 people," Crist said. "Now we're figuring that we have to do it every year, and we're going to try to do it bigger and better every year. But we can't do it by ourselves."Crist said the second festival is "already doubled from last year" with 80 vendors, 15 food trucks and an acre devoted to children's amusements lined up.Caroline County Director of Public Works Ryan White and Director of Emergency Services Mark Sheridan walked into the hallway outside the meeting room to work out some details after Crist's appeal.The town promotes the festival as "home of Caroline County's largest Holiday Light Display and the 2022 Winner of APG Media's Best of the Best Chesapeake Awards for Best Seasonal Attraction, Best Festival/Fair and Best Local Event." 
 
 Caption: Annie Hall of Ridgely, right, and her son Jackson, 5, visit with Yukon Cornelius, Rudolph and the Abominable Snowman from "The Island of Misfit Toys" during the 2022 Winter Festival in Ridgely.

title: Homemade Apple Pies
content:
Homemade Apple Pies

 October 4, 2023 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Page: 17 | Section: News 
 
 1216
 Words 

 Read News Document

 The 31st annual Apple Scrapple Festival will be held in Bridgeville, Delaware, on the second weekend in October - Oct. 13 and 14.The first festival was held in 1992 and has grown larger each year. Bridgeville is well known for its scrapple production because of a popular producer of scrapple - Ralph and Paul Adams - in the town limits. And across town and just outside of town popular apple growers - T S Smith and Sons. These families and their production workers help popularize these two main staples in our kitchens.Today I will work with apples and later this winter we will review those homemade scrapple sandwiches. Mom liked picking her own apples and insisted on it this time of year. Every fall, on a cool crisp Saturday morning Mom would put six to eight baskets in the back of the pickup and off to the apple orchard: we would go.Personal preferences vary, but in general, the best apples for fritters have a good balance between sweetness and tartness. I like honeycrisp apples for their crisp sweetness, which intensifies as they cook. Like apples for pie, Braeburn, Jonagold or Pink Lady apples also work great for apple fritters.When it comes to apple pie, a Braeburn's flavor sweetens and concentrates during cooking to evoke a hint of spice, which makes it a natural pick for pie. And since Braeburns don't release much liquid during cooking, they won't lead to a runny filling or soggy pie crust.If you want extra sweetness without the soft texture, choose gala apples for your pie. Granny Smiths are typically my go-to apple for baking, so I'll always have them on hand during the fall months. Their tart, citrusy flavor makes them perfect for sweet baked goods, where there's sugar in the recipe. I love using these for homemade caramel apples, too.The orchards offered already picked or u-pick and Mom liked getting her own. She separated the apples into three categories - some for homemade applesauce, some for fresh baking and those to eat fresh. What a wonderful smell filled the air as we canned and baked.HOMEMADE APPLE PIE DOUBLE PIE CRUST2½ cups all-purpose flour, 2 tablespoons white granulated sugar, 1½ teaspoons kosher salt, 1 cup unsalted butter cold and straight from the fridge, ¾ cups very cold water divided.APPLE PIE FILLING: ½ small lemon juiced (about 1½ tablespoons), 3-4 whole medium to large apples (pink lady, gala and honeycrisp are my favorites) peeled, halved, cored and thinly sliced, ¼ cup all-purpose flour, ½ cup light brown sugar,1½ teaspoons ground cinnamon,1 teaspoon pure vanilla extract or ½ teaspoon vanilla paste, ½ teaspoon kosher salt, 2 tablespoons sour cream, 1 large egg beaten (for egg wash).In a large bowl, mix together the flour, sugar and salt. Using a box grater, grate the cold butter atop the flour mixture. Transfer to the freezer to chill for 10 minutes. Working quickly, and using your hands, break the butter bits into the flour until they're evenly distributed and resemble the size of teeny, small peas. Add half of the recommended water and mix.The mixture will be shaggy at this point. From here, add 1 tablespoon of water at a time until the dough comes together. Flour your counter and dump the dough onto it. Knead a few times more until it comes together into one cohesive mass. Divide the dough, forming two discs. Wrap the discs in plastic wrap and transfer to the refrigerator to chill for at least 1 hour, ideally overnight.TO MAKE THE APPLE PIE FILLING: You're welcome to peel your apples. This is optional. I personally like to peel the apples. Halve the apples, remove the core and then slice the apples into thin ¼-inch pieces. Or you can use a mandolin and slice them very thinly. Add the apple slices to a large bowl. Squeeze in the lemon juice, being sure to catch any seeds. Next, add the flour, brown sugar, cinnamon, vanilla extract and salt; toss until the apples are evenly coated.TO ASSEMBLE THE APPLE PIE: Remove the first disc of dough from the refrigerator and allow it to come to room temperature for about 5 minutes. Liberally flour your work surface and rolling pin. Begin to roll the dough, being sure to rotate it every so often to avoid sticking to a 13-inch round. Wrap the dough around the rolling pin and unroll it over the pie dish. Gently fit the dough into the bottom and up the sides of the pie tin. Trim the dough around the pie tin, leaving about a 1/2-inch overhang. Recombine the scraps and set them aside. We'll use them for the lattice. Transfer the pie shell to the refrigerator while you roll out the second disc.Remove the second disc from the fridge and repeat the rolling process. Using a knife, cut the dough into 3-inch strips. I cut as many 3-inch strips as I can. Reroll the scraps you have set aside, too, you'll need all of the pie dough. (If at any time your pie dough becomes too soft, transfer to a cutting board and put in the fridge to chill so it's easier to work with.) Fill your pie shell with the apple filling. Lay out five strips of pie dough on top of the filling, leaving about ½-inch of space in between them.Lay the remainder of your strips running perpendicular. This will give you a good idea of how it will go. Next, fold back every strip. Start one at the top, running horizontally. and weave it under and over, rotating, each strip running vertically. Repeat this process until you've worked your way through every stripTrim the edges of the strips, being sure to leave about 1-inch overhang. Going all the way around, tuck the edges under. To make a pronounced crimp, like you see pictured, set your thumb on the outside edge of the crust. With your opposite pointer and thumb fingers, create a v, and push the two together. Repeat this process all the way around the pie crust. Transfer to the freezer to chill for 30 minutes.Meanwhile, preheat the oven to 400 degrees F. Brush the entire pie, liberally, with egg wash and sprinkle with turbinado sugar. Transfer the pie to a baking sheet and place in the oven for 20 to 25 minutes, until the edges are just lightly brown.Turn the heat down to 350 degrees F and bake for another 40 to 45 minutes, until the edges and top are deep golden brown. Be sure to check on it intermittently, if at any time the pie crust begins to turn too dark, use foil to cover those areas to stop browning. Allow to stand for at least two hours so it can firm up before slicing the pie. Serve with ice cream or a dollop of whipped cream!To save some time you make the pie dough ahead. You can make your pie dough ahead of time and freeze it for up to 3 months. To make the pie ahead. You can assemble this entire pie and stick it in the freezer overnight and then bake it off the next day. It'll work very well. Cover lightly with a clean kitchen towel and store on the kitchen counter. I find that the fridge makes the dough soggy because of the moisture.

title: Talbot Interfaith Shelter stages Showdown
content:
Talbot Interfaith Shelter stages Showdown

 October 6, 2023 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Page: 13 | Section: News 
 
 419
 Words 

 Read News Document

 Talbot Interfaith Shelter's (TIS) S4 program - Shelter, Stability, Support, Success - is designed to guide families and individuals from homelessness to self-sufficiency. On Oct. 21, the community is invited to help these neighbors overcome the obstacle of homelessness at the inaugural Shelter Showdown & Hoedown.The Showdown "goes down" at Tardigrade Obstacle Course and Fitness Facility in Cordova, where participants will get the chance to prove that they are "TIS tough." Families and children can join the non-competitive Family Fun Waves from noon to 2 p.m. Registration for this wave is $25 for adults, $15 for children over 5 and free for children under 5.The Competitive Waves begin at 3 p.m. Participants can compete solo or in teams and can sign up to raise additional funds in support of TIS' mission. Registration for the Competitive Waves is $40 per person.The competition is already heating up. The Talbot County Sherriff's Office will be putting a team together to compete and has laid down the challenge for other local first responders to do the same.Sheriff Joe Gamble shares his excitement for this new local event, saying, "Talbot Interfaith Shelter is such an important part of our community, and the Talbot County Sheriff's Office is excited to join them for this fantastic new event. We look forward to meeting our fellow local first responders on the Shelter Showdown starting line, although, we fully expect to be waiting for them at the finish. In all seriousness, I hope to see our whole community out on October 21st having fun together while supporting TIS and its vital mission."All Showdown registrations include admission to the Hoedown, which takes place next door to Tardigrade at Triple Creek Winery from 1 to 6 p.m. The Hoedown celebration is open to the whole community. Admission for non-Showdown attendees is $10 per person, with children under 12 entering for free.Join in the fun for food, beer, wine and entertainment for the whole family. Kids will have a blast on the giant inflatable play course, along with other games and a craft corner. For the big kids, there will be adult axe throwing and archery games. Everyone will enjoy live music by local favorite Justin Ryan from 2 to 5 p.m.Showdown registration and Hoedown tickets are available at talbotinterfaithshelter.org/showdown.The Shelter Showdown & Hoedown offers many advertising opportunities for local businesses. To learn more about becoming a Shelter Showdown & Hoedown sponsor, contact Development Director Laura Richeson at 443-786-6962 or lauraricheson@talbotinterfaithshelter.org. Visit talbotinterfaithshelter.org to learn more about Talbot Interfaith Shelter and how you can help.

title: Here come the vibrant colors of fall - Check out these foliage hot spots throughout the region
author: Abbi Ross; Capital News Service
content:
Here come the vibrant colors of fall - Check out these foliage hot spots throughout the region

 October 6, 2023 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Abbi Ross; Capital News Service | Page: 10 | Section: News 
 
 1064
 Words 

 Read News Document

 With fall officially in season and the summer heat seemingly behind us, there is no better time to start planning trips to see the changing leaves."Western Maryland is arguably the best place to view fall foliage with its dense forests and mountain ranges," Megan McGinn-Meals, public information officer for the Maryland Department of Natural Resources, wrote in an email.McGinn-Meals said that leaf change begins typically in the western region and ends in the southern and eastern portions of the state."Those who want to get a glimpse early, they head to the mountains - they head to Garrett County, Allegany County, Washington County - to see the fall foliage," McGinn-Meals said.With leaves still changing into early November in places like the Eastern Shore, there's the opportunity for people to see the colors change all season long, McGinn-Meals said.Many tree species are prone to early fall color change, including black gum, yellow-poplar, dogwood, black walnut, Virginia creeper and some spicebush, according to McGinn-Meals.The Farmers Almanac predicts peak color for inland Maryland between Oct. 12 and 28 and for coastal Maryland between Oct. 19 and Nov. 4.McGinn-Meals said that leaf peepers might notice some brown edges and a quicker drop in some areas, but it should still be a beautiful fall."You'll see some of the beautiful fall colors, the yellows, the ambers, the reds that we love seeing, but then you'll also see these crisp brown edges around some of the leaves and that's a sign of drought stress."Recent rains and cooler temperatures could help reduce that stress.The Maryland Department of Natural Resources released its Fall Foliage Report Preview Edition on Sept. 18, which includes predictions from state foresters and park rangers in all regions of Maryland. A regular fall foliage report will be released weekly until the end of the fall foliage season.MARYLANDSeneca Creek State Park:11950 Clopper Rd, Gaithersburg, MD10 a.m. to sunset, November-FebruaryHiking, horseback riding, picnicking, bicycling - the options for how one can take in the fall foliage of Seneca Creek State Park this fall are extensive. The Clopper Day-Use Area, where the 90-acre Clopper Lake is located, would make a perfect stop for a fall picnic near the water or a break after a hike.Catoctin Mountain:Visitor Center - 14707 Park Central Road, Thurmont, MDDawn to dusk dailyThose looking for an overnight adventure to see the fall colors should look no further than Catoctin Mountain Park. The park includes space for tent camping as well as historic cabins for rent and includes 25 miles of hiking trails.Gunpowder Falls State Park:7200 Graces Quarters Rd, Middle River, MD (Hammerman Area)Gunpowder Falls State Park in northern Baltimore County offers a number of ways for visitors to get out and enjoy the fall weather. From the Hereford Area's 3,620 acres that are popular with hikers and horseback riders to Central Area, which includes both the Little and Big Gunpowder Falls to the Jerusalem Mill Historic Village, there is something for everyone.Annapolis Rock in South Mountain State Park:Park in the lot on Route 40, one-quarter mile east of Greenbrier. Follow blue blazed trail from the parking lot to white-blazed A.T Turn right to go north on A.T.-The Maryland Department of Natural ResourcesNot sure what trail to hike this fall? Try Annapolis Rock in South Mountain State Park. With cooler temperatures and beautiful colors, fall is the perfect time to take in the view of Greenbrier Lake and Cumberland Valley to the west. The 5-mile trail takes around 2 hours and 15 minutes to complete, according to All Trails.Tuckahoe State Park:13070 Crouse Mill Road Queen Anne, MDSunrise to sunset dailyFor those who prefer to spend their time near the water, Tuckahoe State Park features Tuckahoe Creek, a quaint stream bordered mostly by wooded marshlands, and a 60-acre lake.Valley Overlook in the Hollofield Area of Patapsco Valley State Park:Patapsco Valley State Park - Hollofield Area 8020 Baltimore National Pike Ellicott City, MDThe Overlook located in the Hollofield Area of Patapsco offers up a stunning view of the Patapsco River Valley. The Hollofield Area is located near the center of the park along Rat 40 (Baltimore National Pike).WASHINGTONRock Creek Park:Rock Creek Park Nature Center and Planetarium5200 Glover Road NW, Washington, D.C.Sunrise to sunsetA pocket of peace in the nation's capital, Rock Creek Park is a favorite for a reason. The 1,754-acre city park is home to a number of outdoor and indoor activities for anyone looking to get out and about this fall.VIRGINIASkyline Drive and Shenandoah National Park:Skyline Drive Milepost 51, Stanley, VA (Harry F. Byrd Senior Visitor Center)Open 24/7For those wanting to get out of Maryland to get their foliage fix, Skyline Drive runs 105 miles along the crest of the Blue Ridge Mountains in Shenandoah National Park. Inland Virginia's peak is expected to be between October 12-28, according to the Farmer's Almanac.The park brings in thousands of visitors each year to take in the vibrant reds, golds and oranges of autumn in the mountains. The Shenandoah National Park Service website recommends visitors looking to enter the park purchase passes online to help avoid crowds.WEST VIRGINIAHarpers Ferry:171 Shoreline Dr, Harpers Ferry, WV9 a.m. to 5 p.m.Harper's Ferry in West Virginia marks the unofficial halfway point on the famous Appalachian Trail and offers stunning views of the Blue Ridge Mountains come fall. The quaint town offers 20 miles of hiking trails, great climbing opportunities, museums and a unique 19th-century landscape.TIPS FROM A PROHoward Neufeld is a professor of biology at Appalachian State University and a Frederick, Maryland, native whose research interests in the physiological ecology of plants has led to many years of looking at fall colors.To avoid the crowds, Neufeld suggests going during the week instead of on the weekend. He recommends going early in the day for better colors. When the sun's at a low angle, the colors look more saturated and viewers will get better pictures.Neufeld's final piece of advice is a classic - take the road less traveled."There are a lot of country roads that will offer great color, but be off the beaten track," Neufeld said. "And that way you can have sort of a little more outdoor experience without having so many people around you all the time."

title: Taste of Cambridge returns - Ten restaurants will be there along with distilleries and wineries
author: Maggie Trovato; mtrovato@chespub.com
content:
Taste of Cambridge returns - Ten restaurants will be there along with distilleries and wineries

 October 6, 2023 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Maggie Trovato; mtrovato@chespub.com | Page: 3 | Section: News 
 
 574
 Words 

 Read News Document

 CAMBRIDGE - After four years, Taste of Cambridge is back.On Saturday, from noon to 6 p.m. in downtown Cambridge, residents and visitors will have the opportunity to taste the flavors of Dorchester County and the Eastern Shore.Ten restaurants have committed to the event, as well as a mix of distilleries and wineries - so that event-goers can sip while they taste.And for its first year back since 2019, Taste of Cambridge has expanded its tasting categories. Margaret Knudsen, executive director of Cambridge Main Street, which hosts the event, said that in previous years, the taste category was often crab and one "fun bonus" taste. However, this year the categories are crab, seasonal soup and stew, mac and cheese, apple and pumpkin."So everyone who has a tasting ticket will be able to get a little bit of savory as well as sweet," Knudsen said.A cooking contest, which will go until 4 p.m., will determine the winners of each of these different food categories.Entry to the festival is free and those who want to eat and drink can purchase tickets.This year, there will are a variety of ticket types to choose from, including food only tickets, general admission tickets and VIP tickets. The VIP ticket will give ticket holders the opportunity to taste and sip during a VIP hour from noon to 1 p.m."So if you would like to taste and sip early, you can buy a VIP ticket," Knudsen said. "And that allows you the opportunity to get the food while it's fresh out of the oven and ditch the lines."Compostable silverware will be handed out to ticket holders at check in."We have been told that there was a lot of plastic waste, in previous years, from the event," Knudsen said. "So we were trying to come up with creative solutions to reduce our waste."Although tasting and sipping are the festival's main draws, there are plenty of other things for attendees to do. People can peruse a vendors market full of independent businesses or listen to live performances at one of the festival's two stages.On the main stage in the Blue Ruin Plaza off Gay Street, there will be performances from tranzfusion, the Eastern Shore Dance Academy, Anna Burgess music and SoulCrackers.On the secondary stage at the corner Race and Muir streets, there will be performances from The Folk Villains, Island Fusion with Nancy and Jody and The Terry Koger Duo.Mike Elzey's Guitar Studio will be playing in the Main Street Gallery from 1 to 3 p.m.There will also be a kids' zone complete with costumed princesses, a bubble studio and bounces houses, pending the weather."We will have Belle, Elsa and Mirabel making appearances," Knudsen said.With rain in the forecast, Knudsen said the rain could have a large effect on the event."But thankfully we've been able to be flexible with how we're situating our musicians," she said. "And the restaurants have all been more than accommodating and willing to come out in the rain and support Cambridge Main Street."Knudsen said people should come to the event if they are looking for family fun with different entertainment options."So if you want to come shopping, you can," she said. "If you want to eat, you can. And if you just want to get a picture with Elsa, she'll be there in the kids' zone."

title: 'We will celebrate some of the books that have been challenged' - Library director 'shocked' by efforts nationwide to remove controversial books
author: Laura Tayman
content:
'We will celebrate some of the books that have been challenged' - Library director 'shocked' by efforts nationwide to remove controversial books

 October 9, 2023 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Laura Tayman | Page: 1 | Section: News 
 
 791
 Words 

 Read News Document

 Kent County Library's Executive Director Arnessa Dowell participated in "7 Questions to Ask the Library's Executive Director," while traveling to the branches of North County, Rock Hall and Chestertown and sharing her ideas with county citizens and answering questions they had. Kent County News had the opportunity to ask her questions as well.Dowell was hired in early 2021, when the Kent County Library, like everything else across the country, was trying to adapt to the new norm of living with Covid.Q: What has been your biggest challenge as Executive Director?A: "I got acclimated to everything very quickly," said Dowell. "I oversaw the return of the senior team, putting library staff in place, and finally opening the branches back up." Dowell thanks the community for their support and was pleased that the library has since increased its growth."We've definitely seen an increase in library patrons, with over half the residents now owning a library card," she said.As the world began to get back to the new normal, Dowell and her team shifted focus to upgrading technology and making more of it available to county residents. Today, she and the library's board of directors are now working on improving their current program offerings; developing solutions to the issues raised by patrons in a recent survey; and focusing on how the library is identified in the community today.Q: What are you focusing on currently?A: "I want residents to feel we are inclusive," said Dowell, "like our libraries are really for everyone." New programming, a new website, and more technology for increased access to information for residents are planned for 2024. There are also ongoing discussions about future plans for the Rock Hall branch location.Q: Why did you become a librarian and why did you come to Kent County?A: Dowell says she was born in Mississippi, but grew up in Germany with her military family.Most of Dowell's extended family lived in Maryland, and she moved back and started working at Goucher's and then Towson's libraries. When her mother became ill, it was her librarian friends that got her through it. "They were wonderful and really made me want to work in that profession," said Dowell.Her commitment to increasing the opportunities for residents of a rural area is why she took the Executive Director position in Kent County. She cited examples that have been put in place to support that goal, like the Kent County free laptop program and expanding the e-library offerings.Q: What has been your greatest success so far at Kent County Library?A: Dowell was very excited about the results of this year's summer reading program. Over the course of nine weeks, registered summer readers embraced the "All Together Now" theme at 75 summer library events."Last summer, readers logged over 700,000 minutes, so this summer we set our sights even higher at 850,000 minutes," said Dowell. "The final count for this summer was over 900,000 minutes read!" Q: What is coming up in the fall for Kent County Library?A: Dowell said all county libraries of Maryland have partnered with Maryland Humanities in the "One Maryland One Book" program that aims to bring communities together through the shared experience of reading, discussing, and exploring the themes in a single book. This fall's chosen features author Tommy Orange's work "There There." Released in 2018, the book tells the stories of twelve Native Americans as they converge toward the Big Oakland Powwow. Critics have called it "a riveting portrait of the urban Indian experience." I'm excited to share that the Kent County Library will hold a special presentation with Chief Donna Wolf Mother Abbott, the first Female Chief of the Nause-Waiwash Band of Indians," said Dowell, "She will be speaking about the past, present, and future of the Nause-Waiwash on Maryland's Eastern Shore." Q: What is your feeling about the movement to ban books in other areas of the country?A: "I am just shocked," said Dowell. In fact, Kent County Library will be participating in the American Libraries Association's Banned Books Week this fall. "We will celebrate some of the books that have been challenged that are still on our shelves. Books help people learn and open a door to creativity," Dowell said. "I believe that everybody deserves a voice, and I feel like representation matters." Q: What is your favorite book?A: Dowell said the answer was a simple one-"Oh, the Places You'll Go" by Dr. Seuss. "It's really the theme of a library's purpose," said Dowell. "A really good book or technology at your fingertips can take you anywhere in the world."

title: Blessed are the animals - St. Michaels church blesses 50 local dogs
author: Tom Mccall; tmccall@chespub.com
content:
Blessed are the animals - St. Michaels church blesses 50 local dogs

 Author/Byline: Tom Mccall; tmccall@chespub.com | Page: 9 | Section: News

 Read News Document

 ST. MICHAELS - There was an absence of horses, ferrets and turtles, and there was no presence of even one freaked out cat in a box. Dogs ruled on Sunday October 8, when over 50 were blessed at Christ Church.They strained at their leashes, sniffed around and got in line with their owners to see Rector Steve Mosher, who dressed in a white robe for outside ceremony.A reading from Genesis made God's creative powers known.Mosher read, "Let the waters bring forth swarms of living creatures, and let birds fly above the earth across the dome of the sky God blessed them and said 'Be fruitful and multiply and fill the waters in the seas and let birds multiply on Earth.'" He continued to read that God created the creeping things and saw that it was good.There was a reading from Andrew Carter that mentioned a menagerie of animals. There were badgers and hedgehogs, porcupines and penguins, godwits and chuckawallas.Mosher seemed to delight in the word play, and the crowd smiled along too.Then, participants lined up with their Tibetan terriers, golden retrievers and German shepherds. One at a time Mosher crouched down, touched each animal and gave a blessing.The crowd hung around after the last animal was blessed, enjoying perfect fall weather and their new four-legged friends.

Is that a chihuahua being blessed? Animals large and small all got the same loving touch at Christ Church in St. Michaels on Sunday.

Kirsten Mosher brought her Tibetan terrier for a blessing from her husband, Rector Steve Mosher.

title: Butters makes it back home - Missing cat returns to owners 12 years after being lost
author: Isabella Loy; Stanwood Camano News
content:
Butters makes it back home - Missing cat returns to owners 12 years after being lost

 October 17, 2023 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Isabella Loy; Stanwood Camano News | Page: 1 | Section: News 
 
 471
 Words 

 Read News Document

 All was calm and it seemed like an average day for Angelo and Shelley Castellino as they recently drove to their Stanwood, Washington, home on their 29th wedding anniversary.They had no idea that a phone call would soon give them the shock of their lives.Shelley Castellino received the mysterious call from an unknown number, and at first, she declined it."We figured was a scam call," Angelo Castellino said.Soon enough, the number called again. This time, they decided to answer."The gentleman said, 'I'm from animal control, and I have your cat, Butters,'" Angelo Castellino said."I go, 'Is this some sort of punk call?'" The Castellinos soon discovered it was not a scam - it was Riverside County Animal Control Officer Dalton Churchwell in California, who had found Butters in his yard late at night on Sunday, Oct. 3, and scanned him for a microchip.The couple had been living in San Diego and reported Butters missing 12 years ago in 2011. They had since moved to Stanwood in 2014 and lost hope of ever seeing the cat again.Luckily, the phone number attached to the microchip is the same one Shelley Castellino has today."I was astonished, it was kind of unbelievable," Angelo Castellino said."We figured that he was a meal for some coyotes." Angelo Castellino said he's unsure how Butters traveled so far, but that he was always trying to explore. The couple had adopted Butters and his brother, Barnacles, from a shelter in San Diego as kittens.After the news was shared, the Castellinos knew they wanted to bring Butters to their new home in Stanwood, but the expenses and logistics of flying a cat from California to Washington made for a tricky situation.The Animal Solutions Konnection Foundation, a California non-profit organization supporting the Department of Animal Services, soon heard the story.The organization decided to fund the cost of a flight to Seattle to see Butters safely return to his family."We were thrilled to work with the Department of Animal Services to make this reunion possible," said Carolyn Badger, president of the ASK Foundation, in a news release from Riverside County Animal Control."It was such a wonderful story, and we are very happy to know that Butters is home and safe with his family," she said.Butters' unlikely reunion finally happened Oct. 7, when Riverside County Department of Animal Services' longtime volunteer Larry Rudolph delivered Butters to the Castellanos in Seattle.Butters is now settled in his Stanwood home, and lives happily beside his brother, Barnacles, and the Castellinos' two dogs, Roscoe and Alita.Riverside Animal Services said Butters' defying of the odds was a testament to dedication and teamwork - but also a reminder to microchip pets to ensure reunification.

title: Historical Society remembers Walsh, recalls accomplishments
author: Connie Connolly; cconnolly@chespub.com
content:
Historical Society remembers Walsh, recalls accomplishments

 October 18, 2023 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Connie Connolly; cconnolly@chespub.com | Page: A1 | Section: News 
 
 508
 Words 

 Read News Document

 DENTON - It was an evening of celebrating achievements as well as remembering once again a Caroline County stalwart who contributed much and, with his recent passing, left a huge void.At its annual meeting Oct. 3, the Caroline County Historical Society remembered the achievements and generosity of James Owen Knotts "J.O.K." Walsh, who succumbed to COVID July 13.About 50 members of the society gathered for evening cocktails and hors d'oeuvres at Caroline Country Club.Acting President Charles Andrew welcomed new members and acknowledged local officials, museum docents, leaders of sister historical societies in Preston, Federalsburg and Ridgely, as well as Friends of Linchester Mill.Members renewed the tenure of two directors and elected two more. New on the board are Randolph Moore and Walter Palmer, and staying on are Carolyn Spicher and Jo Ann Staples.With deep ancestral roots in the county, Walsh was elected president of the society in 1987. His mission was to preserve the history, stories and, if possible, structures within the county. Under his leadership, 47 structures were restored, with many serving as tourist destination sites.Treasurer Carolyn Spicher credited Walsh with the solid financial footing of $1.3 million in the treasury.Two donors presented paintings to the society.Caroline native Clarence B. Mollock of Preston brought his 1988 painting of the Mill Dam at Linchester, where he used to swim and fish.Candi Minner of Denton presented a painting of the old Caroline High School by Bill Greenly, a longtime member of the society.Society member Kathy Mackel, Walsh's longtime partner, presented the annual report in a slide show depicting the society's current work projects, including the renovation of the historic Denton Fire House as a heritage center.Diana Lapsley shared memories of Walsh in a tribute that concluded with a suggestion that the center be renamed the JOK Walsh Heritage Center.Calling it "an important legacy," Lapsley said this last project Walsh worked on "is to be an information research center, a meeting place, a further opportunity to illustrate all of the county's rich heritage, and also a place to help visitors and locals to explore, learn about and enjoy all the other Caroline County historical projects." Becoming emotional as she commemorated her friend's legacy, Lapsley said, "I personally thank JOK for his friendship and enthusiasm, tenacity, bravery and generosity, as I know well that, even when busy and under pressure, he would take time to visit, entertain and look after his friends." "My hope is that we will all continue to get the work done that he started," she said. Quoting her granddaughter when she learned of Walsh's passing, Lapsley said, "Who is going to tell the story of Caroline County now?" 
 
 Caption: CONNIE CONNOLLY/STAR DEMOCRAT
 
Caroline County native Clarence B. Mollock, left, of Preston donated his 1988 painting of the Mill Dam at Linchester, where he used to swim and fish, to the Caroline County Historical Society. Accepting the donation is Charles Andrew, acting president of the society.
 
CONNIE CONNOLLY/STAR DEMOCRAT
 
Candid photos of the late JOK Walsh were displayed Oct. 3 at the Caroline County Historical Society's annual meeting.

title: Fashion show to benefit locals in need
author: Contributed
content:
Fashion show to benefit locals in need

 October 18, 2023 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Contributed | Page: 10 | Section: News

 Words 

 Read News Document

 The red carpet will be unfurled for a high-end women's fashion show and luncheon in Easton on Saturday, Nov. 4, to benefit those served by the St. Vincent de Paul Society.All the featured women's apparel, specifically selected for the fall, winter and holiday seasons, will be from the Boutique, operated by the St.Vincent de Paul Society on Canvasback Drive in Easton.All proceeds from the event will assist the St. Vincent de Paul Society in providing food and financial support to disadvantaged residents in Talbot County.The show will be narrated by Janet Schilling, an Easton-based certified image and color consultant who is helping to curate the collection for the runway spectacular. It will be held from noon to 4 p.m. at the Maria Mitchell Social Hall at Saints Peter and Paul Church on South Washington Street.Schilling will narrate the runway walk as the models showcase some trendy looks along with complementary accessories.In addition, she also will offer advice to women in the audience on a range of fashion topics, such as what colors and accessories work best for your skin tone, what profiles flatter specific body types and how to transform your cluttered closet into a wardrobe sanctuary that makes you look great in clothes that fit your lifestyle."My goal is to help women move in the right direction and wear colors and styles that suit their individual personalities," said Shilling."Women who feel good about what they're wearing are more confident." All the clothing at the show will be available for purchase afterward at the Boutique, said Nadine Hilghman, co-chair of the event."Anyone who has not visited our boutique will be surprised by the designer labels we carry, along with such accessories as gold and silver jewelry," she said.The fashion show will also feature two silent auctions, one for a basket of select wines from the Triple Creek Winery in Cordova and the other a gift certificate for a restorative spa treatment.In addition, a limited number of silent auction tickets will be sold for two exclusive social gatherings, which will take place in March 2024 and feature hors d'oeuvres and specially crafted beverages.One of the events will be hosted by Father James Nash, the pastor of Saints Peter and Paul Church, on church grounds. Tickets for previous events hosted by Pastor Nash have sold out in less than an hour.The other will be a Boston Tea Party-themed gathering featuring food and drinks from the "home of the bean and the cod." Society volunteer Lisa Gritti and her husband, Tom Divilio, will host the get-together at their home in Easton and serve guests traditional New England fare, such as clam chowder, Boston cream pie and Cape Codder cocktails.Those attending the Bahhston-themed event will also learn their way around a proper Boston accent.Ticket cost for the fashion show is $65 and must be purchased in advance by calling the Society of St. Vincent de Paul at 410-770-4505 or by mailing a check to SVdP, P.O. Box 783, Easton MD 21601 or at the Boutique, 29533 Canvasback Dr. in Easton.

 CAMBRIDGE - This year's Fun Dog Show at Christ Episcopal Church in Cambridge was a howling success.Parade grand marshal was George Wham and his pup, Oscar, a wire-haired terrier. Best in show was Jax, escorted by Anna Catherine.This was the second year the event was held at the American Legion on Sunburst Highway.The rainy day provided the perfect venue for puppies and people to enjoy the day indoors. title: Study looks at feasibility of Bay passenger ferry
author: Jim Johnson; jjohnson@chespub.com
content:
Study looks at feasibility of Bay passenger ferry

 October 25, 2023 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Jim Johnson; jjohnson@chespub.com | Page: 5 | Section: News 
 
 444
 Words 

 Read News Document

 The last time the Chesapeake Bay had a viable ferry crossing the bay was July 30, 1952.The Bay Bridge opening effectively ended ferry service.That may be changing.A feasibility study of launching a Chesapeake Bay ferry is set to be released in spring.Kristen Pironis, executive director of Visit Annapolis and Anne Arundel County, said the study is taking longer than expected."We want to do it right," she said following a panel discussion about transportation at the Tourism Connect conference in Reho-both Beach Monday. The conference, sponsored by the Delaware Chapter of the Public Relations Society of America, explored the story oftour-ism and its impact on the tri-state area of southern Delaware, Maryland's Eastern Shore and Cape May County in southern NewJersey.The feasibility study on a Bay ferry was initially scheduled for release by the end of the year. "(It's) a little later than that,"Pironis said.A consortium ofcounties - Anne Arundel, Somerset, Queen Anne's, Calvert and St. Mary's - provided matching funds for the $125,000 federal Economic Development Administration grant to complete the study.The focus of the study is not on transportation."This is about a tourism experience," Piro-nis said.During the panel discussion, she talked about "destination management," providing people with things to do at places the ferry docks."People want more to do" she said."We are not experts in ferries, Pironis said, adding that tourism is driving this study.Another expert on the panel was Heath Gehrke, director of operations for the Cape May ferry. He echoed Pironis."It's not just about transportation," he said. "It's about experiences. It's about tourism."He pointed to a third of the riders who ride the Cape May ferry for the experience with many of them buying a round-trip ticket and not getting off in Lewes, Delaware.Pironis' colleague on the panel, Clint Sterling, is director of Somerset County Recreation, Parks and Tourism. He said the study is not about a single county but about the entire region.Visitors to Maryland and the Eastern Shore do not acknowledge where they are as far as a single county. They are there for experiences. That is why the counties are working together to determine if a passenger ferry is feasible."The visitor does not know the county lines," Sterling said. "That's been one of the biggest takeaways of this study."He added: "We are all stronger together. A rising tide will lift all boats and ferries."There are more counties that have expressed interest in the possibilities of a passenger ferry, including Talbot and Dorchester counties.Pironis said the study is exploring the question: Will this be feasible?"This (study) is either the first step of the last step or the first step of many steps."

title: DAR to mark Col. Richardson's grave Nov. 5
author: Connie Connolly; cconnolly@chespub.com
content:
DAR to mark Col. Richardson's grave Nov. 5

 October 25, 2023 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Connie Connolly; cconnolly@chespub.com | Page: 15 | Section: News 
 
 148
 Words 

 Read News Document

 DENTON - The General Perry Benson Chapter of the Daughters of the American Revolution will honor Colonel William Richardson by placing a bronze marker on his grave 1 p.m. Sunday, Nov. 5.The public is invited to attend the ceremony at 23322 Holly Park Drive, Gilpin Point, Preston, the site of his former plantation.Born in 1735 in Talbot County, Richardson was colonel of the Fifth Regiment of the Maryland Line and the Eastern Shore Battalion of the Flying Camp. He fought at the Battle of Harlem Heights. He died in 1825 at Gilpin Point.Colonel Richardson Middle and High schools in Federalsburg are named for him. Members of the high school band will perform at the ceremony.For more information call 609-605-2156 or emailgen-bensondar.org. 
 
 Caption: PUBLIC DOMAIN
 
COL. WILLIAM RICHARDSON
 
HMDB.ORG
 
The ColonelWilliam Richardson historical marker is located at the intersection of Harmony Road and Wilkins Branch Road.

title: Pet Of The Week
content:
Pet Of The Week

 October 31, 2023 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Page: A2 | Section: News 
 
 117
 Words 

 Read News Document

 Caption: TALBOT HUMANE
 
Celia is a 5-year-old spayed female who has lived her life as an outdoor cat. Being at the shelter is very scary for Celia, who would do best in a home where she could be both indoor and outdoor. She has a strong independent spirit and loves the freedom of the outdoors but also loves a warm lap and gentle pets. Celia is shy with new people and takes time to warm up to them. Once she is comfortable, she is a really sweet cat with a gentle personality that is impossible not to fall in love with. She is a well-behaved cat that is relaxed and enjoys lounging around. Find out about adopting Celia by callingTalbot Humane,410-822-0107, or emailing info@talbothumane.org.

title: 'Know that you can make a difference' - Nonprofit for children affected by conflict in Ukraine hosts fundraiser at Avalon
author: Tom Mccall; tmccall@chespub.com
content:
'Know that you can make a difference' - Nonprofit for children affected by conflict in Ukraine hosts fundraiser at Avalon

 November 3, 2023 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Tom Mccall; tmccall@chespub.com | Page: 1 | Section: News 
 
 711
 Words 

 Read News Document

 EASTON - Short videos and still photos were projected across the screen of the Avalon Theater Wednesday night, including one image of a young girl, maybe 10 years-old.Susan Mathison asked those gathered to consider just this one person and her needs for food during the war in Ukraine."Because of our ability to distribute food, that kid and her family ate that week and they will as well next week," she told dozens of locals who had gathered at the theater to learn about Mathison and her partners' work.On Feb. 24, 2022, Russia invaded Ukraine in an escalation of the Russo-Ukrainian War, which started in 2014. It is estimated that tens of thousands of Ukrainian civilians have died and hundreds of thousands of military members.The Common Man for Ukraine, a non-profit aligned with rotary clubs around the world, feeds, clothes and provides sleeping bags for children affected by the war.Along with feeding those in need, The Common Man for Ukraine brings in mental health workers to help young people cope with losing their homes, and in many cases, their families.Mathison is one of the founders of the group. She and three friends - Alex Reyes, Steve Rand and Lisa Murray, all based in New Hampshire - decided they needed to do something about the suffering they had seen from the conflict.None of them were foreign aid workers or diplomats, she said, but they were determined to figure out how to help."The world has a lot of catastrophes right now. And the media and our hearts can be distracted from one to the other, to the other," Mathison said. "Our challenge as humans is to find a cause that matters to you and makes a difference. Find something and know that you can make a difference in the lives of someone, somewhere." "We are just four people.Alex owns a couple dozen restaurants in New Hampshire.Steve is a hardware store owner, I am a retired forester and Lisa is a public health specialist. We had no humanitarian aid experience.Steve and Alex were rotarians.This was a total start from zero." Their approach was to fly to Ukraine, talk to people and find out what they needed."Steve contacted the district governor of all the rotarians in Poland and Ukraine. Alex put up the first million dollars. We are going to raise a match of a million dollars. So we want to help, what can we do?" Mathison said.The Ukrainian Rotarians recommended some projects, which The Common Man for Ukraine was eager to see put on the ground."What is the one thing we can do really well? We decided to work on kids.They seem the most vulnerable, most innocent victims.We wanted to stay out of the fray of politics. 2.5 million kids are in hiding from Russian bombing and kidnapping.They are internally displaced," she said."They are looking for a place to sleep. They are hid in safe houses and secret locations all over Ukraine." The Rotarian connection helped this nonprofit find safe houses and deliver food on a 40-day rotation. Mathison said they have delivered 800 tons of food, 10,000 sleeping bags and 500 generators to date. They keep two warehouses on the Polish border with Ukraine."The Russians have a history of winning wars by starving people out," Rand said. "They are trying to interrupt every line of resupply.If we had a warehouse in Ukraine, it would be a target to be blown up." The organization brings 30 children a month to a safe place in Poland, where they get art therapy, play therapy, talk therapy and perhaps most importantly, they network with others who have lost a parent, said Mathison."Our three legged stool is food, warmth and love.That last leg is mental health counseling," she said.She said her hope is that these kids will be the ones to rebuild Ukraine when the war is over.To learn more about the nonprofit, visit commonmanforukraine.org. 
 
 Caption: TOM MCCALL/STAR DEMOCRAT
 
Steve Rand, in blue vest, hands out cards and receives donations after Susan Mathison is done speaking at the Common Man for Ukraine fundraiser at the Avalon Theater.
 
TOM MCCALL/STAR DEMOCRAT
 
Susan Mathison spoke on the Avalon stage. She helped to start the non profit Common Man for Ukraine, which focuses on helping internally displaced children in Ukraine.

WHCP running membership drive through Nov. 11

 November 3, 2023 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Contributed | Page: 6 | Section: News 
 
 501
 Words 

 Read News Document

 WHCP (91.7 FM) has just come on as a full-service NPR member station for the Mid-Shore with Morning Edition, All Things Considered, and 80% of its schedule devoted to being a "Music Discovery Station." The station offers a diverse lineup of musical styles - big band, neo-soul, blues, indie music, jazz, folk, classic country and deep tracks from the Boomer Tunes era.In addition, the station offers Mid-Shore news updates on Mid-Shore Mid-Day, some of which are provided by partners at the The Star Democrat.Additionally, every day the WHCP Community Calendar is updated, presenting events throughout the Mid-Shore region, along with 20-20 Marine Weather, which offers up-to-date forecasts twice each hour.To support all of these public radio offerings, WHCP is holding a membership drive through Nov. 11."A generous anonymous local donor has made a matching gift of $10,000 so that membership support is automatically doubled until we reach the $10,000 level," said Mike Starling, founder, president and general manager of WHCP."We are excited our new signal on 91.7 reaches roughly 75,000 people on the Mid-Shore (Talbot, Dorchester, and portions of Caroline, plus over 100,000 more in Wicomico and Southern Maryland)," he said. "We are now touting signal coverage, but more importantly the program upgrades as a grassroots community station carrying NPR's most popular programs too." During the station's very first fall membership drive, WHCP said it is proud to be among a select group of 17 NPR member stations that can offer the NPR+ podcast bundle of 16 podcasts as a thank-you gift to those joining or renewing their membership of at least $96 annually ($8 per month).Additionally, Premier Movie Theaters in Cambridge and Easton have partnered with WHCP, and the station is making two passes available to any current members (new, returning or sustaining at the $60 family membership level and above). Passes can be picked up at WHCP's Cambridge studio."New and renewing members are critically important to our program plans for the year ahead," said Starling. "Individual annual memberships start at just $35, and you can become a sustaining monthly member for less than $7 a month, at whcp.org/donate." In addition to its regular programming, WHCP also operates a free public service with the Mid-Shore Reader, a round-the-clock radio reading service for those who cannot read the printed word on their own.Fresh daily readings of books, newspapers and magazines, including The Star Democrat, are read each week by local volunteers, as well as the monthly Attractions, Shore Monthly and Tidewater Times magazines."If you or someone you know suffers from vision loss, or who otherwise cannot see, hold, or comprehend the printed word, this service is available free of charge," said Starling. "Just contact the station at info@whcp.org to learn more or volunteer to be a reader on the Mid-Shore Reader." There are four ways to listen to WHCP Radio - on the air at 91.7 FM, via the WHCP app, online at whcp.org, or simply ask Alexa to "launch WHCP Radio." For more information about becoming a member of WHCP, visit whcp.org or call 443-637-6000.

 EASTON - Talbot Humane has introduced their inaugural holiday ornament.The idea was brought to Patty Quimby, Talbot Humane's executive director, and the TH Board, by the coordinating committee of the TH holiday "Pawsitively Fabulous Pet Boutique." The team presented the concept of establishing a shelter-animal-themed art contest across the community each year, with the winning selection becoming the annual ornament.In the late spring, TH launched the first contest and received a variety of fantastic submissions.While it was a tough decision, Quimby and the board ultimately selected Nicholas Casale's holiday pup design.Kristy Casale, Nicholas' mother, brought her very excited 9 year-old son into the front office of Talbot Humane just minutes before the contest was over.He had seen the contest and excitedly embraced the idea. He loves crafts, drawing and painting and has even landed a supporting role in an upcoming performance of "Elf." "We are thrilled to have a local child's vision of a Shelter Holiday Pup be the very first TH ornament to hang on Talbot County (and beyond) Holiday trees," said the shelter in a press release.The ornament will be sold at the Talbot Humane holiday "Pawsitvely Fabulous Pet Boutique," located directly next to Talbot Humane, from Nov. 2 to Dec. 23. The shop is open Thursday through Saturday, from 10 a.m. to 5 p.m., and is filled to the brim with a wonderful assortment of items that will make great holiday gifts for all pet lovers."The Holidays are a very special time, and it is Talbot Humane's hope that the ornament(s) will become a celebrated family tradition within our community," said the shelter."Please come support our young local artist and Talbot Humane by purchasing your very own ornament.We look forward to sharing this special piece with you every year."

title: REMEMBERING A PATRIOT - DAR dedicates a bronze marker at the grave of Caroline Revolutionary War hero
author: Connie Connolly; cconnolly@chespub.com
content:
REMEMBERING A PATRIOT - DAR dedicates a bronze marker at the grave of Caroline Revolutionary War hero

 November 8, 2023 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Connie Connolly; cconnolly@chespub.com | Page: 1A | Section: News 
 
 890
 Words 

 Read News Document

 GILPIN POINT - Descendants and dignitaries gathered Sunday, Nov. 5, to commemorate the valor and patriotism of a local Revolutionary War hero.Members of the General Perry Benson Chapter of the Daughters of the American Revolution honored the memory of Col.William Richardson by placing a bronze marker on his grave at 1 p.m. on the unseasonably warm and calm day.Richardson's descendants gathered to unveil the marker and place a wreath on his grave. About 100 people attended and participated in the ceremony at Gilpin Point Park near Harmony, on a tiny parcel of his former plantation.Born in 1735 in Talbot County, Richardson was colonel of the Fifth Regiment of the Maryland Line and the Eastern Shore Battalion of the Flying Camp. He fought at the Battle of Harlem Heights. He died in 1825 at Gilpin Point.Colonel Richardson Middle and High schools in Federalsburg are named for him.Colonel Richardson High School alumnus and band director Thomas Cheezum led the school's marching band in a selection of patriotic songs and armed forces hymns."I love it," Cheezum said. "I mean, this is something that I live for because I'm a part time historian, and I am a big believer in truth, justice and the American way." Chapter Regent Jerry Seiler served as mistress of ceremonies and introduced as the first speaker Elizabeth Deering, state vice regent of the Maryland State Society, Daughters of the American Revolution."We are one of the largest women's organizations in the world, with over 3,000 chapters in all 50 states, Washington D.C. and overseas," Deering said. "The placement of markers is a tangible way to honor and connect with Revolutionary War ancestors and to also raise public awareness of their service." "Today we honor a revolutionary war patriot, Col. William Richardson, who served our nation as a Continental Army officer, and later in life as a politician," Deering said. "He helped to decide whether Maryland should ratify the proposed Constitution of the United States." Also participating in the ceremony were other leaders of the Maryland State Societies of the Daughters and Sons of the American Revolution.Speakers included State Sen. Johnny Mautz (R - 37) and Caroline County Commissioner Frank Bartz.On behalf of the Commission, Bartz said the marker is a "symbol of our collective gratitude and a pledge to uphold the memory of those who laid the foundation for our nation" as well as "a lasting reminder of the courage, sacrifice and unwavering spirit that shaped the history of our great nation." Mautz presented a citation on behalf of the Maryland General Assembly."The most significant aspect of today is to have our students and our youth and our next generation here to understand how we got to where we are," he said."Thank you for allowing me to relive fond memories and create new memories today," Richardson descendant Kristen Dukes said. "By mere chance, my family and I have fallen into this honored lineage of a true patriot.We owe much to his great achievements, such as the establishment of Caroline County, his leadership at the Battle of Harlem Heights and his direct involvement in electing George Washington as the first President of the United States." Another descendant, Petty Utermohle, told the crowd her mother "loved to say that he was known as the 'Fighting Quaker.'" "He was a Quaker until he was removed or, as she put it, kicked out of the meeting house because he was a soldier, and they were peaceful people," she said. "Thankfully, he made that decision." Seiler credited Caroline County Parks and Recreation employees for sprucing up the area around the grave, which had become overgrown.Following the marker dedication by Elizabeth Hinson and Suzanne O'Donnell, the descendants gathered at the end of the grave to unveil the marker and lay a wreath.A 3-volley musket salute was followed by a CRHS band member playing Taps.The Rev. Daniel Gedman, pastor of St. Luke's Global Methodist Church in Denton, who prayed the invocation, also concluded the ceremony with a benediction.

 Following an article published Nov. 3, the Star Democrat learned the following about 807 N. Washington St. property: George Lee Whiteley built the original 1,391 square foot home in 1930. He had three chicken houses on the 2.71 acre property until his passing in 1963. They were later moved to a property in Caroline County after his death.The Whiteley's also owned the Easton Candy Company and several hundred acres in Trappe.Whiteley owned a trucking company with his brother Olen Whiteley, who owned Whiteley's Store in Bruceville (Trappe).Their trucks were kept at 807 N.Washington St.Whiteley's wife, Della Whiteley, resided at 807 N.Washington St. until her passing in 1992. Her grandson lived there until 2002. The property was sold in 2021 by the four grandchildren, the heirs to the property.

title: Easton veteran celebrates a family lineage of service
author: Tom Mccall; tmccall@chespub.com
content:
Easton veteran celebrates a family lineage of service

 November 10, 2023 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Tom Mccall; tmccall@chespub.com | Page: 5 | Section: News 
 
 447
 Words 

 Read News Document

 EASTON - Eric Saulsbury comes from a lineage of service.Born and raised in Easton, he is a third generation veteran, having served as an Army paratrooper with the 82 Airborne Division before he retired as a lieutenant colonel."My grandfather fought in the Korean war," he said. "My father did three tours of Vietnam. I served in the Army. My brother Kevin served in the Army. My brother Brian served in the Marines. As far as I know, I am a third generation to serve." Saulsbury's son is taking a little time, but then he also has plans to enlist.Saulsbury enlisted in 1993 and retired in 2023 - a 30-year military career."I lead a battalion of 350 and ran a brigade of 3,500 as a brigade XO - chief of staff. I was second in charge. I took a battery out of country in 2006 of 140 soldiers to Iraq and back," he said. "We did route clearance, and I also shot artillery in combat. I got deployed five times. Three times to Iraq and twice to Afghanistan. I have also been deployed to Haiti. It was a response force." Having experienced both service work in Haiti and combat in the Middle East, Saulsbury said he preferred combat."In combat you were at least helping the people of Iraq and Afghanistan.It was more rewarding to get rid of the Taliban in Afghanistan, and Al Qaeda in Iraq, and Al Qaeda and Isis in Iraq," he said.After jumping out of airplanes and being in combat situations, Saulsbury said he has learned an important lesson - "to live life every day to its fullest." "When you have had that significant emotional event in combat, then you realize that life is short," he said.Saulsbury celebrated his retirement in September, which was attended by friends made throughout his decades-long career.Saulsbury looks at the numbers of his time in service. He brought all 140 soldiers back from Iraq. He gave out ten purple hearts."There were 67 IED attacks.We had humvees and different kinds of gun trucks. We did route clearance and escort and we shot artillery. Cannons with howitzers - 155mm. I did 110 jumps.I feel all 110 now. I got a metal hip from years of wear and tear," he said.And as the life out of the service comes he is pretty clear about what he wants from his community and the Army."The one thing I can say is when you see a service member, it is not the 'Thank you for your service' comment. It is really just have an appreciation for what they do. Only 1% serves in the military," he said. 
 
 Caption: COURTESY OF ERIC SAULSBURY
 
Lt. Col. Eric Saulsbury has served in multiple war zones, including Iraq, Afghanistan and a service assignment in Haiti.

title: Caroline CASA honors armed forces veterans
author: Connie Connolly; cconnolly@chespub.com
content:
Caroline CASA honors armed forces veterans

 November 15, 2023 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Connie Connolly; cconnolly@chespub.com | Page: 1A | Section: News 
 
 540
 Words 

 Read News Document

 DENTON - CASA of Caroline welcomed veterans of the armed forces to its annual Veterans Day Heroes Breakfast Friday, Nov. 10, at the Denton Diner.From a former corporal to a retired lieutenant colonel, local veterans enjoyed the free breakfast hosted by the nonprofit organization that "advocates for the best interest of all abused and neglected children who are in the Caroline County court system through no fault of their own," according to carolinecasa.org.Executive Director Amy Horne welcomed about two dozen veterans. "Anybody who has had the courage to put on the uniform is a hero in my mind," she said.The 7:30 a.m. gathering began with a prayer led by Pastor Don Reynolds of Calvary Baptist Church in Denton. He is also a retired lieutenant colonel with the Maryland Army National Guard.Horne read a lengthy statement from U.S. Sen.Ben Cardin, who expressed his "profound admiration for the unwavering service and sacrifices of our veterans," particularly recognizing Maryland veterans who have served in every armed conflict since the Revolutionary War.Following a moving short video that depicted a military veteran, who is a court-appointed special advocate (CASA) volunteer, helping a young child. A few veterans wiped tears from their eyes."At CASA, we really want to honor and recognize our veterans because veterans are people who protect our freedoms, just like our advocates are the people who protect the rights of the children we serve," Horne said.She said her late father, Talbot County Circuit Court Judge William S.Horne, who was an Army veteran, helped bring the CASA program to the Eastern Shore in 1990.Denton Town Councilman and former Marine Keith Johnson is also president of CASA of Caroline.After some good-natured ribbing of the other service branches, Johnson asked veterans to consider becoming CASA volunteers."Why is CASA, a child advocacy group, hosting a Veterans Day (event)?" he asked, answering the question by listing traits that correlate between veterans and CASA volunteers."Discipline, fighting spirit, leadership, resiliency. We see our veterans as difference-makers in the world.They're mission-ready," said Johnson, whose wife is CASA volunteer Stephanie Johnson."Being married to an advocate, I know that those traits overlap," he said. "Our advocates make a difference every day, our staff makes a difference every day." "As a (Maryland State) trooper, I served about three years as the primary investigator for Caroline County for the Maryland State Police, dealing with child abuse, child neglect," Johnson said. "There's a need in our county for advocates because our children are underserved and our children live as victims of abuse and victims of neglect every day." Johnson appealed to the gathered veterans to consider becoming a CASA volunteer."If you're not an advocate, think about what you can do different this year," he said. "The military focuses on protecting our country, while at CASA we want to protect tomorrow's future - our children." 
 
 Caption: Cousins David Barry of Denton, left, a Navy veteran, and Bob Linkins of Denton, an Army veteran, attend a breakfast and program hosted by CASA of Caroline Friday, Nov. 10.

title: Volunteers 'make a difference'
author: Tamara Forte; Special To The Bay Times Record Observer
content:
Volunteers 'make a difference'

 November 16, 2023 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Tamara Forte; Special To The Bay Times Record Observer | Page: 10 | Section: News 
 
 507
 Words 

 Read News Document

 SUDLERSVILLE - Kindness, enthusiasm and a passion for helping exuded from the front doors at Sudlersville Middle School as 75 households and 130 people were served on Saturday, Nov. 4, at the 10th annual "Make a Difference Day." Tables, chairs and volunteers lined the halls, gymnasium and areas outside of the school.This non-profit and free community event began in 2014 as a way to provide county resources and services for families in need.Housing Program Administrator Kelly Huber said "not only do we rely on the committee, (but) it takes a village of volunteers to assist on the day of the event. We had over 70 volunteers from the community to help - including student volunteers from the Boys Scouts, the sea cadets, adult volunteers, and local school volunteers." Volunteers - of all ages - wore "Make a Difference Day" shirts that said: "Ask me a?" on the back. Volunteers spent the day providing information and services throughout the event.While the Division of Housing and Community Services oversees the event, a large committee plans and executes it. Composed of people from local businesses, agencies, and individuals from the community, many of the original Make A Difference Day board members remain on the committee and are active members in both the planning and in volunteering during the day.Sea cadets volunteered their time and politely welcomed each person in attendance by opening the doors and formally greeting them.Sea cadets are 10 to 17 yearolds who participate in the United States Naval Sea Cadet Corps (USNSCC), a youth leadership development program sponsored by the U.S. Navy.Once through the doors, attendees were given a navigator (who spoke their language) to guide and help them through over 50 tables, services and resources, all conveniently in one location.Each person and family could select the services they needed. Services included: legal aid, social services, meals and food access, education, transportation, housing, personal hygiene, and much more. Eddie the Barber, stylist Ashley Calderone and many Queen Anne's County cosmetology students completed 30 to 40 free haircuts on Saturday.The dental van completed over 30 free dental screenings and provided goodie bags to all.Other services included free flu shots and medical testing (blood pressure, cholesterol and glucose testing).The Lions Club helped more than 10 people with vision needs. Additional services were also offered throughout the day.Giveaways were offered to everyone and were crowd pleasers - toiletries, hats, mittens, blankets, slippers, socks, diapers and wipes, and food from the Maryland Food Bank. Many of those were made possible by donations.The entire event is funded through grants, sponsors and monetary donations from the community. And all donated items found homes that day.

title: More tips on saving every day
author: Mary Hunt
content:
More tips on saving every day

 November 20, 2023 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Mary Hunt | Page: 6 | Section: News 
 
 324
 Words 

 Read News Document

 It's been such a good week, as measured by my bulging email inbox. I just love to wade through reader mail and clever money - and time-saving tips sent in by my dear readers.Enjoy this small sampling.I wash my children's stuffed animals in the dishwasher. I run it on a normal cycle, soap and all (although I use much less soap) and then run an extra rinse cycle. I hang the little critters out to dry on the line after they have gone through the heat cycle, as they are still wet. I've only placed these precious toys on the top rack and you need to make sure their eyes and any pieces are well attached, as they can come off during their bath. - Pam I got this great household tip from a plumber, who happens to be my husband.Dump baking soda down the drain (this can be done with a clogged drain or to prevent the clog) and then follow with apple cider vinegar.This will loosen and eat away any gunk clogging the drains.Allow to sit overnight, then flush the drain with hot water. This is cheaper than drain cleaner and will not harm pipes or septic systems. It's also safer to have around the house with children and animals. - Whitney Put a fresh head of garlic in a plastic sandwich bag and freeze. When you need garlic, just pull off the number of cloves you need and leave the rest of it in the freezer. Let the cloves sit on the counter until thawed enough to chop or press. I've stored garlic this way for years. It really does turn out just like fresh and certainly beats the alreadychopped garlic you buy in a jar. - Jean Would you like to submit a frugal, thrifty tip? Please do, making sure to include your full name and email address at tips@everydaycheapskate.com.Mary Hunt is the founder of EverydayCheapskate.com, a frugal living blog, and the author of the book "Debt-Proof Living."
