title: Girl Scouts care for furry friends
author: Tamara Forte; Special To The Kent County News Star Democrat
content:
Girl Scouts care for furry friends

 November 20, 2023 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Tamara Forte; Special To The Kent County News Star Democrat | Page: 4 | Section: News 
 
 536
 Words 

 Read News Document

 CHESTERTOWN - Excitement filled the Animal Care Shelter for Kent County in Chestertown on Nov. 11, as Claire Anderson-Schultz, Amelia Beach, Clara Gerber and Ayesha Tapia brought in lots of handmade supplies and needed items to the shelter. These four sixth graders earned their Bronze Award for Girl Scouts by setting their sights on helping the cats and dogs at the shelter.To earn their Bronze Awards, the girls from Troop 899 in Centreville had to complete 20 hours of service in a service project. Sharing a love for animals, it was easy to decide that the project would help animals in need. Claire's mom shared that Claire has been visiting animal shelters for years with her grandfather to spend time cuddling the animals after school.This past summer, the girls toured the facility to learn about what the shelter did and what it needed. From June to September, the girls worked independently and as a team to meet these needs. After reaching out and doing research, the girls learned the ACSKC had recently moved into a new building and had many needs.These needs included: a new cat tree, cat and dog toys, pet food and treats, new storage benches, and cleaning items. The girls explained the shelter had to throw out a beautiful, carpeted cat tree due to a sickness that had hit the shelter. The girls quickly began their mission to make a cat tree that was easy to clean and maintain.During these 20 hours or more of time, the girls strategized in meetings (in person and on Zoom) on how to meet these needs and then worked together to create and build the items needed. The cat tree was thoughtfully made, and with a little help from their parents, the girls found a plan that would use easy-to-clean PVC pipes. After making sure the pipes fit, they glued them together and painted them gold. The girls also made Velcro patches of fabric from reused clothing. "These fabric patches were made from my grandpa's old jackets and now they can be velcroed off and on for easy washing" explained Amelia.Shelter worker, Paige Tucker, said they currently have 109 dogs and cats at the animal shelter. Right now, there are 32 animals in need of homes. Allison Otadan, Shelter Media Coordinator, shared the shelter is "so grateful for the efforts of the girls" for the new cat trees and other pet items. She is excited for the new benches, as the current benches are all scratched up. At this shelter, there are special rooms for the animals to freely roam, but that also causes some of the items to get worn down and scratched. In addition to the cat tree and wooden benches, the girls sewed catnip toys, hand tied snuffle mats (where pet treats can be hidden and found), and collected lots of donations from their whole troop, grades kindergarten through fifth grade.If you would also like to help the shelter, they are currently in need of kitten food, cat food, dog food, and cat/dog treats. There is a complete Wish List on their website that includes the specific brands needed at https://acskc.org/

title: 'We just want to feed 'em' - St. Michaels Community Center gives out turkeys for the holidays
author: Maggie Trovato; mtrovato@chespub.com
content:
'We just want to feed 'em' - St. Michaels Community Center gives out turkeys for the holidays

 November 22, 2023 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Maggie Trovato; mtrovato@chespub.com | Page: 1 | Section: News 
 
 590
 Words 

 Read News Document

 ST. MICHAELS - A small line formed outside of the St. Michaels Community Center's temporary location on Talbot Street in the late afternoon on Monday.While some people waited to pick up their usual grocery items from the food pantry, others came for a hefty frozen turkey, pie, a sack of potatoes and a large bag of canned and dry items - all the fixings for a delicious and plentiful Thanksgiving dinner.Food Bank Director Amy DeWitt said that the SMCC has been handing out these "Thanksgiving boxes" to people who might not be able to afford a full Thanksgiving dinner for at least six years."(With) the cost of food nowadays, I think a lot of people just can't afford to go out and buy a turkey," DeWitt said. "And I think it's very important for them to have a meal they can prepare at home for their family." From 4 p.m. to 6 p.m. on Monday, DeWitt and her small team handed out all the turkey day classics for residents to cook on Thursday."The boxes are like an addition to what they already have at home," Mark Singleton, DeWitt's assistant, said."So just to push things along, maybe even press the meal for another day or two." In addition to the Thanksgiving boxes, the SMCC is hosting an eat-in community dinner on Wednesday from 11 a.m. to 2 p.m. Walk-ins are welcome. Those in attendance will be served turkey and gravy from Ava's Pizzeria and Wine Bar as well as cornbread stuffing, garlic mashed red skin potatoes, green bean casserole, dinner rolls and homemade apple and pumpkin pies.DeWitt estimated that they will serve between 150 and 175 prepared meals on Wednesday. She said she had around 75 people taking home Thanksgiving boxes this year.One of those people, Theo Bees, is making Thanksgiving dinner for his mom and himself this year."I love to cook," he said.Bees, who was working as a caretaker but is now taking care of his 92-year-old mother, said he plans to cook the entire meal.Bees said he would love it if everybody could celebrate Thanksgiving with their family."People need to be with family," he said, "every holiday." Kerri Clear, executive chef at the SMCC, who is making most of the dishes for Wednesday's community dinner, said the community is very supportive of what the community center does to help residents."We get a lot of donations," Clear said, "a lot of interest from the community." DeWitt said that all of her clients are "very thankful" for the special holiday meals that the SMCC hands out.Singleton said each person appreciates what they do."They show us every time they come in," he said."They're really thankful." And Dewitt, Clear and Singleton are just happy to help out in the community."We just want to feed 'em," DeWitt Said.

 Page: 3 | Section: News

 Words

 It's the holiday season.There are numerous events slated for Easton, St. Michaels and other parts of the region as Christmas, Hanukkah and New Year's approach. They include ones in Easton and St. Michaels. Here is a holiday sampling of a few of the upcoming yuletide events.Small Business Saturday - Nov. 25There will be a number of Small Business Saturday events across the Shore including in St. Michaels and Easton on Nov. 25. That includes crocheting sessions hosted by Far Eastern Shore Winery in Easton. For more information on the Sip & Stitch event and other happening check out DiscoverEaston.com.Festival of Trees - Nov. 25 to Nov. 28."Caroling, Caroling Through the Town" is the theme for the 2023 Festival of Trees held at The Tidewater Inn from Saturday, Nov. 25 to Tuesday, Nov. 28. The event features decorated Christmas trees that will be for potential purchase. There will also be holiday entertainment from local musicians and musical groups. There will also be a Carols by Candlelight event from 5 p.m. to 7 p.m. on Saturday, Nov. 25, in downtown Easton with choirs, free hot cocoa, food trucks and a holiday marketplace. The event benefits Talbot Hospice.For more: https://festival-of-trees.org/festival-of-trees/Holiday Market at the Ebenezer - Dec. 1.Bluepoint Hospitality is hosting a Holiday Market event at the Ebenezer Theater in Easton on Friday, Dec. 1, from 5 p.m to 8 p.m. There will be plenty of gift options as well as photo with Santa Claus. For more: https://www.pragerarts.com/Holiday Art & Craft Marketplace - Dec. 1 to Dec 3.The Holiday Art & Craft Marketplace returns after a four-year hiatus. The threeday event features the works for more than 30 artisans and will be held at the Waterfowl Building. For more: https://discovereaston.com/marketplace/First Friday, Moonlight Madness - Dec. 1.Art galleries, shops and restaurants will be open in downtown Easton until 9 p.m. on Friday, Dec. 1, for First Friday and Moonlight Madness shopping events.There will also be live free music during the evening festivities.Dickens Christmas - Dec. 1 and Dec. 2.Get a taste of Victorian Christmas in Historic Chester Town with carriage and pony rides, beers, teas, a holiday house hour and visits with Santa.Midnight Madness in St. Michaels - Dec. 2Shops, restaurants and other businesses will be open late on Saturday, Dec. 2 in St. Michaels with plenty of Christmas cheer and festivities.Check out https://www.stmichaelsmd.org/midnight-madness for more info.Santa Claus, Holiday Parade in Easton - Dec. 2 Santa and Mrs. Claus will be at Thompson Park in Easton before the town's annual holiday parade and Christmas tree lighting by Easton utilities. The big man arrives at the park at 5:30 p.m.The tree lighting will be at 6 p.m. and the parade starts at 6:30 p.m. Easton's annual holiday parade runs through the heart of the historic town with bands, floats and community groups. The parade runs along Harrison and Washington streets on Saturday, Dec. 2.There will be plenty more events. Check back next week, in the Star Democrat newspapers and at StarDem.com for more holiday happenings.

title: Be a Santa to a senior
author: Contributed
content:
Be a Santa to a senior

 November 29, 2023 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Contributed | Page: 7 | Section: News 
 
 525
 Words 

 Read News Document

 EASTON - This year, Home Instead is celebrating 20 years of bringing joy to the Easton community with Be a Santa to a Senior, a gift-giving program for older adults who may be overlooked, isolated or alone during the holiday season.Since the program's nationwide inception in 2003, Be a Santa to a Senior has engaged more than 65,000 volunteers, provided more than 2.2 million gifts and shared the holiday spirit with about 800,000 older adults."The holidays can be hard for many older adults, especially those who may not have a companion to share them with and it's incredibly rewarding to see the impact that Be a Santa to a Senior has had over the past 20 years," said Jennifer Marchi, owner of the Easton Home Instead office. "Gifts aside, the true value is the connection Be a Santa to a Senior makes between the community and our older neighbors." This year, program coordinators hope to collect gifts for 800 local older adults.To participate, shoppers can look for Be a Santa to a Senior trees or displays at locations around the area.Ornaments featuring the name and desired gift of an older adult will be on display, and shoppers can buy the requested gift and return it wrapped to the location with the ornament attached.Ornaments will be available until December 1. The gifts will be delivered to local older adults in time for the holidays.Be a Santa to a Senior trees can be found at the following locations:& #8226; Avon Dixon Insurance Agency - 28640 Mary's Ct #100 in Easton & #8226; Bay Vanguard Bank - Idlewild Ave in Easton & #8226; Bay Vanguard Bank - 104 Factory St in Oxford & #8226; Bay Vanguard Bank - 8707 Commerce Dr in Easton & #8226; Bridges Restaurant - 321 Wells Cove Rd in Grasonville & #8226; Brookletts Place-Talbot Co Senior Center - 400 Brookletts Ave in Easton & #8226; Grasonville Senior Center - 4802 Main St in Grasonville & #8226; Hill's Drug Store - 503 Cynwood Dr in Easton & #8226; Ken Island Senior Center - 891 Love Point Rd in Stevensville & #8226; Lewis' Auto Body - 8672 Brooks Dr in Easton & #8226; Londonderry on the Tred Avon - 700 Port St #148 in Easton & #8226; Mid Atlantic Tire - 8105 Teal Dr in Easton & #8226; Morgan Stanley Financial Advisors - 28601 Marlboro Ave Ste 201 in Easton& #8226; Perkins Family YMCA - 300 Seymour Ave in St.Michaels & #8226; Queenstown Bank - 274 N Washington St in Easton & #8226; Ridgley Pharmacy - 7 W Belle St in Ridgley & #8226; Shore United Bank - 212 Marlboro Ave in Easton & #8226; Shore United Bank - 8275 Elliott Rd in Easton & #8226; Shore United Bank - 1013 S Talbot St in St.Michaels & #8226; Shore United Bank - 18 E Dover St in Easton & #8226; Summit Community Bank - 321 Main St in Preston & #8226; Thrifty on 50 Consignments - 111 Chester Station Rd in Chester Be a Santa to a Senior is a true community program.The Home Instead office serving Easton has partnered with local businesses, nonprofit organizations, volunteers, and members of the community to help with gift collection and distribution.For more information, visit BeaSantatoaSenior.com or call (410) 709-1605.To learn more about helping older adults in Easton, visit imreadytocare.com.

title: Cycling Club holds annual Cranksgiving food donation event
author: David Mansfield; Chesapeake Cycling Club
content:
Cycling Club holds annual Cranksgiving food donation event

 November 29, 2023 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: David Mansfield; Chesapeake Cycling Club | Page: 7 | Section: News 
 
 267
 Words 

 Read News Document

 Chesapeake Cycling Club (ridec3.org), based in Easton, held its annual Cranksgiving Food Drive on Sunday, Nov.19. The event was organized by long-time club member, Kevan Full.It was a beautiful and crisp morning for the more than a dozen club members who met at Sprout in Easton and rode about town on their bicycles in casual attire to purchase and gather the designated grocery items.Four teams of cyclists were given a budget of $20 per person to purchase food staples from a list to be donated to Saint Vincent de Paul's local food bank.The cyclists went to Acme, Weis Markets, Target, Harris Teeter and the Plaza Latina Food Market in Easton to buy pasta, sauce, beans, baby food and other essentials.My team came in last, and was urged on at Harris Teeter by an employee, "that the other teams had already been here." While one team claimed victory, the reality is that all the participants were winners. The best benefit was serving an essential need of this community with friends. We also realized how fortunate we were to have this opportunity and to reflect that we helped Saint Vincent de Paul to carry out their mission to serve people in need in our town.Cranksgiving will return next year and enrollment is always open. Next November, please join us, and bring your bike.

Pictured outside of Sprout in Easton are, from left: Meg Roggensack, Eric Griffioen, Todd Ross, Sarah Doelp, Kevan Full, David Burroughs, Gil Passwaters, Richard Marks, Bob Stack, Charlie Leaver, Vince Dongarra, and Laurie and David Mansfield.

title: Beloved Easton holiday parade set for Saturday
author: Natalie Jones; njones@chespub.com
content:
Beloved Easton holiday parade set for Saturday

 November 30, 2023 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Natalie Jones; njones@chespub.com | Page: 6 | Section: News 
 
 486
 Words 

 Read News Document

 EASTON - Easton's long-beloved holiday parade is back again to spread joy and holiday cheer this Saturday, Dec. 2.The annual festivities kick off with Santa's arrival at Thompson Park in downtown Easton at 5:30 p.m., followed by the town's tree lighting at 6 p.m. in the same location.The holiday parade, presented by Preston Automotive Group and supported by Soistman Family Dentistry, starts at 6:30 p.m.The parade route runs from Talbot Town, then heads south on Harrison Street, loops on South Street and then heads north on Washington Street past the panel of judges at the courthouse.Over 60 entrants will be competing across several categories: best nonprofit entry, best commercial entry and best in show.This year's parade will bring a number of firsttime parade participants, said Deena Kilmon, the director of strategic initiatives for Easton Economic Development Corporation.It also marks the first time recently-elected Mayor Megan Cook will lead the parade.There are still opportunities to volunteer or to serve as a parade judge, Kilmon said. Those wishing to volunteer can reach out to Kilmon at deena@eastonedc.com.For Kilmon, who's been working and living in town for over 25 years, the community aspect is what makes the parade and this time of year so special."Coming downtown and seeing your neighbors and just enjoying the absolutely beautiful and charming town that we all live in and sharing that with each other - that's the spirit of the season," she said.Making connections through fun experiences like the holiday parade are crucial to making Easton better." When you have these memories, it makes you a stronger citizen and a person that really wants to work hard for the best of all of us, and that's why we do it," Kilmon said.Two holiday markets will also complement the parade.After a four-year hiatus due to the pandemic, the Easton Holiday Marketplace is back at the Waterfowl Building to feature the best arts and crafts presenters and vendors.The Holiday Marketplace is open Friday, Dec. 1, from 4 p.m. to 9 p.m.; Saturday, Dec. 2, from 9 a.m. to 5 p.m.; and Sunday, Dec. 3, from 10 a.m. to 3 p.m.And for the first time, a holiday market featuring gifts and photo opportunities with Santa will be open in the historic Ebenezer Theater. Live holiday music will regale attendees on Friday, Dec. 1, from 5 p.m. to 9 p.m. Photos with Santa will be available on Saturday, Dec. 2, from 2 p.m. to 6 p.m.Another new element this year is accessible parking and seating for the parade. Sponsored by The Arc Central Chesapeake Region, parking will be available in the Harrison Street parking lot. Those needing special accommodations will have access to a reserved seating area.

title: Toy trains light up EVFD - Holiday Trains Display delights fire department visitors
author: Tom Mccall; tmccall@chespub.com
content:
Toy trains light up EVFD - Holiday Trains Display delights fire department visitors

 November 30, 2023 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Tom Mccall; tmccall@chespub.com | Page: 1 | Section: News 
 
 514
 Words 

 Read News Document

 EASTON - The Easton Volunteer Fire Department was all lit up for Christmas.Their big doors for the trucks were lined in white holiday lights, and there was a gigantic green star up above.But the real holiday fun lay inside the fire station atop miniature train tracks.On Tuesday evening, as part of EVFD's Holiday Trains Display, the building was filled with toy trains running circles through fantastic miniature neighborhoods.Parents brought their kids to see the trains and an odd menagerie that included airplanes, dinosaurs and the Yuengling man bringing frosty kegs home for the holidays.One village mimicked the settings of Charles Dickens. One was staged like the North Pole. The Grinch was there, if you looked for him. There was even a Starbucks.One set of cars is from the Tom Hanks movie "The Polar Express.""We put it on there because it is a steam engine and it is really cool," Tarrang said. "We really like it because of its power. It's a model of the largest steam engine ever built.It is called 'Big Boy,' and there are two that are still in service."And like Where's Waldo, the firefighters asked visiting children to find the tiny donut shop."It keeps the kids entertained for a few minutes," Tarrang said.It took volunteers from Oct. 1 to Black Friday to build the displays."This is Lionel O gage. The train in the back is HF. It is smaller, and we did that to make it look far off in the distance," Tarrang said, showing off the Department's work. "When I was a kid we used our allowance to buy HO trains, which shows how cheap they were. You can't do that anymore.""These are all digitally controlled DCs," he said. "We have two controllers for all the trains. There are certain degrees these trains can handle and it is relative to a real train.These are set up to mimic real trains." Tarrang built all the underpinning structure out of wood to support all the trains.The other person implementing and maintaining the train display is Barry VanVechten, who is also a firefighter.Once enough children were there, the lights were turned off. The train sounds seemed amplified, and the glow from the trains and villages filled the darkness. An audible gasp of wonder came from those in attendance. It was a moment of pure Christmas magic.This toy train spectacle will be open through Christmas Day, with an optional donation requested at the door. During the week, it is open from 6 to 8 p.m., and during the weekends it is open from 2 to 8 p.m. 
 
 Caption: Every kid got to check out the trains and find the Grinch. Leah Maxwell, Caleb Maxwell, and Brooklyn Shortall got fire helmets from the EVFD.
 
An engine passes Santa on a white horse. One could also find the Grinch, a building on fire, a dinosuar and a miniature Easton Volunteer Fire House at the Holiday Trains Display.
 
There are several villages that the trains travel through, like the Dickens Village, the North Pole and the airport.
 
The Budweiser Clydesdale horses with attending Dalmatian dog can be found here.

title: Shore Gives More raises record breaking $310,178
content:
Shore Gives More raises record breaking $310,178

 November 30, 2023 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Page: 9 | Section: News 
 
 273
 Words 

 Read News Document

 SALISBURY - A day celebrating philanthropy culminated in a recording breaking $310,178 raised for participating Lower Shore nonprofits.More than 2,279 donations were made during the ninth annual Shore Gives More Giving Tuesday campaign.Since its inception, the campaign has raised more than $1.8 million to benefit local organizations.Giving Tuesday, held each year on the Tuesday following Thanksgiving, is an international 24-hour online giving movement.The local campaign, known as The Shore Gives More, is hosted by the Community Foundation of the Eastern Shore and assists local nonprofits with the fundraising effort. By providing an online donation platform, marketing and technical support, the campaign makes a significant impact through collective philanthropy."Nonprofits provide critical services to the local community, and fundraisers like Giving Tuesday help charities connect with donors," said Erica Joseph, CFES president. "Giving Tuesday has become its own holiday around the Shore, and the local generosity really shines a spotlight on how wonderful our region is."The Shore Gives More was first launched as a Giving Tuesday campaign for the Lower Eastern Shore in 2015 and raised just under $4,285 in its first year."As the area's leading philanthropic resource, the Community Foundation, understands the complexities around charitable giving, and we work hard to simplify the giving process for both donors and nonprofits," Joseph said."By giving through the Shore Gives More campaign, donors know their gifts will have an impact close to home."The campaign received sponsorships from 47 ABC and Shore United Bank, which significantly increased the campaign presence.To learn more about the "Shore Gives More" Giving Tuesday campaign for local nonprofits, visit CFES.org or ShoreGivesMore.org to view individual nonprofit participants.

title: Life - Rotarians Holding Food Drive In Honor Of Late Lord Scott
author: Contributed
content:
Life - Rotarians Holding Food Drive In Honor Of Late Lord Scott

 December 6, 2023 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Contributed | Page: 6 | Section: News 
 
 473
 Words 

 Read News Document

 EASTON. The Rotary Club of Easton and other community partners are teaming up to host the Drop for Scotty Community Food Drive through the end of December.The food drive is named after the late Lord "Scotty" Scott Sr., who passed away in January 2020.Scott was well-known throughout Easton and Talbot County for hosting his annual Operation Christmas Spirit event at the Easton Volunteer Fire Department.Established in the 1970s, Operation Christmas Spirit made the holidays brighter for thousands through a large community meal and gifts for local children, supported by volunteers and donations."Scotty's kindness and love for the community knew no bounds, and this food drive is a way to honor his giving spirit," said Andrew Walsworth, Easton Rotary president. "Our club is privileged to carry on his legacy, continue his good work and provide direct relief to families in Talbot County during this holiday season." Individuals and organizations may drop off non-perishable food at 2023 designated drop sites: ¡ The ARC Chesapeake on N. Hanson Street ¡ BAAM on Jowite Street ¡ Bay Capital Mortgage on E. Dover Street ¡ BSC Group on Bay Street ¡ Critchlow Adkins on N. Magnolia Street or on Glenwood ¡ Eastern Shore Land Conservancy on S. Washington Street ¡ Easton Visitors Center on S. Harrison Street ¡ Easton Family YMCA on S. Washington Street or Peachblossom ¡ 4H Extension Office on Mary's Court ¡ Harris Teeter on Marlboro Avenue ¡ Mid Atlantic Tire on Teal Drive ¡ Provident State Bank on N. Harrison Street ¡ Queenstown Bank on N. Washington Street ¡ Saints Peter and Paul on High Street or S. Washington Street ¡ Shore United Bank on East Dover Street ¡ Marlboro Ave or Elliott Road ¡ Star Democrat on Airpark Drive ¡ Talbot County Library on West Dover Street ¡ Willow Construction on Commerce Drive.In addition to dropping off food, the community may also make a financial contribution to the Easton Rotary's Youth and Community Fund by visiting dropforscotty.com. Funds raised will be used to purchase additional food and critical supplies.All food and financial donations will stay local and will support vulnerable families in Talbot County.The Rotary Club of Easton Maryland is comprised of nearly 100 professional men and women committed to the Rotary Motto, "Service Above Self." They are part of a global network of more than 1.2 million Rotarians who are changing lives in their own communities and around the world.As the world's first Rotary Club in a town of fewer than 10,000 people, The Rotary Club of Easton celebrated its centennial in 2021. The Rotary Club of Easton meets on Thursdays at noon at Scossa Restaurant, with guests welcome. For more information, please visit eastonrotary.org.

content:

 EASTON - Frosty's Holiday Village was teeming with children having fun Friday.There were gigantic blow up characters, like Rudolph, and there was hot chocolate and cookies. A couple hundred children came to this free event, which was moved at the last minute from the courthouse lawn to the Anchor Church on 620 Goldsoboro Street due to concerns about the weather.Family after family streamed in the church's entrance, passing a giant blow up Frosty, many of their children dressed in holiday finery.There was face painting, professional photos with Frosty and a continuous screening of "Frosty's Winter Wonderland" in the church's sanctuary.A DJ played a continuous round of classic Christmas songs. That is, until he put on the "Electric Slide", during which lines of women formed to do the dance and clap in unison, a fun reminder that the holidays can be terrific and inclusive.For All Seasons, a community behavioral health center, put the whole three-hour extravaganza together. Community sponsors who made the event possible, including presenting sponsors Willow Construction and the St. John Foundation. Each sponsor donated a holiday blow up statue.Additional sponsors include The Chesapeake Bay Beach Club, the Fraternal Order of Police Cambridge-Dorchester Lodge Number 223, Easton Utilities, Tidewater Inn, WBOC, Ewing, Dietz, Fountain and Kaludis, P.A., Construction Services and Supply Inc., Qualifacts, and the Delmarva Pride Center.

title: Holiday Parade Delights Hundreds
author: Natalie Jones; Njones@Chespub. Com
content:
Holiday Parade Delights Hundreds

 December 6, 2023 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Natalie Jones; Njones@Chespub. Com | Page: 1 | Section: News 
 
 397
 Words 

 Read News Document

 EASTON - Despite a misty fog blanketing the Eastern Shore Saturday evening, hundreds of residents flocked to the streets of downtown Easton for the town's festive annual holiday parade.The evening of holiday magic kicked off with Santa's arrival, followed by a 6 p.m. ceremonial tree lighting at Thompson Park.Easton Mayor Megan Cook, joined by four town council members, gathered around excitedly as several children flipped the switch to illuminate the iconic tree.A cheerful spirit was in the air as families staked out prime viewing spots for the parade, talking and laughing with one another. Children, full of anticipation, dashed around, playing tag and dancing in the streets.The parade, organized by Easton Economic Development Corporation, boasted over 60 vehicles and floats from an array of local schools and organizations.Winners in three categories - best band, best commercial entry and best nonprofit - were announced shortly after the parade's conclusion.A longtime favorite, the Easton Middle School band was honored as the parade's best band.Midshore Veterinary Service's elaborate float and dance performance won honor in the commercial category.Easton Utilities won in the nonprofit category with festively decorated trucks, one of which produced a swirl of artificial snow, delighting children with the sight.

 On Thursday, Dec. 14, the Colonel Tench Tilghman Chapter of the Sons of the American Revolution will conduct a meet-and-greet social event at the White Swan Tavern in Chestertown from 4:30 to 6:30 p.m.The local chapter of the SAR is inviting all its members, spouses and anyone interested in learning more about the SAR to come out during the holiday season to enjoy food and beverages and to socialize with members of the SAR.The White Swan Tavern is a historic building located at 231 High Street and has been used since the early 1700s as a tannery, private home and inn.Have you ever considered joining the SAR? To join one must be a lineal descendant of an American Revolutionary War patriot.Did any of your male ancestors:▪Serve in the Continental Army or Navy?▪Sign the Oath of Fidelity to support the cause of independence?Did any of your ancestors, male or female:▪Render material aid to the cause such as furnishing supplies or paying a tax to support the cause?▪Provide any type of civil service to support the new state or provisional government?▪Provide medical assistance (e.g., as a physical, surgeon, or nurse) to aid the wounded?If so, and you can show direct unbroken lineage to one of these individuals, you would qualify to join the Sons of the American Revolution or Daughters of the American Revolution.A member of the General Perry Benson Chapter of the Daughter of the American Revolution will also be present on Dec. 14 to answer questions about the DAR.The Colonel Tench Tilghman Chapter of the SAR serves citizens in in Caroline, Kent, Queen Anne fs and Talbot Counties.The National Society of the Sons of the American Revolution, founded in 1889, is a nonprofit and non-partisan organization dedicated to promoting patriotism, preserving American History and promoting education to future generations.To learn more about the Colonel Tench Tilghman Chapter of the SAR, please visit its Facebook page at facebook.com/ColTenchTilghman.If interested in attending this event, please contact Warren Tewes at wdtewes@gmail.com by Friday, Dec. 8, to RSVP, and advise how many will be in your party.

title: Bigger and brighter - Lights shine through fog at Cambridge Christmas parade
author: Maggie Trovato; mtrovato@chespub.com
content:
Bigger and brighter - Lights shine through fog at Cambridge Christmas parade

 Author/Byline: Maggie Trovato; mtrovato@chespub.com | Page: 5 | Section: News 
 
 540

 CAMBRIDGE - Shrouded in fog, lights twinkled, blinked and glowed at the 74th annual Cambridge Dorchester County Christmas Parade Saturday evening.Although there was no snow for the "Snowflakes on Parade" theme this year, mild weather and a hazy atmosphere made for perfect parade watching conditions.Linda Bramble, who attended the parade with her nine-year-old granddaughter, Emily, said it was a good night for the parade."The wind's not blowing," she said, adding that the fog was a neat addition to the parade.Parade Co-chairman Bruce McWilliams thanked mother nature for stopping rain from pouring down Saturday evening."The fog made for some really nice pictures," he said.There were 105 floats registered in the parade this year, a few of which McWilliams said he knew didn't show.From bright red firetrucks to trucks decked out in wreaths and colorful lights to trailer beds covered in fake snow, residents and visitors watching the parade had a lot to keep them captivated. Floats embarked from Long Wharf Park, traveling down High, Poplar and Race streets before ending on Washington Street.A variety of performances, from marching bands to dance groups were interspersed throughout the parade.Ruby Kreiser, 10, said her favorite part, along with all the lights, was seeing the Eastern Shore Dance Academy, who danced to "The Nutcracker" at different spots along the parade route.Kreiser, who also attends the Eastern Shore Dance Academy said she was able to say hello to her friends dancing in the parade.The Dance Academy took home the judge's choice award in the parade.The National Judges Association out of Pennsylvania judged both the marching bands and floats at the parade. The 10 division winners included Dorchester Emergency Medical Services for best noncommercial adult float, Girl Scout Troop 131 for the best noncommercial youth float, Dorchester Dumpin' for the best commercial float and New Creation Marching Unit for the best marching unit on foot.When it came to marching bands, Snow Hill High School won the best band overall category.For best high school band, North Dorchester High School placed first, Mardela Middle and High School placed second and Crisfield High School placed third.For best middle school band, Salisbury Middle School placed first and North Dorchester Middle School placed second.Since the parade, McWilliams said they have received a lot of "super positive comments." "Everybody has said what a great time, what a great parade," he said.McWilliams said they are "extremely thankful" to the community for their donations as well as the participants for showing up."It was definitely a labor of love for the community," he said.And plans for next year's parade are already underway."Yesterday," McWilliams said laughing during an interview Monday about when plans had begun.For the next year's 75th parade, diamonds will be a major focus."Because it's the 75th annual," McWilliams said."We've got a lot of plans to make the 75th really shine."

title: An Old Wye Mill Christmas
author: Laura Tayman; ltayman@chespub.com
content:
An Old Wye Mill Christmas

 December 8, 2023 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Laura Tayman; ltayman@chespub.com | Page: 8 | Section: News 
 
 493
 Words 

 Read News Document

 WYE MILLS - Christmas shoppers are offered the opportunity to step back in time and travel to the Old Wye Mill just in time to purchase unique gifts in a piece of history.The Old Wye Mill has been grinding grain on Maryland's Eastern Shore for well over 300 years. It supplied flour to a growing nation-and to George Washington's troops during the War for Independence.And it continues to run even today.Prominent colonial owners of the Mill included Richard Bennett III, Edward Lloyd III and IV (owners of Wye House) and Colonel William Hemsley.During the American Revolution, Hemsley was charged with procuring food for the Continental Army, shipping hundreds of barrels of flour across the Chesapeake Bay from Wye Mill and many others like it on Maryland's Eastern Shore. Historians dubbed the Eastern Shore the "Breadbasket of the Revolution." While the historic mill is open to the public during the warmer months, these Christmas Shoppe opportunities allow the mill to open its doors during the colder months. The last one will be held on Saturday, Dec. 16."We have a variety of items available for purchase perfect for the holiday season," said Ken Groves, vice president of the Mill's operations.In additional to multiple flour options made directly by the mill (wheat, einkorn, rye, barley, cornmeal, grits) the offerings also include Amish jams, baked goods (with flour from the mill), lovely needlepoint items, Christmas tree ornaments, glass knick-knacks, and pottery made by a local artist.Proceeds will go to the Friends of Wye Mill, a volunteer-run nonprofit that preserves and operates the Mill with funding from local and state grants, visitor contributions, and retail sales of stone-ground grain products.Volunteer Mary Alice Casey is the one who solicits and arranges the gifts for shoppers. "I'm the one that likes to organize," Casey said.She is also well-versed in the mill's history and came up with the outline of a children's story that is now being used in a published children's book by Talbot County author Timothy Young.The premise is based on a mouse in the mill that travels back in time through being stuck on the revolving wheel.The organization will welcome Young in a book-signing at the mill on May 4, 2024."We are working to include the book in the fourth grade curriculum in the county schools," said Champ McCulloch, another mill volunteer. "It contains so much history about the local area." To purchase grain products when the Mill is closed, please call 410-827-3850.

author: Laura Tayman; Ltayman@Chespub. Com
content:
Crabby Christmas - Watermen Usher In Holidays At Annual Event

 December 11, 2023 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Laura Tayman; Ltayman@Chespub. Com | Page: 1 | Section: News

 With a countdown from ten to one, a large crowd led Santa and Mrs. Claus to turn on a switch and light the three crab basket trees next to Fishermen's Inn at the recent Queen Anne's County Waterman's Association's Tree lighting and Vendor Fair event."I'm surprised that despite the weather we are seeing a steady crowd," Gigi Windley of the Kent Narrows Development Foundation said.
"This is a great cooperative effort from the sponsors to the basket painters to the watermen themselves." The event began during Covid, when Joey and Karen Sadler of Captain's Pride Charters in the Kentmorr Marina said they wanted to create an outdoor benefit event where the community could gather together safely once again.
With the leadership of the Queen Anne's County Waterman's Association, volunteers put the crab basket tree concept together in record time in 2020.
Christy Wilkins coordinates the basket trees effort, starting in October, where crab baskets are sold to local residents and businesses who would paint them and return for the tree display.
This year, nearly 300 baskets were used.
Wilkins said proceeds from the basket sales and the accompanying vendor fair would go towards the watermen's oyster restoration project, to assist watermen who had fallen on hard times because of illness or boat expenses, and, new this year, for scholarships to local high school students in the county.
Over 20 vendors, many with items of a nautical theme, were there for eager holiday shoppers, including Turtles & Tides, the Knotty Mermaid Crochet and Chesapeake Scene Photography.
The Queenstown Lions Club manned the kids craft table, and the Kent Island Rotary sold their "Tales & Tastes of Kent Island" book with students from Club Interact of Kent Island High School. And Fisherman's Inn donated cocoa and apple cider to benefit the Not My Child Program.
As the skies began darkening, the crowd began gathering at the site of the trees, waiting for a special guest to light up the area. Bob Timms of Kent Island Methodist Church gave a blessing of the fleet and Captain Buck Lynch, of the "Stephanie II" Head Boat and representing the Waterman's group, gave moving welcoming remarks.
"We need you and you need us," he told the crowd.
"By working together we can make things better." Sounds of sirens came moments later with shouts of "Santa" by the youngest attendees. Sure enough, here he and Mrs. Claus came, escorted by members of the Kent Island Volunteer Fire Department.
Commissioner Jack Wilson attended the event, and he estimated that the crowd was three times more than in previous years.
"I love this event," Wilson said. "Here we highlight the important work of the watermen in our own community.
This is what small town America is all about."

title: Santa On The Shore: St. Nick, Mrs. Claus Visit Local Firehouse
author: Laura Tayman; Ltayman@Chespub. Com
content:
Santa On The Shore: St. Nick, Mrs. Claus Visit Local Firehouse

 December 11, 2023 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Laura Tayman; Ltayman@Chespub. Com | Page: 4 | Section: News 
 
 378
 Words 

 Read News Document

 Once they entered the firehouse door, the lucky local children who attended this year's Lunch with Santa on Dec. 3, were mesmerized by only one thing in the room. There, sitting in his big chair, was Santa.And it wasn't just any Santa, it was the real Santa.
Even parents were loving the magic.
"I am very happy I got to come to Chestertown today," Santa said. "We've been so busy at the North Pole. And then we had this fog- lucky thing I had Rudolph to guide the way." This year for the first time the fire company was able to welcome Mrs. Claus as well.
"I am usually so busy monitoring the elves who are getting ready for Christmas," she explained.
"But I managed to get away this afternoon." This family-friendly annual event is sponsored by the Chestertown Volunteer Fire Company, whose members are committed to making the holiday memorable for local families.
Along with the choice of pizza or hot dogs, families were offered an enormous display of a variety of cookies, lovingly prepared by company members.
The most popular? "Definitely the s'mores," longtime fire company family member Megan Darling said, "but chocolate chip is a close second." Numerous tables were set up in the firehall, with different crafts at each.
Kids were busily traveling to new spots, making ornaments and snowmen throughout the day.
But the purpose of their visit was to meet Santa and let him know what they were looking for on Christmas morning.
A Barbie Dreamhouse and her pink corvette was one of the most popular requests.
"Do you know that the elves made one for themselves?" Santa asked a little one. "They have the best time driving it around in the snow." Ken Young, a member of the company and professional photographer, was there to catch the moment when children shared some time with Old St. Nick.
"This is my third year doing it," said Young. "I bring my special equipment, including a printer where I can print the photo out for the parents before they leave." Cindy Morris, who organizes the event, said the day wasn't about the funds raised. "This is us supporting our community."

title: St. Michaels Parades Bring Holiday Music, Bright Lights And Candy
author: Maggie Trovato; Mtrovato@Chespub.Com
content:
St. Michaels Parades Bring Holiday Music, Bright Lights And Candy

 December 13, 2023 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Maggie Trovato; Mtrovato@Chespub.Com | Page: 1 | Section: News 
 
 720
 Words 

 Read News Document

 ST. MICHAELS - Visitors and residents of St.Michaels had plenty of holiday-themed entertainment to keep them busy Saturday.
Throughout the day, Christmas in St. Michaels hosted a variety of events, including two parades: the Talbot Street Parade and the Lighted Boat Parade.
The Talbot Street Parade kicked off in the morning, beginning on Talbot Street at Perry Cabin and ending at Seymour Avenue.
A variety of floats, fire trucks, antique cars and boats towed by trucks made their way down the street as parade-goers watched and cheered from the sidelines. Some of those in the parade came on horseback. There were 46 entries in the parade this year.
Instruments, jingle bells and voices rang through town Saturday morning. From "When the Saints Go Marching In" to Christmas classics like "Jingle Bell Rock" and "Santa Baby," there was something for everybody.
Britany Francis was most excited to see her brother, Weston Dunlap, in the parade. Dunlap joined the St. Michaels Fire Department this year.
"I moved here almost two years ago," Francis said. "So this is my first parade, my brother's first Christmas parade."
Danielle Toth brought her two daughters, Emerson, 4, and Camryn, 2, with her to the Talbot Street Parade this year.
Camryn liked the candy the most but also liked seeing Santa as well as the floats that spouted out bubbles to make it look like it was snowing.
Emerson liked seeing the horses from the Tuckahoe Pony Club and the Maryland Rough Riders.
After the sun set on Saturday evening, the second parade of the day, the Lighted Boat Parade, began. Eighteen boats lit up with colorful string lights and different Christmas decorations traveled around St.
Michaels Harbor.
For the Redl family, who live in northern Virginia but have a house in Bozman, this was their first year seeing the lighted boat parade. The three of them said they would definitely come back to see it again next year.
"I think it was cool to see all these people who took their time to put up cool decorations and then come by and show us those lights," Benjamin Redl, the son of David and Amy Redl said.
Benjamin and David Redl's favorite boat in the parade was one that had three Christmas trees, each covered in a different color of lights. Amy Redl liked the boat that had a lighted image of a dolphin wearing a Santa hat.
"It's a lovely thing that the Town of St. Michaels does for families and everyone," Amy Redl said about the parade. "It's really nice."
Jay and Kim Anderson have been coming to the Lighted Boat Parade for seven years now. The couple from Virginia always walks in the Talbot Street Parade with their two Chesapeake Bay Retrievers and then sticks around for the Lighted Boat Parade.
"You don't see this anywhere else," Jay Anderson said. "I mean we live on a lake in Virginia, and they have started doing the lighted boat parade the last couple of years, but just the it's the town, it's quaint."
Ann Law, who has been to six Lighted Boat Parades in the last seven years, said she lives outside Philadelphia and has seen Philadelphia's boat parade.
"But it's too commercial," she said. "This isn't."
The first place winner of the Lighted Boat Parade was Shannon Pickens' boat, Working Girl, with the theme "Christmas in St.
Michaels."
Emma Brown and Bryan Hines' boat, Harbor Shuttle II, came in second place with the theme "Santa's Workshop."
Basil DeLashmutt's boat, Knot Knormal, came in third place with the theme "Take it to Eleven."
Mike Kuperberg's boat, Karisma, came in fourth place with the theme "It's Five o'Clock on the Chesapeake."
Sam Hughes' boat, Samron, came in fifth place with the theme, "Oysters for Christmas."

 FEDERALSBURG - On Dec. 11, all the pageantry of the small town of Federalsburg came out.Pint sized beauty queens, manmade soapy snow and bright red fire engines rolled through the town. There was a judges' stand with the town's bicentennial "200" lit up in bright white beneath their stage.
The ballerinas and marching bands delighted the crowds as little kids gathered candy in the dark streets. If there was a Grinch, there was also a Santa.
All the fire apparatus were polished up from Hurlock to Preston to Denton. Federalsburgs' own volunteer fire crews lead the procession.
Several car clubs revved their lights and showed off their customizations.
One car club rolled by the judges' stand in complete silence, other than laughter from within a cockpit.
This inclusive event brought out the wonder in everybody from toddlers to grandmothers. It was cold. There were seated families wrapped in blankets. But people stayed to watch the whole procession on North Main Street.
There were so many Tootsie Rolls thrown that they languished in the street.
The closer you got to the Town Hall building, the more packed the crowd was. Some families brought sacks to gather the candy strewn from the fire engines. They all smiled when the dancing crew stopped in front of the judges and gave it their sassy best.

title: Holidays - 'Above And Beyond'
content:
Holidays - 'Above And Beyond'

 December 14, 2023 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Page: A3 | Section: News 
 
 451
 Words 

 Read News Document

 Local garden clubs honor Easton Airport with 80th Anniversary inspired Christmas treesResponding to Maryland's First Lady Dawn Moore's request for a holiday representation of Talbot County at the State Capitol Rotunda in Annapolis, the Talbot County Garden Club and the Oxford Garden Club joined forces once again.
After delivering a Waterfowl Festival themed tree to Annapolis in 2022, the garden clubs teamed for a new 2023 tree celebrating the 80th anniversary of Easton Airport.
"Featuring ornaments made of balsa wood, recycled aviation maps, and delicate punched airplane snowflakes, the flight-themed ornaments adorned a splendid holiday tree delivered to the Rotunda on November 29," according to a news release.
Managers at the Easton airport liked the tree so much they request a similar Christmas tree for the terminal building at the Eastern Shore airfield.
"The Annapolis tree features a handmade tree skirt that mimics the view of Talbot County farm fields and Chesapeake Bay watershed, as seen from the skies above.
The Easton Airport 80th Anniversary artwork, featured in posters and banners around Easton, MD, is also displayed in miniature on the festive trees. A hand-crafted model of Easton Airport's Air Traffic Control Tower, contributed by Dave Putman of the Easton Composite Squadron - Civil Air Patrol, sits atop both trees," release continued.
"We are extremely fortunate to have both of these volunteer-led garden clubs doing good work in Talbot County," Easton Airport Manager Micah Risher said.
"They have gone above and beyond to celebrate the holidays while honoring our 80th anniversary."
The Easton Airport recently marked the beginning of the Airfield Modernization Program with a groundbreaking ceremony in October.
"Over the next 6 to 8 years, roughly 80% of the airfield will be reconstructed, and will include the demolition of the Talbot County Business Center, and the shift of the existing Runway 4/22 1,900 feet southwest of its current position," airport officials.
The local garden advocates are also spreading Christmas and holiday cheer throughout the local area.
"The Talbot County Garden Club also gathered recently to decorate greens to enliven the holidays for the local community.
With help from Easton Utilities, the greens have been installed at the Talbot County Court House, Shore United Bank, and Easton Utilities' headquarters. Additional greens were provided to the Talbot County Free Libraries in Easton and St.
Michaels, the Easton Volunteer Fire Department, the Talbot County Visitor's Center/Easton Economic Development Office, and a number of downtown Easton businesses. In addition, club members fashioned 100 tabletop arrangements to brighten the holidays for local Meals on Wheels clients and will provide holiday arrangements to Talbot Hospice and the Talbot Interfaith Shelter," according to the release on the efforts.

title: Hurlock Extends Warm Holiday Welcome
author: Debra Messick; Special To The Dorchester Star
content:
Hurlock Extends Warm Holiday Welcome

 December 15, 2023 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Debra Messick; Special To The Dorchester Star | Page: 8 | Section: News 
 
 445
 Words 

 Read News Document

 HURLOCK - For its first daytime Christmas parade in several years, the town of Hurlock got to celebrate the season under bright sunny skies, enjoying almost balmy temperatures.Despite the decidedly un-December-like weather, on the traditionally frosty month's second Saturday, Dec. 9, young and old alike turned out to line Main Street, eagerly awaiting the scheduled 12 o'clock noon start to the annual event, which this year featured the theme, "May the joy of the season be felt worldwide."
As the procession's dignitaries, marching bands, fire trucks, vintage vehicles, and festive floats found their places in line, parade emcee DJ Buddy Bloom III, situated across from Mom and Pop's Family Restaurant, kept spirits bright with tunes, updating the crowd as 'kickoff' time drew close.
According to parade director John Stitchberry, Jr., 74 participants in 94 individual units were featured in all. As Bloom introduced each, enthusiastic onlookers clapped and cheered, some sporting holiday themed t-shirts under light jackets, many accentuated with an array of Santa hat styles.
Youngsters eagerly clutched buckets and bags, ready to gather up the precious pre-holiday haul of snack sized Milky Ways, Skittles, and other sugar-laden delights, plus perennial favorites, oldfashioned red and white peppermint morsels, generously tossed their way from each slow moving vehicle and parade helpers on foot.
The town, most often noted for its venerable, historic train station (and popular special run each October), showed an equal reverence for the vintage cars, tractors, and other vehicles appearing throughout the parade, lending a nostalgic 'oldtimey' charm fondly invoking Christmases past.
Numerous area organizations, businesses, and churches, and pageant winners got into the holiday spirit as well, traveling atop work trucks and attached flatbeds creatively transformed into visions of miniature winter wonderlands, some complete with 'magically' conjured blowing snowfall.
As the hour-long event wrapped up, Santa and Mrs. Claus made their pivotal appearance, signaling the parade's end, but just the start of the official Christmas season.

 RIDGELY - Benedictine celebrated milestones in service for 50 of its dedicated staff members in early December. The awards were presented to employees with 5, 10, 15, 20, 25, and 30, 45, and 55 years of service.Phyllis Young celebrated 55 years with Benedictine. During her tenure, Young filled many roles in the School residential program, as a Nursing Assistant, Vocational Teacher, Home Economics Teacher and Summer Camp Teacher's Aide.
She was previously honored by the Maryland Association of Nonpublic Special Education Facilities as a recipient of the Inspiring Dreams, Changing Lives Award.
Executive Assistant Carolyn Ebling celebrated 45 years with Benedictine.
"Carolyn, is the person behind the scenes who has positively affected so many people during her time at Benedictine," said Executive Director Scott Evans. "She works tirelessly, never seeking recognition, and her dedication, support and guidance is invaluable."
"Benedictine commends all its staff milestone awardees for their compassion, dedication, dependability and caring devotion for the children and adults they serve and for their commitment to Benedictine," the organization said in a press release. "These traits are demonstrated in their interactions with the people they support and their families, as well as their co-workers and community partners."
Benedictine employs over 350 staff that are dedicated to serving children and adults with moderate to severe developmental disabilities and autism.
For more information on Benedictine's events, services and ways to support, please contact Claudia.cunningham@benschool.org or 410 634 2292.

title: 25th Denton parade draws hundreds - Lighting of the green, Christkindlmarkt also appeal to young and old
author: Connie Connolly; cconnolly@chespub.com
content:
25th Denton parade draws hundreds - Lighting of the green, Christkindlmarkt also appeal to young and old

 December 20, 2023 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Connie Connolly; cconnolly@chespub.com | Page: A1 | Section: News 
 
 557

 Read News Document

 DENTON - Hundreds of people lined Denton's Market Street for the town's 25th Holiday Parade 6 p.m. Thursday, Dec. 7.The mild evening was filled with the sights and sounds of an old-fashioned small-town parade.
Fire trucks blared sirens, horns and flashing lights; floats generated bubbles and confetti; some marchers threw candy and waved flags; and marching bands strutted and played holiday music.
On the grandstand was master of ceremonies Keith Shaffer and three judges: Caroline County Teacher of the Year Rob Honer, His Hope Ministries Director Stefanie Johnson and CASA of Caroline Director Amy Horne.
Trophy winners were Schaefer Farms and Greenhouses, first place float; Pure Country 4-H Club, second place float; Denton Volunteer Fire Company, best fire equipment; Lockerman Middle School, best marching band; Grace Upon Grace Dance Studio, best dance troupe; Maryland Rough Riders, best equestrian unit; Bill and Gail Towers' 1931 John Deere tractor, favorite automobile; Caroline-Dorchester County 4-H Fair Queen Skylar Blunt, favorite royalty; and Chesapeake Culinary Center, best use of lights.
The parade began at the Health and Public Services Building on South Seventh Street, and made its way down Market Street, past the Caroline County Courthouse, where the Rotary Club of Denton hosted the lighting of the historic green, along with the Caroline County Garden Club and Caroline County Recreation and Parks.
Rotary Club President Angel Perez welcomed the crowd, and members of the North Caroline High School chorus sang holiday songs and led the singing of "Silent Night." Shoppers lingered along Market Street and popped in and out of stores as they made their way along the shopping district.
For the first time, the outdoor Christkindlmarkt, sponsored by Downtown Denton Main Street Inc. was held in conjunction with the parade. Starting at 5 p.m. and ending at 8:30 p.m., the outdoor holiday market on the green at Third and Market streets featured a large lighted Christmas tree, craft vendors, food trucks, and Santa and Mrs. Claus.
Patti Wood of Patti's Petals welcomed the combined events. "The more the merrier," she said. "It helps to bring foot traffic in, and that's what we want."

title: 2023 Turkey Trots see another record turnout
author: CONTRIBUTED
content:
2023 Turkey Trots see another record turnout

 Author/Byline: CONTRIBUTED | Page: 6 | Section: News

 EASTON - The YMCA of the Chesapeake announced that the 2023 YMCA Turkey Trot broke records again this year, with approximately 1,800 runners raising nearly $200,000 for the Annual Fund through sponsorship and runner registrations.The Annual Fund supports programming across all eleven YMCA of the Chesapeake branches on the Delmarva Peninsula.
"We are beyond thankful to our participants and sponsors from across the Eastern Shore whose generous contributions made this year's Turkey Trot such a huge success," said Robbie Gill, YMCA of the Chesapeake CEO. "Each year, this wonderful Thanksgiving tradition is a chance to come together, give thanks for our blessings and give back to our friends and neighbors in need." The event's proceeds are dedicated to the YMCA's Annual Fund, which supports a multitude of programs for all ages across the Shore.
This includes local food drives, youth sports, Enhance Fitness (an exercise program for seniors), LiveStrong (a program for adult cancer survivors), Rock Steady (a program for those battling Parkinson's Disease), child care, swim lessons, mentoring programs, before and after school care, and the YMCA's Open Doors Program, which ensures that no member of the community is turned away from a Y facility or program due to an inability to pay.
In-person Turkey Trots were hosted by seven of the eleven YMCA branches across the Eastern Shore, including the Queen Anne's County Family YMCA, Easton Family YMCA at Peachblossom, the Richard A. Henson Family YMCA in Salisbury, the Cecil County Family YMCA in Perryville, the Pauline F. and David Robbins Family YMCA in Cambridge, the Kent County Family YMCA in Chestertown, and the David Landsberger Family YMCA in Chincoteague, Virginia.
In addition, a virtual Turkey Trot was also available.
The top 2023 Turkey Trot sponsors included: Willow Construction, Aetna Maryland, Becker Morgan Group, Life Fitness Division 501, Shore United Bank, Farm Creek Insurance, C & C Drywall Contractors North Inc., Dorchester Family Medicine, LLC, Eastern Shore Tents and Events, FPC Distribution, Iron Works Inc., M & T Foundation, Pepsi Bottling Ventures, PNC Bank, Preston Automotive Group and Tapmans Refrigeration.

title: Rotary club of Cambridge donates to veterans transportation program
author: CONTRIBUTED
content:
Rotary club of Cambridge donates to veterans transportation program

 December 20, 2023 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: CONTRIBUTED | Page: 6 | Section: News 
 
 268
 Words 

 Read News Document

 The Rotary Club of Cambridge recently presented a donation to Santo Grande of Delmarva Community Service to be used for veteran transportation.DCS's Delmarva Community Transportation division provides veterans with transportation when needed. The funds donated were raised through Rotary's Flags for Heroes Project, which runs from Memorial Day for 3 weeks.
"No one honors a Rotarian's motto Service Above Self more than our Nation's military personnel," said Flags for Heroes Chairman Ed Connelly.
The Rotary Club raises money through this program, donating proceeds to a number of veteran and first responder programs.
The Club displays approximately 200 US Flags with organizations, families and friends sponsoring each one.
The Flags recognize heroes who have served.
Over 90% of money raised is donated to a variety of organizations.
"While important, the fundraising aspect of the project is overshadowed by the stories told on the plaques by flag sponsors as to the accomplishments of their hero," said Connelly.
"Honoring those that paid the ultimate sacrifice for us to enjoy the freedoms we all too often take for granted.
Recognizing a teachable moment as a young child walks among the flags with a parent and asks why. Explaining to a recent immigrant the importance of our Memorial Day and seeing the respect on their face when they understand." This year, along with DCS, funds were donated to Project Opportunity, Coastal Hospice, Tunnels to Towers, Fisher House, Patriot's Point and construction of Handicap ramps with Chesapeake Housing Mission.

 December 22, 2023 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Doug Bishop; dbishop@chespub.com | Page: 9 | Section: News 
 
 544
 Words 

 Read News Document

 QUEEN ANNE's COUNTY - This past weekend saw the Wreaths Across America truck convoy headed to Arlington National Cemetery with thousands of Christmas wreaths.Stopping over night Thursday. Dec. 7, for the 14th consecutive year, they were again hosted by Kent Island American Legion Post 278, in Stevensville, under direction of Past Post Commander and the 2023 Maryland State Legionnaire of the Year Nikki Randolph.
Randolph has earned a reputation for her passionate care for all veterans, making sure veteran grave sites are bestowed with American flags and Christmas wreaths at appropriate times of the year, every year.
The yearly tradition began when she was then commander of Post 278 and contacted Morrill and Karen Worcester of Maine, who had already begun the Wreaths Across America program - hauling Christmas wreaths from their state to the nation's capitol to place those wreaths on all veteran's grave sites at Arlington National Cemetery.
Randolph and Legion 278 volunteers provided three meals, dinner, breakfast and boxed lunches to the convoy before they made the final leg of their journey to Arlington.
This year, the Wreaths Across America sent out over 3,000,000 Christmas wreaths across the nation to more than 4,200 locations to be placed on those grave sites. Most were placed on Saturday, Dec. 9.
Eleven wreaths were also presented to families connected to Post 278, whose veterans chose to be cremated rather than buried in a cemetery.
One of those was to the wife of the late George Dashiell, who served during World War II in Germany.
Mrs. Wally Dashiell, now 100-years-old has been a widow for the past 17 years. She said, "I'm truly grateful that the Legion honored George in this way." The wreath was placed next to the urn that holds his ashes, the American flag presented during his memorial service, and a picture of George.
Friday morning the convoy departed from Legion 278 along Route 8, children from both Matapeake Elementary and Middle Schools cheering and waving small American flags. An emotional scene, it was clear the children were excited to participate.
Saturday at noon, American Legion Jeff Davis Post 18 in Centreville, hosted their annual Wreaths Across America ceremony at Chesterfield Cemetery. Approximately 200 people were present, many of them children and teens with their parents. 
 
 Caption: PHOTOS BY DOUG BISHOP

 U.S. Army veteran John Nizer is pictured laying a Christmas wreath for all POWs and Missing in Action veterans at the annual Wreaths Across American ceremony at Chesterfield Cemetery in Centreville, Saturday afternoon, Dec. 9. In the background, Legion 18 member John White takes a photograph and Sea Cadet Unit members stand at attention. Over 3 million wreaths were laid at more than 4,200 locations across the nation of Saturday.

 Pictured at the Chesterfield Cemetery in Centreville, American Legion Vice Commander Ken Huddleston gives opening remarks during the annual Wreaths Across America ceremony there. To his far left, Legion Riders Chaplain Andy "Wizard" Cowley prepares to give the blessing for the event. More than 200 people turned out to help lay wreaths.

 Pre-k children from Christ Episcopal Church Day School wave small American flags at tractor trailer drivers departing from the Kent Island American Legion Post 278, in Stevensville, Friday morning, Dec. 8, as the trucks headed toward Arlington National Cemetery to deliver Christmas wreaths to be placed on military veterans grave sites.

title: Chestertown woman takes home early holiday gift - Lottery players across the state won more than $31 million during week ending Dec. 24
content:
Chestertown woman takes home early holiday gift - Lottery players across the state won more than $31 million during week ending Dec. 24

 December 27, 2023 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Page: 4 | Section: News 
 
 287
 Words 

 Read News Document

 CHESTERTOWN - Maryland Lottery winners continued to claim winning tickets last week as the holiday season was in full swing, including several at the $50,000 level.In the weekly roundup of big winners was one woman claiming $50,000 in the state lottery Money Bag Multiplier. The ticket was sold at Lewes Dairy Market, 840 High Street in Chestertown.
The woman who did not wish to be named was from the area, store owner Hassan Mahmood said, but has redeemed her ticket. It was the fourth winning ticket sold by the store in the last couple of months he said.
Total winnings for the week remained on par with other weeks this year, coming in at $31 million, a figure that includes unclaimed draw game and FAST PLAY wins.
In all, 24 Maryland Lottery tickets worth $10,000 or more were sold or redeemed in the seven days ending Dec. 23. The Lottery paid more than $31 million in prizes during that period.
Winners of prizes larger than $25,000 must redeem their tickets at the Maryland Lottery Claims Center in Baltimore, which is open by appointment only. Prizes of up to $5,000 can be claimed at any of more than 400 Expanded Cashing Authority Program (XCAP) locations.
All Maryland Lottery retailers are authorized to redeem tickets up to and including $600. More information is available on the How To Claim page of mdlottery.com.
The Maryland Lottery encourages players to check their tickets by scanning them at any Lottery retailer or with the Lottery's mobile apps. Draw game winners have 182 days from the date of a drawing to claim their prizes, and scratchoff winners have 182 days from the announced end-of-game date.
Last claim dates for scratchoff tickets are published in the scratch-off section of mdlottery.com.

title: MAKE WAY FOR HOLLY!
content:
MAKE WAY FOR HOLLY!

 December 27, 2023 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Page: 5 | Section: News 
 
 88
 Words 

 Read News Document

 Caption: DOUG BISHOP

 Many aviators arrive Saturday morning, Dec. 9, to the Bay Bridge Airport in Stevensville for the annual Tangier Island Holly Run. Tangier Island has no holly trees, thus, pilots join forces with Chesapeake Sport Pilot School owner and top flight instructor Helen Woods (standing to the right of Santa). A tradition for nearly 50 years, holly is flown to the island where the small community uses the branches to decorate for the holiday season. More than 20 airplanes from around the state made the flight this year.

author: CONTRIBUTED
content:
Cambridge Rotary Club rings in holiday season at Walmart

 December 29, 2023 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: CONTRIBUTED | Page: 8 | Section: News 
 
 119
 Words 

 Read News Document

 The Rotary Club of Cambridge continued its annual tradition of ringing the bell for the Salvation Army.For more years than members can remember, Rotarians have taken a shift at Walmart, sharing a smile and a "Merry Christmas" with shoppers.
In recent years, members of the Cambridge South Dorchester High School Interact Club have joined their Rotary sponsoring club in giving back to the community.
Interact, the high school component of Rotary, is open to students aged 14 to 18. Interact members helping the Rotary Club and Salvation Army were President Mia Jackson, Vice President Tyler Sears, Lily Spedden, Elise Jones and R'Miya Rosado.

title: A spacious and welcoming place - Central branch reopens main floor following a year of renovations
author: Connie Connolly; cconnolly@chespub.com
content:
A spacious and welcoming place - Central branch reopens main floor following a year of renovations

 January 3, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Connie Connolly; cconnolly@chespub.com | Page: 11 | Section: News 
 
 986
 Words 

 Read News Document

 DENTON - Following a year of renovating and redesigning, the central branch of the Caroline County Public Library at 100 Market Street in the county seat reopened its first floor space Dec. 18.The soft reopening is designed to help staff fine tune details as they welcome patrons and visitors. A grand opening celebration is planned when the new elevator is finished in spring 2024.
New carpet, neutral walls, fresh shelving and new furniture create welcoming decor in the more open spaces of the library's main floor. The main desk is bigger and moved away from the wall, making it easier for staff members to see most of the library's interior.
Bennett said she wanted people to experience the library as "bright, open and inviting."
"This is perfect," customer Romont Fletcher of Denton said Dec. 20 as he set up his laptop on the desk attached to an upholstered chair. He had not been in the library for a year and was surprised when he walked in. "This is a great renovation," he said.
"This is good space, and it's flexible space," Executive Director Debby Bennett said. "It's a well-built library." Bennett, who has been with the library since 1983, will retire in June 2024.
"In 1983, people came in, got their books and checked them out and went home," Bennett said. "Now people come to stay, whether it's work on our computer, hang out with their friends in the Teen Zone, a family comes in and spends time looking for materials and just spending time here, small meetings in the study room, research in the Maryland room."
The $2.1 million renovation project began Jan. 2, 2023. Bennett, the Caroline County Board of Library Trustees and library staff met their goal of reopening the first floor to the public before Christmas.
The central branch has experienced many changes in its 62-year history. Card catalogs and hand-stamping due dates have been computerized. Circulating books are still a staple, but today library card holders can check out a Cricut machine, sewing machines and even fishing poles.
The central branch has 13,739 card holders who can check out materials, but visitors can obtain guest passes to use the public computers.
As if to illustrate the changes, two days after reopening, four teenaged young men checked out software to play games on library Xboxes in the Teen Zone.
The renovation was funded mainly by two "highly competitive" State Library Capital Grants, Bennett said.
In addition to replacing the roof slates on the library's 1995 addition, the building underwent extensive first floor renovations.
Phase 2 includes improving the elevator in 2024.
The Phase 1 grant in fiscal year 2023 financed 79%, or $917,000 of the project.
The library board provided the local match of $244,000 from their John Hargreaves fund.
This phase included replacing three HVAC units at the end of their useful life, improving lighting, upgrading the emergency fire alarm system and phone system, enhancing electrical capacity for increased technology, removing the wall dividing the two children's rooms, providing a family bathroom adjacent to the children's areas, increasing seating capacity, improving sight lines and creating quiet areas. The improvements brought the library into compliance with ADA requirements.
The cost didn't include shelving, furniture and other additional costs that were incurred throughout the renovation, about $335,236. The library paid for those costs, except for $78,000 raised by the Friends of the Library for shelving for the adult, young adult and Maryland Room collections.
Phase 2 is being funded by a fiscal year 2024 State Library Capital Grant that pays for 78%, or $467,000, of the project, with the remaining $132,000 provided by the Caroline County Commissioners.
This phase includes replacing the elevator, which is "at the end of its useful life," Bennett said.
The new elevator will comply with ADA requirements and current codes.
The phase also includes replacing the addition's 4,000 square foot roof with artificial slate, which had deteriorated and become a "serious safety hazard," Bennett said.
The elevator provides access to public space, administrative offices and the third floor attic storage area.
"The (two-sided) main service desk is going to work a lot better for staff to both answer basic questions and check out items, and also to be able to work with people with more complex reference questions," Bennett said. "And also we have so much better visibility of the other desks and more areas of library to see who might need help (and) for security."
"Back in 1995 when we renovated and added on, we didn't have cell phones and laptops and iPads," Bennett said, adding that the internet was fairly new then.
"The MakerSpace used to be our reference area in 1995 with 7-foot shelves of reference books. Now, all the reference materials are online."
More square footage not taken up by books "frees up more people space," she said.
There's a lot to figure out," Bennett said. "Half our staff are new and didn't work down here. And for all the staff, it's a new layout. So it's a matter of figuring out procedures and ironing out all the little extra things. So opening like this without a big fanfare - and this is a quiet time of the year anyway - is giving us time to figure a lot so that things go smoothly for staff and customers."
"I've seen a lot of changes, but this library has always been innovative," Bennett said. "It's always been forward-thinking and also thinking: What does the community need? What does community need that they don't even know they need?" 
 
 Caption: From left are Caroline County Public Library central branch staff members Kelly Emory, Mitchell Downes, Executive Director Debby Bennett and Emerging Services Manager Vicki Burchfield.

 "This is perfect," says Romont Fletcher of Denton regarding the newly renovated central branch of Caroline County Public Library.

 The Market Street entrance of Caroline County Public Library's central branch in Denton faces the courthouse.

 New carpet, shelving and furniture add to the fresh look of the central branch.

 The Teen Zone is an inviting space for gaming and online work and research.

title: Brighter Christmas fund assists single mother with holiday gifts
content:
Brighter Christmas fund assists single mother with holiday gifts

 January 4, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Page: 2 | Section: News 
 
 261
 Words 

 Read News Document

 A single mother was struggling to purchase Christmas gifts for her 4-month-old while finishing college and working full time."I support my family by working full time and making sure that my baby's needs are met first," she said. "I am currently a college student working on my bachelor's degree so I can get a better paying job in the future." The mother received assistance with her family's holiday celebration from the Brighter Christmas Fund.
Though awards for this year have already been distributed, your donation to the Brighter Christmas Fund can help families in similar situations provide holiday gifts for their children in years to come.
The Brighter Christmas Fund is a nonprofit charity which helps families in need on the Mid-Shore, may be sent to The Star Democrat, 29088 Airpark Dr., Easton, MD 21601. Donations also may be made online via credit card or PayPal at brighterchristmasfund.org. Click the "Donate" button. Donations are tax-deductible.
The administrative costs for the Brighter Christmas Fund are covered entirely by The Star Democrat and APG Chesapeake, so 100% of donations go to families in need. For more information about the fund, call 410-200-1884.
The total donated for this year's Brighter Christmas Fund to date is $65,165.
Those in the sharing spirit of giving with others this holiday season include: Beth Lawton In Loving Memory of Dr.
Justin T. Callahan & Frances Halsey Callahan David & Brenda Rardin Jacqueline & Sean Mallin Marclyn Hendon Robert Case & Elizabeth Adams In Memory of Dr. and Mrs.
