title: WBOC dropped from Breezeline cable lineup
author: Natalie Jones
content:
WBOC dropped from Breezeline cable lineup

 January 5, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Natalie Jones | Section: Local News 
 
 551
 Words 

 Read News Document

 EASTON — Breezeline, a local cable provider serving viewers in the Mid-Shore region, dropped Salisbury-based news station WBOC-TV from its lineup on Dec. 31, upsetting many customers.The cable provider made the decision to drop the CBS-affiliated news station from its lineup due to WBOC being an out-of-market station to the communities Breezeline serves, according to a statement on the news station's website.
Those communities — some in Talbot, Queen Anne's and Kent counties — are in the Baltimore viewing area, per Nielsen Media Research.
According to Andrew Walton, a spokesperson for Breezeline, the Federal Communications Commission designated WJZ, the CBS affiliate in Baltimore, as the in-market station. WBOC, an out-of-market station, is not significantly viewed, he said in an email.
Nielsen determines the designated market area based on viewing patterns. The designated market areas and stations within those areas are published quarterly, and the FCC has established processes for subsequent modifications.
Breezeline notified its customers in November about the drop of WBOC from its local lineups, Walton said.
Craig Jahelka, president of Draper Media, the company that owns WBOC, stressed that the decision was not a carriage dispute, or made because the station and the cable provider couldn't agree. It was a unilateral decision by Breezeline, he said.
Jahelka, a former journalist, said it was "very frustrating" for the decision to be made for the station by Breezeline executives not in WBOC's coverage area.
"Without us ... people don't know what's going on," he said.
News stations in Baltimore won't cover stories local to the Mid-Shore region, or the area's weather and sports, Jahelka added.
Walton said the discontinuation of carriage was instituted to manage costs for customers.
While there is constant pressure on rates because of large, ongoing increases in content costs, Breezeline works to manage costs where possible to make sure its video service provides a strong value for customers, he added.
"We understand the disappointment that some Grasonville customers feel about WBOC," Walton said via email. "Yet, all Breezeline TV viewers would have been burdened with the cost of both channels when the content on WBOC substantially duplicates that found on WJZ. In addition, local content on WBOC can be accessed on their website for free."
This is not the first time WBOC was dropped from Breezeline's lineup.
In late December 2014, Atlantic Broadband, which was rebranded as Breezeline in early 2022, dropped the news station after a local programming review.
The volume of public outcry then about the decision prompted the cable provider to restore WBOC to its channel lineup within a month, Jahelka said.
While Jahelka can't force the cable provider to add the station back to its lineup, a resurgence of public outcry about the decision could potentially prompt Breezeline to return the channel, he added.
WBOC itself has already been inundated with calls from upset viewers. Some viewers have taken to social media to voice frustration with the decision.
Jahelka encouraged customers to contact Breezeline, saying it's the only way for the cable provider to understand how important WBOC's coverage is to Delmarva residents.
Viewers with concerns or complaints can reach out to Breezeline via email at breezeline@breezeline.com.
But for now, those interested in viewing WBOC's news programs can watch via its website or the WBOC app. News is also available via WBOC's social media.
This story has been updated from an earlier version to include the most current contact information for Breezeline.

title: Appreciating oysters
author: MARIE SAVAGE Country Cooking
content:
Appreciating oysters

 January 9, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: MARIE SAVAGE Country Cooking | Section: Food 
 
 1416
 Words 

 Read News Document

 Having grown up on the Eastern Shore, the oyster has been a much-appreciated seafood in my life.My mother made some of the greatest tasting oyster fritters on the Mason Dixon line. There are no watermen in my family, but we lived close enough to the water to respect the life of the waterman and the delicious delicacies that were a result of their hard work.
In our local area here, the most popular oyster varieties include Malpeques, Well Fleet, Blue Points, Delaware Bay, Chesapeake Bay, Chincoteagues, Apalachicola Bay and Gulf Coast.
East Coast oysters range from slightly salty to sharp salt flavor (Chesapeake, Delaware and Gulf Coast oysters have a light salt taste; all others have a sharper salty taste).
The Chesapeake Bay has been home to oystering since the early 19th century. Chesapeake Bay skipjacks are the last commercial sailing vessels in the United States.
The dredge boats once numbered in the thousands. Today only about a dozen or so remain.
Skip jacks are limited to 150 bushels of oysters daily. The dredging season runs from November through March 1. The recent ice has made it impossible for the boats to get out to perform their work — cutting into the ice and cutting into the pockets of our waterman and their families. Check your local newspapers and the Facebook posts of local fire departments, churches and organizations with upcoming oyster dinners and roast coming up for their fundraising events.
I know that many seafood markets are featuring fresh oysters in the shell or by the pint and quarts or opened for you. I like to open my own — eating them on the half shell or cooking them fresh.
Try going down to the docks and getting them from the waterman themselves. Support a trade that is slowly leaving our Eastern Shore. Thank a waterman who goes out in all kinds of weather laboring in a trade they must love that is full of obstacles. The weather has cleared, and the watermen are returning to the trade they love. I am on the way to the docks for oysters to prepare some of my favorite seafood dishes.
EASTERN SHORE OYSTER FRITTERS
Drain 1 quart of oysters, reserving the juice, and set aside. Beat 2 eggs, add the reserved juice to the egg and add Worcestershire sauce to taste. Add 1 1/2 cups flour with 1 1/2 tsps baking powder and mix well. Add the oysters and lightly mix. Fry in hot oil, browning on both sides. Drain on a paper towel and serve warm. When dropping the fritters in the oil, make sure you have at least 3 oysters to a fritter.
TRADITIONAL MARYLAND OYSTER STEW
In a large saucepan, cook one-pint fresh shucked oysters, with juice, over low heat until edges begin to curl. Add 1 quart of milk, 1/4 cup butter, salt and pepper to taste. You can sprinkle some Old Bay seasoning on top if desired slowly, but do not boil. Serve hot with oyster crackers if desired.
SCALLOPED OYSTERS
In a greased two-quart casserole, place alternate layers of oysters and fresh cracker crumbs, doting each layer with butter. For this process you will need one quart of oysters with liquid, 2 to 3 cups fresh crushed crackers and 1/2 cup butter or 1 stick margarine. You can also sprinkle each layer with salt and pepper to taste. End with a layer of crumbs, and pour one to two cups of milk over the top. Dot the top with remaining butter or margarine and bake at 350 degrees until browned, about 40 to 50 minutes. Makes 6 generous servings.
OYSTER POT PIE
In a large saucepan place 5 or 6 diced potatoes, cleaned and peeled, with 5 or 6 carrots, 2 to 3 cleaned and diced onions, 1/2 pound of chopped ham, and 4 strips of uncooked bacon. Cook until done and add salt and pepper to taste. Sprinkle with 1/2 tsp parsley flakes and 1/2 tsp oregano. Mix 1 pint crushed tomatoes and the liquor of one pint of oysters. Add this to the already cooked ingredients. Bring to a boil; thicken with some cornstarch. When thick, add one pint of oysters. Cook until the oysters have curled edges. Pour into a baking dish lined with your favorite crust and place a crust over the top. Slightly prick the top crust with a fork, bake at 400 degrees until brown. This is so delicious for supper on a wintry day.
BACON OYSTER LETTUCE TOMATO
1 cup all-purpose flour, 1 cup cornmeal, 1 tbsp garlic powder, 1 tbsp onion powder, 1/4 tsp cayenne pepper, Kosher salt, freshly ground pepper, 2 dozen oysters (freshly shucked), 12 slices thick-cut bacon, vegetable oil (for frying; about 5 cups), 8 slices brioche or white sandwich bread toasted, mayonnaise, bibb lettuce, and sliced tomatoes. Whisk flour, cornmeal, garlic powder, onion powder, and cayenne in a medium bowl; season with salt and pepper. Working in batches, toss oysters in flour mixture, transfer to a plate. Working in batches, cook bacon in a large skillet, preferably cast iron, over medium heat until crisp, 10–12 minutes per batch; drain on paper towels. Pour oil into a skillet with bacon fat to a depth of one inch and heat over medium-high heat until oil bubbles immediately when a pinch of cornmeal mixture is added. Working in batches, fry oysters, turning occasionally, until golden brown and crisp, about four minutes. Drain on paper towels, season with salt and pepper. Build sandwiches with mayonnaise, lettuce, tomatoes, bacon and fried oysters and serve.
OYSTER CORNBREAD STUFFING
8 tbsps unsalted butter (divided), 4 stalks celery (finely chopped), 1/2 yellow onion (finely chopped), 1 tsp kosher salt, 1 tsp rubbed sage, 1 tsp dried rosemary, 1 tsp dried thyme, 1/2 tsp coarse ground black pepper, 6 cups cornbread cubes, 18 ounces oysters (chopped, liquor reserved), 2 cups chicken broth, 2 large eggs. Preheat oven to 350 degrees and spray a 9x13 baking dish with vegetable oil spray. Add 4 tbsps unsalted butter to a large skillet on medium heat. Add in the celery and onions, cook for 6-8 minutes until translucent. Add in the salt, sage, rosemary, thyme, and black pepper and stir. To a large bowl add the cornbread cubes, vegetable mixture, and oysters and toss. In a second bowl whisk together the reserved oyster liquor, chicken broth, eggs, and melted butter. Pour the mixture over the bowl and toss gently to moisten the cornbread cubes. Pour the mixture into your baking dish and bake, uncovered, for 30-35 minutes until golden brown.
SINGLE FRIED OYSTERS
1 pint freshly shucked raw oysters, 2 cups buttermilk, 1¼ cup fine yellow cornmeal, ¾ cup all-purpose flour, 1 tbsp Creole seasoning, 1 tsp kosher salt, 1 quart peanut oil. While the oil heats, pour the oysters into a colander or strainer and let them drain. Then, rinse with fresh water to wash off any debris or shell fragments. Pour the buttermilk into a medium-sized bowl and dunk the drained oysters. Let them marinate for 15 to 20 minutes. Place the cornmeal, flour, creole seasoning and salt in a shallow bowl or pie plate and whisk to combine. Remove the oysters from the buttermilk one at a time and dredge them in the cornmeal mixture. Toss gently and make sure they are well coated, then shake any excess bread off. Place the coated oysters on a metal cooling rack until all of them have been coated. Letting them sit for a few minutes helps to fuse the breading and buttermilk and keeps the breading from falling off when they are fried. Place a large stockpot, Dutch oven, or cast iron skillet with high sides over medium-high heat and add one to two inches of oil. When the oil reaches 370 degrees, carefully add the oysters, one at a time to fry. Depending on the size of your pan, it works best to fry in batches and only cook six to eight at a time. You do not want to crowd them. (Maintain a consistent heat of 370 degrees by increasing or decreasing the heat under the pan.)Let the oysters fry for about two to three minutes, stirring occasionally or until the breading is light golden brown and the meat is opaque with the edges slightly curled. Use a wire kitchen spider or slotted spoon to remove them from the oil. Place on a paper towel or wire cooling rack to drain. Repeat until all of the oysters are fried and serve immediately. Optional, garnish with fresh lemon or lime slices and serve with your choice of sauce and sides.

title: Talbot County Garden Club hosts lecture by Leslie Harris
author: Staff Writer
content:
Talbot County Garden Club hosts lecture by Leslie Harris

 January 12, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Staff Writer | Section: Entertainment 
 
 152
 Words 

 Read News Document

 The Talbot County Free Library in Easton will host a free public lecture from the Talbot County Garden Club on Tuesday, Jan. 23. from 11 a.m to 12 p.m."Thoughtful Gardening: How to Combine Sustainability with Beauty in the Garden," will be presented by Leslie Harris of LH Gardens in Charlottesville, Virginia. The event is part of the local garden club's speaker series.
"Harris known for her weekly podcasts, 'Into the Garden with Leslie,' offering a plant of the week, informative interviews, and seasonal tips and tricks. She draws from the experts she interviews (from Delaware's Doug Tallamy to Maine's Chicken Lady) to combine with information from real life experiences in her own garden. From Leslie, you can expect to hear new ways to garden with an eye to your yard as a habitat for both flowers and wildlife," according to an announcement promoting the event from Discover Easton.
For more: https://talbotcountygc.org/ or http://www.tcfl.org/Calendar/

title: A year in review at Londonderry on the Tred Avon
author: LONDONDERRY ON THE TRED AVON
content:
A year in review at Londonderry on the Tred Avon

 January 16, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: LONDONDERRY ON THE TRED AVON | Section: Life 
 
 441
 Words 

 Read News Document

 EASTON — As Londonderry on the Tred Avon reflects on 2023 and looks ahead to 2024, it is thankful for the dedication and enthusiasm of their team, residents and community partners who all played vital roles in this year's success.This same team has set the stage for an even stronger 2024.
A few highlighted achievements include:
Londonderry proudly welcomed new CEO Christine Harrington in September. With Harrington's extensive experience as both an organizational leader and day-to-day manager in the senior living work field, with over 15 years in an executive role, she has been an ideal fit for the community.
"We were thrilled to welcome Christine this past September," said Rachel Smith, Londonderry's sales and marketing director. "Getting to know her and witnessing the unique value she adds to our community and team has been a delight. We're eagerly looking forward to the future and counting on her as an integral part of our exceptional team."
Londonderry also continued its record of community recognition in 2023 winning Best Retirement/55+ Community in the APG Best of the Best Chesapeake Community Choice Awards and being named a finalist in the Senior Living Category.
Other awards included, "Best Residential Community" in Talbot and Dorchester Counties for the fourth year by the readers of Coastal Style magazine as well as "Best Retirement Community" in What's Up Eastern Shore magazine.
Also in 2023, Londonderry was pleased to introduce our New Board President, John Flohr, along with two new additions to our Board, Steve Cades and Jean Rhian.
Jennifer Hughes, Londonderry Controller, graduated from Shore Leadership, a nine-month program where participants learn through face-to-face discussions with local community leaders and experts from organizations and institutions that shape the region's economic structure and culture.
On Oct. 19, Londonderry hosted their annual themed event, with Casino Night being 2023's theme.
The event was attended by more than 100 guests, which included residents, residents' families, members of the Board of Directors, local elected officials and other community members. Guests walked a red carpet, played table games led by a professional croupier with fun money and were entertained by a live band while enjoying casino-themed drinks and appetizers.
"The accomplishments of this past year are a testament to the dedication of our incredible team members, Board of Directors, residents and supportive community business partners," said Harrington. "We are truly fortunate to have so many wonderful people contributing to our commitment of excellence on campus. As we step into 2024, we're excited to enhance retirement living at Londonderry through innovation and advancement."
As the new year gets underway, there are ownership opportunities available. To learn more about what residences are available, please contact Rachel Smith, Sales and Marketing Director at rsmith@londonderrytredavon.com .

title: Specters sought at historic Kitty Knight House
author: WILL BONTRAGER wbontrager@chespub.com
content:
Specters sought at historic Kitty Knight House

 January 23, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: WILL BONTRAGER wbontrager@chespub.com | Section: Local News 
 
 766
 Words 

 Read News Document

 GALENA — On a blustery, wintry Friday night while some were eating salty treats watching football, guests showed up at the inn, ready to spend hours searching for paranormal clues. They dined, and, like a reality show, they got to know each other, sharing stories that drew them to this particular place at this particular time.Eighteen guests met with Tony Avallone, founder of the Mid-Atlantic Paranormal Project, (MAPP), and seven other members for an overnight investigation a the historic Kitty Knight Inn in Galena.
Their goal, to seek out supernatural activity using Avallone's ghost-tracking equipment.
And for a longtime ghost hunter, Avallone, who's had his share of disconcerting experiences, he wants to bring a positive light, even some fun, to this activity. "MAPP's here to help businesses and families understand the unexplained," he said.
Before embarking on their adventure, guests shared past stories, those having left a phantom handprint on their lives from an early age.
Somebody mentioned their deceased grandfather had appeared to her and told him his feet were cold. Later, when she told her grandmother, she was informed he was buried without shoes on. Some had experienced voices and shadows flitting in and out. Some felt heavy oppression at abandoned penitentiaries where tormented spirits lurked.
Others had doors swing wide open without the wind's provocation, and the doorknob shake violently. One couple said they travel far and wide looking for places like this — open to all phenomenal experiences.
Like any group of adventurers and believers, there was a skeptic among them as well. "I'm just along for the ride," he said, arms folded. He was unsure what the night would bring.
The air crackled with positive excitement that only increased when Avallone introduced himself halfway into their meal. Avallone gave them a rundown on what would happen through the night.
Using electromagnetic frequency detectors to follow electromagnetic activity, audio recorders to track electronic voice phenomena and DVR cameras in every room — a total of 12 devices would run for eight hours, from 8 p.m. to 3 a.m., he explained, the time when it's said that supernatural activity peaks.
The house itself has a mysterious history.
Director of Marketing for the Jamestown Hospitality Group, which owns the property said in an interview with Chesapeake Bay Magazine, "We definitely have chatter about the house being haunted. Guests say that doors will shut, or you'll hear voices when no one is there."
Avallone attested that when previously staying in Knight's bedroom he awoke completely cold. Unexplainable because the thermostat wasn't touched when he watched the footage back.
The night started off slow with little responses in the tavern. Then they broke up in teams of three, rotating through the three main "hots spots" — Room 4, Kitty Knight's Room, where Avallone felt that intense cold years back, Room 8 where a spirit of a little boy they call "Captain" is alleged to resides, and the basement — where voices from the Civil War era and voices of children playing had been reported to be heard.
As the evening progressed, guests donned a blindfold and put on noise-canceling headphones. Known as the Estes method, they listened to what Avallone called, "the spirit box," an AM/FM radio that speeds through the dials so fast no words get through.
But when they do, it is believed to be something speaking from beyond.
It was a big thrill for the guests.
Guests on the other side of the room asked questions and if the guest with the headphones answered, that meant something supernatural was speaking to him or her.
The results were both fascinating and disturbing. "Ninety-five percent of the questions were adequately aligned with the questions asked," Avallone remarked.
In the morning, Avallone met the guests at breakfast and answered their questions. It will take weeks for him to comb through the collected data, but he promised to share the results.
In the several years Avallone has been visiting the inn, he's discovered a whispery, hushed, "Hi," and in the basement sounds of of children at play. He's heard footsteps when all was still and an entire conversation that could have revealed knowledge of an earlier time period.
He's also seen a glowing orb, which looked like a lot of insects in a group, yet not moving like bugs, but more like hovering.
He's seen shadows that looked human-like.
But he's never felt threatened by the Kitty Knight Inn experience.
"Whatever is there, enjoys having the company of the guests," he said.
For those intrigued on the next adventure, don't miss out, the Mid-Atlantic Paranormal Project will be having their last public investigation of the season at Kitty Knight Inn on Feb. 3. Find them on Facebook and Instagram @midatlanticparanormalproject

title: Talbot Interfaith Shelter celebrates 15 years of fighting homelessness on the Mid-Shore
author: TALBOT INTERFAITH SHELTER
content:
Talbot Interfaith Shelter celebrates 15 years of fighting homelessness on the Mid-Shore

 January 25, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: TALBOT INTERFAITH SHELTER | Section: Local News 
 
 942
 Words 

 Read News Document

 Talbot Interfaith Shelter started off 2024 with a significant milestone.This month marks their 15th anniversary of serving the community's homeless neighbors. The organization has been through quite a journey to get to this point.
Talbot Interfaith Shelter was formed in 2008 by a group of concerned members of Talbot County faith communities, who were alarmed by a growing number of requests for assistance from those who were hungry, homeless or about to become homeless.
The group, led by founder Evelyn Sedlack, hoped to be able to fill the gap to provide a safe haven for families in need.
For five years, Talbot Interfaith Shelter was a "homeless" homeless shelter — rotating cots, blankets, supplies and support through Talbot's faith congregations during the cold-weather months.
Teams of volunteers from 19 faith communities came together to bring hot meals, drive guests to shower at the YMCA, make bagged lunches and provide fellowship for the shelter's guests. Guests had to leave in the morning and return in the evening to allow the churches and synagogue to conduct their regular business.
Due to fire code restrictions in the houses of worship, Talbot Interfaith was only able to house five individuals per night. This restriction, coupled with the fact that they could not provide daytime shelter or house people year-round, made it nearly impossible to help families under the rotating shelter model.
The shelter began supporting one family at a time in an apartment rented to them in 2011.
Since the need far surpassed the organization's capabilities, Talbot Interfaith began investigating buildings and properties with an eye toward a permanent facility to allow them to function year-round.
After looking at various properties in Easton, shelter leaders began negotiations in early 2014 to purchase Easton's Promise, a former bed and breakfast at 107 Goldsborough Street.
That building, centrally located with five en suite bathrooms, large dining and living areas and a kitchen, offered a tremendous amount of flexibility.
On Sept. 15, 2016, the Maryland Court of Special Appeals upheld the shelter's permit to operate at Easton's Promise, allowing them to finalize the purchase of the building on Nov. 2, 2016.
Having a permanent facility not only enabled Talbot Interfaith to serve more people, but it allowed guests to stay longer, giving the organization the opportunity to develop a program that would address homelessness and its root causes, rather than than simply giving guests a temporary reprieve.
Talbot Interfaith Shelter's innovative S4 Program (shelter, stability, support, success) was designed to address the unique challenges of rural homelessness.
The goal of S4 is to create sustainable change in the lives of local men, women and children, providing them with access to services and tools that can help them break the cycle of poverty and homelessness to reclaim their independence.
The S4 Program incorporates shelter, rigorous case management, connection with local service providers and life skills training to provide a full circle approach to homelessness.
After launching the S4 Program, Talbot Interfaith began building partnerships with the Housing Commission of Talbot and several private landlords to procure more off-site transitional apartments.
In the spring of 2020, when the COVID crisis began, TIS leadership anticipated devastating economic repercussions for many in the community.
In April of 2020, TIS began actively exploring ways to expand their capacity to accommodate more people and help them through the challenges of homelessness. After many months of discussions and planning, the solution presented itself — directly next door to Easton's Promise at 109 Goldsborough Street.
With seven bedrooms, three full baths, a kitchen, meeting space, laundry facilities and more, this is a perfect setting for guests to regain stability as they work towards earning a spot in Talbot Interfaith's transitional housing program.
Appropriately, on Nov. 17, 2020, during National Hunger and Homelessness Awareness Week, the Easton Board of Zoning Appeals (BOZA) voted unanimously to approve Talbot Interfaith Shelter's permit to expand their services to 109 Goldsborough Street.
Dozens of supporters from across the community submitted suggestions to name the new building, and more than 1,000 people voted for the winner, Evelyn's Place, an homage to Talbot Interfaith's founder, Evelyn Sedlack, whose compassion and perseverance was the catalyst for what the shelter had grown to become.
Evelyn's Place was designated as a shelter for single men and women, while Easton's Promise serves families with children.
On June 6, 2022, Evelyn's Place opened its doors for the first time. Within three weeks, every bed was filled with local men and women beginning their journey to self-sufficiency through the S4 Program.
In 2023, Talbot Interfaith Shelter served 112 people, including 27 single individuals and 19 families with 44 children.
Of those served, one family graduated fully from the S4 Program and 16 single individuals and eight families moved from the shelter into one of Talbot Interfaith's 17 transitional apartments or directly into their own housing.
Guests attended classes on basic life skills, poverty, parenting, budgeting, job readiness, relationships, and the Six Pillars of Character.
Case managers helped with everything from recovering lost paperwork or identification to applying for disability and reunifying families.
When asked about how it feels to be celebrating 15 years, Talbot Interfaith Executive Director Julie Lowe said, "What TIS has become today, we owe to that small group of concerned citizens fifteen years ago, who saw their neighbors suffering and knew they had to do something to help. Out of that one meeting grew a community of thousands of volunteers and donors who have changed hundreds of lives for the better. It is incredible to watch our guests thrive and become more confident as they work to rebuild their lives, and we owe that all to this community and our amazing supporters."
To learn more about Talbot Interfaith Shelter and how you can help, visit talbotinterfaithshelter.org or contact Julie Lowe at julielowe@talbotinterfaithshelter.org or 410-310-2316.

title: The Arc is making progress toward August completion
author: TOM MCCALL
content:
The Arc is making progress toward August completion

 January 25, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: TOM MCCALL | Section: Local News 
 
 733
 Words 

 Read News Document

 EASTON — The Arc Central Chesapeake's 24,000-square-foot Port Street Commons center is growing, with concrete monoliths, the beginnings of the new building, reaching into the sky.And as the project takes shape, they are getting closer to providing both affordable housing and support for community members with developmental disabilities, Arc leadership said.
"We started construction on Aug. 14, so yes, we are roughly six months in. That estimates the completion is November 4," said Jonathon Rondeau, the president and CEO of The Arc Central Chesapeake Region.
"It was always designed to be a 14-month build, and we have worked in partnership with our architect, Rauch, and our general contractor, BGC, to keep on top of that," he said.
To speed up the construction process, everything down to bathroom tile has already been chosen.
"There is no design process at the same time, which is a little bit different. We front load everything. That is where delays are, making decisions on site," Rondeau said.
He said the design of the building is meant to mirror what it looked like in Easton 50 or 60 years ago, mimicking architectural styles that were common in the area at the time.
It will be three stories tall and have one elevator.
According to Rondeau, the building will provide space for The Arc to continue to grow in their mission.
"The Arc Central Chesapeake has been providing support and services to people with disabilities in the Mid-Shore region for 20 years," he said. "Over the last five, we have seen a growth in our services by over 80%. The need to have a more established presence here was true when we chose Easton as sort of a central hub for the Mid-Shore and the Eastern Shore as our headquarters 15 years ago."
The Arc been getting support from the town, county and state inspectors.
"Everyone has been aligned to help us to get on that timeline," he said.
This facility has two large goals. One is creating affordable housing, which Talbot County needs for people like EMS workers. The Arc has a specific hourly range in mind.
"Fifteen years ago, The Arc started a housing subsidiary called Chesapeake Neighbors, One, to create better housing for people with disabilities, but also realizing that if we are going to create inclusive and equitable communities, they can't just be people with disabilities," Rondeau said. "Chesapeake Neighbors' vision is to create affordable housing for all."
They have grown from 11 units to over 70. Nine of these will be at Port Street.
"There will be seven two-bedroom apartments and two three-bedroom apartments on this site. It might be for your local Barista or a person who works at Royal Farms. It could be a teacher or childcare worker — people who make $20 to $25 an hour," he said.
Rondeau said that Talbot County's median income is $100,000.
So even if someone makes $80,000, they can't buy or rent easily in the county. Aside from Scotty's Taxi, there is no public transportation.
Where is all this money coming from to build Port Street Commons?
"We have a capital campaign called Expanding What Is Possible. It officially launched two years ago. We have raised about $5.1 million to date," Rondeau said. "The total campaign is $8.5 million. Under Gov. Hogan we received $1 million. Under Gov. Moore we have received $1.5 million. And from the federal government with Sen. Van Hollen and Sen. Cardin, we received $750,000."
He said the Arc is looking to hire direct support professionals. They already have 400 people in that role, but will need more help on Port Street. Applicants do not need a degree, and the Arc will train new employees with 80 or 90 hours. They are looking for people who want to affect change in a person's life.
"I am excited to be taking a piece of land that really didn't have a purpose and there will be something meaningful that the community has needed for a long time, particularly Port Street," Rondeau said. "And there will be a community hub for the people we support, like families with children with disabilities. It will look like a Capital One cafe. The Easton Rotary Club sponsored this room. It will be the Easton Rotary Community Hub."
Rondeau ended with, "There is a huge need in the community. The building is a catalyst for someone to get services. It allows families to feel like they are safe. And The Arc is investing and putting roots in this community."

title: Groundhog Day festivities offer cold pageantry
author: TIMOTHY LLOYD TILGHMAN
content:
Groundhog Day festivities offer cold pageantry

 January 28, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: TIMOTHY LLOYD TILGHMAN | Section: Columns 
 
 739
 Words 

 Read News Document

 I finally experienced the pomp and pageantry of Groundhog Day on Feb. 2, 2023. The 137th annual Groundhog Day radiated a unique and peculiar seasonal American atmosphere that attracts people from all over the country and foreign visitors as well. Everybody comes to see how an oversized brown furry rodent is going to react when exposed to sunlight removed from his little hatch.We did not have tickets to attend the Miss Groundhog Day Banquet held the night before the primary affair. Unfortunately, we walked out of Punxsy Pizza as it was an unsavory episode. I conducted a reconnaissance maneuver of the Gobbler's Knob compound in Punxsutawney to familiarize myself with the grounds. Because Groundhog Day fell on a Thursday, there was less of a turnout than if it had transpired on a weekend date.
My friend was unsatisfied with where we were staying in DuBois and decided to pack up and vacate the premises. This caused us to arrive late and had me worried that we would miss the Big Moment. That morning the wind-chill picked up, and temperatures were registering at 12 degrees F. Somehow, we secured a parking spot, caught the shuttle and arrived at 7:05 a.m. Thankfully the Groundhog Day ceremony was behind schedule.
Gates opened at 5 a.m., but we were still able to position ourselves in a good location to view the annual merriments. Revelers are no longer permitted to party and imbibe in the compound. However, we did miss the confetti cannon, fireworks, and the Gobbler's black top hat and overcoats procession of distinguished gents who paraded through the crowd to the elevated dais. Pyro bursts erupted on stage.
The officiants in top hats and trench coats read a few proclamation scrolls, conducted a groundhog holler back and forth with the crowd, and welcomed those who were brave enough to endure the weather. A dignitary began to knock on Punxsutawney Phil's tree stump at 7:22 a.m. When Phil was held up before the throng assembled, it was determined poor Phil had indeed recognized his shadow.
Discernable boos emerged the audience at the realization that the winter weather would continue for another six weeks. It was announced at the closing of the ceremony that Phil would be returned to Punxsutawney Zoo until this coming Friday for the 2024 ceremony. A bonfire was burning up at the crest of the hill for those seeking some warmth.
Many Groundhog Day visitors are happy to celebrate their Feb. 2 birthdays with an enormous crowd of complete strangers in frigid weather. The Punxsutawney Chamber of Commerce throws an annual Goundhog Day birthday party for those in attendance who were born on Feb. 2. The late Farrah Fawcett was born Feb. 2, 1947.
Estimates last year placed the turnout at 15,000 celebrants. After the ceremony ended, we stopped and shopped inside the Gobbler's Knob gift shop, which features the groundhog image branded on almost any kind of souvenir you can imagine. I bought postcards, coins, a poker chip and, of course, a plush groundhog. When in Punxsutawney ...
The popular 1993 motion picture classic "Groundhog Day" starring Bill Murray is a holiday masterpiece, but it wasn't filmed in Punxsutawney proper. The iconic movie that fictionally highlights the Groundhog Day ceremony was actually shot on location in Woodstock, Illinois. Murray scouted out Punxsutawney, but ultimately had to find an alternative setting.
The next attraction was at Barclay Square, showcasing vendors populated by tourists and locals. There were ice sculptures of Phil and Phyllis Groundhog on display. If you wanted to imbibe or sample libations, you could choose from designer spirits, homegrown wines and microbrews ... too many choices in fact. Jose Del Pino from Santiago interviewed me about Groundhog Day for Chilean TV 13.
We drove out to tour the Jimmy Stewart Museum at Indiana, Pennsylvania. Stewart was truly a fascinating individual and a genuine American WWII aviation hero. I'm glad we made the journey to visit the town library, which hosts the museum. Upon our return, we stopped in at the Groundhog Winery. The proprietor had Junior, their deceased pet groundhog, stuffed and utilizes his image to brand and promote the winery.
By coincidence, we passed by the Cadillac Museum at Greenburg and had to pull over and peek through the glass windows. The coolest automotive example in the rural small-town showroom was an historic 1903 Cadillac Model A Tonneau. You can actually order a miniature replica as your very own desk trophy of this classic Cadillac online.

title: CarePacks awarded $15K from 100+ Women Who Care Talbot County
author: Natalie Jones
content:
CarePacks awarded $15K from 100+ Women Who Care Talbot County

 February 1, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Natalie Jones | Section: Local News 
 
 681
 Words 

 Read News Document

 EASTON — The numbers and members just keep growing.Only four months after 100+ Women Who Care Talbot County held its inaugural meeting, the budding philanthropic group is steadily increasing its membership — and the dollars donated to local nonprofits.
On Monday evening, dozens of group members packed the meeting room at the Talbot County Free Library to hear brief presentations on three nonprofits seeking funding: CarePacks of Talbot County, Chesapeake Multicultural Resource Center and the St. Michaels Fire Department.
After a lightning round of questions and answers, followed by a quick tally of votes cast for the nonprofit members felt was most deserving, CarePacks was selected to receive $15,000 in funding.
Founded by Emily Moody and Easton Mayor Megan Cook, the program serves a large percentage of Talbot County students who rely on meals provided by the school system Monday through Friday, but who may not have access to consistent nutrition over the weekends.
"Kids who are worried about such a basic need as having enough to eat, they simply can't learn," Moody said. "The anxiety of food insecurity is real — it shows up in visits to the nurse for headaches and stomachaches. It shows up on test scores and in classroom behaviors. And sometimes, students will just tell you."
CarePacks serves to comfort the fear and anxiety of food insecurity, she said, and that's done by discreetly placing a bag of meals, snacks and fruit in a student's backpack every week.
Though CarePacks was the clear winner in the number of votes, a desire to help ChesMRC and the St. Michaels Fire Department was evident.
"Are we allowed to vote for two?" one member called out.
While each woman can only cast one vote for the nonprofit of their choice, members can still independently donate to other nonprofits, said Amanda David, one of the group's founding members.
At the group's inaugural meeting in September, one nonprofit that presented but was not selected to receive funding did report an influx in donations the next morning, she added.
Just through bringing local nonprofits in front of a large group of women ready to donate, 100+ Women Who Care raises awareness to funding needs in organizations some community members may not even know about.
"This is a win-win-win situation," David said.
Monday's award was a $2,000 increase from the $13,000 donated to Talbot Interfaith Shelter in September, further marking the group's progression in creating a simple way to engage in local philanthropic efforts.
To Karen Gadson, one of the group's founding members, the concept has "caught fire" primarily due to it being an easy concept.
The group meets for one hour, three times a year. Each woman commits to donating $300 a year — $100 per meeting — to local nonprofits. Members unable to attend in person can cast absentee ballots ahead of time, with group leaders sharing more information about the selected nonprofit afterwards.
"I think it's just been the power of word of mouth," David said of the increase in membership. "I think a lot of women are really impressed with the ease of it, the simplicity behind it, and they've been telling their friends."
And with an already-promising increase from the first meeting, group leaders are working to continue building momentum in Talbot County.
The group is prioritizing weekly communications with members, engaging with local nonprofits and manning a booth at the St. Michaels Farmers Market, David said.
Its social media presence is expanding, too — the group can also be found on Facebook by searching "Women Who Care Talbot County."
David said she was "blown away" by the positive response from women in the community, and her hopes are set high for growing both membership numbers and funding.
"I'd love to fill the Avalon, that would be my goal — our goal is to fill the Avalon and get as many women involved as possible," she said.
The group's next meeting is Monday, May 13, from 5:30 p.m. to 6:30 p.m. at the Talbot County Free Library in Easton.
Members will be considering a new set of nonprofits, including the Mid-Shore Early Learning Center, Tilghman Area Youth Association and For All Seasons.
For more information and to join, visit 100womentalbot.org.

title: Caroline Cares Resource Fair draws around 80
author: TOM MCCALL
content:
Caroline Cares Resource Fair draws around 80

 February 1, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: TOM MCCALL | Section: Local News 
 
 615
 Words 

 Read News Document

 DENTON — Around 80 community members came to St. Luke's Church to have their needs met by dozens of vendors at the Caroline Cares Resource Fair on Jan. 31.Everything from legal advice, to free clothes, to free diapers were offered. There were rows of tables set up, brimming with swag, like stress balls, pens and little flashlights, and the smell of free chili filled the air.
Community service hubs like food insecurity stalwart Aaron's Place and housing-insecurity-focused His Hope Ministries all came together to give back to the community's most in need.
"Our wellness program is offering oral cancer screenings today free for adults, and our vaccine program is offering COVID vaccines and flu vaccines free of charge," said Leigh Marquess, the director of wellness at the Caroline County Health Department.
"We have wellness tables in the other room, and they are offering information about tobacco prevention and cessation for our community. There are around 10 people from the Health Department working here," Marquess said.
She was standing in the doorway to Dr. Adrienne Webb's space, where Webb was offering free oral cancer screening check ups. Across the hall, there were free COVID and flu shots.
Visitors frequented the free coat racks and the free clothes and diapers in the main hall, next to sign-in tables where volunteers helped direct community members to those who could help meet their needs. Some families came from as far as Marydel to get these resources.
Stefanie Johnson is part of the Caroline Homeless Board and is the Executive Director of His Hope Ministries.
"An important part of today is what we call our 'point in time survey' where we try to capture the numbers of those who are actually experiencing a housing crisis in our community. For one day, we go out and see who we can find and see if we can help them," Johnson said.
People experiencing a housing crisis can be found living in cars, couch surfing or in tents. The more accurate the numbers gathered, the more help that can be provided, Johnson said.
She wanted the community to know that there is support and had a whole giveaway room full of food and clothes, like wool hats and scarves and booties, set up at the event. Some of these were hand-knitted by a 94-year-old woman.
"And we have Cheryl Beulah back there of Aaron's Place, giving away food. She works with Amy Cawley of the Maryland Food Bank," Johnson said.
Small white and blue boxes with donors' names written on them were lined up and filled with non-perishables.
"We are a food pantry. We have seven pantries throughout the county. It all fits into the mission of fighting food insecurity. We offer wrap-around services, like helping people get a GED or do early start education, because as we always say, 'Where there is food insecurity, there is something else going on,'" Beulah said.
There was one attendee who was seated in a hallway, taking a break from the bustle. She said she wishes that all the people that need help would just reach out to those who could provide services.
"They need to reach out too. Call the Health Department or Social Services. Tell your friends. They have it every year. I love it. I enjoy it. I love what they do for the community. It is a blessing. Without the grants, they can't do this," said Joanne Clanton of Denton. "If I see stuff I love or like, I am going to get it or I might get it for a family member. It is nice stuff and you socialize. There are people, homeless people, with kids sleeping outside. Let's try to reach out and spread love. Let it be a rainbow across the world."

title: Celebrating 95 years, Vietnam vet reflects on war, rescue efforts
author: WILL BONTRAGER wbontrager@chespub.com
content:
Celebrating 95 years, Vietnam vet reflects on war, rescue efforts

 February 1, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: WILL BONTRAGER wbontrager@chespub.com | Section: Local News 
 
 1031
 Words 

 Read News Document

 CHESTERTOWN — Samuel Tiller, celebrated his 95th birthday on Nov. 25. Although he's safe at home, he sometimes stares up at the ceiling, tears in his eyes, reliving those times in the rice field.That's due to the fact he was in a firefight in the Vietnam War, where he rescued soldiers under him.
After a hellish conflict, he considers himself lucky.
The Army gave him the purple heart and the bronze star for his bravery — luck not mentioned.
On his certificate it read: "Sergeant Tiller distinguished himself by heroic actions during the Operation on 12-14, April 1964, in the Republic of Vietnam."
As much as the military is known for detail, that statement doesn't paint the picture of Sgt. 1st Class Tiller.
In his career he did everything from transporting officers, to drill sergeant to training the Vietnamese army. Starting in Maryland, he went from Germany, to Korea, and ultimately to Vietnam.
And he doesn't have any regrets.
From an early age living in Big Woods, near Worton, Tiller wanted to be a soldier. He got that chance, enlisting during a time when the military was segregated. While in the Army, he suffered prejudice, but also received advice from grizzled World War II veterans.
They told him to advance in rank as a Black man, he had to go to the Korean War front.
Tiller remembered the heaving ocean waves as he and others climbed a rope ladder to get onboard the ship to Korea. He was fortunate being there in the waning years of the conflict.
"I didn't receive a scratch on me," Tiller said.
It was not unproductive. He went from a "nothing to an E-5."
A sergeant, finally, after serving for ten years.
Tiller's time in Korea allowed him to pay for his first car when he returned to Chestertown where Mary, his future wife lived.
Like many, the military life called him back.
Soon after, Tiller was sent to another war, Vietnam, to his wife's great concern.
She'd write him every day until he was home safe.
Tiller's role was to assist the company commander as they trained the Vietnamese army to fight the Vietcong. He moved with the Vietnamese in convoys, mingling with them, while they loaded up their chickens, rabbits, pots, pans and everything they owned.
Close calls while in-country remain fresh on Tiller's mind.
One balmy Sunday, a battalion of Vietcong attacked a village in Tam Phu. Tiller boarded a helicopter along with other companies — 16 Huey choppers and four Piasecki H-21's, called "banana choppers."
Tiller said his helicopter was doorless, and two fifty-caliber gunners thundered fire down on the Vietcong below when they approached the landing zone; an open field. Unable to hear a sound except gunfire and propellers, Tiller and the company commander evacuated, retreating for the tail of the chopper.
Vietcong were in the woodline to the left, firing on Tiller's men.
Hugging the ground, they deployed a "fire and maneuver" action. Some soldiers engaged the enemy allowing others to retreat to the woodline.
Scrambling for it, they jumped into a ditch, pinning them down. Someone threw smoke to show their location to air support, but the dry brush caught fire. Immediately, they were caught between a spreading fire and the enemy.
With bullets bearing down on him, Tiller pulled one of the wounded Vietnamese from the part of the ditch that was closer to the fire. They were in a hopeless situation, but thankfully the smoke did its job.
A tactical fighter squadron dropped a napalm bomb on the enemy, allowing Tiller's company to retreat to the woodline.
Tiller said, "If it wasn't for that plane I wouldn't be here today."
But the Vietcong were a continual presence.
Every time a plane dropped a flare that night, mortars would fire off.
The next morning, they tried to get down a river for pickup, and Vietcong pushed them back to the woodline.
During that conflict, three of Tiller's guys were wounded.
Risking his life, he told the company commander to lay down fire and cover him.
"I brought those guys back by myself, one at a time," Tiller remarked.
The assault continued throughout that day.
Monday evening, a helicopter made an attempt to rescue six wounded. The enemy lurked in the woods. The helicopter had to retreat because they opened up fire again.
For almost three days, the threat of danger and death was imminent.
On Tuesday morning, the violence was drowned out by calm.
Within that silence, a chopper brought the Vietnamese Colonel and an American Major.
This time the enemy didn't fire back.
U.S. forces delivered water to the war-weary and parched soldiers.
Then they marched single-file beside the river towards the special forces camp to get picked up. Tiller was behind 15 men, but he alone set off a land mine. It knocked him down and broke two toes, with the shrapnel from the explosion striking the commander.
Tiller, who carried so many others, was carried himself, then placed on a small boat and then helicopter-bound for Saigon.
Four-Star Gen. Wes Mooreland had visited wounded soldiers in the hospital every Sunday. On one of those times, he asked Tiller how he was. Tiller said he's alright physically but his morale was down. He hadn't received any letters from Mary since he was there.
Orders were given.
If Tiller had any mail in Vietnam, Mooreland would make sure he got it.
That Monday after coming back from the chow hall, there were a pile of her letters on Tiller's bed.
It was the boost Tiller needed.
Tiller recovered and reported to headquarters, received a scolding typical of military life and was soon on the way to the Philippines. He received a hero's steak dinner, and then took a double-decker plane from California back to Philadelphia.
Tiller still sees Vietnam.
"It stays with you," he said.
Tiller retired from the Army in 1967. He became an employee in the Air Force working roads and grounds. A steady job, away from danger, where he could be alone with his thoughts.
He had a good career there. In New Jersey, where he lived, he was known for his impeccably kept yard and as, "Big Sam the Fish Fry Man," cooking fish on weekends.
On his 95th birthday, he celebrated with his family in Chestertown with a big cookout.
Tough-as-nails, a sharp wit, and a natural storyteller, Sfc. Tiller shakes his head, "War is hell. I know. I been through two of them."

title: Talbot County Community Center gymnasium expansion opens
author: Natalie Jones
content:
Talbot County Community Center gymnasium expansion opens

 February 1, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Natalie Jones | Section: Local News 
 
 319
 Words 

 Read News Document

 EASTON — Even though the ribbon hadn't officially been cut yet, a youth basketball team had already hit the court for practice at the Talbot County Community Center's newly completed gymnasium expansion.The young sports stars weren't the only ones eagerly waiting for the spacious new gym to open — roughly 100 community members, several armed with their pickleball paddles, attended the celebratory ribbon cutting ceremony on Wednesday evening.
The expansion project was 20 years in the making, according to Preston Peper, the director of Talbot County Parks and Recreation.
But when it came to construction, things moved quickly. From a ceremonial groundbreaking on March 14 to the ribbon cutting marking the official opening, the project took just under 11 months to bring to life.
The newly unveiled gymnasium is home to two full-size high school basketball courts, bleachers for cheering fans and extra storage for the connected community center.
When basketball teams aren't practicing their dribbles and dunks, the gym can accommodate several volleyball and pickleball courts.
The brightly-lit space can be used for more than sports, too — the community center has already received an inquiry for a wedding and plans to host a trade show, along with job and college fairs, Peper said.
Davis, Bowen & Friedel Inc, a local architectural and engineering firm, completed the architectural work before handing over the reins to Easton-based Willow Construction, who built the gymnasium.
Talbot County Council President Chuck Callahan commended all who were involved in making the new gym a reality, with special thanks to former council members, the county's park board and the Parks and Recreation department staff who were present Wednesday evening.
Callahan also thanked community members, from gym users to youth sports coaches, for their excitement about the project.
"It means a lot to the council — it means to us that it means something to you," he said. "That's what we've done this thing for, we've done it for you guys, the community."

title: CarePacks awarded $15K from 100+ Women Who Care Talbot County
author: Natalie Jones
content:
CarePacks awarded $15K from 100+ Women Who Care Talbot County

 February 1, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Natalie Jones | Section: Local News 
 
 681
 Words 

 Read News Document

 EASTON — The numbers and members just keep growing.Only four months after 100+ Women Who Care Talbot County held its inaugural meeting, the budding philanthropic group is steadily increasing its membership — and the dollars donated to local nonprofits.
On Monday evening, dozens of group members packed the meeting room at the Talbot County Free Library to hear brief presentations on three nonprofits seeking funding: CarePacks of Talbot County, Chesapeake Multicultural Resource Center and the St. Michaels Fire Department.
After a lightning round of questions and answers, followed by a quick tally of votes cast for the nonprofit members felt was most deserving, CarePacks was selected to receive $15,000 in funding.
Founded by Emily Moody and Easton Mayor Megan Cook, the program serves a large percentage of Talbot County students who rely on meals provided by the school system Monday through Friday, but who may not have access to consistent nutrition over the weekends.
"Kids who are worried about such a basic need as having enough to eat, they simply can't learn," Moody said. "The anxiety of food insecurity is real — it shows up in visits to the nurse for headaches and stomachaches. It shows up on test scores and in classroom behaviors. And sometimes, students will just tell you."
CarePacks serves to comfort the fear and anxiety of food insecurity, she said, and that's done by discreetly placing a bag of meals, snacks and fruit in a student's backpack every week.
Though CarePacks was the clear winner in the number of votes, a desire to help ChesMRC and the St. Michaels Fire Department was evident.
"Are we allowed to vote for two?" one member called out.
While each woman can only cast one vote for the nonprofit of their choice, members can still independently donate to other nonprofits, said Amanda David, one of the group's founding members.
At the group's inaugural meeting in September, one nonprofit that presented but was not selected to receive funding did report an influx in donations the next morning, she added.
Just through bringing local nonprofits in front of a large group of women ready to donate, 100+ Women Who Care raises awareness to funding needs in organizations some community members may not even know about.
"This is a win-win-win situation," David said.
Monday's award was a $2,000 increase from the $13,000 donated to Talbot Interfaith Shelter in September, further marking the group's progression in creating a simple way to engage in local philanthropic efforts.
To Karen Gadson, one of the group's founding members, the concept has "caught fire" primarily due to it being an easy concept.
The group meets for one hour, three times a year. Each woman commits to donating $300 a year — $100 per meeting — to local nonprofits. Members unable to attend in person can cast absentee ballots ahead of time, with group leaders sharing more information about the selected nonprofit afterwards.
"I think it's just been the power of word of mouth," David said of the increase in membership. "I think a lot of women are really impressed with the ease of it, the simplicity behind it, and they've been telling their friends."
And with an already-promising increase from the first meeting, group leaders are working to continue building momentum in Talbot County.
The group is prioritizing weekly communications with members, engaging with local nonprofits and manning a booth at the St. Michaels Farmers Market, David said.
Its social media presence is expanding, too — the group can also be found on Facebook by searching "Women Who Care Talbot County."
David said she was "blown away" by the positive response from women in the community, and her hopes are set high for growing both membership numbers and funding.
"I'd love to fill the Avalon, that would be my goal — our goal is to fill the Avalon and get as many women involved as possible," she said.
The group's next meeting is Monday, May 13, from 5:30 p.m. to 6:30 p.m. at the Talbot County Free Library in Easton.
Members will be considering a new set of nonprofits, including the Mid-Shore Early Learning Center, Tilghman Area Youth Association and For All Seasons.
For more information and to join, visit 100womentalbot.org.

title: Jennifer Stanley steps down from Oxford Kids Camp
author: TOM MCCALL
content:
Jennifer Stanley steps down from Oxford Kids Camp

 February 1, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: TOM MCCALL | Section: Local News 
 
 642
 Words 

 Read News Document

 OXFORD — Jennifer Stanley, the founder of the Oxford Kids Camp, is stepping out of the leadership role after more than 40 years.She leaves behind a legacy of bicycles, sail boats, swimming in the Bay and discovering frogs in the mud.
Through the lens of running a kids camp, this president and director has seen many changes in Oxford.
"I moved here when we bought our house in 1979. If I was a kid, this place would be like a playground to me — all the water you wanted, and access to do all kinds of fun things on the water, and all this rural, beautiful countryside. But I didn't see any kids," said Stanley.
She found a group of kids sitting on the steps of the Community Center. Parks and Recreation had the kids playing board games under the porch. She came back to find them in the afternoon, but they were all gone. They had left out of boredom.
"Oxford has fewer families with children living in it (now). The original camp really did serve the community. Families living here, grandparents and children of people who worked here. We had plenty of children then. We have had to open to a larger community. It changes the dynamics a lot. There was that spirit that you got there on your own and got home on your own," she said.
The camp served 50 kids a week and grew to 250 for the summer. Biking and nature gave way to swimming lessons and canoeing.
"That was the idea. Let's do a summer program. We approached the Community Center, who was beginning. I approached them and they said, 'We would love you to use the Community Center, but you have to be independent of us,' which was a good decision on their part. It forced us to think about what kind of an organization we wanted to be," Stanley said.
Stanley, who had previously run education programs with kids at the South Street Seaport in New York City, worked at American Youth Hostels leading bike trips. She had traveled abroad with kids in Canada, Europe and South America.
Oxford Kids Camp came to life in 1982. It has a board and is a nonprofit organization.
"The community really embraced us. Here we were riding around town and people were cautious. If it was a through, it would be different, but we are a dead end, a peninsula. It was ideal," she said.
Elizabeth Wainwright, who taught at New York's prestigious grade school for boys, Buckley, has been part of the camp since she was a girl.
Wainwright has been named as Stanley's replacement at the kids camp.
"Elizabeth was a camper at age five. I can still visualize her. She laughed so hard at the bad boys. She was also a trickster. At one of our campouts, we woke up to toilet paper all over. If I can dream about the perfect person, she would be it. She will keep me in the loop. We haven't figured that out yet, but I am thrilled to be turning over the reins," Stanley said.
Wainwright said, "Both OKC (Oxford Kids Camp) and Miss Jenny had given me experiences as a camper, counselor and co-director that have been among my favorite and most formative. It is hard to imagine camp without Jenny at the helm. She will still be involved significantly, but I am honored to take the tiller for the next leg of the course."
Looking back at what really worked, Stanley said, "The biking was really popular. It was freedom, and even through you are in a line, you are going places that they don't usually get to go to. They love it. There is a lot of laughs and silliness in camp. They knew they were welcome. They could be free and they were free to play hard."
For more information about Oxford Kids Camp, visit oxfordkidscamp.org/.

title: Four World War II chaplains honored at American Legion
author: TOM MCCALL
content:
Four World War II chaplains honored at American Legion

 February 8, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: TOM MCCALL | Section: Local News 
 
 349
 Words 

 Read News Document

 EASTON — There was reverence and patriotism ringing across a room full of veterans at American Legion Post 70 Sunday as the group gathered to honor four chaplains who gave the ultimate sacrifice.The program, held annually by the American Legion, marks the anniversary of the Feb. 3, 1943, sinking of the U.S.A.T. Dorchester. The ship was torpedoed by a German U-boat shortly after midnight, just 90 miles short of its destination.
Aboard were four chaplains, George L. Fox, Alexander D. Goode, Clark V. Poling and John P. Washington, who gave up their life jackets to save the lives of four servicemen.
"They didn't have life jackets when they went down with the ship," American Legion Post Cmdr. Wayne Hall said to those gathered Sunday. "The story goes that they were all holding hands and singing hymns when the ship went down."
During the service, the four chaplains were represented by local religious leaders — Rabbi Peter Hyman of Temple B'nai Israel, the Rev. Jonathon Moyers of Grace Lutheran, the Rev. Gary L. Moore of the Trappe Faith Chapel United Methodist Church and the Rev. Michael Angeloni of Sts. Peter and Paul Catholic Church.
The JROTC from Easton High School presented the colors.
After the color guard cleared, the four religious leaders took turns coming to a lectern up in front of the room. They told narratives that fleshed out the four men who gave their lives on that ship.
After they were finished, a citation from U.S. Sen. Chris Van Hollen (D-Maryland) was presented to Post 77 and Post 70 for honoring the four chaplains.
"It is an important way for the community and society to make sure that the veterans know that their sacrifice and their effort has been appreciated," said local veteran and community liaison for Rep. Andy Haris Mike Detmer, who served in Falluhah during the Iraq War.
"I do a lot of invocations and benedictions at services," said Paula Grimes, Department of Maryland chaplain for the American Legion. "It is from the heart. It is important to spread the word of the sacrifice about these four gentlemen. Everyone should know the story."

 February 8, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Natalie Jones | Section: Local News 
 
 347
 Words 

 Read News Document

 WILLARDS — A Dorchester County man started off his February right with a $5 million scratch-off purchased at a Dash In in Worcester County."We are very grateful for this win," said winner Troy Deneau.
Deneau discovered the second $5 million top-prize winning scratch-off in the 50 Years! lottery game. He stopped by Maryland Lottery headquarters on Monday with his wife Rachel to collect his prize.
The 50 Years! game, which arrived in stores with three $5 million top prizes on Feb. 20, 2023, was part of the Maryland Lottery's 50th anniversary celebration. The first top-prize winner hailed from New Carrollton.
A super fan of the $50 scratch-off, Deneau said it is the only lottery game he currently plays. He's been on a hot streak, too, winning $100, $200 and $10,000 on different 50 Years! instant tickets.
The loyal player caught the big prize when he visited Dash In at 7201 Main Street in Willards on Thursday, Feb. 1. He purchased three 50 Years! instant tickets that day.
Deneau won $75 on the first scratch-off, had no luck on the second instant ticket and found the game's second $5 million top prize on the third scratch-off.
"I am now set for retirement," he said with a big smile.
The 56-year-old is a small business owner, operating a fire-protection company along the Eastern Shore in Maryland and Delaware. He worked for the company for decades before transitioning to ownership eight years ago.
Although he was thinking about retiring after his win, Deneau said he decided to stay with his company.
"At first, I said 'I'm done,' but we have been too dedicated to this company for 30 years to walk away," he said.
The Dash In that sold Deneau the lucky scratch-off is located between Salisbury and Ocean City in Willards.
The business will receive a $5,000 bonus from the Lottery for selling the $5 million top-prize winning scratch-off.
Other large prizes are still unclaimed in the 50 Years! game. In addition to the one remaining $5 million top prize, the game has one unclaimed $100,000 prize, two $50,000 prizes, 18 $10,000 prizes and others ranging from $50 to $1,000.

title: Four World War II chaplains honored at American Legion
author: TOM MCCALL
content:
Four World War II chaplains honored at American Legion

 February 8, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: TOM MCCALL | Section: Local News 
 
 349
 Words 

 Read News Document

 EASTON — There was reverence and patriotism ringing across a room full of veterans at American Legion Post 70 Sunday as the group gathered to honor four chaplains who gave the ultimate sacrifice.The program, held annually by the American Legion, marks the anniversary of the Feb. 3, 1943, sinking of the U.S.A.T. Dorchester. The ship was torpedoed by a German U-boat shortly after midnight, just 90 miles short of its destination.
Aboard were four chaplains, George L. Fox, Alexander D. Goode, Clark V. Poling and John P. Washington, who gave up their life jackets to save the lives of four servicemen.
"They didn't have life jackets when they went down with the ship," American Legion Post Cmdr. Wayne Hall said to those gathered Sunday. "The story goes that they were all holding hands and singing hymns when the ship went down."
During the service, the four chaplains were represented by local religious leaders — Rabbi Peter Hyman of Temple B'nai Israel, the Rev. Jonathon Moyers of Grace Lutheran, the Rev. Gary L. Moore of the Trappe Faith Chapel United Methodist Church and the Rev. Michael Angeloni of Sts. Peter and Paul Catholic Church.
The JROTC from Easton High School presented the colors.
After the color guard cleared, the four religious leaders took turns coming to a lectern up in front of the room. They told narratives that fleshed out the four men who gave their lives on that ship.
After they were finished, a citation from U.S. Sen. Chris Van Hollen (D-Maryland) was presented to Post 77 and Post 70 for honoring the four chaplains.
"It is an important way for the community and society to make sure that the veterans know that their sacrifice and their effort has been appreciated," said local veteran and community liaison for Rep. Andy Haris Mike Detmer, who served in Falluhah during the Iraq War.
"I do a lot of invocations and benedictions at services," said Paula Grimes, Department of Maryland chaplain for the American Legion. "It is from the heart. It is important to spread the word of the sacrifice about these four gentlemen. Everyone should know the story."

title: Ice cream for breakfast?
author: DOUG BISHOP dbishop@chespub.com
content:
Ice cream for breakfast?

 February 9, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: DOUG BISHOP dbishop@chespub.com | Section: Local News 
 
 376
 Words 

 Read News Document

 STEVENSVILLE — Is there anything more fun than eating a big bowl full of ice cream for breakfast?If you were lucky enough to be in downtown Stevensville Saturday morning, Feb. 3, at the Tasty Toucan Ice Cream Shop you'd know the right answer to that question.
Hosting her third annual Ice Cream for Breakfast Day celebration, owner Nikki Neboshynsky said, "I learned about this day as a member of the National Ice Cream Association. They put out information about things like this every year. They told us it was one of the biggest ice cream promotions, so we joined in three years ago."
Neboshynsky, who won a national award at the annual Ice Cream Convention in Las Vegas last year for her handmade natural fruit popsicles, is no stranger to being creative. And she's all about serving quality products.
All of the ice cream sold at the Tasty Toucan is 100%, "cow to cone," made on the Eastern Shore.
The menu included a variety of breakfast-inspired treats, including a donut sundae, a hot cocoa float, a cinnamon-roll-inspired ice cream sandwich, a Pop-Tart milkshake and even a unique bacon sundae.
National Ice Cream for Breakfast Day was started by a mom of six living in Rochester, New York, during the mid-1960s. It was late January, and schools were closed due to a raging blizzard there. It was too cold to go outside, and the children were restless.
The mom, Florence Rappaort, is purported to have announced to her children, "Okay, we're going to have ice cream for breakfast."
The family continued to enjoy the event once every winter. It became a family tradition. Over the years, the family served the ice cream, topping breakfast items such as pancakes, waffles and donuts.
When the children went off to colleges, they shared their tradition with their college dorm colleagues. From there, it grew in popularity with students going home and sharing it with other family members. The tradition continued to spread.
Somewhere in this creation, the first Saturday morning in February became the nationally recognized day of celebration. Neboshynsky notes one of their regular customers recalls her family partaking in the tradition when she was a child.
"We're going to continue to do this the first Saturday in February every year," said Neboshynsky. "It's a lot of fun."

title: Rock Hall's annual muskrat cooking contest draws hundreds
author: WILL BONTRAGER wbontrager@chespub.com
content:
Rock Hall's annual muskrat cooking contest draws hundreds

 February 13, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: WILL BONTRAGER wbontrager@chespub.com | Section: Local News 
 
 365
 Words 

 Read News Document

 ROCK HALL — Over the weekend, Maggie's Coleman Tavern in Rock Hall was affected by rats — in a good way.Nobody had to tuck their pants into their socks or worry about parasites. That's because the bar on Sharp Street opened up to residents and visitors alike its annual Muskrat Cook-Off, where savory recipes were sampled and voted on.
Eight competitors conducted a clinic on how to prepare and cook the web-footed rodent known to hang around Maryland's lakes, ponds, swamps, marshes, smaller rivers and streams.
But why muskrats?
It's a large part of Delmarva's history, according to one of the competitors, Lisa Stottlemyer.
"It was once an important staple on the Eastern Shore. We cook to keep that tradition alive," she said.
During the Great Depression era, muskrat pelts were the mainstay of the winter economy after blue crab season ended, according to Smithsonian Magazine.
Trapping, killing, eating muskrats and using their fur traces back to the Choptank and Nanticoke tribes.
That tradition was alive and well at Maggie's, with an impressive turnout.
Looking around, squinting, owner of Maggie's Carolyn Jones said, "There must be 350 or 400 people here at least."
Beer and punch with a "little kick" were sold while the band, The Everafter, belted out classic rock tunes as people gathered around to sample the muskrat dishes, casting their votes.
Around the smoky tables, muskrat meat was served uniquely.
It was placed in oysters with cheese, made into hushpuppies, mixed into chili, used as a dipping sauce for fries, inserted in a pierogi and a quesadilla, and served with hominy and dumplings.
Around 3 p.m. Jones announced the winner was the team of Alex Cooper and George Parker for their muskrat pierogis. The ingredients were simple, Cooper pointed out: onions, salt and pepper. But what set the dish apart was the homemade dough and being cooked in a cast iron pan.
Jones presented the award to them, a plaque made in the Dirty Cat Garage by Greg Jetton.
The "rat fest," as the competitors called it, is now in its ninth year. Jones said it stemmed from one day sitting around bored, and they decided to do it to escape the cabin fever winter can bring.
"We make our own fun here," said a resident.

title: New Star Democrat reporter loves telling stories
author: TOM MCCALL
content:
New Star Democrat reporter loves telling stories

 February 14, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: TOM MCCALL | Section: Local News 
 
 413
 Words 

 Read News Document

 EASTON — The Star Democrat has hired a new reporter, Veronica Fernandez-Alvarado.This 28-year-old Oregon native has a master's degree in journalism from Georgetown University and speaks Spanish.
She loves to tell stories.
"I have a really amazing local paper back at my hometown of Woodburn, Oregon. And I was one of those kids who went up to adults and said, 'Tell me your story.' I grew up in the community that was first-generation Mexican. I always asked, 'Let me know the stories of how you got to the United States,' she said. "Everyone's story is a little different."
Fernandez-Alvarado said she chose to live in Maryland and work for The Star Democrat after gaining an appreciation for the Mid-Atlantic region while in graduate school.
"Maryland has always been very interesting to me. I went to school in D.C. I lived in Virginia, and a lot of my friends were from Maryland. They spoke very highly of the local papers there," she said. "I was intrigued and wanted to stay in the area."
She is excited to get started and meet the community.
"I really hope to just write stories that reflect the community. I love local journalism," she said. "Journalism in general has been all about community engagement to me. If I am able to find a story about this community and how much they care about what is going on ... even if it was the littlest ways or the biggest ways, I would feel really accomplished with that," she said.
Fernandez-Alvarado said that going through her master's program helped to teach her skills she is eager to put to use at The Star Democrat.
"Persistence was something really big I learned from my master's program. Just bang down on everyone's door. Just not letting go basically. And also a fearlessness of going up to people and talking to them. That was something my journalism program really showed me," she said. "They were taking me to all these different sides of D.C."
Fernandez-Alvarado got to interview some important people.
"One of my professors was a White House reporter. He took us to the White House, and we got to yell questions at President Biden when he landed in his helicopter and was walking in. They were like 'no matter what the situation, come at it fearless,'" she said.
Ultimately, she said, Fernandez-Alvarado enjoys the craft of journalism.
"I love writing. I love talking to people. I look forward to really engaging with everyone and figuring out what makes this a community," she said.
