title: Maryland author takes bestseller lists by storm with self-love book
author: Matt Hubbard mhubbard@chespub.com
content:
Maryland author takes bestseller lists by storm with self-love book

 February 20, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Matt Hubbard mhubbard@chespub.com | Section: Local News 
 
 719
 Words 

 Read News Document

 NORTH EAST — If there was ever a day to launch a book about love, Valentine's Day would be it, as North East author Trista Polo discovered when her first book, "Self-Love Shenanigans", shot to the top of bestseller charts overnight.Polo, 52, described the book — which launched Valentine's Day on Amazon's Kindle store — as a "resource manual for self-worth," which she hopes will help readers to achieve and embrace the power of self-love. Each chapter provides readers with new ways to level up their self-worth, conveyed through a tone that Polo said is fun and inviting.
"The book is called 'Self-Love Shenanigans' because I didn't want it to be too serious," Polo said, "It is a serious topic but it is also fun and I wrote it the same way I would say it."
Polo's inspiration for the book follows her self-love journey and her experiences. Through her journey, Polo said she began to realize that she was developing knowledge and mindsets that other people tend to struggle with.
She explained that she has struggled with self-love and self-worth her whole life and that her book is home to all of the work she has done and what has worked for her throughout her journey.
"Everything that is in the books is all things that I went through in my life and writing the book," Polo said. "I wasn't trying to reinvent the wheel, I just wanted to put it all in one place with my own spin on things by looking at things a bit differently to help people."
Complementing Polo's messages on self-love in the book are numerous activities involving journaling and other growth activities to help readers build a deeper connection with the content.
Polo said that her inspiration to include activities in her book stems from her value of putting action behind learning.
"You can read everything about self-love but without action, I assert, it will not make much difference which is why the activities are important- so people can bring and apply the content to themselves," Polo said.
The 147-page book was mostly written before Polo and her husband moved from New York to a home on North East's Main Street last year. While simultaneously writing her book, Polo started the Self-Love Shenanigans and Stories Collective Facebook group.
The group has over 175 members and serves as a hub for members to share their experiences, self-love tips and new ways to achieve self-love. Since moving to North East, Polo said her value of the community she is creating has grown.
"Walking Main Street every morning really gives me a sense of being part of a community," Polo said. "Being in an area that is this community centered, I started to see the bigger picture and realize that it is not just about myself and my readers, it is about the community that we are creating around self-love and its value."
Polo noted that she hosted a virtual launch party for her book Tuesday night. Readers and supporters from all over the country attended — buying her book the second sales went live on Amazon.
The book is currently on sale for $0.99 cents.
As of press time Thursday, "Self-Love Shenanigans" is ranked number one in several of Amazon's bestseller categories, including Journal Writing, Women's Inspirational Spirituality and the New Age Self-Help category.
Since launch, Polo said she has received overwhelmingly positive feedback from her readers.
"My heart is so full because of the feedback I have received so far," Polo said. "You write something and you hope it is good and makes a difference so to have the book make a positive impact bigger than I could have imagined, it brings me to tears when I think about it."
Currently, "Self-Love Shenanigans" is only available virtually through Kindle. Polo is preparing to deploy the book in paperback within the coming weeks, and plans to collaborate with Cecil County retailers to sell her product.
Polo also plans to work with Cecil County libraries to host events and workshops involving self-love exercises outlined in her book along with other activities.
"My book is not about convincing yourself into something positive you do not believe," Polo said. "It is all about being open to the idea that 'maybe it is true' and starting to believe it and it has been wonderful to be able to help people and share what I know."

title: Chesapeake Fire & Ice Festival warms hearts
author: Veronica Fernandez-Alvarado
content:
Chesapeake Fire & Ice Festival warms hearts

 February 21, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Veronica Fernandez-Alvarado | Section: Local News 
 
 322
 Words 

 Read News Document

 Last weekend, crowds gathered on the streets of downtown Easton for the Chesapeake Fire & Ice Festival. Dozens of well carved ice sculptures decorated Easton's historic district.The event kicked off on Friday night with live music, fire demonstrations and beautifully lit ice sculptures ranging from pianos to ice chests with frozen treasure.
Over the weekend, residents and tourists enjoyed outdoor ice skating, live music, a children's icehouse at the Talbot County Free Library, fire performances and restaurant specials.
Howard Maxwell of Easton bundled up his granddaughter in a warm jacket and hat so she could enjoy the event.
"We brought my granddaughter, and she enjoyed seeing all the different sculptures, and she's having a really great time," Maxwell said.
Featured during the weekend were plenty of musical performances, including Saved by Zero performing during the festival's 80's Glow Party, Jimmy Maguire playing in the Fire Pavillion tent, and DJ Howard Barnett giving a music and light show on North Harrison Street.
Three watermen were shucking oysters in the cold, as a line of people savored the oysters and thanked the watermen while donating money to the Talbot Watermen Association.
Amid the cold, a man with flames covering the torso of his shirt stood in the center of a crowd, waving around long sticks with live flames at the end of it. Carlos Mir, known by his stage name "Cascading Carlos," beamed joyfully as he asked volunteers to blow out the live flames.
Mir said he brings the fire to the Fire & Ice Festival. The Guinness World Recorder winner said Friday evening he was scheduled to perform throughout the festival and teach people how to juggle. He said the committee does a great job with putting together this event.
"They work so hard to make sure that this is so flawlessly perfect," Mir said.
Major sponsors of the festival include The Town of Easton, the Peoples Bank, Merry Maids, Soistman: Family Dentistry and Associates and the Talbot County Free Library.

title: The newly renovated Oaks Waterfront Hotel
author: Veronica Fernandez-Alvarado
content:
The newly renovated Oaks Waterfront Hotel

 February 22, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Veronica Fernandez-Alvarado | Section: Life 
 
 446
 Words 

 Read News Document

 The Oaks Waterfront Hotel in Talbot county recently reopened after a $10 million renovation.Two years ago, owners Tracy and Scott Wagner purchased the historic property and were ready to make a change. Together with their daughter Quin Warner and son-in-law Andy Warner, they transformed the hotel into a thriving family business venture.
"Well, we don't know how to have dinner together and not talk about work. But it's enjoyable," Quin Warner said. "We all have the same vision… we're fully ingrained. We love it. And we have ideas, and it's just how we're going to execute these ideas. We all balance each other out, too."
Quin Warner functions as business manager, and Andy Warner acts as general manager. Together, they balance all the weddings and significant events that keep the hotel booked.
The recently renovated Oaks Hotel dates back to the 17th Century. The entire plot consisted of 740 acres, and over the years, the property transformed into a premier waterfront venue for wedding receptions.
Included in the renovation were interior and exterior changes to the main building. An additional four cottages were built on the property, and over 200 mature trees were planted.
But most importantly, the hotel's owners said, they sought ways to improve accessibility. Scott Wagner explained that they wanted to provide ways for potential grandparents to enjoy the weddings and family reunions often booked on the property.
They installed an elevator, created accessible handicap rooms and renovated the dock to make it easier to use for everyone.
Tracy Wagner describes the vision for the hotel as being comfortable and a fun place to welcome guests and locals alike.
Andy Warner said the community has embraced them, and they have enjoyed hosting events for locals, including holding Easter, Thanksgiving and Christmas dinners, hosting burger nights and galas, and opening the restaurant and bar to locals on Wednesday and Thursday nights.
"We have the best burgers in town, by the way," Andy Warner said, beaming with pride.
Last December, they hosted a Christmas party of between 350 and 400 people. Scott Wagner described the experience as akin to a reunion. Contractors, families, friends and people from every walk of life joined in the fun.
Overall, the owners look forward to having guests discover the beauty of the Eastern Shore. Whether walking through St. Michaels and Oxford or biking through nature, there's something for everyone, they said.
"We've done this for you. We've done this for Talbot County," Tracy said. "We've done this for the brides, for the parents of the bride. And we are proud of this. And we are proud that we've had this opportunity to bring this to Talbot County and to keep this historical place. We've given it a whole new life."

title: One step closer to restoring St. Michael's history
author: Veronica Fernandez-Alvarado
content:
One step closer to restoring St. Michael's history

 February 25, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Veronica Fernandez-Alvarado | Section: Local News 
 
 452
 Words 

 Read News Document

 Attorney Thomas Byrne and a team of history enthusiasts have been working for over 15 years on the restoration project for the historic St. Michaels train station building. Two weeks ago, the St. Michaels Planning Commission unanimously approved moving the project ahead.The plan is to move the building from its 226 North St. address to a new location on Main Street so more people can access, appreciate and learn about this piece of local history.
This restoration project is part of an ongoing effort in St. Michael's to celebrate and share its maritime and railroad heritage through sites like the nature trail and Maritime Museum.
Doug Poore, the curator of the Greater Harrington Historical Society, wrote a letter to the St. Michaels Planning Commission giving his support to the restoration of this building.
"I have been a proponent of historic preservation all my life," Poore said. "The relocation and subsequent restoration of the station is both a chance to preserve history and an investment in your community's future."
Byrne said this station has a rich history that everyone could benefit from learning about. When the station was initially built in the late 19th century, it revolutionized transportation by providing a faster and more reliable method for moving people and goods compared to previous boat and carriage options. This building opened up tourism and commerce for the area.
Byrne explained that the railroad was put out of business for passengers because the ferries began to transport cars and people. From 1928 until 1960, this particular station and the rail lines were still used for transporting cargo. The original railroad line was known as the Baltimore, Chesapeake and Atlantic.
The station was originally located at the end of North Street, near the Rails to Trails. Around 1970, the building was moved to its current location and turned into a house.
Byrne introduced Kurt Grant, a contractor, to the train station about seven years ago. Grant said it sparked his interest right from the start.
"It took this long for it to evolve to get to the point where we are now that we've obtained permission from the zoning board of St. Michaels, and it really brought a new light to it," Grant said. "Many people are involved, and it's a big team effort to make this happen."
Byrne hopes the approval and building permit will be issued in the next few months.
Once the town grants permission, the building will be moved promptly.
Byrne hopes the train station will be turned into a small cafe or ice cream shop after it is carefully restored and moved to its new location. This would allow it to be a functional space while educating visitors through historical exhibits about the railroad's important role in the region's history.

title: Competitive eaters throw down at Cult Classic
author: ERIC SYLVIA Special to the Star Democrat
content:
Competitive eaters throw down at Cult Classic

 Author/Byline: ERIC SYLVIA Special to the Star Democrat | Section: Local News 
 
 769
 Words 

 Read News Document

 STEVENSVILLE — "There's not much else to do on a cold February Saturday — football's over, NASCAR hasn't started and March Madness is still a couple of weeks away," quipped Rohry Flood, owner of Cult Classic Brewing on Kent Island."That's why this event is a perfect way to spend the day," Keith Graffius, organizer of the 14th annual Crawfish Boil and Muskrat Leg Eating Contest held Feb. 17, said.
Graffius has run the event since the beginning, and he says it has grown year over year to its current size. The 2024 event saw more than 1,000 spectators, all eager to witness the competition.
The eating contest didn't kick off until 5:30 p.m., but by noon the taproom floor was already crowded, karaoke was being sung in the listening room, local merchants were selling their wares at one end of the taproom and the food tent was pumping out crawfish and muskrat themed dishes.
The food was provided by Palm Beach Willies, a local favorite in Taylors Island. Willies chef John Butz and his team cranked out quesadillas, spring rolls, muskrat barbecue and steamed crawdads. The line for food was steady, with many of those in line looking to try the signature dish, muskrat, for the first time.
Graffius explained, "We started this event as an add on to the Dorchester County Outdoor Show, but over the years we have outgrown the various venues we've used for past events. Bringing this event to Cult Classic was a perfect way to continue the tradition and provide a premiere event."
Flood added, "Some of the proceeds will go to the Waterman's Association, while others will be used to support a new scholarship fund." The new scholarship fund was set up in the name of Ralph "Peg Leg" Bramble, a two time champion and hall-of-famer who was always a fixture at this event as well as the Outdoor Show. "He did so much to keep these traditions alive — traditions that are at the heart and history of Dorchester County," Graffius said.
Bramble passed the baton and his crown to the 2023 and 2022 world champion, Daniel "Chunky" Hesson. Hesson, a 17-year-old Dorchester native, will be attending Salisbury State next fall.
He has been participating in the event since he was twelve and says Bramble was a mentor. Wearing a t-shirt with a picture of the two of them from a past competition on the front, Hesson said, "Ralph always watched over me during these events, since I am usually one of the youngest competitors."
When asked about the tie-in with crawdads, Graffius explained it is linked to Cameron Parrish, Louisiana that plays host to a similar annual event, the Louisiana Fur and Wildlife Festival. Guests from Cameron Parish made the trek to Dorchester County this weekend for the National Outdoor Show in Church Creek to help crown Miss Outdoors and observe the muskrat skinning semi-finals.
The afternoon saw a steady increase in spectators. The listening room of Cult Classic transitioned into the un-official Blues Emporium of Kent Island as DC Blues legend Jimmy Cole and his Delmarva All-stars took the stage.
The band features a who's-who of blues music, including Ron Holloway on tenor sax, Sam Paladino on the Hammond organ, George Sheppard on drums, Bryan Smith on bass and Jimmy Stepanson on lead guitar.
By 5 p.m. the room was filled to capacity, and the anticipation was palpable as the nine contestants took the stage, one by one. The contestants included Hesson, as well as past competitor Mike Detmer, also of Dorchester County, and several first timers, some of whom had never had muskrat before.
Detmer is known from past contests as "Dirty Legs" Detmer, due to the amount of meat he has been known to leave on the bones during the contest.
As he took the stage for the finale, he stripped off his camo jacket to reveal a gold sequin shirt, which turned out to be somewhat prophetic, as Detmer would go on to win the event by a tenth of a pound over Hesson.
Detmer paid tribute to his fellow competitors, "The rest of the competition is great — they are truly champions and I am surprised I won," he said.
As the event concluded, Detmer accepted the trophy from Flood and Graffius, amid calls for a re-test from Hesson's supporters. First-time entrant Cody Fenzel from Millersville rounded out the top three.
Graffius is hoping to bring the event back to Cult Classic for the 2025 edition. Flood said they were "psyched" to be hosting this year's event.
"It's a perfect partnership between the weird and wonderful things we love about where we live and the crazy creativity of our neighbors," he said.

title: Trapping on the Eastern Shore
author: MARIE SAVAGE Country Cooking
content:
Trapping on the Eastern Shore

 February 27, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: MARIE SAVAGE Country Cooking | Section: Food 
 
 1515
 Words 

 Read News Document

 Back in the late 1950s and early 1960s, my younger brother Ollie would trap and hunt whatever was in season.My dad was very happy when he came home with rabbits and squirrels. The only thing he could not get my dad to eat was the muskrat, better known as the marsh rabbit.
He sold the meat to local folks who loved it, and mom loved it because he sold them as fast as he trapped them.
My brother would save the hides and stretch them on a special piece of board designed to fit the hide. He had them drying out for a certain number of days and then would package them up and ship them to his buyer.
His buyer was the late Mr Clark Harrison Sr. of Preston. After several shipments, Mr. Harrison would send my brother a check.
Years ago, I contacted Mr. Harrison and told him the story of my 14 year old brother, who later retired from the United States Army and did three tours of duty in Vietnam. I will dedicate today's column to those two men — the late Clark Harrison Sr. and Ollie Lowe Hitchens Jr.
Along the Eastern Shore, trapping traditions have been passed down to sons, grandsons and nephews. Living here and working on the water or in the fields near huge ditch banks, it was only natural for these locals to trap muskrats.
They'd set their traps, then go to work farming or crabbing then check the traps for an extra bounty. The muskrat numbers were once estimated to be in the millions here on the Eastern Shore, but that number soon dwindled, as you can imagine with all the trapping.
Just the sight of these animals was enough for me with the fur on, let alone skinning and cooking them.
You guessed it — I've never tasted muskrat, but I've cooked it. The first one I ever cooked was right in my Preston Road kitchen under the guidance of my late husband, John Williamson Sr., who loved them.
JOHN R.'S FAVORITE MUSKRAT
Trap, clean and cut muskrat in half. Soak in a large pot of cold, salted water for several hours — changing water several times. Finally, after draining well, place the meat in a large pot, cover with water, bring to a boil, boiling for 5 minutes. Remove meat from the pot, rinse and clean out the pot well. Then spray the pot with a non-sticking spray, add the meat, half cover with water. Cook until meat falls apart. Add to taste: sage, red pepper, salt and bacon or sausage grease. Don't be afraid of adding any of these ingredients and just keep adding until you can taste all of them. Cook down as much as you want but do not let it cook dry. Serve with a favorite potato dish of your choice and a green vegetable.
MUSKRAT STEW
Clean, cut in pieces and soak three muskrats in cold water and salt. After at least two hours, drain water off and rinse meat well. In a large pot, place the meat and just enough water to cover them. Add 2 teaspoons ground sage, 1/2 teaspoon bacon grease, salt and pepper to taste. Let cook over medium heat for 4 to 5 hours. Start on high heat until it starts boiling, then reduce heat to simmering. Let cook until meat is falling off the bone. Serve over cooked rice.
FRIED MARSH RABBIT
Clean, cut up and soak one or two marsh rabbits in salty water for several hours — changing water several times. Rinse well in several changes of water. Remove from water and pat dry. In a large bowl add flour, sage, salt and pepper. Dredge the pieces of meat in the flour mixture and place in a fry pan with cooking oil and add 2 or 3 strips of bacon. Brown on both sides, adding more sage if needed. When meat is browned on both sides, add some water to the pan, turn heat down and let simmer as the meat becomes tender and a gravy forms.
HOPPING JOHN WITH VENISON
2 full deer shanks, 1 tbsp oil, 1 tbsp your favorite All spice blend, 1 tsp salt, 4 cups beef stock, 3 garlic cloves (smashed), 1 celery stalk (chopped). Hoppin' John: ½ pound of dried black-eyed peas, 3 strips of bacon (chopped), ½ cup diced onion, ½ cup diced bell pepper, 1 clove garlic (minced), 1 celery stalk (diced), 3 cups of the reserved braising liquid, 2 tbsp your favorite All spice blend, 2 tsp salt, 1 cup of yellow rice (rinsed and drained), thinly sliced scallions for garnish. Bring a large pan to high heat on the stove. Rub the shanks with oil, All spice blend and salt. Once the pan is hot, sear each side of the shanks. Turn on the slow cooker and set it to low. Place the seared shanks inside and add the stock, garlic and celery. Allow the mixture to cook for 8 hours or until the meat falls off the bone. I cooked mine overnight. Once cooked, remove the meat from the slow cooker and set it aside. Strain and reserve the braising liquid for the next steps. For the Hoppin' John, place the black-eyed peas into a bowl and cover them with water. Allow them to sit while you complete the following steps. Bring the Dutch over to medium-high heat and stir in the chopped bacon. Brown the bacon and then remove bacon from the pan, leaving the grease behind. Stir in the onion, bell pepper, celery and garlic. Cook, frequently stirring, until the onion turns opaque.
Drain the remaining water from the black-eyed peas. Stir the peas into the pot. Add three cups of the braising liquid from the deer shanks, the All spice blend and salt. Bring the mixture to a boil, reduce the heat to low, cover, and allow to simmer for 45-60 minutes or until the peas begin to soften. You do not want them to completely cook. While waiting, shred the deer meat. When the peas are al dente, there should be about two cups of liquid remaining. Add more if needed. Stir in the rice and the shredded deer and bring the mixture back to a simmer. Cover and allow to cook for 20 minutes or until the rice is done. Serve with the sliced green onions atop, along with some biscuits.
RABBIT STEW
3-4 pounds rabbit, 6 potatoes (quartered), 8 carrots (sliced), 1 medium onion (chopped), 1 tsp salt, 1/4 cup beef consommé, 3/4 cup beef broth, 3/4 tsp pepper, 1/4 tsp basil, 2 bay leaves, 1/4 tsp rosemary, 1/4 tsp thyme. Cut rabbit into pieces. Layer onion, potatoes and carrots in the bottom of a crock pot. Add spices to the pot. Add rabbit, salt, pepper, consommé and about 3/4 cup beef broth. Cover and cook on low for 8 hours. Thicken gravy as desired.
BRAISED RABBIT
2 rabbits cut into serving pieces, 1/4 pound bacon, 3 tbsp olive oil, 1 medium onion (sliced into half-moons), 1 head garlic (cloves peeled but not chopped), white part of a fennel bulb (chopped roughly), a handful of dried mushrooms, 1/2 pound fresh mushrooms, 3 bay leaves, 1 tbsp dried oregano, 1 tsp fennel seeds, 3 cups good stock (chicken or vegetable), 5 spring onions, 1 cup finely chopped fennel fronds, 2 tbsp fresh chopped oregano, salt. Cook the dried mushrooms in 2 cups of hot water. Let them sit, covered, for at least 1 hour. Heat the olive oil in a Dutch oven and cook bacon until crispy. Remove the bacon and turn the heat up to medium-high. Salt the rabbit pieces and brown them well. Add the chopped onion, fennel bulb and the dried mushrooms and saute until they begin to brown. Add the fresh mushrooms and garlic and saute until they begin to brown. Add salt. Add the Armagnac and stir well to combine.
Turn the heat all the way up and add back the rabbit, the bacon, and add the bay leaves, fennel seeds and dried oregano and mix well. Pour in just enough stock just to cover the rabbit. Do not totally submerge it. Bring to a simmer, taste for salt (add more if need be), cover and set over low heat for an hour, or 45 minutes if you are using chicken or domestic rabbit. After an hour, test to see if the meat is tender. You want it to be practically falling off the bone. At this point you can pull the rabbit from the pot, remove from the bone and add back to the pot or keep it in the pot on bone. Add the green onions, garlic and fennel fronds and stir to combine. Simmer uncovered for 3 minutes or until you believe it is done. Be careful to not overcook.
There are a few opportunities coming up for you to enjoy a great muskrat dinner without having to stare down skinned muskrats. There will be a chance to get this wonderful DelMarVa Delicacy at the West Side Volunteer Fire Department, located at 21045 Nanticoke Road Bivalve, on Saturday, March 9, from 11 a.m. until they are all gone.

title: Empty Bowls event feeds body and soul
author: TOM MCCALL
content:
Empty Bowls event feeds body and soul

 February 28, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: TOM MCCALL | Section: Local News 
 
 392
 Words 

 Read News Document

 EASTON — Talbot Empty Bowls raised around $30,000 for Talbot County food pantries on Saturday at St. Mark's United Methodist Church by combining the community's good will with handmade bowls and local restaurants' soup making abilities.There, guests, each of whom paid $30 for admission, were able to select one of about 400 painted bowls, all created by members of the community. The bowls were made in a variety of places, including Kiln Born Creations, high school art classes and The Academy Art Museum's pottery studio.
With their selected bowls, guests were then treated to a variety of soup options, all provided by local restaurants.
Around 250 people attended the event, and it brought different parts of the community together for a good cause. People from Tilghman to Easton to Bellevue filled a bowl.
"It was amazing. We had a really great event. The turnout was wonderful. The soups were amazing and were donated by local restaurants. We had music by The Royal Oak Musicians, and it was a festive upbeat event for the community," said volunteer Amy Jacobs.
"It is a glimpse into what I think our community should be like. It was a lot of different people from the community that are all coming together and they are all sharing a meal and just getting to know each other, talk and support a great cause," Jacobs said.
The soups were donated by The Ivy Cafe, Piazza, Garden and Garnish, Hambleton House, Pope's, Tea at the General Store, Bluepoint Hospitality and the Bistro. Bread was donated by Panera.
Some of the soups included chicken dumpling, venison chili, vegetable barley with tomato, cream of mushroom, white bean winter vegetable and cured duck legs, pasta fagioli and butternut squash.
The food pantries that received support include Care Packs, the Neighborhood Service Center, Harvest of Hope Church of God, Royal Oak United Methodist, The Scott's United Methodist Church, St. Michaels Community Center and the Tilghman Food Pantry. A new food pantry has been established at Chesapeake College, and it too benefited from this event.
There was a crew of 20 volunteers, many who came from local high schools and churches.
Qlarant provided a grant to allow groups like BAAM and The Multicultural Center to paint bowls at no cost.
Sponsors included Bette Kenzie and Ellen C. Evans.
Since 2009, when the event began, Talbot Empty Bowls has distributed $320,613, Jacobs said.
To learn more, visit talbotemptybowls.org.

title: Caroline Sportsmans Bash draws 450
author: Connie Connolly
content:
Caroline Sportsmans Bash draws 450

 February 28, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Connie Connolly | Section: Local News 
 
 454
 Words 

 Read News Document

 DENTON — The sign outside the door said "Sold Out."Inside 450 sportsmen, dressed in camouflage and caps, filled the Caroline County 4-H Park main building near Denton to take their chances on a variety of firearms and door prizes during the second annual Sportsman Bash Saturday, Feb. 24.
Proceeds benefit the Caroline/Dorchester County Fair. Last year's event netted about $25,000; this year's bash was expected to bring in $35,000.
Mitchell Conneely of Denton is the president of the fair board.
"Last year we were probably 50 shy of selling out; this year we sold out," Conneely said. "Everybody's enjoying themselves. The food is great. Prizes are great. Everybody seems to be happy."
The doors opened at 10 a.m., with the first prize drawn at noon. A $60 donation included entry, gun and cash raffle, food and drinks, including beer, until the last drawing at 4 p.m. A $30 ticket included chances on the 14 firearms and cash prizes awarded at 15-minute intervals. Winning numbers were posted on the fair board's Facebook page.
But there was more. Various chances were sold throughout the day for 50/50 raffles and gun door prizes. Most of the firearms were hunting shotguns and rifles. All winners had to be 18 and older and were required to pass a National Instant Criminal Background (NICS) check.
Jay Davis of Smyrna, Delaware, served as the event's announcer. The Farmer's Daughter Barbecue and Catering of Federalsburg served an all-day buffet. Seventeen businesses and individuals sponsored the event.
St. Michaels waterman Doug Morris and his grandson Jacob Sadler shucked three bushels of oysters for the Sportsmans Bash.
On its Facebook page, the fair board thanked everyone who made the day a success. "It's all for the 4H/FFA kids to make their county fair an experience they will not forget," the board posted.
"Last year (at the fair), we had a mechanical bull, we were able to open up some laser tag in the evening for the community free, that type of stuff — anything we can do to get better entertainment and bring more people out to the community and have a good time," Conneely said.
The Amish Outlaws will be back this year, along with the Reagan Years, an 80s tribute band (who will be performing March 1 at the Avalon Theatre in Easton) and local favorites The Jones Boys.
The bash proceeds "increases our ability for better prizes for exhibitors and make improvements to the barns and so forth, and open it up, hopefully, to get more people from outside to come show," Conneely said.
"Everything goes towards funding the fair," he said. "So hopefully we can do as good for the fair this year as we did last year."
This year's fair is Aug. 7 to Aug. 10. For more information, visit carolinedorchestercountyfair.com.

title: Celebrating 250 years of Caroline County
author: STAFF REPORT
content:
Celebrating 250 years of Caroline County

 March 6, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: STAFF REPORT | Section: Events 
 
 251
 Words 

 Read News Document

 It has been 250 years since Caroline County was created, formed from inland sections of Dorchester and Queen Anne's counties.It was named for Lady Caroline Eden, sister of the sixth Lord of Baltimore and then Lord Proprietor and wife of the royal governor.
The weekend of March, 15, the Caroline County community will commemorate the past 250 years and the changes that have taken place since the county's founding.
Festivities will kick off with a VIP celebration event hosted by the Caroline County Historical Society on Friday, March 15, from 5 to 8 p.m. at the Museum of Rural Life.
Guest speaker Julie Markin, director of archaeology at Washington College, will present on a recent dig at Barwick's Landing, the presumed location of a tavern operated by James Barwick until 1783.
Refreshments will be offered, and tokens will be given, redeemable at participating downtown Denton businesses.
Tickets are $50 and are available online at donorbox.org/250th-anniversary-vip-event-tickets.
Continuing the celebration March 16, Market Street between Second and Fifth Streets in Denton will be closed to traffic to accommodate pedestrians for a St. Patrick's Day themed event.
The Chamber of Commerce will host a scavenger hunt with cash prizes. Registration will be open at 8 North Second Street during the event.
The event will feature a petting zoo, trike races, a cornhole tournament, cooking demonstrations, street bowling and potato spoon races.
There will be a DJ and performances from the North Caroline and Colonel Richardson High School jazz bands, To the Point Dance Studio and the Arts Center Drums and Dance Circle.

title: CWDI Board President shares progress at Cambridge Harbor
author: MAGGIE TROVATO mtrovato@chespub.com
content:
CWDI Board President shares progress at Cambridge Harbor

 March 6, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: MAGGIE TROVATO mtrovato@chespub.com | Section: Local News 
 
 261

 CAMBRIDGE — In a Feb. 29 news release, Cambridge Waterfront Development Inc. President Angie Hengst touched on some of the developments taking place at Cambridge Harbor.According to the news release, CWDI will unveil concept plans for a tree park and Memorial Garden along Byrn Street "shortly."
This park and garden is part of the larger Cambridge Harbor project that will develop space along the Cambridge waterfront. This project will include public spaces, a boutique hotel and residential and mixed-use spaces.
In the news release, Hengst said the tree park and garden will preserve Maryland's Champion English Elm tree and its twin, as well as honor those who worked at the former Dorchester General Hospital.
Also in the news release, Hengst shared that CWDI's Planning Committee met in February to discuss design plans for the East Gateway Park, at Route 50 and Maryland Avenue. Hengst said concept plans for this are almost complete. She said CWDI will share them with the public when they are complete.
For this project, Hengst said CWDI is working with local muralist Michael Rosato to create a new mural installation that would incorporate the current mural at the park along with new images that highlight Dorchester heritage.
"The park itself will have an educational component as well as provide visitors with a jumping off point to explore the rest of the city," she said in the news release.
CWDI's board will hold its next meeting at 4 p.m. on March 20 in the Dorchester Chamber of Commerce conference room. The open session portion of the meeting is open to the general public.

title: Dyer achieves Eagle Scout
author: TOM MCCALL
content:
Dyer achieves Eagle Scout

 March 7, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: TOM MCCALL | Section: News 
 
 519
 Words 

 Read News Document

 ST. MICHAELS — A crowd of family, politicians, civic leaders and Boy Scouts assembled in the Scout House on St. Mary's Square to present the Eagle Scout Badge to Vincent Thomas Dyer Sunday.Multiple candles were lit to commemorate different aspects of his journey that started when he was 5. This is the highest honor a Scout can achieve and only about four in 100 Scouts reach it.
Dyer's sash had 26 merit badges on it, and his final project was raising $2,000 to raise a flag pole honoring veterans in Cordova. Of course, this achievment took hours of input from his family, his Troop 741 leaders and his fellow Scouts.
"It is now time to formally present you with Scouting's highest badge of accomplishment. The symbol of your success is the Eagle Scout badge and neckerchief, which will now be presented by your parents," Scoutmaster Brendan Beers said.
One of the most touching moments was when his parents, Paul and Kimberly, attached the Eagle Scout pin. He then attached pins on them for being a supportive Eagle Scout mom and dad.
Vincent's brother Paul Jr., also an Eagle Scout, said, "What does the rank of Eagle Scout represent? To me it represents saying you are going to do something and then doing it. It represents goals realized, focus and strength of character. When the pressure is on and others would run around and panic, the Eagle Scout stays calm, cool and collected in the face of atrocity."
Another person who was there to guide and bear witness is Steve Bealefeld, assistant scoutmaster.
He said, "He is a hard-working young man who has always had his head on straight."
Vincent's father listed many of the places the Scout troop went to go camping like the C & O Canal, Dorchester County and Tennessee. The biggest test was a 10-day hike at Philmont in New Mexico.
There was a testament to Vincent's leadership in the field. He was said to be an excellent cook with a Dutch oven. He can make peach cobbler and chicken pot pie.
"When he was in the lead, you were never going in the wrong direction. In the spartan wilds of Philmont, this was no small feat. Vincent is an excellent navigator. Vincent's attitude was equally as unflagging as his physical stamina. There is a deep keeled steadiness to his emotional thermostat," scout leader JoRoy Lizewski said.
Then it was time for the politicians to offer large citations. President of Town of St. Michael's Commission David Breimhurst, Del. Tom Hutchison (R-Caroline, Dorchester, Talbot, Wicomico), community liaison to Andy Harris Mike Detmer and Maryland state Sen. Johnny Mautz (R-Caroline, Dorchester, Talbot, Wicomico) all spoke briefly. Vincent was given the United States flag and the Maryland Flag.
Vincent had the last word.
"I am so proud. I am happy that all my friends from 190 and 741 were here to celebrate this event with me, because it has been a long time coming. It is a bittersweet moment. I am glad I got Eagle Scout, but I will miss Scouting as a whole," Vincent said.
He tentatively has plans to attend University of Maryland at College Park in the fall.

title: Shelter seeing success
author: ANDREA GRABENSTEIN
content:
Shelter seeing success

 March 8, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: ANDREA GRABENSTEIN | Section: News 
 
 705
 Words 

 Read News Document

 CENTREVILLE — Queen Anne's County animals continue to be in "good paws" as officials presented updates to ensure the safety and wellbeing of those in their care to the Queen Anne's Board of County Commissioners Feb 27.The Queen Anne's County Animal Control Commission (ACC) introduced updates to the Animal Control Comprehensive plan, Chapter 9.
While there have certainly been changes over the years, the Animal Control ordinance has never seen a line by line holistic review of documents such as this before, said Jennifer Nowak, commission chair.
"It needed a major upgrade," she said.
Revisions were especially needed to make the ordinance more applicable for animal control cases, Nowak noted. The extensive revision includes housekeeping items and definition changes to make the documentation flow better.
Updates to the animal control ordinance include three full document reviews, hundreds of hours of work and strong collaboration from officials including Animal Control, emergency services and animal services, according to Nowak.
A public hearing regarding the ordinance is expected at the commissioner's March 26 meeting.
In other business, Queen Anne's County Animal Services (QACAS) presented 2023 overviews and 2024 projections to the county commissioners.
Animal Services Chief of Services Kelly Hamilton presented a year in review and projections for the shelter moving forward.
The shelter continues to lead the way in providing care care for forlorn animals of the Eastern Shore with an impact stronger than ever, she said, it was a very successful year of diligent volunteers, engaging events, and successful community support and 2024 only looks to continue.
The organization considers itself a quintessential No-Kill Shelter of the state of Maryland and the Eastern Shore, Hamilton said, with the Live Release Rate determined by the number of animals leaving the shelter via adoption, returned to the owner or transferred to another shelter.
The national standard to be considered a No Kill Shelter is 90% and with a 94.6% rate, QACAS is proud to be one of 12 such shelters in Maryland, she said.
A total of 1,324 animals entered the county's shelter in 2023, whether as strays, seized or transferred in, a 29% increase from 2022, according to Hamilton.
Through QACAS, 679 animals found their "furr-ever" families in 2023, she announced.
Nearly 900 surgeries were performed onsite ranging from routine neuters, to life saving procedures.
The shelter has ramped up its social media presence including facial recognition software to instrumentally connect owners and pets and help 166 animals find their way back home in 2023.
"It's amazing, the technology is there," Hamilton said.
Hamilton credited volunteers and foster families as the "true heroes" for their tireless dedication to the animals.
"It really takes our team to invest all this time and energy in these animals to get them ready for that adoption floor," she said.
Foster families are imperative to provide valuable insight into an animal's behavior outside of the shelter to provide "purr-fect" placement for prospective adopters.
Programs include doggy day trips in hopes of enticing new foster families with a day of play away from the kennels, which can often snowball into full blown adoptions.
IQACAS participated in a National Clear the Shelter Event to roaring success, seeing nearly 100 animals find homes in a very short amount of time, she said.
Other community events include Puppy Yoga, donation drives, and partnering with the Parks and Recreation Department for the first annual "Pawing in Love" Fun Run.
Moving forward, the shelter expects to see an increase in community involvement including school education programs and "bigger and better" fundraisers, Hamilton said.
The facility has undergone remodeling to include updated in house dental machines and a new lobby layout. The shelter is now home to new cat condos, improved yard spaces, and even surround sound speakers at the dog kennels to provide calming ambiance.
With its newly improved yard space, they plan to offer additional enrichment programs for dog training including daily doggie play groups.
A complimentary behaviorist class is available for all newly adopted dogs. This program will serve residents who may be considering surrendering animals to the shelter for behavioral concerns or are in need of training tips, according to Hamilton.
QACAS looks to continue leading the pack as a local No Kill Shelter with updated technology and infrastructure improvements to provide community critters the best care "pawsible."
More information about the QACAS, including upcoming events can be found at www.qac.org/1425/Animal-Services.

title: The Navy’s 'best kept secret'
author: TAMARA FORTE Special to the Star Democrat
content:
The Navy’s 'best kept secret'

 March 8, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: TAMARA FORTE Special to the Star Democrat | Section: Local News 
 
 815
 Words 

 Read News Document

 GRASONVILLE — "Do your best. Remember to breathe. Remember why you are here.''On Saturday, March 2, this encouragement echoed through an almost silent room at the Veterans of Foreign Wars Post 7464 in Grasonville during the annual inspection for the Maryland Division of the U.S. Naval Sea Cadet Corps. While many 10 to 18 year olds relax at home on a rainy Saturday morning, 21 Sea Cadets and eight League Cadets stood at attention.
Their uniforms carefully pressed and prepared, shoes shined and haircuts and hairstyles well groomed according to the set regulations. They were prepared and ready for their yearly inspection.
The purpose of annual inspection is to prepare for combat. Although these young men and women are not going into combat, they are preparing to be productive citizens now while also preparing to be future leaders who positively impact the world around them.
Many do not know about this extraordinary program. But, some call it "the Navy's best kept secret."
Established in 1958 by the Secretary of the Navy, the U.S. Naval Sea Cadet Corps are comprised of young men and women aged 10 through 18.
There are two programs within Sea Cadets, the Navy League Cadet Corps for middle school students aged 10 to 13, and the Naval Sea Cadet Corps for ages 13 through the end of high school.
Through the program, values of discipline, accountability and teamwork are instilled, giving cadets a chance to step outside of their comfort zones and helping them thrive.
Today, the corps has 380 units and 9,000 enrolled. Although this program is supported by both the U.S. Navy and Coast Guard, the goal is not to recruit for the military but to create respectable citizens in life — no matter what their career path may be.
Lt. Maryjoe Phillips, Sea Cadet Corps supply, finance and division officer, explains that she started with this program about 10 years ago as a "drop off mom," when she would drop her daughter off to the Sea Cadet program.
Not knowing much about the Sea Cadet program, Phillips was recruited by the master chief to help.
Ten years later, she is one of the driving forces behind this Sea Cadet unit.
"The program means a lot because we are turning out really great young men and women that are going to be beneficial to our society," Phillips said. "We are raising patriots, which this country needs so badly."
She called the program "a breath of fresh air."
"With some of the turmoil going on in the world, I have seen these Cadets do some really amazing things," Phillips said. "I get so proud of them even though they are not my children. I'm amazed at what can be done."
Starting with only five cadets in 2018, the program has grown to 29 cadets and is still growing.
In April 2018, the Maryland Unit formed and was commissioned in May 2022. Before this unit formed, many parents drove their children over the bridge to Annapolis for drills and training.
Kent Island High School senior, Evan Newcomer, explained how he started his Sea Cadet training as a League Cadet in Annapolis at age 10. His parents said there were many families traveling back and forth at that time.
Newcomer's parents asked to bring this program to Maryland's Eastern Shore. He now leads as a Naval Sea Cadet Corps petty officer second class.
His experience as a League Cadet and Sea Cadet has helped grow him into the leader he is now.
"I always had a dream of serving," Newcomer said, "and I knew the military was always appealing to me. And the whole mission of all the branches was something that kind of shined to me. My uncle was a Naval Academy Grad. He inspired me to pursue that course as well as the other, older cadets in the program. (They) impressed me and made me want to pursue that dream."
After Saturday's inspection finished, the unit and their families celebrated Evan's acceptance to West Point as a life sciences major studying pre-med.
Cadets and families come from Centreville, Easton, St. Michaels, Prince Frederick and everywhere in between, as the Maryland unit is the only unit on Maryland's Eastern Shore.
Interested young persons ages 10-17 can join a drill weekend to learn more about the program. The unit is looking for adults that can give trainings (gun safety, medical and public safety) or help develop a new marksmanship program. Any interested adult volunteers that could help the program run smoothly or hold a position are welcome to contact Lt. Maryjoe Phillips at pti00803@ gmail.com or visit seacadets.org

title: 250th anniversary proclaimed in Caroline County
author: TOM MCCALL
content:
250th anniversary proclaimed in Caroline County

 March 13, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: TOM MCCALL | Section: Local News 
 
 353
 Words 

 Read News Document

 DENTON — Historian Chad Dean came to the Caroline Commissioners' meeting March 12 to read a 250th anniversary proclamation for Caroline County.The county was formed in 1773.
"This is very enjoyable to put together as have all the 250th anniversary events so far," he said. "We are hoping to plan and execute many more in the future."
He delved into the history of the early people who created the county.
"Where as a pragmatic acknowledgement of a desire of late colonial dwellers and planters near and along the banks of the Choptank River, Tuckahoe Creek and Marshy Hope Creek to duly enjoy more convenient access to the services of the county seat," they created Caroline County, Dean said.
He went on to read that Caroline was formed on November 5, 1773, from portions of Dorchester and Queen Anne's County. He listed all kinds of vocations that have emerged from Caroline, like artists, doctors and military personnel.
"Now it is hereby resolved that we, commissioners of Caroline County, proclaim March 15, 2024, to be the official commencement of the celebration of the 250th anniversary of this venerated place and encourage all loyal friends of the green garden county to reflect on, participate in and support the many planning events and activities of our Jubilee Year," Dean said.
There will be a VIP celebration of the green garden county on from 5 to 8 p.m., Friday, March 15, at the Museum of Rural Life, located at 16 N. Second St., Denton.
Guest speaker Julie Markin, director of Washington College archaeology, will talk on the topic of "Melville's Warehouse and Barwick's Inn." Beer, wine and hors d'oeuvres will be served.
Tickets cost $50 per person and can be found at donorbox.org/250th-anniversary-vip-event-tickets. For more information, go to carolinehistory.org.
The next day, there will be a St. Patrick's Day event from 2 to 4 p.m. on Market Street from Second to Fifth streets. This family-friendly event will include tricycle races, bowling, corn hole contests, face painting and arts and crafts with the Caroline County Arts Council.
There will be jazz bands from both North Caroline and Colonel Richardson high schools. Market Street will be closed to traffic.

The open house celebrated the 75the anniversary of the Ladies Auxiliary, and there was a scavenger hunt for the Children.

title: Eclipse 2024: America gets ready for next month’s big celestial event (VIDEO)
author: Mike Sunnucks APG National Enterprise Editor
content:
Eclipse 2024: America gets ready for next month’s big celestial event (VIDEO)

 March 20, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Mike Sunnucks APG National Enterprise Editor | Section: Travel 
 
 1382
 Words 

 Read News Document

 Mansfield, Texas, and Mansfield, Ohio, are more than 1,100 miles and a 17-hour drive from each other.But the two cities share more than a name.
Like communities from Texas to Maine, the two Mansfields are expecting a surge of visitors for next month's total solar eclipse.
On Monday, April 8, the total solar eclipse will cross North America with at least a partial view of the moon blocking out the sun throughout the continental U.S.
As many as 4 million people could travel to viewing sites across 13 states in the path of totality to view the moon completely blocking out the sun for between 3 and 4 minutes.
That path starts in Mexico and then traverses Texas and 12 other U.S. states including Oklahoma, Missouri, Kentucky, Illinois, Ohio, New York and into New England.
"It's simply the most spectacular sight you will see in your life," said Michael Zeiler, a self-professed eclipse chaser who operates GreatAmericanEclipse. com. He's been viewing celestial events since 1991.
There will not be another similar celestial event in the continental U.S. until 2044, according to Angela Des Jardins, a physics professor at Montana State University, who is a lead researcher in a NASA initiative deploying 1,000 faculty and students from dozens of colleges and schools throughout the country to analyze the eclipse.
Special glasses and viewers are needed to watch the eclipse in order to avoid potential eye and vision damage from staring at the sun.
TOURISM BOOST
In Mansfield, Ohio, Jodie Snavely expects as many 250,000 people to visit Richland County (which sits between Cleveland and Columbus).
"We have not had anything like this before. The last total eclipse in our region was 1806. But it's exciting to see the creativity of what the local businesses have planned before and during the eclipse for the residents and visitors," said Snavely, special projects director for Destination Mansfield — Richland County.
Eclipse viewing events will be held at Kingwood Center Gardens and the historic Ohio State Reformatory (a former prison where "Shawshank Redemption" was filmed and is celebrating its 30th anniversary.)
Snavely said some of Mansfield's eclipse marketing is tied to the movie.
Other creative events range from watching the eclipse during a yoga class at the Ohio Bird Sanctuary or with alpacas at a local farm to a weekend music festival and "You'll Burn Your Eye Out" eclipse watch party hosted by a local brewery.
Snavely said the area could see a $7 million tourism and economic boost from the event.
Tim Roberts, marketing and promotions manager for Mansfield, Texas' Convention & Visitors Bureau, said his town moved its spring musical festival to April 6 and renamed the Music Alley Eclipse Fest to coincide with the event.
"We are fully expecting 8,000 to 10,000 people based upon our hotel bookings. Our hotels are mostly booked that weekend," Roberts said, adding that some room rates are as high as $500 per night.
Mansfield — 34 miles southwest of Dallas — is also hosting eclipse watch parties. Roberts said he's seen interest from visitors as far as Europe including Poland.
Texas is the prime U.S. spot to view the event with the longest totality times (how long the moon will darken the sun), according to eclipse chasers and astronomers.
Zeiler said he is viewing the April event from Fredericksburg, Texas (70 miles northwest of San Antonio). He said Texas is the ideal U.S. spot because it is more prone to have clear weather on eclipse day and Fredericksburg is near multiple highways in case cloudy or inclement weather necessitated relocating to clearer skies.
'COMING FROM ALL OVER'
Many eclipse travelers are looking at camping options to enjoy the event.
Many campgrounds along the U.S. route have already or will sell out for the weekend leading up to the Monday eclipse.
"We've got them coming from all over," said Monica Garcia, general manager of Mystic Quarry, a camping site in Canyon Lake, Texas (in between Austin and San Antonio) that offers cabins, tents, teepees and spots for RVs.
Garcia expects to be sold out by eclipse day with remaining cabins and teepees running $230 per night.
The early April combination of spring break travel and the eclipse path near major population centers could make for one of the busiest travel periods in U.S. history.
OTHER TOP DESTINATIONSAixa Diaz, a spokesperson for AAA, said the likes of Cleveland and Dayton, Ohio; Buffalo and Syracuse, New York; Indianapolis, Little Rock, Arkansas and Burlington, Vermont; join Texas cities as the top eclipse destinations.
And, she said travelers are paying hefty prices.
"Flights to cities along the path of totality are averaging 28% higher compared to last year and hotels are 48% more expensive during the eclipse weekend compared to that same weekend in 2023," Diaz said.
In Ohio and other states, tourism bureaus, campground operators and universities are centering events around the eclipse.
Zeiler said northern Ohio on the shores of Lake Erie and spots along Lake Ontario in upstate New York could also offer clear viewing weather for viewers.
In the southeastern part of the state, Defiance County, Ohio and Ohio University are among those hosting events leading up and on April 8 including at the latter's Chillicothe campus.
Many astronomers and solar researchers are traveling to experience and analyze the event in person.
"Most of the solar specialists in our department (and actually around the country) are going to be in meetings or events that are in the path of totality for the eclipse itself," said Rachael Filwett, a physics professor at Montana State University specializing in space physics.
Des Jardins said 53 research teams (which include college and some high school students) will release high-altitude research balloons to study the impacts of the eclipse, including on the atmosphere and climate.
'ECLIPSE FLIGHTS'
Other cities and towns in the totality path — from Rochester, New York to Paducah, Kentucky — also have events planned the weekend before as well as eclipse day.
"Paducah was in the path of totality for the 2017 Great American Eclipse, so this is a 'twice in a lifetime event for the city," said Liz Hammonds, director of marketing and communications for the local convention and visitors bureau.
The Kentucky town, which sits at the confluence of the Ohio and Tennessee rivers between Nashville and St. Louis, will host an "X Marks the Spot" festival April 7-8 to celebrate the crossroads of the two eclipses.
Hammonds said an estimated 150,000 visitors are expected in western Kentucky including an influx of aircraft flying for celestial happening.
Southwest Airlines, Delta Air Lines and United Airlines also have flights coinciding when the solar eclipse travels across sections of the U.S.
United has five flights from Chicago and four from Houston on April 8 that will traverse the eclipse path, according to Remy Milburn, an airline spokesperson.
She said outbound bookings from San Antonio after the eclipse are up 288% compared to last year and destinations such as Cleveland and Little Rock are also seeing increased travel demand.
Southwest Airlines had eight flights on April 8 that could offer aerial views of the event including routes from Dallas to Pittsburgh, St. Louis to Houston and Austin to Indianapolis.
Grant Myatt, a spokesman for Delta Air Lines, said an eclipse flight from Austin to Detroit is sold out and there were limited seats left for another one from Dallas to Detroit.
The few seats left for those flights have fares running at $660 or more one way (and that's before fees and taxes).
AAA's Diaz said Niagara Falls is also a popular destination and the auto club's travel agents have also seen bookings for eclipse cruises on the Panama Canal and vacation packages to Mexico.
'BLOWN AWAY'
There will also be livestreams of the moon meeting the sun hosted by NASA as well as the Exploratorium in San Francisco.
Des Jardins said teams from Montana State and 74 other schools are working with those two groups. She's also interested to see how animals and insects react.
Robyn Higdon, senior project director and executive producer at the Exploratorium, said the museum will broadcast eclipse livestreams from Torreon, Mexico and Junction, Texas.
The museum partners with NASA and has numerous events and webinars with local schools, planetariums and museums across the country.
Higdon first got interested in eclipses in 1998. "I was just blown away," she said.
Higdon and Des Jardins will be part of a contingent viewing the eclipse from Junction. Texas.
"If anyone can travel to the eclipse in person the experience is worth it," Higdon said. "It's an all body, just incredible experience."

title: Caroline County celebrates 250th anniversary
author: Angela Price
content:
Caroline County celebrates 250th anniversary

 March 20, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Angela Price | Section: Local News 
 
 932
 Words 

 Read News Document

 DENTON — The Caroline County Historical Society hosted a VIP event to kick off the county's 250th anniversary celebration Friday, March 15, with special guests, presentations, food and more at the Museum of Rural Life in Denton.Maryland Delegate William Richardson of Gilpin Point, portrayed by Rick Culotta, addressed the standing-room-only crowd.
"We're gathered here today to celebrate and explain to one and all of you the results of many requests that a new county be formed so as to better accommodate those having business with the court," Richardson said.
An attempt was made as early as 1745 to organize a new Eastern Shore county, to be known at that time as King William County. That effort failed.
"Twenty-nine years later, in this same area, it pleases me to introduce you to our new county," Richardson said.
He said the inland sections of Dorchester and Queen Anne's counties had developed, becoming rich and productive, and trade as well as population had increased.
"With regret I must also report to you that crime has also increased, and the carrying of prisoners from here to Queenstown in Queen Anne's County or to Cambridge in Dorchester has naturally become a problem," Richardson said. "Having in mind your needs, all your needs, of a growing population, increased trade and rising crime, I found it of great importance to petition the General Assembly of the Colony of Maryland in Annapolis to organize this new county."
The new county, known as Caroline after colonial Gov. Robert Eden's wife, was formed from 200 square miles of northern Dorchester and approximately 120 square miles of eastern Queen Anne's. The land was paid for with tobacco.
Richardson introduced the bill on Nov. 5, 1773, and it passed Dec. 15, 1773. The new justices met March 15, 1774, at Millvill's Warehouse, which served as the county courthouse, and selected Thomas White as the county's first delegate.
Richardson went on to become a colonel in the Revolutionary War. Colonel Richardson Middle School and Colonel Richardson High School are named in his honor.
Millvill's Warehouse served as the county courthouse from from 1774 until 1791. Other nearby buildings included Barwick's Ordinary (a tavern) and a jail.
Returning to the present day, Cheryl Smith recounted how her husband Joe was using a backhoe to bury the remains of some brush he had burned on their property on Smith Landing Road in 2015 when he unearthed a brick foundation.
They knew the original courthouse had been located somewhere nearby and wondered if that could be it. They started using a metal detector and found numerous artifacts on the site.
The late J.O.K. Walsh contacted the state archaeologist, who "wasn't really interested in helping Caroline County for some bizarre reason," Smith said. "But he retired, and then a younger gentleman named Matthew McKnight took over as state archaeologist, and he was extremely interested."
McKnight got Dr. Julie Markin, director of anthropology and archaeology at Washington College, involved, Smith said, and they have conducted archaeological digs on the property for several years.
Markin was the evening's special guest, presenting a slide show, "Barwick's Ordinary: Tavern Life on the Choptank," and talking about their discoveries on the Smith property.
A slide showed an overhead view of the property, with outlines marking different features located. The orange areas showed magnetic anomalies, such as coins and bits of horse tack, while the lighter, whitish areas were rectangularly shaped, indicative of manmade structures.
"So, we have something that is cultural, that is human-made," Markin said. Then the question is, when is it from? That's when Washington College started working with the Archaeological Society of Maryland. Caroline County Historical Society provided lab space in Greensboro for processing artifacts.
In an area eventually determined to be a trash pile, they found slag, nails, fish bones and lots of fish scales. Other artifacts found included coins, buttons, military buttons, straight pins, toys and stoneware.
They have identified several features as outbuildings, one possibly a dairy. They believe the largest is the tavern's cellar.
Their most exciting find this past year came on the last day of the dig, Markin said. They uncovered a beam and, beneath the beam, the remains of a large, green glass bottle.
Pieces of glassware uncovered on the property range in quality, telling of a time when people were shifting from necessities to luxuries, searching for things that made life more comfortable and convenient.
"Now in the Chesapeake, there's still a social hierarchy, so you find them present in different quantities according to class, but they're all trying to get the same goods," Markin said.
She used tea sets as an example: Lower class citizens might have sets of lesser quality and mismatched cups, while upper class citizens might own tea sets of fine porcelain.
Tea, like tobacco, was important in colonial times. After the Boston Tea Party, Britain passed the Intolerable Acts, and Caroline County responded, passing the Caroline Resolutions.
They were written and signed at Barwick's Ordinary House on June 18, 1774, and represent the next Caroline anniversary celebration. The resolutions will be reenacted on June 18 at the Wharves at Choptank Visitor Center with dignitaries reading each of the 11. Food and spirits will be served. For more information, contact Caroline County Historical Society.
Historical Society President Charles Andrew said Friday was just the first of many events planned this year to celebrate the county's 250th anniversary.
CCHS received proclamations from the Governor's Office, State Sen. Johnny Mautz and the Caroline County Commissioners. Every historical society in the county was represented, and Andrew invited each to make a brief presentation.
Food for the event was provided by Earth Tones, Caroline's, Market Street Pub, Pizza Empire, Night's Kitchen Bakery and Cafe and the Chesapeake Culinary Center.

title: From the courtroom to the pulpit: New Newark pastor left a law career to join the ministry
author: Josh Shannon jshannon@chespub.com
content:
From the courtroom to the pulpit: New Newark pastor left a law career to join the ministry

 March 22, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Josh Shannon jshannon@chespub.com | Section: News 
 
 774
 Words 

 Read News Document

 As a defense lawyer, Dan McKenty represented corporate clients in front of judges at the courthouse in Wilmington, Delaware.In his new job, he helps his flock stay accountable to an even higher power.
Last month, McKenty was hired as senior pastor at the First Presbyterian Church of Newark, his second pastoral role after making a mid-life career change and joining the ministry.
"People make jokes, they say, 'Well you get up and talk in front of people, so there are a lot of transferrable skills," McKenty said. "And I say, well yeah, but in this job, I really do have to get the evidence right."
Though his path to the pulpit was unorthodox, there's nowhere McKenty would rather be.
"I'm doing what God wants me to do," the 63-year-old said.
McKenty grew up in West Chester, Pa., and attended a Presbyterian church with his family.
As an adult, while he never lost his faith, religion took a backseat as he built his career and grew his family. Eventually, he made his way back to church, and he couldn't shake the feeling that he was destined for something greater.
"God has a way of not being ignored, so I was called to the ministry," he said
"It wasn't really a blinding moment on the road to Damascus like Paul had," he added. "I'm not going to lie to you and say it was that. It was just this growing passion for spreading the gospel."
McKenty would work all day as a lawyer, then drive to Philadelphia to take night classes at a seminary school. After four years of classes, he did a year of chaplaincy at Nemours Children's Hospital, giving him a crash course in comforting people in the worst moments of their life.
"That's my view of God," he said. "God is in the emergency room when it all goes to hell. He's sitting there amongst a mascara-streaked mess of it all, feeling as [lousy] as everybody else. That's the God we have, and thank God we have that God."
His first pastoral job was at a small church in Ocean City, Md. After seven years, he was looking for a new challenge, and First Presbyterian was looking for a new pastor.
In the Presbyterian system, pastors are chosen by the congregation, not assigned by a bishop. Churches looking for a new pastor can search a computer database of candidates and then do interviews.
A committee at First Presbyterian chose McKenty as a finalist, and McKenty came to the church to do a guest sermon.
"He wowed us with the sermon, and it was a unanimous vote," church elder Don Tancredi said.
The new pastor's laid-back, welcoming style has already won praise.
"You sit here and have a conversation with Pastor Dan, it's like I've known him for a long time," Tancredi said.
For McKenty, coming to Newark is a homecoming of sorts, considering he used to live in West Chester and work in Wilmington. He and his wife now live in Strasburg, Pa.
"This church has a lot of talent in it and has a great potential to expand the ministry that is already healthy and is already here," he said. "So it was really an opportunity to do more than I was afforded in Ocean City."
McKenty hopes to lead First Presbyterian toward expanding its ministries.
"I'm going to take a little bit of time and get to know the area, and then together we're going to move forth joyfully and boldly in enlarging our footprint," he said, adding he wants to find more ways to take the church out into the community. "Basically we want to live the gospel by meeting people where they are."
One particular focus will be the drug recovery community, which already uses the church for support group meetings.
"Those are people who are tackling a big uphill climb, and it takes a lot of bravery to begin and to reach the summit," McKenty said. "I think it's a vital part of the gospel that we help in that."
The church recently completed a renovation project that enhanced its 600-seat chapel, including new pews, new carpet, new lighting and investments into equipment for live-streaming services.
First Presbyterian, which will mark its 190th anniversary next year, sits on a 14-acre campus on West Main Street, including three buildings.
Its 5,000-square-foot Westminister House — located between the main church and the Newark Country Club — presents a particularly exciting opportunity. The building is currently unused, and church officials are working on a plan to use it for programs that benefit the community.
That could include giving service organizations like the Newark Area Welfare Committee a permanent space there, Tancredi said. The church is also considering hosting a regular farmers market in the parking lot.

title: Protecting each other
author: Staff Writer
content:
Protecting each other

 March 24, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Staff Writer | Section: Editors Inbox 
 
 392
 Words 

 Read News Document

 Being a good Catholic does not mean turning one's head to crime committed by priests or anyone else.My six siblings and I were fortunate to attend Catholic School. As adult professionals, we credit the nuns with our integrity.
All the nuns at our school were strong women. They were tough Germans who fled Germany as Adolf Hitler came to power. I stayed in touch with many of the nuns over the years.
Due to their background, they insisted that we look out for one another, for protecting each other, and correcting any aspect of life that would place one in a harmful situation. Sitting down when seeing evil was not an option for them.
It is that teaching that brought me to reporting a priest in our Maryland parish for inappropriate contact with small boys in 1987. Seeing things with my own eyes, I reached out to one of the nuns that I trusted. The parish settled the cases, and the priest was defrocked.
Defrocked. Removed for good. He would have no more Catholic school playgrounds to select his next victim nor another innocent parent to convince that his or her child spend the night with him in the rectory.
Last year at Eastertime, the Maryland Attorney General released a report on the sexual abuse of children within the Baltimore Archdiocese. Due to the stigma of sexual assaults especially for boys, it is impossible to calibrate the exact number of victims.
That report sat poorly with one of the local devout Catholics. She seemed to not understand why the state of Maryland would increase the statute of limitations for child victims. She condemned the amount of money available to the victims and categorically and alarmingly published, while defending the church, false statements: "No new cases have been brought up for over 25 years and most of the clergy who were involved are not even alive today."
That is like stating a crime like drunk driving has been extinguished throughout the country in the last 25 years.
The upset parishioner is considered one of the pillars of the church. Thus, she has a good vantage point to observe. With that comes duty. And one of the duties is to take the blinders off, get educated on child victims and report any inappropriate conduct upon a child. That makes us good Catholics because praying alone does not extinguish pedophilia.
CATHY LINDBERG JAROSZ
Easton

title: College students travel to every Easton in US
author: TOM MCCALL
content:
College students travel to every Easton in US

 March 24, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: TOM MCCALL | Section: Local News 
 
 626
 Words 

 Read News Document

 EASTON — Three students and a recent alumna at Lafayette College in Easton, Pennsylvania, had a crazy idea.What could be discovered traveling to every incorporated "Easton" in America? The last stop on their voyage of discovery was Easton, Maryland, where they met Mayor Megan Cook last weekend.
One of the group members, Remy Oktay, was a pilot, allowing them to travel by single engine airplane to each town. There was no way to get to these towns by commercial flight so barnstorming in the four-seater made sense.
The tour criss-crossed the United States, taking off from Easton, Pennsylvania, to fly to Easton, Illinois. Then it was on to Easton, Kansas and Missouri.
From there, they headed south to Easton, Texas, before heading north to Easton, Minnesota, and Easton, Wisconsin.
More Eastons were visited in Michigan, Connecticut, Massachusetts, Maine, New Hampshire and New York.
"And now we are in Maryland," Oktay said. "This is the last stop."
Elisabeth Seidel said that Wikipedia lists 21 Eastons in the United States. They decided to visit the incorporated ones.
What makes a town? Is it a high school? A mayor? A Lion's Club? Often there was little on Wikipedia, the group found.
They took a one-hour walking tour of downtown and looked through a book of old photos with their guide from the Talbot Historical Society.
"She knew everything," Seidel said. "I am very interested in the preservation of local history."
The hardest part of the trip was keeping the weight down in the small craft. They kept collecting souvenirs along the way. Shipping the mementos back to school was the only solution to remain five pounds under regulation weight.
The trip was a mix of personal and academic. The students are not getting credit, but an alumnus paid some of their expenses. The school paid for hotels, food and transportation. They plan to cowrite an article for their school newspaper about the experience.
"We found an alum who is into aviation and was like, 'This sounds cool. Here are a few thousand dollars. Go have fun,'" Oktay said. Their biggest cost was aviation fuel.
The search for Eastons began with cookies.
"Trebor and I did an article for the newspaper. We tried all of the chocolate chip cookies in Easton, Pennsylvania, that we could find. We tried them all, ranked them all. We compared them. They were ranked on a scale of one to five milks," Seidel said.
Then they got to thinking what else they could explore.
"I had known there were other towns called Easton. It started off as a joke. We thought we could go to maybe three or four over spring break. Then we were talking to Remy, who is a pilot, ... and things spiraled from there," Seidel said.
When asked if they had a favorite Easton, the answers came quick: "No comment. Restricted information. We cannot say."
"There were real people that we have made friends with in the last 10 days," Trebor Maitin said. "Everyone has their own unique thing to bring to the table."
They found people to be friendly once Easton residents realized what their motive was.
"We have been stopping people in the streets and even doing some door knocks to chat with the locals and get a better understanding of the history," Lucie Lagodich said. "We have met people whose families have lived in these Eastons for generations."
Whenever they were in doubt about whom to contact in a town, they went to the local bar. As soon as they told their story, the bar stools would invariably swivel toward them.
"It is really amazing to see all these towns. It really changes the way you view America," Lagodich said.
"This trip has made me a better reporter and a better person," Maitin said. "I feel a lot more comfortable walking into a situation where not everybody looks like me."

Soups will be chicken noodle, vegetable beef, and peas and dumplings for dining in and carry out at $5 per cup meal or $8 per quart with biscuits. Free delivery is available for four or more. Call to preorder for carry-outs and delivery, 410-228-4910. Must use Glasgow Street entrances for easy access and parking.
