title: Maryland Stories: U.S. Army veteran honored for 50 years with the DAV
author: Michael Reid mreid@somdnews.com
content:
Maryland Stories: U.S. Army veteran honored for 50 years with the DAV

 May 7, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Michael Reid mreid@somdnews.com | Section: News 
 
 643
 Words 

 Read News Document

 Ralph Gough began working with the Disabled American Veterans when he was medically discharged from the military in 1974, and last month — a half century later — he was recognized for his work.The Lexington Park resident, who serves as a judge advocate, received an award on April 27 for his 50 years of service with the St. Mary's DAV Chapter 26 in Lexington Park.
"It's a wild moment," Gough said as he sat at a picnic table at the Leonardtown Wharf a few days before the ceremony. "Where has the time gone? I look at it from the time I've come in and I look around [now]. A lot of friends have passed on and I wish they could have been here. It's been rewarding. It makes me feel that that I reached someone [to help]."
"It's cool," said DAV Chapter 26 Vice Commander James Williams, who has been a member of the St. Mary's chapter the past three years. "He won't tell you but he's the go-to guy. If you have questions or problems he has the information."
Gough said the DAV is an important resource for veterans; its website provides a calendar of upcoming events, services and 28 links veterans can click on to access forms and information.
"It's helped improve communication with other veterans," he said, "and it does [benefit] claims which helps us increase our compensation, and for those who don't get compensation it helps them get theirs."
The DAV Chapter 26 is open 10 a.m. to 1 p.m. Wednesdays at the Local Lodge 4 Machinist Union hall at 21795 Shangri-La Drive in Lexington Park. It has moved a few times over the past couple years.
"We don't have a home and we've been fighting that for years," Gough said. "And if we did have a home where we could be open eights hours a day or whatever, we as veterans could come in and get together."
Gough was asked if the DAV is a type of fraternity for veterans.
"Yes it is, and once you get to know [the vets] and they start to come in and there's a bond that you never break," he said. "My only downside is that I've met a lot of people who went to Vietnam and I had no overseas experience. I'm glad I didn't [have to go overseas], but it can be hard to bond [with those who have]. They have the stories and I can't imagine."
Gough graduated from Great Mills High School in 1968 and was drafted two years later. He was sent to Fort Holabird in Baltimore, then to Fort Dix, N.J., for eight weeks of basic training. He later attended Redstone Arsenal, Missile and Munition Center & School in Huntsville, Alabama, before being assigned to the 200th Ordnance Detachment GMGS Unit Training Command to begin on the job training. The GMGS is a type of grenade launcher.
He later went to Quartermaster School at Fort Lee, Virginia., to become a missile repair parts specialist, which he did the rest of his military career and made him eligible for promotion to E-5 Special Fifth Class.
Because of an injury to his foot, Gough received a medical discharge on Oct. 11, 1972.
"It helped me a lot," Gough said of the services he received from the DAV in the 1970s. "They do it all for you. I've stayed around for 50 years just to see if I could help people."
"It's the most rewarding job I've had," Williams said. "Every Wednesday my mind is set to help veterans, because every veteran has a different story."
He began working at the DAV in 1974 and has held several positions, including a stint as commander from 1993-1995.
"As long as I can move and have a little breathe [in me]," Gough said, "I'll always be there to help people."
For more about the St. Mary's County DAV Chapter 26, call 240-925-5439 or go to www.davch26stmarysmd.com.

title: Sugar Buns Cafe and Bakery serves creativity at the Easton Airport
author: Veronica Fernandez-Alvarado
content:
Sugar Buns Cafe and Bakery serves creativity at the Easton Airport

 May 12, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Veronica Fernandez-Alvarado | Section: News 
 
 530
 Words 

 Read News Document

 EASTON — Susan Leonard created sugar buns, a cross between a cinnamon roll and a croissant. The pastry is a staple of Leonard's business, Sugar Buns Cafe and Bakery, and it also reflects her journey to her love for providing comfort food to all those seeking it, which has involved a lot of creativity.Leonard said she came to owning her cafe the same way she came to all her past careers: through a mixture of boredom and curiosity.
From her two decades career as a flight attendant to receiving her master's in Chinese medicine and practicing acupuncture at Johns Hopkins Hospital, to real estate and mortgage banking and even to being one of the first women to receive an acceptance letter for the FBI training program, Leonard has gains a wide range of life experiences.
Her only consistency through all these career changes has been her love for food.
"My joy comes from making people happy and seeing them really appreciate good food," Leonard said.
Leonard was raised by what she describes as a "meats and potatoes" traditional father and an "ahead of her time" mother who encouraged her to seek independence and "pave her own path." Leonard kept curiosity at the forefront of her life.
As a flight attendant, she would take cooking classes during layovers in places like Paris, Barcelona and Athens.
That combination of cooking and air travel is reflected in Sugar Buns Cafe and Bakery's menu.
Leonard said she tries to make her menu leave an impression through humor and decided to use airport codes for all her hamburgers, including LAX, CDG and London Heathrow, which was named so because it is a double-decker burger.
The cafe is located in the terminal at Easton Airport.
Jessica Gibbs, the waitress at Sugar Bun Cafe, said she tries to provide an open, free-flowing and friendly atmosphere. Customers often come in to enjoy a meal while watching planes land and take off, she said.
Gibbs said she also enjoys the celebrities that have come down for a meal, including John Travolta, Harrison Ford, Adam Sandler and a handful of senators and representatives.
Besides sugar buns and hamburgers, the menu includes a variety of breakfast and lunch items, including the signature "Crabzilla," a large sandwich with six pieces of bacon, thick tomato slices and a large crabcake between Texas toast, finished with two olive eyes.
Calvin Johnson, chef of Sugar Buns Cafe, said he enjoys working there and his creative freedom with the menu, especially since almost all the food is made from scratch and they refuse to use frozen food in meals.
"All the stuff here is comfort food, and I've been around a bunch of different places, but I've been here a long time," Johnson said. "Me and Susan are kind of like Batman and Robin."
Through all her adventures, Leonard said she has always tried to follow her gut and chase curiosity, which is what she advises young girls to do, similar to what her mother modeled for her.
"You take a true accounting of your gifts and challenges and then what your heart wants to do," Leonard said. "It's usually a good match, like the old saying 'if you do something you love, you never have to go to work.'"

title: BAAM Celebrates new Soccer Field and 20 Years
author: TOM MCCALL
content:
BAAM Celebrates new Soccer Field and 20 Years

 May 15, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: TOM MCCALL | Section: Local News 
 
 663
 Words 

 Read News Document

 EASTON — Not only did Building African American Minds mark 20 years of service Saturday, but the organization also celebrated the creation of a great space where children can play.BAAM has refurbished a soccer field for children with new Bermuda grass. They had a ribbon cutting to open the new field near Moton Park on May 11.
Located in Easton, the nonprofit provides scholarships, afterschool programing, summer camp, and more to empower at-risk youth in the community.
A white tent full of local government officials listened to different speakers at a podium set up right in front of the field.
Frank Gunsallus, president of the Easton Town Council, said, "I want to extend special thanks to everyone involved in making this project a reality. From our dedicated town staff to our numerous community volunteers and generous sponsors."
The small crowd of officials clapped as the colors were raised on either side of the podium.
"Let's continue to support and invest in our parks and recreational facilities to ensure that Easton remains a vibrant and engaging community for everyone," Gunsallus said.
Del. Tom Hutchison (R-Dorchester, Talbot, Wicomico) and Sen. Johnny Mautz (R-Caroline, Dorchester, Talbot, Wicomico) came up to the microphone.
Hutchison said, "You have done such great things for the community. This is a great addition for the children and youths that are here."
He presented citations to BAAM for U.S. Sens. Chris Van Hollen and Ben Cardin honoring BAAM's 20 years of service.
Mautz said, "If you had been standing here 20 or 30 years ago, you wouldn't recognize where we are standing. I am looking forward to everybody kicking soccer balls out here."
The sound of DJ Hector could be heard in the distance as Amy Kreiner, president of the Talbot County Chamber of Commerce, came to the microphone to give a glass award to BAAM.
"It is my honor to present Derek and Dina Daily with this 20th Anniversary plaque on behalf of the Talbot County Chamber of Commerce and blessings for the next 20 years," Kreiner said.
Then they stepped onto the pitch for a large red ribbon cutting to open the field up.
William Ryan is president of the board of directors for BAAM. He was smiling as he wore a BAAM sweatshirt.
"We want to get our kids out playing as much as possible. It is part of the town park. It is open to all. If you want to have an event, you have to check with the town. We started out small and we have just been steadily growing," Ryan said.
There were members of the construction crew that actually built the field. It was a lot more than siting a rectangle. Lucas Lees, coastal and land designer of Unity Landscapes, had a three man crew that got the drainage on the field just right.
"We ran into water lines we weren't expecting, but since we were putting in irrigation it was convenient that the town already owned them. It really transformed this space and completed the park," Lees said.
Unity Landscape built it in 45 days.
Derick Daly, founder of BAAM, said that key is being long-term. The relationship with the town, the donors and the staff were all long-term.
"We wanted a place where kids could come and call it their own. We are opening up the soccer field with the partnership of the town of Easton developing with this field for youth soccer. Come out here and just have fun. Play and enjoy yourself, get out and exercise. This could be an incubator for kids to get exposure and take it to another level," Daly said.
Looking past the new soccer field, there was BAAM Fest going on closer to the community pool. There were 31 community partners, whose colorful tents lined a winding sidewalk.
"We started BAAM Fest to give out information about what we are doing. It turned into offering a meal to everyone. We have free lunch for everyone. We have a band as you can hear, face painting — the kids love it. We have community partners," Daly said.

title: Community BBQ hosted to show support for DCPS middle schooler
author: MAGGIE TROVATO mtrovato@chespub.com
content:
Community BBQ hosted to show support for DCPS middle schooler

 May 15, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: MAGGIE TROVATO mtrovato@chespub.com | Section: Local News 
 
 841
 Words 

 Read News Document

 CAMBRIDGE — Circulating videos of an incident where a Mace's Lane middle schooler's hijab was pulled off her head brought people from near and far to the corner of Washington Street and Greenwood Avenue for a community barbecue.The May 8 event, organized by mosques in Baltimore and Philadelphia, was created to support sixth grader Tori Gibbs, who is Muslim, and to give attendees the opportunity to learn about Islam.
"Everybody's invited," Anwar Wright, an administrator at the Germantown Masjid in Philadelphia, said at the event.
The community barbecue came to fruition after religious leaders at Masjid Al-Hidaayah in Baltimore received videos of the incident, which happened off of school grounds.
"What was relayed was our young Muslim sister was being bullied," said Sabur Carter, an administrator at Masjid Al-Hidaayah. "Us Muslims, we're not going to tolerate that. That doesn't mean, as everybody may think, that we're going to react with violence. We're going to react with education."
According to a letter signed by Baltimore's Masjid Ad-Da'wah Ilat Tawheed Imam Raha Batts, the videos shows Gibbs "being verbally and physically attacked with her hijab being violently snatched from her head."
The letter says that those involved chanted Islamic phrases to "taunt" Gibbs. It also says Gibbs was physically assaulted in the presence of the assailant's father.
Gibbs' mom, LaToya Gibbs, said in an interview May 9 that it's been heartbreaking and devastating to see her daughter go through this.
"It's been really hard on her mental health and mine," she said.
She said Tori Gibbs will be doing home hospital schooling through the end of the year due to her mental health.
Carter said that when he saw the video, he felt outrage.
"Everybody should feel safe," he said.
At the barbecue, organizers grilled hamburgers and hot dogs and offered pamphlets and books about Islam for people to peruse.
Along with offering learning opportunities to people in the community, Carter said they came to help foster a peaceful resolution between the children and parents involved in the incident. He said he was able to help make that happen in the early afternoon before the barbecue began.
"We're not protesting or anything like that," Carter said about the event. "But we are calling for change. We're calling for education, and we're calling for change."
The same day as the barbecue, LaToya Gibbs said she and faith leaders sat down with Dorchester County Public Schools Interim Superintendent Jymil Thompson. Although she said the district had given her "the runaround" in the past, she said the meeting was a positive one.
"Unfortunately it took for my brothers and sisters to make a post and bring more awareness than I could," she said about finally getting that meeting.
LaToya Gibbs said that at the meeting, she talked to Thompson about how better communication with parents could have stopped the situation from getting as bad as it did.
According to a statement from DCPS, Thompson called the meeting constructive and said the Gibbs family's concerns were taken seriously.
"The school and community need to work together to prevent small issues becoming big," he said about Imam Raha Batts' suggestion to work together on a bullying awareness program. "It is sensible to use school, where the community's youngsters come together, to further education against bullying. I look forward to working with the Imam on this project."
In an email, DCPS Communications and Community Outreach Specialist Valerie Goff said that following the meeting, Thompson will be monitoring the situation and checking in with the family.
In an interview May 9, Cambridge Police Chief Justin Todd said that on April 5 the department began investigating the incident, which took place outside a Mace's Lane Middle student's home on March 26. He said police did a detailed investigation that included getting video footage of the incident from social media and from city street cameras.
Todd said Rian Johnson, a parent of one of the children involved in the incident, has been charged with conspiracy of assault in the second degree, conspiracy of reckless endangerment, reckless endangerment and contributing to the condition of a child. He said one of the children involved was identified as a juvenile offender but has not been charged. He said the Dorchester County State's Attorney is looking into whether the offender's actions could be considered a hate crime.
LaToya Gibbs said the community barbecue resulted in five attendees taking their Shahada, which means they made the decision to convert to Islam. She said two of those five attendees were the fathers of girls in the video that showed Tori Gibbs being attacked.
Tori Gibbs' great aunt, Kandy Waller, said she just wants her niece to be OK. She said the bullying has been a constant, and she hopes the barbecue results in an end to the bullying and harassment.
"I just want her to be able to enjoy her childhood like everybody else without the threat of violence," Waller said.
LaToya Gibbs said the barbecue had a positive effect on her Tori.
"She did say she was more confident (seeing) all the people come together and show support for her," LaToya Gibbs said.
This story has been updated to include comments from DCPS.

title: 'A nonstop smile': Delaware boy enjoys dream vacation thanks to fundraiser
author: Josh Shannon jshannon@chespub.com
content:
'A nonstop smile': Delaware boy enjoys dream vacation thanks to fundraiser

 May 20, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Josh Shannon jshannon@chespub.com | Section: State News 
 
 378
 Words 

 Read News Document

 A Delaware boy born with serious medical challenges recently enjoyed a dream vacation, thanks to money raised by a local golf tournament.Bruce Johnson Jr. and his family visited the American Dream Mall in East Rutherford, N.J., which features North America's largest indoor water park and a number of other attractions, including a Nickelodeon theme park, a Ferris wheel, a mini golf course, an ice skating rink, an aquarium, a Legoland playground and a wave pool.
"This trip allowed Bruce to enjoy activities such as an amusement park and water park that he would not have been able to do," his mother, Amy Wilson, said. "He had a nonstop smile. We are so blessed for the entire experience."
Bruce, a third-grader at Delaware School for the Deaf, has a medical condition that prevents him from spending too much time outside, so the indoor attractions at American Dream Mall were just what he needed.
"He can't do regular kid things because he has heat intolerance so bad, which affects his lungs," Wilson explained. "So if we can do everything inside, he can be a normal kid."
Bruce was born with microtia/atresia and bilateral hearing loss. Microtia is the absence of an ear or an underdeveloped outer ear, and atresia is hearing loss due to the absence of an ear canal.
Bruce uses hearing aids, which use vibrations to send sound from the outside through his skull to his auditory nerve. He is also fluent in American Sign Language.
The Newark boy and his family were the beneficiaries of the 27th-annual Sunshine Scramble golf tournament, held Oct. 9 at the Newark Country Club. The tournament raised an estimated $15,000 to answer Bruce's dream and other children's dreams.
The Sunshine Foundation answers the dreams of children who have profound, lifelong medical conditions such as spina bifida, cerebral palsy, severe autism, Down syndrome, hydrocephalus, severe epilepsy, sickle cell disease, blindness, deafness or trauma from abuse. Many of those children may be turned away from other wish-granting organizations that require a life-threatening or critical diagnosis.
Bruce said he loved the entire trip and had trouble picking a favorite part.
"I enjoyed the amusement park as I've never been able to experience it," he said. "I also loved riding on electric animals and chasing my mom and Aunt Angie. It was so fun."

title: Ribbon cut for St. Michaels Community Center renovation
author: Veronica Fernandez-Alvarado
content:
Ribbon cut for St. Michaels Community Center renovation

 May 21, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Veronica Fernandez-Alvarado | Section: News 
 
 464
 Words 

 Read News Document

 ST. MICHAELS — On Monday morning, many community members gathered for the ribbon cutting ceremony for an approximately $4.5 million renovation project to help serve the community of St. Michaels.The St. Michaels Community Center has been operating for over 30 years and has provided various supports through community pantries, events, senior and adult programs, youth programs and community gardens.
Lori Morris, the center's board chair, said she is excited to continue serving the community 2,500 meals a week and distributing groceries to neighbors in need.
"The outstanding center staff, both past and current, many of whom are here, not only provided ongoing input to the design and construction process but kept as many of our programs running as possible while we were out of the building," Morris said.
The approximately 5,700-square-foot building now houses a modern commercial kitchen, two classrooms, a technology center, a gallery and upstairs offices for staff. The main level of the building will serve multiple uses, including cafe seating, a space for speakers or performances and a place where people can pick up items from the center's community pantry.
The 800-square-foot commercial kitchen will serve the new Culinary Arts & Hospitality Workforce Development Program and the center's Community Cafe, which serves chef-made meals free of charge to anyone experiencing food insecurity.
The two classrooms on the other side of the gallery will be used primarily for children's programming but also for adult programs.
A technology center will have desks and computers for different organizations and nonprofits.
During the ribbon cutting ceremony, Morris praised her predecessor Langley Shook, former chair of the board of directors.
Morris said that Shook's leadership was the foundation of the project. The renovation was his vision, and he and his wife, Karen Shook, threw themselves into the fundraising, representing the committee before the town commissioners and the Historic District Committee.
Shook spoke about the work that many put into the project and thanked everyone involved in making the community center what it is today.
"The programs have been expanded, the staff has been strengthened," Shook said. "Our fundraising has made this platform possible and successful, and I think our greatest days are yet to come."
One of the speakers, State Sen. Johnny Mautz (R-Caroline, Dorchester, Talbot, Wicomico), requested that all people who had attended St. Michaels Middle or High School come to stand with him as he presented the St. Michaels Community Center board of directors a citation in recognition for the work that was put into the community project.
"Because we do citations and we do projects, and it's part of the government doing something, but this is the will of the people," Mautz said. "This is what the town needed. This is what the town wanted, and by golly, this is what the town was going to get. So it's a great day for everybody."

 CENTREVILLE — Saturday afternoon, May 11, the Queen Anne's County Animal Services hosted their second annual volunteer celebration. The event was held again at Conquest Beach Park, just north of Centreville.Volunteer Coordinator Sarah Rondeau welcomed all who attended, thanking them for their service to the homeless animals the facility works very hard to find loving, forever homes for. Rondeau said, "You are people who are truly special. You share love with these animals that makes a difference. You're more than volunteers — you're heroes."
She was followed by Director Kelly Hamilton, who added, "We're also recognizing those who volunteer to provide foster care for these animals while we look for permanent loving homes. Last year, 390 animals were fostered. You took the pets home with you, some only for a weekend, as time would permit you to do. But, that time was well invested in each animal to keep them socially working with people until we could find them a home. Thank you, again."
Adoption and Foster Coordinator Sara Taylor was also present at the event Saturday, and played an essential role in helping find foster care homes last year.
The first ever "Paws for Heroes" Spotlight Award, was presented to QA Sheriff's Office Sgt. George Sewell for his continued work with animals, particularly dogs. Sheriff Gary Hofmann submitted Sewell's name to the Animal Services facility to be recognized.
"The intention is to recognize someone in our county each month for this award," said Hamilton. "If you know someone who is deserving, please contact Sarah Rondeau with your recommendation."
The volunteers who attended the appreciation were provided a catered lunch, music, games and encouragement to continue their good works.

title: Caroline County Public Library celebrates renovation
author: Tom McCall
content:
Caroline County Public Library celebrates renovation

 May 22, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Tom McCall | Section: Local News 
 
 505
 Words 

 Read News Document

 DENTON — Politicians, law enforcement, children and librarians all met at the Caroline County Public Library on Saturday to celebrate the completion of a years-long renovation.Over and over, people said the space feels brighter and more open. But beyond the library's physical appearance, the renovation project was designed to help the library continue to function as a hub of the community, offering a variety of programming for library patrons of different ages.
"We have got gaming stations in the teen zone and for adults we have study rooms and zoom meetings for tutoring," Nancy Pollen, a library associate said. "We make it so much fun. We have puppet programs and read to a beagle."
The group gathered for a ribbon cutting amidst the stacks of books.
Years of effort went into raising money and designing the new space. An architect of the project, Connie Kumor of RMM Architects, brought her family to the grand opening.
"A lot of the design was making the space more friendly and open," Kumor said. "When we started the project, especially the children's area, there was a big dividing wall right down the middle, and there were no restrooms for families to use while they were in this space, and the lighting levels were a bit tough for a library environment. We really wanted to open up the space for everybody and make it more inviting."
Kumor said that all the renovation work was done to the interior and that the original footprint of the building did not change. She noted that Executive Director Debbie Bennett has been planning this project for a long time, and Kumor was happy to see it completed.
Bennett, who is retiring at the end of June after decades of service, was whirling around in the midst of many wellwishers.
"This is terribly exciting," Bennett said. "We started in the fiscal year of 2019. We did a space utilization study and a design plan, then the renovation of the first floor, finally the replacement of the slate on the back pitched roof and a major upgrade on the elevator."
She said that this is one of her major legacies. It continued the effort that was started by the library founder John Hargreaves in 1961.
She also cited the Maryland State Library Capital Grant and all political support the library got from state legislators. There were also several large donations and hundreds of small donations from the community.
"We have a small but mighty Friends of the Library," Bennett said. "I asked them to raise $50,000 for furniture, which wasn't included in the grant. They raised $78,000."
Irene Padilla, the state librarian who was present at the ribbon cutting, said, "We know what a great resource this is for Caroline County. Libraries play an important role in the success of any community.
"Beyond the 1,000s of books that you have on your shelves, there is the access to computers, the internet, makerspace, printing services and a myriad of digital resources. Thank you to the professional staff. We all need their help to succeed in the 20th century."

Enjoy a story or two to learn more about areas fairies like most and why they can be so hard to find. Then we will try our own hands at building and decorating fairy homes for our elusive and magical friends to live in! We'll then take a short walk and find the perfect spot for our small shelters for fairies and other creatures to enjoy. This program is geared for children ages 2-5 and their adult companion. Sign up at https://pickeringcreek.org/programs/upcoming-programs/
WEDNESDAY MORNING ARTISTS, weekly at 9:30 a.m., 900 Peachblossom Place, Cambridge. All are welcome, from beginners to pros. There is always opportunity and something interesting to learn and see. Group shares our artwork at meetings and collaborates with many different forms of media. Artists' work displayed in the window of Vintage Venue on Race Street in Cambridge. Facebook: wednesdaymorningartists. Email is: wednesdaymorningartists@gmail.com
'OUTLAW GUNNER', 2 p.m., Talbot County Free Library, 100 W. Dover St., Easton. The Talbot Historical Society will host Joe Walsh at the Talbot County Free Library. Joe will discuss his father, Dr. Harry Walsh, and his book "The Outlaw Gunner," which has recently been republished.
BEEKEEPING FUNDAMENTALS, 1 to 2:30 p.m., Easton Family YMCA or via Zoom. Immersive two days into the fascinating and rewarding world of beekeeping. Led by local beekeeper, Jim Scoggins, this course will provide insights into the world of hobbyist, sideliner and commercial beekeepers. Two sessions, May 15 and 22, including a visit to a local apiary 7883 Fox Harbour Lane, St. Michaels. $30. To register, visit chesapeakeforum.org.
THE TALBOT COUNTY OF FREDERICK DOUGLASS, 10 to 11:30 a.m., Easton Family YMCA. What can Frederick Douglass, Talbot County's most famous native son, teach us as America continues struggling with racial divisions, the legacy of enslavement, and the quest for a just, free, and embracing society? Join Jeff McGuiness and Lance Morris in a discussion of the eloquent words penned by Douglass himself, juxtaposed against the very landscape that bore witness to the genesis of his quest for a society that transcends differences and dismantles the constancy of hate. Two sessions, May 22 and 29. $30. To register, visit chesapeakeforum.org.
'JOIN OR DIE' SCREENING, 6:30 to 8 p.m., Easton Branch, Talbot County Free Library. A screening of the documentary film "Join or Die" will spark a community conversation about the need for more people of all ages to adopt the practice of being a "joiner" in local civic organizations, clubs and volunteer corps.
BUCKETS OF WARM SPIT, 10 to 11:30 a.m., Easton Family YMCA or via Zoom. Join Raymond Vergne, M.D., as he turns his focus on the intriguing lives and careers of selected vice presidents from the 20th century. This course is the final chapter in his comprehensive series, offering a deep dive into the often overlooked but fascinating world of Vice Presidents. Three sessions, May 23, 30 and June 6. $40. To register, visit chesapeakeforum.org.
FRIDAY NIGHT DINNER, 5 to 7:30 p.m., VFW Post 5118, 355 Glebe Road, Easton. Community invited. Held every Friday.
A SENSE OF PLACE, 10 to 11:30 a.m., via Zoom. This course is a discussion and exploration of our perceived special places. It celebrates the individuality and mutability of places and times. Readings will be suggested. Participation is a requirement. Three sessions, May 17, 24 and 31. $40. To register, visit chesapeakeforum.org.
EASTON FARMERS MARKET, 8 a.m. to 1 p.m., 100 Block North Washington St., Easton. Open rain or shine. Live music at 10:30 a.m.
ST. MICHAELS FARMERS MARKET, 8:30 to 11 a.m., 206 S. Talbot St., St. Michaels. Open rain or shine.
MUSEUM OF RURAL LIFE, 11 a.m. to 4 p.m., 16 N. Second St., Denton. World War I and II, a sharecropper's cabin, new Buffalo Soldier exhibit, among many other artifacts and stories about Caroline County. A docent is on hand for tours. Free to the public. Info: carolinehistory.org or 410-479-2055 and leave a message.
YOGA CLASS, Oxford Community Center, 200 Oxford Road. 9:30 a.m. Intermediate yoga with Suzie Hurley. Info: 410-226-5904 or oxfordcc.org.
BOY BAND REVIEW, 7 p.m., Avalon Theatre, 40 E. Dover Street, Easton. Boy band tribute show. boybandreview.com.
SPRING FESTIVAL, 8 a.m. to 1 p.m., Neck District Volunteer Fire House, 954 Cook's Point Road, Cambridge, 11 miles west of Cambridge. Food, flea market, plant sales, and other vendors. title: Seniors experience a 'groovy' time at annual summit
author: ANDREA GRABENSTEIN agrabenstein@chespub.com
content:
Seniors experience a 'groovy' time at annual summit

 May 23, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: ANDREA GRABENSTEIN agrabenstein@chespub.com | Section: News 
 
 398
 Words 

 Read News Document

 CENTREVILLE — Celebrating Older Americans Month with tie dye and flowers, the Queen Anne's County Department of Community Services Area Agency on Aging presented its 19th annual Senior Summit at the 4-H Park in Centreville May 17.Grooving to a 1960s theme, seniors and members of the community were welcomed out for a day of resources, prizes, and community togetherness to recognize the contributions and influence of older adults in society.
Queen Anne's County proclaimed May 2024 as Older Americans Month and this year's theme, "Powered by Connection," highlighted the significant role social connections play in promoting the health and well-being of the local older population.
More than 40 vendors from across Talbot, Kent and Queen Anne's counties made up the summit, welcoming the community to discover programs and services and interact with the organizations that make up their community.
Booths displayed a wide variety of services within the county for seniors, including the new YMCA facility, assisted living facilities, the public library bookmobile, Queen Anne's County Emergency Services, hearing centers, funeral homes, AARP, senior centers and housing representatives, as well as local assisted living and and home care services.
Acknowledging animals are often another member of the family, Compass Regional Hospice presented information about its newest program, a Pet Remembrance Service to be held June 15 at 11 a.m. at the Millstream Park Pavilion in Centreville. More information about this bereavement program is available at compassregionalhospice.org.
The University of Maryland Shore Medical provided information about services as it prepares to welcome its new regional hospital in Easton by 2028.
Other businesses participating included Edwards Pharmacy from Centreville, Queenstown Bank, crisis response and behavioral health services, and a wide variety of entertainment — D.J. Jennifer Cox, Paracise demonstrations by Shirley McNatt, dancing with Ann Monego, as well as antique car displays. Engaging games of bingo were also held for the first time this year.
The Tri-County Ruritan provided a free lunch to all attendees ages 60 and over.
Bus shuttle services brought in attendees from neighboring retirement communities and senior centers to ensure all members of the community were included.
The annual Senior Summit continually provides a platform for connecting the community and supporting independence while addressing issues such as isolation and loneliness.
Next year's Senior Summit is already scheduled for Friday, May 16, 2025.
More information about Older Americans Month events and initiatives in Queen Anne's County can be found at www.qac.org and search Area Agency on Aging.

title: Maryland stories: College hosts Memorial Day ceremony and flag planting
author: WHIG STAFF REPORT
content:
Maryland stories: College hosts Memorial Day ceremony and flag planting

 May 24, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: WHIG STAFF REPORT | Section: News 
 
 200
 Words 

 Read News Document

 The Cecil College Student Veterans Club hosted a Memorial Day Commemoration Ceremony on the school's campus honoring those who died during war and in military service to the U.S.Cecil College faculty, staff and students were joined by the members of the local community as well as local veterans, who gathered to plant flags in memory of a veteran special to them on Monday, May 20, and Tuesday, May 21.
At noon during both ceremonies, TAPS was played. The traditional closing bugle call honored the sacrifice of those who gave their lives in defense of America.
The college also put up a "Static Flag Display" featuring the flags of different branches of the military surrounding the American flag. According to college officials, the display will remain on exhibit through Memorial Day on Monday.
Alongside the ceremony, the Student Veterans Club hosted a contest which asked community members to answer the question: "What does Memorial Day mean to me?"
Contestants were encouraged to submit written, video and photographical entries, which were reviewed by a panel of judges.
The winning entries were an essay by Gavin Roger and a drawing by Ashley Kifer, both students at Bohemia Manor High School. Both Roger and Kifer attended the event.

title: Lip Sync fundraiser nets $112,000 for shelter
author: Staff Writer
content:
Lip Sync fundraiser nets $112,000 for shelter

 May 26, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Staff Writer | Section: News 
 
 399
 Words 

 Read News Document

 EASTON — Talbot Interfaith Shelter staged a successful eighth annual Lip Sync Battle fundraiser on April 27 at the Waterfowl Building in Easton.After raising nearly $83,000 last year, Talbot Interfaith Shelter surpassed this year's $100,000 fundraising goal to the tune of $112,000 by the end of the live show. Attendees enjoyed an evening of music, laughter and joy as the community gathered to support the shelter's mission of providing shelter, stability, support and a path to success for local families and individuals in need.
This year's vibrant showcase of talent and generosity kicked off with a heartfelt thank you from shelter Executive Director Julie Lowe and hosted by crowd favorites Jayme D, Jay Hudson and Ricky Vitanovec. The distinguished panel of judges included Talbot County Commissioner and CEO of Foundation of HOPE Keasha Haythe, Easton Mayor Megan Cook and John Horner, president and chief operating officer of Easton Utilities.
Participants took the stage to deliver captivating live team lip sync performances, intercut with clips from the Online Video Competition teams — all in the spirit of raising crucial funds for the Talbot Interfaith Shelter.
Nineteen teams competed for the top fundraiser titles and the coveted Lip Sync Battle trophies. Many familiar faces returned to the stage alongside fresh talent, with notable newcomers including Playa Bowls, Rise Up Coffee and Capriotti's. All eight live show teams rocked the stage during the initial freestyle round followed by the unpredictable and hilarious roulette round.
The following teams taking home trophies at the end of the evening: Best Fundraiser (Live Show): The Country School faculty; Best Fundraiser (Online Video): Team TIS; Best Live Show Performance (tie): Black Wizard and The Country School faculty; and Best Online Video Performance: The Factory. The show was recorded and can be streamed online: talbotinterfaithshelter.org/lsb
"We are still glowing from the beautiful and uplifting experience of Lip Sync Battle 2024," Executive Director Julie Lowe said. "It's more than just a fundraiser; it's a celebration of community spirit and resilience."
The 2024 Lip Sync Battle was made possible by the support of Platinum Record Sponsor Sun Management Rising Technologies and a host of dedicated local sponsors.
Talbot Interfaith Shelter is a homeless shelter and transitional housing program based in Easton, MD and serving the five counties of the Mid-Shore (Talbot, Caroline, Dorchester, Kent, Queen Annes). To learn more about the organization and how to help, visit talbotinterfaithshelter.org or contact Julie Lowe at 410-310-2316 or julielowe@talbotinterfaithshelter.org.

 Author/Byline: PHIL REED Rotary Club of Cambridge | Section: Life 
 
 323
 Words 

 Read News Document

 Hugh Middleton, Patriot Point vice president of operations and development, and his wife, Joy, hosted a tour of Patriot Point for the Rotary Club of Cambridge. Hugh spoke about the history of the retreat and its mission."Patriot Point is the Military Bowl Foundation's 294-acre retreat that provides safe, secure and tranquil outdoor recreational retreat facility for wounded, ill and injured active duty service members, veterans and their families and caregivers who face daily struggles related to their time spent defending our great nation," he said.
Hugh said some come to hunt or fish while others come just to enjoy time away. Each group coming determines what they are looking for, and Hugh and Joy provide what is needed. Located between Madison and Taylor Island in Dorchester County, Patriot Point was formed in 2016 purchasing the property and formalized the concept of the previous owner, Jim Buggs. Buggs, a sportsman, businessman and conservationist, informally hosted recovering service members.
Since purchasing the property, significant improvements have been made to provide upgrades without losing the original rustic appearance. Most groups coming range in size with the average being about 10.
Hugh graduated from The Citadel with a degree in business administration followed by several years of experience in Naval Special Operations and multiple civilian senior management positions.
A former Navy SEAL, he had various overseas assignments. His work experience was varied after leaving the military. His first visit to Patriot Point was as a guest for a duck hunt sponsored by the Grand National Waterfowl Association. Initially as a volunteer, his passion to help wounded veterans led to his current position.
Bringing his wife on board, Joy's passion for the veteran and first responder communities made her a perfect fit for the retreat. Along with her husband, Joy's task is to provide the guests whatever is needed to make their experience positive.
Owned and operated by Patriot Point LLC, their sole member is the Military Bowl Foundation Inc., a nonprofit organization.

title: Centreville YMCA readies for outdoor pool
author: ANDREA GRABENSTEIN agrabenstein@chespub.com
content:
Centreville YMCA readies for outdoor pool

 May 28, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: ANDREA GRABENSTEIN agrabenstein@chespub.com | Section: News 
 
 397
 Words 

 Read News Document

 CENTREVILLE — Opening the newest community YMCA in Centreville in October, Robbie Gill, CEO at YMCA of the Chesapeake, presented updates to the Queen Anne's County Commissioners regarding the Queen Anne's County Family YMCA May 14.Opening with 2,400 members, as of May the YMCA now has a constant stream of 6,400 members, according to Gill.
"Being a member of the Y, you can participate at any YMCA, not only the Eastern Shore but across the county," Gill said.
The vision of the YMCA is a place for all members of the community to come together, Gill said. The YMCA does not turn anyone away due to financial limitations and currently provides about $15,000 a month in assistance, he said.
"It's a place where everyone is kind of connected," he said.
Queen Anne's County Family YMCA is estimated to reach 8,000 members by the end of 2025, and with that, Gill projected the Y to give away $400,000 in assistance a year by then.
"Which equates to about one in three folks receiving assistance in some capacity," he said
About 80 staff serve the Centreville location's approximately 1,000 daily visitors, including members, and community partner trips, including the County Active Aging Center and local schools.
"So it's a very busy place," he said.
The YMCA is currently addressing growing pains, including that only the front of the building is easily accessible by wheelchair, while most of the parking is in the facility's rear, he said.
Site work has begun for the final phase for the Centreville YMCA, which includes a rear parking area with an extension to Little Kidwell Avenue, an outdoor pool and pickleball courts, Gill said.
Total cost estimates for the pool, pavilion and the site work is about $1.8 million. The Y has raised about $800,000 of the necessary funds and is confident the remaining amount could be raised in time for a groundbreaking in September, Gill said. Opening of the YMCA's new outdoor facilities is expected in time for next Memorial Day, he said.
The entire price tag for the Centreville YMCA project was nearly $25 million through, "primarily private funding with some county help and some help from the state as well," he said.
Gill noted the project has been an excellent example of community partnership and credited local support in bringing it to fruition.
The Queen Anne's County Family YMCA is located at 210 Vincit Street Centreville, more information can be found at ymcachesapeake.org/locations/queen-annes-county-family-ymca.

title: 'Dancing Crab' christened in Sassafras paddle
author: WILL BONTRAGER wbontrager@chespub.com
content:
'Dancing Crab' christened in Sassafras paddle

 May 28, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: WILL BONTRAGER wbontrager@chespub.com | Section: State News 
 
 342
 Words 

 Read News Document

 BETTERTON — Two row clubs showed up in Betterton on May 18 to test their canoeing skills: Kent Island Outrigger Canoe Club and New Hope Canoe Club Ministry Atlantic.They had their vessels in the water despite dark clouds threatening. Two members from Philadelphia also joined the Kent Island team.
When the sun peeked out, pastor of New Hope, David Schofield blessed the maiden voyage of Kent Island's newest canoe.
Michelle Reid, president of the Kent Island team, said, "This is a great opportunity for the two clubs to come together, kick off our season, have some fun and experience the nice exercise here, and just get out there and do some paddling."
All of the canoes get a Hawaiian name, and carrying on that tradition, all affiliates formed a big circle around the new canoe and prayed over it, blessing its first time going out.
"The idea here is love and light," Schofield said. "We can all agree that's a good thing."
The name they gave it was Hula Papa'i, meaning Dancing Crab.
Once the Dancing Crab was christened, all canoes were in the water.
They traveled six miles along the Sassafras River Trail to Lloyd's Creek and back as part of their Hawaiian voyage paddle.
Doug Klepfer, a member of the Kent Island Outrigger Canoe Club, found it peaceful, enjoying nature, "spotting beautiful eagles and blue herons along the way."
The water was calm, he said, and after the rain, they had the whole river to themselves, no boat traffic.
The first journey of the Hula Papa'i (Dancing Crab) sliced through the water with great stability, quietness and speed, he said.
They returned to Betterton around 1:30 p.m., enjoying their team-building exercise.
This is one of many events planned, Klepfer said.
"We look forward to the Chesapeake Bay Paddle race around Kent Island on Saturday, July 20, offering a 35-, 10-, and 3-mile paddle with a post paddle festival to help protect the bay," he said.
The event takes place at the Kent Island Yacht Club, and everyone at all levels of experience are welcome to register, Klepfer said. For more information visit baypaddle.org

Two sessions, May 22 and 29. $30. To register, visit chesapeakeforum.org.
PLANNING FOR OUR FUTURE BEFORE IT REACHES US, 1 to 2:30 p.m., Easton Family YMCA or via Zoom. Two sessions, May 29 and June 5. $30. To register, visit chesapeakeforum.org.

Sign up at pickeringcreek.org/programs/upcoming-programs/.
BUCKETS OF WARM SPIT, 10 to 11:30 a.m., Easton Family YMCA or via Zoom. Food pantry, 4 to 7 p.m. Thursday, 7 to 9 a.m. Saturday, 10 a.m. to 1 p.m. Monday. Aaron's Place Pantry at Greensboro Connects, 111 S. Main St., side entrance.
Winter/spring storytime, 10:30 a.m. Tuesdays. North County Branch library, Greensboro. Half an our of fun songs, stories and fingerplays for early learners, up to age 5.

title: Strawberry Festival welcomes hundreds to Martin Sutton Memorial Park

content:

 Author/Byline: ANNIE HASSELGREN Special to the Star Democrat | Section: Local News 
 
 135
 Words 

 Read News Document

 RIDGELY — One of Caroline County's most popular events was well attended Sunday at Martin Sutton Memorial Park in Ridgely. This year's 43rd annual Strawberry Festival was host to a steady stream of hundreds of people and kicked off with its Strawberry Chase 5K Walk and Fun Run.The festival is the Ridgely Lions Club largest fundraiser and helps support charities and community service projects of importance to the organization.
Musical entertainment, a parade, food vendors and kids' activities kept event goers busy, entertained and well-fed. The event included a songwriters' showcase from talented artists from the Eastern Shore and beyond.
Dozens of volunteers gave their time for the fundraiser to help support the Ridgely Lions Club's mission: to help where help is needed with unmatched integrity and energy. The organization looks forward to next year's event.

title: Remembering friends and neighbors on Memorial Day
author: MAGGIE TROVATO mtrovato@chespub.com
content:
Remembering friends and neighbors on Memorial Day

 May 29, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: MAGGIE TROVATO mtrovato@chespub.com | Section: Local News 
 
 562
 Words 

 Read News Document

 CAMBRIDGE — Marine veteran and Dorchester County Council Vice President Mike Detmer has a vivid memory of a small moment that occurred while he was serving in Fallujah, Iraq in the early 2000s.Detmer was sitting on his rack, or bed, when he saw his friend and platoonmate Brad Arms enter the room shared by lance corporals and private first class Marines. Arms had just arrived back from patrolling with the infantry outside the city for multiple days. On these patrols, you could forget about hot water, phones and internet. There were no "creature comforts," as Detmer put it.
"It was a dirty and miserable place," he said. "And that was not considering the danger that was connected to it."
Detmer watched Arms enter the room that day and look toward the large and overflowing plywood trashcan.
"That trashcan would get heaped up," Detmer said. "And it would usually take a sergeant or an angry corporal coming in there and fussing at somebody to take it out and put it in the trashcan outside."
Detmer can remember Arms, who had just returned from that "dirty and miserable" patrol rotation, setting his things down and going over to take out the trash; Assuming responsibility for something he hadn't contributed to.
"Not one piece of that trash in that trashcan came from Brad Arms," Detmer said. "Brad Arms was out in hardship and danger that whole time that trashcan had filled up."
Arms, who was later killed while serving in Iraq, was one of the five fallen heroes that Detmer spoke about at a Memorial Day service hosted by American Legion Post 91 in Cambridge on Monday, May 27. Detmer also spoke about two other friends, Andy Aviles and Jesse Strong, and two Dorchester natives, Cecil "Butch" Jenkins from Taylors Island and Adam Mooney from Cambridge.
In sharing each of their stories, Detmer pointed out the similarities of the five men. They were bright and well-regarded in their communities. "The cream of the crop," he said.
Along with that, as illustrated in Detmer's story about Arms, these men were not selfish.
"They were also people who I don't believe — even knowing (the) price that they were eventually called to pay — I don't think they would have shirked it," he said.
At the American Legion on Memorial Day, prayer and song were a part of the service dedicated to those who gave their lives serving in the military. Former state senator and Post 91 Historian Richard Colburn told attendees they could "certainly" grill hotdogs and crack open a beer in the afternoon.
"But to honor those that gave us supreme sacrifice is the most important thing we can do on Memorial Day," he said.
At the service, Dorchester County Orphans Court Judge Rev. George Ames gave an invocation, the City of Cambridge Color Guard presented arms, Amy Bennett sang "The Star-Spangled Banner" and "God Bless America," Sheila Hickman read the poem "In Flanders Fields," Cole Kesselring played the bagpipes and Pastor Steve Bloodsworth gave a benediction.
At noon, the firing of a cannon indicated the American flag had been raised from half-mast, in honor of Memorial Day, and "Taps" was played.
In his speech, Detmer said that it is important to honor and memorialize fallen heroes through holding these events, creating physical monuments dedicated to them and telling their stories.
"Understand that these sons and daughters of these families, they were our friends and neighbors too," he said.

Embark on a fun journey through time and horsepower with our exclusive "Car Talk" tour of the Classic Motor Museum of St. Michaels. This immersive experience offers a unique opportunity to delve into the captivating world of automotive history, featuring a curated collection of vintage cars spanning from the iconic Model T to the sleek Mustang and Stingray. $35. To register, visit chesapeakeforum.org.

Join experts Gordan Fronk and Elena Sallitto as they demystify estate and elder planning, ensuring that you are well-prepared for the future. "Planning for Our Future Before It Reaches Us," delves into the intricate world of estate and elder law to safeguard your assets, make informed decisions, and prioritize the well-being of your loved ones. Two sessions, May 29 and June 5. $30. To register, visit chesapeakeforum.org.
POPLAR ISLAND TALK, 10 to 11:30 a.m., Easton Family YMCA or via Zoom. Learn about Poplar Island's unique story and continuing habitat successes in this talk given by Kristina Motley from Maryland Environmental Service. Poplar Island is an environmental restoration project located in the Chesapeake Bay of Talbot County, Maryland. The beneficial use project, started in the 1990's, relies on dredged material collected from the approach channels to the Baltimore Harbor to restore lost remote island habitat within the Chesapeake Bay. Two sessions, Wednesday June 5, and a field trip Monday, June 10, to Poplar Island from 9 a.m. to noon. $40. To register, visit chesapeakeforum.org.
BUCKETS OF WARM SPIT, 10 to 11:30 a.m., Easton Family YMCA or via Zoom. Join Raymond Vergne, M.D., as he turns his focus on the intriguing lives and careers of selected vice presidents from the 20th century. This course is the final chapter in his comprehensive series, offering a deep dive into the often overlooked but fascinating world of Vice Presidents. Three sessions, May 23, 30 and June 6. $40. Join experts Gordan Fronk and Elena Sallitto as they demystify estate and elder planning, ensuring that you are well-prepared for the future. "Planning for Our Future Before It Reaches Us," delves into the intricate world of estate and elder law to safeguard your assets, make informed decisions, and prioritize the well-being of your loved ones. Two sessions, May 29 and June 5. $30. To register, visit chesapeakeforum.org.
POPLAR ISLAND TALK, 10 to 11:30 a.m., Easton Family YMCA or via Zoom. Learn about Poplar Island's unique story and continuing habitat successes in this talk given by Kristina Motley from Maryland Environmental Service. Poplar Island is an environmental restoration project located in the Chesapeake Bay of Talbot County, Maryland. The beneficial use project, started in the 1990's, relies on dredged material collected from the approach channels to the Baltimore Harbor to restore lost remote island habitat within the Chesapeake Bay. Two sessions, Wednesday June 5, and a field trip Monday, June 10, to Poplar Island from 9 a.m. to noon. $40. To register, visit chesapeakeforum.org.
BUCKETS OF WARM SPIT, 10 to 11:30 a.m., Easton Family YMCA or via Zoom. Join Raymond Vergne, M.D., as he turns his focus on the intriguing lives and careers of selected vice presidents from the 20th century. This course is the final chapter in his comprehensive series, offering a deep dive into the often overlooked but fascinating world of Vice Presidents. Three sessions, May 23, 30 and June 6. $40. title: Beloved school crossing guard retires after 54 years
author: KONNER METZ kmetz@chespub.com
content:
Beloved school crossing guard retires after 54 years

 June 12, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: KONNER METZ kmetz@chespub.com | Section: Local News 
 
 491
 Words 

 Read News Document

 EASTON — For 54 years, when school let out, Charles Jenkins worked his magic, directing traffic and ensuring Easton Middle School students walked home safely.Tuesday morning was unique, though, as the longtime crossing guard was honored for his last day on the job, waving to hundreds of cars, trucks and buses at the intersection of S. Washington Street and Peachblossom Road.
"I'm gonna miss every bit of it because I've been doing it all my life," Jenkins, who is best known by his nickname 'Nut,' said. "Just like starting driving your first time, you want to keep right on driving. That's what I felt about this.
"I've enjoyed every bit of it, working with the community and working with my fine officers and everything. …(I) give them respect, and they give me respect."
Jenkins, 81, has 54 years of service at schools in Easton, along with over 20 years in the St. Michaels community on the weekends. He's been manning the intersection for decades, managing the chaotic, busy scene of buses departing, students walking home and parents picking up their children.
"Wait 'til I tell them to go, don't go on your own," Jenkins said of his longtime message to the students. "Wait until I turn around to tell you to go, but they're great for that. They really do (listen)."
Josepha Price and Carla Beavers, who each have children that just wrapped up sixth grade at EMS, led an effort to honor Jenkins Tuesday morning. Price and Beavers worked with the school's Family Teacher Organization to have students and parents drop off cards.
They energized a large part of the Easton community prior to Tuesday morning with a Facebook post, which garnered hundreds of likes, and a wealth of appreciation for what Jenkins has done for pedestrian safety in Easton.
"He's tough on us parents that drive, but so soft and enthusiastic to our children," Price wrote. "You know wherever he is, the kids will be safe, and I can't think of any greater purpose than protecting children."
As Easton Middle's early dismissal on its last day commenced, Price and others held up "Honk for Mr. Jenkins" signs in front of the Idlewild Park fountain, down the street from the school. Some students walked over to embrace Jenkins and say goodbye.
Once dismissal finished, EMS administrators, teachers and staff all walked down to the intersection to greet Jenkins, who was accompanied by one of his two daughters.
"They all respect me and everything with my work, and I respect all of them by being here," Jenkins said.
In 2022, he was presented a Governor's Citation by former Gov. Larry Hogan for his dedication to keeping the community safe.
Jenkins' plans moving forward are to spend time with his daughters and "take it easy and relax."
"I just wish I was 30 years younger," Jenkins said.
When asked if he would do it all over again for another 50-plus years, the beloved crossing guard had no hesitation.
"If I could, I really would," Jenkins said.

author: Staff Writer
content:
Rotary Clubs unite for Men's Clothing Drive to empower communities

 June 12, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Staff Writer | Section: Local News

 The Rotary Club of Kent Island, in collaboration with Rotary Clubs in Denton, Centerville, Chestertown and Easton, alongside partners including the Queen Anne's County Chamber of Commerce, Tides of Grace and Grasonville Community Center, announced a transformative initiative aimed at making a difference in the lives of men in need.From June 1 to July 31, these organizations will join forces to conduct a men's clothing drive to support the work of Sharp Dressed Men.
The drive seeks donations of dry-cleaned suits, sports coats, slacks, ties, laundered dress shirts, dress shoes and belts. Additionally, clothing that has not been laundered or dry cleaned will be accepted, with arrangements made to have items cleaned at local cleaners and laundries.
Sharp Dressed Men, renowned for its commitment to empowering individuals through professional attire, will be hosting an event at the Grasonville Community Center on Aug. 2. The clothing collected during the drive will directly support this event, providing men with the attire and confidence they need to pursue employment opportunities and achieve self-sufficiency.
"This collaborative effort embodies the spirit of community and compassion," said Candi Cook, president of the Rotary Club of Kent Island. "By coming together with our fellow Rotarians and esteemed partners, we have the opportunity to make a meaningful impact on the lives of men in our communities, helping them take strides toward a brighter future."
Individuals interested in supporting this initiative or seeking further information are encouraged to reach out via email at rotaryofkentisland@gmail.com.

title: Maryland couple celebrates 70th wedding anniversary
author: Jane Bellmyer jbellmyer@ceciwlhig.com
content:
Maryland couple celebrates 70th wedding anniversary

 June 14, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Jane Bellmyer jbellmyer@ceciwlhig.com | Section: News 
 
 645
 Words 

 Read News Document

 When Wayne Smythe and Joan Bines got married 70 years ago today, Dwight David Eisenhower was president, On the Waterfront was big at the box office, Sh-Boom by The Crew Cuts was the hot song on the radio and the first Jonas Salk polio vaccines were being administered.He was 20 and she was 16 when they stood before The Rev. Jack Patterson at Hopewell United Methodist Church in Port Deposit and got married.
"My father was strict," Joan recalled. "I wasn't allowed past the sidewalk after 8 p.m."
So the young couple eloped June 14, 1954. They had been dating about a year.
"I met him through his cousin," Joan said. "I think we clicked right away." Dating meant driving around, talking and going out to dinner.
"We'd go to the one (restaurant) in North East and one in Chesapeake City," Wayne recalled.
"The one in North East you could sit and watch them cook through the window," Joan added.
Then came 'The Day.'
"I proposed to him," Joan said. It was one of several days she had ditched school to hang out with Wayne.
"I was just being silly. I asked if he'd marry me. He said, 'yeah,'" Joan said, adding, "I wasn't expecting that."
For the wedding, Joan wore a dress from her own closet.
"I snuck off wearing a dress I already had," she said. "It was a purple dress with a black bolero and black suede shoes."
She also wore a white corsage; a gift from Wayne.
Wayne wore his uniform. He was in the US Air Force from 1953 to 1957. Trained as an aircraft mechanic during the Korean War, he spent 15 months in the Philippines and also served in the Formosa Islands, among other stops.
"It was good to see what other people lived like," Wayne said of his service years. "They didn't like the U.S. and they still don't."
After a short honeymoon in the Poconos, the couple lived with her cousins — Gert and Frankie Bines — for a time before buying their first home.
"We found a little house on Richmond Street (in Perryville) for $4,000," Wayne said. "When we had that house we used to have all the kids over with big dinners."
Those five kids led to 12 grandchildren and now 26 great grandchildren. Big family dinners are a thing of the past.
Except for the house Wayne built in Port Deposit near Burlin Road, the couple has always lived in Perryville.
From Port Deposit, they moved into Joan's parents' house for 43 years, then into a smaller rancher about 15 years ago.
"This has everything on one floor," Joan noted.
The secret of their success
According to the American Psychological Association, more than 30% of first marriages end in divorce.
So how have the Smythes made it to 70 years?
"No arguments over money," Wayne said simply. "Money is what breaks a lot of people up. I brought home all the paychecks to her."
"With a large item to buy, we'd discuss it," he added.
Joan worked until she had their first child, Joanne, when she was 18. After Wayne Jr, Douglas, Michelle and Jennifer were old enough, she went back to work while Wayne worked as many as four jobs. That included his own oil burner service company.
"I raised a bunch of kids. He worked all the time," she said. "It has paid off."
He did have some fun in between all those working hours.
"He bought an old bakery truck and turned it into a camper," Joan said, remembering all those fun trips as a family.
"I used to have classic cars," Wayne added. The one he admits to missing the most is a 1962 Chevrolet Corvette. "I also had a Ford Coupe, a Mercury and a Thunderbird."
Now as they approach their Platinum Anniversary, Wayne looked back and commented he was "just a plain country boy" when he and Joan got married, and they have had a good marriage.
"I have no regrets in my life," Wayne said.

title: Cat lovers, groups work to save feral cats
author: KONNER METZ kmetz@chespub.com
content:
Cat lovers, groups work to save feral cats

 June 16, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: KONNER METZ kmetz@chespub.com | Section: Local News 
 
 628
 Words 

 Read News Document

 EASTON — Up and down the Eastern Shore, "cat colonies" thrive. Feral cats exist in groups that live in a specific location with a reliable food source, such as a farm, and often have serious health problems.At Talbot Humane, Laura Koeneman, adoption and foster coordinator, and Nancy Benner, program coordinator, head up a "TNR" program meant to encourage people to trap, neuter and return feral cats.
"There's absolutely tons of research over the years about how bringing feral cats in and euthanizing does not help at all," Benner said. "TNR'ing, the numbers go down."
Talbot Humane offers help with trapping cats and encourages those unfamiliar to contact the organization for tips and tricks. "All of us have struggled with trapping cats before," Koeneman said.
Then, cats are spayed or neutered, as Talbot Humane hosts a clinic each Thursday, where Benner works to schedule as many as possible. The group typically takes in kittens and cats from Talbot and Dorchester, as there's a noticeable gap in services in the latter county.
"I have people from Dorchester County that have standing appointments," Benner said. "There are a bunch of ladies that are just going around, trapping cats because there's a huge problem there."
Once fixed, Koeneman and Benner both emphasized the importance that the cats are returned to their original homes if it's safe. Talbot Humane removes ear tips as a universal sign to signify feral cats that have been brought in.
SAVING A FERAL CATWhen Karla Wieland-Cherry first met her cat Tom, he was bloody and infested with fleas, in desperate need of care.
He had been living in a chicken manure shed on a farm, eating raw, dead chicken and living with feral cats. He was brought to Snip Tuck, an organization in Secretary that fights against feline overpopulation, where Wieland-Cherry volunteers.
After Tom was neutered, Wieland-Cherry asked the owner of the property that Tom was living at if she could keep him. The owner agreed, and Wieland-Cherry brought Tom in, though he was not socialized to humans.
"He was one that really needed a home," Wieland-Cherry said. "He was dripping in blood from complete flea infestation. When I talk about red, I mean red, blood red."
Almost two years later, Tom is perfectly accustomed to people and lives inside Wieland-Cherry's home in Trappe, with many other feline friends — 25 to be exact. It wasn't an easy process domesticating him, though, as Wieland-Cherry spent about a year building a routine and rapport with the young, American shorthair.
"One day, I reached my finger, I touched his cheek and started petting him," she said. "He kind of pulled away and gave me this look. … He didn't eat my finger, so that was a good sign."
AVOIDING EUTHANASIAWhile Tom's transition from feral cat to lovable pet is impressive, it "isn't the norm," Koeneman said. Most feral cats Talbot Humane sees cannot be domesticated, meaning the best option is to return them to their familiar area. Or else, euthanasia is a possibility.
"It's not humane to euthanize perfectly healthy cats just because they aren't socialized," Koenaman said. "… They live perfectly long, healthy lives just like indoor cats."
Sometimes, kittens come in at around 6 weeks or younger, an age where they can still be socialized. Wieland-Cherry is one of Talbot Humane's volunteers that takes in "spicy kittens," ones that have feral tendencies but can be changed.
Benner and Koeneman said that most people are receptive to understanding that most adult cats are better off being fixed and returned, rather than living through a "high level of stress" in the center.
"The only times that we have issues with that is if the people in that area if they're making threats that they may hurt the animals," Koeneman said. "Or have expressed that if we don't keep them, they're just going to kill them."

title: Leo Club makes a roar with Queen Anne's County teens
author: ANDREA GRABENSTEIN agrabenstein@chespub.com
content:
Leo Club makes a roar with Queen Anne's County teens

 June 16, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: ANDREA GRABENSTEIN agrabenstein@chespub.com | Section: Local News 
 
 368
 Words 

 Read News Document

 QUEENSTOWN — With a focus on youth involvement, Queenstown Lions Club welcomes younger generations to serve their community with the introduction of its Leo Club, a teen-based club.LEO stands for "leadership, experience and opportunity" and seeks to foster commitment to community service for younger members.
The youth group assists in main Lions Club events while taking charge of its own unique activities including fundraising, according to Queenstown Lions Club President Crystal Sipes.
"It's all about building leadership, giving them experiences, and getting their foot in the door," she said.
The Leo Club started in January as an extension of the Lions Club for younger members when current Lions realized they had younger family members seeking involvement, Sipes said.
The Leos have been at the forefront of events including the Ronald McDonald House Red Shoe Shuffle and community fairs and festivals, Sipes said.
The Queenstown Leo Club is growing and currently consists of about 10 members who are students at the Gunston School and Kent Island High School, dedicated to lending a hand throughout their community.
The Leo Club meets twice a month at the Queenstown Moose Lodge and is always looking for additional teens to join the hardworking community fun, Sipes said.
Upcoming events spearheaded by the Leos include a supply drive in June planned to benefit Chesapeake Cats and Dogs and Haven Ministries as well as plans for a bingo fundraiser to benefit St. Jude Children's Hospital in October.
The Leo Club is a prime opportunity for students to achieve community service hours and build pride in their community, all while they give assistance to those who truly need it, Sipes said.
"It's all about giving back," she said.
Chartered in 1935, the Queenstown Lions Club is one of the oldest continuous community service organizations on Maryland's Eastern Shore and will soon be celebrating its 90th anniversary, Sipes said.
The Leos will also be available during the Queen Anne's County 4-H Fair Aug. 12 -17.
Sipes encouraged anyone interested to check out the Leo Club at various upcoming events including the Queenstown fire carnival and stop by to see what the group is all about for themselves.
Information on how to be part of the Queenstown Leo Club can be found by contacting Crystal Sipes at 410-739-6038 or sipeschester@atlanticbb.net.

author: WILL BONTRAGER wbontrager@chespub.com
content:
Torch Run sees LEOs and community out in support of Special Olympics

 June 19, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: WILL BONTRAGER wbontrager@chespub.com | Section: Local News

 CHESTERTOWN — On Monday, the police were out on the streets.Officers participated in the Law Enforcement Torch Run for Special Olympics as athletes prepared for the summer games at Towson University on June 22 to 24.
The Torch Run is the largest public awareness vehicle and grassroots fundraiser for the Special Olympics. The law enforcement members are called Guardians of the Flame, and annually more than 100,000 officers carry the "flame of hope."
Senior Director of Special Events Betsy Jiron said the police run so that over 2,000 athletes can compete at the games completely free.
Jiron added participants walking/running will join police all over the state to light the cauldron that ushers in the summer games.
This year, troopers from the Chestertown Police Department, the Kent County Sheriff's Office, Queen Anne's County Sheriff's Office, employees from Washington College, the Department of Social Services and the Steve Meehan Law Firm all tied up their sneakers.
Bright and early at 9 a.m., they ran, walked, and took turns carrying the special torch and waving the flag representing the torch run. Their route consisted of High Street, Mill Street, then along the Wayne Gilchrist Trail to Wilmer Park, their destination.
After that, the tourch was brought by boat to Elkton Police Department Ofc. Anthony Devine in Cecil County.

title: Train Station tells charming history of the 'Dream City'
author: KONNER METZ kmetz@chespub.com
content:
Train Station tells charming history of the 'Dream City'

 June 19, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: KONNER METZ kmetz@chespub.com | Section: Local News 
 
 535
 Words 

 Read News Document

 RIDGELY — Railroad tracks, antique glass train station windows and old ticket stubs are all part of the historical charm on West Railroad Avenue in Ridgely, where the town's 1892 railroad station is preserved.Owned by the Town of Ridgely, the station is maintained by the Ridgely Historical Society. The nonprofit group hosts tours of the station on the first Saturday of each month.
Ridgely Historical Society President Cathy Schwab and her husband, Rick, are heavily involved in the upkeep and tours.
The role of historian wasn't something Cathy ever expected when they moved to Ridgely in 2004.
"We have become very attached to this building," she said, adding that the society has a "good rapport with the town."
Originally tailored for passengers, Ridgely Train Station fit into the town's hope of becoming a booming city on the East Coast. But developers from the Maryland and Baltimore Land Association failed financially in the early 1900s, and the town never became the "Dream City" many had envisioned.
Ridgely was a hotspot for the growing and shipping of strawberries by the crate up to cities like Wilmington and New York. "This town exploded during picking season," Cathy Schwab said.
The station closed in 1976, but the building remained, housing businesses and the Ridgely Town Hall in the 1990s.
During tours, Schwab takes guests through the station's history, adding in surprising facts about its surroundings when Ridgely was being developed with a big city feel in mind. Guests get to explore inside the station — which includes two rooms and a ticket booth space — and learn about the many preserved artifacts.
Schwab said the late James Owen Knotts "JOK" Walsh was critical in restoration of the train station. Walsh, who died last July, was the president of the Caroline County Historical Society and helped secure a grant from the State Highway Administration.
"We were all devastated," Schwab said. "He had such a memory… He inspired us."
Originally, the restoration project looked to receive grant funding from the Highway Administration as a visitor's center in 2010. Schwab said when they came back to the state in 2013 and applied for a Transportation Alternative Program grant as an interpretive center, the state was more receptive.
It created the need for a quick turnaround for the Ridgely Historical Society, as the goal was to have the restoration complete by the town's 150th anniversary in 2017.
Restoration included conducting a paint analysis for the station's original colors, installing air conditioning and a bathroom, and cleaning up the outside of the station itself to make it more presentable.
Before receiving the grant for the station, Ridgely Historical Society also worked on restoring a red caboose adjacent to the train station building. Built in 1931, the caboose is originally from Reading, Pennsylvania and was donated to the town in 2006.
There's still work to be done at the station, Schwab says. But for such a small town, a captivating and unique history continues to be uncovered at and around Ridgely's railroad.
"Ridgely has a lot to offer," Schwab said. "... We have not even scratched the surface."
The next open tour of the Ridgely Train Station is Saturday, July 6, from 10 a.m. to 1 p.m. For questions or to schedule a personal tour, contact Cathy Schwab at 410-991-8225.
