title: Fair Food: What in the world are watermelon fries?
author: Carl Hamilton cahamilton@chespub.com
content:
Fair Food: What in the world are watermelon fries?

 July 26, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Carl Hamilton cahamilton@chespub.com | Section: News 
 
 1463
 Words 

 Read News Document

 FAIR HILL — Watermelon fries are like regular fries — in name and shape only.Contrary to what they are called, watermelon fries are not fried (nor baked, broiled, roasted, seared, grilled or cooked in any fashion whatsoever). They are cool to the touch.
Watermelon fries look like fries because of their finger-like shape and because those strips are served in a little, cardboard basket.
Those strips, however, are made out of watermelon — not potatoes — and they are dipped into a small container of strawberry yogurt — not ketchup — before every bit. And it's probably not a good idea to shake salt onto watermelon fries (Editor's note: We acknowledge, of course, that there is no accounting for personal preference.)
It's also important to note that watermelon fries are pinkish-red in color — not golden, tannish-yellow in hue.
With all of that said, the watermelon-fries menu item is an example of some of the interesting food choices offered at the Cecil County Fair, which started on Friday (July 19) and runs through Sunday.
Watermelon fries is the brainchild of Dan McGrath, who owns and operates the Real Deal food truck. Watermelon fries are sold during the fair at a Real Deal vending tent that is beside the Real Deal food truck.
"It's usually hot at the fair, so he was looking for something refreshing and different and came up with watermelon fries. This is the first year," outlined North East-area resident Alicia Sipe who, along with her husband, Dan, operated the watermelon fries tent on Wednesday night. "It's also a healthier alternative to other foods."
Watermelon fries sales have been OK, according to Sipe, who referred to fairgoers in general and opined, "They don't understand what they are."
Granted, watermelon fries certainly are a tad unusual when compared to the standard fair food, such as thin-crust carnival pizza slices, Italian sausage brimming with fried onions and green peppers on a sub roll, hotdogs, hamburgers, cheesesteaks, funnel cake and ice cream.
But watermelon fries, as it turns out, isn't the only food that causes double-takes and even some grinding halts to make inquiries when attendees see the item listed on a vending tent or food truck menu while walking on the fairgrounds.
"Yeah, there's some weird stuff out there," chuckled Cyn Marie Schafer, whose Cyn Marie Concessions is next to the Real Deal watermelon fries tent.
Not too far out there, either, geographically speaking.
"We have deep-fried pickles," Schafer said. "We make ours with fresh batter and we put a little hot sauce in that batter. We use pickle spears to make ours. We coat the pickle spears in the batter and then deep fry them. Each serving comes with ranch dressing, so you can dip the fried pickle spear in the dressing."
She acknowledged that fried pickles are nothing new under the sun, before explaining that Cyn Marie Concessions puts its own spin on the culinary creation. "The fried pickles you get at restaurants are breaded, round pickle chips that are frozen. We make our own fresh batter and the hot sauce in it makes them just a little bit spicy, but not overly."
Looking for something different, Schafer came up with the recipe a few years ago. Schafer admitted that she had some reservations while attempting to create a dish that would appeal to other palates, not necessarily her own.''
"I honestly thought it would be gross," said Schafer, who was pleasantly surprised with the result.
There has been some trial-and-error along the way, according to Schafer, who commented, "The first couple of years, we tried putting Hershey's chocolate syrup on the fried pickles." That sweet option did not attract many followers, though. But that's OK because Cyn Marie Concessions' version of the deep-fried Oreo cookie is quite popular. A deep-fried Oreo cookie was a cutting-edge specialty years ago, but now is pretty common.
(Schafer owns and operates Cyn Marie Concessions with her husband, Wayne, who also has owned and operated a Pennsylvania-based barbecue catering company called Big Fat Daddy's since 1982.)
Then there are the hugely-popular loaded baked potatoes sold at the Gifford's Farm stand, which can be found simply by looking for the longest line of customers on the fairgrounds. (Service is swift, and the lines move very fast.)
Sure, loaded baked potatoes can be found at many places in and outside Maryland, even at some fast food restaurants. But they likely pale in comparison to the overstuffed versions made by the Gifford family and their helpers.
The baked potatoes used to make the dish are roughly the size of Idaho. (Editor's note: Slight exaggeration there.)
The names of the varieties of stuffed baked potatoes include Maryland Loaded and Piggy Potato. For those with an appetite surpassing the satiation that would be provided by the colossal Piggy Potato, there is the Double Piggy Potato. It features melted butter, cheese, pork BBQ, bacon, Old-Bay corn, sour cream and chives. It weighs about 50 pounds. (Editor's note: Another slight exaggeration.)
"We've already had one this week, and we're back again," said Elkton resident Christy Kluh on Wednesday night as she and her husband, Tom, waited in line at the Gifford's Farm loaded potato stand.
There were at least 25 people ahead of them in line, but Tom and Christy were not discouraged as they kept their eyes on the prize.
"It moves pretty fast, and it's worth it," Kluh said, breaking into a smile.
Kelly Gifford, one of the family members working steadily to serve the crowd, told the Cecil Whig that the stand would go through 120 cases of spuds during the week-long Cecil County Fair, which translates to approximately 5,000 big potatoes. (Sweet potato versions of the loaded potato also are offered.)
Providing more information to show the briskness of the loaded potato business during the fair, Kelly's sister, Kacey Gifford, reported that the stand was expected to use 600 pounds of sour cream.
Gifford's Farm & Feed on Joseph Biggs Highway (Route 274) near Rising Sun typically sells the loaded baked potatoes for a limited time in the fall, when the farm's beautiful sunflower fields are in bloom, and once again during the annual week-long Cecil County Fair.
Unlike the Kruhs, North East-area resident Mark Bowers ate his first Gifford's Farm loaded baked potato on Wednesday night, after wondering what all the buzz was about.
"I heard about this and had to try it," Bowers said, some four or five hearty forkfuls into his Maryland Loaded. "It's good."
Brian Williams described eating a Gifford's Farm loaded potato as a "Cecil County Fair rite of passage" and noted that the loaded baked potato's good reputation precedes it.
"I break food down into two categories: Convenience and destination. The Gifford's Farm loaded baked potato is definitely one of those destination foods for the fair or for anywhere. People will travel specifically to get one," Williams opined.
That is a pretty big compliment, too, because Williams is quite knowledgeable about preparing delicious food that makes customers come back for more. Williams and his wife, Natalie, own and operate the popular CRAVE Eatery in Elkton and the equally-popular CRAVE food truck, which is stationed on the fairgrounds this week, selling its style of smash burgers, tacos and other dishes.
Beneath a canopy beside that food truck, CRAVE also is selling fresh limeades prepared in an interesting way. Instead of putting the limes in a conventional blender, which typically is powered by electricity and uses metal agitators to break down the limes, Natalie Williams and other servers place the limes into a pneumatic blender, which uses compressed air to do the job.
Generally speaking, a conventional blender pulverizes whatever is put into it — limes, in this case — while a pneumatic blender gently presses the limes.
"It (the pneumatic blender) presses the lime but doesn't break it down. Breaking it down causes oil and flavor to escape. Pressing the lime keeps the oil and flavor," Natalie explained, noting that mashing the limes results in a bolder lime flavor after the juice and pressed limes are mixed with other ingredients, including ice and water, to create the limeade.
Now back to those watermelon fries or, more specifically, the guy who came up with the idea to make them.
Dan McGrath created watermelon fries so he Real Deal business would have a cool, healthier item on the menu. But make no mistake, the Real Deal food truck sells Italian sausage smothered in fried onions and green peppers and similar foods more in line with typical fair fare.
Real Deal also sells a pretty interesting dish called The Mac Attack, which is listed on the menu as a "fair special." It features the Real Deal potato stacker topped with nacho cheese, macaroni and cheese, pulled pork and barbecue sauce and, by all accounts, it is quite delicious and super filling.
The Mac Attack is hot and gigantic and, compared to watermelon fries, it clearly falls on the other end of the food spectrum.

While mentions of business practices and entertainment elements exist, the core subject is the Cecil County Fair as a local cultural and social phenomenon.

title: Chrome City fundraiser revs up Benedictine's Ridgely campus
author: Tom McCall
content:
Chrome City fundraiser revs up Benedictine's Ridgely campus

 July 30, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Tom McCall | Section: Local News 
 
 392
 Words 

 Read News Document

 RIDGELY — On July 27, Benedictine School held its 22nd annual Chrome City Fundraiser. The event drew hundreds of car and motorcycle enthusiasts. There were many Chevys and Harleys all polished up.Spectators paid $35 to take in the custom cars, classic cars, hot rods and motorcycles, and event proceeds went to support the school and its mission. Each person who registered got a Chrome City t-shirt.
There was live music by the "Stoneflies," a Paul Reed Smith employee band, and a guitar signed by Mark Tremonti of Creed to be raffled off.
Megan Efland, director of supply chain for Paul Reed Smith said, "We are here to support Benedictine School. Our COO has a son who is a student here. It is a great cause."
PRS had a few entries, including a vintage Rolls Royce and a BMW motorcycle, in the competition too.
There were many food trucks serving up delicious offerings including lobsters, shaved ice and barbecue.
Scott Evans, Benedictine's executive director said, "We can't hold these events without sponsorship and the support of other community members. We also can't hold this event without volunteers."
He noted the success of the event, saying it raised over $100,000 last year to support the non-sectarian service provider that cares for individuals with developmental disabilities and autism.
"The support for this event continues to grow," Evans said. "New people learn about Benedictine. We have people who come out that don't know anything about our mission or what we do, but it is important to get them on campus, because we are so remote.
"They can see the people we support and interact with our students," Evans said. "My favorite part is walking around and seeing the cars and bikes. It is like I am a little kid."
The judges of the car and motorcycle show were Jack and William Higginbottom.
Best in Show winners were awarded a gold statue. The Best in Show motorcycle was a 1949 Vindian Replica Chief prototype owned by Bill and Debra Bugaj. The Best in Show car was a 1938 Packard Model Eight owned by Craig and Diane Postlewait of St. Michaels.
Sponsors of the event included: A.H. Hatcher, Acruise, Blue Ruin, Bullocks Deli, Choptank, Coast Country Cares with Spicer Bros, Fresh Air Concepts, The Jetty, Koons Easton Toyota, Pepsi Bottling Ventures, PRS Guitars, Queenstown Bank, Red Knights Motorcycle Club, South Corrosion, Dukes-Moore Insurance Agency, Torchio Architects, and PepUp.

title: Sense of Wonder
author: Carl Hamilton cahamilton@chespub.com
content:
Sense of Wonder

 August 2, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Carl Hamilton cahamilton@chespub.com | Section: Sense Of Wonder 
 
 727
 Words 

 Read News Document

 NORTH EAST — I stopped in my tracks and chuckled when I saw 10-year-old Cooper Ambruster and his two companions in a grocery store aisle at the North East Walmart the other day."So what's this all about?" I playfully asked Cooper.
Without missing a beat, Cooper answered, "I'm 30."
And that was the extent of the explanation given by Cooper, whose youthful face was accented by a mustache, goatee, sideburns and a unibrow — all dark black, all made of felt.
The faces of his 4-year-old brother, Cullen, and Cooper's friend, Kamryn Johnson, 12, had been accessorized in similar fashion.
There is a little backstory, according to Tiffeny Pietro, who is Cooper and Cullen's mom and who, evidently, is a kid at heart.
"I bought a bag of 200 mustaches. I thought it would be fun to have them around," she said, noting that felt sideburns, goatees and eyebrows of different styles also were inside the bag.
Unable to resist, Pietro had applied one of those fake mustaches to her face earlier that day before entering a family room where Cooper, Cullen and Kamryn were playing on their electronic devices.
Deeply immersed in their activities, the boys were oblivious.
"I said, 'Is there something on my face? I feel like there is something on my face.' I kept trying to get them to look up from their electronic devices," Pietro recalled.
When she asked the question again, the boys looked up and noticed the mustachioed woman in the room.
"They put their electronic devices down and started laughing," she said.
With their electronic devices lying nearby, essentially forgotten by the youngsters, they sampled the assortment of fake facial hairpieces.
And what followed was some old-fashioned fun.
"They spent the next 45 minutes getting in front of the mirror and putting on the mustaches and cracking up," Pietro said.
A little bit later, she informed the boys that she was going grocery shopping at Walmart and that they had to accompany her.
It's important to note that the boys had been in tow on countless trips to Walmart in the past and that a grocery store is a boring place for a kid, especially on a sunny day amid summer vacation.
But it's equally important to note that children are blessed with a sense of wonder. It often enables them to excitedly look forward to something — even a mundane thing like grocery shopping with an adult.
"They said, 'Can we wear them in the Walmart?' They were so excited about it," Pietro said.
Pietro gave the boys permission.
"The pharmacist was the first one who noticed them. We went through the drive-thru because Cullen was asleep at that point," Pietro said. "The pharmacist asked me, 'Do you have some sophisticated, refined gentlemen with you?'"
That playful comment sparked laughter from the boys.
"That's exactly what they were looking for — to get noticed," Pietro said.
And that was just the beginning. During the shopping trip, several smiling customers noticed the trio of "sophisticated, refined gentlemen."
As I had mentioned earlier, I was one of those shoppers who noticed the comically incognito youngsters. I identified myself as a Cecil Whig reporter to Pietro, and then, after receiving her permission, I took photos of the boys.
I wasn't precisely sure why I felt the need to do so.
Although I'm a little jaded after writing predominantly about crime for the past 40 years, I still sensed in some indescribable way that there was some sort of story there — something bigger than meets the eye, maybe something even magical.
Searching myself for the answer in the days that followed, I started thinking about when I was a kid, and then it hit me: some of my really good childhood memories aren't linked to major events.
Instead, the source of some of my fondest childhood recollections are those seemingly trivial pockets of time that materialized out of nothing.
Like that massive, super fun kick-the-can game beneath the corner streetlight one warm evening when, only an hour or so earlier, no neighborhood kids seemed to be around. And like that bike ride I took with friends in a gentle, steady summer rain while wearing, for no particular reason, dish rags on our heads.
And hopefully Cooper, Cullen and Kamryn will look back someday, decades from now, and smile as they remember that summer day when they were "sophisticated, refined gentlemen" in the local Walmart.
Pietro holds that same hope.
"Absolutely, this will be a very good memory for them," she said.

title: 'Everything burned to pieces but our Bible is completely intact': Woman credits faith with family surviving fire.
author: WILL BONTRAGER wbontrager@chespub.com
content:
'Everything burned to pieces but our Bible is completely intact': Woman credits faith with family surviving fire.

 August 2, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: WILL BONTRAGER wbontrager@chespub.com | Section: News 
 
 496
 Words 

 Read News Document

 What could have been even more of a tragic event from a fire was prevented by divine intervention, Kay Markow said.On the morning of July 25, at Duck Neck Campground, she, along with her 12-week-old daughter and siblings, and her mother Jessica, escaped their burning camper, receiving no injuries.
But they lost everything else, she added.
The entire 30-foot aluminum structure with attached living quarters was reduced to ash.
No, not everything, Markow corrected.
"Everything burned to pieces but our Bible is completely intact," she replied.
She credits her faith in Jesus Christ for their escape.
And even as they're uncertain to where they're laying their head down, Markow's keeping her spirits up.
"God is good," she exclaimed.
She also thanked others who helped them including members of her church, Grace Apostolic in Kennedyville, residents from the Duck Neck Campground along with Felix Property and the fire department.
The fire was first discovered by the owners of the camper.
Jessica Markow said her daughter's husband woke to feed their baby. He saw smoke and started screaming for everyone to get out.
"I grabbed the baby and ran to call 911 and as I did that I seen flames under the camper," she recalled.
Despite her boyfriend attempting to use a fire extinguisher, the flames already had caught the trees.
"It was out of control," she said.
She explained that Crumpton Volunteer Fire Department arrived fifteen minutes later after they discovered the fire.
The fire was reported shortly after 4 a.m. Crumpton Fire Department was the primary responding agency, with a total of 24 firefighters on-scene.
Once there, it took the fire department 30 minutes to control, but the damage was done. According to the fire marshal's report, a structure loss of $100,000, and loss of contents worth $20,000 was reported.
The marshal further stated that the area of origin of the blaze came from the underside of the camper due to an unspecified electrical failure.
As Markow awaits a visit from her pastor she'd appreciate any help from the community.
"We didn't have much to begin with," she said. "So losing what we did put us in a deep hole."
She said the family is still trying to process this turn of events and are in shock. As a precautionary measure, they took the baby to the hospital to be evaluated.
On the Duck Neck Campground Facebook page, there's a call to action to help them.
The family are in need of clothes, shoes, diapers and any other necessities.
Woman small, girl child size 10, toddler size 4t, baby girl 3-6 months, pull-ups diapers size 5t. Flip flops are needed too. Shoe sizes: girls, 6-7, 3, 4, and 7 women.
"Let's come together as a community and help this family," the campground's post read.
The church backs them up too, being one of the first on the scene to support them. They are organizing a clothing drive and has put up the funds to help them stay in a hotel for several days.
If anyone wants to help the family, the pastor for Grace Apostolic Church can be contacted at dtrombley@myantioch.org.

title: Cordova Country Fair draws a crowd
author: Tom McCall
content:
Cordova Country Fair draws a crowd

 August 3, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Tom McCall | Section: Local News 
 
 565
 Words 

 Read News Document

 CORDOVA — On a steamy Aug. 1 night, a large crowd of people came to the Cordova Country Fair.There were rides on an antique shiny red fire truck with sirens blaring. There were funnel cakes, grilled hot dogs and quarter games like the dunk tank. This was a family event, and families gathered to take in the festivities.
Jimmy Eason, vice president of Cordova Volunteer Firemen's Association, said the fair is the fire department's biggest fundraiser of the year.
"In 2026 the fire company will be celebrating 100 years. The fair — we are going on like 60-something (years)," he said. "This is a community event with good cheap food. It is family-oriented. Prices are low. 100% of what is spent on these grounds, stays on these grounds. We have no outside vendors."
The association has a big expenditure coming next year. They have to buy a new fire engine with a $1-million price tag.
"It is nothing extravagant. It is just what we need for the next 30 years," Eason said.
Bill Dulin is a trustee and engineer with the association.
"Today we are prepping to make this fundraiser a success. We have been at it for a week and a half. The rides are our big draw. The kids like to hear that siren and stuff," Dulin said.
There were lots of strollers and little kids chasing each other around the grounds.
"This is a family thing. People make sure they are not on vacation for this weekend. This is the only time they see some people this year. They are sitting around in lawn chairs. It gets people out," Eason said.
Katie Dulin, president of the fire association, said, "It is a good time for community. Inexpensive entertainment with the games. We have our Little Miss and Miss Fire Prevention Contests. We have fire truck rides and hay wagon rides. I am here under our recruitment and retention tent in case anyone has interest."
Robert and Barbara Saathoff live so close to the fair that they walked.
"We have been here ever since this fair started. We have been married 63 years," Barbara said.
Robert said, "When I got out of high school in 1958, I went to work for her dad. I got the farmer's daughter."
Around 8 p.m., the excitement for the Little Miss Cordova pageant began to rise. The girls' hair was done up, and their party dresses were just right.
Courtney Fike, reigning Miss Cordova, was the emcee for the competition. She wore a sash and a tiara.
"We are just here to support the girls. I will be asking them questions out of the fishbowl, so they have to think off of their toes," Fike said.
The winner will be in a lot of parades in the coming year, from Easton, to Preston, to Federalsburg, to Trappe and Ocean City.
"I like watching the little girls open up more into it, because a lot of them have never done this before. I did it when I was their age," Fike said.
After the contestants had been delivered by a tractor pulled cart with hay bales for seats, they were asked fire-related questions like, "Do you know your 911 address for an emergency?"
The winner, Aubrie Stichberry, 5, was asked what fire prevention means. She is going into kindergarten at Chapel Elementary.
She said leaving the stage, "I am going to keep my crown on."
The Cordova Fair continues on Saturday. More details are available at facebook.com/events/11868144 95659325.

title: Hummingbird Inn: a bed and breakfast filled with love and community
author: Veronica Fernandez-Alvarado
content:
Hummingbird Inn: a bed and breakfast filled with love and community

 August 3, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Veronica Fernandez-Alvarado | Section: Business 
 
 769
 Words 

 Read News Document

 EASTON — Owning a bed an breakfast was not a dream Eric Levinson had on his own. The plan was created alongside his late husband, Kevin Woloshyn.The Hummingbird Inn, located on North Aurora Street in Easton, is a product of their shared love of traveling and hospitality.
The foundation of the inn and their love began many years ago online, when computer monitors had one color and there were no graphics, according to Levinson. Levinson, who at the time was working in Manhattan, New York, in IT management, went on Internet Relay Chat and began talking to Woloshyn, who was from Alberta, Canada. They connected and soon began sending letters to each other and talking on the phone.
Eventually, they made the decision to have Woloshyn move to New York. Same-sex marriage was not legal at the time, and the couple had to find alternatives to be together through work visas, but once they, did they did not want to be apart.
"He was one of these life-of-the-party guys," Levinson said. "He would walk into a room, and everybody was just enamored with him. He was very charismatic, and outgoing, and funny and silly, but extremely intelligent. He spoke seven languages. He and I traveled the world together."
Levinson said Woloshyn was determined to help him find his passion. Bit by bit, Levinson tried to hone in his interest of traveling, cooking and connecting to people. He enrolled in the New York Culinary Institute and began working in a couple of restaurants in Manhattan.
Eventually the idea of opening a bed and breakfast came to the couple, and they decided it would be a project they could do together in the future.
After years of being together Levinson and Woloshyn moved to Canada, where same-sex marriage was legal, and got married. The plan was to wait for same-sex marriage to be legalized before moving back to the U.S., and at the time the issue was being presented to the Supreme Court.
But just before same-sex marriage was legalized, Woloshyn was tragically killed by a drunk driver.
"Ever since Kevin was taken away, I realized that tomorrow is not guaranteed," Levinson said. "You have to live every life to the fullest."
With the help of his sister Brooke Drake and his realtor (and future best friend) Jana Mewedith, Levinson found what is now the Hummingbird Inn.
It has become a popular bed and breakfast where Levinson hosts events such as weddings, dark dinner experiences, annual Pride events, halloween parities, tea events and fundraisers for local nonprofits.
Drake said she is proud of her brother and the success he has found in Easton.
"It was their dream, and he's done a great job to bring that dream to life," Drake said. "We, me and my husband, have just been so happy for him to have him be able to change his life like this and move forward into a wonderful community that's embraced him and made his inn a success."
Levinson is known as an "ambassador of Easton" by many of his guests.
Dan Schumacher, a former guest and current Easton resident, credits Levinson's hospitality for bringing him and his husband to the town.
"Eric and the Hummingbird Inn have been instrumental in attracting new residents to the town of Easton," Schumacher said. "I know a number of couples who visited because the inn allows dogs, can host weddings or because it's LGBTQ friendly (the latter of which attracted my husband Rob and I) … Many of us have purchased homes here and now call Easton our home."
Throughout the inn, hummingbirds can be found in every room, framed on many walls and tiny crystal birds floating on every ceiling. In the entrance, there is a wall of framed cards and art of hummingbirds sent by guests called a "charm" wall, since that is the official name of a group of hummingbirds.
Levinson said that for the vast majority of his life, he had no connection to the bird. But after his husband died, he began receiving many sympathy cards with hummingbirds on them.
For a while, he was confused by all the hummingbird cards. After a bit of research, he learned of the lore associated with the bird.
Hummingbirds are thought to take on the spirit of people who were charismatic and full of life after they had passed, Levinson said.
"I used the hummingbird as a remembrance symbol after he died, and then when the inn started to actually come together, I knew I was going to rename it," Levinson said. "… Knowing this was something that Kevin and I were originally planning to do together, that's why it's called Hummingbird Inn — because it's in his memory."

title: Just Peachy: Sudlersville Peach Festival celebrates 10 years
author: ANDREA GRABENSTEIN agrabenstein@gmail.com
content:
Just Peachy: Sudlersville Peach Festival celebrates 10 years

 August 5, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: ANDREA GRABENSTEIN agrabenstein@gmail.com | Section: Local News 
 
 143
 Words 

 Read News Document

 SUDLERSVILLE — Sudlersville Volunteer Fire Co. and Godfrey's Farm once again partnered to bring a festival dedicated to all things peaches with the 10th annual Sudlersville Peach Festival.Hot weather couldn't keep hundreds of visitors from turning out to the annual event at Godfrey's Farm Aug. 2 and 3.
Antique cars, a petting zoo, pony rides, food and craft vendors from across the area joined in the community festivities alongside raffles to benefit local organizations.
Musical talent included Swamp Donkey, West Street Revival Band and the Ryan Keith Band.
The highlight of the festival is always the fresh-picked peaches from Godfrey's orchard, including peach ice cream, peach pie and peach slushies.
Godfrey Farm goods including fresh produce and local products are available during the peach festival
Godfrey Farms is open through Labor Day at 302 Leager Road in Sudlersville.
More information about Godfrey's Farm can be found at godfreysfarm.com.

title: Community block party brings resources and fun together
author: ANDREA GRABENSTEIN agrabenstein@chespub.com
content:
Community block party brings resources and fun together

 August 8, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: ANDREA GRABENSTEIN agrabenstein@chespub.com | Section: News 
 
 292
 Words 

 Read News Document

 CHESTER — Strengthening neighborhood spirit, a warm evening of collaboration brings a festival of resources and organizations for a community night out block party to the United Methodist Church in Chester Aug. 2.The annual community block party is a multi-organization collaborative event brought forth music, food vendors, resources and giveaways.
Blending everything in the county in one central hub: the warm evening of collaboration provided an opportunity for citizens, law enforcement, faith-based organizations, county agencies, civic organizations, neighborhood organizations, and businesses to come together and address prevention issues.
Sponsored by CSAFE, the Collaborative Supervision and Focused Enforcement Group, and in collaboration with the organizations including the Queen Anne's County Department of Health Alcohol and Drug Abuse Prevention Services, Citizens Against Smoking Tobacco Coalition, the Office of the Sheriff and the Wellness Coalition, the annual community-building campaign promotes police-community partnerships to make neighborhoods safer.
Thankful to be part of the diverse landscape that makes up Queen Anne's County, Dorine Fassett has been organizing community events to bring resources to surrounding neighbors for years.
"I love to see people come out and support each other," Fassett said.
Community festivals are excellent ways for neighbors to learn more about the resources and organizations surrounding them in a casual, fun environment, she said.
Alongside local vendors, raffles and activities for all ages, other participating organizations included the Queen Anne's County Sheriff's Department, the County Health Department, and the Maryland Army National Guard.
National Night Out is a nationwide event that brings law enforcement and the community together and is traditionally held on the first Tuesday in August. Fassett and her organizers love to hold a community event on the first Friday prior to giving the community more events to attend and more opportunities to get out and meet their neighbors, she said.

title: Leonard, CWDI 'mutually agree' to terminate Leonard's contract
author: Maggie Trovato
content:
Leonard, CWDI 'mutually agree' to terminate Leonard's contract

 August 8, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Maggie Trovato | Section: Local News 
 
 725
 Words 

 Read News Document

 CAMBRIDGE — Matt Leonard is no longer Cambridge Waterfront Development Inc.'s executive director.According to a Thursday news release from CWDI, the organization and Leonard have "mutually agreed" to terminate his contract, effective immediately.
In an interview with the Star Democrat, CWDI Board President Angie Hengst said that all board members and Leonard made this decision and signed an agreement on Thursday.
"It was just a mutual agreement, just deciding that moving forward it was best for both parties," she said.
Hengst said she could not elaborate on why it was best for both parties.
Leonard was hired as CWDI's executive director in January 2022. In the last year, Leonard and CWDI have been in the spotlight. The Cambridge Harbor project — a project to develop land along the Choptank River — has become a frequent topic of conversation in Cambridge.
In May, tensions between CWDI and the City of Cambridge came to a head when the city filed a lawsuit against CWDI alleging the organization had violated a transfer agreement it entered into with the city in June 2021. Later that month, the city and CWDI entered into mediation before a retired judge.
Hengst said the ongoing mediation had no part in the decision to terminate Leonard's contract.
"The board thanks Matt for his tireless efforts and commitment to the organization and its mission," Hengst said in the news release. "He has played a significant role in the success of the project to date. We enjoyed our time working together, and we wish him well in his future endeavors."
Some of the progress CWDI made during Leonard's time as executive director includes securing grant funding; creating Waterman Way, a new street on the Cambridge Harbor property that has yet to be paved; and moving the project to extend the promenade along the waterfront forward.
The news release says Leonard chose to retire to Cambridge five years ago after he fell in love with the city.
"I answered the call to help my chosen forever home by joining the CWDI team," Leonard said in the release. "All of the CWDI board members I worked with are talented professionals dedicated to CWDI's community-first mission. I'm proud of what we accomplished together. I wish them all the best going forward and look forward to enjoying the fruits of their efforts for a long time to come."
According to the news release, in the interim, CWDI's Board Secretary-Treasurer Frank Narr will serve as CWDI's "day-to-day contact," and the organization will "continue with its active projects" and continue working with its partners to advance the Cambridge Harbor project.
In an interview with the Star Democrat, Narr said he has been involved with the project for almost 31 years. He said he is passionate about what can and should be done at Cambridge Harbor and wants to do it right.
Hengst told the Star Democrat the CWDI Board of Directors hasn't started looking for a new executive director to fill Leonard's position and, at the moment, won't be.
"Unfortunately, based on our financials, which we presented at our board meeting, we do not have the funds to take a new executive director," she said.
At the most recent CWDI Board meeting on July 31, Narr brought up the need for CWDI to sell property so that it can use that money to pay for other things. Since the lawsuit was filed in May, CWDI has not sold a piece of property it has been planning to sell to Yacht Maintenance Company. That property is part of the land that the city transferred to CWDI in the 2021 transfer agreement.
Narr also told the board that CWDI is $200,000 over budget when it comes to legal expenses, which is due to litigation with the city.
Hengst said Narr will serve in the day-to-day role and the board will work through things as best it can without an executive director "for the time being." She said the board's financial situation will determine when it can begin the search for a new executive director.
Hengst said the organization's financial situation did not play a part in the decision to part ways with Leonard.
"We just really thank Matt for his time and efforts that he put into CWDI and the Cambridge Harbor project," she said. "He put in a lot of work, a lot of hours, and we couldn't have gotten to where we are today without him."

title: Giving to the community — teaching the next generation
author: Staff Writer
content:
Giving to the community — teaching the next generation

 August 9, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Staff Writer | Section: News 
 
 937
 Words 

 Read News Document

 Henry and Beth Covington have a long history in Queen Anne's County. Both of their families arrived in the United States in the 1700's. Eventually, the Covingtons' settled in Queen Anne's County. Beth's ancestors landed on the Eastern Shore of Virginia and migrated to Mississippi.Henry's great-grandfather, also called Henry, was a Methodist minister at three local churches, Burrisville, Starr, and Salem near Church Hill. His son (Henry's grandfather), Edward, was a preacher and tenant farmer. Henry's dad, Henry Sr., preached for a while, but then began a career with New York Life Insurance.
In 1979, Henry Sr. and his wife Kathryn, bought the Peace and Plenty Farm from the Wright family and started farming. Henry Sr. always said there were two things his father approved of during the year other than work and going to church; attending the 4-H fair and riding to Rehoboth Beach for the day! To get there, all nine kids piled in the back of a 6-wheel truck filled with straw! Henry's mother, Kathryn, was raised on the Richard family farm near Templeville, along with her 12 siblings.
Beth was born in Mississippi where her maternal grandparents, the Dilworths, farmed. She moved to Kent Island at the age of 4, when her dad began working for Maryland DNR. Beth's family also had their faith, it was a big part of growing up and they attended church regularly. After graduating from Chesapeake College, Beth attended the University of Maryland Dental School, earning her degree in dental hygiene.
Henry graduated from the University of Delaware with a degree in Plant Science. Spring of his junior year, he attended a semester at Chesapeake College and met Beth. Henry was recruited by some high school friends at Chesapeake to play baseball. At one baseball practice, Henry noticed one of the softball players. She was wearing red shorts and Henry asked one of his teammates "who is that girl in the red shorts?". Henry was told it was Beth, his friend Earl's little sister. Beth mentioned "since she was a couple years younger than her brother, no one noticed her until college!". After the chance meeting at baseball and softball practice, they dated and were married in 1982.
In 1980, Henry started working at Agrico and Crop Production Services, selling fertilizer and Pioneer seed. Henry had his first opportunity to rent a farm on his own from Gladys Cahall. His grandmother was Cahall's Sunday school teacher so she knew Henry's family very well.
Henry enjoyed farming with his dad for many years. After 10 years, Henry became a full time Pioneer sales rep while also farming over 1300 acres. Henry and Beth dreamed of owning their own farm, and in 2001 that dream came true. They bought a farm near Centreville, and named it Broadland. After 30 years, Henry retired from the seed business in 2021. A good friend, Anton Roe now continues the business as a local Pioneer sales rep. Henry and Beth continue to farm.
Henry and Beth have three children; Will, Ben, and Sarah. Will graduated from Washington and Lee University and is now working as a systems engineer for Communications Electronics Systems Integrated. Ben graduated from Iowa State University. He works for the University and John Deere as an agricultural and biosystems engineer. Sarah graduated from the University of Richmond with a degree in Biology. Sarah teaches biology at Queen Anne's County High School.
Beth had worked off the farm as a part-time dental hygienist for 38 years. This allowed her to take care of the kids and help on the farm. Their three kids were actively involved in 4-H, showing pigs, steers, and rabbits, and entering indoor exhibits. Henry was recruited by Paul Gunther to help with the open farm crops at the fair and to assist the Godfreys with open vegetables. Henry and Beth gladly did this for over 30 years.
After the kids had all left home and Beth retired as a dental hygienist, she had time to work on one of her hobbies, quilting. She said, "My grandmother sewed and taught me to sew. I started out making doll clothes and then made clothes for myself, and later, my kids. After the kids left home, I started to quilt". Beth has been generous in her quilting talents, giving quilts as gifts and donating them to people in need.
About the same time Henry started collecting old tractors. His first was a 1958 John Deere 730. The 730 was one of his favorite childhood toys and 1958 was the year in which he was born. At some point Beth mentioned she would like to have a Farmall cub, like the one she remembered Mr. Ernest Porter owning. Henry found a 1960 cub right away (the same year she was born!) Mr. Ernest Porter was a wonderful Christian man who was very dear to both Henry and Beth. Mr. Ernest Porter was a big influence in Henry's life. "He never seemed to get upset" Henry said. He was also a faithful member of Beth's church on Kent Island.
Henry and Beth consider themselves so very blessed to have had all the experiences that come with living in our farming community. They have thoroughly enjoyed supporting and serving others through their church, 4-H, and school activities. Henry said with a smile "people are generally good and giving back to your community keeps our community close". He said "my father never missed a 4-H Fair up until his passing and I feel the same way. The fair is a good way to stay involved and see people…Everyone should give some of their time to their community. That's how we teach the next generation."

title: Community block party brings resources and fun together
author: ANDREA GRABENSTEIN agrabenstein@chespub.com
content:
Community block party brings resources and fun together

 August 9, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: ANDREA GRABENSTEIN agrabenstein@chespub.com | Section: Life 
 
 290
 Words 

 Read News Document

 Strengthening neighborhood spirit, a warm evening of collaboration brings a festival of resources and organizations for a community night out block party to the United Methodist Church in Chester Aug. 2.The annual community block party is a multi-organization collaborative event brought forth music, food vendors, resources and giveaways.
Blending everything in the county in one central hub: the warm evening of collaboration provided an opportunity for citizens, law enforcement, faith-based organizations, county agencies, civic organizations, neighborhood organizations, and businesses to come together and address prevention issues.
Sponsored by CSAFE, the Collaborative Supervision and Focused Enforcement Group, and in collaboration with the organizations including the Queen Anne's County Department of Health Alcohol and Drug Abuse Prevention Services, Citizens Against Smoking Tobacco Coalition, the Office of the Sheriff and the Wellness Coalition, the annual community-building campaign promotes police-community partnerships to make neighborhoods safer.
Thankful to be part of the diverse landscape that makes up Queen Anne's County, Dorine Fassett has been organizing community events to bring resources to surrounding neighbors for years.
"I love to see people come out and support each other," Fassett said.
Community festivals are excellent ways for neighbors to learn more about the resources and organizations surrounding them in a casual, fun environment, she said.
Alongside local vendors, raffles and activities for all ages, other participating organizations included the Queen Anne's County Sheriff's Department, the County Health Department, and the Maryland Army National Guard.
National Night Out is a nationwide event that brings law enforcement and the community together and is traditionally held on the first Tuesday in August. Fassett and her organizers love to hold a community event on the first Friday prior to giving the community more events to attend and more opportunities to get out and meet their neighbors, she said.

title: 13th annual Watermen’s Appreciation Day draws a crowd
author: Veronica Fernandez-Alvarado
content:
13th annual Watermen’s Appreciation Day draws a crowd

 August 12, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Veronica Fernandez-Alvarado | Section: News 
 
 437
 Words 

 Read News Document

 ST. MICHAELS — Hundreds of people enjoyed boat docking contests, steamed local crabs, live music and family activities to celebrate the 13th annual Watermen's Appreciation Day hosted at the Chesapeake Bay Maritime Museum on Sunday.Watermen's Appreciation Day brings people together to celebrate the longstanding history of watermen on the Eastern Shore, as well as fundraise for the Talbot Watermen's Association.
Jeff Harrison, president of the association, said the event began in 2010 and has grown throughout the years. For Harrison, the number of people attending every year shows the local community's support for watermen.
"There is this appreciation for the local watermen in this area and, of course, all over the Bay," Harrison said. "And we are actually trying to grab a hold of that in some of our fundraisers and to let people know that we do appreciate them and that we're glad that they appreciate us also."
Harrison, dressed in a yellow volunteer shirt, was part of a team of over a 100 volunteers assisting attendees and contestants.
The Harrison family were all part of the volunteer team. Ashley and James Harrison, along with a group of five boys under the age of 13, stood behind a volunteer table near crowded bleachers awaiting the boat docking competition.
Ashley Harrison said volunteering at the Watermen Appreciation Day event is a family tradition she married into and has decided to establish in her family. This tradition stems from her husband, who comes from a family of watermen and who began volunteering when he was a young boy.
"We like doing stuff for the children," Ashley Harrison said. "We have three of our own, and we love seeing them have fun at events as well. And we like helping our community and showing our visitors that come here that this is a really great place to come and we're a tight knit community."
Under the sun, hundreds of people crowded and squeezed together to catch a glimpse of the boat docking contest. Boat owners of all ages showed off their skills and embraced cheers and support from the crowd.
Shannon Mitchell, vice president of engagement for the Chesapeake Bay Maritime Museum, said this event is a part of a partnership between the museum and local watermen to benefit the watermen in their fundraising, sponsorship and silent auction work. The museum benefits from the admission intake, she said.
"This one is very much mission-focused in supporting our local watermen," Mitchell said. "It's a big piece of why the museum exists to begin with. They tell a big story about the Chesapeake Bay and our region, so it's really exciting to see everyone come out and support them."

title: Tangier Post Office serves island community
author: MILES LAYTON APG Media
content:
Tangier Post Office serves island community

 August 13, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: MILES LAYTON APG Media | Section: News 
 
 531
 Words 

 Read News Document

 TANGIER, Va. — A small town post office is a community gathering spot and a lifeline to the mainland for a small island in the Chesapeake Bay.Tangier is about 12 miles from the mainland at Crisfield, Maryland, with the mail boat, the Courtney Thomas, running six days a week, weather pending, across the Tangier Sound between Maryland and Virginia.
Postmaster Dolores Daley is a familiar face to many with her glasses and warm smile — she talks to everyone as they check their mail. Daley explained what she likes best about working at the post office, a centerpiece for the town.
"I like that I can stay right in my hometown, and I like that everybody comes to me," she said. "I know everybody on a first-name basis."
There's no mail delivery to home or business addresses on the island, so Tangier's 400 residents receive their mail in tiny post office boxes that have served the community for decades.
"Because of our location and how close everybody is, we don't have any mail carriers," Daley said.
Daley said folks can pick up their mail anytime, but afternoons are when the latest mail arrives so that is "when people tend to visit the post office the most to talk and share news about their friends, family or neighbors."
Remember the term "golden ticket" from the movie "Charlie and the Chocolate Factory"? When someone sees a golden ticket — a yellow post office letter announcing the arrival of a package — then folks get excited because they know they've received something good from the mainland. Whether it's rubber boots for wet weather or a laptop for a soon-to-be college student, many packages from Amazon arrive each day.
"The golden ticket is the card — the yellow card — that says come and get your package," Daley said with a smile. "And when the package is too big, which most of them are, to go into the post office box, we put that card in and you bring it in to get your package. Most people like the yellow slips, and they call them golden tickets."
A lifelong resident of Tangier, Daley, 67, has worked for the post office for 38 years.
"Yes. Absolutely — we get everything," she said. "We get grass cutters through here occasionally. We get a lot of things through here. We just got chicks the other day. We've received caterpillars for the island's school to turn into butterflies when they do science projects."
Important announcements from Town Hall or residents are taped to the windows by the front door leading into the post office, whether it's the time and date for the island's annual homecoming or news of a funeral service.
"We've always been a big part of the community," Daley said. "We have a bulletin board of the things that are happening in the town because everyone is going to stop by the post office."
Married to a longtime waterman, Mickey Daley, now retired, Dolores said she loves island life.
"I love living here, being here," she said. "People here — we can go off and tend to anything we need on the mainland and come back when we've had enough. Living here in Tangier is my most favorite thing."

title: Preston Bethesda Methodist Church hosts 22nd Peach Festival
author: KONNER METZ kmetz@chespub.com
content:
Preston Bethesda Methodist Church hosts 22nd Peach Festival

 August 14, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: KONNER METZ kmetz@chespub.com | Section: News 
 
 349
 Words 

 Read News Document

 PRESTON — Hundreds gathered at the Preston Volunteer Fire Company on Saturday to enjoy peach ice cream and desserts at the Bethesda Methodist Church's 22nd annual Peach Festival.Inside the fire hall, church members and volunteers served attendees peach and vanilla ice cream adorned with freshly-cut peaches. Peach cobblers, donuts, cakes and pies, along with other sweet treats, were for sale at the event.
Mark Butcher, who lives a few blocks from the Preston Fire Hall, helped the church sell its baked goods on Saturday. He also baked over 20 bags of cookies in advance of the festival.
"The whole town was baking yesterday," Butcher said.
Family-owned and Preston-based Heritage Orchard, which has around four acres of peach orchards, sold white and yellow peaches at a table. Run by the Whaples family, Heritage Orchard also provided fresh peaches for many of the church's homemade baked goods, Bethesda Methodist Church Pastor Nate Weaver said.
Weaver greeted festival-goers as they walked around the hall, which included more than 20 local vendors. Saturday was Weaver's first Peach Festival. He said with the help of around 20 members, the church made 111 peach cobblers in the two days leading up to the event.
Weaver said "everyone's on board" and that it's a full church effort to pull off the festival. He noted the biggest challenge is having "manpower where we need it" to ensure the event runs smoothly.
"We have committee meetings prior to the Peach Festival, and we get people together," Weaver said. " … We figure out where they're going to be working, what they're going to be doing, (and) give their jobs."
Jim Michael, a member of the church, cooked soft crabs Saturday, part of the festival's menu, which included hot dogs, hamburgers, scrapple sandwiches and peach milkshakes.
As hundreds of people walked in and out of the fire hall late Saturday morning and early afternoon, the church was making strides for its yearly fundraising efforts. Weaver said it's the biggest event of the year.
"This is our main fundraising portion for the church," Weaver said. Without the festival, he added, "we don't have the funding for the church."

title: Couple converts school bus and hits the road
author: Tom McCall
content:
Couple converts school bus and hits the road

 August 15, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Tom McCall | Section: News 
 
 544
 Words 

 Read News Document

 EASTON — It took three years to convert the old diesel school bus into a coastal-chic wandering machine.Now, Easton couple couple Caroline Petosa and Brandon Lund are ready to set off on their adventure.
The couple, who used COVID downtime to plan their adventures and renovate their Canadian-made 2004 Blue Bird bus, are scheduled to leave on a cross-country voyage Thursday.
"We got the bus on Facebook Marketplace out in Blackwater. That was three years ago," Petosa said. "We knew we both liked to travel a lot. We were stir crazy during COVID, and you really couldn't fly, so how could we travel by land? The dream was born during COVID."
Petosa has spent lots of time on boats and knows about their tiny showers and kitchens. A lot of her design choices keep in mind the economy of space that both a boat and a school bus require.
The bus has a shower, a bedroom, a living room and a sumptuous leather driver's chair fit for a king.
The design features coastal motifs, including a large blue octopus painted on the outside of the bus. The vehicle has a flowing name that goes with the decor.
"Her name is Auwana, which is Hawaiin for wander," Petosa said.
The 28 years olds both have remote jobs, and they will be taking their two dogs on the road as soon as the renovations are complete.
Lund, who works as an economist for the federal government, is good at working with the mechanics of the old bus. From pulling out rusty tail pipes to installing solar panels on the roof, he can figure it out.
"Before I got my bachelors, I was trained in automotive technology. Engines, suspension, brakes and electrical work on a 12 volt system. Carpentry is not my stong suit, but I have come leaps and bounds. There is a huge online presence for schoolies that I have learned from," he said.
One of the couple's favorite parts of renovating the bus was the two months of demolition. They took everything out, including the bus seats, which they sold on Facebook Marketplace.
As one of the final steps towards setting off on their journey, the couple sold their house.
"We did it for a little bit. We lived in our house for three years. I am glad we did it, but it is time for something different," Petosa said. "It was too much space. I never went into half the rooms. We don't need to be locked into one spot, especially because we both work remotely."
Petosa took over ownership of online wedding resource My Eastern Shore Wedding. She is an expert at social media, so their upcoming journey will be well-documented.
They plan to start out their journey in New England, where they will have six weeks to just explore. Then, over the winter, they will head to the warmth of the Florida Keys. They have two inflatable paddle boards on the bus.
Some bucket list items include going to Banff, Canada, and Alaska next summer, but they are open to seeing other parts of the country and finding a place they love.
When they are done traveling, they said they have no plans to sell Auwana.
"No, probably not," Lund said. "We put too much blood sweat and tears in this thing."
To follow their adventure, visit auwanabus.com.

title: Summer Youth Program Graduation at EVFC
author: Tom McCall
content:
Summer Youth Program Graduation at EVFC

 August 17, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Tom McCall | Section: Local News 
 
 583
 Words 

 Read News Document

 EASTON — In a joyous graduation program at the Easton Volunteer Fire Department on July 14, 46 students completed the Upper Shore Workforce Investment Board youth program. The six-week work program gives students with learning disabilities and handicaps not only a path get out into the workforce, but many retain their jobs after completing the course.These teens do all kinds of things across five counties like washing dishes, taking movie tickets at a theater and working at a day care center. There are lots of different businesses who are willing to work with these students like Aaron's Place, Dorchester Parks and Recreation and the Kent County Animal Shelter.
One student learned data entry so thoroughly that he was teaching his employer a few tips.
As their names were to get their diploma, some were shy and some were triumphant with their arms in the air. Most were dressed up for the event. The crowd clapped enthusiastically for every kid. There were tears of joy as parents snapped cell phone pictures of their child in front of the balloon-covered backdrop.
"We are here to celebrate our summer youth connections program that we do for youth in the Upper Shore from Kent all the way down to Dorchester," said Dan Schneckenburger, executive director of Upper Shore Workforce Investment Board. "Students with any kind of learning disabilities or handicaps, we place them with the employer. We off job coaching along the way."
He said this was the culmination of their achievement and their first job. He says they work with employers and with Division of Rehabilitation Services, which is part of The Maryland Department of Education.
"For a lot of these kids this six-week program is their first paid work experience. YMCA, animal shelters, restaurants. One kid liked IT. We placed him at the St. Michael's library," he said.
Case manager Elizabeth Chiocca watched with pride as the kids got their diplomas.
"It is hard for local youth to find jobs and this gives them a stepping stone that they need," Chiocca said. "Some of the businesses are actually hiring our students."
Youth coordinator Deborah Boulden said she likes the intake part, where other people have written these students off.
"Because they do have a disability, some people write them off," Boulden said. "We take them as they are and don't write them off. And we make diamonds."
Boulden spoke to the crowd from a lectern. She was proud of many students who not only completed the six-week program, but stayed at their place of employment to keep working.
Mason Callis worked as a "dishwasher at Mamma Mia's in Sudlersville, Maryland. Clean dishes, sweeping floor out in the lobby and in the kitchen. And washing and more dishes. I like my job very much, and I am a hard-working person."
Savannah Quinn had a clerical job at Chesapeake College with tasks like shredding paper and making name tags for folders.
One successful multi-year participant in the program is Connor Swann. He is 21 now and was a keynote speaker at the event.
"Miss Debbie and Miss Elizabeth helped me get jobs. I started in ninth grade. One job was Chesapeake Cats and Dogs and the other was Talbot Humane Society. That helped me get great skills toward working with animals," Swann said. "Right now I work at Dogwood Acres Pet Retreat in Kent Island. I am starting to train people now. I completed the veterinary assistant program at Chesapeake College. I am getting my associates degree in liberal arts. Then it is off to the real world of working."

title: Bay Country Bakery owners celebrate 25 years of ownership
author: MAGGIE TROVATO mtrovato@chespub.com
content:
Bay Country Bakery owners celebrate 25 years of ownership

 August 17, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: MAGGIE TROVATO mtrovato@chespub.com | Section: Local News 
 
 680
 Words 

 Read News Document

 CAMBRIDGE — Neither Gena nor Dave Levy had lifelong goals of owning their own bakery.Gena said they fell into it. The couple had been working in fine dining before they took a leap and purchased Bay Country Bakery from Robert and Connie Minn in August 1999.
The pair had just learned Gena was pregnant when they decided to buy the bakery, a longtime Dorchester establishment.
"The bakery came up for auction at kind of the same time," Dave said. "We got a little bit of help from our family to buy some equipment and ..."
"... we just started," said Gena, finishing Dave's sentence.
"We just went for it," Dave added.
Twenty-five years and 28 years of marriage later, the couple has found success in their business and been able to grow it, moving to a larger location and adding a cafe. The business is now located on U.S. Route 50 on the east side of Cambridge.
In that time, they've been able to take part in something generational. They've watched children and grandchildren come in to try the doughnuts that their parents and grandparents grew up on.
"It's very cool," Dave said.
When they purchased the bakery, the Levys inherited the beloved doughnut recipe from the previous owners.
"They stayed with us for one week," Gena said about the Minns. "And I remember thinking, 'Wow, OK that's nice.' And then now I'm like, 'A week, God, that was like nothing."
When the Levys first took over, there were some people in the community that had concerns.
"We were strangers," said Gena, who grew up in Trappe. "And any local community, they're like, 'Who are these people? What are they doing? Are things going to change?'"
The Levys have kept the tried and true doughnut recipe from before their ownership for all these years. But they've added some of their childhood favorites to the menu. They use Gena's grandmother's peach pie recipe and some of Dave's grandmother's Christmas cookie recipes.
"She had Christmas cookies up the wazoo," Dave said about his grandmother. "She would spend months making Christmas cookies."
When Gena and Dave met in culinary school, one of the things they bonded over was their strong grandmothers.
"We had similar backgrounds," said Gena, who noted that they both came from food-oriented families.
Although getting to work at 1:30 or 2:30 a.m. to make baked goods from scratch can be rough, the production team at Bay Country Bakery and Cafe keeps spirits high. Those especially early risers listen to podcasts together in the morning, and as more people trickle in, they switch it over to music.
Taylor Warfield, who has worked in production at the bakery for nine years, starts her workday around 8 a.m., after she's dropped off her 5-year-old daughter, Luna, at school.
As she formed pie crusts, she said she learned to bake from her grandmother.
"She decorated cakes when I was growing up," Warfield said. "So I wanted to bake."
Though owning the bakery can be challenging at times — from dealing with changes in the economy (when they started, a dozen doughnuts cost $4.75 compared to $16 now) to juggling owning a business and raising two children to having to work unusual hours — Gena and Dave like what they do every day.
"I don't like waking up in the middle of the night and going to bed (early)," Dave said. "I miss a lot of life. I've sacrificed a lot in that respect but also gained a lot from it."
For the Levys, it's a rewarding job. Dave is reminded of that every time he sells their goods at the farmers market in Salisbury.
"People coming week after week, rain or shine, to stand outside and buy stuff," he said. "That's what keeps me going."
Dave and Gena don't yet have a plan in place for when they decide to hang up their aprons and retire. They hope they can pass on the business, whether to their children or someone new, like when the Minns sold the bakery to them 25 years ago.
The couple doesn't know what the next 25 years will bring, but there's one thing Gena hopes will still be around: "This place," she said.

title: Betterton dedicates late restaurant owner with bench in his honor
author: WILL BONTRAGER wbontrager@chespub.com
content:
Betterton dedicates late restaurant owner with bench in his honor

 August 20, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: WILL BONTRAGER wbontrager@chespub.com | Section: Local News 
 
 771
 Words 

 Read News Document

 BETTERTON — While Betterton Day was in full swing, Saturday, Aug. 3, up the hill a bench was dedicated to the late Francis Marzella, restaurant owner for over 52 years.His wife, Maureen and their son, Michael, christened the bench, situated near the Betterton Volunteer fire house, and across from their restaurant, Marzella's By the Bay.
Almost 50 people came out to pay their honors to Francis. Leading the dedication was Dick Story, a close friend.
Francis died in the early hours, Tuesday, March 19, after putting in a shift at the restaurant. He worked hard, but also in these years here, he enjoyed the slower paced lifestyle of Kent County, specifically in Betterton.
His son coming in from California, told the Kent County News, this was just the place for his parents after decades of serving students at Ursinus College in Pennsylvania. There, the demand never stopped. Alumnus have fond memories of eating at his establishment.
During the bench ceremony, under the shade of a maple, Maureen recalled with humor the time they discovered Betterton.
They were being shown real estate in Kent County when they came across the road sign pointing to the town.
At first sight, Maureen knew right away that old firehouse was special.
"We saw it, and I wanted it, and I was surprised my husband didn't shoot it down. He said if we can get it at a reasonable price, you got it. And you know what ... I never want to leave."
Michael thanked all the people for coming out to honor his father.
"This community has been wonderful to my parents, and it's been a great place to spend their retirement years."
Maureen added some background. When Francis and Maureen purchased the firehouse in 2002, they just so happened to have a worker who got accepted into Delaware State, training as an airplane pilot.
He needed a place nearby to stay and needed a job. Not only did the old firehouse work for that, it helped eventually develop Marzella's by the Bay, opening it for business on weekends.
That place eventually drew the owners in 2013, as Kent County tends to do, with the loveliness found on the Eastern Shore.
Francis and Maureen moved from college town to beach town in 2013, where they've ingratiated themselves to the community ever since.
Nothing explains any better their dedication to the town than a message from the Betterton Volunteer Fire Department during an emergency in January 2019.
"On behalf of the Betterton Vol. Fire Company members, I would like to thank Frank and Maureen Marzella for getting up and opening their business 2 a.m. this morning during the major Apartment building fire that Betterton Vol. Fire company had. Mr. and Mrs. Marzella fed over 45 Firefighters with pizza, sandwiches, and coffee and then stayed open the rest of the day serving all the customers that dine there everyday."
From Francis and Maureen's early start as restaurant owners, they've showed that kind of dedication to their community.
It's what they've done ever since 1960, when they sold a one-size, 12-inch pizza for $1.25 each, at a pizza shop in Collegeville, Pennsylvania. The first location had only two tables.
After a decade they moved to 488 Main St. across from Ursinus College, quickly building a legacy, where they extended their menu.
Always adapting, they expanded, shipping their products nationwide because Ursinus College alumni couldn't shake those indelible memories and savory dishes from their college years.
Then in 2013, the couple approaching their 70s, longing for a quieter life, moved to Howell Point Road, in Betterton, deeming the restaurant, Marzella's by the Bay.
There they had the freedom to reduce their hours, and meet the ever-growing demand for their delicious strombolis.
The family atmosphere, warmth and witty, whimsical stories from Maureen combined with Francis' tradition of excellent food continues to this day.
That was evident with the amount of support at the bench ceremony. Story said it didn't take long to find a way to pay for the bench, the plaque and fly Michael in from California.
"This is really so nice," Maureen said, overwhelmed by the attentiveness.
Story said that they'd be honored for Maureen to christen the bench, the first "sit."
With a smile, and a slow shake of her head, Maureen pointed out that technically that wasn't true. She wasn't the first. Earlier she saw some cute little boys sitting on it.
Which she said was all right too.
Francis probably would have wanted it that way, she replied. She added that as much as the community misses her husband, she misses him even more.
Marzella's continue to serve great food. They're open from Tuesday to Sunday, offering pizza, hearty sandwiches and more.
The bench, like Marzella's, is open for business as well, Story announced.

title: Community turns out for boy in hospice's 10th birthday
author: Tom McCall
content:
Community turns out for boy in hospice's 10th birthday

 August 22, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Tom McCall | Section: Local News 
 
 424
 Words 

 Read News Document

 CAMBRIDGE — On Aug. 19, Jeremiah Shaw had a 10th birthday bash for the ages.The town of Cambridge turned out in droves to make sure this boy felt appreciated with a parade down Foxtail Drive. There were bikers, school buses, fire trucks and tractor trailers.
The whole point was to ride by and put a smile on Shaw's face.
Shaw has struggled with Lennox-Gastaut Syndrome, a neurodegenerative disease that causes him to have seizures. His mother, Maschell Hines, said he has been recently put in to hospice care and that this could be his last fall season.
"He is out of meds. There are no other meds they can give him. It is come and go. All we can do is change his diet and pray," said Jeremiah's father Chris Shaw.
"The condition is pretty hard. He has been dealing with it since he was two years old. We didn't find a diagnosis until he was five. The hospital is like our second home. Hospice has been very hands-on. Very sweet. We started about a month ago. They work well with him. He has all types of seizures and runs a sudden risk of death," said Maschell.
His father says Jeremiah struggles with memory. Pictures may be all he remembers of this parade in his mind, so they shot the whole thing with their phones.
"He loves bikes, motorcycles, fire trucks and ambulances," Hines said. "This is his thing."
Happy with the huge turnout, Hines looked at all the fire trucks coming to her normally quiet neighborhood.
One man jumped out of his truck and handed the boy a crisp $100 bill. The Cambridge Fire Rescue Company stopped and gave him a stuffed dalmation and an authentic fireman's helmet.
Jeremiah Shaw gave the bent-arm trucker's salute to get them to blare their horns.
Towards the end, the Dorchester County Sheriff's K-9 unit pulled out a dog for him to pet.
"Thank you for everybody that came out to support him and show him love. It is really appreciated," Hines said.
Chris Shaw said, "I definitely appreciate the turnout. It has definitely been amazing. Especially the community and the people you don't know. The main thing is his condition. A lot of people think it is just his birthday, but it might be his last birthday."
After about half an hour, all the sirens, horns and waving people had run their course, and Foxtail Drive got quiet. In front of his house was a pile of presents for Jeremiah Shaw to open. His new fireman's helmet was there too.
Seeing all that fanfare, Jeremiah said, "I am happy."

title: American Legion Post 77 looking to jumpstart Hometown Heroes banner project
author: KONNER METZ kmetz@chespub.com
content:
American Legion Post 77 looking to jumpstart Hometown Heroes banner project

 August 22, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: KONNER METZ kmetz@chespub.com | Section: Local News 
 
 428
 Words 

 Read News Document

 EASTON — An effort to honor past and present veterans, firefighters and police officers gained momentum at the Easton Town Council on Monday evening.Joan Harris-Brooks, speaking on behalf of Blake-Blackston American Legion Post 77, asked the council to partner with the group in creating a banner program so that families of Talbot County veterans, firefighters and officers can honor their loved ones.
Harris-Brooks said the banners would be placed on Ward 4 roads such as Glenwood Avenue, Port Street and West Street. Her father, John Harris Jr., and her uncle were members of Post 77, which operates on Glenwood Avenue.
With members of Post 77 in attendance, council members expressed nothing but support for the project.
"I think that this is a great endeavor," Ward 4 Council Member the Rev. Elmer Davis said. "(It's important) that we don't lose the memory of those persons who fought for our country. I believe it's our responsibility to help out with this project. Secondly, it doesn't cost the town a dime."
The Hometown Heroes Banner program began in 2006 in Harrisburg, Pennsylvania. Today, Mid-Shore towns including Federalsburg, Hurlock and Preston showcase banners honoring past and present veterans.
Harris-Brooks said the banners would cost $200 each. There will be no ask of the council to provide any money for the project.
She asked that the town office hold blank applications for interested families, in addition to applications being advertised on social media and at Post 77.
"It will instill a sense of pride and unity in Easton and for our country," Harris-Brooks told the council. "It is our goal that you grant us approval. And we believe that if you grant us an approval, this will make a landmark for you as our councilmen."
Council members unanimously approved the request. Prior to voting, the council expressed hopes that the banner project could extend to the entire town.
Harris-Brooks said that Post 77 will accept donations from the community that can help families who cannot afford the cost of a banner. She added that Post 77 will work with American Legion Talbot Post 70, Easton Utilities and the town as the project comes to life.
"I think our children need to be aware," Harris-Brooks said. "We still have young people still enlisted in the service. I will just very passionately say my uncle was a member of Post 77 … He gave his ultimate self serving."
Commander Victor Middleton thanked the council for their support following the approval.
"When people say thank you for your service, it really lifted me up just now to a higher level," Middleton said. "And I thank you all."

title: Community donates vessels to Charity Boat Auction
author: Tom McCall
content:
Community donates vessels to Charity Boat Auction

 August 30, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Tom McCall | Section: Local News 
 
 524
 Words 

 Read News Document

 ST MICHAELS — A wide array of boats, from kayaks to 40-foot vessels, were on display at the Chesapeake Bay Maritime Museum Thursday evening ahead of the museum'a annual Charity Boat Auction.The auction, held each year over Labor Day Weekend for more than two decades, will take place Saturday, raising money for the museum and its efforts in the community.
On Aug. 29, there were was a preview event for members of the museum. And although no bids were cast, there was a lot of interest in these boats, all of which have been donated to the museum.
Each boat has a story. Kristen Greenaway, president and chief executive officer of CBMM, knows many of these stories. On Thursday, she noted a little wooden sailboat with a well-maintained sheen. It was designed in the 1930s.
"This is a Chesapeake Bay locally designed boat," she said. "The chap who designed it put a couple of designs together. It was great for sailing upwind, and when it was sailing downwind, it would kind of flop from one side to the other. The wife of the chap he asked 'What did it look like?' She said it looked like a penguin waddling from side to side. So he named it 'penguin' and they are all painted with a black hull," Greenaway said.
The auction has a large reach.
"People come from far and wide to come in here and just have a phenomenal day kicking fenders, not kicking tires. And just having fun and maybe finding something to take home," she said.
This is the first year the museum has implemented reserves, or minimum bids.
The range of possibility is staggering. There was a 46-foot trawler with $15,000 minimum. There was jet ski with just 40 hours of running time. There was a whole section of boats at the auction that were floating at the dock. Some of the boats needed some care, but most were ready to hit the water.
Lad Mills, is longtime CBMM worker who retired five years ago. He just came to observe and scope out the offerings for a friend. He had some thoughts as man who helped found the auction event.
"You have to have enough, having is cleaned, and presented properly and having the proper crowd. Auctions are fun to watch because people get excited. People get emotional and people don't want anyone else to get their boat," Mills said.
"It does people a lot of good to be able to get rid of boats they have and don't want. I like old boats. I still fiddle with old boats. I am not a perfectionist, but I like to resurrect boats," Mills said.
The boat auction is important for the museum, Greenaway said.
"The boat donation program as a whole is extremely important because the funds from the sales of the boats go directly into the mission. It is phenomenal that people actually trust us enough to donate their vessels to us so we can sell them to put that revenue back into achieving the mission," she said.
The Charity Boat Auction will take place on Saturday ,Aug. 31. The doors open at 8 a.m. and the bidding starts at 11 a.m.
