title: Greensboro Car Show & Music Fest a big hit for locals
author: KONNER METZ kmetz@chespub.com
content:
Greensboro Car Show & Music Fest a big hit for locals

 September 3, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: KONNER METZ kmetz@chespub.com | Section: Local News 
 
 421
 Words 

 Read News Document

 GREENSBORO — Hundreds of cars and even more car enthusiasts gathered on the fairgrounds of the Greensboro Volunteer Fire Department Saturday for the annual Greensboro Car Show & Music Fest.The first half of the event included a bevy of vintage and modern automobiles for attendees to take in. A burnout contest even attracted a trucker and a motorcyclist, both engulfing the applauding crowd in smoke.
As judges walked up and down the rows of cars, a number of entries stood out across 13 separate classes, which included imports, police vehicles and motorcycles.
Sponsors Easton Auto Care and Denton Auto Care selected the top award on Saturday. Kevin Mezick, from Delmar, won the Best of Show trophy with his red 1969 Ford Mustang.
One of the most popular cars of the afternoon was the "Batmobile," designed like the car from the Batman comics and cartoons. Darrell Hughes, who runs the group Heroes for Happiness, brought the car to Greensboro after it won an award earlier in the day at a Houston, Delaware car show.
Hughes said the group goes around Delaware and the Eastern Shore dressing up as superheroes for children's birthday parties and at children's hospitals. The Batmobile was named one of the top five 1980-2000 entries at the Greensboro Car Show on Saturday.
Also awarded a trophy was Rick Miner for his 2004 Harley-Davidson. Miner, from Harrington, Delaware, said he's had his motorcycle for four years.
Miner said many are surprised when they find out his motorcycle has a Harley-Davidson engine but a Volkswagen transmission. He added that he rides it often and that it's not just for show or collecting dust in a garage.
The event was sponsored by many local organizations and businesses. Brandon Cunningham, the town's public works supervisor and one of the car show's organizers, thanked the sponsors.
"Without the help and the support of over 70 sponsors throughout the community, (this event) would not be possible, so thank you to everyone," Cunningham said.
At the conclusion of the car show, local band Rivers & Rhodes entertained fans before headliner and Nashville-based recording artist Trea Landon performed. It was Landon's first live performance in Maryland.
The event, which was free to all attendees, raised money to support the Greensboro Police Department's community basketball program.
Cunningham said the funds will help improvements at Greensboro's park and potentially other nearby parks. Proceeds help the program so that it can continue to be offered for free to local kids.
"Our goal is to venture out to help multiple areas, so we want to thank everybody," Cunningham said during Saturday's event.

BIRDING AND BOATING THE HARRIET TUBMAN BYWAY, 2 to 6 p.m., Linchester Mill, Preston. DCHS YARD SALE, 4 to 6 p.m., Dorchester County Historical Society, 1003 Greenway Dr., Cambridge. Historical society members only.

FRIDAY NIGHT DINNER, 5 to 7:30 p.m., VFW Post 5118, 355 Glebe Road, Easton. Community invited. Held every Friday.
SHOE DRIVE, Cordova Firehouse. Collection of gently used shoes for the Volunteer Fire Department Ladies Auxiliary . Shoes can be dropped off at the Cordova Firehouse until Sept. 13. This drive is to raise funds for the firehouse needs.

He will be joined on the Avalon stage by Betty Soo, a world-class vocalist.
DCHS YARD SALE, 7 a.m. to 4 p.m., Dorchester County Historical Society, 1003 Greenway Dr., Cambridge. Open to the public.

YOGA CLASS, Oxford Community Center, 200 Oxford Road. 9:30 a.m. Intermediate yoga with Suzie Hurley. Info: 410-226-5904 or oxfordcc.org.

CONCERT IN THE PARK, 4 to 7 p.m., James T. Wright Memorial Park, Preston. Home Brew is a trio of local musicians with two guitars, good vocals and tight harmonies. They play an eclectic selection of acoustic music to please all ages. Free to attend with treats available from Jaha Ice.

DCHS YARD SALE, 7 a.m. to 4 p.m., Dorchester County Historical Society, 1003 Greenway Dr., Cambridge. Open to the public.

Facebook: wednesdaymorningartists. Email is: wednesdaymorningartists@gmail.com.

RSVP at oxfordcc.org.

ST. MICHAELS FARMERS MARKET, 8:30 to 11 a.m., 206 S. Talbot Street, St. Michaels. Open rain or shine.

YOGA CLASS, Oxford Community Center, 200 Oxford Road. 9:30 a.m. Intermediate yoga with Suzie Hurley. Info: 410-226-5904 or oxfordcc.org.

The legendary Glenn Miller was one of the most successful of all dance bandleaders back in the Swing Era of the 1930s and '40s. A matchless string of hit records, the constant impact of radio broadcasts and the drawing power at theatres, hotels, and dance pavilion, built and sustained the momentum of popularity.

MUSIC ON THE NANTICOKE, 4 to 7 p.m., River Pavilion, 114 Water St., Vienna. Free concert with Randy Lee Ashcraft & The Saltwater Cowboys.

title: Talbot community remembers victims of 9/11
author: Tom McCall
content:
Talbot community remembers victims of 9/11

 September 11, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Tom McCall | Section: Local News 
 
 401
 Words 

 Read News Document

 EASTON — Around 100 people gathered at the corner of Dover and West streets Wednesday morning in a solemn and patriotic remembrance of the Sept. 11, 2001 attacks. A fire engine ladder with a giant American flag waved above the gathering.There was prayer and the laying of a wreath as the prelude.
Easton Mayor Megan Cook, Talbot County Council Member Keasha Haythe and Council Vice President Pete Lesher all came to the podium. Council President Chuck Callahan gave the greeting.
"We are here today for a day to remember 9/11, The National Day of Service and Remembering," Haythe said.
"On this day of remembrance, on this day of service, our focus is on what we have in common, what we value together as a community and as a nation," Lesher said.
The ceremony featured musical tributes, including performances by the Easton Middle School band and a spirited group of singers, including Thalia Turner, who sang the "Star Spangled Banner " Deputy John Coleman, who sang "God Bless America " and Ta'Vea Roberts, who sang "America The Beautiful."
The crowd was solemn as the silver bell was tolled by firefighter Rich Williamson. He rang out three sets of five, symbolizing the code for loss of life of a firefighter. It is an honorific signal for the ultimate sacrifice.
2,977 people died on 9/11, Callahan said. On Sept. 11, 2001, 19 terrorists hijacked four commercial airliners, crashing the first two planes into the World Trade Center in New York City and one into the Pentagon in Arlington County, Virginia. The fourth plane crashed in rural Pennsylvania during a passenger revolt.
Easton Mayor Megan Cook said, "We are here today to ensure its lessons of courage, of loss and of unity are never forgotten. Let us forever honor the bravery of first responders, who without hesitation ran towards danger."
Dressed in formal wear, Talbot County Sheriff Joe Gamble and Easton Chief of Police Alan Lowery placed a wreath in the memorial space across from the library. The stone bench behind them was carved with "You Are Not Forgotten."
Pastor Reginald Pinkett of Asbury United Methodist Church invoked the holy presence. And Pastor Dave Griffin of Grace Fellowship gave a short sermon.
Pinkett said, "We comfort the firefighters, the paramedics, the police officers, all the ones who gave lives trying to help and protect on that crucial day."
Many heads were bowed. Many hands were crossed as the victims of 9/11 were brought to mind.

While 9/11 is a national event, the focus is on Talbot County's local observance, making 'Local Life' the most precise category. 'Public Safety' is tangentially related to 9/11 but not the event's core focus.

title: Birding and boating the Harriet Tubman Byway
author: Tom McCall
content:
Birding and boating the Harriet Tubman Byway

 September 14, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Tom McCall | Section: Local News 
 
 711
 Words 

 Read News Document

 DENTON — On Thursday afternoon, a tour group traversed the Harriet Tubman Underground Railroad Scenic Byway while also spotting 25 species of birds.The event, "Birding & Boating the Harriet Tubman Byway," was hosted by Alex Green and Jim Rapp. It aimed at highlighting Tubman's accomplishments while also celebrating the nature of the Eastern Shore.
Jeanea Blair came all the way from Baltimore for the excursion.
"I love that we can combine history and nature, which I think traditionally people don't combine those things. It shows you can't really separate one from the other. The land informs our history and the history informs our land. It is cool to see that intersection and learn more about all of our history," Blair said.
The tour featured several sites that are central to the life and work Harriet Tubman, an abolitionist and social activist who escaped from slavery in Dorchester County and became well-known for her work on the Underground Railroad.
Green, owner of Harriet Tubman Tours, gave context to each site.
Rapp, owner of Delmarva Birding Weekends, was the second guide. He had a pair of binoculars around his neck and was listening for chirps, watching attentively for birds.
"Alex is interpreting the reason why Linchester Mill, The Webb Cabin and the Caroline County Courthouse has so much importance to the Underground Railroad. Then on the boat we are still interpreting both things, but I step up and do the birding portion. We sort of tag team. This tour is about Harriet Tubman's work on the Underground Railroad," Rapp said.
Many sites were visited by the caravan of cars who followed the guides. Several participants said they had driven by the Underground Railroad signs on the road, but had never stopped.
The Harriet Tubman Underground Railroad Scenic Byway is a self-guided driving tour through Caroline and Dorchester Counties, with significant sites marked with signage. It continues north to Philadelphia.
One stop was the Leverton House, which was owned by Quakers Jacob and Hannah Leverton, supporters of the Underground Railroad. It was a dairy farm at the time. Although the Levertons were wealthy, hiding and clothing those escaping slavery was a risky undertaking. Now the private home has a long dusty road with corn fields all around, turkey vultures flying overhead.
Rapp said most birds can't smell a thing.
"Vultures have a huge nasal opening and a lot of senses in there. They are sniffing for stinky, rotten stuff," Rapp said.
There was sturdy but small cabin in Preston, which was owned by James Webb. The tour went inside and got to see the "potato hole," a trap door beneath the house, under which Webb would hide people escaping on the Underground Railroad.
"This is where James Webb worked his farm and lived and worked the Underground Railroad. He was a farmer and an Underground Railroad agent," Green said.
Standing in front of the Caroline County Courthouse, where slaves were sold, Green said the land affected the slave trade. The current courthouse replaced one that burned down.
"The menacing building of the time with slave auctions would be somewhat of a fanfare. It is just like going to a car auction. This is where they sold African Americans. A lot of commerce comes up and down the river. From here you can go anywhere you need to go in the world by the Choptank River all the way to the Atlantic," Green said.
There was a former school teacher of history on the tour. She wrote her senior thesis on abolitionists.
"It is great. I am learning things that I didn't know before and supplanting things I already knew," Betty McAdams said.
When Rapp saw a handful of hummingbirds, they filled the air with a buzzing sound.
He said, "Our predominant hummingbird on the East Coast is the ruby throat. Males have a bright, shiny metallic-looking throat."
The history buffs turned into avid naturalists as the tiny birds flitted around orange jewel weed blossoms. Later in the tour the saw a red tailed hawk.
At the end, the group boarded a 33-foot tritoon named Ellen B. The captain, Allan Thomason, had his daughter Ali Thomason as first mate.
Though birding and Underground Railroad history are a unique pairing, Green and Rapp bring life to both subjects.
In the winter they come together to do a different tour in Dorchester County that focuses on Tubman's early life.

title: Wheatley Methodist Church celebrates 240 years, new renovations
author: MAGGIE TROVATO mtrovato@chespub.com
content:
Wheatley Methodist Church celebrates 240 years, new renovations

 September 18, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: MAGGIE TROVATO mtrovato@chespub.com | Section: Local News 
 
 593
 Words 

 Read News Document

 RHODESDALE — A mix of church members and residents packed the Wheatley Methodist Church Sept. 15 to celebrate the church's 240th anniversary and see the newly-renovated building."I haven't seen the church that full in forever," Pastor Barbara McShain-Keyser said about the event.
Along with tours of the space, a dedication service was held. The service included prayer, a presentation of the building and a consecration of the church. After the service, attendees went next door to the Community Hall for food and drink before gathering outside to listen to a gospel concert featuring the Jones Boys.
Member Suellen Wheatley Wilkins said she printed 125 church bulletins for the event, and they were all gone by the end of the service.
For Wilkins, a church renovation had been in the back of her mind for years.
"I always wanted to see a wood floor back in here and that ugly brown paneling off the walls," she said. "And I wanted the aluminum siding off to expose the (clapboard) siding on the exterior."
The church was built in 1784 on land that was granted by King George II to William Wheatley around 1750, according to Wilkins. Since the church was built, it has continuously served the community as a church.
In the 1970s, the floor fell through, and it was replaced with carpet covering plywood. Paneling was placed along the walls to cover damage to Victorian-pressed tin panels, and aluminum siding was installed on the exterior of the building.
During a 2019 project to restore part of the church, the building's underlying structure was looked at, and the church was condemned. Members chose to salvage the church, and a plan to restore and preserve it was made.
Now the aluminum siding on the exterior is gone and the carpet covering plywood has been replaced with reclaimed hardwood. Most of the tin on the interior is gone, and wide boards, painted white, that run along the walls have been exposed.
Wilkins, who is a descendent of William Wheatley, said the church has stayed around all these years because God intended it to. She said that when she sits in the church, memories come back to her.
"I can see my grandparents in here," she said. "I see all the old people that I thought were ancient when I was little."
McShain-Keyser said many churches have closed, but God keeps the Wheatley Methodist Church going. She said the dedicated members, who have made her feel "part of the family," also work very hard to keep things going.
"It's amazing because you don't see many churches like this," she said.
Wilkins said that around 2010, there would be somewhere between three and six people at the church for Sunday service. Over the years, the number of members has increased. Wilkins said the church now has 15 or 16 members. She said about 28 people come on Sunday mornings.
Beverly Wheatley, who has been coming to the church since she was about 5 years old, said the church looks different, but very nice.
"I think it's just nice that they repaired this church and didn't let it fall down," she said.
Annette Henry called the newly-renovated church "inviting."
"I had been in it before they started working on it," she said. "So it's very obvious that its improvements have been fantastic."
When talking about the success of the dedication event, Wilkins mentioned a grant the church was awarded from the Bartus Trew Providence Preservation Fund. She said requirements of the grant award include making the place available for people with like interests to visit and for education.
"That has been met 10 times over today," she said.

title: 'This is hard. It is history': Barber shop closing after more than a century
author: Josh Shannon jshannon@chespub.com
content:
'This is hard. It is history': Barber shop closing after more than a century

 September 19, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Josh Shannon jshannon@chespub.com | Section: News 
 
 988
 Words 

 Read News Document

 After more than a century of serving Delaware, the Main Street Barber Shop in Newark will close its doors for the final time on Friday.Kim Teti, the sixth owner of the shop, is retiring after 31 years and moving to Florida. The shop, which is part of the Klondike Kate's building, will be turned into a merchandise shop for the restaurant or possibly be used as a dedicated place to pick up to-go meals.
It's a bittersweet moment for Teti, who has spent the past few weeks saying goodbye to longtime customers, many of whom have become like family.
"I am very sad, a little choked up right now," Teti said. "This is hard. Because it's closing after 100-some years, it is history."
The barber shop is located in the iconic Exchange Building, which was built in 1880 and is on the National Register of Historic Places. It was originally built as a grange hall and has housed a meat market, post office, pool hall, general store, movie theater, courthouse, jail, skating rink, gas station and — since 1979 — Klondike Kate's restaurant. One constant through the years has been the barber shop, which according to Newark Post archives, has been there in one form or another for at least 130 years.
Teti's long association with the barber shop began on a whim.
After growing up near Wilmington, she learned to be a barber while attending Delcastle Technical High School. She honed her skills working at a barber shop in the Hotel DuPont, where she learned from old-school Italian barbers working there, and then worked at a barber shop in Greenville.
Teti was driving through Newark one day when she saw the Main Street Barber Shop and decided to stop in and ask about part-time work. The owner at the time, Ralph Burchard, spent summers in Maine and was planning to close the shop for the summer unless he found someone to fill in for him.
"A week later, he gave me the key to the shop," Teti recalled. "He went from Memorial Day all the way to Labor Day, and I worked the entire summer all by myself."
She filled in for Burchard a couple more times and then, in the summer of 1993, a fire damaged Klondike Kate's and the barber shop. Burchard, then 81, decided to retire instead of dealing with the expense and stress of repairing the damage.
Teti decided to take over the business full time and her husband, a tile contractor, worked to restore the historic shop, which reopened a few months later.
Over the years, she has strived to keep the business in the style of what she calls an "antique barber shop," with a barber pole outside, high ceilings, large windows, original cabinets, old-style barber chairs, pictures of Frank Sinatra and Marlon Brando on the walls and a tile mural depicting Main Street of yesteryear.
"I never wanted to modernize it," Teti said. "I always wanted it to stay like turn of the century."
Though the barber shop hasn't changed much, Main Street has, Teti lamented.
"When I first came here, it was Jimmy's Diner, the Post House, and Eagle Furniture was up there. It was a mom-and-pop town," she said. "And then it changed. I liked the way it was. It was awesome."
When Teti took over the shop, she charged $7 for a haircut. Now, she has to charge between $20 and $25 to keep up with rising costs.
The addition of a covered deck for Klondike Kate's a few years ago made the barber shop a lot less visible, making it harder to draw in foot traffic.
"You can barely tell it's a barbershop," Teti said. "Back in the day, it stuck out like a sore thumb, and then they built the deck."
She has also seen the type of customer change. She used to get a lot of university students, but "now they go to the shops where they play the loud rap music and stuff like that," she said.
Still, the shop serves an eclectic mix of customers, some of whom started coming decades ago when Burchard was still in charge. At least one older customer recalls getting his hair cut at the shop when he was a kid, Teti said.
"We get all walks of life in here, everybody from politicians to construction people, lawyers, doctors, everybody comes here," she said, noting that she even cut the hair of future Super Bowl MVP Joe Flacco when he played for the Blue Hens.
Teti has kept the shop going as Klondike Kate's changed hands twice, each time promoting worry that the new owner might want a different use for the barber shop space. She expressed gratitude to current owner Gianmarco Martuscelli, who told her when he bought the restaurant in 2016 that she was welcome to stay for as long she liked.
"Gianmarco was nothing but happy for the barbershop to go on," she said. "But he did tell me a long time ago when he bought the building that when I was done, he had plans for it."
Teti had planned to keep the shop going even longer, but her husband recently suffered an injury that forced him to retire, so the couple decided it was time to move to Florida and take advantage of the second home they bought a few years ago.
She's looking forward to the warmer weather but doubts that she's hung up her barber shears for good.
"Most barbers work until they're in their 80s and can't work no more. I'm too young to really retire at 64 years old," she said, adding that she may find part-time work in Florida.
Teti said she'll miss her customers the most.
"It's not a hard job, and you make friends along the way. You don't get rich off of it, but it's a good career," she said. "I can honestly say that I never got up and said, 'Oh God, I gotta go to the job today.' It was always a happy place to come to."

title: Easton flying event gets women up in the air
author: Maggie Trovato
content:
Easton flying event gets women up in the air

 September 20, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Maggie Trovato | Section: Local News 
 
 615
 Words 

 Read News Document

 EASTON — Women who have always wanted to experience of being up in the air in a small plane got their opportunity last weekend at the first ever Let's Fly Now event in Maryland.The event, held at Easton Airport on Sept. 14, gave a group of 21 women the chance to learn about planes and sit in the passenger seat as a pilot takes flight.
Let's Fly Now was put on by the Maryland Chapter of the Ninety-Nines, an international nonprofit organization made up of licensed women pilots from around the world. Maria Esparraguera, who has been a member of the Ninety-Nines for about 5 years and is currently the Maryland Chapter secretary and the Mid-Atlantic Section vice governor, piloted two different flights during the event last weekend. She said that both of the women she flew were "very enthusiastic."
"Both of them (had) always wanted to go up in a small airplane," she said, "never had a chance."
One of the women Esparraguera flew told Esparraguera that her father had flown planes.
"She actually asked me to take a picture of her in the same pose that she had seen her father have a picture taken of him in his airplane," Esparraguera said.
Cheryl Mohrmann, who was an organizer of the event, said she saw the event as an initiative to get more women flying planes.
"The women are out there," she said, adding that even though they barely advertised the event, it filled up in a matter of hours.
Although a lot of the 21 women and teens who signed up were local, some came from different parts of Maryland. Mohrmann said one woman even drove all the way from Brooklyn, New York.
During the event, attendees spent about an hour in ground school learning all things planes: the different parts of a plane, a plane's axes, how to do a pre-flight inspection, how to remain safe in air and more. After that, participants were taken into the air by licensed pilots.
Up in the air, the women got a chance to take the yoke — which is used to control the plane — if they wanted.
The Let's Fly Now event was specifically for women who are of the age eligible to fly a plane. Mohrmann said the event — which was advertised to women between the ages of 15 and 99 — brought women of a range of ages. She said about four of the attendees were under 18 years old.
Both Mohrmann and Esparraguera said some of the pilots involved with the event took notice of attendees' strong engagement.
"They felt like some of these people are really going to do this," Mohrmann said about the attendees becoming pilots one day. "It made a big difference to (the pilots) that they were able to contribute in that way."
Mohrmann said that although there aren't yet plans for another event, there is a lot of interest. She said after the event, everyone said, "I can't wait for the next one."
Esparraguera said the event last weekend reminded her of a Women in Aviation conference she attended where a flight simulator was brought in. She said that she loved seeing all the women in line for the flight simulator at the conference.
"And that they didn't have to kind of push their way in," she said. "Because I think that that's what happens a lot."
She said the event Sept. 14 gave women who "have an inkling toward aviation" an opportunity to try it out without being "pushed aside."
"And so this kind of gave them (a) 'Hey, look. This is for you. We set this up for you. Nobody's going to cut in line ahead of you. Just go ahead. Just go ahead and try,'" she said.

title: Edna Parks celebrates 110th birthday
author: KONNER METZ kmetz@chespub.com
content:
Edna Parks celebrates 110th birthday

 September 21, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: KONNER METZ kmetz@chespub.com | Section: Local News 
 
 349
 Words 

 Read News Document

 EASTON — Hymns, roast beef and chocolate cake made for a perfect day for Edna Parks.Surrounded by family and members of the community, Parks celebrated her 110th birthday at The Dixon House in Easton on Tuesday afternoon, four days ahead of her actual birthday Saturday.
Linda Elben, executive director of The Dixon House, an assisted living facility, said Parks requested to have her favorite foods for lunch as she celebrated: roast beef and mashed potatoes, chocolate cake and Coca-Cola made it a complete birthday celebration.
Scott Clausen, choir director at St. Mark's United Methodist Church, and organist Ranee Reitz performed a set of hymns as everyone joined in to sing. Hymns included "Amazing Grace" and Parks' favorite, "How Great Thou Art."
"Very good," Parks said after the last verse of her favorite hymn was sung.
Parks, who has lived her whole life in Talbot County, has lived at The Dixon House for five years. She lived independently until she was 102.
Parks still walks and uses the exercise room, activity director Shelly LaRoque said. She had been known to be one of the first to the activity room in the past, always ready with her calendar in hand. Even as recently as six months ago, Parks was still crocheting.
Parks' daughter-in-law Betty Parks said just a few weeks ago, Edna joined members of The Dixon House in going down to St. Michaels to take a tour on The Patriot, a historic cruise operated by the Chesapeake Bay Maritime Museum. "When they go, she's ready," Betty Parks said of her mother-in-law.
Edna's longevity can been attributed to multiple factors, family members said.
"Well it's a miracle, that's what it is," Betty Parks said. "She's blessed."
Her son and daughter-in-law said she's never had major surgeries and avoided hard labor during her life. That, along with a daily soda, has kept her healthy.
"She has her Coke every day, doctor's orders," Betty Parks joked. "We made him write it down on the paper."
Edna's son, Roger, was grateful for The Dixon House's celebration and for another year of life for his mom.
"She's doing great, and she's happy there," Roger Parks said.

title: Venerable Chestertown bookseller celebrates 20 years
author: LISA J. GOTTO Special to the Star Democrat
content:
Venerable Chestertown bookseller celebrates 20 years

 September 26, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: LISA J. GOTTO Special to the Star Democrat | Section: News 
 
 639
 Words 

 Read News Document

 CHESTERTOWN — "Let's open a brick-and-mortar bookstore," wasn't exactly the phrase on many entrepreneurs' lips in 2004 when a newcomer to Chestertown saw the potential in a storefront in the 100 block of Cross Street.As owner Tom Martin tells it, he and wife Lizzie had only been in town a couple of times when they started exploring real estate with the intention of having a weekend home option.
And then Lizzie's hairdresser turned Martin's attention to a commercial property, an empty storefront on Cross Street.
Since leaving a political post in his mid-50s, Martin said, he set out on a personal journey that would hopefully have him figuring out what he wanted to do with the rest of his life. In the current vernacular, this "pivot" included working in both small- and large-scale bookstores in Washington, D.C.
The plan was to spend six months in this particular sector of retail, which he said he took to, "like a fish to water."
"When I got that job, it took me two days to say, 'Man, this is fun," Martin said.
And yet, when the storefront opportunity presented itself, he was not quick to put two and two together.
"How this all happened was very strange," he said. "It didn't happen by design; I was not looking for a bookshop."
But eventually he signed lease at 112 Cross Street, despite Lizzie's best efforts to dissuade him. Martin vividly recalled their exact conversation, which took place at Bethesda's Tastee Diner over breakfast one morning.
"You're going to what?" he said was his wife's reply when he revealed that he had decided that he wanted to move forward with opening a used bookstore in Chestertown.
"What would you even call it?" she replied skeptically. Martin relayed that he looked down at the beautiful breakfast on the table before him and replied, "I'm going to call it The Bookplate."
And so it began, with the books from his own vast collection, finds from local outlets like Dixon's Auction at Crumpton, and the good will of many who wished to donate either personally or from estate collections.
Fast-forward 20 years, and The Bookplate is thriving. The place is now home to some 50,000 old and new volumes, give or take, and has seen its fair share of customers, cultural events and milestones.
Since opening in 2004, Martin has not stressed over the effect technology has had on reading habits. Rather, he balances his approach to tome-centric retail by leaning into the sense of community he can build around books and reading.
This connection to the community goes way back, he said. Prior to the pandemic, the store had a small stage and was the place to be for local music, plays and impromptu poetry festivals.
That is the state of play at The Bookplate; there is always something going on in and around the store.
Martin said as a bookseller he chooses not to be influenced and prefers to cast a wide net when it comes to genres and titles.
When the occasion of the store's 20th anniversary on Sept. 11 came around, Martin said, the staff thought to recognize the day with some sort of celebration. At first, Martin said he downplayed the idea because of the way he approaches every day in his life. As a member of an alcohol recovery program for several decades standing, Martin said he is more than grateful for what he has been able to accomplish, in part, because he has been successful in maintaining his sobriety. He also feels it's important to convey the message to others who may be struggling that they should take heart that there is longevity in the program.
"Because of who I am and where I'm coming from, I'm just grateful to have the store. Life was turned around and it worked out well. And so, every time somebody comes through that door, I mean, that's a celebration."

title: Volunteers donate $10K to Chesapeake Housing Mission
author: MAGGIE TROVATO mtrovato@chespub.com
content:
Volunteers donate $10K to Chesapeake Housing Mission

 September 27, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: MAGGIE TROVATO mtrovato@chespub.com | Section: Local News 
 
 645
 Words 

 Read News Document

 CAMBRIDGE — Chesapeake Housing Mission board member and project engineer Dave Mayonado knew he would be building a ramp for a Cambridge resident Thursday morning with the help of a group of volunteers from Regal Rexnord. But he didn't know the volunteers would be donating more than their time.As the group gathered outside Ben Parks' home early Thursday morning to build a ramp, Mayonado was handed a check for $10,000 to be put toward the nonprofit's mission of offering home repair services to low-income families in Dorchester, Somerset, Wicomico and Worcester counties.
"This is super timely because it really is needed at this point," he said to the volunteers. "Particularly in this county here."
This is the third year that Regal Rexnord, an international manufacturing company with a facility in Cambridge, has organized a volunteer day with Chesapeake Housing Mission. Regal Rexnord's human resource business partner Beth Hancock said the company offers 16 hours of paid volunteer work and sets up multiple volunteer opportunities for employees each year.
Mayonado told the group that when COVID-related funding was available, it was easier to build ramps and offer other home repair services to families in need.
"But that's gone now," he said. "So we're having some funding agencies telling us they don't have the money."
Although Chesapeake Housing Mission is made up of volunteers, the organization needs money to buy materials for the projects they complete. Mayonado said every project costs about $2,000 to $3,000. He said the money comes through funding agencies and donations.
"So a situation like this (where) we have an opportunity for them not only to do the job, but then they're going to pay for these materials and maybe two more jobs, or maybe even three — it's pretty cool," he said.
Hancock said one of the reasons Regal Rexnord chose to donate money to Chesapeake Housing Mission was because there are many people in Dorchester County in need of health care services. She said there are people who can't get to doctors appointments because their family members can't get them out of their homes.
"So this is something that just goes so much further," she said. "And it just could be life-changing for someone who needs to get to the doctor."
Regal Rexnord materials manager Aurora Arriaga, who was volunteering with Chesapeake Housing Mission for a second year, said for people who have difficulties walking, a ramp affects not only where they can go, but how they feel. She said not being able to leave your house can feel isolating.
"So I think being able to help the people not feel so isolated, especially nowadays, is just an amazing thing to do," she said.
The group built a ramp outside of Ben Parks' front door. Parks, a retired waterman, hasn't been able to leave his home in about three months due to medical issues. The ramp built on Thursday will allow him to get in and out of his home safely.
As 14 of the Regal Rexnord employees moved and sawed lumber, the 15th employee, Cole Collins, removed vegetation from Parks' driveway. Although that task was not a part of the Chesapeake Housing Mission project, Collins — who owns Peninsula Dirt Works LLC along with being the manufacturing engineering manager at Regal Rexnord — noticed during a pre-construction meeting that the Parks' driveway is not level and is hard to walk on. He decided to bring his tractor to redo the driveway on Thursday.
Collins, who is a Dorchester County native, talked about the importance of giving back to the community.
"It's huge when businesses are able to give back to our local community," he said. "... And I'm glad to be able to give back as well. It's not much, but it's something."
Mayonado talked about the rewarding feeling of getting a hug from someone "who has been locked in their house and now is free."
"That's the reason we do it, honestly," he said.

title: Molly's Place brings outdoors lovers together for fun fall event
author: WILL BONTRAGER wbontrager@chespub.com
content:
Molly's Place brings outdoors lovers together for fun fall event

 October 1, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: WILL BONTRAGER wbontrager@chespub.com | Section: Local News 
 
 593
 Words 

 Read News Document

 KENNEDYVILLE — Molly's 14th annual fall tent sale returned bigger and better, rebranded as the Maryland Outdoor Festival this year.All through the weekend, Sept. 20-22, Molly's Place set up a massive tent courtesy of Eastern Shore Tent and Events, packed with savings from favorite hunting, fishing and outdoor brands, offering up to 70 percent off purchases.
In addition, there were giveaways like four Yeti coolers worth $250 a piece, autographed by Orioles players and a Sunday Sweeps with a Traeger Grill package.
For three days, residents enjoyed the comfortable weather, browsing the sales, seeking familiar brands like Benelli USA, Hevi-Shot, YETI and many more.
But Molly's tent sale is not just for the hunters and anglers. Rebranded now, the staff aims to create an event enjoyed by the entire community.
One of the organizers Prakash "Chikki" Shajwani emphasized this point, "We wanted to give back to the community. This is a way of getting kids outdoors and for families to get together."
Marketing Director Sara Dion echoed his statements, mentioning the new vendors this year to do that: the decoy table, duck and goose call makers, and some fun activities for kids along with food trucks.
Under the tent with the callers and decoy makers, there was a wealth of information from experts of their craft, people willing to discuss their workmanship, honed from years of experience.
Like Sean Mann the World Goose Calling Champion of Champions. He won championships for duck calling and for making his own calls.
Working beside his son, Ian, who shows his talent for making calls, Mann said he owed his career path to the late Dan Edwards, an instructor at Anne Arundel College and a good friend.
"He made the dream possible. Without him none of this would have happened," Mann said.
These awe-inspiring stories weren't limited to just the vendors.
Looking at crossbows, Delaware resident Rene Swing casually mentioned how she once got a bear using a Horton Legacy crossbow, in a deer stand, in Maine.
These outdoor stories were all over the place, uniting residents and visitors.
Outside the tent, children enjoyed climbing the bouncy castle, The Triple Shots 4-H crew taught kids archery and beside them was a BB gun range run by the National Wild Turkey Federation along with the Queen Anne's County High School Clay Target Team, ensuring proper safety.
With cold beverages and good food there was also a nice mix of local talented musicians entertaining while spectators sat on hay bales.
The Quinn Arnold Band played on Friday, Joe Bryan sang and strummed classics on Saturday, and newcomer Elena Barnett with musician Justin Singleton, closed out Sunday with country, blues and rock covers.
For three days Molly's was bustling with activity.
Dion said last year they drew approximately 15,000. They anticipated recording as many this year, if not more.
Shajwani showed appreciation to all the volunteers such as the Chestertown Lions Club for helping park cars, the Kennedyville Volunteer Fire Company selling beer, and the Maryland State Police for helping on that busy stretch of road navigating people who came as far as Virginia and Baltimore for the event.
And he thanked the community recalling when the place was called Vonnie's noting how it was a hub for Marylanders to meet.
With their tagline, "Fuel your adventure," Shajwani said Molly's shows that same appreciation to the location's history and the culture while making their own mark.
Dion said, "We want to express our gratitude to the wonderful members of our community who attended the event and continue to support Molly's. Kent County holds a special place in our hearts, and we are honored to be part of this remarkable community."

title: Frederick Douglass Day continues to share abolitionist's legacy
author: WENDY WEITZEL wweitzel@chespub.com
content:
Frederick Douglass Day continues to share abolitionist's legacy

 October 2, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: WENDY WEITZEL wweitzel@chespub.com | Section: Local News 
 
 577
 Words 

 Read News Document

 EASTON — The first time Harriette Lowery heard that Frederick Douglass had grown up in Talbot County was when she moved back to Easton with her husband in the early 2000s.Lowery was surprised to hear of Douglass' local origins. She had grown up in Talbot County, but she had never known it was the famed abolitionist's birthplace.
"The historical society had put a notice in the paper asking for people to respond to a question — 'Is anybody interested in honoring Frederick Douglass in some way since he's our native son.' And I read that and thought, 'I knew a lot about Frederick Douglass, but I did not know he was from Talbot County,'" she said Saturday, surveying the crowd outside the Talbot County Free Library that had assembled for the annual Frederick Douglass Day celebration.
"... I was a little embarrassed by that but more interested in doing something because of that," Lowery said.
Lowery and her late husband became founding members of the Frederick Douglass Honor Society, the group that spearheaded the process of having a statue of Douglass erected on the Talbot County Court House lawn. The statue was unveiled to a crowd of thousands in June, 2011, after years of sometimes tense back-and-forth between the honor society, members of the community and local governments.
Frederick Douglass Day evolved from that unveiling ceremony in an effort to continue the honor society's mission of educating the community about Douglass.
"Since 2011, the Frederick Douglass Honor Society decided that it wanted to continue efforts to continue the legacy of Frederick Douglass," said Walter Black, another founding member of the Frederick Douglass Honor Society. "So the main thing that we concentrated on is the Frederick Douglass Day."
On Saturday, Frederick Douglass Day filled downtown Easton with a parade, a ceremony, a lecture, a children's village and a city block filled with vendors, nonprofits and live entertainment.
"The event gets bigger and better every year," said Debbi Dodson, the Frederick Douglass Day event coordinator. "More people get involved and more people attend, so that is a sign that people appreciate it and really support it."
The keynote speaker for this year's event, Keidrick Roy, said that although this was his first time visiting Talbot County, he has been working with the Frederick Douglass Honor Society for several years.
Keidrick Roy, a fellow at Harvard University, signed copies of his new book, "American Dark Age: Racial Feudalism and the Rise of Black Liberalism," at the event. Roy said Douglass is heavily featured in the work.
"I've always wanted to be in the place where Frederick Douglass walked and talked and had many of his formative experiences, so it's very special for me to be here to do this," he said. "I loved the celebration this morning, seeing so many people from different parts of the city, different parts of the town come out and honor Douglass in a variety of ways."
In holding the event every year, Lowery said the honor society hopes to ensure that all members of the community are aware of Douglass's ties to Talbot County and of how the principles of equality and freedom that Douglass espoused are still relevant today.
"What we wanted was for everybody to look at Douglass as an American hero and not an African American hero," Lowery said.
On Saturday, Lowery remarked that Talbot County had made progress toward that goal since 2011.
"We're always growing and getting better, or we should be anyway," she said. "Every year, I know that there's progress."

 CENTERVILLE — Winners of the 2024 annual Fishing Derby received recognition during the Centreville Town Council meeting Oct. 3.Sponsored by the Town of Centreville Parks Advisory Board and the Corsica River Conservatory providing rods, bait and advice, this year's annual day of fishing fun welcomed a record-breaking 54 participants ages 2 to 15 and their families to the Wharf Park Sept. 14, Sandy Simpson of the Parks Advisory Board said.
With a seven-inch white perch, Zane Foulger, 3, tipped the scales in not only catching the largest fish for his 2-to-5-year-old age group, but also the reeling in the fish of the day, Simpson said.
In the 6 to 9 age category, Sophie McNiece, 7, and Conner Khamvongsa, 9, each hooked 11-inch catfish.

title: Harvest Party: Sultana Foundation welcomes fall with free event
author: WILL BONTRAGER wbontrager@chespub.com
content:
Harvest Party: Sultana Foundation welcomes fall with free event

 October 11, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: WILL BONTRAGER wbontrager@chespub.com | Section: News 
 
 402
 Words 

 Read News Document

 With exceptional weather on Saturday, Oct. 5, beside a freshwater pond, marsh and forest, banjo music played to a crowd.Ringing in the autumn season, Sultana Education Foundation threw their Sultana Harvest Party in Chestertown, inviting the community to the Lawrence Wetlands Preserve, free-of-charge.
Founder Chris Cereno said ever since the preserve had their ribbon cutting last fall, they haven't really had any community events there.
So they were expecting maybe 70 people.
Despite many other festivities throughout Kent County, he was pleased and surprised to see, what he guessed, was more like 300, partaking in the festive activities volunteers offered.
People showed up to celebrate autumn, bringing their own blankets with them. They found a cozy spot in the woods or mingled with neighbors.
"We're thrilled that we have a lot of younger families here. We've got a petting zoo, games for kids, all kinds of things. The concept was to have a family-friendly event in a nice, relaxing atmosphere."
Volunteers also handed out free pizza, in a hut — literally a pizza hut.
Animals like a mini horse, a mini donkey, goats, rabbits and ducks were petted and combed courtesy of Party Animals LLC. out of Sudlersville.
Fearless little toddler Betty Herr donned her goggles to pet the shaggy goat; her mom was amused.
Nearby, on the bocce ball court, volunteer Melissa Lane guided a boy on how to play the beloved sport of the County, with a holiday twist, using pumpkins instead of balls. Pumpkins don't quite roll as nice but the kids enjoyed them, Lane said.
Live music was provided from Flatland Drive, a bluegrass band with modern stylings. Volunteers handed out regional beer or wine while the band played some originals and covers.
The woods added enough shade for adults to have a comfortable spot to relax.
Nature lovers enjoyed the gravel path that follows the Gilchrist Rail trail.
That trail opens out to a pond with a nice view of the woods and the Sultana building. In Saturday's case, folks got a view of the musicians and the people gathered around them while the sun cast shadows over the water.
Cereno noted that first-time visitors are a little surprised of all the wildlife back there.
The wetlands is a 8.5 acre urban nature center featuring a variety of ecosystems. "We're still in the town but it doesn't feel like it," Cereno said. "It's really beautiful out here."
He encouraged visitors and residents to check out the trail, open from sunrise to sunup.

 514
 Words 

 Read News Document

 This Saturday and Sunday the attention across Southern Maryland will be focused on the St. Mary's County Fairgrounds where the Rotary Club of Lexington Park will host the 58th annual U.S. Oyster Festival, featuring fresh seafood and sufficient oyster shucking competition.Considering that the county boasts over 500 miles of shoreline, providing fisherman and local residents with an abundant variety of seafood, it only seems fitting that St. Mary's County hosts the annual event.
Hosted once again by the local rotary club, the U.S. Oyster Festival which food and fun for the whole family and proceeds from the event will be used to fund local community projects.
On Saturday will be the 45th annual National Oyster Cook-Off with cash prizes available in three different categories. Local residents have more their held their own in recent years in the cooking competitions. Deborah Reynolds of Waldorf took first-place in the 2022 event, while Ellynne Brice Davis of Leonardtown was third in that category. Reynolds also boasts a first-place finish in the Soups & Stews category.
"This festival was started to highlight the importance of the oyster harvest to the entire region and there are so many events surrounding it now that it is really a two-day event," said Teri Moore, chairperson for the 2024 U.S. Oyster Festival Committee. "The National Oyster Shucking Competition brings people from all over the country to compete."
On Saturday, the 45th annual National Oyster Cook-Off will highlight the festivities as contestants will be competing for cash prizes in three different divisions — Hors d'ouevres, Soups & Stews and Main Dishes. Grand prize for first place is $300, second place is $200 and third place will earn $150, although the winners will be entitled to immeasurable bragging rights throughout the year.
Organizers promise that the genuine "one and only" U.S. National Shucking Competition will be a "shell-shucking good time" with supporting events that include pony rides and a petting zoo, bouncy houses, an axe throwing exhibition, live music, a tasting tent, food vendors and craft vendors. A dozen local businesses have signed on as corporate partners.
"Not only does the winner of the local competition get a prize, they get to compete in the International Championship next September," Moore added. "Best of all, after the competition the contestants give the shucked oysters to anyone nearby interested at eating them."
If you go
The 58th annual U.S. Oyster Festival will take place Saturday and Sunday, Oct. 19 and 20, at the St. Mary's County Fairgrounds in Leonardtown. Hosted by the Rotary Club of Lexington Park, the U.S. Oyster Festival will offer guests with ample food and fun with an oyster shucking competition literally taking center stage.
On Saturday, Oct. 19, gates will open at 10 a.m. and close at 6 p.m., then on Sunday, Oct. 20, gates will open at 11 a.m. and close at 4 p.m. Entry at the gate is $15 each day, although a two-day ticket is available for $20, while kids 10 and under are free. Saturday will be the 45th annual National Oyster Cook-Off, which includes cash prizes in three different divisions.

title: Aurora borealis burns bright over Eastern Shore
author: Tom McCall
content:
Aurora borealis burns bright over Eastern Shore

 October 11, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Tom McCall | Section: Local News 
 
 323
 Words 

 Read News Document

 EASTON — The northern lights came south for a rare and colorful display Thursday night. One local self-taught astronomer and self-described "star geek" stayed up late to see it all.Julie Heikes fell in love with the heavens decades ago.
"I got interested in astronomy with comet Hayakutake in 1995. It was before Hale-Bopp, and the tail of it, I could see it all the way across the sky one night. That was when I was determined to figure things out," Heikes said.
Although she has telescopes to look at Saturn and the moons of Jupiter, this celestial event was strictly enjoyed with the naked eye.
The naked could see the event, but having and iPhone or bigger camera, yielded a clearer picture of the celestial event.
"It was so cool. It may happen again. The phone picks up more than the eye can. When we couldn't see anything, Margaret's (Enloe-North) iPhone was picking up some green glow," Heikes said.
"It would morph and blob around, and then like a really intense line of green would show up. That would fade and a pink blob would come up over there. There were rays coming up. It is just cool," she said.
The aurora borealis, also known as the northern lights, are a natural light show that occurs when the Earth's magnetic field interacts with charged particles from the sun during an event called a solar storm. Because these particles are attracted to the plant's magnetic poles, these events typically happen around the Earth's furthest north and south latitudes.
But the storm Thursday was big enough to reach beyond the normal arctic arena.
"I saw a picture that someone took in Big Pine Key, Florida. It reached at least down to the Florida Keys," Heikes said. "He said it is so weird to see the Northern Lights with palm trees in the foreground. Rare. I Hope the people in North Carolina got to see it. It would be good for the soul."

title: Paper keeps community informed
author: Staff Writer
content:
Paper keeps community informed

 October 12, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Staff Writer | Section: Editors Inbox 
 
 300
 Words 

 Read News Document

 Locked door and a lock box. No chance of seeing through the blackened window. That's how I found the entrance to the Circulation Department of the Star Democrat one day last February.My heart sank, and not because I would have to get on the phone with them about my subscription. My heart sank at this symbol of an unfree press.
What's wrong? I asked someone who would know. I got information on the hours when one could go to the front entrance and get to visit the newsroom, and mention of the attack on the Annapolis Gazette five years ago.
So, a question of security. But the memory of the locked door and the blackened window remained in my mind as a portent of things that could come.
One of the first items in a dictator's bag of tricks is to shut down the free press and retain one news outlet as the voice of the regime. Did you hear Donald Trump say, after his debate with Kamala Harris, that ABC should lose its license? Trump talks often about shutting down news outlets; he has sued 20 of them. Advisers such as Steve Bannon and Kash Patel have openly talked about plans to seek revenge against journalists.
And here we are in Talbot County, Maryland, proudly celebrating 225 years of continuous news coverage of this community. Over those years the local press has risen from ashes a few times, had its equipment wrecked, and, during the Civil War, lost a Southern-sympathizing editor to exile.
Our local newspaper keeps the community informed about itself, and we're damned lucky to have it. But what if — in a second Trump administration — somebody came over from Washington with the authority to shut down the Star Democrat? There is every reason to consider that possibility.
MARGARET BARTON DRIGGS
Easton

title: Taste of Cambridge brings delectable treats to downtown Cambridge
author: JIM JOHNSON jjohnson@chespub.com
content:
Taste of Cambridge brings delectable treats to downtown Cambridge

 October 15, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: JIM JOHNSON jjohnson@chespub.com | Section: Local News 
 
 297
 Words 

 Read News Document

 The weather was perfect Saturday, drawing a large crowd to the 16th Taste of Cambridge event."We were extremely thrilled with the turnout," said Christina Wingate-Spence, Cambridge Main Street executive director. More than 300 Taste of Cambridge tickets were sold and the overall crowd in downtown Cambridge was upwards of 800, Wingate-Spence said.
The event — the second hosted after a hiatus during the COVID-19 pandemic — featured 11 cook-off contest competing for best crab soup, best crab cake, best Eastern Shore fare and best desserts.
Winners were:
Crab soup: Blue Ruin bar and restaurant.Crab cake: Blue Ruin bar and restaurant.Eastern Shore fare: Vintage 414 wine bar.Dessert: Blackwater Bakery and Eats.
Ticket holders voted for the people's choice award, which went to Blue Ruin's crab cake.
The judges for the four awards were: Laurie Forster, an author and national expert on all things wine; Tami Weber, WBOC morning show host; and Gena Levy, owner of Bay Country Bakery in Cambridge.
In addition to the cook-off contestants there was a Kid Zone, featuring a face painter and bounce houses. A giant crab balloon archway created by Cabin Fever Play Centre was the backdrop for many selfies.
Two stages featured a variety of entertainment. On the main stage at the intersection of Race and Gay streets, the Soul Crackers, an 11-piece ensemble from the Washington, D.C., area, made a repeat performance. They were followed by the Radio Pilots, a rock cover band, which received an enthusiastic welcome from the crowd.
On the second stage, located at the intersection of Muir and Race streets, a variety of students performed; along with Inland Fusion featuring Nancy and Jody; and Jayme D., a solo artist.
The event drew people from across the Eastern Shore and Washington, D.C. Wingate-Spence said the downtown shops had a large influx of customers throughout the day.

title: Easton Airport Day a roaring success
author: Tom McCall
content:
Easton Airport Day a roaring success

 October 16, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Tom McCall | Section: Local News 
 
 492
 Words 

 Read News Document

 EASTON — The 14th annual Easton Airport Day drew hundreds on a blue-skied fall day, Oct. 12, to see the roaring spectacle of WW II planes, Naval Academy parachute jumpers and tidily kept up biplanes.The keynote speaker was Gustavus McLeod, the executive director of the Glenn L. Martin Maryland Aviation Museum.
"Look up into this cloudless sky. It is like you can see forever," McLeod said.
Event attendees were allowed to explore some of the aircraft on the tarmac, like the Maryland State medevac helicopter Trooper 6. Kids put on flight helmets, and aviation enthusiasts took the opportunity to come aboard.
Trooper 6 does more than carry the sick and injured. The team also does search and rescue missions and can work with their camera to assist with police chases. The camera is so strong that it can identify what kind of beer you are drinking from a mile and a half away said Cpl. Jeff Kelly.
"It is a lot of fun just to talk to people. We get to surprise people because a lot of people don't know what we do. If you put in a call for help, there is no charge for that. The citizens of Maryland have decided that we collectively have to pay for this," Kelly said.
For $7, attendees could climb into the Spirit of Freedom, which flew in the 1949 Berlin Airlift and gave Franklin D. Roosevelt a ride.
When planes got into formation and buzzed overhead, everybody looked up and shaded their eyes from the sun.
The food tents were bustling with the smell of bacon and funnel cakes.
Congressman Andy Harris addressed the crowd.
"The airport is such an important part of the economy and this runway extension project is going to keep us the premier general aviation airport in the whole region," Harris said.
Micah Risher, the Easton Airport manager, seemed to be enjoying the festivities, though pulling this show together is logistical feat.
"We have been planning this for about a year," he said. "Every event is a little different. We have so many elements to make it special, like the paratroopers and seeing Placid Lassy taking off and lead the mass formation. When engines start and for the next 90 minutes, it is going to be an amazing display. This is a celebration of our history. Our airport has been here since 1942."
There is a connection between these warbirds and the airport, which was built to support the war, he said.
The climax of the event was the rubber chicken drop contest. Flying planes tried to hit the target of a truck on the airfield with rubber chickens.
There were loudspeakers throughout the event that broadcasted both PSAs and hitmakers like Eric Clapton.
This perfect fall day brought out families. There were lots of kids, some with noise-canceling headphones, pretending to be airplanes while their parents watched.
"There are lot of beautiful airplanes out and a lot great things to look at," said Sarah Andrew. She was with her husband and 4-year-old daughter.

title: 9th annual Easton BeerFest brings community together
author: Veronica Fernandez-Alvarado
content:
9th annual Easton BeerFest brings community together

 October 16, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Veronica Fernandez-Alvarado | Section: News 
 
 381
 Words 

 Read News Document

 EASTON — On Saturday, over 700 people attended the 9th annual Easton Beer Fest. The fundraiser gathered participants from throughout the Mid-Shore region to raise money for the Easton Volunteer Fire Department.This festival featured over 40 breweries, wineries and distilleries sharing over 120 craft beers, ciders, seltzers, wines and spirits from the region. Packed with live music, a variety of food, raffles and games, the Beef Fest, has become a staple on the Eastern Shore.
Chris Hash, Easton Beer Fest organizer and treasurer of the Easton Volunteer Fire Department, said this fundraiser provides community engagement and a chance for residents to support their local fire department.
"It's a key fundraising event for the Easton Volunteer Fire Department and allows us to purchase equipment and do things necessary to live up to our motto, 'service for others,'" Hash said.
According to Hash, the event began in 2016 as a way to replace previous fundraising events such as Casino Night and Bull Roast. Now, nine years later, Beer Fest has become a large community event in Easton with a wide attendance from across the Eastern Shore.
Doug Greene, an attendee of Beer Fest, said major highlights of the event were the live music by local band Black Dog Alley and the opportunity for locals and visitors alike to support local businesses.
"I think it's a great way to be a part of the community, to engage in different industries and also, obviously, support the fire department," Greene said. "And one thing that I've always noticed is that a lot of people, after the day of the event, they go into town, they go to restaurants. They may stay for the night or the rest of the day. They really get involved in the area."
Cameron Swell, another attendee of the event, said Beer Fest is not only good for the community but helps attendees expand their horizons with local beers and helps them support local craftsmen and tradespeople from wineries to distilleries.
"(The Fire Department) had a ton of breweries, a bunch of rare beers, and they do one of the best jobs I've ever seen for an event, let alone a beer fest," Swell said. "They put a lot of heart and soul into it, and I know every year they look to improve on the previous year."

title: Hogan Visits Port Street
author: Tom McCall
content:
Hogan Visits Port Street

 October 18, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Tom McCall | Section: Local News 
 
 358
 Words 

 Read News Document

 EASTON — Port Street got a distinguished visitor at the Neighborhood Service Center. Former Gov. Larry Hogan is running for the open U.S. Senate seat and stopped in Easton Friday to talk with people at the service center.He visited the facility on 126 Port Street and asked questions.
The Responsible Father Initiative, founded by Corey Pack and co-facilitated by Lou Dorsey, is an outreach program to help men become better fathers. It is a nonprofit and is all confidential. It provides food, clothing and first month's rent to people in need. These men gave Hogan the tour of the center.
Pack spoke to the governor about what they teach.
"We go over what is called the three E's. Emotion, energy and expression. And we talk about effective listening skills," Pack said. "We run through the 7/38/55 rule. 7% of the way we communicate is verbally. 38% is with our tone and 55% is with our body language."
The governor listened closely.
"I did not realize that," Hogan said. "That is an important lesson for me to learn."
He listened to more about the program.
"We try to develop more nurturing and caring fathers in this program. Most of the guys grew up in a home without a father. Some have been incarcerated with no contact with their children. It is great for them to see their children and establish a relationship with their children," Dorsey said.
Hogan recognized that a lot of men needed these services and saluted their dedication to helping these men flourish.
"It sounds like you guys are doing really important work here," Hogan said.
One of the Neighborhood Service Center workers asked Hogan to run for president. He smiled.
Hogan toured spaces intended for children. Then he went into the kitchen and in another room saw where they store clothes to give away.
At the end of tour, he was give two T-shirts and a coffee mug that touted the Neighborhood Service Center.
After his visit he stopped to do an interview in the parking lot. Hogan said his campaign is focused on the economy and crime.
"We are meeting voters every day," he said. "The people of Maryland know me after eight years of being governor."

title: Carol's Kitchen brings food back to Dorchester airport
author: MAGGIE TROVATO mtrovato@chespub.com
content:
Carol's Kitchen brings food back to Dorchester airport

 October 18, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: MAGGIE TROVATO mtrovato@chespub.com | Section: Local News 
 
 368
 Words 

 Read News Document

 CAMBRIDGE — For those who enjoy entertainment while they dine, Carol's Kitchen has reopened in a new location: the Cambridge-Dorchester Regional Airport.During a ribbon-cutting ceremony hosted by the Dorchester Chamber of Commerce on Thursday, Oct. 17, community leaders congratulated the restaurant's owners, Carol Short and Grady Wilson.
"I wish you a lot of success," said Kevin Hill, chairman of the the Dorchester Chamber of Commerce board. "Congratulations on the expanded space. It's great to see this space reactivated."
Once Short cut the ribbon outside the restaurant, attendees of the event went inside to enjoy lunch with a view.
The restaurant, which was previously located on Glasgow Street in Cambridge, opened at the airport in early September. Short and Wilson said the new location offers a great view where they can serve up food the community loves at an affordable price.
Airport Director Steve Nuwer said the restaurant "brings life" to the airport, which he considers a gateway to Dorchester County. He said there are a lot of people from nearby states that fly to the airport just to have lunch.
"So it's a great opportunity for people that are not familiar with this area to come in and experience Dorchester County," he said about the airport. "The restaurant helps bring them in here."
Nuwer joked that having a restaurant so close to where he works isn't good for his health.
"But they've got really good food," he said.
Although the airport has had restaurants in it in the past, it has been without a restaurant since the beginning of 2022 when Katie's At The Airport closed.
Dorchester Chamber of Commerce President Bill Christopher said having a restaurant back at the airport is good because the airport is easy to get to and has great parking. Christopher said Carol's Kitchen serves up good portions of good food at a reasonable price.
"It's a good environment to be in," he said. "I think they'll do well."
Christopher called the restaurant "a natural draw" for people to come to the airport. He said sitting in the restaurant and watching planes take off could also spark career ideas for young people.
"Bringing them out so they can eat and see and start thinking, 'I might want to be a pilot someday,'" he said.

title: Prayer breakfast attracts the faithful
author: Tom McCall
content:
Prayer breakfast attracts the faithful

 October 18, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Tom McCall | Section: Local News 
 
 681
 Words 

 Read News Document

 EASTON — There was praise, solemnity and song as eggs, bacon and biscuits were served. Over 200 people came to the sold out 7 a.m. annual prayer breakfast held at the Easton Volunteer Fire Department. On Thursday amens from the dressed-up crowd reached to the rafters.Sheriff Joe Gamble was the master of ceremonies who introduced the 13 speakers at the event. They focused on their faith and how their life stories shaped their relationship with God. Some were pastors and reverends. Some were politicians, educators and business leaders. Many hugs were given and hands were held high in reverence. Biblical passages from protective wings to deadly pestilence were read.
Gamble said, "We are really excited with a sellout crowd, and we have got some great speakers today. We have 230 or 240 people. We can't thank the Volunteer Fire Company enough. They donated the space today."
Prayers were directed to leaders of the town. There were prayers for first responders, educators and the nation at large. There was a special acknowledgement to Paul Carroll who has kept the 41-year tradition of the prayer breakfast alive. He serves on a committee that keeps the prayer breakfast going.
"We realize the importance of prayer and we need to continue this," Carroll said. "It is a different venue, but we are happy to have it. After the food, we have two speakers Jimmy Rogers and Wendy Palmer."
Rogers told how he died and came back to life convinced in his faith. He served in Vietnam as a Marine and then joined the Easton Police Department. Although he had to read his remarks because of a traumatic brain injury, he held the audience's attention.
"I would like to share with you the story of God's incredible works in my life," Rogers said. "It includes miracles, forgiveness, incredible acts of healing, redemption and saving a person totally unworthy of such acts."
He had a heart attack and died in his bathroom. His wife found him.
"She found me on the floor, not breathing and no pulse. She called 911 and started CPR. This was not a near-death experience. It meets all the clinical criteria for death," Rogers said.
When the EMTs arrived, they shocked him multiple times and tried to revive him for 20 minutes. One last effort induced a weak pulse. They rushed him to the hospital.
"I had a 98% blockage in the coronary artery known as the widow maker," he said.
In that death experience, he had a vision of a friend who had died two years earlier.
"I was walking through the woods. The sun shining more than you can possibly imagine. The leaves had incredible colors. The air was crisp and clear, and I came to a stream of crystal clear water cascading over the rocks. It was absolutely heavenly, and I have never felt such peace. I never wanted to leave this place," Rogers said.
He saw his friend on the other side of the river. The friend told Rogers to go back. Then Rogers awoke from his coma. He wonders if it was a glimpse of the after life or just a drug-induced dream. As Rogers told his story, the room was silent, the crowd engrossed in his testimony.
The second testimony came from Wendy Palmer, director of chronic diease and prevention programs at the YMCA of the Chesapeake. She spoke of service both in her role as a 31-year restauranteur and now helping people to get moving at the Y.
"It is never to late. At 57 on December the 19th, I was born again. I was baptized," Palmer said.
She says she is in her infancy of faith but is a lifelong learner.
"I get to help people move and feel good and be in community. And I tell our staff and our team at the Y that everybody comes to our Y — the front porch of the community as Robbie Gill refers to the Y — to be seen, to be heard and to be loved," Palmer said.
"If we can do that everyday in a way that magnifies our Lord, He will be so proud of us and our work."

title: Community parade celebrates Dan Tabler’s 100th birthday
author: ANDREA GRABENSTEIN agrabenstein@chespub.com
content:
Community parade celebrates Dan Tabler’s 100th birthday

 October 19, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: ANDREA GRABENSTEIN agrabenstein@chespub.com | Section: Local News 
 
 213
 Words 

 Read News Document

 CENTREVILLE — A parade of emergency vehicles, American Legion Riders and community members lauded a life well lived during a 100th birthday celebration for local community legacy Dan Tabler Oct. 13.Orchestrated by the Goodwill Fire Company, in which Tabler has been a member for over 75 years, the parade took off from the firehouse and made its way to the Tabler residence on Elm Street for a celebration of the century alongside friends, family and the Centreville community.
Commending Tabler's outstanding contributions to the community and the American Legion,
Jason Miller, American Legion vice commander of the Detachment of Maryland and Jeff Davis American Legion Post 18 member, presented certificates of recognition.
Centreville's Jeff Davis American Legion was chartered in 1935 with Tabler one of its charter members, Miller said.
According to Miller's research, at 90 years of membership, Tabler stands as one of the longest serving Sons of the American Legion members in the country.
Tabler is former editor, writer and longtime columnist for the Record-Observer.
Tabler was grateful for the recognition from the community and credited his success and dedication to the local community as, "love what you do."
Surrounded by friends, family and an appreciative community, Tabler presented one of his trademark lines when asked about how he feels, "I've never felt better in my life."

title: St. Michaels announces gingerbread contest, ornament
author: Staff Writer
content:
St. Michaels announces gingerbread contest, ornament

 October 19, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Staff Writer | Section: Life 
 
 421
 Words 

 Read News Document

 Bakers and pastry chefs of all ages and talent levels are encouraged to get their gingerbread house games on with the return of the Christmas in St. Michaels Gingerbread House competition this December and a purse totaling $2,000 in prizes up for grabs.The competition is an important component of the fundraising the all-volunteer organization achieves with the annual event, with the creations highlighted and on display at the Gingerbread "House" Preview Cocktail Party at the Woman's Club of St. Michaels on Thursday, Dec. 12, beginning at 5 p.m.
"We are encouraging participants to donate their creations for our silent auction, to be held the evening of the cocktail party," says this year's Gingerbread House Competition Co-Chair Michele Lowe. "All auction proceeds support the beneficiaries of Christmas in St. Michaels."
Entrants can pick their category for participation, which includes master chefs and caterers, adults, young adults, children, children with adults, kit-made houses, and non-profit organizations. Participation is free, with pre-registration needed at christmasinstmichaels.org/events.
The 2024 Christmas in St. Michaels Collectors Ornament has also been announced and is the 21st in the series. This year's ornament depicts the Chesapeake deadrise workboat with its crew and a friendly canine companion. The image was provided by St. Michaels artist Sherry Smith.
The boxed ornament is available for purchase at select local retail shops and the weekend-long Christmas in St. Michaels Marketplace and Sweet Shoppe. Online purchases can be made at www.christmasinstmichaels.org/ornament.
The deadrise workboat has been a staple among Chesapeake watermen for decades. "Deadrise" refers to the almost flat, V-shaped hull that provides a shallow draft to accommodate the waters in creeks and rivers of the Eastern Shore. Boats range from 25-45 feet in length and are powered by large, inboard four- or six-cylinder engines, usually diesel-fueled.
Workboats typically sport women's names on the transom or bow, paying tribute to wives and daughters. Others, such as the one in this ornament, refer to the town, river or creek the boat calls home port.
"It is typical to see dozens of these deadrise workboats plying the waters of the Eastern Shore in the wee hours of the morning as they seek the day's catch, returning to the pier in the early afternoon to get their catch to market," says Christmas in St. Michaels Chair Pat Martin. "We're honored to add this limited-edition ornament to our collection to pay tribute to watermen and their boats in the St. Michaels area and the Chesapeake Bay region at large."
Event details, online ticket and ornament purchases, and more about Christmas in St. Michaels are at christmasinstmichaels.org.
