title: Boarders can now drop-in to new Terrapin Skate Park
author: ANDREA GRABENSTEIN agrabenstein@chespub.com
content:
Boarders can now drop-in to new Terrapin Skate Park

 October 25, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: ANDREA GRABENSTEIN agrabenstein@chespub.com | Section: Local News 
 
 380
 Words 

 Read News Document

 Giving skaters of all ages a local place to safely hone their skills, Queen Anne's County welcomed a ribbon cutting of Terrapin Skate Park in Stevensville Oct. 18.Complete with quarterpipes, ramps, rails, hubba ledges and more, Terrapin Skate Park is crafted to suit all level of skaters stands as the county's first permanent skatepark, according to Queen Anne's County Parks and Recreation Director Steve Chandlee.
Over two decades ago the parks department established a makeshift skating area but it was hidden away and not utilized well, he said.
Utilizing county owned property, an important aspect of the Terrapin Skate Park project was insuring it was in a visible location, Chandlee said.
In 2022, youths were instrumental in voicing a need to the commissioners and the Parks Advisory Board, including Kent Island High Schooler Dylan Cannon and Violet Baudean, who was a then seventh grader, created a petition highlighting the need for a skatepark.
"We knew upfront this was a great project," Chandlee said.
Now a Kent Island High School sophomore, Baudean is excited to share a love of skating with the community.
Public skateparks highlight a sense of community and offer an outlet for all ages, especially for those who don't drive, according to Baudean.
"There's something here for all skill levels, " she said.
Baudean credited county officials for their support of the project.
While skating is not a team sport, the skating community is very welcoming, always encouraging each other, Chandlee and Baudean said.
"It is a team of support for individuals," Chandlee said.
Funding for the park was made possible through a grant with the Department of Natural Resources Local Parks and Playground Infrastructure, he said.
Breaking ground in April, 12 weeks of construction opened the park to the public in June before stormwater management and tree planting completion officially welcomed the park, according to Chandlee.
More improvements are on the horizon for the park, including bleachers thanks to PRS Guitars and a restroom, he said.
The park has already become a welcome addition of the community with the hope to reach skaters far and wide.
"No matter what, try skateboarding," Baudean said.
Terrapin Skate Park is open sunrise to sunset and patrons are reminded to be respectful of the site and neighbors.
Cars are permitted in the designated parking area and should not be parked in the cul-de-sac or on the roadway.

title: Years in the making: John Wesley Church in Oxford completes renovation
author: KONNER METZ kmetz@chespub.com
content:
Years in the making: John Wesley Church in Oxford completes renovation

 October 26, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: KONNER METZ kmetz@chespub.com | Section: Local News 
 
 621
 Words 

 Read News Document

 OXFORD — When he moved to Washington, D.C., Wayman Pinder often traveled back to his Eastern Shore hometown down the unassuming Oxford Road.On the way, he saw a dilapidated building that he almost couldn't recognize. It was the John Wesley Methodist Episcopal Church, no longer used for services and worsening in condition by the year.
"I had to ride by this church where I used to be the organist, where I went all my life," Pinder said.
Following the church's closure in the mid-1970s, its exterior deteriorated, with roof problems, an unkempt cemetery and outhouse, and a lack of what once was a thriving group of community residents to look after the church. Pinder, now back in Oxford, felt it was ready to fall down at any moment.
"And to see it look like that, it hurt," Pinder said.
Pinder and his sister, Virginia Gibson, are just two of the many community members who have poured endless hours into renovating and rededicating the John Wesley Church. Earlier this month, the church celebrated a formal ribbon-cutting for its renovation — which has been an ongoing effort since 2003.
Renovations have included extensive roof repairs, a new wheelchair-accessible ramp, chimney and siding replacements and significant archaeological work on the cemetery that surrounds the building.
In the 2000s, the church was lifted to repair the foundation. Gibson notes that archaeological surveying found buried bodies beneath the church, which are now memorialized with gravestones in an expanded cemetery.
Upon walking in today, the church is welcoming and clean, with names of restoration donors and volunteers on the pews and window panes. It doesn't host services anymore, but it has hosted weddings and funerals.
"The inside of that church is just wonderful compared to what (it was)," Pinder said.
The restoration process wasn't always smooth sailing. Former John Wesley Preservation Society Vice President James Hollis founded the restoration efforts in 2003, Gibson said.
"We were spinning wheels for about five or six years," she said. Gibson attributed much of the credit to former Oxford Commissioner Kathleen Radcliffe, the preservation society's former president.
"She really mended (it) together," Gibson said. "She really was the person."
Through weekly and monthly meetings, board members rallied community support, hosted fundraisers and gathered the needed permits to fix up the semi-abandoned piece of history.
The preservation society gained official nonprofit status in 2014. Restoration took off thereafter, with major repairs performed by local contractors both outside and inside of the church.
Adjacent to the church is the Nellie Brooks Leatherberry Cook Shop, which Gibson said acts as the society's meeting room. An original stove used in the building still remains today. Nellie Leatherberry, born in Oxford in 1908, provided meals to churchgoers.
"People would actually sit in here and eat the best food ever made," Pinder said.
The cook shop became Talbot County's first African American Museum site in 2015. The church next to it has just as much history. Originally bought in 1838 as Oxford Neck Church, documents show it was a mixed congregation, with 31 white members and 26 Black members.
In 1875, the church was rebuilt to the single-room white building it has been since, becoming a part of the Oxford community and the Eastern Shore Black community until its closure in the 20th century.
Though the church hasn't hosted weekly services for decades, it has remained a cornerstone of the Oxford community. It's been home to quilt shows and community gatherings, and even served as a water stop for local cycling races.
Many board members and community volunteers have memories associated with the church, Pinder and Gibson both said. Whether they were members or their parents or grandparents were, many Oxford residents seem to resonate with the small but chronicled building off of Oxford Road.
"For us, it's personal history, too," Pinder said. "We experienced it."

title: Tench Tilghman: A Talbot County-born revolutionary hero
author: KONNER METZ kmetz@chespub.com
content:
Tench Tilghman: A Talbot County-born revolutionary hero

 October 26, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: KONNER METZ kmetz@chespub.com | Section: Local News 
 
 795
 Words 

 Read News Document

 EASTON — One of George Washington's most trusted men has roots in Talbot County, and this week he was celebrated by a local chapter of the Maryland Society of the Sons of the American Revolution.The SAR's Colonel Tench Tilghman Chapter honored its namesake after receiving proclamations from Easton and Talbot County for the inaugural Tench Tilghman Week from Oct. 19 to 24.
Tilghman, born in Talbot County in 1744 and educated there during his youth, was a primary aide-de-camp for Washington during the Revolutionary War. Wes Hagood, chapter president, has deeply researched Tilghman and his critical role as one of Washington's right-hand men.
In 1776, Tilghman joined Washington's staff. Washington often referred to him as "family" in written letters, Hagood said.
"He became, in a lot of ways, like a son to Washington," Hagood said. "… They carried on a relationship until Tilghman died."
Tilghman's calling card was his duty of delivering the notice of British surrender following the Battle of Yorktown. Surrender came on Oct. 19, 1781, and Tilghman arrived in Philadelphia on Oct. 24 to confirm the news to the Continental Congress.
"It's probably one of his most recognizable accomplishments," Hagood said.
Hagood described Tilghman as "hard working" and smart, adding that he "probably would have had a role in the future government had he lived." He provided leadership to patriot soldiers and often was responsible for finding food to sustain the troops, Hagood said.
In a letter to Continental Army General John Sullivan in 1781, Washington spoke highly of Tilghman.
"This gentleman came out a captain of one of the light infantry companies of Philadelphia, and served in the flying camp in 1776," Washington wrote. "In August of the same year he joined my family, and has been in every action in which the main army was concerned. He has been a zealous servant and slave to the public, and a faithful assistant to me for nearly five years, a great part of which time he refused pay."
Following the victory, a portrait of Washington was commissioned in 1781, depicting Tilghman and Marquis de Lafayette. Maryland-born Charles Willson Peale painted the portrait, which is displayed today in the Maryland State House.
Tilghman died in 1786, leaving behind his spouse, who spent many decades thereafter in Oxford on Tilghman's father's plantation. Today, Tilghman is buried at the Oxford Cemetery after being reinterred in 1971 from his original burial site in Baltimore.
MARYLAND 400
Hagood, who has read all of the letters Tench Tilghman wrote to his father during the war, pointed out the Talbot County native's critical role in the Battle of Brooklyn in 1776. At that battle, a larger and more experienced British army posed a significant threat to patriot troops.
Owen Lourie, "Finding the Maryland 400" project director at the Maryland State Archives, calls that the "first major battle." Lourie says the troops known as the Maryland 400, along with some from Pennsylvania and Delaware, reformed to attack the enemy after a damaging British charge.
While there were massive casualties, Lourie says the Maryland 400 "bottled up" the British and prevented them from delivering a "final death blow" to the other continental soldiers that were escaping.
"It is probably not too much of an exaggeration to say that they saved the Continental Army," Lourie said.
Witness to the heroic efforts, Tilghman applauded the Col. William Smallwood's 1st Maryland Regiment, Lourie notes. "No Regular Troops ever made a more gallant Resistance than Smallwood's Regiment," Tilghman wrote in a memoir.
Lourie and the Maryland State Archives are working to identify and write biographies on as many of those soldiers as possible. There were more than 1,000 Maryland troops, and his historian work has helped identify over 800. He says he's focused on "telling the small stories" of those Marylanders that may not have been thought of in hundreds of years.
Lourie is presenting a history of the Maryland 400 at the Talbot County Free Library on Saturday at 11 a.m., an event sponsored by the Tench Tilghman Chapter which wraps up Tench Tilghman Week.
Dana Newman, library director, says registration is open online at tcfl.org, with limited spots remaining. It will also be livestreamed on Talbot Library's YouTube channel.
Hagood is excited for Tench Tilghman Week to return next October and for years to come.
"What better way would there be for us as a chapter to fulfill our mission of educating current and future generations about all of this than to have a week dedicated to Colonel Tench Tilghman," Hagood said. "And this year, just start with one event. But the idea is, we'll do this every year."
Following the Maryland 400 presentation on Saturday, a free program on how to join the Sons of the American Revolution and Daughters of the American Revolution will be held at the Talbot County Free Library from 2 to 4 p.m. in the Frederick Douglass Room.

title: Thousands of oyster lovers sip, slurp, savor at annual Oysterfest
author: Tom McCall
content:
Thousands of oyster lovers sip, slurp, savor at annual Oysterfest

 October 30, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Tom McCall | Section: Local News 
 
 544
 Words 

 Read News Document

 ST. MICHAELS — Smoked, fried or raw — local oysters were served to over 3,000 bivalve lovers attending the Chesapeake Bay Maritime Museum's OysterFest Saturday.There was an oyster stew competition and an oyster slurping eating competition. Two live bands, Swamp Donkey and JCT 33, lit up either end of the museum's campus.
"We have people coming in to sample six different local restaurants that have provided oyster stews. Each with their own recipe. They get to vote a, b, c, d, e, f, and we will reveal the winner after all the ballots have been cast," said Pete Lesher, the chief historian at CBMM.
The oyster stew competition had three winners. Third place went to Gourmet by the Bay, second place to The Oaks Waterfront Inn and first place to Bistro St. Michaels. It was a double blind system where even the neutral ladlers serving the voters didn't know who made their soup.
Glistening silver raw oysters on the half shell were enjoyed as pristine white historic nautical craft gleamed on the docks.
The oysters came freshly caught by the Talbot Watermen Association and freshly farmed from the Choptank Oyster Company. Slow Descent Oysters provided smoked oysters with butter, garlic and hot sauce or with smoked gouda, onion and maple bacon.
For the adults, there were craft beers, cocktails and oyster shooters with bloody Mary mix and vodka. There were workers checking IDs as customers queued up.
There was even an oyster slurping contest. Contestants slurped six oysters fast to become "Slurp King or Queen."
Although the food offerings were the primary draw for the event, vendors offered everything from belts with the Maryland state flag on them to maritime crafts.
Eve Johnson pulled in a vintage Bluebird bus and put out her Wild Raven Boutique clothes on the boardwalk.
"This is a boho vintage hippie mixture. Usually it is what I am wearing that people want, like these palooza pants. This might be a our fourth time at this event. Great food, great people, great music, great shopping and beautiful views," Johnson said.
Younger visitors had a whole children's section with wooden model sailboat building and a little pool to launch them in. Cheerful volunteers made it all come together.
A big draw for the crowd was the American Chesapeake Club Retriever demonstrations. Handsome Chesapeake Bay retrievers showed off their retrieving abilities as an announcer educated on the finer points of the breed and its talents. The fit, golden-brown dogs charged across a decoy-strewn lawn to get to the plastic target and bring it back. The audience cheered and the dogs' tails wagged.
There were several presentations, including one by author Eric Cheezum, who gave a cultural history lecture on Chessie. The sea monster is said to have first been sighted in 1978.
There was also an lecture about oyster reef building with discarded hockey sticks called Rink2Reef.
Logan Clark, event and group services lead for CBMM said, "Incorporating both sides of the campus is a challenge and making sure there is entertainment on both sides. There is music, vendors and oysters on both sides. This year we have a big slate of programs happening in the VLA (Van Lennep Auditorreum), including a cooking demo."
No matter what drew the crowds to the museum, this year's turnout was impressive. Parking overflowed down Talbot Street to Perry Cabin.

title: Denton Fall Festival brings out costumes, community
author: Tom McCall
content:
Denton Fall Festival brings out costumes, community

 October 31, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Tom McCall | Section: Local News 
 
 288
 Words 

 Read News Document

 DENTON — Painted pumpkins, candy and a miniature bride of Frankenstein all flocked to the downtown park for a family friendly Fall Festival Oct. 30.There was a costume contest that gathered adults and children alike. A face painter worked past sundown as the fairy lights twinkled during a spectacular sunset. There were vendors selling essential oils, lemonade and cheeseburgers. There was a haunted house that would only take four people at a time.
Isabel O'Brien caters at the Culinary Center and had a table at the event. She had a chef's toque and thin mustache drawn on her upper lip.
"This is my first time being a part of this event specifically. I am just so glad to see that there are so many opportunities for the kids to come out and get as much candy as they can," O'Brien said.
Director of Downtown Denton, Jessica Jean Willoughby, was the primary organizer of all this spooky fun. She loved seeing all the families dressed up and making memories.
Jill Pugh, president of Downtown Denton Main Street, said, "We run several events each year and this Fall Festival is one of them."
Willoughby has written roughly $50,000 worth of grants to stimulate Denton's downtown. She wants to bring businesses and community together.
"I bring community together with all of the festivals. If you bring kids downtown, you bring families. I want to bring lighting all the way down the street. The ones that go across the street. I want to bring people together and just have a good time," Willoughby said.
Alicia Moxley, a member of Downtown Denton Main Street said, "Downtown Denton is a beautiful space, but we still have room to grow. This is a great opportunity to bring people into our town."

title: Kent Island Community Garden relocates
author: ANDREA GRABENSTEIN agrabenstein@chespub.com
content:
Kent Island Community Garden relocates

 October 31, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: ANDREA GRABENSTEIN agrabenstein@chespub.com | Section: Entertainment 
 
 410
 Words 

 Read News Document

 A local garden will now find a fresh home in the community as the Queen Anne's County Commissioners approved a lease agreement with Kent Island Community Garden, Inc. for relocation to 210 White Pine Lane in Stevensville Oct. 8.The community garden formerly located in the Harbor View section of Chester used the land next to Galilee Lutheran Church for about ten years, group representative John McKnight said. Following the land sale from the church, the garden had to look for a new home and McKnight reached out to the County Commissioners over the summer for assistance.
Formed in 2015 as the Galilee Community Garden, the Kent Island Community Garden serves the need for a community garden in the Harbor View area of Chester and has since blossomed to include church volunteers, local Master Gardeners, Boy Scout Troop 495 and neighbors of all sorts ready to get their thumbs green.
The community garden also partners with the University of Maryland Extension Master Gardeners Program for educational opportunities.
The garden offers many beds of vegetables, flowers, and a separate herb garden with an irrigation system and compost area.
The Maryland Food Bank cites that one in three Marylanders face hunger. "With several of our gardeners in independent living facilities and one handicapped gardener, we realize how critical it is to establish a new space for our community garden," McKnight said.
Voicing their appreciation for the garden, the county Commissioners approved a $1,500 grant to help the garden blossom at its new location.
The new location's property next to the offices of the Fire Marshal is an ideal location to offer sufficient land for growth along with the necessary utilities as well as close proximity to the Cross-Island Trail, local schools, and the public library.
"It's going to be a great resource for the county," McKnight said.
The Kent Island Community Garden is always looking for new gardeners and civic minded groups to help build garden beds, according to McKnight.
The all inclusive garden stakes claim in having the only handicapped-accessible garden beds in the county, he said.
"We are a diverse and unique group of twenty gardeners and are the only community garden in Queen Anne's County that is open to all, " McKnight said.
Looking ahead, the garden hopes to build a few garden beds before winter sets in and In the spring seeks funds to install a deer fence around the perimeter, he said.
More information about Kent Island Community Garden can be found by contacting McKnight at McKnightJohn143@gmail.com or 202-257-3754.

title: History and mystery: Haunted High Street tour shares Cambridge folklore
author: MAGGIE TROVATO mtrovato@chespub.com
content:
History and mystery: Haunted High Street tour shares Cambridge folklore

 October 31, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: MAGGIE TROVATO mtrovato@chespub.com | Section: Local News 
 
 546
 Words 

 Read News Document

 CAMBRIDGE — Walking past the grand, historic High Street homes on a sunny day, ghosts might not be top of mind.But after the sun has set, Chesapeake Ghost Tours brings history lovers and thrill seekers alike on a journey down the haunted street, telling stories of local history and strange happenings.
Mindie Burgoyne, founder of Chesapeake Ghost Tours, considers Cambridge's High Street the most haunted street in Maryland. She said those that come on the tour will be "entertained by the mystery and informed by the history."
The tour — which was primarily developed using the folklore collections at Salisbury University's Edward H. Nabb Research Center, books, newspaper articles and personal interviews — begins right outside the Dorchester County Circuit Courthouse. Guides take tourgoers down High Street toward the Choptank River before looping around and coming back up the street. The tour ends at the graveyard attached to Christ Episcopal Church.
On Friday, Burgoyne led a small group around the street, stopping in front of homes to tell stories about mischievous ghosts, cat ladies and even murder.
Burgoyne believes that in areas like High Street that have had a "high injection of emotion," it creates a hole in the "veil between the dimensions." She said that over the years, people would hear things while walking in the area of High and Spring streets.
Past the courthouse and toward the water, Burgoyne told the story of an old murder that took place in the foyer of what is now the Cambridge House Bed and Breakfast at 112 High St. Burgoyne said two men had an altercation in the foyer of the house that involved an umbrella and a fireplace poker. She said the incident ended with a gunshot.
The previous owners of the bed and breakfast would find umbrellas and fireplace pokers missing, Burgoyne said. When she interviewed them, they told her the story connected the dots for them.
"Well no wonder our pokers and umbrellas are missing," the previous owners told her.
The bed and breakfast is one of many properties on High Street that Burgoyne can share history and stories about. Her favorite stories are about the Josiah Bayly House at 207 High St. Built in the 1700s in Annapolis and moved to Cambridge by barge, the Bayly House is known as the oldest house in Cambridge.
Burgoyne said one woman she interviewed who lived there said she always had a sense that they weren't alone in the house.
The tour ends under fragrant yew trees in the graveyard of the Episcopal church. On Friday, as tourgoers pointed their phone flashlights at old gravestones, Burgoyne told a few last stories and shined a light on one grave stone practically enveloped by a yew tree, poking out just enough to be noticeable.
Shasta Ingram, who lives in Howard County, said she didn't have one particular story on the tour that was her favorite.
"I just liked looking at the houses and hearing the history," she said. "Because, you know, there's so much history."
Those interested in taking the tour on High Street, or doing another ghost tour through Chesapeake Ghost Tours, can book online at chesapeakeghosts.com. Walking tours are available most weekends from March through October and parts of November. In December through February, the company often has bus tours in areas not covered on the walking tours.

title: One year in, Centreville Y nears 7,000 members
author: DOUG BISHOP Special to the Star Democrat
content:
One year in, Centreville Y nears 7,000 members

 November 1, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: DOUG BISHOP Special to the Star Democrat | Section: News 
 
 497
 Words 

 Read News Document

 CENTREVILLE — The Centreville YMCA opened in October 2023. A year later, according to the local Executive Director Brian Byrnes and Membership Director Laura Feller, it has grown to 6,692 members.According to Mid-Shore YMCA Director Robbie Gill, that doesn't count the 535 Active Aging Center members (who are 55 and older) or those "people engaged in our free chronic disease programs; Rock Steady Boxing for Parkinsons, LiveStrong Cancer Survivor Program, Enhanced Fitness, and the dozens of our partnerships that are using the Y for programs.
"The Centreville Y is serving over 10,000 people," he said.
Gill, who was part of the planning for the new, much larger Centreville location more than a decade ago, added, "It's exciting seeing the Queen Anne's County Family YMCA/Active Aging Center making a positive impact in the lives of over 10,000 community members."
Gill said he couldn't be more proud of the Y staff team, volunteers and the work of the Active Aging Center staff and volunteers.
One of the main goals of the Y is to make everyone feel like family.
Since the beginning in Centreville, there has been a partnership between the Y and the Queen Anne's County Department of Community Services, Department of Aging, sponsoring the Active Agency Center within the Y building. The Active Aging Center is for all people 55 and over. Registration and participation is free.
Within the Active Aging Center, there is a wide and growing variety of free services for seniors. Monday through Friday, lunch is served, with a donation of $6.30 asked for those ages 55-59. For those 60 and over, a donation of $3 is asked.
One regular participant in the daily luncheons is Arden Weiss, 85, of Queen Anne. Weiss said, "This is the healthiest food I've eaten in my entire life." Weiss comes to exercise each morning and enjoy the food with others each weekday.
The meals are catered by a contracted group. They provide the same service at the three county senior centers — Kent Island, Grasonville and Sudlersville each weekday.
Bethany Brennan is the Active Aging Center manager. She said, "While the manager organizes some of the activities, we encourage members to start their own groups or clubs too. It doesn't have to be overwhelming — it could be as simple as a card-playing group that meets on a specific day or a history club for those who share that interest. In the coming year, members can look forward to seeing some familiar events along with a variety of new ones."
Ed Kaczmarczyk, 65, was elected this past year as president of the Site Council at the Active Aging Center in Centreville. Kaczmarczyk said, "We meet monthly to discuss how the existing programs are going, and to make recommendations for changes and/or to organize different activities our seniors want to do." All Active Aging Center members are welcome to attend the Site Council meetings.
The Active Aging Center at the Y only exists at one other Y in the Mid-Shore area, located in St. Michaels in Talbot County.

title: Boys and Girls Club, Mace's Lane Community Center work on closing funding gap
author: MAGGIE TROVATO mtrovato@chespub.com
content:
Boys and Girls Club, Mace's Lane Community Center work on closing funding gap

 November 1, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: MAGGIE TROVATO mtrovato@chespub.com | Section: Local News 
 
 568
 Words 

 Read News Document

 CAMBRIDGE — With hopes to begin the third phase of a project to create the Mace's Lane Community Center, the Boys and Girls Clubs of Metropolitan Baltimore and community center are working to close a funding gap.When complete, the community center will host a Boys and Girls Club. The facility will have a gym, tech lab, game room and classrooms. It will also have a museum and cultural center to honor the area's African American history during and following segregation.
"We have a lot of work to do," Jeff Breslin, president and CEO of the Boys and Girls Clubs of Metropolitan Baltimore, said during a Dorchester Chamber of Commerce luncheon on Oct. 29. "We're still fundraising every single day."
With about $8 million raised so far, Breslin said there is a $4.5 million funding gap. He said they feel confident in getting $3 million of that funding and so they are pushing for the final $1.5 million.
Breslin said so far, the building — which is the vacant Mace's Lane High School — has had its roof and windows replaced and its facade updated. He said there have been remediation efforts inside, including asbestos removal.
"But really, we're just about shovel-ready to get the inside done," he said in an interview.
Breslin said the start of the project's third phase, which they hope to begin in early 2025, is dependent on funding.
The Rev. Keith Cornish said raising the remaining funds for the project will ensure "everyone wins."
"Every part of our society will be impacted," he said about the community center.
Cornish is board president of Mace's Lane Community Center, a nonprofit that was formed by the Good Shepherd Association and the Mace's Lane High School Alumni Association. He compared the Boys and Girls Club at Mace's Lane Community Center to fertilizer for the school system.
"When they come alongside and help the school system, everyone benefits," he said.
Breslin said across the country, every dollar invested in the Boys and Girls Clubs returns $10.32 in economic benefits to club members, their families and society. He said in Maryland, every dollar invested in the Boys and Girls Clubs returns $7.64.
Breslin said that since opening the Boys and Girls Club at Leonards Lane in Cambridge in 2021, there has been a 35% decrease in juvenile crime within 0.3 miles of the club. He said that percentage has been controlled for recent juvenile reform laws.
"Ultimately it just means that when kids have somewhere safe and predictable and hopeful to go, we know what it does for the community," Breslin said.
During the lunch, Breslin introduced Leonards Lane Club Manager Gabe Butler and the organization's Manager of Community and Youth Support Kentavius Jones.
Butler said when kids come into the club, they are given dinner and time for homework help and tutoring before going through Boys and Girls Club programming. Programs deal with health and wellness, career and workforce readiness, social emotional wellness, and more. After programming, the children are given time to "just have fun and play," Butler said.
Jones talked about the importance of focussing on social emotional learning. He said COVID-19 had a negative impact on the social emotional wellness of this generation of kids.
"So learning healthy connections, how to relate to people, how to express what you're thinking, what's going on — our kids are struggling with that," he said.
Those who are interested in donating to the Mace's Lane Community Center project can donate at bgcmetrobaltimore.org/donate or maceslanecc.org/.

author: WILL BONTRAGER wbontrager@chespub.com
content:
Lions Halloween parade celebrates over 50 years

 November 1, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: WILL BONTRAGER wbontrager@chespub.com | Section: News 
 
 259
 Words 

 Read News Document

 CHESTERTOWN — In a tradition of more than 50 years, the Chestertown Lions Club held its Halloween Parade on Saturday along High Street.Performing this year was the Kent County High School marching band led by Jodi Bortz, the Sudlersville Middle School Marching Band led by Ronald Demby and the Delmarva United Marching Band led by Mark Mumford.
The parade began at 1 p.m., and in addition to the bands, the Chestertown Volunteer Fire Company came through, rumbling their engines and tossing candy.
Floats added to the fun, like the Pirate's Cove float and the Radcliffe Creek School float driven by a storm trooper from "Star Wars."
Grand Marshal was Roger Williams, a Lions member for 53 years, who received the Melvin Jones Award from the Lions International Foundation for dedicated Humanitarian Services. Williams served in many roles within the County over the years as well.
Following the parade, club members were available to judge contestants for the costume contest, emceed by Brian Moore of WCTR. The contestants also marched in the parade, from groups preschool, elementary, middle, high school/adults and, new this year, a category for pets.
There was an array of costumes, from super heroes, pirates, dinosaurs, princesses, video game and anime characters, providing a fun yet tough time for the judges to decide on the best of each group.
Winners received cash prizes and hearty applause from the impressive number of people in attendance lined up on both sides of the street.
The day went off as Lions member Dwight Wilmot expected, fun and worry-free.
"What a gorgeous day to be out," he said.

title: Glad to have post office back
author: Staff Writer
content:
Glad to have post office back

 November 2, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Staff Writer | Section: Editors Inbox 
 
 134
 Words 

 Read News Document

 After over two years of being closed for renovations, the Trappe Post Office has finally reopened after a sudden closure in October 2022. Our community was never informed of construction progress (or the lack thereof) that seemed to drag on forever.The post office is a central feature of any small town, and we are very glad to have our post office back.
For all of this time, those of us with post office boxes have driven to Cambridge to pick up our mail. I extend gratitude to the postal clerks at the Cambridge post office who took on the extra workload processing our mail, always with a smile and a helping hand.
Special appreciation to our own postal clerk, Jasmine, who spent those years away working in Cambridge, and now is welcomed back home.
ANN FROCK
Trappe

title: Local brewer collaborates with brewery to unveil beer for Waterfowl
author: Maggie Trovato
content:
Local brewer collaborates with brewery to unveil beer for Waterfowl

 November 7, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Maggie Trovato | Section: Local News 
 
 599
 Words 

 Read News Document

 EASTON — Some people keep lists of potential baby names. Doug Greene keeps lists of potential beer names."I have a whole list on my phone of beer names," he said.
The Bird Nickel Brewing Company owner's passion for making beer started with a home brewing kit in 2009. Eight years later, Greene took a beer business course, and 10 years later, he incorporated Bird Nickel Brewing. In 2021, he graduated from American Brewers Guild, a brewing school in Vermont.
Although he's still looking for a brick-and-mortar brewery, Greene has done contract brewing, where he employs another brewery to brew beer for him. Through contract brewing, he has created brews with names like "Slick Calm Chesapeake Ale" and "Quite the Mixture."
Greene said the beer names often come from observation or overheard phrases. Slick calm, he said, is a term for when water is "smooth like glass."
Bird Nickel Brewing's latest creation — a limited edition collaboration with Salisbury-based Burnish Brewing Company and Waterfowl Festival Inc. — is "In Flight," a winter lager.
The beer will be released for the Waterfowl Festival so that attendees can sip on the limited edition brew while they throw back oysters and chow down on other Eastern Shore fare.
The lager has subtle notes of cinnamon, nutmeg and pear. Greene said different people might pick up on different notes.
"What we didn't want to do is overwhelm people with cinnamon," he said. "We want to make it enjoyable for everyone."
Waterfowl Festival Executive Director Deena Kilmon said the beer goes perfectly with hors d'oeuvres like oysters.
"Like when you're getting ready to eat dinner and you just really have something special to start," she said.
Greene, an Easton native, has "always wanted to do a beer for the Waterfowl Festival." The festival has been a part of his life for years, whether volunteering as a "duck sitter" in high school or walking the festival on the hunt for food trucks as an adult.
Greene's favorite memories of the event are walking down Harrison Street and seeing all the different vendors.
In the summer, Kilmon reached out to Greene about making a beer for the festival. This is the first year the festival is collaborating with brewers to make a special beer. The idea was one Greene had brought up to Kilmon years ago.
"When I became executive director in March, it was one of our first conversations about how we finally felt like it was the right year to launch it," Kilmon said.
Once Greene got Burnish Brewing on board, it was all systems go.
The label wrapped around the can is also a local effort. Maggii Sarfaty, an Easton artist, designed the label. On it, the festival's mission of conservation, education and research to protect local wildlife and habitats is written.
A portion of the proceeds from beer sales will go toward the Waterfowl Festival to fund education and conservation, Kilmon said.
Greene said having his beer at the festival is an important milestone.
"Especially for my business," he said. "And being able to create something for the festival instead of just being a resident or a ticket holder. I'm actually a part of it."
In Flight will be available at the festival's Premier Night on Nov. 7 in all the art pavilions. It will be free to VIP ticket holders while supplies last. Throughout the weekend, VIP ticket holders can request In Flight in the VIP hospitality suite. In Flight can be purchased at the new Duck Blind Bar located within the Avalon Theatre. Festival participants will also be able to sample the beer in the tasting pavilion located on Dover Street with the purchase of a tasting pavilion ticket.

title: 'It's an honor': American Legion Post 77 Hometown Heroes project takes off
author: KONNER METZ kmetz@chespub.com
content:
'It's an honor': American Legion Post 77 Hometown Heroes project takes off

 November 7, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: KONNER METZ kmetz@chespub.com | Section: Local News 
 
 454
 Words 

 Read News Document

 EASTON — The American Legion Blake-Blackston Post 77 and the Town of Easton are working to line downtown streets with banners honoring veterans in the community ahead of Veterans Day.The joint effort began Nov. 1, when town public works employees erected the first banners on telephone poles at Glenwood Avenue, across from the Post 77 headquarters. Those included banners for the post's founders, Nelson Blake and John Blackston, both U.S. Army veterans.
William Griffin, current Post 77 commander, reflected on the project as the initial banners were hung. His banner was included in the first order as well, recognizing his service in the Army during the Cold War.
"It's an honor," Griffin said. "It's just an honor where, when I'm dead and gone, my grandkids can ride down this street and see their pop-pop."
This is the first year the banners have been hung in Easton. Joan Harris-Brooks helped organize the ordering and erection of the banners. The first two orders contained 13 banners each. A third order was on its way, she said.
The Hometown Heroes Banner program began in 2006 in Harrisburg, Pennsylvania. Today, Mid-Shore towns including Federalsburg, Hurlock and Preston showcase banners honoring past and present veterans, part of the motivation to bring the initiative to Easton.
Harris-Brooks' father was a life member at Post 77, bringing that much more meaning to the project's culmination, she said. She hopes the banners bring awareness of all local veterans and first responders have done to better the Easton community.
"Not only did they serve in the country, but they served this community, which is very dear to all of us," Harris-Brooks said.
Easton Mayor Megan Cook, Town Council President Frank Gunsallus and Ward 4 Councilmember the Rev. Elmer Davis all stopped by on Nov. 1 to witness some of the first banners go up. Gunsallus' father will be on one of the banners.
Griffin encourages people to stop by Blake-Blackston Post 77 to learn the stories behind the faces on the banners. He pointed out Harry Dobson, Post 77's first commander, and Robert Poney Sr., a talented musician remembered by any current members of the post.
"You may look at the picture, but you don't have a story behind it," he said.
With banners planned for streets such as Glenwood Avenue, Port Street and West Street, Harris-Brooks hopes the Hometown Heroes banners expand to other areas within town. So far, there's been "overwhelming support," she says.
"This is something that should've been done years ago," Griffin said. " … There's so many people who should (be) recognized. The old saying, 'You may be gone, but you're not forgotten.' And the only way you don't forget them is by putting something up like this, to remember those who paved the way before I did."

 EASTON — Around a table in the Blake Blackston American Legion Post 77, five veterans of various histories talked about what brings them all together.The scars of war are sometimes obvious and sometimes hard to see, they said.
"We have been through situations where we have lost friends and lost part of ourselves. If you don't talk about your experience, you will never know someone else's. You never know what you have to say is going to help him out," said retired Chief Master Sergeant from the United States Air Force Victor Middleton. He served for 30 years in two combat wars.
Providing support to fellow veterans is about "family more than just camaraderie," Middleton said. It's been part of the VFW post's mission since its inception.
"The history of Blake Blackston Post 77 is named after two missing in action veterans that never came back. There names were Nelson Black from Unionville and John Blackston from Trappe. The original post was on The Hill. For 40 or 50 years this place has been packed," Staff Sergeant William E. Griffin said. Griffin is the commander of the post.
Since, post members said, the VFW has served as a place where not only history is honored, but so are the struggles and issues that affect veterans today.
Griffin said, "We can't forget about the thousands and thousands of veterans here who are homeless. They didn't get the help that I got, or maybe they just don't know where to go.
"The American Legion is here to help these veterans out — those that suffer from PTSD, those that don't know how to retrieve their benefits. This is our job to support them. There are too many homeless veterans and their families who don't have it as good as we do here."
Army Staff Sergeant Noreen Wilson did eight years of active duty in the Army. She is the adjutant at Post 77, and remembers how veterans were treated when she was younger.
"I remember Vietnam Veterans being pushed to the side, and that bothers me," she said. "People ignored them and didn't do much for them when they came home. If it wasn't for the American Legion, they wouldn't be taken care of as much as they are now."
Through tears, Middleton recounted losing friends, being wiped out by loss and having the resolve to keep going.
"Friends in Vietnam and Thailand. There are lot of things that happened in Thailand that had to do with the Vietnam War. When I do funeral services for our Legionaires, I can't help but cry. I have been the historian, chaplain, commander- first and vice. Of all of them, I have enjoyed the chaplain the most. My feeling is when we go, we deserve to go with dignity," Middleton said.
They are in this together.
But not all the bonding the happens at the VFW is over shared hardship, the five veterans said. Most look back fondly on their time of service.
"We got a chance to see the world and see people all over the world. I bet I know someone in every state. The military changed my life, made me a better person," said Michael Waller, who served three years in the Army and is the finance officer at Post 77.
Kirk Henson, who is on the board of American Legion Post 77, said being in the military put him ahead of his high school class who were looking for jobs.
"By the time I got out, I had seen a whole lot more that the people I would have graduated with. I had my high school diploma and boom, boom, boom, I got to see the world — Germany, Greece, and Fort Raleigh, Kansas," Henson said.
Wilson said, "It is a whole different thing versus being in the regular civilian world. You just have this camaraderie. You look out for each other."
This camaraderie is what drives and bonds members of Post 77 to serve the military community and the Easton community as a whole.
For those looking to get involved, the veterans said, there is always a seat at the table.

title: Veterans Day Roundup
author: Staff Writer
content:
Veterans Day Roundup

 November 8, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Staff Writer | Section: News 
 
 481
 Words 

 Read News Document

 The origins of Veterans Day in the U.S. date back to 1921 with the burial of an unknown World War I American soldier on a hillside overlooking the Potomac River in Arlington National Cemetery.England and France had already memorialized the end of WWI with burials of unknown soldiers and ceremonies on the 11th hour of the 11th day of the 11th month in 1918, the day the war came to an official close.
An annual commemoration of the formal cease fire was first known as Armistice Day.
A Congressional resolution in 1926 officially named Armistice Day, and it became a national holiday 12 years later.
But according to the U.S. Department of Veterans Affairs, in 1947 in Birmingham, Alabama, the first celebration under the name Veterans Day was held with parades and other festivities to honor all veterans.
Communities throughout the nation, including Barron County, continue the tradition of holding Veterans Day ceremonies. Here is a snapshot of some opportunities on Monday, Nov. 11, to thank veterans for serving their country.
Rice LakeRice Lake Middle School, 204 Cameron Road, will host a 2024 Veterans Day service with a free program open to the public beginning at 10 a.m.
The event will be live-streamed on the Rice Lake Community Media Channels and via the website ricelaketv.com, and a photo gallery will be available to view on Chronotype.com.
The program will include the presentation of Honor Banners honoring 21 service members to their families.
Rice Lake Main Street Association spearheads the banner project. The banners bear the picture and name of a veteran, their branch of service, and how many years or wars in which they were involved.
The banners were hung on Memorial Day weekend along Veterans Lakeshore Drive and were taken down on Patriot Day on Sept. 11 to be washed in preparation to be presented to the veterans' families at the ceremony.
Biographies of the 21 veterans can be found at rlveteransdrivepro.wixsite.com/rlvdprojects. To nominate veterans for next year's project email a service members name and rank, military branch, years of service/war(s) and a photo to rlveteransdriveprojects@gmail.com.
HaugenHaugen Elementary School's Veterans Day Program begins at 1:45 p.m. at the school. The program will include student performances, and fourth-grade students will be setting the missing man table with the audience learning what the different pieces of the table represent.
The program is scheduled to conclude by 2:15 p.m.
CameronCameron High School is hosting a Veterans Day program at 9:45 a.m. in the high school gymnasium, featuring music from the band and choir. Guest speaker is U.S. Army Master Sergeant Justin Imlo. The public is welcome.
The FBLA will be hosting a brief appreciation gathering afterwards with snacks and drinks for veterans. The program should take around 30 minutes.
BarronVeterans Day Programs will be held at Barron High School at 8:20 a.m., Woodland Elementary School at 9 a.m., Riverview Middle School at 10 a.m., Almena Elementary School at 10:30 a.m. and Ridgeland/Dallas Elementary School at 2 p.m.

title: World War II veteran looks back on his life
author: Maggie Trovato
content:
World War II veteran looks back on his life

 November 8, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Maggie Trovato | Section: Local News 
 
 401
 Words 

 Read News Document

 CAMBRIDGE — Ninety-nine-year-old World War II veteran Reese Hurley doesn't remember a whole lot from his days in the war."It's been too long," he said on a Tuesday afternoon last month.
The Cambridge native remembers having to eat spam — of which he is not fond. "Spam, oh God!" he said, remembering his distaste for it. "Don't want to see it."
He remembers that he enlisted in the U.S. Navy in 1942 and served as an aviation electrician. In that role, Hurley was a crew member on "PBM planes," or Martin PBM Mariner planes.
The aircraft, designed in 1937, was created by the Martin Company, according to the National Museum of the U.S. Navy. It's initials stand for Patrol Bomber, Martin. According to the Smithsonian National Air and Space Museum, the Martin PBM Mariner is one of the least known patrol aircrafts of World War II, but is considered "one of the most successful."
The war is where Hurley learned the trade that would become his career.
"That's where I learned," he said about becoming an electrician.
In his career, Hurley became a chief electrician. He owned a small business in Cambridge at one time.
"I was trained in electronics and circuitry," he said.
Sometimes, Hurley would get called to factories to help fix machines.
Hurley and his wife, Agnes, had one son, Luther. Agnes has since passed, and Luther lives in North Carolina.
For Hurley, the war stories have faded over the years, becoming more distant in his memory. The stories he remembers most are those of his days as a missionary and minister. He said he is most proud of his ministry work.
"I was more active probably as a missionary than I was in the Navy," Hurley said.
Although Hurley didn't have a close relationship with God when he was in the war, he did later on in life. As a missionary, he traveled more than 33,000 miles, he said. He's been all over the world, including Central America, South America and Asia.
Hurley said he's seen a lot of hunger and suffering.
"I've been in three war zones," he said. "They were fighting when I went there, fighting when I left."
Hurley said one mission trip he especially enjoyed going on was to India. He recalled a mother coming to him and handing him her unresponsive baby, asking him for help.
Hurley said he took the child, held him up, spoke to God and, lo and behold, the baby started to cry.

title: Donations ease financial needs
author: Staff Writer
content:
Donations ease financial needs

 November 9, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Staff Writer | Section: Editors Inbox 
 
 339
 Words 

 Read News Document

 The Maryland Association of Social Services Boards (MASSB) Foundation is composed entirely of volunteers who serve on local boards in all 23 counties in the state of Maryland.For those of you who are not familiar with the Caroline County Department of Social Services' Advisory Board, our mission is to provide assistance to support families in financial crisis that do not meet federal and/or state program eligibility but need assistance.
Under the auspices of the Maryland Association of the Social Services Boards, an established nonprofit, the Caroline County Department of Social Services' Board of Directors oversees the Community Assistance Fund, which responds to unmet needs that are fundamental to the safety, health and well-being of Caroline County's children and adults.
Since its inception in 2012, Caroline's Community Assistance Fund has assisted county residents with rental, utilities arrearages and food insecurities. Additionally, the fund provides support in the form of medical supplies and emergency repairs for the elderly.
As you may be aware, there continues to be a growing number of county residents with unmet needs. As we move into the winter months and the holiday season we anticipate an increased need for holiday assistance for families with children and our elderly who are not as fortunate. Any assistance garnered through this drive will also go towards assisting our seniors in need.
We would like to thank you for the generous support you've provided in the past and encourage you to donate whatever you can to our organization to help our less-fortunate neighbors. Please make your checks payable to MASSB Foundation and mail them to:
Juanita A. Webster, Board Chair; Caroline County Department of Social Services; P.O. Box 400; Denton, MD 21629.
Donations can also be made via credit card at massbfoundation.org. Please add a note that your donation is in support of Caroline County Department of Social Services. All donations are 100% tax deductible.
MASSB is an all-volunteer organization so you will have the comfort of knowing that your funds will go directly to those in need.
Thank you for your kindness and your support.
JUANITA A. WEBSTER
Denton

title: There's plenty to eat in Easton: Fest-goers feast on food and drink
author: MARTY MADDEN mmadden@somdnews.com
content:
There's plenty to eat in Easton: Fest-goers feast on food and drink

 November 10, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: MARTY MADDEN mmadden@somdnews.com | Section: Local News 
 
 519
 Words 

 Read News Document

 EASTON — The hordes of people converging on Easton on foot, some pushing strollers and others walking dogs, got enough exercise to work up a waterman's appetite Saturday.The Waterfowl Festival street vendors and those with stations under tents were ready for them.
"It's going great, it's a good turnout," Angie Tyler of Rusticana Pizza said of her business' first time at the 53-year-old fest. "We're a family business, we've been around for 40 years."
While the Waterfowl Festival is known for its seafood vendors, Tyler said Rusticana offered "a little something different" with New York-style pizza that's "always homemade."
RaR, a Cambridge-based brewery with an eclectic menu, attracted customers anxious to sample Eastern Shore comfort food. RaR (which stands for Real ale Revival) had location set up on Harrison Street. Marcy Harrison, RaR's catering director, said it was the first time the brewery has had such a location at the festival.
Among the menu items for sampling was venison chili. RaR chef Victoria Tanner said this is a "traditional chili" with black, kidney and pinto beans, using traditional spices and light tomato sauce. The venison is purchased from "local vendors."
"It's nice and traditional," Tanner said. The spicy chili was augmented by a slice of cornbread.
Whether looking to enjoy alcoholic beverages or something less spirited, fest-goers got samples of both at the tasting pavilion.
Monika Mraz of Doehrn Tea Company in Oxford said her products are imported from mostly Asia — China, India and Sri Lanka — where popular black and green teas are grown. Teas that are caffeine-free, grown in South Africa, are also part of the inventory.
"I'm discovering we have a great tea-drinking community," said Mraz, who noted she has customers who start their day with coffee "and then they move onto tea. It's a little less harsh on the stomach. Tea is a lot more like wine than coffee."
Wine lovers also had their favorite libation at the pavilion.
Candace Donahoe of Layton's Chance Vineyard and Winery had samplings of dry and sweet wines.
"We grow a great variety of grapes," Donahoe said. "We do lots of events."
The Layton family first planted grapes at their Dorchester County farm in 2007 and opened the winery three years later.
Some of the other Eastern Shore farm-to-food basket items available for sampling at the festival included Pepper's Pickles of Chestertown.
"We sell our products at farmers markets and through online shipping," co-owner Nikita Bocharv said.
Among the first-time food vendors was Experience Smith Island. While touting excursions on the classic deadrise workboat Circuit Rider, business owner Carole Ann Landon, a Smith Island Native, sold samples of the iconic Smith Island Cake.
"This is our four year of business and our first year at the Waterfowl Festival," Landon said.
The cake has been popular for centuries, and in 2008 the General Assembly designated it as Maryland's State Dessert.
The eight-to-nine-layer treat is no piece of cake to make, either. Fortunately, Landon does provide as part of her business' programs a Smith Island layer cake demonstration, available off island at a venue of customers' choice.
The cake and everything else consumable provided just another slice of good eating and thirst-quenching satisfaction at the annual Waterfowl Festival.

title: Virtual horse race goes to fund Christmas basket
author: WILL BONTRAGER wbontrager@chespub.com
content:
Virtual horse race goes to fund Christmas basket

 November 12, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: WILL BONTRAGER wbontrager@chespub.com | Section: News 
 
 253
 Words 

 Read News Document

 BETTERTON — Two times a year, the stakes are plenty high at the Betterton Volunteer Firehouse.On Saturday night, almost 200 Kent County residents and nearby neighbors showed up, betting on the horse races as the Still Pond/Betterton Lions Club hosted their 46th Virtual Race Night.
On a large screen, horses raced while folks cheered in a rambunctious, enjoyable manner. On a large screen, they watched a DVD from the "Night at the Races," a gaming company that records real horse races.
Most races were close, some having photo finishes, and the jubilation of the winners watching was contagious.
This year's proceeds went to the Kent County Lions Christmas basket, and winner of the 50/50 raffle was Carol Calloway winning $776. She was congratulated by Emcee, Dick Story and new Lions member Jean Leverage.
During the races, patrons exchanged their regular money placing their bets, chatting with neighbors while they waited in line.
It was not an uncommon occurrence to see popcorn, red raffle tickets, white tickets, funny money, and the program strewn across the tables in a kind of organized, fun, frenzy.
That along with smiling, familiar faces.
There were 12 races, sponsored by local companies and also companies or individuals could sponsor the horses too.
This race is becoming a beloved Betterton tradition that is also a good recruiting tool for the Lions as well as an effective fundraiser.
Debi Cornelius Betterton/Still Pond Lions member thanked everyone for their continued support of the Bettertown/Still Pond Lions Club.
"I hope to see you at our next race on March 8," she added.

title: Haven Ministries welcomes opening of Jacob Sloan Center
author: ANDREA GRABENSTEIN agrabenstein@chespub.com
content:
Haven Ministries welcomes opening of Jacob Sloan Center

 November 12, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: ANDREA GRABENSTEIN agrabenstein@chespub.com | Section: Local News 
 
 464
 Words 

 Read News Document

 QUEENSTOWN — Providing more than just a space to go during the day, the recently opened Jacob Sloan Center is a respite and an assurance of kindness to those in need.Serving as an extension of Haven Ministries emergency shelter and carrying on the kindness of one local boy, the Jacob Sloan Center opened with a ribbon-cutting at the Shore Christian Fellowship Church Oct. 31.
The space at the Shore Christian Fellowship Church was offered by Pastor Tom Chandler, and the Jacob Sloan Center developed to not only provide a place for clients of Haven Ministries Emergency Shelter to spend time during the day but also to be an education center to help individuals to learn life skills to help them to lead sustainable lives.
At the Jacob Sloan Center, guests can shower, do laundry, find respite and take part in education classes such as resume writing, finances, computer literacy and life skills, according to Peter Grim, Haven Ministries executive director.
Haven Ministries has long envisioned a day center where guests can gain vital skills to transform their circumstances and improve their lives, Grim said.
Food and shelter are essential, but so are educational programs that can help lift individuals and families out of poverty, he said.
The next steps for the center include kitchen enhancements, said Mary Ella Jourdak, a Haven Ministries volunteer.
"This is the first step in providing the under-resourced more dignity," she said.
The center filled with hugs and greetings of community supporters last Thursday as members of the Sloan family embrace and reconnect with each other through the memory of Jake Sloan.
Inside the Jacob Sloan Center, a wall is home to a photo collage of memories and smiles of Jake, who was killed in a car accident in Queen Anne's County in 2018 when he was 12.
Jake's parents, Mary and Peter Sloan, were proud to once again partner with Haven Ministries to continue their son's legacy and the opportunity for Jake's name to be a part of bettering the lives of the community.
"He was a friend to all. He went out of his way to make a difference every day with kindness and giving,' Mary said.
The Jacob Sloan Foundation has provided hundreds of thousands of dollars in funding to support various organizations and families in need.
"Just by being kind, you can make a difference," she said.
The mission of Haven Ministries to provide hope and support to those in need fits perfectly with Jake's lifelong dedication of always kind: a commitment the Jacob Sloan Foundation now fulfills with honor, according to Mary,
"It takes a village, and you are all of ours," she said.
Funding for center furnishing and equipment was also made possible by Tim and Linette Miller.
More information about Haven Ministries can be found at haven-ministries.org.
More information about the Jacob sloan Foundation can be found at jacobsloanfoundation.com.

title: Veterans Day brings together Marylanders who served for breakfast at American Legion
author: MAGGIE TROVATO mtrovato@chespub.com
content:
Veterans Day brings together Marylanders who served for breakfast at American Legion

 November 13, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: MAGGIE TROVATO mtrovato@chespub.com | Section: Local News 
 
 531
 Words 

 Read News Document

 CAMBRIDGE — Serving in the U.S. Army gave Gov. Wes Moore (D) the chance to see parts of the country and world he never knew existed.The experience also gave him the opportunity to create lasting bonds with people different from him.
"I can tell you that some of my best friends on this planet are people who society tells me I shouldn't even be talking to," he said during a Veterans Day breakfast at American Legion Post 91 in Cambridge. "And these are my brothers now. And my sisters."
Before shaking hands with Maryland veterans and serving them breakfast, Moore — who was deployed to Afghanistan in 2005 — talked about the military's ability to unite people and the importance of unity in a time of division.
"I could not tell you the political affiliation of people that I served with," he said. "Because we didn't talk about it. ... Because it didn't matter. We fought for each other."
Moore said he and the people he served with had one goal: Making sure they got home. He talked about standing with each other and fighting for each other, even when disagreements arose.
There is a lot society can learn from veterans, he said.
"This Veterans Day, I think it becomes incredibly important that we hold those values dear and that we understand that even in the darkest moments, that it's faith that is what's going to drive us through," he said.
In his speech, Moore also talked about Maryland's efforts to support veterans. He mentioned tax relief for veterans as well as the Time to Serve Act, which extends military leave for state employees who serve in the National Guard or Reserve.
Along with Moore, American Legion Department of Maryland Commander David Heredia and Maryland Secretary of Veterans and Military Families Anthony Woods spoke at the breakfast event that drew an array of American Legion members from different posts.
Woods announced grant awards to the American Legion through the Maryland Veterans Trust Fund. He said Post 70 and Post 193 would receive funding for capital projects.
"This is a beautiful post right here," Woods said about Post 91. "But we want to invest in those posts because we know the role that the posts play in building community amongst our veterans."
The state is also giving $10,000 to the American Legion Department of Maryland to be invested in the American Legion's Be The One campaign, a national effort to reduce veteran suicide rates through offering supports and resources to veterans and working to destigmatize mental health support.
Steve Williams, who served in the U.S. Air Force from 1964 to 1968, said medical care and homelessness are two of the most important issues when it comes to supporting veterans. He said he thinks Moore is "pretty well on top of" what the issues affecting veterans are because Moore is a veteran.
Williams, who is the judge advocate for Post 91, said the event went "wonderfully."
"Seeing the different Legion posts all come together with state officials, you don't see that very often," he said. "I'm Really, really proud of it."
Post 91 Commander Rich Colburn said there were no Democrats, no Republicans and no independents in attendance at the event Veterans Day morning.
"Just veterans," he said.

title: CASA is grateful for its volunteers this holiday season
author: CASA OF THE MID-SHORE
content:
CASA is grateful for its volunteers this holiday season

 November 15, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: CASA OF THE MID-SHORE | Section: News 
 
 313
 Words 

 Read News Document

 At CASA of the Mid-Shore, we are committed to advocating for children under the protection of the Talbot, Dorchester, Queen Anne's and Kent circuit courts due to abuse, neglect or abandonment. Our nonprofit organization's mission is to ensure that every child has the right to thrive in a safe and permanent home.CASA (Court Appointed Special Advocate) volunteers play a vital role in this mission. As caring and involved adults, they work to identify the unique needs of each child, advocate in court for essential services, and collaborate with agency partners to facilitate timely and safe resolutions.
Most importantly, CASA volunteers become trusted figures in the lives of the children they serve, often providing stability, support and consistency.
This commitment is especially significant during the holiday season. For many children, this time of year is about creating joyful memories with family. However, for those placed in foster care, the holidays can be a stark reminder of their circumstances and what they are missing. CASA volunteers offer vital support, helping these children find hope amidst the challenges.
"Speaking up for children is our guiding principle," said Robin Davenport, CASA's executive director. "It reinforces our belief that a brighter future is possible for every child we serve... As we approach the holiday season, we are profoundly grateful for our extraordinary CASA volunteers. Their unwavering dedication to vulnerable children is a true treasure in our community."
National studies confirm the value of CASA — findings show that children are more hopeful when a CASA is in their lives.
CASA volunteers come from all walks of life, have varied experiences and professions, and are at least 21 years of age. After completing the application and screening process, individuals participate in pre-service training before being sworn in as officers of the court. CASA welcomes volunteers from all cultures, races, ethnicities and backgrounds.
To learn more about becoming a volunteer, visit casamidshore.org or email jc@casamidshore.org.

title: Never forgotten: Veterans Point at Wells Grove holds ribbon cutting
author: ANDREA GRABENSTEIN agrabenstein@chespub.com
content:
Never forgotten: Veterans Point at Wells Grove holds ribbon cutting

 November 15, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: ANDREA GRABENSTEIN agrabenstein@chespub.com | Section: News 
 
 652
 Words 

 Read News Document

 KENT NARROWS — In Queen Anne's County, the National Anthem comes accompanied by the sound of bay waves lapping the pier and the cries of gulls overhead.With a clear sky, a light bay breeze wafted Old Glory at the Wells Grove pier where veterans and their community honored all who served with the dedication of Veterans Point at Wells Grove Nov. 11.
The project was spearheaded by the Queen Anne's County and Center for the Military and Veteran Family, operated by the Veteran and Military Support Alliance (VAMSA).
Through collaboration with community organizations and county departments and representatives, Veterans Points at Wells Grove serves as a physical manifestation of Queen Anne's County's dedication to the sacrifices made by the military and their families, Eric Johnson, VAMSA executive director, said.
The memorial stands not just a tribute to those who fought and fell, but all who have served and the sacrifices made by waiting families and supporting communities, said Master of Ceremonies Wes Guckert, United States Air Force and Vietnam veteran and VAMSA board of director member.
"This place now marked in the heart of Kent Narrows serves as a sanctuary where memories will be honored and history will be remembered," he said, noting the dedication ceremony as a "momentous occasion."
Guckert teared up as he shared the impetus behind the memorial sought to ensure the loneliness experienced by returning Vietnam veterans never happened again.
VAMSA believes in operationalizing "thank you for your service" and works to address needs along with their families, according to Johnson.
"For every veteran that comes in with a need, there is a member of that family that is also in crisis," he said.
For All Seasons serves as a strategic partner with VAMSA for mental health services and healing and Beth Anne Dorman, Executive Director, noted services are available to families as well as the community
Open access telehealth provides help for those who need it regardless of ability to pay and a new no wait list system provides services quickly, she said.
"We're able to say to veteran families, your service means something, you are valuable as a community member and we are here," she said.
Remembering that freedom and liberty are not free, keynote speaker USMC Lieutenant General (Retired) John Sattler urged honor, education and encouragement: honor those who have served, educate others on the sacrifices made, and encourage instilling core military values and carrying on an 'If not me then who?' mentality just as generations of veterans before have shown.
Bagpiper Randy Welch said it was always an esteemed honor to bring memories back into the lives of veterans as they listen to him play, whether they spring to their feet as their branch of the armed forces medley plays or when their eyes shine with pride with America the Beautiful.
Singing of the National Anthem was performed by United States Air Force TSgt. Megan May.
Having a local spot commemorating veterans is incredibly meaningful, according to veteran and VAMSA volunteer Sarah Stallings, "It shows the community cares."
VAMSA serves as an extended family to all veterans and their families and connects them with the resources they need. "We're all in this to help each other," she said.
The monument was built by Chester River Landscaping.
Funding was made possible by the W. Earl and Barbara Griffin Foundation and Chair Micheal Foster hoped for Veterans Point at Wells Cove to be the first of many projects together with VAMSA.
Invocation services were performed by Mark Hamilton, chaplain of Kent Island American Legion Post 278 and benediction services were provided by Rabbi Jason Goldstein of Beth Tfiloh Congregation of Baltimore.
At a lunch reception at the neighboring Bridges Restaurant, veterans reminisced and shared stories of service.
With community as the heart and soul, officials seek Veterans Point as a place of reflection and welcome families to use the space as a way to honor legacies and carry the spirit of endurance as it continues to inspire.
More information about VAMSA can be found at qacveteransupport.org.

title: Cranksgiving riders collect food for those in need
author: DAVE MANSFIELD Chesapeake Cycling Club
content:
Cranksgiving riders collect food for those in need

 November 16, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: DAVE MANSFIELD Chesapeake Cycling Club | Section: Life 
 
 259
 Words 

 Read News Document

 Chesapeake Cycling Club, a growing organization based in Easton, held its annual Cranksgiving Food Drive on Sunday, Nov. 10.The event was again organized by longtime Chesapeake Cycling Club member Kevan Full.
It was a beautiful and crisp morning for the eight members who made up in enthusiasm for slightly lower turnout. They met at Eat Sprout in Easton and "raced" on their bicycles in casual attire to purchase and gather the designated items.
Two teams of four cyclists had a budget of approximately $20 per person to purchase food and other staples from a list to be donated to Saint Vincent de Paul's local food bank. The riders went to Acme, Weis Markets, Target, Harris Teeter and the Plaza Latina Food Market in Easton to buy pasta, sauce, beans, baby food, peanut butter and other essentials.
While one team claimed victory, the reality is that all the participants were winners, participants said.
The local 4-H Club independently collected and donated a significant amount of food and other staples.
We also realized how fortunate we were to have this opportunity and to reflect that we helped Saint Vincent de Paul to carry out their mission to serve people in need in our town.
Eat Sprout provided complimentary coffee to participating club members.
Cranksgiving will return next year and enrollment is always open. Please join us and bring your friends and family with bikes to help our community to be a better place to live for everyone.
Chesapeake Cycling Club is more than just cycling. The Club is welcoming new members to join in the recreation and fun.

title: Be a Santa program serves Mid-Shore seniors
author: Tom McCall
content:
Be a Santa program serves Mid-Shore seniors

 November 22, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Tom McCall | Section: Life 
 
 737
 Words 

 Read News Document

 EASTON — Usually when it comes to holiday gifts comes, children are top priority, but according to organizers of a program serving multiple Mid-Shore counties, there is another deserving population for shoppers to keep in mind.Senior citizens will receive a small gift and some community connection through the "Be a Santa to a Senior" program this holiday season.
"A simple, thoughtful gift can bring immense happiness to an older adult who may not have family around to celebrate with," said Jenna Marchi, owner of the Home Instead office in Easton, which is coordinating the effort. "Being a Santa to a Senior is about more than presents—it's about showing care, love, and letting these individuals know they are not forgotten."
The program aims to help combat the loneliness many seniors feel around the holiday season.
There are trees with seniors' names on the ornaments at 20 different locations from Easton, to Grasonville, to Preston. Those interested in purchasing a gift for a senior are asked to select an ornament, buy the gift listed on it, and return the gift and ornament to the location where they found it.
Childlene Brooks is the Senior Center manager at Brookletts Place in Easton.
"All of the name tags are gone. Some of the gifts are back. We had 23 names to start with. They wanted stacked baskets, slippers, sweaters, hats, perfume and bath towels. Word games and gloves. Nothing costly. The last ones came off the tree on Friday," Brooks said of the tree at Brookletts Place.
The tags that go on her tiny tree have the recipient's first name, a code number and whether they are male or female. "It also indicates what they want," Brooks said.
Her favorite part is to help seniors in the community out.
"They probably don't have any other avenue of obtaining some of these things or any family to help them out. I am one for helping. If I can help in any way, that is what I want to do. A lot of them are still living alone. They need contact with other people," Brooks said.
The Ridgely Pharmacy has been participating in the program for over 10 years.
"It is going wonderfully. I think we are one of the top ones that help. We try to do over 200. It is very rewarding to help these seniors. We have six left to go," Brenda Walls said. She is the owner of The Ridgely Pharmacy.
There were gifts like a lap blanket, shoes, lotion, cleaning products and a cane listed on ornaments at her store.
"I have a following now. As soon as I put it on my Facebook page, we had people coming in. It is all about giving back to our community," Walls said.
Although there is a physical transaction, the emotional one is just as crucial.
"This program is about so much more than giving gifts—it's about creating moments of joy and connection between older adults and the community," Marchi said. "There's nothing more rewarding than seeing the smile on a senior's face when they open their gift and feel the love behind it."
Home Instead is a senior home care provider and has an office on 8626 Brooks Drive in Easton.
For more information to get involved, call 410-822-1230. Gifts must be returned by Dec. 1.
