title: Tides of Grace presents 5th annual Christmas Magic Toy Drive
author: ANDREA GRABENSTEIN agrabenstein@chespub.com
content:
Tides of Grace presents 5th annual Christmas Magic Toy Drive

 November 22, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: ANDREA GRABENSTEIN agrabenstein@chespub.com | Section: Local News 
 
 348
 Words 

 Read News Document

 STEVENSVILLE — Ensuring the joy of Christmas is spread throughout the Eastern Shore community, Tides of Grace once again welcomes the return of its signature Christmas Magic Toy Drive.This year's annual drive anticipates serving nearly 1,000 children and is currently collecting gently used toys for infants through teens. The drive serves as a perfect way to make room for new gifts this holiday season and show children the joy of giving, Leann Rhodes, Tides of Grace executive director, said.
Toys will be collected from drop off locations starting at midnight, Dec. 6 and volunteer elves will come out for an extravagant Christmas pajama party at The Edge Arena to sort and lay all the goodies across the 25,000 square-foot edge arena.
From 7 a.m. to 9:30 a.m. Dec. 7, Christmas magic will welcome registered parents to shop for free toys for children ages infant to 17.
This jolly big event is designed for parents only, with children left at home to maintain the element of surprise.
No income verification is required, but parents must register ahead of time.
This event takes a total of 200 volunteers from the community starting from midnight on Friday, Dec. 6 through the morning hours of Saturday, Dec. 7 to make it possible.
"It's really awesome to see the community come together in such a big way," Rhodes said.
The annual event began in 2020 with a group of moms wanting to spread holiday cheer, and it has grown tremendously over the years, from helping 100 children in 2020 to over 600 children in 2023, she said.
Donators are asked to ensure toys are in working condition and keep all parts together with a bag to prevent them from getting lost during sorting.
The drive is not accepting stuffed animals, used clothes, or books this year.
Drop off locations are located throughout the Eastern Shore with volunteers available to arrange pickups if donations can't be dropped off in person.
"Together, we can spread joy and ensure that every child in our community feels the love this holiday season," Rhodes said.
More information including child registration and drop off locations can be found at tidesofgraceinc.org/christmas-magic.

title: Thanksgiving made simple: Top tips for hosting small gatherings
author: Laura Sampson Food Drink Life
content:
Thanksgiving made simple: Top tips for hosting small gatherings

 November 22, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Laura Sampson Food Drink Life | Section: Life 
 
 807
 Words 

 Read News Document

 As we move through life, there will be times when smaller gatherings of friends and family naturally happen. We can't change it, we can't pretend that it's anything different. But we can accept and embrace it.Maybe it won't always be this way. Or you may decide to change how you celebrate completely. Whatever happens with that is in the future. You can make changes in the future.
The only way to move forward this year with a smaller gathering is to embrace the good things about it, even if you don't want to. You might discover a few things about yourself or come up with new ways to enjoy family gatherings.
Celebrate with small gatherings
Cooking for fewer people allows you to change how you've always done things. If you're struggling with change or celebrating when you just don't feel it, that's okay.
Moving forward with a traditional dinner with fewer people can be a blessing. Fewer people means less money spent, which can be nice in the pocketbook. But other things are amazing, too.
Try new things
You can change up what you usually make. Instead of a 20-pound turkey, you can try a small prime rib, turkey breast or something else fancy, perhaps a beef Wellington or a roasted duck.
If you don't need a huge turkey, you can relax a little and sleep in it, or you can make a special breakfast that morning instead of making and stuffing a bird at 5 am. With no reason to be up so early, you can sleep in, make a leisurely breakfast and still get everything done in time.
Streamline the menu
Because you're making a dinner that doesn't include the world's biggest turkey, you're free to cut down on stuffing recipes, cranberry sauces and all that jazz. Even if you're making a turkey, you don't need that much food.
That means it's the perfect time to try something new, like corn pudding or fresh bread. Or the ultimate homemade pie with homemade pie crust. The sky is the limit here, so pick something and perfect it, then amaze your guests.
Make it a potluck
If you are having a smaller gathering, it's the perfect time to call for a potluck. You can make a main dish or two because you'll be doing less in other places. And everyone else can bring sides. Assign them to people so they know what to make and what will be on the menu.
You can serve a potluck buffet style if that's interesting to you. Then, the table is simple, clean and elegant.
If you're serving potluck style, you can keep your current table the size it is. That means no stuffing people into a small space or finding and dragging out more chairs and stools. Plus, no table prep means more time to relax or clean the house.
Speaking of tables
If you're making a smaller, cozy dinner for fewer people, it's the perfect time to do something new and different with your table this year. Add a tablecloth, beautiful candles, pumpkins, flowers or anything else your creative mind desires.
Pull out the fancy special dishes and the silver and make beautiful, small feasts. Just because it's smaller doesn't mean it isn't special or meaningful.
Less pie stress
When you have a house full of guests, you often feel like you have to whip up several pies or desserts. With fewer guests, you can make one and be done. Or go fancy and order from a bakery that will make you the dessert of your dreams.
Change it up
Try new things this year. Instead of having dinner at your regular time, try a new time. Or insist everyone bring their favorite game and host a game night with friends or family. Kick off the Christmas season by choosing a favorite movie and enjoying it together. There's no end to ways you can innovate the day with family or friends.
It's just smaller, not less important
Thanksgiving doesn't have to be a grand affair to be meaningful. Sometimes, embracing a smaller gathering allows us to focus on what truly matters: The people around the table, the flavors we love and the moments we share.
This year, rather than seeing a smaller gathering as something or somebody missing, try to view it as an opportunity to create a more intimate, relaxed celebration. A simplified menu, a cozy setting and a slower pace can make this Thanksgiving feel refreshingly different.
It's a chance to try something new, let go of old expectations and perhaps even start new traditions that feel just as special. Whatever the size of the gathering, the spirit of Thanksgiving lives on in the connections we make and the gratitude we feel.
Laura Sampson of Little House Big Alaska is on a mission to teach modern family-oriented home cooks how to make old-fashioned foods new again. She shares her passion for home cooking, backyard gardening and homesteading on her website and blog.

Holiday season kicks off on the Mid-Shore

 Words

 EASTON — The holiday season is here, and with it comes an array of events from ice skating to Christmas parades on the Eastern Shore. For those looking for a holiday adventure take a moment to preview upcoming events.Immediately following Thanksgiving is ice skating at Hyatt Regency Chesapeake Bay. Hyatt Regency Chesapeake Bay Golf Resort, Spa and Marina is debuting a synthetic ice-skating rink and winter village in celebration of the holidays and winter season. The rink will be available throughout the winter.
On Dec. 5 at 9 a.m., the Chesapeake Curling Club will be hosting 90-minute learn to curl sessions. During this event, attendees will learn proper technique in delivering a granite curling stone and sweeping techniques.
The 75th annual Cambridge-Dorchester County Christmas Parade, one of the largest nighttime Christmas parades in the state, kicks off at 5 p.m. on Saturday, Dec. 7. Pre-parade entertainment will be provided by artist Rebecca Bailey starting at 4:15 p.m. at the reviewing stand located at Craig's Drugstore parking area. The parade can be viewed on High Street, Poplar and Race streets, ending at Washington Street.
Also on Dec. 7 is the Easton Christmas Parade, which draws visitors to the town each year. Before the parade, Santa arrives in Thompson Park at 5:30 p.m., followed by a tree lighting at 6 p.m. Parade starts at 6:30 p.m. Street closures begin at 6 p.m. The Chamber of Commerce will have collection boxes at Thompson Park during the parade to collect for Toys for Tots.
In Ridgely, the Lions Club's annual Christmas Parade will light up downtown Dec. 7. Line-up for the parade begins at 6:15 p.m. at the Martin Sutton Park Fourth Street Parking Lot. The parade begins at 6:45 p.m. Santa will be at the train station after the parade for visits.
On Dec. 8, visitors can tour five gorgeous homes decorated for the holiday season in and around Cambridge, in addition to historic Waugh Chapel United Methodist Church and Sycamore Cottage. The Cambridge Holiday House Tour takes place from 1:30 to 4:30 p.m. Tickets are $35 and can be purchased day-of at 417 High St.
The annual Santa Chase will be held in Martin Sutton Park in Ridgely on Dec. 13. The dog- and family-friendly two-mile run or walk and costume contest (judged by Santa himself) costs $20 per person or $72 per group of four, plus $5 for each dog. The event is produced in partnership with Lions International and the Ridgely Lions Club.
Starting Dec. 13 to 15, the Oxford Holiday Market will be up and running. This event will take place in Oxford and will offer a weekend filled with unique artisan gifts, food and holiday music.
That weekend also marks the 38th annual Christmas in St. Michaels. From Dec. 13 to 15, St. Michaels will host a variety of holiday events including a gingerbread house contest, two parades and a tour of homes. More details and a schedule for the festivities can be found at christmasinstmichaels.org.
At noon on Dec. 14, Denton will host its first ever Wreaths Across America event at the Denton Cemetery. The event is being organized by local boy scout Billy Quick as his Eagle Scout service project. It will honor veterans by placing wreaths on their graves.
For those looking for family-friendly fun, Santa's Workshop will be open at Wharves of Choptank Visitor & Heritage Center in Denton on Saturdays, Dec. 7, 14 and 21. The event, where families can create toys with "elves" and meet Santa, has a suggested donation of $15 per child. Registrations can be made at carolinearts.org/events/santas-workshop-in-the-island-of-misfit-toys/.

title: Iota Alpha Alpha provides turkeys, meals to hundreds of Easton families
author: KONNER METZ kmetz@chespub.com
content:
Iota Alpha Alpha provides turkeys, meals to hundreds of Easton families

 November 26, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: KONNER METZ kmetz@chespub.com | Section: Local News 
 
 417
 Words 

 Read News Document

 EASTON — Hundreds of turkeys and packaged meals were handed out to Easton residents Saturday afternoon on Glenwood Avenue.Iota Alpha Alpha, an Easton chapter of the national Omega Psi Phi fraternity, organized the distribution, which was held at the American Legion Blake-Blackston Post 77. Residents lined up around noon Saturday to pick up turkeys and meals.
Doug Rogers, a member of Iota Alpha Alpha, and Mayor Megan Cook each spoke at the start of the distribution.
"This is a great opportunity to give back to your community," Cook said.
She thanked the local organizations for their contributions that will help Easton residents not just the week of Thanksgiving, but throughout the entire holiday season.
Rogers said organizations such as the Dock Street Foundation, Chesapeake Multicultural Resource Center, Neighborhood Service Center and Building African American Minds Center were important partners with Iota Alpha Alpha for the event.
"This truck, it was filled to the brim," Rogers said of the truck that held the meals and turkeys. "… We passed out over 200 turkeys and 200 certificates for meals. And if people don't come and pick up those turkeys, it's great, because we're going to give the overflow to the Neighborhood Service Center. If they don't eat today, they'll eat next week."
The men of Iota Alpha Alpha joined with sister organizations and community members to not just pass out food, but to give away winter clothing to those in need as well.
It was the chapter's first Thanksgiving distribution at Blake-Blackston Post 77. Rogers said he hopes it continues and grows in future years.
Founded in 1911 at Howard University, Omega Psi Phi is predicated upon public service, Rogers said. A motto of the fraternity is "friendship is essential to the soul," something Rogers says the Easton chapter strives to do in the local community.
"When we start talking about giving, we start talking about (what) the Lord calls us to do, (He) calls us to serve people," Rogers said. "We're a service organization first and foremost. We're called to serve people. The little bit that we can do, the little bit that we can gather, is about serving God as people. So that's at our core."
Rogers said Saturday's cheerful and upbeat turkey and meal distribution was an example of the Iota Alpha Alpha chapter carrying out its mission and helping local residents in need during what can be trying times.
"It makes us feel good as men, is that we're able to stand up and be able to serve," Rogers said. "… We're living our creed."

 GRASONVILLE — Saturday evening, Nov. 16, Talisman Therapeutic Riding hosted its second annual Horseshoe Heroes Awards Banquet at the Hyatt Place hotel, located at Kent Narrows.Event Chair and emcee Audrey Scott welcomed those in attendance, explaining the purpose of the banquet was to recognize those in the community who have supported the mission of Talisman Therapeutic Riding, an organization providing horse therapy to disabled military veterans, children, and other individuals.
Following dinner, guest speaker U.S. Coast Guard Captain Carrie Wolfe spoke briefly, talking about related services the Coast Guard provides to members of the military, particularly those struggling with mental health issues. She stated, "We not only use horses for therapy treatments, but other animals such as dogs and others, to help members of the military improve their quality of life."
Scott was joined by TTR Chair Diana Saquella and Queen Anne's County Commissioner Jim Moran during the presentations. Moran read a biography of each honoree.
Talisman Therapeutic Riding has been in existence for more that a decade. Executive Director Noelle Douglas said, "This banquet is held to recognize our volunteers and members of the community who go above and beyond to help Talisman."
The Talisman farm and facility is located at 172 Blue Ribbon Lane in Grasonville. For more information, visit talismantherapeuticriding.org or call 443-239-9400.

title: Ridgely sports new model train station
author: KONNER METZ kmetz@chespub.com
content:
Ridgely sports new model train station

 November 28, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: KONNER METZ kmetz@chespub.com | Section: Local News 
 
 437
 Words 

 Read News Document

 RIDGELY — The Town of Ridgely has a new display of its historic railroad station.Bob Anderson, 86, built a model of the Ridgely Train Station, a part of the town's unique charm that dates back to the 19th century. Anderson's model mimics the train station's antique glass windows and green roofing that are still seen today on West Railroad Avenue.
Anderson said despite some cramps in his hands and wrist, he was able to finish the model in around six months. His daughter, Ridgely Clerk-Treasurer Stephanie Berkey, helped him complete the project.
"I've never built anything like it in my life," Anderson said. "We tried to make it as authentic as we possibly could."
On Nov. 4, Anderson's model station was presented to the Ridgely Town Commissioners and placed in the Ridgely Town Hall. It will eventually be taken to the Ridgely Train Station, Ridgely Historical Society President Cathy Schwab said.
"It was awesome. I was so happy and proud, mostly happy for him," Schwab said. As part of its mission, the historical society works to maintain and preserve the railroad station and its history.
Anderson, a longtime Eastern Shore resident who spent time in the Coast Guard, said building models has become a hobby for him in recent years. His next project will be constructing a model of the USS Enterprise that played a crucial role during World War II.
The train station took lots of patience and attention to detail, Anderson said, placing wood planks down one by one. Anderson said there are more than 1,000 wooden planks on the deck of the model station.
"Each one was done one at a time," Anderson said. "I like to make things right. … I don't rush. I do not rush."
The train station fit into the town's hope of becoming a booming city on the East Coast. But developers from the Maryland and Baltimore Land Association failed financially in the early 1900s, and the town never became the "dream city" many had envisioned.
It closed in 1976, but the building remained, housing businesses and the Ridgely Town Hall in the 1990s. Town historians view it as a centerpiece of the small town.
"It starts out and still is the heart of Ridgely," Schwab said. "If the train had not gone through the town and stated that we needed to have a station and a hotel, there would be no town."
Anderson called the station on West Railroad Avenue "a relic" and said he was happy to contribute to the town's preservation and recognition of the historic railroad. Schwab echoed the same.
"To preserve what we had is just a wonderful reminder of who we are," Schwab said.

title: Look backward, not forward
author: Staff Writer
content:
Look backward, not forward

 November 30, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Staff Writer | Section: Editors Inbox 
 
 376
 Words 

 Read News Document

 I caught an article in a recent Star Democrat mentioning funds that were possibly going to be allocated for a new kids playground. (Full disclosure: Anything we can do to keep our young population pointed in the right direction I am all for.)But it got me thinking of how things have changed in the half century since I was one of those kids growing up in Easton.
For us, a playground was simply where we stopped and the action of the day began. A garden shed could become Command Central, our secret fort of the day. Almost any out-of-the-way spot could be commandeered as GI Joe's headquarters.
Talbot Town Hill was the go-to skateboard challenge – on homemade boards of course – and no helmets, naturally. Playing cards clothes pinned to our bikes sent a clackety warning to anyone who happened to see us – we meant business. No surprise, we built the bikes ourselves too.
Looking back, I give us credit for being resourceful. Hand lines, earthworms and Kool-Aid for fuel were the necessities for fishing trips to any bridge. (Aside: I remember checking the mailbox daily for three agonizing months waiting to get my free Kool-Aid pitcher).
We went through a Wild West stage, converting a couple of old wagons to "covered" wagons. Freedom had few boundaries. Our curfew was simply when it got dark or when we got hungry.
When I was 10, my family moved to Glebe Villa on Goldsborough Creek into an aptly named haunted house, and the good times went up a notch. The water became our streets and boats became our wheels. Waterskiing, the original boogie boards, bridge jumping and more fishing.
Mock orange fights with my new clan the "villa gorillas." Neighborhood football, many a campfire. Walking in the woods, my first pocketknife. Ahh, those were the days.
Friendships I have to this day were members of this then — "exclusive" club. Well I guess I am starting to look backward more than forward these days.
"You're turning into your dad," someone recently told me. What an honor, I said to myself. Thanks again, and lots of love to all of my friends and family.
P.S. Please reach out to this great community and lift someone's spirit, there are many ways, be yourself, it's free.
ROO WOOD
Easton

title: Country Cooking: Christmas cookie making fun
author: MARIE SAVAGE Country Cooking
content:
Country Cooking: Christmas cookie making fun

 December 3, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: MARIE SAVAGE Country Cooking | Section: Food 
 
 1335
 Words 

 Read News Document

 Stepping back in time reveals a lot of memories for me. Holiday baking was extra special, as my mother, my sister and I each liked to bake different desserts.Mom loved making pies, cakes, puddings and custards. My sister liked making candies of all kinds "and especially fudge."
I was the cookie maker. They would not have hit Betty Crocker's list, but my late brother-in-law, Sonny, loved them. He ate them perfectly baked, burned or mushy. He also said they were the best.
Brother Ollie said even the chickens wouldn't eat them when he threw them into the poultry yard.
I have improved through the years, and now each holiday I have a grandson, Colin, who joins me in the love of cookie baking. As a matter of fact, we do our first batch on Thanksgiving evening.
It is so much fun baking with the children, watching them be so excited to do this "on their own."
I am going to begin this cookie column today with my mom's favorite cookie.
GINGERSNAPS1 1/2 sticks unsalted butter, 1 1/4 cup granulated sugar, 1/4 cup lightly packed brown sugar, 1/3 cup molasses (not black), one egg, 1/2 tsp salt, 2 tsps baking soda, 1/2 tsp ground ginger, 1 tsp ground cinnamon, 1/4 tsp ground cloves, 2 1/4 cups all purpose flour.
Preheat the oven to 350 degrees. Line baking sheets with parchment paper. In a large bowl using an electric mixer, beat butter, 3/4 cup granulated sugar, and brown sugar until light and fluffy, about two minutes. I use the paddles on the mixer for this. Add molasses and egg and beat again until well combined. Add in salt, baking soda, ginger, cinnamon, cloves and flour and beat until well combined. In a shallow dish add 1/2 cup granulated sugar. Scoop the dough into 1 1/2 tablespoons balls, roll into the sugar in the dish and place on the baking sheet, leaving plenty of room for cookies to spread. Bake for 15 minutes or until cookies have spread and the surface looks cracked. Let the cookies cool completely on the baking sheets before moving to wire racks. Store cookies in an airtight container. This recipe makes 28 cookies. I use Brer Rabbit or the Grandma's brand of molasses. Enjoy.
CHRISTMAS SWEET AND SALTY TOFFEE35 saltine crackers, 1 cup butter, 1 cup packed brown sugar, 1 3/4 cups semisweet chocolate chips, 1 bag red and green holiday M&Ms, 1 jar holiday sprinkles.
Preheat the oven to 350 degrees. Line a baking sheet or jelly-roll pan with tin foil and coat with cooking spray. Line the baking sheet with Saltine crackers. Set aside. In a medium-sized saucepan, melt butter and brown sugar. Bring to a boil, stirring continuously, and let cook until bubbling, about 2 minutes. Pour mixture over crackers in an even layer and bake for 12 to 15 minutes. Top immediately with chocolate chips and let melt. Smooth chocolate out into an even layer, then top with red and green M&Ms and holiday sprinkles. Cut into squares, then cool until the chocolate has hardened.
CHOCOLATE CRINKLE COOKIES1 3/4 cups all-purpose flour, 3/4 cup unsweetened cocoa powder, 1 tsp kosher salt, 1 tsp baking powder, 3/4 tsp baking soda, 1/2 cup butter (melted), 3/4 cup granulated sugar, 1/2 cup packed brown sugar, 3 large eggs, powdered sugar for rolling.
In a large bowl, combine flour, cocoa powder, salt, baking powder and baking soda. In a medium bowl, whisk together melted butter, sugars and eggs until well combined. Pour into dry ingredients and mix until just combined. Cover bowl with plastic wrap and refrigerate for two hours. Preheat the oven to 350 degrees and line two large baking sheets with parchment. Place powdered sugar in a small bowl. Scoop about 2 tablespoons of dough and roll into a ball. If dough is too sticky, wet your hands slightly to help roll dough. Roll dough into powdered sugar, coating well and then place on a prepared baking sheet two inches apart. After rolling all the dough in powdered sugar, roll each piece again in powdered sugar. This will help get a more dramatic crinkle when the cookies bake. Bake cookies until cookies puff and crack, about 14 minutes. The edges will just be set, but the cracks will still look slightly underdone. Let cool on a baking sheet.
CANDY CANE SNOWBALLS2 cups butter (softened), 1 cup confectioners' sugar, 1 tsp vanilla extract, 3 1/2 cups all-purpose flour, 1 cup chopped pecans, 8 ounces white candy coating (melted), 1/3 to 1/2 cup crushed peppermint candies.
Cream butter and confectioners' sugar until light and fluffy, 5-7 minutes. Beat in vanilla. Gradually beat in flour. Stir in pecans. Refrigerate, covered, until firm enough to shape, 3-4 hours. Preheat the oven to 350 degrees. Shape dough into one-inch balls. Place two inches apart on ungreased baking sheets. Bake until lightly browned, about 15 minutes. Remove from pans to wire racks; cool completely. Dip tops of cookies into candy coating, allowing excess to drip off; dip into crushed candies. Let stand until set.
OLD FASHIONED CHOCOLATE COOKIES1 1/2 cups all-purpose flour, 1/2 tsp baking soda, 1/2 tsp salt, 1/3 cup shortening, 1/3 cup butter (softened), 1/2 cup granulated sugar, 1/2 cup brown sugar, 1 egg (beaten), 1 tsp vanilla, 1 6-ounce package semi-sweet chocolate chips, 1/2 cup chopped nuts (optional).
Preheat the oven to 375 degrees. In a medium bowl, sift together flour, salt and baking soda. Set aside, In a large bowl, cream together shortening, butter, sugars, egg and vanilla. Gradually combine half of the flour mixture into the wet mixture. Use a rubber spatula to incorporate the other half of the flour mixture if the dough gets too thick for the mixer. Stir in the chocolate chips. Roll the dough into tablespoon-sized balls. Place on a baking sheet lined with parchment paper, two inches apart. Bake for 7-10 minutes. Remove from the oven when cookies are slightly golden around the edges and soft on the tops. Leave cookies on the pan for 2-3 minutes to continue cooking outside of the oven. Let cool until firm to touch. Serve immediately or store leftovers in an air-tight container.
ITALIAN THUMBPRINT COOKIES2 1/4 cups all-purpose flour, 1 cup salted butter (firm but not cold), 2/3 cup granulated sugar, 1 1/2 tsp vanilla extract (could be substituted), 2 large eggs (yolks and whites divided), 1 cup unsalted pistachios (finely chopped), 1/2 cup strawberry preserves, 4 ounces white chocolate or semi-sweet chocolate (melted).
Preheat the oven to 350 degrees. In the bowl of an electric stand mixer fitted with the paddle attachment and set on medium-high speed, whip together butter, granulated sugar and vanilla bean seeds until mixture is pale and fluffy, about 4 minutes. Blend in egg yolks (setting egg whites aside in a small bowl). With the mixer set on low speed, slowly pour in flour and mix until combined (mixture will seem dry at first but will start to come together). Form dough into a ball, cover with plastic wrap and refrigerate for 30 minutes. Whisk egg whites with 2 teaspoons water until frothy. Place chopped pistachios in a small bowl. Remove cookie dough from refrigerator and scoop dough up 1 tablespoon at a time and shape into balls. Drop each ball into egg white mixture and toss to evenly coat, then immediately transfer to bowl with chopped pistachios and roll to evenly coat sides and bottom with pistachios (I just left a circle on top uncoated for indenting). Transfer cookie dough balls to Silpat or parchment paper lined baking sheets (fitting 15 per sheet). Using your thumb, make an indentation in the center of each cookie and fill each indentation with a heaping 1/2 tsp of jam. Bake in a preheated oven 14-16 minutes. Allow to rest on a baking dish several minutes before transferring to a wire rack to cool. Cool cookies then fill a piping bag or small Ziploc bag with melted chocolate and cut a small tip off the corner and drizzle with melted chocolate. Store cookies in an airtight container.
See you next week for more Christmas recipes.

title: Greensboro kicks off Whoville, 2 weekends still to come
author: KONNER METZ kmetz@chespub.com
content:
Greensboro kicks off Whoville, 2 weekends still to come

 December 4, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: KONNER METZ kmetz@chespub.com | Section: Local News 
 
 296
 Words 

 Read News Document

 GREENSBORO — A popular holiday attraction for families and children of all ages kicked off last weekend in Greensboro. The town's sixth annual Whoville Village Holiday Park opened Friday at the Greensboro Volunteer Fire Company Fair Grounds.The annual event, inspired by Dr. Seuss' fictional town, features activities for all ages, decorations, light displays and photo opportunities with the Grinch.
Whoville continues during the next two weekends, open Dec. 6-7 and Dec. 13-14. Admission is free.
The town requests $5 parking donations, though donations are not required. Parking revenue is split between the Greensboro Volunteer Fire Company and next year's Whoville efforts.
Amanda Weaver, Greensboro's community programs coordinator, said around 1,500 people attended Whoville last weekend.
"The first weekend was slower than (it has been) historically," Weaver said. She said that's partly due to the town opening the attraction in November for the first time ever.
Sunday was a special night for Greensboro residents, in which 150 town residents enjoyed Whoville without the usual "commotion" and packed crowd.
"We loved that," Weaver said. "They all had a great time."
Typically, there are 2,000 to 3,000 attendees per day, according to Weaver. She said the town is expecting a similar turnout looking toward this weekend.
Around 12 student volunteers from the local schools chipped in to make opening weekend a success, Weaver said. They will continue helping throughout the upcoming weekends.
This Friday, Saint Paul's United Methodist Church Pastor Bonnie Shively will accept her nomination as Whoville's honorary mayor.
Weaver said on Dec. 11, Whoville will have its sensory night. Loud music and flashing lights will be minimized to accommodate visitors with sensory sensitivities, and the trails will be designed for accessibility.
Reservations for sensory night can be made by calling Greensboro Town Hall at 410-482-6222. The Whoville attraction runs 5 p.m. to 8 p.m. on all nights.

title: St. Michaels Shop with a Cop event brings holiday gifts a few weeks early
author: Maggie Trovato
content:
St. Michaels Shop with a Cop event brings holiday gifts a few weeks early

 December 4, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Maggie Trovato | Section: Local News 
 
 420
 Words 

 Read News Document

 EASTON — In a winding line at register 10, St. Michaels' youngest residents snacked on popcorn and waited for their new toys, clothes, beauty supplies and other goods to be scanned through and wrapped up.During the St. Michaels Police Department's Shop with a Cop event Monday evening at the Target in Easton, 44 kids were able to each pick out $100 worth of anything they wanted.
As children scanned the aisles for the coolest toys and cutest pajamas, St. Michaels Police Chief Jeffrey Oswald and Officer Kristian Bailey ambled the store, checking in on families and making sure things ran smoothly. Before shopping was in full swing, Oswald said he and Bailey would help out a little bit in the shopping process, but would try to stay out of the way.
"And let them have a little bit of fun," he said.
On Thursday, the children's picks will be presented to them during a party in front of the police station, complete with Santa, hot cocoa, a DJ and the entire police department crew.
Oswald said these events "create a great excuse to come together."
"It's not all about gifts," he said. "It's about bonding with the police officers. Getting to know them by their name instead of just police, solely. You know, we're individuals and we care. So that's why we do it."
Tiffany Sweeney, the department's administrative assistant, said the St. Michaels community really invests in the program to get gifts to kids in town. This year, 44 children registered.
"It's a good amount of kids for our small town," Sweeney said.
Jimmy Grimley, 4, came to the Target Monday evening with hopes of finding the "better t-rex ever." By the time he got to the register, Grimley had multiple dinosaur toys in his cart.
Sisters Summer and Sophia Smith filled their carts with books, makeup, clothes and skin care products. The 12- and 14-year olds, respectively, participated in Shop with a Cop last year. Sophia said they decided to participate again because it's fun.
Heather Beecher, the mother of 11-year-old Sophia Showacre, called the event "a blessing."
"I'm thankful," she said next to her daughter's cart, which was filled with an Owala water bottle, press-on nails and other goodies.
At the end of the checkout line, volunteer Glenn Glasgow donned a Santa hat as he put colorful gift bags into carts so that the gifts could be picked up and taken to the police station for Thursday's party. This being his second year volunteering, Glasgow said it was nice to participate. He called it a "great, feel-good experience."

title: With countdown to Christmas on, Christmas Angels garner support
author: ANDREA GRABENSTEIN agrabenstien@chespub.com
content:
With countdown to Christmas on, Christmas Angels garner support

 December 5, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: ANDREA GRABENSTEIN agrabenstien@chespub.com | Section: News 
 
 400
 Words 

 Read News Document

 QUEEN ANNE'S COUNTY — There is still time to be part of the Christmas magic to ensure new toys and goods for local children through the QAC Christmas Angels this season.Local nonprofit QAC Christmas Angels works year round to ensure every child in Queen Anne's County has a merry Christmas and upcoming community events invite everyone to once again be part of the magic.
In its fifth year of spreading holiday joy, QAC Christmas Angels currently serves 1,500 county children and is continually growing, providing not only clothing and toys, but essentials such as hygiene kits, blankets and pillows to support families in the community that are going without due to circumstances beyond their control, organizer Linda Austin said.
Community collaboration has ensured the success for the QAC Christmas Angels for the holiday season and this year is no different, including upcoming SantaCon 2024 festivities.
While it's not a reindeer, El Jefe Mexican Kitchen/Tequila Bar will be home to a mechanical bull Dec. 7 from 5 p.m. to 10 p.m., $5 or a new toy donation will provide the opportunity to see how long you can hang on for a wild ride.
An escape room inviting everyone to "save Christmas" will take place at Kent Island Resort Dec. 12. Starting at 5:30 p.m., the evening includes dinner, a glass of champagne, dessert, a cash bar and a unique Christmas themed escape room.
Tickets are $75 per person or $65 per person with a table of eight and more information can be found at shoreupdate.com/savechristmas.
All designated proceeds will go toward QAC Christmas Angels to benefit county children.
QAC Christmas Angels falls under Queen Anne's Advocates for Youth, and with a 100% volunteer crew that operates out of a donated space, it is immensely proud of having no overhead, Austin said.
"Every dollar goes to the kids," she said.
QAC Christmas Angels are continuously collecting new goods and seeking volunteers and sponsorships to get a head start on next year's planning, Austin added.
Monetary contributions, no matter how small, are greatly appreciated. Amazon Wishlist and Paypal donation links are available through the QAC Christmas Angel Facebook page.
The QAC Christmas Angels were recently presented with a $15,000 donation from the county commissioners, who lauded the nonprofit for its dedication.
"We have seen tremendous support from the community," Austin said.
More information about the QAC Christmas Angels and how to get involved can be found by contacting Austin at 410 829-3136 or contacting linda.austin@longandfoster.com.

title: Frosty’s Holiday Village brings holiday cheer to Easton
author: Veronica Fernandez-Alvarado
content:
Frosty’s Holiday Village brings holiday cheer to Easton

 December 7, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Veronica Fernandez-Alvarado | Section: Local News 
 
 369
 Words 

 Read News Document

 EASTON — Frosty's Holiday Village came back Friday evening at the Anchor Church bringing with it holiday cheer, family friendly activities and community engagement.Hosted by For All Seasons, a community behavioral health center, Frosty's Holiday Village is in its fourth year of providing winter festivities to the residents of the Eastern Shore.
Katie Theeke, vice president of marketing and communications at For All Seasons, said the event's mission goes beyond bringing holiday cheer to residents. The event is also meant to help lift spirits throughout the community during a time when mental health concerns grow.
"We know that the holidays can be like a really lonely time of year for many people, and we also know that for many folks too, it can be expensive to take your family out, and we wanted to just have a really fun, festive evening of connection in the community that was free for everyone and that brought people together to just enjoy a night out," Theeke said.
Theeke said the attendance of the event over the years has grown significantly. Last year there was an estimated 1,000 people in attendance. This year, the For All Season team anticipated a bigger turnout of 1,500 people.
Similar to previous years, there was a line of excited children waiting for their turn to have a professional photo with the famous Frosty and friends. They enjoyed complimentary cocoa, cider and additional winter treats as "Frosty's Winter Wonderland" played on a big screen.
Nearby, a crowd of enthusiastic families in awe of Cascading Carlos the Juggler. Adored in his iconic black shirt with flames, the award-winning juggler and Guinness World Record holder engaged with children and parents alike to take part in his performance. Sharing his love for juggling with attendees of all ages.
This year, included with the wide variety of activities, there was an additional 20 new inflatables and a second holiday movie for all to enjoy.
Presenting sponsors include The St. John Foundation and Willow Construction. Additional sponsors include Willow Construction, St. John's Foundation, Jacob Sloan Foundation, Tri Gas and Oil/Pep, Parker Counts, Hearthstone, Talbot County Health Department, Construction Services & Supply, Inc., Chesapeake Building Components, La De Da!, Grauls Market, Julianne Rosela Foundation, Mid-South Audio, and Creative Training Solutions.

title: A Mission Impossible Thanksgiving accomplished in Easton
author: Veronica Fernandez-Alvarado
content:
A Mission Impossible Thanksgiving accomplished in Easton

 December 7, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Veronica Fernandez-Alvarado | Section: News 
 
 643
 Words 

 Read News Document

 EASTON — Six days before Thanksgiving, Sandra Adams and Amanda Dow took it upon themselves to organize and execute a dinner for those in need. With help from local organizations and dozens of volunteers, they were able to accomplish something beyond their expectations.In the course of less than a week, Adams and Dow organized a full Thanksgiving dinner serving over 70 meals to families from the Eastern Shore and gave out essential goods such as winter coats and hygiene products.
For Adams, helping those in need is not a new experience. She began the nonprofit Friends Helping Friends Network based on her experiences of being a single mom and her struggles of trying to make ends meet for her family.
"No matter how hard I worked, I never made enough money, and I was always told that I made too much money, even though I knew I didn't and I've ended up homeless several times myself, and just different experiences of struggling," Adams said.
Dow said she would help Adams during previous events hosted by Friends Helping Friends Network and said Adams is the kind of person who always finds a way to assist the people around her, whether it be helping someone find temporary housing or assisting in resume reviews for those who need work.
For Dow, working with Adams on this dinner reminded her of the work she did growing up, when her parents had a nonprofit. When Adams started talking about a potential Thanksgiving event for the community, Dow was more than eager to help make it happen.
"We had decided that no matter what, we were going to do something, we just weren't quite sure what that would look like," Dow said. "And the owners of the Spaghetti House were gracious enough to come back and say, 'You know what, it can't hurt to help. So you guys, do your thing, make sure you're safe.'"
According to Dow, by the time Spaghetti House approved the use of their venue, Dow and Adams had only six days to make the dinner happen. They asked business owners in the community to donate as much as they could but had low expectations for turnout due to the short timeline.
What none of them expected was the rush of community support they received to make the event happen.
Food donations began to come in from Teddy Bear Fresh, Legal Assets, Blu Miles Seafood and Grill, Hot Off The Coals and Darnell's Grill and Catering, who donated several cooked turkeys.
The amount of food donated allowed them to go beyond their plans of a simple meal. Adams and Dow were able to give attendees a feast.
Additionally, Tahlia Pabon, owner of Tahlia's Virtual Solutions, LLC and co-host of the event, offered attendees with free resume services.
Adams said through donations they were also able to provide coats, scarves and other necessities.
When Thursday evening finally came, Adams said the venue was packed with over 40 volunteers and dozens of families, each enjoying their meals while the room filled with music provided by DJ Jason Young.
Dow said attendees came with expectations of a meal and left with filled stomachs, bags of donated food, coats and other necessities for long-term care.
Beyond the event, she plans to continue care for those who need it and encourages anyone who would like to volunteer to contact her on Facebook and to come with an open mind and heart.
"We never know what everyone is going through. And I just ask that people look in other people's eyes and see their heart and know that even if people are stuck or homeless, they need a hand up," Adams said. "(Friends Helping Friends Network's) motto is 'taking those around us to help those around us,' because it's not just about me helping them, it's about all of us jumping on board to lift up that hand and that's what we plan on doing."

title: Family fights Dunkirk cemetery's plan to move plot
author: MARTY MADDEN mmadden@somdnews.com
content:
Family fights Dunkirk cemetery's plan to move plot

 December 10, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: MARTY MADDEN mmadden@somdnews.com | Section: State News 
 
 508
 Words 

 Read News Document

 According to her daughter, it was in 1989 that Gloria Moseley purchased two plots at Dunkirk's Southern Memorial Gardens. It was supposed to be a modest resting place in a quiet rural setting.Laura Dodgson, Moseley's daughter who now lives in North Carolina, said her sister died in 1994 and her brother died four years later. Urns containing their ashes were buried side-by-side on the site.
Gloria Moseley died in 2002 and eight years later her husband, Robert, passed. Both were laid to rest at the family gravesite.
Southern Memorial Gardens has had different owners since 1989, when the Moseleys purchased the plots.
Now the cemetery owners say mistakes have been made. Their solution has brought distress to the family.
In a letter to Southern Maryland News, Dodgson said she received a phone call from cemetery officials back in September.
"They stated that my family had been buried in the wrong plot and that they would have to be dug up and moved," Dodgson wrote.
During a phone conversation with Dodgson after the letter was received, Southern Maryland News learned cemetery officials, via mail, told her to sign papers for moving the family members to another location.
"I don't want them moved," Dodgson said.
When Southern Maryland News contacted the cemetery about the situation, the employee answering the phone provided contact information for the business's attorney, Kevin Vitelli.
"It happens at every cemetery," Vitelli said of the Moseley family's situation. "Mistakes were made in 1989. We're just trying to make it right."
Vitelli, whose law practice is based in Pennsylvania, said the relocation of the family's plot would be done at no additional cost.
The local cemetery has a well-documented history of problems.
Nearly 20 years ago, fraudulent activity on the part of former owner, Larry Deffenbaugh, came to light after a Maryland State Police investigation. Deffenbaugh was later convicted of defrauding over 500 people out of funeral and memorial items.
He had entered an Alford plea, which is not an admission of guilt, but an acknowledgment that prosecutors have evidence to support a charge, received a 15-year suspended sentence and ordered to pay restitution to the victims.
Deffenbaugh's story then gets more convoluted, as he was summoned back to court for a violation of probation hearing but failed to appear. Apparently not wishing to go to prison, Deffenbaugh reportedly fell off a fishing boat. He was, however, recaptured in 2010 and sent to prison.
Dodgson said her late sister's daughter, Pam, filed court papers to have her mother's urn removed from the cemetery and given over to her. Dodgson and another family member confirmed that the urn was flooded with water.
Dodgson said she fears the disturbance of the plot could result in the collapse of the vaults where her parents' coffins are laid.
The family has been in contact with attorneys for a possible breech of contract and gross negligence lawsuit.
"There were some mistakes made by prior owners," Vitelli said of the Southern Memorial Gardens situation. "We have to correct those mistakes."
The attorney added that while aggrieved plot owners have been urged to file suit, "nobody has filed any action against the cemetery."

title: Residents brave the cold for Denton Holiday Parade
author: Maggie Trovato
content:
Residents brave the cold for Denton Holiday Parade

 December 11, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Maggie Trovato | Section: Local News 
 
 461
 Words 

 Read News Document

 DENTON — Bundled up in coats, gloves, hats, scarves — and even blankets — Caroline County residents braved the cold and the wind to watch the town's annual holiday parade.At the start of the parade on Thursday, the weather was 31 degrees Fahrenheit but felt like 12 degrees.
As the wind put a sway to the colorful string lights above Market Street, John Bell and Linda Allen-Bell waited for the parade to begin. The two, wrapped in blankets, didn't want to miss the parade after missing it last year. Allen-Bell said they love small town parades.
Down the street, Rachel Tull stood with her family, trying to stay warm. She said that the kids were most excited for the candy that would soon be tossed from parade floats. Tull, on the other hand, was most excited for the meatloaf she had waiting for them at home.
As attendees waited for floats to glide down the street, some checked out the vendors at the corner of Market and Third streets.
It was Ridgely resident Haley Wondrash's first year selling the cups she makes at the parade. She said she makes her cups, which have different designs on them, for different people to express themselves. There's a cup for everyone, she explained, from sports lovers to Taylor Swift fans.
"I make a lot of Taylor Swift cups for all the Taylor Swift girlies out there," she said.
JP Morris, who attended the parade with his two sisters and his parents, was most excited for the candy that parade participants toss to the crowds. He, along with other children at the parade, cleaned up the candy from the sidewalks as floats made their way down Market Street.
Morris said he wasn't too cold. His mom, Meagan Morris, said the family of five has spent their last couple Christmases in Maine, "so this ain't nothing," she said, laughing.
Once the parade began, attendees heard local marching bands play Christmas music, watched bright red firetrucks and pickup trucks decorated in lights make their way down the street, and kept their eyes open for Santa and Mrs. Claus, who closed out the parade.
A variety of creative floats were in attendance this year, from the 4-H float blasting fake snow into the air to the Caroline County GOP float toting a cardboard cutout of President-elect Donald Trump standing next to a decorated Christmas tree.
Kyra Ringgold took her son Kyro, 3, to the parade for the first time this year. Seeing Santa and getting candy and chocolate was Kryo's favorite part of the experience.
After Santa and Mrs. Claus made their way down the street, people gathered in front of the courthouse for the Lighting of the Green. A drumroll slowly ushered in the turning on of green and red lights on the trees outside the courthouse.

 EASTON — Downtown Easton buzzed with anticipation Saturday evening as people — some decked out in Christmas-themed gear — waited for the town's annual holiday parade to begin.Although it was dark out, colorful lights shaped like candy canes and candles helped light up the night before the vibrant, festive floats arrived. The parade, which brought music and candy to Harrison and Washington streets, was preceded by a visit from Santa and a tree lighting at Thompson Park.

Mayor Megan Cook said that one of the best parts of living in a small town is events like these that bring the community together.
"The parade, to me, is one of the highlights of the whole year," she said.
Cynthia Spence has been coming to the parade for a about five years now with her daughter Sofia, 7, and now her daughter Nevaeh, 4. She said they return because her children like watching the parade.
"They like seeing different floats and ..."
"Don't forget the candy," Sofia jumped in as her mother spoke.

Their mother Jess Taylor said that although they normally attend St. Michaels' parade every year, they came to Easton's parade to support Ella this year.
From Easton school marching bands to a kazoo choir, music filled the air at Easton's Holiday Parade. Floats, vintage cars and firetrucks traveled slowly along the parade route as parade participants on foot weaved in between them, handing out candy and other small items.

title: Easton Elks Veterans Affairs Committee hosts a USO dance
author: Veronica Fernandez-Alvarado
content:
Easton Elks Veterans Affairs Committee hosts a USO dance

 December 12, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Veronica Fernandez-Alvarado | Section: Local News 
 
 525
 Words 

 Read News Document

 EASTON — On Saturday evening, Bridget O'Brien, 2024 Miss Maryland, opened the dance floor at Easton Elks Lodge by singing the "Star Spangled Banner." Couples, of all ages, gathered on the dance floor under USO military-themed decorations for a benefit in honor of disabled veterans.In an effort to provide continued care for disabled veterans at Pleasant Day Adult Day Care in Cambridge, the Easton Elks 1622 Veterans Affairs Committee hosted a USO event in an effort to raise funds for disabled veterans. Over a hundred people attended the event that included dancing, food, a silent auction and a raffle.
Michael Feehley, chair of the 1622 Veterans Affairs Committee and a lead planner for the event, said the committee believes in doing what they can to provide for those veterans in need and this event was a way to raise funds for veterans that are often overlooked.
"We believe in taking care of veterans, the veterans that use services at Pleasant Day, whether it's just for two meals, whether it's for medications, whether it's to meet with medical people, whether it's transportation to their medical appointments, they're only funded for two days a week through (Veteran Affairs), we feel it's necessary to fund those guys for five days," Feehley said.
Throughout the event, veterans were honored by attendees and volunteers but also by potential new recruits. Feehley said Easton High School's Navy Junior Reserve Officers' Training Corps members assisted in functions such as drawing tickets, helping people to their seats and any assistance needed including putting away chairs at the end of the evening.
Tom Carlson, Vietnam veteran and member of the Easton Elks 1622 Veterans Affairs Committee, said the event provided him the opportunity to be around more veterans and talk about their experiences between enjoying the music and dancing.
Carlson said he was surprised by the enjoyment of the guests when it came to the music being played. Guests of a variety of ages were in attendance that evening singing along to songs of Carlson's youth and flooding the dance floor.
"It wasn't just people in their 60s and 70s and 80s. There were a lot of people in their 20s and 30s, and they had a great time too," Carlson said. "It's amazing that some of these youngsters really knew the music. They know our songs that we grew up with."
Feehley said he was proud of the ability to organize an event to honor veterans in the area, and he advises anyone who comes across a veteran to take the time to honor them even in the smallest ways.
"When you see that Army hat or the Coast Guard bumper sticker on the back of a car, or anything that says, 'Hey, I was in the service,' say, 'Thank you for your service.'"
"Because that veteran, the person who wears that hat, or the person who drives that car, they gave an awful lot of themselves," Feehley said. "They took time away from their families, away from home, in some but not all cases, they put themselves in danger, so you and I can do what we do today, and who are we not to give back to those people."

title: Rescue Fire Company Train Garden celebrates 90 years
author: MAGGIE TROVATO mtrovato@chespub.com
content:
Rescue Fire Company Train Garden celebrates 90 years

 December 12, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: MAGGIE TROVATO mtrovato@chespub.com | Section: Local News 
 
 309
 Words 

 Read News Document

 CAMBRIDGE —Rescue Fire Company Train Garden Chairman Gary Hickman's father was visiting the train garden on Gay Street the day of the Pearl Harbor attack in 1941."He was just here that day as a child," Hickman said.
Eighty-three years later, the RFC Train Garden — the longest continually running train garden in the country — is celebrating its 90th anniversary.
Hickman said this milestone is so important because "the gentlemen back in 1934 had the forethought to be able to put this together for the community and the children of the community."
Hickman remembers coming to the train garden as a kid. He said he loved trains as a child.
"I used to come here as many times as I could during the Christmas season when it was open," he said.
That love never drifted for Hickman, who plans to continue on with his role as chairman for as long as he can.
On a Monday evening, families slowly made their way in and out of the old City Hall on Gay Street, where the train garden is located. Quaid Windsor, 4, walked around the train garden with his parents as he snacked on popcorn. He said he liked the trains the most.
Hickman said support from the local business community makes it possible for the train garden to keep chugging along.
"When I was growing up as a kid, it was a hobby, and it was an affordable hobby," Hickman said. "And now things are so expensive. ... And all of these sponsors re-sponsor us every year and they give us money so we can continually change and add things and buy new engines and upgrade things as we go along."
Hickman said that with continued volunteer support from the fire company, he sees the train garden making it to the 100-year mark in another decade.
"As long as I'm around, we're going to continue," he said.

The town held their annual Christmas event, Light up the Park, sponsored by Molly's and Dixon Valve, drawing nearly 100 people this year.Through the archway made of colorful gifts with ribbons creatively put together, attendees were treated to a Santa wearing floaties, next to a boat of Christmas lights, some reindeer, a gingerbread man, multiple light displays, a fire to stave off that winter chill, and plenty of family activities.
In addition to lighting up a 20-foot Christmas tree, Council member Sarah Merrell noted they had Santa escorted by the Galena Volunteer Fire Department, children's coloring activities and a few vendors, all while the Galena Lions Club offered hot chocolate and cookies.
At 7 p.m., under the tent, they had their fourth movie night of the year, playing the 2000 family/comedy "How the Grinch Stole Christmas," starring Jim Carey.
Mayor John Carroll said movie night has been growing in popularity, and the screen they purchased with American Rescue Funds money, has turned out to be a good community investment.
And he was pleased with the annual Christmas event overall, growing too big to contain at their previous location.
Over the years, they held the event at Town Hall, he noted, but after 100 kids showed up, they felt the park was the best way to expand it and allow the kids to have space enough to play.
Next year, Carroll said, they are going to try to develop squares around the whole park for families to decorate.
"Hopefully we can grow each year and make this a nice tradition," Carroll said, thanking volunteers, the community, the fire department and their sponsors for making all this possible.

author: ANDREA GRABENSTEIN agrabenstein@chespub.com
content:
Garden Club 'decks the halls' in Centreville

 December 13, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: ANDREA GRABENSTEIN agrabenstein@chespub.com | Section: Entertainment 
 
 429
 Words 

 Read News Document

 The festive scents of seasonal pine and holly filled American Legion Jeff Davis Post 18 as the Queen Anne's County Garden Club Members prepared the town with festive cheer Dec. 5.The long-standing annual decorating is traditionally the Thursday before the Centreville Christmas parade, according to club president Laura Blaylock.
"This is the highlight of the year," she said, and is a favorite among all members who, with a potluck breakfast and lunch, and many of whom in yuletide sweaters, spend all day together preparing.
Throughout the hall, stations were set up for wreaths, swag, garland, bows, and putting the final touches on holiday magic to decorate Centreville in a glow of greenery.
Members also designed over 100 floral arrangements to be hand delivered to hospice care and home bodies in need of Christmas cheer.
"It is our way of getting in the Christmas spirit and getting others in the Christmas spirit as well, " Blaylock said.
Member Jane Chambers, of Kent Island, has been a garden club member for about 50 years and said her favorite part is seeing the finished product displayed throughout the season "and it's a fun group that does good for the community," she said.
With help from local department staff, wreaths, garland, and long lines of blooming swag adorned historic aspects all through town, including the Queen Anne's County Library, Shore United Bank, the Tucker House, the Historic Courthouse, and Chesterfield Cemetery.
From wreath decoration design to floral arraignments, "It never ceases to amaze me the amount of creativity from everyone," Club Vice President Robin Lanham said.
During Arbor Day, the club celebrated its 90th anniversary with a tree planting honoring first responders at the Fallen Heroes Memorial at Route 18 Park in Centreville.
The club recently decorated crab pots to create a crab tree unique to Queen Anne's County and pay tribute to the watermen and preside over the Annapolis state house.
"It made quite a splash, people loved it," club treasurer Paula Kumar.
The object of the garden club is to stimulate the love of gardening, to aid in the protection of native plants and birds, to encourage civic planting and beautification, and to teach children to love and care for all growing things, according to Blaylock
Covering a wide spectrum of horticulture topics including guest speakers and field trips, the club is always seeking new members and anyone interested in not just gardening but local pollinators, native plants, floral design or seeking to enhance their green thumb.
Queen Anne's County Garden Club is part of the Federated Garden Clubs of Maryland Inc. District 1.
More information can be found by contacting Blaylock at laura.blaylock804@gmail.com.

title: Tides of Grace toy drive creates holiday magic
author: ANDREA GRABENSTIEN agrabenstein@chespub.com
content:
Tides of Grace toy drive creates holiday magic

 December 13, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: ANDREA GRABENSTIEN agrabenstein@chespub.com | Section: Local News 
 
 415
 Words 

 Read News Document

 STEVENSVILLE — While children lay dreaming of visions of sugar plum fairies, parents made their way to the Edge Arena bright and early to select toys as part of Tides of Grace fifth annual Christmas Magic Toy Drive Dec. 7.The area filled with community donated gently used toys as Volunteers welcomed parents and guardians as they selected community-donated gently used toys as part of Tides of Grace's mission to ensure every child has something during the holidays.
The Christmas Magic Toy Drive began in 2020 with a group of moms wanting to spread holiday cheer, and it has grown tremendously over the years, helping 100 children in 2020 and over 600 children in 2023, according to Tides of Grace executive director Leann Rhodes.
Now bigger than ever, 500 families with over 1,000 individual children were registered this year.
At opening, 40 parents were allowed in the arena at a time with 15 minutes to select six toys per child and one large item per family.
After 9:30 a.m., the floor was opened for anyone to take anything that was left.
"No toy gets left behind," Rhodes said.
Generous community support and collaboration continually makes the event what it is, Rhodes said.
Skillfully organized by gender and age group, dedicated volunteers held a pajama party all through the night to unload and sort toys, and prepare the arena.
The toy drive also received immense support for its Amazon Wishlist to provide gifts for teens, who are often the most difficult to shop for.
Chestertown mother of two Megan Ingledue drove an hour to Stevensville to ensure everyone her family gets something during the hard times.
"We couldn't ask for something better," she said.
Members of Tides of Grace provide hope and kindness and understand the hardship for families who don't know how they will provide during what is supposed to be the happiest time of the year.
For families that are struggling, the uncertainties about how to provide can put a significant damper on what is supposed to be the happiest time of the year.
Seeing the joy on parents' faces is what it's all about for Tides of Grace Board member Mary Himmel has been with the nonprofit since its inception.
Himmel considered the annual Christmas Magic Toy Drive, "the best day of the year" that helps alleviate concerns for struggling parents who don't know how they will provide Christmas gifts.
"When they leave here, it's like the weight of the world is lifted," Himmel said.
More information about Tides of Grace including volunteer opportunities can be found at tidesofgraceinc.org.

 I concur with the letter to the editor in the Dec. 7-8 edition of the Star Dem, entitled, "Carrier did stellar job," by Joan Wetmore.Andre Thurman delivered the newspaper to my home for more than five years, and was the best newspaper delivery person that I can remember, (and I'm in my 80s).
I shall quote words from his Christmas note, received early December.
"It's hard to say goodbye.
If I could turn back time.
If I could just find a way.
If I could do it again.
Then it would be me delivering your
paper each and every day."
It is also my Christmas wish that Andre would again be delivering my Star Dem newspaper.
Now the paper gets to my community mailbox usually after 5 p.m., as it's the last stop on the postal route. I retrieve it the following morning. Not a bad walk to the mailbox when the weather is good, but not so in a cold and windy rain.
Please let Mr. Thurman deliver the Star Dem to my home. Far better than using the postal service!

Easton

title: Cemetery Christmas wreaths honors veterans, military's fallen
author: Michael Reid mreid@somdnews.com
content:
Cemetery Christmas wreaths honors veterans, military's fallen

 December 14, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Michael Reid mreid@somdnews.com | Section: News 
 
 647
 Words 

 Read News Document

 Martha Hyde and her father honored all those who served in military conflicts, while Larry Hill will spend some time thinking about his comrades.The remembrances were part of the 18th annual Wreaths Across America, took place at churches, cemeteries and memorials across Maryland on Saturday, Dec. 14.
At participating cemeteries, relatives of those interred and the general public were invited to lay a wreath at the site of each veteran, and the latter were encouraged to say the veteran's name and learn about their service.
"We encourage young families and kids to come out and say the names of these service members, learn their history, take time to actually learn about those people who are actually in your community and their families," Wreaths Across America Director of Communications Amber Caron said. "It's a time where it's important to take your family and pause and say 'Thank you' to our service members who keep us all free and able to celebrate how we choose in this country."
Mt. Zion United Methodist Church in Mechanicsville participated in the event for the fourth year.
"It's a busy time of the year; I know people are off doing other things," said Larry Hill, who is a member of the United Methodist Men's Group that coordinates and sponsors the event for the church, "but this is an opportunity to recognize the veterans at Christmas."
The event at the Mechanicsville church featured guest speaker Rear Adm. John Lemmon. A bugler played Taps" while Hill read the names of the 75 veterans interred in the cemetery, which go "all the way back to the Civil War, both sides of the Civil War," Hill said.
In Pomfret, St. Joseph Catholic Church held a mas, followed by the event. Duncan S. Moore will play the national anthem on the bagpipes, parishioner Karen Kleyle will read "A Soldier's Poem" and guest speakers will be the Rev. Harry Stokes and La Plata American Legion Post 82 Commander and retired Chief Master Sgt. Jamie Zayas, who had a 37-year military career.
"Women parishioners were saying prayers during November, which the Catholic Church reserves that month for the Holy Souls in Purgatory, and that's when we noticed how many veterans were buried there," St. Joseph Catholic Church Wreaths Across America Coordinator Tammy Hilburn said of the approximately 100 veterans. "And we felt that it had to be addressed, so that set the whole event in motion."
All Saints Episcopal Church is Sunderland held its third Wreaths Across America event.
Bugler Eric Pfeiffer played "Taps," Malinda Markland sang the anthem and a moment of silence was held across the church's Sunderland campus before the laying of 38 wreaths.
"I just think it's a very spiritual ceremony as well and it's a way to not only reflect on the veterans and express gratitude for those that are buried in our cemetery, but also express gratitude to those veterans that are still living and serving," said All Saints Wreaths Across America Coordinator Martha Hyde, who added she has a couple of generations of relatives interred in the cemetery.
Also attending was Hyde's 99-year-old father, Gordon Grahame, who was drafted as an 18-year-old and served as a SeaBee in Okinawa, Japan.
Caron said 4,909 participating locations nationwide will be holding Wreaths Across America events, an increase of 740 over last year, with about a million volunteers.
According to the Wreaths Across America website, Merrill Worcester donated surplus wreaths from his Maine-based Worcester Wreath Company to Arlington National Cemetery beginning in 1992 as a way of saying thanks to veterans. In 2005, a photo of wreaths on tombstones after a snowfall at the cemetery went viral and Wreaths Across America began as a nonprofit in 2007.
"As a veteran I think we owe it to those who served before us," said Hill, who was drafted in 1972 and spent three years in the Army, including 15 months in Germany.
For more information on Wreaths Across America, go to www.wreathsacrossamerica.org.

11th annual Shop with a Hero builds lasting connections

 STEVENSVILLE — Community children fostered relationships with local first responders while picking up the perfect gift during the Kent Island Optimist Club's 11th annual Shop with a Hero event at Stevensville Target Dec. 14.Partnering one-on-one with a police officer or firefighter from surrounding agencies, over 60 children were selected this year to participate in the shopping extravaganza through recommendations from local schools.
Each child was provided $200 to spend as they pleased for everyone on their Christmas list, and creating unforgettable memories, the 11th annual day once again filled with smiles, laughter, and the true spirit of the season to connect the community.
Understanding, for most people, the only interaction they get with police is when something bad happens, and Shop with a Hero aims to build positive experiences and foster relationships between youth and see first responders in the right light, according to Kent Island Optimist Club President Jennie Hager.
The day provides festive spirit for children who might not otherwise be able to, alongside the community, for children, their families, and local first responders. Shop with a Hero has grown exponentially over the years and the group couldn't be more thrilled to be able to provide for local children, Hager said.
Along with generous community donations, the Optimist Club raises money all year round to completely fund the shopping expedition, including a lip sync battle at Cult Classic Brewing company in October, she said.
Back at American Legion 278, heroes, kids, families and the community enjoyed a hearty breakfast and photos with Santa and Mrs. Claus.
Participating hero organizations included the Queen Anne's County Department of the Sheriff, Maryland Transportation Authority, Queenstown Fire Department, Kent Island Fire Department, Maryland State Police, Maryland Transportation Authority Police, Centreville Police Department, Greenbelt Police Department, Maryland Department of Natural Resources,, QAC Department of Emergency Services, Grasonville Volunteer Fire Department, United Communities Volunteer Fire Department.
Also in attendance was the Kingsman Motorcycle Club, ready to step in and help cover any shopping costs needed.
"It's all about the kids," biker Bobby Deal said.
The likeminded community and youth focused mission of the American Legion provides the hall space and breakfast and countywide volunteers from various organizations lend hand in wrapping all the goodies.
"Everyone just jumps in, it's a total community effort," Hager said, "It never ceases to amaze me, it's the community coming together."

title: Cambridge PD provides holiday cheer with Shop with a Cop
author: Veronica Fernandez-Alvarado
content:
Cambridge PD provides holiday cheer with Shop with a Cop

 December 16, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Veronica Fernandez-Alvarado | Section: Local News 
 
 425
 Words 

 Read News Document

 CAMBRIDGE — On Saturday afternoon, police sirens rang as dozens of children were escorted by Cambridge police to Walmart for the annual Shop with a Cop event.The children were met with warm welcomes from police officers before they raced inside for this holiday tradition.
Shop with a Cop provides the opportunity for underprivileged children in the community to spend quality time with local police officers and purchase Christmas presents.
Sergeant Antoine Patton from the Cambridge Police Department, said this event began in 2015 in an effort to help families throughout the area during the holiday season.
"We realized that in today's economy that everyone doesn't have the funds, and we as a police department here, wanted to make sure that we could help as many families as possible," Patton said. "We wanted to see as many smiling kids on Christmas as we possibly could."
Through a live raffle system, families and loved ones of local children apply to have the children participate. Each drawing is broadcast on Facebook Live.
After names are picked, Patton calls the families to let them know their child has won. Then, a small group leaves the station to pick the children up from their homes and take them to Walmart.
Each child then gets to spend $100 on "anything of their choosing." This year 30 children were chosen during the raffle.
According to Patton, this is the first year that all funds for the event were entirely made available through donations. Patton said several organizations, including Paul Davis Restoration of Delmarva, The Lions Club, the Friendship Methodist Church of Aireys, and private donations provided funds for gifts.
On Saturday, the children were split into small groups and assigned a police officer, who guided them through the toy aisles. With the help of the officers, children choose toys from Nerf guns to pink tea sets.
Lydia Travers, a parent of a Shop with a Cop winner, said her mother sent her son Zyonn's name into the Shop with a Cop raffle and they were lucky enough to be chosen.
According to Travers, this event allows the community to come together and help each other.
Patton said the children aren't the only ones benefitting from Shop with a Cop. Police officers have shared positive experiences with the children outside of the event.
"It helps us out tremendously, because the children get to see us doing something fun and positive," Patton said. "And these children don't forget. I have children that we took maybe three or four years ago, and they still remember me, say, 'Hey Mom, that's the guy took us Christmas shopping.'"

title: Garden Club 'decks the halls' in Centreville
author: ANDREA GRABENSTEIN agrabenstein@chespub.com
content:
Garden Club 'decks the halls' in Centreville

 December 17, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: ANDREA GRABENSTEIN agrabenstein@chespub.com | Section: Local News 
 
 430
 Words 

 Read News Document

 CENTREVILLE — The festive scents of seasonal pine and holly filled American Legion Jeff Davis Post 18 as the Queen Anne's County Garden Club Members prepared the town with festive cheer Dec. 5.The long-standing annual decorating is traditionally the Thursday before the Centreville Christmas parade, according to club president Laura Blaylock.
"This is the highlight of the year," she said, and is a favorite among all members who, with a potluck breakfast and lunch, and many of whom in yuletide sweaters, spend all day together preparing.
Throughout the hall, stations were set up for wreaths, swag, garland, bows and putting the final touches on holiday magic to decorate Centreville in a glow of greenery.
Members designed over 100 floral arrangements to be hand delivered to hospice care and home bodies in need of Christmas cheer.
"It is our way of getting in the Christmas spirit and getting others in the Christmas spirit as well, " Blaylock said.
Member Jane Chambers, of Kent Island, has been a garden club member for about 50 years and said her favorite part is seeing the finished product displayed throughout the season "and it's a fun group that does good for the community," she said.
With help from local department staff, wreaths, garland, and long lines of blooming swag adorned historic aspects all through town, including the Queen Anne's County Library, Shore United Bank, the Tucker House, the Historic Courthouse, and Chesterfield Cemetery.
From wreath decoration design to floral arraignments, "It never ceases to amaze me the amount of creativity from everyone," Club Vice President Robin Lanham said.
On Arbor Day, the club celebrated its 90th anniversary with a tree planting honoring first responders at the Fallen Heroes Memorial at Route 18 Park in Centreville.
The club recently decorated crab pots to create a crab tree unique to Queen Anne's County and pay tribute to the watermen and preside over the Annapolis state house.
"It made quite a splash, people loved it," club treasurer Paula Kumar.
The object of the garden club is to stimulate the love of gardening, to aid in the protection of native plants and birds, to encourage civic planting and beautification, and to teach children to love and care for all growing things, according to Blaylock
Covering a wide spectrum of horticulture topics including guest speakers and field trips, the club is always seeking new members and anyone interested in not just gardening but local pollinators, native plants, floral design or seeking to enhance their green thumb.
Queen Anne's County Garden Club is part of the Federated Garden Clubs of Maryland Inc. District 1.
More information can be found by contacting Blaylock at laura.blaylock804@gmail.com.
