title: Talbot Street Parade brings festive cheer to St. Michaels
author: Veronica Fernandez-Alvarado
content:
Talbot Street Parade brings festive cheer to St. Michaels

 December 17, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Veronica Fernandez-Alvarado | Section: Holiday 
 
 229
 Words 

 Read News Document

 ST. MICHAELS — On Saturday morning, the streets were filled with families in holiday getup as dozens of floats made their ways through the center of the town for the Talbot Street Parade.The Talbot Street Parade is a time-honored holiday tradition in St. Michaels that includes marching bands, antique cars and boats, horses and representatives of the town's vibrant business and nonprofit community.
Ashley Russ, a parade attendee and St. Michaels native, said as a child her family would take her to the parade every year. Now as an adult with her own family, she is happy to pass down the tradition to her son.
Russ said her son most loved the fire trucks, which opened the parade, and the horses that decorated with festive tinsel, vines and reindeer horns.
Maydeen Merino, an attendee of the parade, said she enjoyed the motorcycle Santas that made an appearance and the Chesapeake Bay Retrievers and their well-dressed dogs who adorned sweaters, scarves and bandanas.
"It's a really cute community event, and I love how enthusiastic the whole town was for this parade," Merino said.
The parade is a part of a weekend-long fundraiser event known as Christmas in St. Michaels. Beginning in 1987, Christmas in St. Michaels has raised more than $1.7 million for local nonprofit organizations including Critchlow Adkins Children's Centers, St. Michaels site, St. Michaels Community Center and the St. Michaels Fire Department.

title: Remember, honor, teach: Wreaths Across America visits KI
author: ANDREA GRABENSTEIN agrabenstein@chespub.com
content:
Remember, honor, teach: Wreaths Across America visits KI

 December 17, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: ANDREA GRABENSTEIN agrabenstein@chespub.com | Section: News 
 
 478
 Words 

 Read News Document

 KENT ISLAND — On a mission to once again ensure all veteran graves are remembered and adorned in the spirit of the holiday this season, the official Wreaths Across America Convoy stopped at Kent Island American Legion 278 on Dec. 13.For 15 years, the legion has been the last stop for the convoy before it makes its final push to Arlington and takes part in the wreath laying ceremonies in Washington, D.C, said Nikki Randolph, 2nd senior vice commander of the American Legion Department of Maryland.
Arriving in Kent Island Dec. 12, the convoy was treated to dinner by the legion as well as breakfast the next morning and box lunches for the last ride together to Washington.
Over breakfast inside the American Legion 278 hall, alongside community supporters, including first responders, convoy participants were recognized and honored for their esteemed work.
The convoy is an annual parade of tractor trailers, wrapped vehicles carrying veterans and Gold Star Families, law enforcement and motorcycle riders leading an escort of wreaths to Arlington for ceremonial placement.
Starting from Maine, and traveling over 1,000 miles for eight days through 10 states and Washington, the convoy of 55 vehicles, including 14 tractor trailers, takes part in 21 ceremonial events, as many as three times a day, according to Janine Roberts, Wreaths Across America logistics law enforcement liaison.
"It's about honoring all that have served and their families," she said.
Randolph noted it is events like Wreaths Across America that showcase "a true representation of who the American Legion is and what we do. This is it. We take care of our community, we take care of our veterans. American people taking care of American people."
The Legion continually collaborates with the community, especially schools as it is important to teach children the values of what it means to be an American and respecting freedoms made possible by sacrifices made along the way, Randolph said.
With fundraisers throughout the year and tremendous community support, American Legion 278 is on a mission to put a wreath on every veteran grave in Queen Anne's County. Thus far, American Legion 278 has raised money for over 900 local veteran grave wreaths.
According to Randolph, through its help to Wreaths Across America, Post 278 has been recognized for setting the bar of service, not just in Maryland, but across the country.
"Its pretty cool that this tiny little island has such an impact on Wreaths Across America," she said.
Departing Kent Island, the convoy joined ceremonies throughout Washington for National Wreaths Across America Day 2024.
Members of the American Legion wished the convoy, now become an extended family over the years, a safe trip as they continued their mission to ensure those who have served are never forgotten.
"Our hearts ride with you," Randolph said.
Donations to support local American Legion wreaths, as well as more information about how to continually remember, honor, and teach can be found at wreathsacrossamerica.org.

title: Wreaths Across America honors veterans graves
author: Lilly Howard lhoward@chespub.com
content:
Wreaths Across America honors veterans graves

 December 17, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Lilly Howard lhoward@chespub.com | Section: State News 
 
 396
 Words 

 Read News Document

 Cecil County organizers partnered with gas station chain Sheetz helped facilitate deliveries of holiday wreathes to various cemeteries in Cecil County, including Rosebank and St. Mary Anne's, last week to be used in Wreaths Across America across the county. Wreaths Across America is an annual tribute to our nation's veterans, honoring those who served by placing a wreath on their graves around the holidays.Julia Swoboda initiated the first Wreaths Across America event in Cecil County nine years ago at St. Mary Anne's, after she attended the annual Arlington National Cemetery wreath ceremony in 2016 — where the initiative first began in 1992, and where nearly 400,000 veterans and their families are buried.
"After that, I was really inspired to come back to Cecil County and start our event," Swoboda said. "I think anyone who's done that [gone to Arlington's ceremony] really understands the impact that makes on you and then just inspires you really to see what you can do in your community."
Once Swoboda brought the initiative to St. Mary Anne's in North East, it spread across the county to other cemeteries, such as Rosebank in Rising Sun.
"It's really been a way for me to kind of stay connected to honoring the sacrifices that our community members have made," Swoboda said.
This year's Wreaths Across America theme is "live with purpose," which Swoboda says encapsulates the event perfectly for her.
"When you're there you see the people coming are not only honoring the people who have lived with purpose in our community, but they're also finding a way to be involved and honor those and integrate it in their purpose of their life," Swoboda said. "And that's something really beautiful to see in our community, especially at a time where things are really divisive. This event is something that seems to bring everyone together."
All the wreaths were placed on veterans' graves across Cecil County Saturday, Dec. 14.
"We have so many veterans who continue to worship at our church, plus those whose family members who are interred here, and those who've come before us," said St. Mary Anne's Pastor John Schaeffer.
He pointed out that the historic church cemetery holds graves of veterans who served in the Spanish American War and the Revolutionary War all the way up to the more recent Iraq War and Afghanistan War. This initiative honors all veterans throughout time, ensuring their service is never forgotten.

title: Thousands attend Christmas in Ridgely Winter Festival
author: KONNER METZ kmetz@chespub.com
content:
Thousands attend Christmas in Ridgely Winter Festival

 December 18, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: KONNER METZ kmetz@chespub.com | Section: Local News 
 
 495
 Words 

 Read News Document

 RIDGELY — Thousands braved frigid temperatures to stroll the streets of the Ridgely Saturday for its annual, award-winning Christmas in Ridgely Winter Festival.Attendees walked up and down W. Railroad Street and W. Belle Street, enjoying vendors, massive displays of holiday lights, and a wide array of activities for families and children.
Many children ice skated — some for the first time — outside of the Ridgely Town Hall, while couples young and old posed for photos underneath the town's mistletoe sign. At the other end of the festival, kids enjoyed an area full of inflatable slides, bounce houses and games.
In between the town hall and inflatables, the historic Ridgely Train Station welcomed visitors in for pictures with Santa and a Christmas tree display from the students and parent-teacher association at Ridgely Elementary School.
Garret and Pat Falcone, a couple from Chestertown, were enjoying their second trip to the festival. There was no doubt in their minds that they would come back for another year after last year's experience.
"The people. Everyone is so nice," Garret Falcone said of why he loves the event.
"I love the decorations. They're really cool," Pat Falcone said.
Ridgely Clerk-Treasurer and event organizer Stephanie Berkey said the town stuck to its usual strong suits this year, namely horse-drawn carriage rides and train rides for attendees. She said holiday characters, such as Elsa, Olaf and Buddy the Elf, were new additions to the event.
People from as far away as New Jersey and southern Virginia made the trip to Caroline County, she said. As always, Berkey's favorite aspect of the event was the smiles it brought to children.
"Seeing kids try to ice skate for the very first time, it's so much fun to see," she said. "And when you see all the parents that are taking the pictures of them having such a good time, that makes it all worth it. It's the happiness that it brings to everybody."
Around $50,000 was raised to make the Winter Festival a go, Berkey said. Keeping it a non-ticketed venture is the town's aim.
"The big thing that we've always said is that if we ever get in a position where we can't cover those costs and would have to charge, we don't want to do it any longer," Berkey said. "We want to be able to give the people of this area something they can bring their whole family to, where they can make a Christmas memory and they don't have to bring any money."
Planning for the town's marquee event in 2025 has already begun. Berkey said there may be some new offerings to keep things fresh for loyal festivalgoers.
"We are thinking that next year, we would like to try and maybe add something new, some kind of a new attraction, just to keep people interested in it," she said. "We don't want it to be stale next year. We want to still have all the charm and have everything that we have, but maybe add another attraction to it."

title: Star shines bright over Still Pond nativity scene
author: Staff Writer
content:
Star shines bright over Still Pond nativity scene

 December 20, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Staff Writer | Section: Life 
 
 363
 Words 

 Read News Document

 STILL POND — Just off Route 292, on a chilly Friday night, the star that church lay minister Justin Bitter created using welded scrap metal and an LED rope light, burned brightly in the trees. The Christmas hymns that were sung resonated with the 85 in attendance for the nativity scene beside the road.At the creche, maintained year-round by hardworking volunteers, local children dressed in robes and sandals. Telling the story of Jesus, Joseph, Mary, the wisemen, shepherds and animals, was Eddie Taylor, board member of Still Pond-Betterton Methodist Charge.
The reading of the gospel story followed by classic hymns with audience participation is a beloved tradition, now in the 10th year.
As night fell, seated atop bales of straw, attendees endured the cold sipping hot cocoa, enjoying Christmas cookies, and singing along as Taylor narrated the gospel scenes.
The story was told with Taylor's wit and affection, followed up by a hymn introducing the kid actors and actresses.
As Taylor read, "He is Christ the Lord. And, this is how you will know who he is….you will find a baby wrapped in swaddling clothes and lying in a manger," congregants sang the first verse of "Angels We Have Heard on High"; the angels of Still Pond were introduced, making their way to the manger.
During the production, Noel the donkey, Rosie and Annie the sheep, and Cookie Dough and Lollipop the goats were provided by Party Animals LLC., from Sudlersville, a company the church has relied on regularly during this event.
Owner of the company, Ashley Winterstein regretted she could not personally be there this year as this is her favorite holiday event. She was on a float with their 4-H club at Sudlersville's first annual Christmas Parade and Tree Lighting.
"Taylor is my favorite narrator," Winterstein added.
Pastor Greg Boege, replacing the late and greatly missed Pastor Bill Carroll, was pleased with how the event came together.
"Everybody did their part and we pulled it off," he said.
Boege said for those interested in a similar service, without the animals, in a more meditative, reflective atmosphere, they will hold their Christmas Eve service in Betterton at 5:30 p.m. followed by a service at the Still Pond location at 6:30 p.m.

 Making an evening merry and bright, Sudlersville started a new community tradition with its first ever community Christmas parade Dec. 13.Immediately following the parade, Sudlersville hosted its first ever tree lighting with hot chocolate at the Town Office Friday.
The tree was donated by town attorney Tom Yeager and will be located out front of the town office through the season.
With a dedication to give back to the local community, the highly successful inaugural parade was hosted by the Sudlersville Ruritan Club in partnership with the Sudlersville Volunteer Fire Department.

title: All I want for Christmas: a chimney ... and pony
author: JAMES L. SNYDER
content:
All I want for Christmas: a chimney ... and pony

 December 21, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: JAMES L. SNYDER | Section: Columns 
 
 874
 Words 

 Read News Document

 The best holiday for me is Christmas. I enjoy everything about Christmas except paying for many gifts. But looking back, it's all been worth it. I can't think of anything I would ever change.It's the one time of the year that families get together who usually aren't together during the year because of work schedules and so forth.
I look forward to our great Christmas gatherings. There was a time in our family when the number of family members increased every year. I thought when we had children, that would be the end of it. But wouldn't you know all of our kids decided to have their own kids? And it's even come to the point where some of our grandkids are having their own kids.
Oh boy, when will this stop?
Actually, I hope it doesn't stop.
Everybody looks forward to the Christmas holiday and everything associated with it. It is very hard to have a bad Christmas, no matter what seems to happen.
After our Christmas holiday, I was sitting in my easy chair drinking coffee and reflecting on all the Christmases I had as a child. Those were fun times. I got to see relatives I haven't seen the rest of the year.
It was then I remembered something — the worst Christmas I ever had. I had forgotten about this, but all of a sudden, it came to mind.
When I was young, before I became a teenager, my parents would take me and my siblings downtown to meet Santa Claus. We would sit on his lap, take a candy cane from him, and tell him what we wanted for Christmas.
When we were done, he would say, "Ho, ho, ho," give us a Merry Christmas look, then send us back to our parents.
I vividly remember the first time I told him that I would love to have a pony for Christmas. He agreed to bring me a pony, and then he did his "ho, ho, ho" routine.
When I got up that Christmas, I noticed no pony under the Christmas tree. As I thought more about it, I realized that nothing was under the Christmas tree that I had asked Santa for. I couldn't understand it. My parents told me Santa would bring me the Christmas presents I asked for. Of course, I believed them.
Several Christmases passed, and the same thing happened or didn't happen. And I was just a little bit confused about this guy called Santa Claus. Why wasn't he good to his word?
I remember the year I turned 13. I was now a teenager, and so I had graduated to that smart level of being a teenager.
At school, we were having some kind of Christmas party, and they were talking about Santa Claus coming down the chimney to put presents under the Christmas tree and in the stockings hung by the fireplace. I didn't think too much of it at the time.
That Christmas Eve, as we were getting our Christmas tree all "holidayed" up, I felt that something was missing with our Christmas decorations. Then, it hit me rather strongly.
"Dad," I cried in alarm. He looked at me and said, "What's wrong son?"
I looked at him angrily and asked, "Dad, where is the chimney?"
With a curious look, he responded, "What are you talking about?"
"It's beginning to make sense," I seriously said to my father. "I now know what's wrong with our Christmas. I now know why I haven't got my pony."
My dad had no idea what I was talking about and asked me to explain.
"This week in school they were telling us all about Christmas and Santa Claus and Rudolph the red nose reindeer. One of the things they told us was that Santa Claus comes down the chimney to bring his gifts."
I paused for a moment and then continued, "So, that's why I've not got my pony for Christmas. Dad, where is our chimney?"
My dad was momentarily confused and had no idea how to respond to what I was saying.
"Well, son," my father said, "we don't have a chimney. We don't even have a fireplace so we don't need one."
"How then is Santa going to get me my Christmas presents under our Christmas tree I asked for while sitting on his lap?"
Thinking back over that now, I couldn't help but laugh. My father had a hard time explaining to me why we didn't need a chimney for Christmas time. Every year, just before Christmas, I ask, "Dad, will we have a chimney this year?"
After a while, he got tired of hearing me ask that question and refused to come up with any more excuses.
I was confused about Santa Claus and Christmas, not knowing what to believe. It took me some time to sort out the Christmas holiday.
As I reflected on this, I thought that many things in life need sorting out. We believe something and then find out it wasn't the truth.
Jesus addressed this in John 8:31-33, "Then said Jesus to those Jews which believed on him, If ye continue in my word, then are ye my disciples indeed; And ye shall know the truth, and the truth shall make you free."
The truth about Jesus and His birth sets us free, and that truth can only be found in the Word of God.

title: Mother can't find work with lack of child care
author: Staff Writer
content:
Mother can't find work with lack of child care

 December 25, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Staff Writer | Section: News 
 
 296
 Words 

 Read News Document

 After her mother moved away and couldn't help with child care, a single mother lost her job, which was not able to accommodate the hours she needed to take care of her 10- and 13-year-old children."Her moving away really makes it hard for us with hours being able to work because she can help watch my kids," the mother said. "It's just me."
With the holidays approaching, this mother wasn't sure how she would find the money to provide her kids with Christmas gifts.
This mother received assistance with her family's holiday celebration from the Brighter Christmas Fund.
Your donation to the Brighter Christmas Fund could help local families in similar situations provide a holiday celebration for their children.
The Brighter Christmas Fund is a nonprofit helping families in need on the Mid-Shore. Donations may be sent to The Star Democrat at 29088 Airpark Dr., Easton, MD 21601. Donations also may be made online via credit card or PayPal at brighterchristmasfund.org. Click the "Donate" button.
Donations are tax-deductible.
The administrative costs for the Brighter Christmas Fund are covered entirely by The Star Democrat and APG Chesapeake, so 100% of donations go to families in need. For more information about the fund, call 410-200-1884.
The total donated for this year's Brighter Christmas Fund to date is $55,855.42.

title: Tides of Grace expands into new center, opens to community use
author: ANDREA GRABENSTEIN agrabenstien@chespub.com
content:
Tides of Grace expands into new center, opens to community use

 December 25, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: ANDREA GRABENSTEIN agrabenstien@chespub.com | Section: News 
 
 227
 Words 

 Read News Document

 CENTREVILLE — The holiday season brought Tides of Grace a new community resource center to share with all, a gift that will keep giving.The new center in Centreville is a huge upgrade from the 500 square foot building the nonprofit has worked out of in Stevensville for two years, Leann Rhodes, executive director said.
The new building at 207 C N. Liberty Street is about 2,200 square feet, with plenty of space to take in monthly donations and host community outreach events throughout the year, she said.
Setting a foundation of community love, community members are more than welcome to schedule usage for different events they may have. Just this month, a special needs group utilized the space for gingerbread house making class, according to Rhodes.
"This is exactly what we envisioned for our new building, a welcoming space where the community can come together, connect and create lasting memories," she said.
At Christmas, Tides of Grace held their fifth annual toy drive helping over 1,000 children this year.
Tides of Grace's next community event in the new space will be a pop-up prom boutique for seniors, with free suits and dresses.
"We can't wait to see all the ways our community resource center will bring joy and support to our community," Rhodes said.
More information about Tides of Grace, including upcoming events and how to get involved, can be found at tidesofgraceinc.org.

 EASTON — Cars lined up on North Washington Street to view a large display of holiday lights and the Easton Church of God's Drive-Thru Live Nativity on a cold and rainy Friday evening.Those that pulled into the Easton Church of God and drove around were greeted by an array of Christmas lights, music, decorations and inflatable holiday characters. Gift bags and hot chocolate were handed out, and Santa greeted attendees.
Easton Church of God Family Pastor Josh Maxwell said the live nativity has been going on for a little more than a decade.
"We set up Christmas lights with the different scenes around the back for the live nativity and the Christmas story," Maxwell said. "It's just another opportunity for us to help create traditions for families in the community."
In the drive-through, biblical scenes included Mary hearing about the birth of Jesus from the angel Gabriel, baby Jesus in the manger, the Last Supper and the resurrection of Jesus.
Maxwell said everyone has come to love the annual event that tells the story of Christmas, making it a tradition not just for the church, but for the entire community.
"It's incredible," Maxwell said. "We hear comments and stuff from the community, the kids talking about how they look forward to it."

title: Miles River Yacht Club's Annual Angel Tree event brings holiday joy
author: Veronica Fernandez-Alvarado
content:
Miles River Yacht Club's Annual Angel Tree event brings holiday joy

 December 25, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Veronica Fernandez-Alvarado | Section: Christmas 
 
 543
 Words 

 Read News Document

 ST. MICHAELS — The Miles River Yacht Club's annual Angel Tree event is bringing holiday cheer to the Eastern Shore.Through this time-honored tradition, members of the yacht club come together to celebrate and provide local children with presents and other essentials for the holidays.
This collaboration is in conjunction with the Head Start of Shore Up, a program focusing on children's social and educational development, and the event has recently roped the Benedictine School in an effort to grow the number of children who benefit from the Angel Tree program.
Nick Simpson, commodore at the Miles River Yacht Club, said this year they are providing gifts to over 30 local children. Simpson said this event has showcased the most generous characteristics of their members and the volunteer opportunities that the club promotes for all its members.
"Our mission statement has a lot about boating and doing things on the water, but part of the mission statement is also to give back to support the local community," Simpson said. "The club donates a lot throughout the year. This is just kind of the culmination of it."
Simpson said outside of this Angel Tree event, the club provides meals to those in need during Thanksgiving and members donate school supplies through the Community Center in St. Michaels for children. But the Angel Tree is by far the most anticipated event by members.
According to Simpson, Head Start of Shore Up identifies children in need, then they work to get a list of toys that they want as well as clothing sizes for the children.
Then a tree at the yacht club is decorated with cardboard or construction paper ornaments, and each ornament has two or three toys, as well as clothing items and sizes, requested by the children. Club members select an ornament, purchase the listed items, and return them to the club to be distributed to the children.
Simpson said members will often race to obtain these ornaments.
Jackie Tate, a volunteer at Head Start of St. Michaels, said the children picked for the Angel Tree range from ages 2 to 4. Tate said the program has been going on for well over a decade and she has loved the joy brought to families.
"That's why I continue to do it, because you never know what the parents are going through because they don't tell you and if I can help a family that's in need, do this for them. My heart is satisfied," she said.
Tate said parents will often not know when their child is picked to be part of the Angel Tree, and she recalls a time about 10 years ago when she called a mother and told her that her child had been picked for the program and she needed to come down and pick up the gifts bought for her.
When the mother came to the classroom, she was overwhelmed with gratitude and began to cry.
"(The mother) said, 'Miss Tate, I thank you so much because I didn't know what I was going to do for Christmas for my child, because I've been laid off from my job.' And that touched my heart to know that we could, just as a yacht club, help these children and these families, because you don't know what they're going through," Tate said.

 The Londonderry Satellite Rotary Club is thinking of the folks who suffered through hurricanes Helene and Milton some months ago. The club was able to help somewhat when three members traveled to Greenville, Tennessee, in early November to donate over 50 blankets, 20 child-sized throws and 15 tents that could hold eight people each.The people who would have received these supplies are in our thoughts today. It is good to know that those supplies might be bringing warmth and comfort to folks at this special time of year.
As we gather around our home fires, enjoying the holidays feeling comfortable and secure, we are hopeful that we have been able to ease their hardship in this small way.
The Christmas message has always been peace, love and joy. That never changes, in good times and bad. When people believe, Christmas always comes.
PATRICIA BRADLEY
Easton

title: Service dog group names pup after late veterans affairs secretary
author: MARTY MADDEN mmadden@somdnews.com
content:
Service dog group names pup after late veterans affairs secretary

 December 30, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: MARTY MADDEN mmadden@somdnews.com | Section: News 
 
 500
 Words 

 Read News Document

 Not every hero needs a bronze statue or a painted portrait hanging in a prominent building to be remembered. Sometimes a dog will do just fine.Earlier this year, an organization called Warrior Canine Connection announced it was naming a service dog after George Owings III.
Owings, a Calvert County resident, Vietnam veteran, Marine and former secretary of Maryland's Department of Veterans Affairs, died Oct. 31, 2023.
In February 2020, under Owings' leadership the Maryland Veterans Service Animal Program bestowed on Warrior Canine Connection $30,000 in funding to help support the placement of service dogs with wounded armed forces veterans.
The Montgomery County-based organization's leadership was pleased with the allocation.
"It's no secret that service dogs are an amazing tool to help in the veteran recovery process and by making them more available, together, we can help serve more of our nation's heroes," Rick Yount, the founder and executive director of Warrior Canine Connection, said at the time.
"For our veterans who have honorably served in the military and who have also given so much to our state and nation, this is but one way we can give back," Owings remarked after the $30,000 in funding was presented to Warrior Canine Connection in 2020.
The impetus for that bestowal was launched three years earlier when an Anne Arundel County state lawmaker, Sen. Bryan W. Simonaire (R), sponsored a bill that, when passed, established the Maryland Service Animal Program.
Josh Marks, a Carroll County resident who is a veterans advocate, nominated Owings this year to have a service dog named in his honor.
"George was an honorable man," Marks said. "Honor is simply the morality of superior men. What better legacy to leave?"
The connection's announcement that a fledgling service dog would be named "Owings," recounts the actions of U.S. Marine Sgt. George W. Owings III during his four years of service during the Vietnam War.
The citation noted Owings earned the Navy and Marine Corps Medal "for heroism in rescuing the crew of an OH-23 helicopter on the evening of Aug. 3, 1967. Upon observing the helicopter crash approximately 200 yards off the beach at Marine Corps Air Station Chu Lai Republic of Vietnam, Sgt. Owings took immediate action to assist downed crew members. He, along with other marines, immediately ran to a 750 pound fiberglass boat positioned 50 yards from the water, which could obviously be used in a rescue attempt. Sgt. Owings and the other marines began struggling with the heavy boat to launch it into the water."
Despite the challenging waters, Owings and other marines were able to subsequently save three injured crewmen from the downed chopper, guiding the vessel back to shore so the survivors could receive medical attention.
In addition to the Navy and Marine Corps Medal, Owings received a Presidential Unit Citation, a Navy Unit Commendation with Bronze Star Badge and the Vietnam Service Medal with Silver Star Badge.
Owings, the service canine, was raised by a Germantown couple and as of this writing, remains in training.
To learn more about the Warrior Canine Connection, go to warriorcanineconnection.org.

title: Woman needs held after taking in best friend's grandson
author: Staff Writer
content:
Woman needs held after taking in best friend's grandson

 January 1, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Staff Writer | Section: News 
 
 293
 Words 

 Read News Document

 A woman took in her best friend's 6-year-old grandson earlier this year after the woman's friend and her husband, who were raising the boy, died 10 days apart.Both of the child's parents are not in his life.
"I didn't want this child to go to live with anyone who he didn't know," the woman said. "... I have been in his life since he was born, so I went to the court and got custody of him.
"... It's been a struggle financially, but faith always has come through for us."
The woman, whose own children are adults and on longer live at home, was accustomed to supporting just herself on her modest salary. With the extra moth to feed, her resources have been stretched thin.
With the holidays approaching, she wasn't sure how she would find the money to provide the boy with Christmas gifts.
She received assistance with their holiday celebration from the Brighter Christmas Fund.
Your donation to the Brighter Christmas Fund could help local families in similar situations provide a holiday celebration for their children next year.
The Brighter Christmas Fund is a nonprofit helping families in need on the Mid-Shore. Donations may be sent to The Star Democrat at 29088 Airpark Dr., Easton, MD 21601. Donations also may be made online via credit card or PayPal at brighterchristmasfund.org. Click the "Donate" button.
Donations are tax-deductible.
The administrative costs for the Brighter Christmas Fund are covered entirely by The Star Democrat and APG Chesapeake, so 100% of donations go to families in need. For more information about the fund, call 410-200-1884.
The total donated for this year's Brighter Christmas Fund to date is $62,626.42.
Those in the sharing spirit of giving with others this holiday season include:
Kay Schaar-Wagenblatt
Jacqueline Smith
Mary King
In Honor of our Grandsons, Jaxson and Carter Fox
Sean Mallin.

title: January events: Oysters & Ice Festival, movie night, murder mystery event
author: Staff Writer
content:
January events: Oysters & Ice Festival, movie night, murder mystery event

 January 2, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Staff Writer | Section: News 
 
 409
 Words 

 Read News Document

 There are a number of fun, local happening this month, according to a January rundown from Discover Easton — which puts on and promotes local events.Here's some of January's top events, according to Discover Easton (https://discovereaston.com/).
Cambridge Oysters & Ice Festival
Friday Jan. 17 and Saturday, Jan. 18
Icelab and the Dorchester Chamber of Commerce are putting on the Cambridge Oysters & Ice Festival with events throughout downtown Cambridge. That includes interactive ice sculptures, oysters, live music and free family fun as well as an ice skating rink at the Hyatt Regency.
For more: https://iceoysterfest.com/
Movie Night at The Ebenezer: Tinker Tailor Soldier Spy
Friday, Jan. 10 — 7:30 pm
Enjoy movie night at the Ebenezer Theatre for the 1975 spy novel by John Le Carre. Venture back to the days of intrigue in the bleak days of the Cold War, as espionage veteran George Smiley is forced from semi-retirement to uncover a Soviet Agent within M16.
The.movie event at the Prager Family Center for the Arts features tables for two with beverages and pizza slices from Roma Alla Pala.
For more: https://www.pragerarts.com/
Murder Mystery Dinner
Saturday, Jan. 18 — 5:30 p.m.
Join the Tidewater Inn for a Murder Mystery Event on Saturday, Jan. 18 at 5:30 p.m.. The Mardi Gras-themed mystery, features The Mystery Krewe, where not everyone survives the ball. Enjoy a 4-course paired menu crafted to complement the intrigue. Tickets are $120 per person, including the experience, menu, gratuity, and tax. The Tidewater Inn is also offering Murder Mystery Hotel Package, featuring discounted accommodations and two tickets.
For more: https://tidewaterinn.com/
Bugatti: Reaching for Perfection
Exhibit at Academy Art Museum
An exhibit at the Academy Art Museum features five rare Bugatti cars from an Eastern Shore collection: two grand prix race cars, two Type 57 touring cars, and a miniature "Baby." and eight bronze sculptures from the Arsidi-Scuderi Collection of Lugano, Switzerland. The two collections have never been displayed together before. The exhibit runs through April 13.
For more: https://academyartmuseum.org/
Call Me Dancer
Friday, Jan. 17
The Chesapeake Film Festival and Maryland State Arts Council are presenting a free back-by-popular-demand screening of the critically acclaimed film "Call Me Dancer" at the Talbot County Free Library in Easton,n Friday, January 17, at 4:00 PM. Call Me Dancer tells the story of a young street dancer from Mumbai whose passion and determination lead him on a transformative journey to pursue his dreams of becoming a professional dancer against all odds. This movie is suggested for adults.
For more: https://chesapeakefilmfestival.com/

title: Brighter Christmas Fund provides holiday gifts for almost 500 kids
author: Staff Writer
content:
Brighter Christmas Fund provides holiday gifts for almost 500 kids

 January 8, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Staff Writer | Section: News 
 
 340
 Words 

 Read News Document

 The 41st annual Brighter Christmas Fund raised over $60,000 this holiday season as part of its yearly effort to bring joy to children on the Mid-Shore.The effort's main focus was to help Santa provide children in need presents to open during the Christmas season.
"As a challenging economy played a big role in contributions in 2024, I was surprised and very grateful that so many local individuals stepped up to provide help to our community's children," said Orestes Baez, regional president of APG Chesapeake, which oversees The Star Democrat. "Of course, we wish — and I know our donors do as well — we could help more and more each year, but we are thankful for the support of so many. Truly heartwarming."
This holiday season, the Brighter Christmas Fund helped 495 children receive holiday presents. This included 126 children in Caroline County, 114 children in Dorchester County, 73 children in Kent County, 34 children in Queen Anne's County and 148 children in Talbot County.
The 2024 Brighter Christmas Fund raised $64,126.42 to go to local families in future years.
The Star Democrat donates all the fund's administrative operating costs.
From late October through the end of January, The Star Democrat published stories daily about families in Talbot, Caroline, Dorchester, Queen Anne's and Kent counties who were struggling to provide a Christmas for their children. These stories were the only way The Star Democrat solicited donations for the Brighter Christmas Fund.
The Brighter Christmas Fund is a nonprofit charity which helps families in need on the Mid-Shore,
Donations may be sent to The Star Democrat, 29088 Airpark Dr., Easton, MD 21601. Donations also may be made online via credit card or PayPal at brighterchristmasfund.org. Click the "Donate" button. Donations are tax-deductible.
The administrative costs for the Brighter Christmas Fund are covered entirely by The Star Democrat and APG Chesapeake, so 100% of donations go to families in need. For more information about the fund, call 410-200-1884.
Those sharing the spirit of giving with others this holiday included:

Bonnie Haynes
Carla Howell
George and Helen Albury
Diane M. Marquette

title: Cambridge Ice & Oyster Fest to return for fourth year
author: MAGGIE TROVATO mtrovato@chespub.com
content:
Cambridge Ice & Oyster Fest to return for fourth year

 January 8, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: MAGGIE TROVATO mtrovato@chespub.com | Section: Local News 
 
 565
 Words 

 Read News Document

 CAMBRIDGE — Ice sculptures and ice games are coming back to Cambridge — and will be served up with a side of oysters — for the fourth annual Cambridge Ice & Oyster Festival on Jan. 17 and 18.Put on by the Dorchester Chamber of Commerce and Ice Lab, with help from Cambridge Main Street and Dorchester County Tourism, the festival will bring ice sculptures carved from more than 400,000 pounds of ice, live ice sculpting demonstrations, a slide made of ice and more frozen fun to Cambridge.
There will also be frozen versions of classic games such as corn hole and tic-tac-toe, an '80s-themed ice bar and two stages featuring live music.
Dorchester Chamber of Commerce President Bill Christopher said the family-friendly festival is "always a blast." This year, there will be some new ice sculptures, including a Jersey skiff you can pose inside of and a target you can shoot at with paintballs, he said.
"We have a lot of interactive ice, which I think is different than some of the other festivals," Christopher said.
According to a news release about the event, some of the festival's featured ice sculptures include an ice hockey table, locomotive engine, flock of geese and tractor and trailer. The more than 40 sculptures have been or are being carved by Ice Lab.
Ricky Fitzhugh, chief ice officer of Ice Lab, said the time it takes to carve each sculpture depends on the detail of the sculpture.
"But it could (be) anywhere from an hour to five or six hours of carving," he said.
Sponsored by the Hyatt Regency Chesapeake Bay Golf Resort, Spa and Marina and a variety of other Mid-Shore businesses and organizations, the event will be held in downtown Cambridge, at the Packing House and at the Hyatt. Shuttles will provide transportation between locations.
For the oyster part of the festival, the watermen of Dorchester County and some of the region's top oyster farms will be selling oysters. Christopher said that along with raw oysters, there will be oysters prepared in different ways, like roasted oysters.
"The Dorchester Seafood Heritage Association will be serving wild caught oysters," Christopher said. "And then we will have five other aquaculture guys that are all local that grow the oysters local. Each of those oysters are slightly different. They've got different salinity, different taste."
According to the news release, local oyster farms that will be at the event include Choptank Terrapin Oyster Co., Farm Creek Oyster Co., Madhouse Oysters and Madison Bay Seafood.
With all the ice, festival-goers will be able to warm up at fire pits and make s'mores.
The festival will also have beverages to keep everyone — including those who are 21 and older — warm. From coffee to hot chocolate to craft beer and cocktails, attendees will be able to take their pick.
The event will kick off at the Packing House on the evening of Friday, Jan. 17. That night, there will be ice skating at the Hyatt Winter Village and interactive ice sculptures in downtown Cambridge. On Saturday, Jan. 18, events will be held throughout the day in downtown Cambridge and at the Hyatt Winter Village. There is no cost for admission to the festival.
The Rescue Fire Company Train Garden will be open during the festival.
More information about the Cambridge Ice & Oyster Festival can be found on the festival's website at iceoysterfest.com. Entertainment schedules and weather updates will be posted on the festival's Facebook page.

title: Easton residents, aiming to bridge political divide, bring workshop to Talbot County
author: Konner Metz
content:
Easton residents, aiming to bridge political divide, bring workshop to Talbot County

 January 10, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Konner Metz | Section: Local News 
 
 500
 Words 

 Read News Document

 EASTON — Easton residents Ronnie Halperin and Sharon Harrington have seen political division worsen over time to the point where they have hesitated to openly discuss their viewpoints or place political signs in their yards.That trend, escalated during recent elections, motivated the two residents to bring an event to the Talbot County Free Library this Saturday. It's a workshop by Braver Angels, a volunteer-led nonprofit organization that aims to bridge political division in local communities.
Halperin says the idea to bring Braver Angels to Easton was birthed when she realized the lack of political diversity within her community book club.
"We realized that everyone in the book group was a Democrat," Halperin said. "And we know that our community is only — at most — half Democrat. So we felt kind of bad about that. What did that mean? It spoke to the polarization that exists now."
One of the book club's members discovered the Braver Angels website. Watching an example workshop video, Halperin said the nonprofit's work struck her as "really effective and really meaningful."
After being trained by the Braver Angels group, Halperin and Harrington are organizing Saturday's event, which is free to the public and takes place from 9:30 a.m. to 12:30 p.m.
The purpose of Saturday's workshop — titled "Depolarizing Within" — is not to change anyone's political beliefs or discuss specific issues. Instead, it's to teach those on both sides of the aisle how to converse with others "in a way that doesn't include rancor and demonizing and dismissiveness," Halperin said.
"I don't want anybody to walk in there thinking this is a group that's going to try to change my mind," Harrington said. "That is not our goal."
Braver Angels is a New York-based organization that was founded after the 2016 presidential election. It defines itself as the "nation's largest cross-partisan, volunteer-led movement to bridge the partisan divide for the good of our democratic republic" on its website.
A professional moderator will be at Saturday's workshop. The two organizers say they've had pre-registrations come in from both liberal- and conservative-leaning residents, though they're hoping for more of the latter to achieve a balanced discussion.
Talbot County has had its share of political divide in recent elections. Prior to 2024's November election, local political committees reported vandalism of yard signs.
The presidential race was a dead heat in Talbot County, with 11,125 residents voting for Republican nominee and President-elect Donald Trump and 11,119 voting for Democratic nominee Kamala Harris.
Harrington believes Saturday's workshop is a step in the right direction to bridging the partisan nature in the region.
"In the past political year, we've been aware that people have been uneasy about expressing their preferences and have kind of gone underground because of animosity or hurt feelings or things of that sort," Harrington said. "And we wanted to bring something to the town where people could find a way to talk about their differences without going the ugly route or without escalating."
To register, visit braverangels.org/event/depolarizingwithin-4/. For more information, contact Ronnie Halperin or Sharon Harrington at halperinandharrington@gmail.com.

title: Goodbye to a colleague with ink in his veins
author: Staff Writer
content:
Goodbye to a colleague with ink in his veins

 January 11, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Staff Writer | Section: Editorials 
 
 690
 Words 

 Read News Document

 There are many people who work to deliver your Star Democrat every day.You recognize the names of the reporters. Their names top their stories and are easily spotted. Editors' and managers' names are listed in every edition of the newspaper.
Advertisers recognize the account executives who help them reach their customers.
Yet there are many, many people who work behind the scenes to produce the paper — press operators, mailroom workers, page designers, graphic artists, accountants and technology experts. These people are unseen by most of our readers, but without their dedicated work, the newspaper could not be produced.
One of those people is Dale Massey, who makes the plates that go on our printing press.
Friday was Dale's last day at the newspaper. He retired after a career that spanned nearly 50 years, a career that has seen quantum leaps in the technology used to produce newspapers.
Dale joined the Seaford Leader the day after he graduated from high school in June 1976. The Leader then was part of Chesapeake Publishing, the precursor to Adams Publishing Group that now owns the Star Democrat.
Dale's first job was running the darkroom, but he also took photos for advertising copy. At one time, he found a side gig doing wedding photography.
In those days, long before computers eased the process of producing newspapers, type was set in lead. Now reporters and editors type on a computer and the words are digitally sent to production.
Dale worked with then Leader sports editor Ron MacArthur. He learned on the job how to be a sports photographer. In 1983, Dale became the sports editor in Seaford. He eventually went back to darkroom work and shooting advertising photos.
In the mid 1990s, the Seaford Leader was named best of show for the overall newspaper in all of Delaware, Maryland and the District of Columbia, one of the proud moments of Dale's career.
In 1996, the company moved its printing operations to Easton, and Dale began commuting from Seaford, something that continued until his retirement on Friday.
While he continued doing photography and sports, he added other duties, including making and working with the negatives that were used to create plates for the press. A single color page in the newspaper requires four plates, one each for black, magenta, cyan and yellow inks. Those four plates, with screens of different intensities, create all of the different colors on a newspaper page.
A giant camera, the size of a room, was used to make the negatives to create those plates.
In 2003, that giant camera and the negatives went away, and the newspaper began sending pages directly to plate.
"I've seen a lot of technology," Dale said. "It's evolved; it's the evolution of doing things."
That technology, that evolution has meant there are fewer people doing the job than there were when Dale started nearly 50 years ago. The pre-press department that makes the plates for the press once had 10 people. Now there are two.
Much of the work is automated. Dale now sits at a computer and sends pages to a plate-making machine.
The plates roll out, about one every 30 seconds. In the old days, each plate would take almost 15 minutes to produce.
The job has evolved over the years, but one thing has stayed consistent, Dale's love for newspapers.
"It's like you have ink in your blood," he said.
Dale is just one of nearly 100 employees at the Star Democrat, many of whom say the same thing, they have ink in their blood. There's something about working at a newspaper. It's not just a job. Our employees help tell the stories of our communities. In a way, their jobs are part of preserving democracy in this country.
It's not just a job. It's a calling.
You might not know all of their names, but each one is an essential part of producing the Star Democrat and getting that newspaper to you.
Dale is not sure what all he will be doing in retirement, but he knows he'll be spending much more time with his 9-year-old grandson.
On Friday, colleagues stopped by to wish Dale luck as he moves on to the next phase of his life.
"I'll miss this place," Dale told one.
We'll miss Dale.

title: YMCA back to normal operations after Saturday fires
author: WENDY WEITZEL wweitzel@chespub.com
content:
YMCA back to normal operations after Saturday fires

 January 12, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: WENDY WEITZEL wweitzel@chespub.com | Section: Local News 
 
 559
 Words 

 Read News Document

 EASTON — Peter Hyman was in his gym clothes and already on his way to the YMCA on Peachblossom Road around noon on Saturday when he learned there had been a fire at the Y.When he arrived moments later, Hyman, who is president of the YMCA's board, said he saw members of the community and Y staff gathering, many visibly upset by the event.
"The staff was upset. It was an upsetting moment, and I just did what I could to help both in terms of the emotions of the folks as well as the physical reality of the situation," he said Sunday morning.
The fire, which involved a second-floor closet at the Y, was one of two that the Easton Volunteer Fire Department and other departments responded to at the YMCA Saturday, according to Easton Fire Chief JR Dobson.
At around 5:30 p.m., firefighters were once again called to the Y, where an HVAC unit was on fire on the building's roof.
Neither fire resulted in any extensive damage to the building, according to YMCA of the Chesapeake CEO Robbie Gill.
Dobson said the first fire was extinguished by the Y's sprinkler system before firefighters arrived at the scene. The second fire was quickly extinguished by firefighters using a fire extinguisher after gas feeding the HVAC unit was shut off, the fire chief said.
The fires closed the Y for the remainder of Saturday, but regular operations resumed Sunday morning with all facilities but the racquetball courts open for use. The racquetball courts were largely undamaged, Gill said, but due to their proximity to the first fire, a sprinkler had gone off over them, meaning they had to be closed Sunday while staff worked to dry the area.
"We were fortunate there wasn't a substantial amount of damage to the building," Gill said. "And now we're working with local authorities to provide any information we can to help them investigate."
While the second fire's cause was ruled by the Office of the State Fire Marshal to have been a mechanical failure with the HVAC unit, Dobson said, the cause of the first fire is still under investigation.
Gill said the first fire is not believed to have been caused by any mechanical or similar failure.
Though the fires did not cause extensive damage to the facilities, Hyman said the events were particularly upsetting for Y staff and regulars because of the role the YMCA plays in the Easton community.
"We're lucky," he said. "Our YMCA is not just a place to work out and exercise. It really is a community. It's a very wonderful group of people… I've been a member of the Y for years, and it really is a community across cultures, all kinds of folks. And it's a really special place."
Dobson said multiple departments, including the Easton, Oxford and Trappe volunteer fire departments and Talbot County Emergency Services, responded to the events Saturday. These departments worked with staff and others on the scene to evacuate the building and secure the area.
Gill said although Saturday was "a little bit of a traumatic day," the coordinated community response to the fires served as a reminder of the importance of the YMCA.
"The Y has been around for 168 years, so it's an institution in the community that serves one in three people, and it's wonderful to see so many people care for it at that level," Gill said.

title: Community leaders honored at MLK Youth Basketball Classic
author: Konner Metz
content:
Community leaders honored at MLK Youth Basketball Classic

 January 20, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Konner Metz | Section: Local News 
 
 409
 Words 

 Read News Document

 EASTON — Hundreds gathered at the Talbot County Community Center on Monday for the 18th annual Martin Luther King Jr. Youth Basketball Classic, where four members of the community were recognized.Kids in fifth through eighth grades from Caroline, Dorchester and Talbot counties competed in games throughout the morning. They then participated in 3-point, free throw and half-court shooting contests.
The Mid-Shore partnership was established in 2007. During Monday's event, four community members were honored for making marks in their local communities. They were presented with the 2025 Martin Luther King Jr. Image Award.
Former Talbot County Council President Corey Pack helped hand out the awards, thanking the four recipients for their community dedication.
This year's recipients were: Joseph Brummell (Talbot County), Gabriel Butler (Dorchester County), Heather Harding (southern Caroline County) and Cheryl Beulah (northern Caroline County).
Brummell is a longtime Talbot County resident who is the founder of Brummell Does LLC, a landscaping company in Easton. Easton Director of Parks and Recreation Lorraine Gould introduced Brummell, noting that he's very involved locally, including as a youth baseball and basketball coach.
"Joe is always looking for a challenge," Gould said.
Butler is a youth pastor in Cambridge and club manager at the Boys & Girls Clubs of Metropolitan Baltimore.
Cambridge Police Department Sgt. Antoine Patton pointed out Butler's significant impacts on the local youth that "(keep) the dream of Dr. King alive."
"Since the opening of the club, Gabe Butler has added over 200 members of the club there and has touched over 850 children in our community in outreach programs," Patton said.
Harding, the southern Caroline County recipient, is the judy center coordinator at the Federalsburg Judy Center. She previously served stints on councils and commissions in the Town of Federalsburg.
Harding was thanked for her efforts in bringing National Night Out to local communities.
Beulah, the northern Caroline County recipient, is the executive director of Aaron's Place in Denton, a food pantry serving hundreds of local families every month.
"I feel really humbled to be representing the community and serve in the community," Beulah said in an interview. "We serve a lot of folks, and to be recognized, it's very humbling and very honoring."
Beulah said when she was first notified she'd be receiving the award, she was shocked. "'Oh my God, why me? Why Aaron's Place?'" she recalled thinking.
"I don't look at us as some extraordinary place, I really don't," she said. "I just look at us as being able to serve the community. I'm thankful and very humbled."

title: Ice & Oyster Festival brings crowd to downtown Cambridge
author: MAGGIE TROVATO mtrovato@chespub.com
content:
Ice & Oyster Festival brings crowd to downtown Cambridge

 January 21, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: MAGGIE TROVATO mtrovato@chespub.com | Section: Local News 
 
 488
 Words 

 Read News Document

 CAMBRIDGE — Although Friday's comparatively warmer temperatures kept the more than 40 ice sculptures off the streets of downtown Cambridge for the first day of the Cambridge Ice and Oyster Festival, they didn't stop festival-goers from having a good time.As Caleb Stine strummed his guitar at the Packing House Friday, people mingled and filled their stomachs with everything from grilled oysters with cheese, bacon and salsa to steaming hot gumbo.
Cambridge resident Kathy Ridgely said she loves the live entertainment, variety of vendors and seafood the event offers every year.
"It's just a great opportunity for community," she said.
Along with the Packing House, the two-day, admission-free festival was held at the Hyatt Regency Chesapeake Bay Golf Resort, Spa and Marina and in downtown Cambridge. Shuttles offered festival-goers easy transport between locations.
Dorchester Chamber of Commerce President Bill Christopher said although it was too warm to set up the ice sculptures until about 9:30 p.m. Friday night, the Packing House was "packed."
"And the shuttle was full, running people around up to the ice skating rink at the Hyatt," he said. "So people had plenty to do even though we didn't have the sculptures for them to look at downtown. The restaurants were still open, shops were still open."
Gayle Quillin, a Cambridge resident who arrived at the Packing House Friday evening with a group of friends and family, said they first went downtown Friday, but nothing was going on yet.
"So we came over here," she said.
Quillin said she always looks forward to the people at the festival every year.
"We just love all the people down there and getting to see our neighbors," she said.
Sponsored by the Hyatt Regency Chesapeake Bay and a variety of other Mid-Shore businesses and organizations, the event was put on by the Dorchester Chamber of Commerce and Ice Lab with help from Cambridge Main Street and Dorchester County Tourism.
Christopher said he wanted to thank the numerous sponsors of the event, whose sponsorship supports downtown Cambridge businesses.
"Because that's what this is all about," he said. "Bringing people into downtown to get folks into the restaurants and the shops in the January timeframe, which is normally very slow. And I think we were successful at making that happen again."
Ice sculptures, once they were set up, remained up for attendees to marvel over and interact with all of Saturday.
"I mean, the temperature was probably better for humans than ice," Christopher said. "But the fact that it was overcast helped the sculptures hold up really well for the day."
Last year, weather also had an affect on the festival. The event's first day was canceled because of warm weather.
Christopher said the Chamber has received overwhelmingly positive feedback about the fourth annual event. He said the Chamber estimates the festival brought in as many people as last year. He said Saturday was busy and he thinks the restaurants and shops got a lot of business.
"It's nice to see Cambridge alive and breathing," Ridgely said.

title: Cambridge resident remembers involvement in 1965 march from Selma to Montgomery
author: Maggie Trovato
content:
Cambridge resident remembers involvement in 1965 march from Selma to Montgomery

 January 21, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Maggie Trovato | Section: Local News 
 
 520
 Words 

 Read News Document

 CAMBRIDGE — Cambridge resident Roy Davis remembers approaching Edmund Pettus Bridge for the first time during the march from Selma to Montgomery, Alabama in 1965. He was 14 years old."As we were coming up to the bridge, you could hear horses, dogs, screams," he recalled.
Once Davis reached the center of the bridge, he could see what he had been hearing: horses, dogs and people getting beaten with billy clubs and sprayed with tear gas.
"I was scared," Davis, a Selma, Alabama native, said.
During a Martin Luther King Jr. Day commemoration event at Christ Episcopal Church in Cambridge on Monday, Davis shared his recollection of the famous Alabama marches, which took marchers three times before they were able to cross the bridge.
Davis said they marched about 15 or 16 miles each day until they arrived in Montgomery.
"It wasn't bad on me," he said about the distance. "I was 14 years old. I could run and walk all day."
His mother didn't know about Davis' involvement in the first march, but she was proud when she found out. "She was calling my relatives in Chicago, New York and everything," he said.
MARCHING ONDavis remembers being on the playground during recess after he had gotten back to Selma from the march.
"And kids were coming to me (saying), 'Roy, you're on Newsweek Magazine,'" he said.
Davis didn't believe them. But sure enough, on the cover of the April 5, 1965 edition of Newsweek, Davis is seen marching with two other young men on the road to Montgomery.
Almost 60 years later, Davis continues to champion issues important to him. These days, that issue is homelessness in Dorchester County.
"These people have no business being homeless," he said. "Can't get nothing to eat. ... And that's what we are doing these days. Helping them try and get housing."
After the event, attendee Lametha Elbert said Davis' experience in the march and as a kid in Alabama in the 1960s struck her. She talked about the importance of people sharing their experiences.
Dorchester County Democratic Central Committee Chair Sarah Gavian said the event had "universal appeal," bringing people together.
"It comes on a day that's very important for people, certainly for Democrats, to be turning their energies forward constructively and figuring out how to be more community (service-oriented) and engage better." Across the bridge in Washington, D.C., Republican President Donald Trump had been sworn in a few hours earlier.
Along with Davis' story, the Martin Luther King Jr. Day event — hosted by the Dorchester County Democratic Central Committee — included a variety of speeches and songs. First United Methodist Church of Hyattsville Rev. Yvonne Wallace Penn and Cambridge Mayor Lajan Cephas' fiancé Joe Johnson-Bey both spoke. Vocalist Maris Wicker sang "This Little Light of Mine" and "Balm in Gilead." Marie Anderson closed out the evening singing "If I Could Help Somebody."
Johnson-Bey spoke for Cephas, who couldn't be at the event. He shared the importance of loving each other through everything.
Wallace Penn said that King lived love.
"He said, 'I have decided to stick to love' because I don't have time to waste to hate anybody. But I have time to love you," Wallace Penn said.

title: Ralph Bartz credits a life of activity for his 100 years
author: AHMAD GARNETT agarnett@chespub.com
content:
Ralph Bartz credits a life of activity for his 100 years

 January 22, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: AHMAD GARNETT agarnett@chespub.com | Section: News 
 
 586
 Words 

 Read News Document

 FEDERALSBURG — Born Jan. 21, 1925, Ralph Barth celebrated 100 years of life Tuesday.Barth's family wanted to surprise him at his daughter Melinda Peugh's house on his birthday, but he knew a week before that something was going to happen.
"I had a feeling what was happening the week before that it might be something, and I expected maybe five or six people there with maybe cake and ice cream," Barth said. "But it was quite a crowd there, and I got quite a few gifts."
Dozens attended his birthday party on Sunday evening, braving the snowy weather to get there.
Barth has seen many things in 100 years, including living through World War II and surviving polio at 15 years old, which he credits, in part, for helping him reach his age.
Polio is a contagious disease that attacks the nervous system and is often fatal. For Barth, it attacked the right side of his body, leaving him in a wheelchair for a period.
Polio taught him to take his health more seriously, he said.
"I was in the University Hospital in Baltimore for about six or seven weeks," Barth said. "... and I think when you're really sick when you're younger, you respect your health more as you grow up."
Barth began his career as a 13 year-old boy in Howard County. Barth stopped going to school to help his family of 10 siblings work on their farm. His father had to go back to work to make more money because the farm wasn't making enough. Barth took over and worked the family farm until he got polio.
"I managed to farm. I did all the farm work. We had cows, horses, all kinds of chickens and poultry. And at 13, and I did all the field plowing, putting crops and things like that."
Barth had many jobs. He worked at a defense plant for the Army making copper brass. He then moved to be a lumber manager at a hardware store for 20 years, and then to the post office for 18 years.
In Barth's first marriage, he adopted two children, who he said he loves dearly.
He married his second wife, Clara Barth, on July 8, 1984. They moved to Caroline County in 1989 and opened and operated a store for 12 years. The store sold baked goods and candy, sorted mail and much more.
Barth's career didn't end until just five years ago.
"I worked in Queenstown for an estate," Barth said. "I was a carpenter helping the Kenny family build a new home on a big ranch. I also did trim work in the house, and after we finished the trim we built a new three-car garage."
Barth's stepson got him the job at the estate, but after his stepson left he stayed for another 12 years as the family's maintenance man.
"I stayed there for another 12 years after he left," Barth said. "I did maintenance work and I did outside work. I trimmed about eight acres of woods out in Lake Central Park and planted the grass and did the mowing and painted everything as maintenance on a 32 acre land."
Barth's credits his hard working mentality as the reason he has lived to 100 years old.
"All my activity, all these years, when you stay active, it's much better for you," Barth said.
He also credits a good mental outlook on life.
"I looked at the good side of everything," Barth stated. "I think the mental outlook makes a big difference in your health, too. You try to look at the good side of anything."

title: Mail call! American Legion auxiliaries partner with Operation We Care to support troops
author: ANDREA GRABENSTEIN agrabenstein@chespub.com
content:
Mail call! American Legion auxiliaries partner with Operation We Care to support troops

 January 22, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: ANDREA GRABENSTEIN agrabenstein@chespub.com | Section: News 
 
 455
 Words 

 Read News Document

 QUEENSTOWN — Members of the community and American Legion auxiliaries packed 70 boxes for service members deployed in Jordan and South Korea as part of Operation We Care, an Eastern Shore nonprofit, at the Queenstown American Legion on Jan. 18. The cooperative effort aims to bring troops overseas a taste of home.Filled to the brim, each box contained comforts of home with snacks, essentials, and toiletries as well as Valentine's Day cards crafted by local students.
Started in 2007, Jeff Merritt and his wife Diana of Salisbury knew there must be something they could do to assist the Easton Army National Guard units deployed to Iraq at that time.
"We had no money, no forward plan, and no idea what we were doing," he said.
Starting with simple packages with thoughtful reminders of hope and well-wishes, the nonprofit has since taken off to regularly ship thousands of packages a year and collaborated with numerous team members and partnerships through the strength of community support, he said.
Merritt presented kudos to the amazing team of Operation We Care and the wonderful partners who have thrown their hat in the ring in supporting the mission, including Fisher's Popcorn, of Ocean City, whose donations ensure kernels make it into every box.
During the height of the pandemic, dedicated volunteers continued to package from home as Operation we Care also sent out thousands of packages to local hospitals, fire departments, and police stations to ensure support and voice appreciation to support first responders and let them know they are appreciated, Merritt said.
OWC regularly hosts boxing days, including as recently as November in which volunteers packaged more than 1,000 boxes in two hours, Merritt said.
The nonprofit's largest expense is postage, spending about $40,000 a year, he said.
Especially for some unit members who wouldn't otherwise receive packages, receiving a box can truly mean the world to someone far from home.
"They serve as morale boosters," Merritt said.
Volunteer Enid Kelley and her husband Josh have been part of the operation since 2013. Josh was originally a member of the Easton National Guard unit that received the inaugural packages 18 years ago. Josh credited Operation We Care as a worthwhile organization that brings the community together in supporting troops.
"Its great to pay it forward to future units now," he said.
"It means a lot to have been able to see the entire process first hand," Enid said.
Sons of the American Legion State Commander and Centreville Jeff Davis 18 Commander Jason Miller noted Operation We Care serves an imperative mission in reminding service members they are not forgotten and to thank them for everything they do.
"It's the little bit we can do to give back," he said.
More information can be found at Operation We Care can be found at https://www.operationwecare.org.

title: World War II veteran celebrates 100th birthday
author: Carl Hamilton cahamilton@chespub.com
content:
World War II veteran celebrates 100th birthday

 January 24, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Carl Hamilton cahamilton@chespub.com | Section: News 
 
 1226
 Words 

 Read News Document

 Private First Class Kernie Thompson's nickname was "Young Boy" when he served overseas in the U.S. Army's 599th Ordnance Ammunition Company during World War II.That's because Thompson, at age 18, was the youngest of the 40 soldiers assigned to that all-African-American unit when he joined in 1943, the start of a two-year stint in which fought alongside his comrades in England, France, Belgium, Holland and Germany.
On Wednesday (Jan. 15), that veteran once known as Young Boy celebrated his 100th birthday, a milestone marked by a party in the Community Living Center at the Perry Point VA Medical Center, where the Baltimore native has resided since 2020.
There were party hats, lots of balloons, a beautiful birthday cake and Thompson's favorite candy — Hershey's Kisses, which he calls "silver bells." The party room was packed with people, including Thompson's fellow veteran residents, VA staff and members of his church family.
Among the party guests were Army officials, including Maj. General John Cushing, who is the Commanding General; and U.S. Army Combat Capabilities Development Command (DEVCOM) Command Sgt. Major Brian Haydt.
Thompson reportedly was his usual upbeat self during the party. Thompson relies on a wheelchair and is "not able to eat regular by mouth," but he remains "sharp as a tack" mentally, one longtime friend described. The new Centenarian has outlived his children and his friends from childhood and young adulthood.
Also at the party was the woman Thompson married more than 40 years ago, Clarice Thompson, his second wife, whom he nicknamed "Reesey." Thompson reportedly gets excited whenever he hears her name or learns that "Reesey" has come to visit him.
"He is the love of my life," Clarice said, before referencing his necessary VA residency and remarking, "I miss him, but I know that he is where he is suppose to be."
Thompson is soft-spoken and is strong in his Christian faith, according to a few party attendees who were interviewed.
He served more than 40 years as the chaplain at the oldest African-American owned and operated nursing home in the state, Maryland Baptist Aged Home in Baltimore, where he volunteered once a week.
A longtime member of a city Baptist Church, where he served as a deacon until age 94, Thompson also was active for more than 40 years in the Baptist Deacons Conference of Baltimore. In addition, Thompson provided usher, or deacon, training to parishioners throughout Maryland and other states, as part of an usher ministry associated with another one of the faith-based groups that he served.
"He's the kind of man who walks humbly and talks humbly. When he speaks, you listen," Clarice said. "He's the kind of man I would recommend any young people to just take a photograph of him in their mind and take on some of his characteristics — other than Jesus' characteristics."
Clarice added, "Not only was he disciplined in the military, he's a disciplined man as he walks with God."
One of the party attendees, Joseph Miller, president of that Baptist Deacons Conference of Baltimore, and his wife have been friends with Thompson and Clarice for more than 30 years.
"He is a wonderful guy. His smile is what gets you. He seems like a quiet person. His mannerism is quiet until you start talking to him. He's powerful. He talks softly, but carries a big stick," Miller commented with a chuckle. "He loves to talk."
Along those lines, Thompson's favorite topic of discussion: The Bible.
"He loves the word of God, and he will share it with you. When I come here to the VA center and talk to the residents, they always tell me what he taught them about the word of God," Miller said.
After retiring from his career as a Baltimore City maintenance worker, Thompson worked as an usher during Baltimore Orioles home games. He had that gig for three decades and was quite popular among spectators and all employees in the Baltimore Orioles organization.
"I was there when he got his 30-year ring, and he was proud of that (ring). They knew him well at the Baltimore Orioles, from the general manager, the manager, the players, the vendors, the mascot, and they all loved Kernie Thompson," Miller said.
An only child with an interest in woodworking, Thompson entered the U.S. Army at the tender age of 18 in 1943. Defending this country during World War II is among the many admirable contributions Thompson has made during his 100 years on this earth, thus far.
Thompson left his parents' West Baltimore home and traveled to Georgia, where he completed basic training. The military then sent Thompson to Camp Breckinridge in Kentucky, where he was put in the Army's 599th Ordnance Ammunition Company, which saw combat action after its deployment to Europe.
During a Cecil Whig interview two years ago, Thompson recalled, "Being overseas at war was a great experience, but some days were pleasant and some days were scary."
The following is an excerpt of some of the World War II remembrances Thompson shared during that interview:
Thompson noted that he enjoyed talking to not only his fellow soldiers, but citizens of the countries they were deployed to about their life and what it was like living in their country.
"They would ask about the United States and we would ask about their country and we would always talk to the people, we had a good relationship," Thompson said. "With the soldiers, we would play cards and everyone always had something to say to make you laugh."
But when Thompson and his fellow soldiers weren't playing cards, telling jokes or talking with citizens, they were receiving ordnance shipments, supplying soldiers with ammunition and exercising their knowledge from basic training — something Thompson said his survival was contingent upon.
"What they teach you is important to your life, especially in combat," said Thompson. "Your life might depend on what you were taught in basic training."
Thompson recalled that that training saved his life late one night in 1944, when his company was waiting for the arrival of a munitions shipment. After his group laid down to rest before the shipment arrived, they were awakened by the sight of enemy flares falling from the skies.
According to Thompson, flares were used to illuminate areas at night so planes and infantry could properly identify enemy soldiers, weaponry and other valuable targets — such as the ammunition holds that Thompson's unit was responsible for.
"Basic training taught us that when they drop flares, don't move and turn your face to the ground," said Thompson. "If you look up, the planes could see the glare of your face and it could mess up the dilation of your eyes. It was a scary night."
In 1945, after two years of his service, Thompson — who was then 21 — received word that the war was over.
"When we heard the war was over, it was a big joy," Thompson said. "We shouted and we celebrated. When I got back, the first thing I did was go with my mother to see my grandmother and we had a nice dinner and celebrated."
Following the war, Thompson got married, had a daughter and worked.
Reflecting on his wartime military service, Thompson commented, "Being a part of the Army and serving my county was one of the most rewarding things because I felt like I was fulfilling a duty that I owed to my country and it makes me feel good,"
Thompson then remarked, "I am a blessed man to be here."
