title: 'Heartbeat of Easton Utilities' legacy lives on
author: JOHN ENGLEHART
content:
'Heartbeat of Easton Utilities' legacy lives on

 January 25, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: JOHN ENGLEHART | Section: Columns 
 
 1208
 Words 

 Read News Document

 On Jan. 13, Vicki Petro retired as vice president of human resources at Easton Utilities after 31 years of dedicated service. To some, this may seem like the closing chapter of just another HR career. But to those of us who had the privilege of calling Vicki a colleague, a mentor or a friend, this marks the end of an extraordinary era in the Mid-Shore community.Vicki began her journey with Easton Utilities on Nov. 2, 1993, as the organization's sole HR professional, reporting to the business manager. Over the past three decades, she has shaped the careers of countless employees, directly overseeing the hiring of 324 individuals during her tenure, guiding many through the retirement process and supporting the training and development of many more.
She's ensured payroll ran seamlessly more than 750 times, served as a trusted adviser to two CEOs and been the go-to resource for employees seeking guidance to navigate their careers. She has served as mentor to many at Easton Utilities and in the Mid-Shore community, having a profound impact on them both professionally and personally.
I first met Vicki in 2021 when I interviewed for a position with another organization. She had been invited to serve on the interview panel to lend her expertise and help them make an informed decision. From the moment she spoke, I was struck by her professionalism, warmth and rare passion for HR — a field where such genuine excitement can sometimes feel scarce.
I remember thinking, If I ever have the chance to work for her, I'll take it, because there's so much I could learn from someone like her. That opportunity came in 2023, and over the past two years, I've grown immensely—not just as an HR professional, but also as a leader and as a person—thanks to her guidance.
Easton Utilities, like any organization, can be thought of as a living body. The linemen could be viewed as the muscles, the water/wastewater operators perhaps viewed as the backbone, the customer service representatives perhaps the face, and—if you ask the engineers, they might claim to be the brain. But at its core, Human Resources is the heart. It keeps the organization alive and thriving, circulating energy and support to every part.
For 30 years, Vicki was Easton Utilities' heartbeat, sustaining the organization through storms, challenges, and triumphs alike.
Her impact reaches far beyond Easton Utilities' walls. If a gas technician safely resolved a leak in your home, it's likely Vicki played a role in hiring them. If a Velocity technician helped you as a rural customers get connected to much needed high speed internet, chances are Vicki was there to interview them. When linemen braved ice storms to restore power to your neighborhood, she likely contributed to their onboarding. And when you've interacted with our professional and compassionate customer service staff, you've experienced the result of Vicki's discerning eye for talent.
In sum, if you've been impressed with Easton Utilities' service over the past 30 years, it's because Vicki had a hand in it — not only by selecting individuals who embody Easton Utilities core values but also by shaping the training that helped them excel. She has also been a great mentor to others through her Leadership Maryland classmates, impacting professionals around the State of Maryland.
Vicki's influence wasn't confined to hiring or compliance—it was deeply human. She understood that when employees face challenges, they carry those burdens home to their families. Time and again, she offered them support, showing them how to navigate their struggles so they could be present for their loved ones.
As her retirement approached, Vicki demonstrated the same grace and foresight that defined her career. This graceful departure reminds me of a lesson from sports. As a Baltimore football fan, I think of the legendary Johnny Unitas. He was the greatest quarterback of all time, but even he struggled to hang up his cleats. In a twist few like to remember, Unitas ended his career not in Baltimore but in a San Diego Chargers uniform, a move that seemed out of place for such an icon. It's a lesson in knowing when it's time to step aside. Vicki, however, has shown impeccable timing. She embraced the evolving needs of the organization, mentored her successors, and made way for the next chapter—all while ensuring Easton Utilities' heart continues to beat strong. Some leaders struggle to step aside, holding onto their roles even as the times and needs of their organizations evolve. But not Vicki. She embraced the opportunity to mentor and prepare the next generation, ensuring Easton Utilities' heart continues to beat strong long after she steps away.
One of my favorite movies is The Dark Knight. A memorable quote from that movie is Harvey Dent's reflection on heroes: "You either die a hero or live long enough to see yourself become the villain." In my years of observing HR leaders, I've seen this sentiment play out. Many HR Directors depart their roles amid controversy or burnout, others retiring from their organization leaving behind employees that are happy to see them go rather than admiration. But Vicki defied that trend. She is retiring on her own terms, as a universally respected leader—beloved by employees, admired by executives, and deeply respected throughout the mid-shore community.
After Jan. 13, as the days, weeks, months and years go by, Vicki's name will be heard less and less around Talbot County and Easton Utilities. New employees will join, and those who knew her best will retire. The stories of the great things she achieved as the heart of Easton Utilities will fade, as the stories of legends often do. But I can guarantee her name will be spoken one more time, 20 years from now …
When my time comes to retire, and I am the "old-school" HR director trying to understand the up-and-coming HR leaders looking to replace me, I'm sure I will observe them make some kind of mistake — fall flat on their face in a way that only experience can teach to avoid. And just like Vicki, I'll be there with some kind of sage advice to help them learn from it. When they ask me, "Who taught you that?" my answer will be simple: "Vicki Petro taught me that."
And with that the legend of Vicki Petro will continue.
No one asked or paid me to write this. I did so because some contributions deserve recognition, and Vicki's story is one of them. Over the past two years, I've had the honor of working with her and witnessing her remarkable leadership firsthand. Vicki has been an exceptional HR professional, a trusted advisor, a compassionate mentor, and an inspiring leader. She has not only shaped Easton Utilities but has left it stronger and better for the next generation in our mid-shore community.
For now, Vicki rides off into the sunset to begin the next chapter of a legendary life — as a grandma spending time with her grandbabies, traveling with her husband to new places across the globe and enjoying the fruits of her labor. And I'm sure in those new adventures, she will be the heartbeat of those moments, just as she has been the heartbeat for so many years at Easton Utilities and the Mid-Shore community.
Enjoy your grandbabies, Vicki. Thank you for everything.

 Author/Byline: AHMAD GARNETT agarnett@chespub.com | Section: News 
 
 516
 Words 

 Read News Document

 DENTON — Multiple vendors at Caroline Cares Community Resource Day Wednesday were reminded how amazing it is to do community work and help others.His Hope Ministries Youth Director Desiree Jefferson distributed winter clothes at the event. She was one of many vendors who had previously attended the event not to distribute resources, but to receive them.
"It's really refreshing to be able to give back," Jefferson said. "Just a couple years ago, I was somebody that was coming through the doors and receiving services myself, so it's good to see that we can help families in need."
The Caroline Cares Community Resource Day featured around 40 vendors providing information, help and food to the community.
"This is what it's all about," said Stephanie Johnson, His Hope Ministries' executive director and board member for Resources Day. "Just getting all the resources in one building so that it can be kind of an easily accessible for those who need them the most. Being able to bring those providers under one roof, on a specific day, to get those services out to everybody who needs them is huge."
One of the main focuses for Resource Day is providing many different types of help for many different people.
Some attendees face expenses they can't afford or are just in a bad financial situation, and some people are homeless. Resources Day helped with a variety of situations.
Directors expect 100 to 150 county residents experiencing homelessness to attend Resources Day every year, and they have a plan to make sure homeless residents can find shelter.
"With this particular event, they have access to walk around, talk to the vendors and see what exactly what their services are that they provide," Johnson said. "However, like when it comes to those who are actually experiencing homelessness, we have a separate room set aside for them to really dig into what their needs are and see how we can connect them with services."
Caroline County Public Schools officials attended, providing information for children on enrollment in school and many different resources for mental and physical health. United4Caroline provided free diapers for families with infants.
Chesapeake College's nursing program provided free blood pressure checks for all people in attendance. Nursing students gained experience and enjoyed serving the community.
"Oh, I love this, and I'm actually from Denton myself, so to give back to the community is amazing," Katie Reuwer, an assistant professor at Chesapeake College, said. "It's a great experience for the students to really learn about community service and helping others. I've already had some really good feedback from the students about how much they enjoy it."
Staff from Studio 107 Hair Salon in Kent Island and Edwards All Star Barbershop in Denton enjoyed providing free haircuts and styles at Resource Day, something both shops provide every year.
"There's no better feeling," Lisa Milligan, owner of Studio 107, said. "You're helping people that are maybe down on their luck or they're just getting out of jail or they're just going for jobs. It's every aspect, older people that can't afford to get their hair cut especially in this economy. So it's great to give back."

title: Tragedy underscores value of local journalism
author: ORESTES BAEZ
content:
Tragedy underscores value of local journalism

 January 31, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: ORESTES BAEZ | Section: Editorials 
 
 515
 Words 

 Read News Document

 At 8:43 p.m. on Wednesday, a tragic mid-air collision occurred over Washington involving an American Airlines regional jet and a Blackhawk helicopter from Fort Belvoir, Virginia. Both aircraft plunged into the Potomac River, and, sadly, all lives aboard were lost. As rescue operations transitioned to recovery efforts, the nation was left mourning this horrific event.While this tragedy has gripped the country, it also has highlighted the crucial role that local journalism plays in providing timely, in-depth information to communities. Let me explain.
Within minutes, The Associated Press notified national, regional and local media outlets, including the Adams Publishing Group, of the incident. Thanks to these real-time alerts, news platforms across the country, including ours, immediately shared updates through digital news feeds and live video streams.
This national coverage provided essential early updates. However, as the night turned to morning, local journalism began to take center stage, offering the in-depth, community-focused coverage that national outlets often overlook.
As soon as the news broke, Southern Maryland News — our closest newsroom to the crash site — mobilized its team. Jim Johnson, our executive editor, and Jesse Yeatman, managing editor, organized reporters to uncover how this tragedy impacted local residents.
By coordinating resources across our network, we learned that seven passengers on the flight were from Charles County, Maryland. Our reporters spoke with sources in the community, including family members, neighbors and friends, to piece together the stories of these individuals and posted the story online mid-morning.
Our production team delayed the publication of Southern Maryland News to include this crucial local angle in the Friday newspaper. We prioritize community-centered coverage — the kind that connects with readers on a deeper level.
Meanwhile in Delaware at another APG newspaper, Newark Post Editor Josh Shannon learned a figure skating coach and two young skaters were among the passengers, posting that story online for our Delaware readers.
National media may provide broad details about tragic events, but they often lack the time and resources to delve into the local impact. At most, they might air a brief mention of a local resident or include a paragraph in a larger feature.
Local newsrooms, however, are committed to covering these stories in greater detail. We highlight the lives affected within our communities, share heartfelt stories and bring light to even the darkest moments. Our role is to inform, engage and support our readers during times of crisis.
This localized approach is made possible by your support. Subscribing to local news platforms funds the journalists, editors and production teams working tirelessly to keep you informed. Without your help, local journalism would struggle to provide the essential coverage our communities need.
By subscribing to and engaging with our content, you ensure that we can continue to respond quickly to events like this. Your contributions help sustain the critical infrastructure of local journalism, allowing us to report stories that matter most to our readers.
We thank you for your continued support and ask that you keep the victims of this tragedy and their loved ones in your thoughts and prayers. Together, we can help our communities heal by sharing their stories with compassion and care.

title: Easton Postal Service short staffing causes late mail deliveries
author: AHMAD GARNETT agarnett@chespub.com
content:
Easton Postal Service short staffing causes late mail deliveries

 February 1, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: AHMAD GARNETT agarnett@chespub.com | Section: News 
 
 287
 Words 

 Read News Document

 EASTON — Easton resident Bart Pelstring has experienced late mail delivery for about two months now, and he believes his neighbors and other Easton residents have experienced the same issue.Pelstring said that he has consistently received his mail between 1 and 3 p.m. But for the past few months, Pelstring said delivery times have been "unacceptable."
"I noticed that there were times when no mail was delivered," Pelstring said. "I have neighbors that said the same thing, and then we noticed that mail was being delivered at seven or eight o'clock at night, and sometimes later than that."
Pelstring called the Post Office to speak to the post master and the response he got alarmed him, he said.
"I called to speak to the postmaster, and they told me he was out delivering mail," Pelstring said. "The girl I talked to, she said, 'well we're short staffed, we don't have enough people anymore, and we don't have backup people.'"
Mark Wahl, a strategic communications specialist for the postal service in Washington, D.C., Maryland and Virginia, detailed the Easton location's recent challenges.
"We recently experienced challenges with employee availability that did impact mail deliveries," he said. "We have taken specific actions to continue service to our valued customers."
The actions Easton Post Office plans to take include:
Authorizing overtime to allow employees to work the time necessary to deliver mail.Expanding mail deliveries to earlier in the morning and later in the evening.And using additional carriers from nearby offices to maintain mail deliveries.
"We appreciate customers' patience and understanding and expect staffing to be restored to normal levels soon," Wahl said. "With our carriers delivering later in the evening, often when it's dark, we kindly ask customers to keep porch lights on for our employees' safety."

title: Family moves into newest Patuxent Habitat for Humanity house
author: Madison Bateman Special to Southern Maryland News
content:
Family moves into newest Patuxent Habitat for Humanity house

 February 4, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Madison Bateman Special to Southern Maryland News | Section: State News 
 
 700
 Words 

 Read News Document

 Surrounded by friends and family, LaToya Carroll and her 10-year-old daughter Callie, with giant golden scissors, cut the ribbon on their new home in Lexington Park on a recent Saturday.The pair were overjoyed to now be owners of a new home built on Loudon Lane through Patuxent Habitat for Humanity.
Carroll is a St. Mary's County native, educated in local public schools and has worked in the county her whole life. She said she enjoys her work at a local high school and watching her daughter grow up.
"This is so surreal for me," she said. "I'm still waiting for it to sink in later tonight … I'm incredibly grateful."
Carroll will spend this week moving into the home.
She said Habitat for Humanity works with the community to be able to help people get into homeownership.
In May 2024, the nonprofit hosted a groundbreaking ceremony on the site of their 22nd home build. Over the next eight months, local companies and organizations pulled together to complete the house.
"It is a humbling experience to be part of such an amazing organization," said Phyllis Trouard, president of Patuxent Habitat for Humanity. "To watch the Carroll family cut the ribbon on their home was a joyful occasion. … I look forward to our next build and watching another family have the same experience."
W.M. Davis Inc. general contractors worked to complete Carroll's house, which has three bedrooms and one and a half bathrooms. Sponsors included Jerry Lewis Roofing, Barron's Lumber, C & C Plumbing and Septic, KING Electric, B&D Siteworks, Hilltop Signs and Graphics, St. Mary's County commissioners and others.
"It is through our corporate sponsors and individual donors that we can build these wonderful homes," Trouard said.
Catherine Shipman, executive director of Patuxent Habitat, explained people can apply to be chosen for this project via the nonprofit's website. The most eligible person is selected by a committee.
Individuals are eligible for a Habitat home if their present housing is not adequate and they are unable to obtain adequate housing through other conventional means. Lack of adequate housing may include problems with the present structure; water, electrical or sewage service systems; heating system problems; or failure to meet property maintenance standards.
Also taken into consideration are the number, ages and gender of children compared to the number of bedrooms in a family's current home, according to the organization's website.
A family will be considered if their annual total income is between 30% and 50% of the median income for Calvert and St. Mary's counties.
A Habitat house costs approximately $150,000 to $190,000 to build. A new Habitat homeowner will only pay what it cost to build the house through a mortgage. The average monthly payment is between $650 and $750, depending on house style, location and length of the mortgage; this includes an escrow payment for taxes, termite bond and insurance, but does not include any utilities.
Habitat acts as a lender for a 30-year interest-free mortgage. The money that families pay back is channeled into the construction of more Habitat homes for other families.
The organization requires that a family puts "sweat equity" into the home build and that they earn enough money to pay the mortgage payments. While some Habitat homeowners may receive public assistance, most have jobs.
Habitat for Humanity works in good faith with people who are at-risk financially, knowing that owning a home is not the answer to every problem, but can be an important step-often the first step-toward breaking the cycle of poverty.
Every year, Habitat for Humanity makes it their goal to complete one home build for a local family in need.
"We are currently exploring options for buildable land in Calvert County, potentially in the Prince Frederick area," Trouard said. "We are looking for houses in need of repair, donated homes or a vacant lot. We consider purchases as well as receive donations of land/homes. It is common for children to inherit a home from their parents and then find the need to sell or donate the home. We accept these estate homes, remodel or update them, and then place a deserving family in them for a reasonable mortgage. We hope to have a location and timeline by this spring so we may begin the process of our next build."

title: 14-year-old on his way to becoming a minister
author: AHMAD GARNETT agarnett@chespub.com
content:
14-year-old on his way to becoming a minister

 February 5, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: AHMAD GARNETT agarnett@chespub.com | Section: News 
 
 786
 Words 

 Read News Document

 EASTON — Javion Jones has been living his life through God since a very young age.When Javion was just 5 years old, his mother Taryn Bell can recall him setting up his toy cars, pencils, and decks of cards as his congregation to preach too.
"He would take number two pencils, and that was his church," Bell said. "He would sit there and preach to the pencil or if there were toy busses he used to have little toy cars, that was his church. Or he would play with just playing cards. I mean, I would have cards all spread out."
Now at just 14 years old Javion is further along in his career choice than most others his age. He works at Benny Smith Funeral Home as an assistant, and he is a minister in training at Union Baptist Church.
His potential for the craft was discovered years ago by many former Pastors of the church but Rev. Demetruis A. Price truly took Javion under his wings.
The Rev. Demetrius A. Price, pastor of Union Baptist Church, came to Easton from Washington, D.C., in May 2023.
Early in his time at the church, Price was going over the schedule for the installation service and wanted to have every age group accounted for. A member of the church suggested Javion to pray.
During the prayer, Price said he saw the anointing of God upon Javion's life.
"When he prayed, I felt and saw the anointing of God upon his life, and I knew right then and there that God had called him into the ministry," Price said.
PATH TO MINISTRYWhen Price arrived at Union Baptist Church, he asked God to allow him to be able to pour back into someone young who came into ministry young, just like him.
"I come to this church, and I see a country church, family church, different than across the bridge, and I'm like, 'why here?'" Price said. "And then when I met Javion, then I realized God had answered my prayer."
Price was called to ministry at 16, a couple years older than Javion. He knew what Javion would face and wanted to be there for him.
Javion's call to ministry was no surprise to anyone, but Javion didn't think it would come so soon.
"I was listening to two preachers one night," Javion said. "I was like, 'man, I want to be like them.' So the Lord had just spoke this to me. He was like, 'you're called. I'm walking to your calling.' Never to know that this calling would be so soon. I thought, like, I would be preaching at the age of like 20."
Bell was very happy that Price was here at the church when Javion got the call. She was not surprised that her son was called to ministry but she was happy that Price was here to mentor him.
"I think I always knew," Bell said. "I always knew he had it in him. So when Rev. Price and I talked, I felt so proud. I was happy that Rev. Price had came to me and told me his story and wanted to put Javion under his wing."
Javion's new position, minister in training, is difficult. He is in a rigorous year-long course in which he must learn the Bible and other essential lessons. When he is finished in April, he must do a trial sermon.
Also with his role, he is a regular minister in rotation at his church. He is in rotation with other ministers to get up on Sunday mornings and read scriptures and pray. He also will go to the hospital to visit sick or shut-in church members.
When Javion graduates the class, he will know everything that it takes to properly conduct himself as a minster.
Being a minister in training and a assistant at a funeral home is a lot of responsibility for a 14-year-old, but Price believes he can handle the sacrifices and the responsibility.
"That was the one thing that really amazed me with him, and again, I think it spoke to really his anointing," Price said. "Because when a person is anointed to do a work, with the anointing comes capacity to do it, and that's what I notice about him. The boy goes to school, he works with the funeral homes, and if he's not in this church, he's in somebody else's church."
The most challenging and most rewarding part for Javion is the responsibility of educating his peers. He says when he started ninth grade at Easton High School, everyone including students and teachers, called him "preacher" because of the way he carried himself.
The way Javion wants to engage his peers is to teach them the word of God.
"The word of God is how I can touch a generation," he said.

title: 'We are a big family here': Bringing joy and love to local seniors
author: WILL BONTRAGER wbontrager@chespub.com
content:
'We are a big family here': Bringing joy and love to local seniors

 February 6, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: WILL BONTRAGER wbontrager@chespub.com | Section: Entertainment 
 
 955
 Words 

 Read News Document

 In the year and a half since Colleen Upp became Activity Coordinator of the Amy Lynn Ferris Center at 200 Schauber Road, Chestertown, she has been having a blast, conducting new dance classes, art activities, crafts, and crazy games. Before she was there, the center had one exercise class and bingo twice a week, she said.That's changed under her watch. The parking lot there is filled, depending on what day and what fun activity, said board member Cathy Quesenberry.
"We are a big family here," Upp said with the youthful energy she exudes to anyone who walks through those doors.
It is a fun occupation, but it also is a very important job, requiring possessing a level of care ranging beyond the center, since the senior members she works with can be widowers, often live alone, and some may not have immediate family close by.
Such was the case with one member, 90-year-old Dean Wood. His wife passed away two years ago and since then, he has been religiously attending lunches there, amusing staff with his quirky mannerisms.
But one day last fall, Wood was not there — unusual for him. Upp noted that he did not miss many, if any, meals, and would ask for double helpings when he could, followed by a kind of catch phrase he adopted, "Well, you know me!"
Additionally that day, receptionist Cathy Smith told Upp and Shift Coordinator Michaela Wilson that the Meals-on-Wheels volunteer Joy Grace went by his house but he did not answer the door.
Upp and Wilson decided to drive to Wood's home to check on him.
Upp hollered for Wood, and after a while, she heard him through the window in his usual tone, a booming voice, hearing impaired.
"What? Who is that?", he cried.
"Are you ok? Dean, it's Colleen," she responded.
The silences were too far in between and Upp knew something was wrong. She was ready to climb through the window, but Wilson was already on the phone with the police. When they arrived they had to break down the door where they found Wood laying in the hallway.
He had fallen, but maintaining that distinct personality, he looked at Upp while awaiting medical transport.
"Dean, I knew something was wrong when you didn't come to lunch," she said.
Not missing a beat, his smile turned to a frown and said, "You mean I missed baked potato day? You know me, I never miss a meal!"
Wood's humorous response highlights the care, respect and appreciation, Upp, Wilson and the entire staff show towards their seniors.
Knowing Wood's habits and routines enabled them to possibly save his life. If not for their concern, he may have been in that position all weekend since Meals on Wheels only delivers on Mondays, Wednesdays and Fridays.
Wood, according to medical personnel, was likely dehydrated and malnourished leading to his fall — it could have been fatal.
Instead, he spent five weeks recovering in the hospital, first in Christiana, then in Corsica Hills where he expressed discomfort of the beds there.
Wood is happy to be back home now.
On the day of this interview, it was lunch time on a Wednesday. They were serving up roasted pulled barbecue chicken, succotash, jasmine rice, fruit, milk and juice.
Wood showed up, back in his place, and sat down and wanted milk and juice with two straws, as is his usual custom.
His eyes shined when he saw Upp, and it was evident he looked forward to seeing some of his friends, chatting with them and other staff members.
All of the seniors who came in were greeted warmly showing that these gestures of kindness, and dignity, mean as much to seniors as the meals the center serves. Vanolia Brown, of food services, asked one member where they were at yesterday, playfully chiding them.
It was this kind of personal attention that protected Wood that day.
Upp said, "Every one of us know where the members are and we know when something is off. For instance, we know the day one of them might go to AquaFit, or have an appointment with the VA hospital, or are visiting their son every Wednesday. We see their routine."
It is a vital and often under appreciated responsibility that the whole staff share.
"We love them all. We see them everyday and interact and care for them. It is extremely rewarding work," Upp said. "It takes all of us to do it."
It is this personal attention that keeps senior's minds and bodies active as well. The chance to do all the activities that Upp has planned is something they can look forward to each week.
What love she gives, she gets back in full. On her wall, in her activity room, displaying exactly how much residents appreciate her — are memories from Colleen Appreciation Day on July 11, last year.
Hanging on a hook is a whip one of her residents made for her, to poke fun at her intensity leading her exercise routines. Dancing is a joy for her, tracing back to her mother, Arlene Blanke, a former Rockette in New York, who started a dance troupe called The Happy Hoofers," while in a senior center in Virginia. Upp's vibrance and energy come thorough when in conversation.
There are countless cards of appreciation on the wall but one card sums up the great impact she has made.
"Colleen's dedication, determination, imagination, ingenuity, and enthusiasm have all made the Amy Lynn Ferris Center more fun and has encouraged new people to participate."
Quesenberry said, "She has been wonderful. We're so lucky to have her."
And what of Wood?
He is back, saying blunt things very loudly for all the tables to hear, and never passing up on a great meal.
Well...you know Dean!
For information of the activities for the center call 410-778-2564. Their hours: Monday-Friday 8 a.m. to 3:00 p.m or go to: https://www.uppershoreaging.org/centers.

title: Dorchester County auctioneer earns state title after serious injury
author: MAGGIE TROVATO mtrovato@chespub.com
content:
Dorchester County auctioneer earns state title after serious injury

 February 8, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: MAGGIE TROVATO mtrovato@chespub.com | Section: Local News 
 
 707
 Words 

 Read News Document

 EASTON — Dave Yearsley has put in the hard work and overcome challenges to continue on with his love for auctioneering.From winning a competition with a 103 degree fever that was so bad he could barely see the bidders to becoming the 2025 Maryland Bid Calling Champion after experiencing a truck accident that resulted in a brain injury, Yearsley has persevered for his passion.
Since his first auction at the Ward World Championship in the early 1970s — when he was just a preteen — Yearsley, a Dorchester County resident, has auctioneered all over, from Texas to Missouri to the United Arab Emirates.
It all started with a daring decision.
Yearsley was 11 years old when he entered "the ugliest duck you ever saw" into a competition at the Ward World Championship, he said. His parents took him to the event in Salisbury, which also had an antique decoy auction. Sitting in the stands as Walton P. Taylor auctioned off antique decoys, Yearsley noticed Taylor's rhythm and told himself, "Wow, that's something I gotta learn to do."
"So I went home and I practiced all year long," Yearsley said, "and was terrible."
The next year, Yearsley was back at the championship with his parents and another "ugly duck" he had carved.
"So I'm 12," he recalled. "I got away from my mom and dad on purpose because I knew what I was going to do."
Yearsley ducked under a roped off area where the auctioneer, Taylor, was. With security guards watching, he went up to Taylor and shook his hand. "And I said, 'Mr. Taylor, my name's Dave Yearsley, and I want to sell decoys with you today.'"
After what felt to Yearsley like "the longest minute," Taylor said, "Young man, anybody that's got the guts to stand in front of me, you're damn right you're going to sell ducks with me today."
At this point, Yearsley's parents were searching for their son. Yearsley's mom was not happy when she found him onstage.
"She came racing up in front of the stage," Yearsley recalled. "'David, you get down here right now!' (she said)."
When Yearsley asked Taylor what he should do, Taylor replied, "It's time for you to learn not to listen to your parents."
From there, Taylor took Yearsley under his wing.
"He was my mentor," Yearsley said.
It took Yearsley two years to "get somewhat competent" at auctioneering, he said. To improve his speed, he practiced over instrumental bluegrass music.
"Instrumental bluegrass music has a definite beat," he said, adding that he got every instrumental bluegrass album he could to practice over.
In auction school, Yearsley learned tongue twisters, like "Betty Botter bought some butter," to improve his craft.
AGAINST THE ODDS
In September 2018, Yearsley got into a serious truck accident. His vehicle rolled over and he came out of it with a brain injury. It was possible he would not be able to walk or talk again. Eventually, both abilities came back to him, although his speech would slur.
"I didn't have good tongue control," he said.
Yearsley was told he would probably never be able to auction again. He said his doctor told him to keep trying because practicing might help bring back the skill.
"And that's what happened," Yearsley said.
In January, Yearsley was named Maryland's Bid Calling Champion by the Auctioneers Association of Maryland.
Lynne Zink, a past president of the association and the chair of the contest, said the annual competition brings auctioneers from across the state to vie for the title.
"Once someone has won the championship, then they don't get to compete again," she said. "So David will always be our 2025 champion."
Yearsley didn't think he would win it.
"I don't cry much — and I didn't let anybody see me do it — but I cried," he said about his response to winning the award. "I said, 'My god, how could I ever do this?'"
Yearsley wasn't the only one to shed a tear after he won. Zink, who is also an auctioneer and has known Yearsley for years, was happy to see Yearsley win the Maryland title.
"Whenever you see something like that, it's encouraging because he can be a role model for others," she said. "So when the doctors give you a prognosis and then you beat the odds, gosh, it makes everybody happy. Some of us were teared up."

title: Community, vendors cut the ribbon on The Market at Dover Station
author: Konner Metz
content:
Community, vendors cut the ribbon on The Market at Dover Station

 February 12, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Konner Metz | Section: Life 
 
 352
 Words 

 Read News Document

 EASTON — A revitalized property in Easton officially cut the ribbon to celebrate its first phase of development and a flourishing new marketplace.Dover Station LLC is a project led by local developer Sevan Topjian and his wife, Keri. Its marketplace, The Market at Dover Station, brought together many local vendors and Easton community members Thursday for a ribbon-cutting ceremony.
So far, more than 100 artists, artisans and vendors are involved with The Market at Dover Station. It's become a destination for goods, services and antiques.
Keri Topjian, who manages the market, said the feedback from the Easton community has been "incredibly positive."
"I have people walk in that cry," Topjian said. "They either cry, they get the chills or they start pinching themselves and dancing."
Dover Station sits on a Dover Road property that was formerly Easton Wholesale Grocery, built in 1912. It was recently a roofing supply center and fell vacant before Sevan Topjian began the revitalization process.
Sitting along the Rails to Trails and in an accessible area of town, the property, he felt, presented the perfect opportunity for a central hub tailored toward Easton residents and visitors alike.
"It is such an honor to work on this beautiful building," he wrote. "We really wanted to showcase the incredible craftmanship of previous generations and to create a retail destination in town that features its original charm."
Keri Topjian says anchor vendors such as The Zebra Gallery and Savington & Hill Floral Co., among others, have helped kickstart the marketplace as a local shopping destination.
Speaking to a large crowd Thursday, Sevan Topjian encouraged the community to come up with creative, interactive ideas for events and collaborations at the marketplace.
Already, the market is bringing businesses and people together. Keri Topjian said it's reminded some people of European markets and others remark that "'this is what Easton needs.'"
"There's a crazy amount of connections that happen here," she said. "There's a lot of cross-collaboration among artists and artisans. There's just a lot of positive energy in the building."
The Market at Dover Station is open Monday through Saturday from 10 a.m. to 5 p.m. and Sunday from Noon to 4 p.m.

title: National Outdoors Show slated for Feb. 21, 22
author: Maggie Trovato
content:
National Outdoors Show slated for Feb. 21, 22

 February 13, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Maggie Trovato | Section: Local News 
 
 310
 Words 

 Read News Document

 The National Outdoor Show in Dorchester County is coming back for its 78th year.The show — which celebrates wildlife, as well as the trappers, watermen and sportsmen of Dorchester County — will be held Friday, Feb. 21, and Saturday, Feb. 22, at South Dorchester School in Church Creek. Bringing residents together to celebrate the county's culture, the show has it all, from a live auction to pageants to exhibits to demos and competitions that include calling, trap setting, skinning and oyster shucking.
This year, 13 young women will vie for the title of Miss Outdoors, with the pageant to take place Friday night. On Saturday, 22 girls and three boys will vie for the respective titles of Little Miss Outdoors and Little Mister Outdoors.
The National Outdoor Show also hosts the World Champion Muskrat Skinning Competition, where competitors race to skin a muskrat fastest.
During a Dorchester County Council meeting Feb. 4, the council proclaimed the month of February to be National Outdoor Show month in the county.
"And we hope that in doing so, the people of Dorchester County will see the beauty of our wildlife and gain a new appreciation of our natural resources," Council Vice President Mike Detmer read from the proclamation during the meeting.
The proclamation was received by the show's 2024 royalty, which includes Miss Outdoors Laila Insley, Little Miss Outdoors Rose Bloodsworth and Little Mister Outdoors Edwin Bramble.
"We want to thank you for being representatives of our beautiful county," Council President Lenny Pfeffer said to the three before the council handed them Dorchester County pins for their muskrat pelt sashes.
Doors to the 2025 National Outdoor Show will open at 5 p.m. on Friday, Feb. 21, with the show beginning at 7 p.m.
On Saturday, Feb. 22, doors will open at 9 a.m. At 6 p.m., the 2025 pageant winners will be introduced and a live auction will be held.

title: Trapping on the Eastern Shore (copy)
author: MARIE SAVAGE Country Cooking
content:
Trapping on the Eastern Shore (copy)

 February 19, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: MARIE SAVAGE Country Cooking | Section: Food 
 
 1623
 Words 

 Read News Document

 Back in the late 1950s and early 1960s, my younger brother Ollie would trap and hunt whatever was in season.My dad was very happy when he came home with rabbits and squirrels. The only thing he could not get my dad to eat was the muskrat, better known as the marsh rabbit.
He sold the meat to local folks who loved it, and mom loved it because he sold them as fast as he trapped them.
My brother would save the hides and stretch them on a special piece of board designed to fit the hide. He had them drying out for a certain number of days and then would package them up and ship them to his buyer.
His buyer was the late Mr. Clark Harrison Sr. of Preston. After several shipments, Mr. Harrison would send my brother a check.
Years ago, I contacted Mr. Harrison and told him the story of my 14-year-old brother, who later retired from the United States Army and did three tours of duty in Vietnam. I will dedicate today's column to those two men — the late Clark Harrison Sr. and Ollie Lowe Hitchens Jr.
Along the Eastern Shore, trapping traditions have been passed down to sons, grandsons and nephews. Living here and working on the water or in the fields near huge ditch banks, it was only natural for these locals to trap muskrats.
They'd set their traps, then go to work farming or crabbing then check the traps for an extra bounty. The muskrat numbers were once estimated to be in the millions here on the Eastern Shore, but that number soon dwindled, as you can imagine with all the trapping.
Just the sight of these animals was enough for me with the fur on, let alone skinning and cooking them.
You guessed it — I've never tasted muskrat, but I've cooked it. The first one I ever cooked was right in my Preston Road kitchen under the guidance of my late husband, John Williamson Sr., who loved them.
JOHN R.'S FAVORITE MUSKRATTrap, clean and cut muskrat in half. Soak in a large pot of cold, salted water for several hours — changing water several times. Finally, after draining well, place the meat in a large pot, cover with water, bring to a boil, boiling for 5 minutes. Remove meat from the pot, rinse and clean out the pot well. Then spray the pot with a non-sticking spray, add the meat, half cover with water. Cook until meat falls apart. Add to taste: sage, red pepper, salt and bacon or sausage grease. Don't be afraid of adding any of these ingredients and just keep adding until you can taste all of them. Cook down as much as you want but do not let it cook dry. Serve with a favorite potato dish of your choice and a green vegetable.
MUSKRAT STEWClean, cut in pieces and soak three muskrats in cold water and salt. After at least two hours, drain water off and rinse meat well. In a large pot, place the meat and just enough water to cover them. Add 2 teaspoons ground sage, 1/2 teaspoon bacon grease, salt and pepper to taste. Let cook over medium heat for 4 to 5 hours. Start on high heat until it starts boiling, then reduce heat to simmering. Let cook until meat is falling off the bone. Serve over cooked rice.
FRIED MARSH RABBITClean, cut up and soak one or two marsh rabbits in salty water for several hours — changing water several times. Rinse well in several changes of water. Remove from water and pat dry. In a large bowl add flour, sage, salt and pepper. Dredge the pieces of meat in the flour mixture and place in a fry pan with cooking oil and add 2 or 3 strips of bacon. Brown on both sides, adding more sage if needed. When meat is browned on both sides, add some water to the pan, turn heat down and let simmer as the meat becomes tender and a gravy forms.
BISHOPVILLE BULLFROG LEGS2 lb or 14 sets fresh or frozen frog legs, 1/3 cups milk, 2/3 cups corn flour, 1 tsp salt, 1/2 tsp red pepper, shortening, or cooking oil for deep frying, lemon halves, 1/2 tsp accent food enhancer, 1/2 tsp garlic powder.
In a medium bowl combine corn flour, salt, pepper, accent and garlic powder. Coat Frog legs with corn flour mixture, In a saucepan or deep fryer heat about 2 inches melted shortening or cooking oil to 375 degrees. Fry coated frog legs a few at a time in deep hot oil for 1 to 2 minutes or until done. Drain on paper towels.
HOPPING JOHN WITH VENISON2 full deer shanks, 1 tbsp oil, 1 tbsp your favorite All spice blend, 1 tsp salt, 4 cups beef stock, 3 garlic cloves (smashed), 1 celery stalk (chopped). Hoppin' John: ½ pound of dried black-eyed peas, 3 strips of bacon (chopped), ½ cup diced onion, ½ cup diced bell pepper, 1 clove garlic (minced), 1 celery stalk (diced), 3 cups of the reserved braising liquid, 2 tbsp your favorite All spice blend, 2 tsp salt, 1 cup of yellow rice (rinsed and drained), thinly sliced scallions for garnish. Bring a large pan to high heat on the stove. Rub the shanks with oil, All spice blend and salt. Once the pan is hot, sear each side of the shanks. Turn on the slow cooker and set it to low. Place the seared shanks inside and add the stock, garlic and celery. Allow the mixture to cook for 8 hours or until the meat falls off the bone. I cooked mine overnight. Once cooked, remove the meat from the slow cooker and set it aside. Strain and reserve the braising liquid for the next steps. For the Hoppin' John, place the black-eyed peas into a bowl and cover them with water. Allow them to sit while you complete the following steps. Bring the Dutch over to medium-high heat and stir in the chopped bacon. Brown the bacon and then remove bacon from the pan, leaving the grease behind. Stir in the onion, bell pepper, celery and garlic. Cook, frequently stirring, until the onion turns opaque.
Drain the remaining water from the black-eyed peas. Stir the peas into the pot. Add three cups of the braising liquid from the deer shanks, the All spice blend and salt. Bring the mixture to a boil, reduce the heat to low, cover, and allow to simmer for 45-60 minutes or until the peas begin to soften. You do not want them to completely cook. While waiting, shred the deer meat. When the peas are al dente, there should be about two cups of liquid remaining. Add more if needed. Stir in the rice and the shredded deer and bring the mixture back to a simmer. Cover and allow to cook for 20 minutes or until the rice is done. Serve with the sliced green onions atop, along with some biscuits.
RABBIT STEW3-4 pounds rabbit, 6 potatoes (quartered), 8 carrots (sliced), 1 medium onion (chopped), 1 tsp salt, 1/4 cup beef consommé, 3/4 cup beef broth, 3/4 tsp pepper, 1/4 tsp basil, 2 bay leaves, 1/4 tsp rosemary, 1/4 tsp thyme. Cut rabbit into pieces. Layer onion, potatoes and carrots in the bottom of a crock pot. Add spices to the pot. Add rabbit, salt, pepper, consommé and about 3/4 cup beef broth. Cover and cook on low for 8 hours. Thicken gravy as desired.
BRAISED RABBIT2 rabbits cut into serving pieces, 1/4 pound bacon, 3 tbsp olive oil, 1 medium onion (sliced into half-moons), 1 head garlic (cloves peeled but not chopped), white part of a fennel bulb (chopped roughly), a handful of dried mushrooms, 1/2 pound fresh mushrooms, 3 bay leaves, 1 tbsp dried oregano, 1 tsp fennel seeds, 3 cups good stock (chicken or vegetable), 5 spring onions, 1 cup finely chopped fennel fronds, 2 tbsp fresh chopped oregano, salt. Cook the dried mushrooms in 2 cups of hot water. Let them sit, covered, for at least 1 hour. Heat the olive oil in a Dutch oven and cook bacon until crispy. Remove the bacon and turn the heat up to medium-high. Salt the rabbit pieces and brown them well. Add the chopped onion, fennel bulb and the dried mushrooms and saute until they begin to brown. Add the fresh mushrooms and garlic and saute until they begin to brown. Add salt. Add the Armagnac and stir well to combine.
Turn the heat all the way up and add back the rabbit, the bacon, and add the bay leaves, fennel seeds and dried oregano and mix well. Pour in just enough stock just to cover the rabbit. Do not totally submerge it. Bring to a simmer, taste for salt (add more if need be), cover and set over low heat for an hour, or 45 minutes if you are using chicken or domestic rabbit. After an hour, test to see if the meat is tender. You want it to be practically falling off the bone. At this point you can pull the rabbit from the pot, remove from the bone and add back to the pot or keep it in the pot on bone. Add the green onions, garlic and fennel fronds and stir to combine. Simmer uncovered for 3 minutes or until you believe it is done. Be careful to not overcook.
There are a few opportunities coming up for you to enjoy a great muskrat dinner without having to stare down skinned muskrats. This year, the 76th annual National Outdoor Show will be held Feb. 21 and 22, located at the South Dorchester K-8 school at 3485 Golden Hill Rd. in Church Creek. The muskrat will be served on Saturday only at 1 p.m.

title: Demolition begins as developers wait for Easton Crossing project approval
author: Maggie Trovato
content:
Demolition begins as developers wait for Easton Crossing project approval

 February 19, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Maggie Trovato | Section: Local News 
 
 442
 Words 

 Read News Document

 EASTON — Demolition of the abandoned silos and storage buildings on Brookletts Avenue is underway.The tearing down of the former Perdue AgriBusiness operation is one step in The Arc Central Chesapeake Region's plan to build Easton Crossing, a mixed-use development, on about 6.29 acres between Brookletts Avenue and South Street.
Ross Benincasa, who is senior vice president of community development at Chesapeake Community Development, a subsidiary of The Arc Central Chesapeake Region, said the demolition will take six months. He said some of the material from the silos will be salvaged for potential future use.
Although demolition has begun, the project still requires site plan approval from the Easton Planning Commission. It is scheduled to go before the Planning Commission on Thursday. Following site plan approval, the project will need standard grading and building permits.
Easton resident Maury Schlesinger was walking his dog Monday when he noticed demolition was underway. Although he has some concerns with future plans for the site, Schlesinger said he thinks the demolition is "appropriate."
"Something has to happen there," he said.
According to the draft site plan for Easton Crossing, if approved, the development would create 123 multi-family units, including 29 affordable apartments priced below the market rate. It would also bring parking, stormwater management and landscaping to the property.
The property would have six buildings, with some buildings that include commercial spaces. The first building, which would have 15 units, is expected to open in December 2027 if the plan is approved.
Benincasa said project plans "emphasize public green spaces."
"We want the community as well as our tenants to enjoy the space, which is why nearly 30% of the property will be open public space," he said.
According to Planning Commission documents, town staff would like the developers to address scale and consistency concerns with one of the proposed buildings.
Schlesinger also has concerns with that building. He said it would bring too much density to one area of the property.
"I think it needs to be relooked at," he said.
Schlesinger brought up concerns with traffic and the need for traffic improvements.
"I'm not opposed to a redevelopment project on that site, and I think that there's some really good stuff they're trying to do here," he said. "It just could be moved from being a good project to a really great project that the town could be really proud of and could show off as good, small-town urban redevelopment."
Benincasa said community feedback has been helpful. He said feedback helped the developers define what types of units are wanted in the area as well as determine which materials are "more reflective" of the town's historic architecture.
Schlesinger said he hopes the Planning Commission "does the right thing."

title: 'Check' this out: Young and old gather for chess meet-up
author: Michael Reid mreid@somdnews.com
content:
'Check' this out: Young and old gather for chess meet-up

 February 19, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Michael Reid mreid@somdnews.com | Section: News 
 
 636
 Words 

 Read News Document

 There were plenty of kings, queens and knights at the Lexington Library on Sunday, Feb.16 but it had nothing to do with a Renaissance Fair.Instead, they were all confined to a space of about 157 inches as the branch held a chess meet-up.
"There are places to play online, this is a real good way to get into the community we have," St. Mary's Library Team Librarian Jake Parsons said, adding that about 25 players took advantage of the weekend event.
Players ranged from five years old to older adults, and one player was even dressed in a Scooby-Doo costume.
"I think with the internet so common nowadays we're getting some brain rot," Jason McCauley of Lexington Park said as he pondered his next move against Tom Hollinghead of Great Mills, "and chess kind of helps me get back into thinking. I use my mind more."
"We had a big family so we all played against each other and then I went away from it a long time and now I'm getting back into for a lot of the reasons he's talking about," Holinghead said. "I'm a firm believer that it really helps in getting the gears turning and exercises your brain in different places.
And where did Hollinghead stand when it came to family supremacy on the board?
"I rose to the top," he said.
The two-hour drop-in event was open to all levels and ages.
"I had some professors I wanted to show up, and it's one of the few things I feel where you can sit down and focus on for six straight hours," Mason Brady of California said when asked why he took up the game.
A few years back, he was the Class E New Mexico state champion as a college sophomore and the following year claimed the Class D New Mexico state championship.
"I'm not a great attacker, and at the end of the day you're not going to win unless your opponent makes a mistake so I like to sit back and wait for that to happen and hope I'm not the one to [make a mistake]," Brady said.
Stewart Smith, who is co-founder of PAX CHESS & Strategy, said the 1,500-year-old game is making a comeback of sorts.
"I would say so. It's a combination of things," he said. "During the pandemic a lot of people had a lot of extra free time and there was online chess, which people were familiar with the idea of playing," he said, adding the Netflix series "The Queen's Gambit," about a 1960s female chess prodigy, has also helped in the game's resurgence.
"The other thing that I think has helped chess make a comeback is its very accessible, you can play it very quickly, and with the addition of all the [various time formats] people can play it very casually or seriously and so that addition of people being able to play on their phone has caused a lot of people to get into the game more," Smith said. "The online experience is not the same, you don't get to meet new people, and you're facing random players around the world anonymously."
A few feet away, Bryce Klindworth, 6, of Great Mills battled his mother Danielle while wearing his Scooby-Doo costume while 5-year-old Gryffin Daniels of California needed to stand on a chair in order to see the pieces on the board.
"I would say because I just like the pieces and it's just a lot of fun," said Ryan Thomsen, 8, of Hollywood, whose favorite piece was the coveted queen. "It makes it fun because it's nice to play with other people and a lot of people play it. I play with my brothers and parents and I beat at least everyone in my family once. If you haven't played chess, you should try it. It's really fun and there's a lot to learn."

title: State, county leaders join Frederick Douglass descendants to unveil new plaque
author: Konner Metz
content:
State, county leaders join Frederick Douglass descendants to unveil new plaque

 February 21, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Konner Metz | Section: Local News 
 
 482
 Words 

 Read News Document

 EASTON — Exactly 130 years after Frederick Douglass' death, the Talbot County-born abolitionist and civil rights leader was honored for his lasting impact on freedom, equality and education.Descendants, county leaders and state transportation officials gathered to unveil a historical marker honoring Douglass at the Talbot County Courthouse Thursday morning. They were joined by Lt. Gov. Aruna Miller.
Miller spoke at the unveiling, noting that Douglass' calls for justice still demand answers to date. She pointed out the crucial role he played in advancing education for Black Americans during a time when it was not widely accepted.
"Frederick Douglass dared to see beyond the chains that bound him," Miller said. "He knew that true liberation was not just freedom of the body, but freedom of the mind."
The marker, one of nearly 800 official historical signs created by the Maryland Department of Transportation, will be placed at Tappers Corner Road and Route 303, just northeast of Cordova and near Douglass' birthplace.
Julie Schablitsky, cultural resources chief for the Maryland Department of Transportation, said after working with Douglass family descendants and community members, an addition was made to the text on the historical marker: Anna Murray.
Murray, Douglass' first wife, was "strong" and "loyal," Schablitsky said. Many speakers Thursday maintained that Murray's fight for equality and justice was just as important as Douglass'.
Schhablitsky noted Murray was crucial in Douglass' escape from slavery, sewing the sailor suit he used to disguise himself while fleeing north.
Kenneth Morris Jr., Douglass' great-great-great-grandson, called Murray an "equal partner" to her husband.
"It was Anna who made his escape possible," Morris said. "Her strength, sacrifice and unwavering support ensured that his journey to freedom was not just his alone, but part of a greater fight for justice that continues today. I'm just as proud of her as I am of him."
"Her story reminded me that during difficult and challenging times, we must rely on each other and sometimes risk our own safety for the ones we love," Scablitsky said.
Other local and state officials spoke during the event, including Department of Transportation Secretary Paul Wiedefeld, Talbot County Council President Chuck Callahan and Easton Mayor Megan Cook.
Edward "Boots" Robinson, president of the Frederick Douglass Honor Society, and Tarence Bailey, Douglass' five-time great nephew, provided words as well.
"No place is more important to mark his footsteps than where Frederick Douglass experienced his first taste of freedom while living with his grandparents, enjoying those few spiritful, joyful years," Robinson said.
Bailey said that when he was growing up in Easton, many of his elders didn't openly discuss the history of slavery in the area. Descendants of Harriet Tubman weren't allowed to talk about Tubman outside their houses, Bailey said.
The roadside marker will give the younger generations a chance to learn about that history and the local legacy of Douglass, Bailey said.
"We didn't have this," Bailey said. "So to be able to give it to the next generation is really special."

title: Talbot County’s United States Colored Troops fought with valor and honor
author: PAUL W. CALLAHAN Talbot County Historical Society
content:
Talbot County’s United States Colored Troops fought with valor and honor

 February 22, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: PAUL W. CALLAHAN Talbot County Historical Society | Section: Local News 
 
 566
 Words 

 Read News Document

 Though President Lincoln's Emancipation Proclamation, issued on Jan. 1, 1863, did not free the enslaved people in Maryland, it allowed African Americans throughout the nation to serve in the Union Army as part of the United States Colored Troops. This gave Black Americans the opportunity to fight not only for their nation, but also for their freedom and citizenship — and fight they did.Frederick Douglass, a native son of Talbot County and a leading African American abolitionist, writer, orator and newspaper publisher, placed steady pressure on the Lincoln administration to include African Americans in the Union Army. Douglass met with the president, used his influence to the fullest, and has received great credit towards the creation and support of the United States Colored Troops.
During the Civil War, nearly 180,000 African Americans served in the Union Army, with almost 80,000 recruited from states that remained in the Union. Of this number, 8,718 were from Maryland. Talbot County led all Maryland counties in total enlistments.
By the start of the war, African Americans in Talbot County were nearly equally divided, with half enslaved and half free. Many enslaved individuals from Talbot earned their freedom by enlisting in the United States Colored Troops.
The Civil War saw the first draft in U.S. history to enroll men for battle. There were four draft rounds during the war, but Talbot County was only subjected to the first. The enlistment of Talbot's African Americans counted toward the county's quota of men required for the Union Army. Because so many Black men enlisted, no white men from Talbot were drafted after the first round.
Many senior Union commanders voiced skepticism about how African Americans would perform in battle and questioned their willingness to fight. Many formerly enslaved men had little experience with firearms and could neither read nor write, as they were often prohibited from learning. Time and time again, Black soldiers proved their mettle in combat, exhibiting great valor, courage and a ferocious fighting spirit.
Men from Talbot County served in every United States Colored Troops regiment formed in Maryland and in the United States Navy. They participated in major battles in Virginia, North Carolina and South Carolina in 1864 and 1865, including the battles to capture Petersburg and Richmond.
Talbot County soldiers were also involved in the final battles leading to the defeat of General Robert E. Lee's army and were present when Lee surrendered at Appomattox Courthouse.
This May, the Talbot Historical Society, located in downtown Easton, will present an exhibit titled "With Valor and Honor — Talbot County's United States Colored Troops During the Civil War."
This exhibit will feature numerous images and artifacts that tell the story of the courage, honor and valor displayed by these men.
"They served their nation at a time when many Black people in the Union states were still enslaved, and those who were free had no rights of citizenship," the Historical Society said in a press release. "Our staff has been working diligently to research this history and, most importantly, to identify the names of the men who served. To date, we have uncovered the names of over 550 men from Talbot County who served in the Union's United States Colored Troops — and we are still discovering more."
During this exhibit, the Talbot Historical Society will have these men's military records available so those who are interested, including these men's descendants, can have direct access to this rich history.

title: VFW plans parade to welcome Vietnam veterans home 50 years after end of war
author: WENDY WEITZEL wweitzel@chespub.com
content:
VFW plans parade to welcome Vietnam veterans home 50 years after end of war

 March 1, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: WENDY WEITZEL wweitzel@chespub.com | Section: Local News 
 
 374
 Words 

 Read News Document

 EASTON — When Kenley Timms returned home from the Vietnam War, he did not receive a warm welcome."I was never spit on, never thrown trash at, but when I landed at National Airport in Washington, I walked into the airport, and there was a lady and her child, probably 5, 7 years old, and I spoke to the child, and that woman picked that child up like I was the devil," Timms said.
Other returning soldiers faced even more hostile receptions upon returning to a country where political tides had turned and the Vietnam War, unbeknownst to those deployed, had become deeply unpopular.
"And at the time, I didn't know about it because when I was in Vietnam, I didn't know what was happening back in the United States," Timms said.
Now, 50 years after the war ended, Timms, the commander of VFW Post 5118, and a collection of other veterans at the post in Easton are seeking to give their fellow service members the welcome home they never got.
On March 30, the VFW post plans to hold a wreath laying ceremony before a parade through downtown Easton and a short program in honor of Vietnam veterans.
"I'm hoping that we'll have a couple thousand people standing in the streets, waving to us," Timms said. "You'll see a lot of veterans walking or riding, ones that are able to walk, tears rolling down their face."
The parade route, which has already been approved by the Town of Easton, will begin at the intersection of Dover and Washington streets, then make its way down Washington Street and Glebe Road to the VFW. Event organizers plan to distribute American flags for spectators to wave.
But beyond event attendance, the Vietnam veterans behind the event are hoping to gather parade participants and gain assistance with transportation for veterans who are unable to walk the parade route.
"We need transportation, but we don't want a bus. We want something where people can see them, the public can wave to them," Timms said.
"What we're looking for is people to participate," added Wayne Hall, president of the VFW's Vietnam Veterans Chapter. "If anybody has any military vehicles, the collectors, we'd be glad to have them."
Those who wish to be involved in the event can contact 410-310-5748.

title: A yacht to do: Bay Bridge Boat Show comes to Kent Narrows
author: ANDREA GRABENSTEIN agrabenstein@chespub.com
content:
A yacht to do: Bay Bridge Boat Show comes to Kent Narrows

 March 5, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: ANDREA GRABENSTEIN agrabenstein@chespub.com | Section: News 
 
 601
 Words 

 Read News Document

 KENT NARROWS — Setting sail into the boating season with a new charter, the Bay Bridge Boat Show is coming to the Kent Narrows area at Safe Harbor Narrows Point April 11 through April 13.After 26 years at the Bay Bridge Marina, the new venue at Safe Harbor Narrows Point promises to retain the spirit attendees love while strengthening community fellowship alongside even more amenities and better parking.
"We are extremely excited that we were able to keep the Bay Bridge Boat Show in Queen Anne's County and think the new location at Safe Harbor Marina Kent Narrows will only enhance the economic impact to the region," Heather Tinelli, director of Queen Anne's County Economic and Tourism Development said. "It is our hope that patrons of the boat show will stay overnight, enjoy all of our wonderful dining options, shop locally and of course buy a boat."
Whether boat enthusiasts looking to buy a new vessel or those looking for a day on the banks of the Chesapeake Bay, the powerboat show is complete with services, products, exhibitions and shipshape retail therapy.
Community and conservation are a focus of this year's spring power boat show, according to Annapolis Boat Shows' President, Mary Ewenson.
Committed to sustainability and conservation and environmental impacts, the boat show is proud to welcome numerous non-profits, and environmental organizations highlighting resources with free seminars, including the Department of Natural Resources, Coastal Conservation Association of Maryland, and the Department of Agriculture.
"Getting people excited about boats is a good way to get excited about the Chesapeake Bay. If you don't get out on the Bay you don't know it needs protecting, Ewenson said.
She is excited that by partnering with local businesses and building connections with the community, the show really connects with the community and emphasizes local involvement.
Welcoming attendees by land and water, both local and away, the boat show offers a unique opportunity to showcase the culture of the surrounding Kent Narrows, including additional shopping, restaurants, hotels, businesses, and the Cross Island Trail.
"It will really benefit the whole area. This is not a convention center, this is people's lives and businesses," Ewenson said of this year's show venue.
In addition to showcasing the local area, the boat show also seeks to provide accessibility to anyone with maritime interests, with onsite hands-on training available to make any land lubber sea worthy of a new vessel.
With new powerboats on the market to behold, an expanded demo dock will offer attendees the opportunity to climb aboard a wide array of powerboats of every style and size. From fishing boats and trawlers to pontoon boats and luxury cruisers, last year's powerboat show saw more than 250 boats, and at least as many are expected this season, she said.
"If you're a seasoned boater or a first timer, the show will offer something new for everyone to explore," said Annapolis Boat Shows' General Manager Sheila Jones.
Marine industry career networking opportunities will also be available alongside information about nearby boating clubs and schools.
And a great aspect of spring shows is that you can take your new boat out on the water right away, she said.
"Whether you're here for the boats, the education, or the food and entertainment, it's always a ton of fun. And the beautiful new venue means visitors may board even more exciting new powerboats and shop everything from gear and accessories to electronics, communication equipment, education, clubs, and more."
Shuttles will run between the lot at the old outlets off Exit 41 and the show.
An event certainly not to 'skiff', you can 'ketch' more information about the Bay Bridge Boat Show and other local shows at BayBridgeBoatShow.com.

title: Family, friends celebrate Mary O'Donnel's 100th birthday
author: Konner Metz
content:
Family, friends celebrate Mary O'Donnel's 100th birthday

 March 5, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Konner Metz | Section: Local News 
 
 234
 Words 

 Read News Document

 EASTON — Mary O'Donnel was surrounded by family and friends Wednesday afternoon to celebrate her 100th birthday.Many gathered around at HeartFields Assisted Living in Easton for lunch, cake, birthday photos and the singing of "Happy Birthday." Family and staff decorated the lunch room with flowers, banners and balloons.
Mary O'Donnel, adorned in a 100th birthday pin and sporting high spirits, blew out her birthday candles with her grandson Liam. The birthday cake featured her favorite colors — blue and orange.
Mary O'Donnel said the key to so many years has simply been "good living." Her grandson said she's "feisty" and always has stories to tell.
"She shoots from the hip," Liam O'Donnel said.
Joining the celebration were cousin Patsy McEneaney, family friends Riley MacIntyre and Mary Moreton, and Ladonna Fowler, Liam O'Donnel's girlfriend. HeartFields Assisted Living staff members and fellow residents joined the celebration, too.
Mary's late husband, Richard, would've celebrated his 98th birthday Thursday, born exactly two years and one day after his wife of over 75 years. They lived in Severna Park for many years.
Moreton drove all the way from Philadelphia to attend Wednesday, and said she wouldn't miss the celebration for anything.
Since she was five, Moreton knew Mary and Richard O'Donnel, who previously lived in Drexel Hill, Pennsylvania. She recalled camping memories and the impact Mary O'Donnel has had on her life and values.
"She's taught me about love and life and hard work," Moreton said.
