title: VAMSA makes history with AI assistance to support veterans
author: ANDREA GRABENSTEIN agrabenstein@chespub.com
content:
VAMSA makes history with AI assistance to support veterans

 March 7, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: ANDREA GRABENSTEIN agrabenstein@chespub.com | Section: Local News 
 
 1119
 Words 

 Read News Document

 The Queen Anne's County Veteran and Military Support Alliance (VAMSA) has made history recently as the first veteran service organization in the nation to leverage artificial intelligence (AI) to strengthen Veterans Assistance (VA) disability claim submissions.Signing a memorandum of understanding with Vet Mentor AI Feb. 22, VAMSA is utilizing technology to strengthen disability claims support programs and streamline processes of support for all veterans.
Anyone who has ever had to submit a claim can understand the rigmarole necessary to jump through and the often overwhelming process involved.
One who knew such first hand struggles of facing denied disabilities claims was U.S. Marine Corps veteran and Vet Mentor AI founder and CEO Paul Hylenski who initially created a personal program to help him and his friends process information before quickly realizing it could be turned into an application to assist others.
Along with the challenges service members can face returning to civilian life, such as delayed impact from experiences like PTSD, many vets don't know how to apply for benefits and are unsure of their eligibility, according to Hylenski.
Vet Mentor AI supports veterans throughout the entire process of filing successful benefits claims by streamlining the process, he said. The goal of Vet Mentor AI is to ensure that every veteran has access to the support they deserve, making the complex claims process more accessible and effective.
The process which previously could take months if not years of organizing paper work now can be available in a manner of seconds, he said.
Offering personalized seamless support to simplify complex processes for user ease, humanistic AI avatar guides include a Denied Claims Assistant, a Virtual Veterans Officer and a Compensation and Pension Exam Simulation.
The program will be able to scour the internet to provide concise and specific aspects needed for a specific claim.
The program is specifically designed to streamline the process, officials will be able to get answers to questions much faster and even tell the strength of a claim.
In addition to detecting human error made to denied claims, the program will make significant headway in eradicating "claim sharks" or non-VA-accredited affiliations that try to charge for phony filing assistance, he said.
VAMSA officials were over the moon for the opportunity to bring the program to the community and expand their services by performing at a much higher level efficiency rate, according to Eric Johnson, VAMSA executive director and Air Force veteran.
The Eastern Shore has fewer resources compared to western shore counterparts, according to Johnson.
Whether appealing denied decisions or establishing new claims, VAMSA spends the most amount of its time on claims, according to Johnson, who was sold "immediately" withVet MentorAI and noted a "minimum" of 75% staffing time will be cut through through the program.
"Eastern Shore residents often feel the overall resource availability is like a resource desert when compared with what is available on the Western Shore — VAMSA [alongside County partners] are working very hard to counter this perception," Johnson said.
With the workload saving, Johnson said, they will be able to expand service reaches, expand the organization's services and mission to address inequity faced by veterans and their families across the Eastern Shore.
VAMSA has been asked to be the face of the organization's expanding mission and inequity faced by veterans and families on the Eastern Shore.
"I can't say enough about the capabilities," Johnson said.
With the streamlined services, VAMSA will be able to do more of what it is meant to do:spending time with clients and further strengthening service resources across the Mid-Shore region.
Safety and support is a crucial aspect of the program and VAMSA access support will be available through every step of their claim's journey, according to Johnson.
The program is versatile and whether for those computer savvy or those who are not, clients will never be left on their own to navigate the technology.
VAMSA officials can help walk applicants through the process, or applicants can use the program from the comfort of their own home, Johnson said.
"At the end of the day it's going to give us valuable information and we're still going to deliberately go through it and add the human touch," he said.
The tool will scrub the internet for research and academic sources studies to support service based conditions in a timely manner that even the most diligent VSO can't accomplish.
"It's taken people years to get answers, and this, it's literally taken seconds," Chad Baker, VAMSA board member and Army veteran said.
The program can tell the applicant what aspects are still needed and probably most importantly, The HIPAA certified program will never store or send out personal information and perhaps most importantly, Vet Mentor AI will never under any circumstances make up information it does not know the answer to, Hylenski emphasized.
"This is setting veterans up for success," said VAMSA board member and Navy veteran Cynthia Arnette. As a member of the Department of Veterans Affairs assisting veterans and their families get benefits for decades, Arnette could remember the old school filing days of pen and paper.
"Now look how far we've come," she said proudly.
Like many, Arnette was wary of the growing rise of AI, but was "elated" at the prospects of VetMentor AI to assist claims and streamline the service.
The program will not be replacing Veteran Service Organizations, "but strengthening them," according to Baker, who noted support for veterans assistance is a crucial need in the country. Decisions are made everyday that not only affect veterans, but the livelihood of spouses.
Baker looked forward to the program eventually being utilized across the country and assisting long time coming support, especially Vietnam vets and their families and eliminating millions of dollars in backlog from human error.
"I really believe by using this tool, it puts something in the hands of the VA (Veterans Assistance) that they can act on exponentially more quickly, " Johnson said, adding somberly, "People literally die waiting for their claim."
Transforming the lives of veterans one claim at a time, "You are the reason I credited this tool, " Hylenski said to the members of VAMSA, noting their passion in assisting veterans was nothing less than inspirational.
"This is going to change the world," he said.
VAMSA will never lose sight of its human touch in assisting local veterans and coupling the advanced AI with its team of dedicated expertise to make advancements for those who have more than earned it.
"As long as there is a human element on both ends checking and validating, that's how you do artificial intelligence," Johnson said.
The VAMSA office is located at 301 Pier One Road Stevensville.
More information about VAMSA, including events for veterans can be found a.
More information about Vet Mentor AI can be found at https://www.vetmentorai.com.
This story has been updated to correct a quote by Eric Johnson referring to availability of resources and resource deserts.

While the national significance of being the first such organization is mentioned, the primary context is local implementation and regional challenges, aligning most closely with 'Local Life.'

title: Pair of World War II vets honored as they turn 100
author: MARTY MADDEN mmadden@somdnews.com
content:
Pair of World War II vets honored as they turn 100

 March 11, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: MARTY MADDEN mmadden@somdnews.com | Section: News 
 
 505
 Words 

 Read News Document

 A salute earlier this month to two Maryland men who served in World War II and are reaching the age of 100 was as much a celebration of citizenship as it was age and military service.The birthday celebration for Calvert Count yresidents John William Mackall Sr. and Robert Augusto Padilla was held at a jam-packed Lusby American Legion. The chance to say "thank you" to a remarkable generation drew the attention of several community leaders.
"The World War II generation is just something different," Brandon Temple, chairman of the Calvert Commission for Veterans and Military Families, said.
The event was a collaborative effort by the American Legion and the Veterans of Foreign Wars.
In fact, it was VFW Post 2632 in St. Mary's County that received an inquiry that led to the special event.
Marco Padilla wanted to make sure his grandfather's contributions eight decades ago would be remembered for his 100th birthday. Robert "Roberto" Augusto Padilla turned 100 on Tuesday.
"We all knew he was going to live to be 100," Marco told Southern Maryland News. "He's incredibly healthy. We just wanted to honor him. We reached out to the VFW, we went to their website."
Roberto Padilla's story is a wartime odyssey that led to U.S. citizenship that was paid forward from day one.
"He was born in Guatemala," Marco said. "His father was a diplomat. He lived in Italy until he was 17."
When Roberto's family moved to the U.S., the teen enlisted in the U.S. Army and became part of the U.S. Army's 23rd infantry.
"He was a medic," Marco said of his grandfather, who served from July 1943 to May 12, 1945.
Roberto saw action during the Normandy invasion in 1944, which helped librate Europe.
For his bravery and as one of the country's newer citizens, he was awarded the European-African-Middle Eastern Campaign Medal and an overseas service bar.
When his military service ended, Roberto Padilla settled in Maryland, established a successful business in Washington, D.C., and raised seven children.
"He's our patriarch," Marco said. "We're incredibly proud. We owe everything to him."
Mackall, who enlisted in 1944, embarked on a 24-year career with the U.S. Army, retiring in 1968 as a staff sergeant.
During his military career, Mackall earned the National Defense Service Medal with Oak Leaf Cluster and the Army Commendation Medal. He is also recognized as an expert marksman.
Post-military, Mackall served the Sunderland community as its postmaster for 20 years and has been active with the American Legion's Gray-Ray Post 220 in Prince Frederick.
While Mackall's American Legion membership has spanned 80 years, Padilla had no prior veterans organization tie. That situation was remedied Sunday when the local legionnaires presented him with a membership.
Joe Cicchollo, the Veterans of Foreign Wars' Maryland commander, told the audience the who participated in the World War II campaign truly are "the greatest generation," making contributions to labor, economics and civic organizations.
"We have to say 'thank you' to the veterans," Cicchollo said.
"We've got a lot of good veterans here in Southern Maryland," Harry Pool, Post 2632 commander, said of the members who aid others in the community.

 CENTREVILLE — Queen Anne's County High School will honor the legacy of Vietnam veterans with a distinguished Veterans Day ceremony at the QACHS auditorium March 29 at 2 p.m.Veterans, their families, and the public are invited to attend the distinguished ceremony to honor all who served during the Vietnam Era during the 50th anniversary of the official end of the Vietnam War.
A day of fellowship to honor and remember the valiant service of all Vietnam War veterans, all are welcome to ensure their legacy is preserved for future generations. All Vietnam Era service members who served on active duty anywhere in the world are invited for a pinning ceremony.

A proclamation will be presented by the Queen Anne County's Board of Commissioners with participation from Boy Scout Troop 278 and the U.S. Naval Sea Cadet Corps.

title: $10 rentals?: Exploring Maryland's old boarding houses
author: MARTY MADDEN mmadden@somdnews.com
content:
$10 rentals?: Exploring Maryland's old boarding houses

 March 19, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: MARTY MADDEN mmadden@somdnews.com | Section: News 
 
 466
 Words 

 Read News Document

 With today's high housing costs, it maybe hard to believe there was a time when you could rent a room in Maryland for $5 or $10 a week. Note, however, it was almost a century ago and the atmosphere wasn't posh.In less than 50 minutes, Grace Mary Brady of the Bayside History Museum gave attendees of a lecture, held March 16 at the North Beach Town Hall, a black and white pictorial tour, south to north, of some of the boarding houses, motels and businesses with second-floor rooms that provided lodging in southern Maryland.
"Where did we stay, where did we go?" was the theme of the lecture, which was cosponsored by the museum, Calvert Library and the John Hanson Daughters of the American Revolution.
"The whole county was full of boarding houses," Brady said of the 1940s, which predated construction of the Chesapeake Bay Bridge, a project that helped end Calvert County's stature as a top getaway location for residents of the Washington, D.C., metropolitan area as the Eastern Shore and Atlantic Ocean towns became much more within reach.
In additional to the Twin Beaches in northern Calvert, Solomons in the south was booming with visitors during the 1940s as World War II was underway.
One popular location in Solomons, according to Brady, was Sunset View, which accommodated wives of U.S. servicemen who were stationed in the area.
Another structure providing homes to the families of servicemen was Barreda House at Drum Point Landing. Brady said the house was demolished after World War II ended.
In addition to the photographs of many houses and businesses that were either burned down or demolished, Brady had drawings of some large hotels that were planned but never built.
"Chesapeake Beach was intended as a resort for the wealthy," Brady said in revealing a sketch of a massive hotel that had been planned in 1894.
A hotel that was built in the beach town at the turn of the century was the Belvedere, which was constructed "to attract gambling." Brady said the Belvedere burned down in 1923.
Other photos that drew some audible reactions from the audience included one of Franchi's Restaurant in North Beach and an image of the original Woodburn's in Solomons.
All of the museum's winter lecture series presentations are available on the facility's YouTube page.
Other presentations in the Bayside History Museum's lecture series this year have included Stephen Godfrey's "Fossil Roadshow," a talk on the history of Camp Chesapeake and accounts of "Southern Maryland Before the Naval Base."
The final in the series is scheduled for March 30. Local author Don Shomette will present a talk on "The Canadian Campaign Before the American Revolution."
The Bayside History Museum, which will mark 20 years this October, is located on 4th Street in North Beach and is open year round Wednesday through Sunday from 9 a.m. to noon.

title: Lip Sync Battle fundraiser returns April 26
author: Staff Writer
content:
Lip Sync Battle fundraiser returns April 26

 March 19, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Staff Writer | Section: Local News 
 
 431
 Words 

 Read News Document

 Get ready to rock and roll as Talbot Interfaith Shelter's Lip Sync Battle fundraiser returns to the Waterfowl Building in Easton on Saturday, April 26.It promises to be another epic event to raise funds in support of the shelter's mission to fight homelessness on the Mid-Shore by providing shelter, stability, support and a path to success for local families and individuals in need.
This is the ninth year for the organization's signature event. What started out as a way for Talbot Interfaith Shelter to stand out in a sea of local fundraisers has turned into something more.
"There are so many amazing events for so many worthy causes in our community," shares shelter Executive Director Julie Lowe. "When we first started the Lip Sync Battle, our goal was simply to put on an event that would capture people's attention. But over the course of nine years, it has meant so much more for our organization than we ever could have imagined. So many people from all areas of our community participate in Lip Sync every year, whether they are competing, volunteering, donating, or attending the live show. It has been the catalyst for building an incredibly strong community around our mission and around the neighbors we serve."
Lip Sync Battle has grown so much that last year's event raised more than $112,000 for Talbot Interfaith Shelter. This prompted an ambitious goal of $125,000 for this year's event, which is being presented by Sun Management Rising Technologies.
Fans do not have to wait until April 26 to get their Lip Sync fix. The competition is already underway, and teams from across our community are currently vying for votes to win one of two competitions. The Live Show Competition teams will be performing on stage at the main event at the Waterfowl Building, and the Video Competition teams have created musical masterpieces that will be shown online and during the live show.
Teams can win in their respective competitions in one of two ways. Each team is duking it out to see who can raise the most in support of Talbot Interfaith Shelter. Community members can vote by donating directly to their team, or selecting their team when purchasing event tickets or signing up for an event sponsorship. In addition, a panel of impartial judges will decide the winners of the best performance award in each category.
Visit talbotinterfaithshelter.org to meet the teams, purchase tickets and vote for your favorites. For questions about the Lip Sync Battle, or to learn more about sponsorships, contact Talbot Interfaith Shelter Director of Development and Marketing Laura Richeson at lauraricheson@talbotinterfaithshelter.org or 443-786-6962.

title: On a mission of love: Hope Warehouse welcomes grand-reopening
author: ANDREA GRABENSTEIN agrabenstein@chespub.com
content:
On a mission of love: Hope Warehouse welcomes grand-reopening

 March 20, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: ANDREA GRABENSTEIN agrabenstein@chespub.com | Section: Business 
 
 490
 Words 

 Read News Document

 QUEENSTOWN — Providing the community with quality low cost furniture to support its mission of community support, Haven Ministries welcomes the grand reopening of its used furniture and home furnishings outlet Hope Warehouse in Queenstown March 15.More organized and with better selections than ever before, "It's gorgeous, it's like a new boutique," said Cheryl Valentine, of Stevensville.
Complete with beautiful lighting and new paint, following six weeks of renovations, the store is now organized by home section type, including living room decor, dining room, living room selections, bedroom furniture and a "scratch and dent" section, for those looking for a fixer upper project along with their furniture.
"Picker's Paradise" is now a less overwhelming one spot section dedicated to a catch all of treasures from tools to equipment to small appliances and toys.
Amanda James, Haven Ministries food pantry director was grateful for the community support, noting on reopening day items were already flying off the shelves.
Visiting the Eastern Shore from Georgia, Sylvia Schneider came to the reopening with her grandmother Pat Helvey, of Stevensville. An avid Haven Ministries supporter, "she has been looking forward to this for a long time," Schneider said.
Coming away with a pile of choices including a table, a dining set, as well as children's toys, "We'll definitely be back," she said.
Lee Markley, of Stevensville, said she came in on a mission to the furniture store looking for a specific swivel rocker recliner. "And I found two and I bought both," she said.
Markley recommended the store as a place for anyone looking for new- to them furniture as well as anyone looking to clean out their home of furniture no longer needed, "Now I have to go home and see what I will donate to replace them with," she said with a laugh.
With donations coming in everyday, "You never know what you're going to find," James said.
Supplying the largest food pantry in Queen Anne's County, and providing sheltering assistance for the community's most vulnerable, Haven Ministries also provides vouchers for clients needing furniture, she said.
Whether its items are directly sold out of the store, or provided to clients by voucher, all proceeds go right back into supporting Haven Ministries' mission, James shared.
Proceeds from the warehouse support Haven Ministries' other ministries in the community, including its seasonal homeless shelter and Jacob Sloan Day Center in Stevensville, Homes of Hope long-term housing assistance program, emergency food pantry in Queenstown, and food pantry satellite location in Sudlersville, thrift store in Chester, street outreach, and resource center and benevolence fund.
Photos of clean, salable donations can be texted to 410-490-8498, and if accepted can be scheduled or one of the free weekly pick ups.
Hope Warehouse is located at 6527 Friels Road in Queenstown. New store hours are Tuesday through Friday, 10 a.m. to 5 p.m., Saturday, 10 a.m. to 6 p.m. andSunday, noon to 4 p.m. The store is closed Monday.
More information about Hope Warehouse and Haven Ministries can be found at haven-ministries.org.

title: 'Nothing better': Land surveyors shed light on profession's unique draw
author: Konner Metz
content:
'Nothing better': Land surveyors shed light on profession's unique draw

 March 26, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Konner Metz | Section: Local News 
 
 684
 Words 

 Read News Document

 ST. MICHAELS — Five years ago, Grant Foster didn't know much about the field of surveying.After graduating from college and completing an internship in an office, he was looking for a change in pace. That's when he took a job as a surveyor at Lane Engineering in 2022.
"I fell into it, and I loved it," Foster said.
Foster, 24, has been a crew chief for two years. Instead of a 9-to-5 office job, he's in the field working on construction sites and properties across the Mid-Shore.
Land surveying includes a wide variety of field work, often at construction sites and homes, such as denoting property boundaries, measuring land or locating utilities.
Local leaders in the industry say the demand for surveyors is high, particularly for young surveyors. Jeff Hubbard, Lane Engineering's chief of surveys, said there's a limited number of surveyors overall, making their time especially valuable.
As development on the Mid-Shore increases, that demand only rises. Surveying on the Shore comes with its unique challenges, Hubbard notes, from property lines meeting with the Chesapeake Bay to ensuring environmental regulations are followed.
Hubbard, who represents Eastern Shore counties on the board of the Maryland Society of Surveyors, said surveying "has always had a marketing issue."
"When kids go to school, they don't think about becoming surveyors," Hubbard said. "They think about becoming engineers. They think about becoming doctors, lawyers."
But for those who do find the field, it's sometimes a perfect fit. Heinlein enjoys that his job has him working in nature and with animals.
"Any kid who likes the outdoors, it's almost the perfect job for it," Heinlein said. "You are outside all the time, seeing gorgeous views."
TECHNOLOGY
Hubbard has been in the field since 1974 and has been a licensed land surveyor since 1986. He's seen surveying change drastically due to technology — compasses, rulers and protractors have been replaced by geographic information systems that can store and analyze points on a map.
"The ability to digitize all that has been a game-changer for the survey industry," Hubbard said. "Today, those same people are out there locating the same things, but we don't have to pull a tape to find out how far away we are."
Once field surveyors gather the data, licensed surveyors work their magic inside, creating maps, designs and drawings often necessary for construction approvals from local agencies or commissions.
But two-dimensional, paper drawings haven't gone away yet, Hubbard says.
"At the end of the day, we still work in a world where the counties (and) approving agencies still are using paper," he said.
He hopes that Lane Engineering can continue to prioritize technological advancements, though some of that is limited based on what agencies require.
Foster said technology initially captivated him when he began the job years ago.
"It will never be boots on the ground," Foster said. "So, yes, technology helps us do our jobs better, but I don't think it'll ever take the surveyor out of the field."
"This isn't going anywhere," crew chief Michael Mitchell said. "It's one of the oldest professions, and it's going to be necessary going forward. Whenever there's civil engineering going on, you're going to need surveyors to implement it."
UNIQUE FIELD
At Lane Engineering, field crews often work at multiple sites in a day. The crew chief and a survey technician work together in what they say is an independent job.
Mitchell, who's been in the field for more than five years, enjoys that aspect.
"There's a lot of autonomy that goes with the job," Mitchell said. "I'm given a task. I come out here, and I figure out what I think is the most effective way to get it done and it's up to me. I kind of get to call the shots out here within reason."
Earlier this month, Mitchell was at Gannon Range in Easton, a construction site for a housing development coming to Matthewstown Road. He was marking the buffer area for where utility lines could be run.
Playing a role in important construction work is a neat part of the job to Mitchell.
"You see a lot of development and you're like, 'I remember when that was a field,' and now we're driving down the road," Mitchell said.

title: Events planned to mark 50th anniversary of end of Vietnam War
author: STAFF REPORT
content:
Events planned to mark 50th anniversary of end of Vietnam War

 March 28, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: STAFF REPORT | Section: Local News 
 
 338
 Words 

 Read News Document

 Saturday, March 29, is National Vietnam War Veterans Day, a national day of observance for those who served during the 20-year conflict. This year marks the 50th anniversary of the war's end.Several Mid-Shore organizations will host events this weekend to commemorate the occasion and recognize those who served.
Easton parade, ceremony
On March 30, Veterans of Foreign Wars Post 5118 plans to hold a wreath laying ceremony before a parade through downtown Easton and a short program in honor of Vietnam veterans.
The event begins at 1 p.m. Sunday.
The parade route, which has already been approved by the Town of Easton, will begin at the intersection of Dover and Washington streets, then make its way down Washington Street and Glebe Road to the VFW. Event organizers plan to distribute American flags for spectators to wave.
Those who wish to be involved in the event can contact 410-310-5748.
QACHS commemoration
Queen Anne's County High School will honor the legacy of Vietnam veterans with a distinguished Veterans Day ceremony at the QACHS auditorium Saturday, March 29, at 2 p.m.
Veterans, their families, and the public are invited to attend the distinguished ceremony to honor all who served during the Vietnam Era during the 50th anniversary of the official end of the Vietnam War.
The keynote speech will be led by Jack Farley, retired judge with the United States Court of Appeals for Veterans Claims and wounded Vietnam veteran.
A proclamation will be presented by the Queen Anne County's Board of Commissioners with participation from Boy Scout Troop 278 and the U.S. Naval Sea Cadet Corps.
For more information, contact sdpeterson71@gmail.com.
Caroline County observation
On Saturday, March 29, at 1 p.m., Caroline American Legion Post 29 invites all legion members and Caroline County residents who served anywhere in the world between Nov. 1, 1955, and May 15, 1975, to a special recognition event as part of the National Vietnam War Commemoration.
The event will take place at the post.
Widows of servicemen during this period will also be acknowledged and recognized for their strength and resilience. Light refreshments will be served.
Call 410-200-5640 to RSVP.

title: Vietnam vets still deserve thanks, 50 years later
author: Staff Writer
content:
Vietnam vets still deserve thanks, 50 years later

 March 29, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Staff Writer | Section: Editorials 
 
 498
 Words 

 Read News Document

 It may not be the most celebrated or well known anniversary, but this weekend marks the 50th anniversary of the end of the Vietnam War.Many Vietnam veterans still carry the scars — physically and emotionally — of their experiences during the struggle in Southeast Asia that lasted until the fall of Saigon in 1975.
The time the United States was involved in the Vietnam War was a difficult period for our country. While many cried out that America shouldn't be involved, more than 58,000 Americans died during the war. The war divided families, friends and politicians, often generationally.
We will not debate the morality of the country's involvement, but we need to note the tens of thousands of lives lost, and the hundreds of thousands more who brought the war home with them, inside, in a number of ways.
The U.S. Department of Veterans Affairs designated March 29 as the day for the department to commemorate the 50th anniversary of the war, by expressing gratitude and support through numerous planned ceremonies across the nation.
Here in Easton, Veterans of Foreign Wars Post 5118 plans to hold a wreath laying ceremony before a parade through downtown Easton and a short program in honor of Vietnam veterans. The event begins at 1 p.m. Sunday.
The parade route will begin at the intersection of Dover and Washington streets, then make its way down Washington Street and Glebe Road to the VFW. Event organizers plan to distribute American flags for spectators to wave.
The Vietnam War was, no doubt, a controversial one, and the ripples that ran through protestors at home and veterans upon arriving home took years to settle. It was how veterans of the Vietnam War were negatively treated upon returning stateside that caused Americans to band together and ensure we would support our troops returning home from modern conflicts in Iraq and Afghanistan.
Many veteran support programs have been created since the end of the Vietnam War, and military organizations like the American Legion, the Veterans of Foreign Wars and Disabled American Veterans offer help in countless ways.
Still, much is left to be done. Veterans don't always have visible signs of battle, such as a lost limb due to an IED or facial scars caused by shrapnel. The psychological effects of battle are direct causes of post-traumatic stress disorder, a leading cause of suicide among veterans.
More needs to be done to help veterans suffering from the effects of war, both mental and physical, and that responsibility rests with us, the citizens whom our military men and women fight to defend.
We learned many lessons from Vietnam, and hopefully the greatest one is that while we may not agree with the reasoning behind sending soldiers to fight abroad, we need to welcome them back with open arms for the selfless service they offered and extend to them the support they need.
To our Vietnam veterans on the Eastern Shore, we salute you. We're sorry America wasn't always there for you when you returned home. But we're here now.

author: Staff Writer
content:
Farmers market aficionados

 March 29, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Staff Writer | Section: Editors Inbox 
 
 178
 Words 

 Read News Document

 In a 2015 article from the Stardem titled "Parking Problems — Perception or Reality," statistics were quoted citing 900 available parking spaces in Easton.True not every space puts you right in front of your intended destination, but compared to dealing with parking garages and exorbitant hourly rates, Easton has a sweet deal.
I'm not sure what the problem is with the Farmers Market location.
Steve Mangasarian was quoted as saying trash was a problem — is he saying it is the vendors or the patrons? He also states the impact on merchants, but most stores are not open when the market opens at 8, and downtown Easton is not hopping in those early morning hours.
We, my spouse and I, are farmers market aficionados.When we go on extended vacations our first stop is a farmers market. It's where we learn about local specialties and food customs.
Over the years we have developed relationships with vendors at the Easton market, and I am grateful to have a vegetable on my plate that has not traveled 1,200 miles to grace my table.

title: Easton parade welcomes home Vietnam vets 50 years after end of war
author: Konner Metz
content:
Easton parade welcomes home Vietnam vets 50 years after end of war

 March 31, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Konner Metz | Section: Local News 
 
 640
 Words 

 Read News Document

 EASTON — Kenley Timms struggled to hold back tears after Sunday's Welcome Home parade for Vietnam veterans.Timms, commander of Easton VFW Post 5118 and a Vietnam veteran, had high hopes for the parade, stocked full of veterans, families and local service organizations.
"But our concerns were there was not going to be anybody," said an emotional Timms in front of more than 100 people at the post-parade ceremony held at the VFW post.
"I didn't know we were going to have people from the town show up, and it was quite obvious they did. Thank you."
People lined the streets of Easton Sunday as the parade made its way down Washington Street and Glebe Road. Vietnam veterans from Easton, Talbot County and the entire Mid-Shore were honored for their service 50 years after the war's end.
Those young, old and in between waved American flags and saluted veterans of the Vietnam War and families of those who gave their lives serving the nation in the conflict.
It was a welcome home that many never received.
Following the end of the war in 1975, many soldiers weren't welcomed back with open arms, but with hostility. The war and its brutal nature divided the country and became increasingly unpopular as it went on.
"Time has a way of softening the edges and revealing truths," said Joe Cicchillo, commander of the Maryland VFW. "The nation has come to see what you've always known. That you are — the veterans of Vietnam — our heroes. You served not because it was easy, because it was your duty."
Mike Detmer, a Dorchester County Councilman and Marine Corps veteran, said when he returned from his time in Iraq, Vietnam veterans gave his unit the welcome back they were never afforded.
"The warmest reception that I got was oftentimes from men and women that had those Vietnam campaign ribbon colors on their hats," Detmer said. "And more than one of them told me that they wanted to ensure that we got welcomed back in the way that was appropriate."
"You're our treasure," Detmer said of Vietnam-era veterans. "You're a treasure to this country."
During the ceremony inside VFW Post 5118, Vietnam veterans and their families were honored, as were those who never returned home.
Talbot County First Class Deputy John Coleman led the crowd in singing the national anthem and "God Bless America."
Ngung Van Le, a former Vietnamese commando who worked for the CIA and a special United States intelligence operation during the war, was honored during the ceremony, receiving a standing ovation from the entire crowd.
The post held a solemn roundtable ceremony, with five veterans surrounding a table that symbolized those who were killed in action or became prisoners of war.
Cicchillo lauded the Vietnam veterans in attendance for their service during the war and their strength afterward.
"Vietnam was not just a war that was fought overseas," he said. "It was a war that followed you back. When you returned, you didn't always get the welcome you deserved. Some of you faced silence, some of you faced scorn. And yet through it all, you held your head high.
"You knew all along of what you've done. You knew the sacrifices you made. You knew that freedom is not free, and it is paid for in sweat, blood and quiet moments of resilience that no one sees."
Timms said the mission moving forward is to ensure the country's treatment of Vietnam vets upon their return after the war never repeats itself.
"We have members in this post that were spit on," Timms said. "They were told when they hit the United States before they got off of that plane, make sure you do not go out in your uniform. That's disgraceful.
"We hope we'll never, ever see that again. As Vietnam veterans, we're going to support every unit, every army, navy, every veteran we can to make sure that never, ever happens again."

title: Last sailor on the pier': Hollywood couple celebrate 65th wedding anniversary
author: Michael Reid mreid@somdnews.com
content:
Last sailor on the pier': Hollywood couple celebrate 65th wedding anniversary

 April 1, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Michael Reid mreid@somdnews.com | Section: News 
 
 518
 Words 

 Read News Document

 Roy Hart Jr. desperately wanted to dance with the pretty girl, but he was flatly rejected.But Hart refused to give up, got the girl and on March 26, he and wife Jane Hart of Hollywood celebrated their 65th wedding anniversary.
"We've had a great marriage," said 88-year-old Roy.
The couple celebrated the anniversary with lunch at Capt. Pat's Seafood in Drayden.
Hart worked 40 years at The Enterprise and The Calvert Recorder, while Roy served 23 years in the U.S. Navy before becoming a broker with Hart & Lyle in California.
They have three children — Lisa Barrios, who lives in Virginia, Roy Hart III who lives in Baltimore and Pamela Renee Johnson, who lives next door — along with four grandchildren and three great-grandchildren.
"There has to be a lot of give-and-take and a lot of patience on both sides," 82-year-old Jane said.
And it was Roy Jr. who exhibited plenty of patience at the onset.
It was the early 1950s when Roy spied Jane across the hall at a USO dance in Charleston, S.C., and he was immediately smitten. He said he "thought she was a good looking girl" and told Jane Brewer's friend he'd like to dance with Jane.
But the attraction certainly wasn't mutual.
"Me? Dance with that old man? He's too old for me," said Jane, who was 15 at the time of the 21-year-old Roy Jr.'s advance. "And he didn't know how to dance very well."
But Roy persevered. He called his mother later that night and told her he'd met the girl he was going to marry and Jane's parents adored him and invited him to dinner every Sunday. He even took dance lessons at the Arthur Murray Dance Studio.
Even though Jane lied and told Roy Jr. she was about to turn 18, her feelings slowly started changing and they started dating.
"I began to like him more and more," Jane said.
Roy was deployed aboard the U.S.S. Orleans Parish, a flat-bottom tank landing ship, shortly after, and when he returned he waited along with his shipmates for loved ones to pick them up.
"Here I am standing there waiting, waiting," Roy said. "I was the last sailor on the pier."
"I was late," Jane admitted.
The couple got engaged and married in 1960 at Citadel Square Baptist Church in Charleston.
Because of Roy's military obligations, the couple lived in Charleston before moving to Massachusetts and then Italy, and Roy's first day at Allied Forces in 1962 was one to remember.
He received a call from the adjutant of a four-star admiral that Jane had parked in his space.
The following is the couple's version of events:
"I beat my feet over and Jane was two buildings over at a beauty salon. I told her, 'You have to move your car right away.'"
"But my hair's not done yet. He'll just have to wait."
"He won't wait. Get out and move that car right away."
"But my hair's not done. Who does he think he is anyway?"
"I'll tell you who he is. He's the admiral."
Jane eventually moved her car.
The couple eventually relocated to Hollywood after Roy was assigned to Naval Air Station Patuxent River. And that's where they reside to this day.

title: Welcome home: QAC honors Vietnam era veterans
author: ANDREA GRABENSTEIN agrabenstein@chespub.com
content:
Welcome home: QAC honors Vietnam era veterans

 April 3, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: ANDREA GRABENSTEIN agrabenstein@chespub.com | Section: News 
 
 503
 Words 

 Read News Document

 CENTREVILLE — Proving it's never too late to say "welcome home", a special commemoration honored the service, valor, and sacrifice of Vietnam Era veterans at the Queen Anne's County High School Auditorium March 29.Commemorating the 50th anniversary of the end of the Vietnam War, the ceremony led by Vietnam veterans presented recognition for some decades in the making.
Ceremony speaker Jack Farley, served as a U.S. Army captain in Vietnam and acquired four Bronze Stars, two Purple Hearts and left a leg behind.
Farley said, "Those who decide to go to war are generally not the ones who fight," and the lessons of the war can be found in the more than 58,000 names etched into the national Vietnam Veterans Memorial wall in Washington D.C.
No matter the branch of the armed forces, American service members answered the call to serve the country and were treated the same upon their return, according to Farley.
At that time, many Americans were vocal in their disdain for the war and connected that to the soldiers as well, he said.
Returning service members realized that the county they went off to fight for was no longer there when they returned, Farley said, and highlighted the need to "separate the war from the warrior."
Farley was especially glad to see so many younger people in the ceremony's attendance to share legacies, keep history alive and resolve to ensure the reception military members received from their countrymen during Vietnam never happens again.
Joe Sikes, along with Boy Scout Troop 278, led a missing man table ceremony recognizing the sacrifice of those lost. As a member of the United States Naval Academy Class of 1968, the ceremony was particularly significant for him in losing classmates to the war.
To this day, remains from those missing in action continue to be identified and brought home, he said, and for some, the war never truly ended as some families are kept waiting. Sikes said he himself never heard a thank you for his service until well into the 1980s and seeks to connect the community, especially the younger generation to remember the battles fought and the sacrifices made in duty in Vietnam.
Alongside music performed by the Centreville Middle School Symphonic Band, a pin ceremony honored all members who served in active duty anywhere in the world from 1955 to 1975.
March 29 was established as National Vietnam Veterans Day in 2017 and local ceremonies are crucial in continually providing recognition to noble service members, according to Farley.
Navy veteran in Vietnam and organizer Dave Peterson led recognition of the five Queen Anne's County residents who died in the Vietnam operating theater and their Gold Star families.
The ceremony's Presentation of Colors was performed by the U.S. Naval Sea Cadet Corps Maryland Division. The National Anthem was presented by the Quee Anne's County High School Chorus.
Taps was performed by Stephanie Shields.
Prayer was led by Rev. Reginald Ryans.
Participants and sponsors also included Centreville Veterans Information Center (CVIC), Veteran and Military Support Alliance (VAMSA), American Legion Jeff Davis Post 18 and Compass Regional Hospice.

author: Lilly Howard lhoward@chespub.com
content:
Bed racers bring racing fun to the streets of Maryland town

 April 4, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Lilly Howard lhoward@chespub.com | Section: News 
 
 329
 Words 

 Read News Document

 The fourth annual Cecilton Bed Races brought April Fools fun for everyone on Tuesday, as families, friends, and community members came together to observe creative contraptions get pushed across the finish line for an April Fools fiesta.Six beds — manned by ages young and old — competed for the top three prizes. From a neon green vehicle inspired by Hot Wheels toys with a small but mighty team of three, to a mattress atop four bicycle wheels — which unfortunately took a tumble — there was a spectacle for all lining the track on Rebecca Smith Way.
Teams continued to race one versus one in a bracketed competition, with one person riding and up to three pushing the "beds" on wheels.
"Eveland Arms" represented the hunting and sporting goods store in Earleville, and secured the first place trophy. A local family entered their second "Bed on a Budget" contraption — bright pink bunk beds on wheels — and took home second place and best design after winning first place with the original "Bed on a Budget" last year, which was made of milk crates.
A group of young locals used their vehicle to campaign for Sue Katzmire — the organizer of the bed races — who is up for re-election to Town Council. They decorated their structure on wheels with "vote for Katzmire" signage and patriotic decor.
Katzmire organizes the bed races on April Fools each year as a fundraiser for Faith In Action, a local nonprofit food pantry.
Katzmire grew up in upstate New York, where she was first introduced to bed races in her neighborhood. When she moved to Cecilton she felt right at home, so decided to bring the bed races to the small Maryland town, and the people love it.
"When I was a little girl, my hometown was a lot like Cecilton and we did this every year," Katzmire said.
To offer informative resources for community members, theCecilton Judy CenterandCecil County Health Departmentwere tabling along the sidelines of the racetrack.

title: 'You are all God’s gift': Volunteers honored for dedication, service to seniors
author: WILL BONTRAGER wbontrager@chespub.com
content:
'You are all God’s gift': Volunteers honored for dedication, service to seniors

 April 4, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: WILL BONTRAGER wbontrager@chespub.com | Section: Seniors 
 
 550
 Words 

 Read News Document

 Susan Higgs of Upper Shore Aging Inc. showed appreciation for the many volunteers dedicated to serving the Retired and Senior Volunteer Program, RSVP, of which she is project director."We're a team and I can't say enough. You are all God's gift and I thank you," Higgs said at their annual recognition event on Friday at the Amy Lynn Ferris Adult Activity Center on 200 Schauber Rd.
Upper Shore Aging, Inc., a non-profit organization, is a designated Area Agency on Aging by the State of Maryland, serving over 31,000 seniors in Caroline, Kent and Talbot counties. Over a catered dinner from Out of the Ordinary Catering, run by Robert Yalley, Upper Shore celebrated 50 years of service.
Higgs, using a PowerPoint presentation, showed that when they first began the Retired and Senior Volunteer Program there were only a few cells of busy bees.
But over the years, Kent County has produced more than 100 volunteers, who this year already put in more than 7,000 hours.
Each volunteer agency is called a station with a station manager. The Kent Association of Riding Therapy's (KART) station manager is Sue Caswell. Her volunteering duties involve walking with the horses and helping children with disabilities with them. She said it is an extremely rewarding experience.
Another station is the Museums of Kent, and with 11 museums, it can be a busy one, run by station manager Carolyn Sorge.
The list of Program stations is long in the county and getting longer, Higgs pointed out. Their goal as stations, volunteers or busy bees, is to produce honey, a sweetness to the community — to establish and build connections creating a better quality of life for everyone.
As they do this this year, they face some challenges.
Upper Shore Executive Director Herb Cain pointed out their funding comes from the Maryland Department of Aging, which may be facing federal and state cuts. Cuts to that department means potential cuts to Upper Shore, which may fall to county government to support some programs in their jurisdiction.
Cain has already visited the Kent County Commissioners and expressed his concerns, and so far, all the counties have been supportive, he noted.
But there is a level of uncertainty, he acknowledged, especially in the federal funding.
In this financially unstable environment, Higgs said, volunteers are needed more than ever. Having professional, knowledgeable seniors active and involved benefits the community. Placing older adults in these high-quality positions improves their quality of life as well.
Higgs said with 10,000 baby boomers retiring since COVID-19, isolation and loneliness can set in. Volunteering provides purpose, decreases loneliness and adds a sense of fulfillment.
Higgs' positive energy and optimism is an example of the benefits of volunteering, and she encouraged residents to reach out to them if interested at shiggs@uppershoreaging.org.
Upper Shore Aging's website for the Retired Seniors Volunteer Program, volunteersontheshore.org, is a centralized place for anyone seeking a volunteer opportunity in Kent, Caroline or Talbot counties. The site includes information on the enrollment process and a listing under each county of volunteer opportunities.
In Kent County, a handful of these organizations include the Chester River Hospital Center Auxiliary, Amy Lynn Ferris Adult Activity Center, Meals on Wheels, Kent Association of Riding Therapy (KART) and many more.
"To me this is a very special program. We're still here and making things happen and living life. Look at us now!" Higgs said.

title: Sail Selina II to set sail in St. Michaels for final season
author: Maggie Trovato
content:
Sail Selina II to set sail in St. Michaels for final season

 April 12, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Maggie Trovato | Section: Local News 
 
 661
 Words 

 Read News Document

 ST. MICHAELS — After nearly a century on the water and more than two decades guiding passengers along the Miles River, the Sail Selina II will be sailing into retirement later this year.Following its upcoming season, which begins next week, Captain Iris Robertson will be retiring. But before it departs the Bay following the end of its season in November, Sail Selina II is going out with a bang.
The boat is joining the National Park Service's Chesapeake Gateways Network, a network of places that offer opportunities for visitors to learn about and enjoy the Chesapeake Bay.
Robertson said in the last 25 years, she estimates close to 60,000 people have stepped aboard Sail Selina II. Some of those passengers, she said, might not have gotten out on the water otherwise.
"The Bay is very fragile," Robertson said. "It's at risk right now. And (for) folks that live in Pennsylvania, (it's) out of sight, out of mind. But they're on the watershed. And Selina's just been a wonderful way for people to connect to something that they participate in even though it's not necessarily in their backyard."
On April 24, there will be a ribbon cutting ceremony at the Harbour Inn Marina in St. Michaels to welcome Sail Selina II into the Chesapeake Gateways Network for its final season. The event will include remarks from National Park Service Chesapeake Gateways Superintendent Wendy O'Sullivan.
GENERATIONS ON THE WATERAlthough Robertson, who lives in Royal Oak, has been the captain of Sail Selina II for 25 years, her history with the boat stretches back to before she was born.
In 1926, Robertson's grandfather had the boat commissioned. Her grandparents kept the boat for 36 years before passing it down to Robertson's parents in 1962. In 2001, Robertson became Sail Selina II's third steward.
"From the time I was about 12, even though I've got older siblings, everybody knew she would come to me," Robertson said. "I was the kid that was aboard, participating, had the interest."
Robertson made the decision to charter the boat so that she could afford to maintain it.
After Sail Selina II's final charter season, Robertson plans to pass the yacht down to her niece, who happens to live in Greenport, New York, where Sail Selina II was built.
"It's like a full-circle thing," Robertson said about the sailing yacht. "She's 100 years old. She's going back to the town she was built in."
Robertson said she knows her grandparents and father, who have since died, would be so proud of the boat's Chesapeake Gateways designation.
"I think they'd be tickled pink to know how much she has contributed to people's joy and experience over the last 25 years," Robertson said.
STEPPING ABOARDWith a 1,000-square-foot canvas sail, the 44-foot-long Sail Selina II is a "stable" and "regal" sailing yacht, Robertson said.
"We have a lot of guests that have never been on boats before, and they're a little bit nervous when they first step on," she said. "But by the time they get off, they go, 'Oh my God, this was like being on a flying magic carpet ride.'"
From wine and beer tasting cruises, to sunset sails, to engagement cruises, to weddings, to private sailing lessons, there are many options for those who want to set sail on Sail Selina II. Robertson said the standard two-hour tour takes passengers around St. Michaels Harbor before cruising out to the Miles River and putting up sails.
"We let the wind determine our course," Robertson said. "And before you know it, two hours has gone by."
Repeat passenger Gene Pisasale said he and his wife love sailing on Sail Selina II because they love being out on the water and they love sailing with Robertson.
"She's got to be the friendliest boat captain on the Chesapeake," said Pisasale, who lives in Pennsylvania. "And she is just a gem, a real gem. A pleasure to sail with."
To charter Sail Selina II during its last season, visit sailselina.com/ or call 410-726-9400. The season will go from April 18 through Nov. 2.

title: Fashion show raises record funds for Kent animal shelter
author: STAFF REPORT
content:
Fashion show raises record funds for Kent animal shelter

 April 15, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: STAFF REPORT | Section: News 
 
 257
 Words 

 Read News Document

 CHESTERTOWN — A local fashion show fundraiser at the Elks Lodge raised more than $4,500 for the Animal Care Shelter of Kent County, setting a new record in its third year.The annual event, organized by Michelle Timmons, owner of Jerry Moe's and Houston's Dockside Emporium, featured 13 models showcasing outfits and styles from her stores.
"Best year ever, gets bigger each year," Timmons said. The fundraiser has shown consistent growth, raising $3,000 in its first year and $4,000 in its second.
The fashion show featured five men, four women and four children modeling the latest styles. Most models were friends of Timmons, including her husband, who initially was skeptical participating.
"He's kind of a ham now," Timmons said of her husband, who has participated all three years.
The fundraiser's success was bolstered by community donations. The Mill of Kingstown paid for the hall rental and donated raffle baskets containing garden supplies and other items.
The event also included a silent auction. Haven Harbour in Rock Hall donated a two-day stay, while Images Salon and Spa in Kennedyville, Bad Alfred's Distillery and The Bluebird contributed gifts as well.
"It's a fun event and so worthwhile," Timmons said.
Attendees received a 10% discount coupon for Timmons' stores in exchange for their ticket.
Timmons, a former board member from the Animal Care Shelter of Kent County decided to continue the annual event after stepping down, and is glad to keep it going for the cause. The fourth fashion show is already scheduled for early April next year and she hopes to see the community come out again.

title: Power, balance and discipline displayed during black belt testing
author: WILL BONTRAGER wbontrager@chespub.com
content:
Power, balance and discipline displayed during black belt testing

 April 16, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: WILL BONTRAGER wbontrager@chespub.com | Section: News 
 
 684
 Words 

 Read News Document

 CHESTERTOWN — Kicks and punches flew over the weekend, but safely, under the watchful eyes of local martial arts masters.On Saturday, at Eastern Shore Tang Soo Do, instructors of the Korean martial arts known for its practical self-defense techniques and physical fitness training, held Black Belt/Advanced Testing for students.
The judges (the masters) were Mark Pagano, owner of Eastern Shore Tang Soo Do; Derek DePaolis, owner and head instructor at Synergy Martial Arts in Odenton, and his son Michael, with Masters Lacy Reedich of Synergy Do Jang in Crownsville; and Bob Campbell, co-owner with Pagano of Eastern Shore Karate and Fitness.
They reviewed students as a group, in areas like basic blocking and kicking techniques, Hyung (meaning form or pattern), self defense skills, board breaking, sparring, endurance and terminology.
Pagano was pleased with his students overall but agreed with other instructors they need to improve their sparring, focusing on control over ferocity. "Sparring is about exactness of technique and speed and control," he said.
Guiding the students in these six areas, instructor and 3rd degree blackbelt, Stephen Marvel piggybacked off Pagano's statements. When sparring an opponent, especially a fellow karate student, it is important to exercise a "good attitude, good energy and good spirit," he said.
You are not trying to injure an opponent during sparring, he added.
Pagano explained their testing examines every thing students learn — each skill builds on another. Tang Soo Do teaches control of body and mind instilling discipline and showing respect at all times to the instructors.
Students learn serious lifetime skills, yet the family friendly atmosphere promotes a joy in what they do, with good natured ribbing and jokes between them all.
Marvel guided the students through the tests, assisted by 4th degree blackbelt Master KT Pagano, lending her many years of expertise to the class. Now a Washington College student, KT Pagano balances out her time training, showing boundless energy when teaching.
In the basic move portion of the test, students were told by Michael DePaolis to make every motion sharp. Every movement should be made with focus and attention, even something as simple as keeping hands tight to the body.
During the Hyung testing, (forms) students showed their graceful techniques, memorizing a series of movements. KT Pagano went through a rigorous series of Hyung forms, showing power, grace and determination in her sequences.
In self defense testing, students demonstrated relying on instincts and training to take away the sword, knife, or gun from their opponents, utilizing balance and leverage.
During board breaking, students elbowed, chopped or kicked a board breaking it in two. Derek DePaolis said to break a board, it's about following through, generating power from exhaling and breath control. Oldest to youngest broke them successfully.
The next test was endurance, with non-stop kicks or punches for a time period judges determined. Nobody dropped out or stopped their movements.
The last test was a challenge to most students. They had to recite terminology from some of their basic tenets, often made more difficult when asked to do it in Korean. The Masters lent a lot of help in this particular area.
After the approximately three-hour testing period, Masters encouraged the students with sound advice and urged them to attend the Tang Soo Do World Championships {span}July 24 through the 29, {/span}to take full advantage of everything available.
The keys to success will be hard work, masters said.
"Train with sincerity," Michael DePaolis noted.
"We want students to be better than us," his father, a 6th Degree black belt added.
Pagano, also a 6th degree black belt, will give out promotions on June 22, at Tuckahoe State Park at their annual picnic.
He said the students can hold their heads up high at their performance. "They showed great heart, focus and concentration. I couldn't ask for any better."
Pagano has been training in the area since 2009, producing many black belts, and pointed out it is more than a martial arts school; it is a family-oriented community, training students of all-ages to bring Pyung Ahn into their lives — Korean for "well balanced, calm, peaceful, safe, confident, and comfortable."
Anyone interested in training can find them at 903 Washington Ave. #3, Chestertown, or online at easternshoretangsoodo.com/.

title: Women to Watch event recognizes 212 leaders
author: WENDY WEITZEL wweitzel@chespub.com
content:
Women to Watch event recognizes 212 leaders

 April 16, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: WENDY WEITZEL wweitzel@chespub.com | Section: Local News 
 
 409
 Words 

 Read News Document

 EASTON — Shawna Payne issued a reminder to more than 100 people gathered in the Avalon Theatre April 9 — "You have been chosen."The phrase was a call to action. Despite any self-doubt, Payne said, those gathered in the theater that evening were there to celebrate their own accomplishments and honor their potential to initiate positive change.
In the crowd were some of more than 200 nominees for this year's Women to Watch magazine, an annual publication by APG Chesapeake recognizing the contributions of women to Mid-Shore workplaces and communities.
The women, who were nominated via an online portal by coworkers, friends, spouses and loved ones, represented a wide swath of Mid-Shore change-makers.
"It was a wonderful evening to celebrate the power, success and perseverance of women to watch in the Mid-Shore," said Orestes Baez, regional president of APG Chesapeake. "Everyone had a great story to tell and a great energy to share. APG Chesapeake did a wonderful job putting all the pieces together. We are thankful for the opportunity to share it with the public."
The event marked the launch of the fifth Women to Watch magazine, a preliminary printed version of which was unveiled at the Avalon that evening. The magazine will be inserted into the Star Democrat and available online April 23.
Payne, who works through her nonprofit The BE Academy to empower women entrepreneurs, is one of 14 women featured in this year's edition. She was the first of three speakers to offer advice to those gathered April 9.
Yixin Qiu, co-founder of Apollo's Dream Foundation and a technical project manager for Qlarant, shared how she has worked to generate positive change in the Eastern Shore community that welcomed her as an immigrant a decade ago. Qiu helped found a nonprofit aiding senior citizens with digital literacy.
Jackie Wilson, senior vice president at Burke and Herbert Bank, shared advice for women experiencing change or uncertainty in their careers. She encouraged women to embrace change and rely on their expertise and the expertise of their teams to navigate challenges.
"What an uplifting evening," said Betsy Griffin, APG Chesapeake general manager for sales and marketing. "It was great to see Mid-Shore women connecting and networking with other leaders. We are honored to provide a refreshing evening celebrating these women who serve in the community and excel in their workplaces. The friends, husbands, business associates, sons and daughters also all came out to join in for these special moments. This was especially nice to see."

Sign up: 443-448-4611.
Bingo, 7:30 p.m., Tuesdays, American Legion Post 29, 9238 Legion Road. 5 p.m. doors open, 7:30 p.m. games start. Info:410-479-2708.

title: 5,000 Easter eggs bring excited children to Cambridge park
author: Maggie Trovato
content:
5,000 Easter eggs bring excited children to Cambridge park

 April 21, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Maggie Trovato | Section: Local News 
 
 510
 Words 

 Read News Document

 CAMBRIDGE — Some in lunge positions and some clutching the police tape marking the starting line, around 200 children waited eagerly as Capt. Antoine Patton counted down the seconds to the start of the annual Cambridge Police Department Easter Egg Hunt.When he got to one, children aged 2 to 12 leapt forward with excitement and began to search for the 5,000 eggs spread across Gerry Boyle Park Saturday. Many children inspected the park closely for golden eggs, which, when found, could be taken to the prize table and traded for an Easter basket full of toys and candy.
After 6-year-old Johana Green found her golden egg, she received an Easter basket almost half as tall as her. The basket was complete with candy, a dart board, foam darts, a spinner, a slingshot and more.
Green said she was excited to open the basket and was looking forward to trying out the slingshot.
And Green was not the only kid to walk away from the hunt with a haul to bring home. Many children left with baskets filled to the brim with eggs.
Patton said the police department began spreading out thousands of eggs across the park at 8 a.m. so all the children there would be able to put eggs in their baskets.
The department started putting on the egg hunt about 10 years ago when the county stopped hosting it, Patton said.
"We actually started 10 years ago with about 100 eggs and maybe 25 kids on Pine Street," he said. "And it got so large that we ended up coming here. So we went from 100 eggs to now 5,000 eggs and a lot of people."
Patton said he was excited for the event because it gives kids the opportunity to participate in an Easter egg hunt and helps the police department build a relationship with the community.
Along with the hunt, children could take pictures with the Easter Bunny, paint eggs with The Garden Church and get food and drink from the Salvation Army. For the adults, a sack race was held immediately after the egg hunt.
"It is a beautiful day," Patton said as warm breezes glided through the air. "I don't think we could ask for a better day."
After learning about the event in the newspaper, Cambridge resident Chuck Pinkston brought his two sons, Corey, 8, and Carter, 6. Like many of the other older kids at the hunt, Corey and Carter were determined to find a golden egg.
Pinkston said even though he told his sons to stay together, Corey ran out to find a golden egg with his younger brother chasing behind him. Later in the hunt, Corey helped Carter fill his basket with eggs.
April and Levi Jarman, who brought their 4- and 1-year-old children to the hunt, said even though there were a lot of people, there were a lot of eggs.
"I'm just glad that they put this on for the community," April Jarman said. "It was nice to get everybody out. I've seen some old coworkers, so that was nice. Just nice to get out with the family, do something."

title: Church Hill Park welcomes StoryWalk
author: ANDREA GRABENSTEIN agrabenstein@chespub.com
content:
Church Hill Park welcomes StoryWalk

 April 23, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: ANDREA GRABENSTEIN agrabenstein@chespub.com | Section: News 
 
 167
 Words 

 Read News Document

 CHURCH HILL — Combining the great outdoors with a really good book, Queen Anne's County Library welcomed a new StoryWalk at Church Hill Park April 22.As a way to enjoy local parks, explore new places and bring library resources outside the walls, StoryWalks are fixed display stands of books for readers of all ages to read along the trail, according to Allison Wood, Queen Anne's County Library marketing outreach manager.
Trail books are regularly switched out, and other StoryWalks locations can be found at the Route 18 Park in Centreville and Sudlersville Park, she said.
"Bring the family and walk the trail, enjoy a story, and celebrate this fun and engaging way to read outdoors," Wood said.
StoryWalks are a community collaboration with county parks and recreation and funding for the Church Hill Park StoryWalk was made possible through United Way of Queen Anne's County as well as Friends of the Library, she said.
More information about Queen Anne's County Library, including programs and events can be found at qaclibrary.org.

title: Law enforcement and Easter Bunny make holiday appearance at area hospitals
author: Submitted News
content:
Law enforcement and Easter Bunny make holiday appearance at area hospitals

 April 23, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Submitted News | Section: Local News 
 
 193
 Words 

 Read News Document

 CHESTERTOWN — Sheriff Gary Hofmann and members of the Queen Anne's County Office of the Sheriff delivered Easter bunnies to patients and staff at area hospitals.This effort aims to bring a moment of comfort and connection to those spending the holiday away from home, the sheriff's office said in a press release.
Each year, the Queen Anne's County Office of the Sheriff partners with neighboring law enforcement agencies to carry out this initiative. This year, Sheriff Gary Hofmann visited the University of Maryland Shore Emergency Center at Queenstown, joined Sgt. Cory Willey from the Talbot County Sheriff's Office at University of Maryland Shore Medical Center at Easton, and was accompanied by Kent County Sheriff Dennis Hickman during the visit to University of Maryland Shore Medical Center at Chestertown.
The Easter Bunny also joined the team, helping bring smiles to both patients and staff throughout the day.
"We do this every year to put a smile on the faces of those who may not get to be home with their families for the holiday," Hofmann said. "It's a simple gesture, but one that means a great deal to us and, we hope, to those we visit."

title: Rock Hall’s Bun Run raises $6,000 for rescue rabbits
author: STAFF REPORT
content:
Rock Hall’s Bun Run raises $6,000 for rescue rabbits

 April 23, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: STAFF REPORT | Section: News 
 
 350
 Words 

 Read News Document

 ROCK HALL — The Eastern Shore Rabbit Rescue and Education Center hosted its fifth annual Bun Run on Saturday, April 19, raising both funds and awareness for abandoned pet rabbits.The event, held in Rock Hall for the first time, drew 56 in-person participants and nine virtual registrants, raising approximately $6,000 to support the nonprofit's mission.
The 5K kicked off at 10 a.m. with participants taking a scenic route that included views of the Chesapeake Bay, Swan Creek and the harbor. Participants could walk or run at their own pace, and medals were awarded to the top finishers in four categories: adult male, adult female, youth male, and youth female. Each category winner received a free entry to the Savage Race obstacle course in Kennedyville.
The medalists included:
Youth female first place: Phoebe Fritz of Chestertown (fifth overall).Female adult first place: Margaret Randolph of Millington (fourth overall).Youth male first place: Jonathan Smith of Berlin (first overall).Adult male first place: Chris Blanchard of Rock Hall (second overall).
Rescue President Cora Dickson, who also participated, thanked the community for its support and shared in welcoming remarks from Rock Hall Mayor James Cook.
The Bun Run raised awareness about the large number of rabbits abandoned after being purchased on impulse during the Easter holiday. The event is part of the organization's ongoing efforts to highlight the importance of long-term commitment and specialized care for rabbits.
The Eastern Shore Rabbit Rescue and Education Center, established in 2014, has placed nearly 500 rabbits in new homes, and the Bun Run is an essential fundraising effort for the organization, which spends most of its funds on veterinary expenses, including spaying, neutering, and vaccinations.
This year's event also featured fundraising competitions. The top fundraising team in the business category was Brampton 1860 of Chestertown, which raised $500, and the top individual fundraisers, each with $300, were Cora Dickson and William Fielder.
The Bun Run, initially organized as a virtual event in 2021 during the COVID-19 pandemic, has continued to grow, with in-person events in Salisbury and now Rock Hall.
More information about the Bun Run and how to support the rescue's efforts is available at esrrec.org/bun-run.

title: The Star Democrat's top 10 online stories this week
author: STAFF REPORT
content:
The Star Democrat's top 10 online stories this week

 April 26, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: STAFF REPORT | Section: Local News 
 
 419
 Words 

 Read News Document

 Here are the 10 stories that attracted the most page views on The Star Democrat's website this week. The stories are ranked in order of number of page views as of Wednesday evening.1. Easton Planning Commission approves Zaxbys on Route 50
The planning commission approved new designs for a Zaxbys being build on Route 50.
2. Easton council rejects Gunsallus' proposal to delay introduction of campaign finance law
Town Council members held a heated discussion Monday on a proposed ordinance mandating campaign finance reporting in town elections.
Before the opening Pledge of Allegiance and prayer, council President Frank Gunsallus moved to remove the campaign finance law's introduction from Monday's meeting agenda. The remaining council members voted to proceed with the introduction.
3. Dorchester County proposes tax increases to balance FY26 budget
In an effort to address a $6.2 million deficit, the Dorchester County Council introduced a draft fiscal year 2026 budget that raised taxes.
The $91.96 million proposed operating budget presented Tuesday includes proposals to increase property taxes, remove the municipal tax differential, increase local income tax and eliminate tax rebates offered to municipalities.
4. TCPS announces leadership changes for coming school year
Talbot County schools will have several new principals and vice principals next school year.
5. With crab season open, Talbot watermen tracking weather and economy
As Maryland's blue crab season begins, local watermen have their eyes on the weather and the economy.
Jeff Harrison, president of the Talbot Watermen Association, said last week that he's expecting this year's crabbing outlook to be fair, perhaps slightly better than last year.
6. Counties approve Chesapeake College budget request, shift cost of tech center
In a joint meeting Thursday, officials across Caroline, Dorchester, Kent, Queen Anne's and Talbot counties approved a shift in county cost shares for Chesapeake College's new technical building.
7. Easton house fire causes $1.5 million in damages
Forty-seven firefighters responded to a house fire on Locust Grove Road that caused $1.5 million in damages, according to the state fire marshal. No injuries were reported.
8. Talbot County introduces $161M budget with a focus on conservatism
Talbot County officials introduced a $161 million budget proposal, emphasizing their intention to flatten spending after multiple years of significant increases.
9. Fire marshal: Pool intentionally set on fire
A pool at a vacant property was intentionally set on fire, according to the Office of the State Fire Marshal.
10. Point-in-time count shows Mid-Shore homelessness is up
A point-in-time count conducted in January showed a 50% rise in people experiencing homelessness on the Mid-Shore since last year, according to results released earlier this month.

title: CASA of the Mid-Shore celebrates its volunteers
author: Maggie Trovato
content:
CASA of the Mid-Shore celebrates its volunteers

 April 26, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Maggie Trovato | Section: Local News 
 
 400
 Words 

 Read News Document

 EASTON — Over appetizers, drinks and good conversation, CASA of the Mid-Shore thanked its volunteers Thursday with a special event at the Avalon Theatre in downtown Easton."The people who bring our mission to life are our CASA volunteers," Executive Director Robin Davenport said.
CASA of the Mid-Shore assigns volunteer court appointed special advocates in Dorchester, Kent, Queen Anne's and Talbot counties to advocate for children who are considered to be at significant risk in their current homes and have been placed under court protection.
Advocates are tasked with identifying a child's needs and advocating for necessary services so those needs can be met.
During the celebration Thursday, Davenport shared a story of the impact volunteers can have on the children they advocate for. She said a retired volunteer, Sally, was at the doctor's office recently when she discovered her nurse was a child whose case she was appointed to a decade ago.
Davenport said Sally had never known if she had made a difference in the child's life. At the doctor's office that day, the now-nurse told Sally she got through high school and college because of what Sally said to her.
"And so we're here tonight because everyone in this room talks the talk and walks the walk," Davenport said. "And that is really important to us, but certainly to the future of the kids who we're working with."
Volunteer Geoff Searle said he got involved with CASA of the Mid-Shore in 2022 after retiring. He said social workers often have large caseloads, and CASA volunteers are able to focus solely on one child.
Larry Neviaser, who became a volunteer this year, said one of the things that drew him to the organization is its focus on finding the best outcome for every child.
"We don't represent anybody else except the child," he said.
Neviaser said he feels supported by CASA of the Mid-Shore's staff.
"They recognize the value of the volunteers, and (that) it really makes the organization," he said.
Along with being thanked and served up food and drink, CASA volunteers heard a presentation from author and speaker Frank Kros about making positive impacts on children that can last generations.
Weaving in stories about his own childhood, Kros talked about the mindset of children who have been through abuse and gave tips on how to encourage children.
"It's incredible what we can do when someone genuinely believes in us and provides us the support that we need," he said.
