title: Childlene Brooks, Kenley Timms win awards at Talbot Day
author: Konner Metz
content:
Childlene Brooks, Kenley Timms win awards at Talbot Day

 April 28, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Konner Metz | Section: Local News 
 
 533
 Words 

 Read News Document

 EASTON — Childlene Brooks and Kenley Timms were honored Friday for their outstanding community service.During a Talbot Day ceremony, an annual celebration for the county's April 25 birthday, the county presented Brooks with the Lifetime Service Award and Timms with the Ripple Effect Award.
Brooks is manager of the Brookletts Place Senior Center, and Timms serves as commander of VFW Post 5118.
Talbot County Council members Lynn Mielke and Keasha Haythe spoke on the impact of the winners' work in the Talbot County community.
"Childlene's name is synonymous with service to Talbot County," Mielke said. "Through her leadership at Brookletts Place, her tireless volunteerism, she's guided, mentored and uplifted generations. Her service has not only filled gaps, but has built bridges."
"A Vietnam veteran and longtime VFW commander, Kenley's legacy is one of action and compassion," Haythe said. "Whether organizing welcome-home parades, helping homeless veterans, supporting first responders, or simply showing up for those in need, Kenley leads with heart. His efforts have not only made a difference, they've inspired movement."
Brooks volunteers for nonprofit organizations along with leading the Brookletts Place in its mission to serve the county's growing senior population. Timms recently organized a Welcome Home parade for Vietnam veterans and families, an event that brought hundreds to the streets of Easton.
A 1983 proclamation originally declared April 25 as the county's birthday. The County Council led a charge to reinvigorate Talbot Day by signing a new proclamation to create the holiday in 2023.
In all, the county recognized 17 nominees for community service, part of the new tradition.
Haythe noted that the county created the award ceremony to continue the tradition of a now-defunct state program dating back to the 1980s, which honored community service leaders.
"Although the statewide program ended in 2022, the Talbot County Council chose to carry the tradition forward," Haythe said. "We renamed it the Talbot Citizen and Service Awards, continuing its legacy of recognizing those who give their time and heart to our community."
Talbot Day also brought around 100 residents to the lawn of the Talbot County Courthouse to celebrate the county's history. Mike Mielke, a local farmer, waterman and historian, served as Friday's guest speaker.
Mielke said a range of local organizations, schools and volunteer groups make Talbot County a special place to live. He pointed out towns such as Oxford, St. Michaels and Easton for bringing a unique way of life to the Eastern Shore as well as being a "mecca for weddings."
And for unincorporated areas such as Tilghman Island or Neavitt, Mielke said it's a neat mix of residents.
"The people do get along, the newcomers and watermen and stuff," Mielke said. "They get along pretty darn well."
"It's still the land of pleasant living," Mielke said of Talbot County. "Talbot's my home, and I love it."
Talbot Day Poster Contest winners: Maddy Calabro, Division I; Toni Wilson, Brianna Johnson, Meyers Hannah and Leah Bell, Division III.
Talbot Citizen and Service Awards nominees: Carlton "Corky" Greene, Childlene Brooks, Christine Dorset, Daphan Smith, Della Andrew, Doris Dobson, Mary DeShields, Jennifer Stanley, JR Burkhardt, Karla Wieland-Cherry, Kenley Timms, Khalid Kurtom, Lonnelle Green, Nancy Andrew, Raymond Bonner, Sonny Diefenderfer, Virginia Capute
This story has been updated to correct the spelling of Talbot Citizen and Service Award nominee Sonny Diefenderfer.

title: Women and Girls Fund presents 2025 awards, grants
author: Maggie Trovato
content:
Women and Girls Fund presents 2025 awards, grants

 April 30, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Maggie Trovato | Section: Local News 
 
 394
 Words 

 Read News Document

 EASTON — During its annual luncheon at the Tidewater Inn Monday, the Women and Girls Fund of the Mid-Shore presented its 2025 awards and annual grants.Kathy Deoudes was presented with the Women and Girls Fund Award. The annual award honors members of the community who have made contributions toward understanding and addressing women and girls' needs.
Deoudes, who retired in 2010 after spending seven years as a legislative aide for former Sen. E.J. Pipkin, currently serves as chair of the University of Maryland Shore Regional Health Board of Directors.
In her speech, Deoudes thanked her friends, family and colleagues for their support.
"And then to everyone else in this room, your philanthropy, your volunteerism and your compassion is what provides a safety net for members of our community who need it all the time or some of the time," she said. "And for that, I am very grateful."
For All Seasons President and CEO Beth Anne Dorman was presented with the Sheryl V. Kerr Award. Given in memory of Kerr, the award recognizes individuals or programs that are significant to women, according to the Women and Girls Fund.
In her speech, Dorman said mental health matters and spoke about how important it is that women remember to prioritize self care.
"To know that it's OK if you need support, its OK to reach out and that sometimes the people that are leading and the people that are smiling and holding things need to be checked in on too," she said.
The Women and Girls Fund, which uses pooled resources to improve the lives of women and girls on the Mid-Shore, aims to support programs and initiatives geared toward women and girls and facilitate collaboration and partnership among organizations.
During the luncheon, a total of $64,970 in grants were distributed among 18 organizations.
Women and Girls Fund President Beth Spurry said the organizations recognized at the luncheon are ones that invest in young girls' ability and right to "soar."
"They will be the leaders of tomorrow," she said. "So a prom dress or a 5K race on its own doesn't save a life, but being told that you are valued, that you deserve the spotlight too and that you are strong and can do hard things, may just give these girls — who will be women — the raw material to move beyond the barriers imposed on them from the circumstances of their lives."

title: Stronger together: Rebuilding Together wraps up Rebuilding Month with appreciation lunch
author: ANDREA GRABENSTEIN agrabenstein@chespub.com
content:
Stronger together: Rebuilding Together wraps up Rebuilding Month with appreciation lunch

 May 1, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: ANDREA GRABENSTEIN agrabenstein@chespub.com | Section: News 
 
 444
 Words 

 Read News Document

 CENTREVILLE — Wrapping up National Rebuilding Month and celebrating its first appreciation lunch following its merger, Rebuilding Together Eastern Shore recognized volunteers and supporters at the Centreville United Methodist Church April 26.Rebuilding Together Eastern Shore provides free, critical home repairs for income eligible homeowners in Kent and Queen Anne's counties the whole month of April kicked projects into high gear to provide vital repair needs across the area, completing six projects including fresh off of two that very Saturday, said co-President Larisa Thomas.
Providing more resources and personnel to help more residents, the recent merge of the Kent and Queen Anne's counties departments has made Rebuilding Together even stronger together, Thomas said.
Thomas started as a volunteer swinging a hammer 15 years ago and credited the non-profit as making a difference in local lives.
Before rebranding, Rebuilding Together originated nationally as Christmas in April in 1973 and started in Queen Anne's County in 1994 and in Kent Count in 2004, according to Executive Director Genevieve Croker in a presentation to the Queen Anne's County Commissioners April 22.
Keeping the human aspect along with the housing aspect, Rebuilding Together recognizes everyone has the right to live comfortably, and works to repair homes, revitalize communities, and rebuild lives, Croker said.
All work is done at no cost to the homeowners who meet the income limits and other criteria. Typical projects can include painting, installing ramps and grab bars, repairing floors, plumbing, electrical, and other areas needed to ensure safe and healthy housing for homeowners.
"We say what we're going to do," Community Service Coordinator Cory Palmer said.
Rebuilding Together seeks to establish safe homes and communities for all and addresses the housing crisis by improving property values and preserving affordable housing stock, noting it is often cheaper to repair a home than build a new one and help aging homeowners age in place, Croker said.
Helen Fisher, of Crumpton, was one such homeowner utilizing volunteer services including smoke detector installation, outside lighting installation, and improved home skirting. At the appreciation luncheon, Fisher credited volunteers as professionals who get the job done.
Rebuilding Together welcomes volunteers of all calibers, whether with repairs or behind the scenes fundraising. "There is a role available for you," Thomas said.
Palmer encouraged anyone struggling with home repair costs to apply for services, noting income requirements and guidelines can change.
Volunteer Dan Hercher, of Church Hill, recently celebrated his first completed project with Rebuilding Together. Experienced with repair work, he said he loved seeing the change made to the homes and what it means to the homeowners.
"Some people don't have the tools or resources, so it's nice to help," he said.
More information about Rebuilding Together Eastern Shore can be found at rebuildingtogethereasternshore.org.

title: National Day of Prayer draws big crowd in Caroline County
author: AHMAD GARNETT agarnett@chespub.com
content:
National Day of Prayer draws big crowd in Caroline County

 May 2, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: AHMAD GARNETT agarnett@chespub.com | Section: News 
 
 280
 Words 

 Read News Document

 DENTON — Hundreds of Caroline County residents joined together on the county courthouse green to pray Thursday afternoon.The Caroline County Christian Clergy Association hosted National Day of Prayer ceremony, an annual event highlighted with prayers and singing.
"As a part of this community for so many years, it's just wonderful to see everybody come out for prayer and to recognize that we need God at work in our land in order for him to do great and mighty things," said Doug Morely, Greater Impact pastor and president of Caroline County Christian Clergy Association.
The Caroline County Sheriff's Office presented the colors for the national anthem. Grace Notes, the choir at Calvary Baptist Church in Denton, sung the anthem and multiple songs throughout the event.
Grace Notes has sung at every National Day or Prayer event in Caroline County, except for last year's.
"It's a privilege," Maureen Twining, singer and pianist, said. "Especially two of us are going through some really difficult times physically, and we know that it's a blessing that we're here today. It's wonderful."
Denton Mayor Abigail McNinch, Caroline County Commissioners President Travis Breeding and Caroline County Sheriff Donnie Baker shared proclamations at the event.
Paul Twining, National Day of Prayer coordinator and pastor at Calvary Baptist Church in Denton, presented the keynote speech, highlighting multiple scriptures and reasons why prayer is so important in 2025.
"The response of the people today and the people that participated, I thought it was so on target," Twining said.
After the keynote, multiple clergy members began to pray for various groups in the county, including churches, government, families, media, schools, military, first responders and businesses.
After all prayers, Caroline County municipalities served free hot dogs and chips to residents.

title: Country Cooking: Mom's recipes
author: MARIE SAVAGE Country Cooking
content:
Country Cooking: Mom's recipes

 May 6, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: MARIE SAVAGE Country Cooking | Section: Food 
 
 1354
 Words 

 Read News Document

 We are celebrating Mother's Day on Sunday, and this year I decided to gather favorite recipes from many moms around the countryside. I am constantly sharing my mom's cooking, and I appreciate the many wonderful comments I receive, but let's share your favorite mom recipes.As I made my calls, emails and text messages to my readers, it was amazing to find how alike our mom's recipes were.
Remember how moms dumped in, sprinkled, spread, eye measured and judged the size by holding the product? They held recipes by "memory instead of measurement."
Years ago, I asked my mom to write down some recipes and she replied, "I'll try."
When I speak of and recall Mother's Day, there are many definitions of a mom or mother. This person can be our birth mother, adopted mother, step mother, sister who replaced a mother, aunt, grandmother, close family friend who stepped in to help, father who served as both parents — it does not matter who they are.
But what does matter is they were, or still are, there to fill those shoes of a loving adult guiding your life forward.
My mom was a blessing, and her love and guidance will forever be treasured by all who knew her as Mom, Grandmother, Great Grandmother or Miss Laurie.
MRS. HOLLAND'S GREEN LIMA BEAN SOUP
Mrs. Holland is now in her late 80s and remembers her mother making this soup any time of the year to help feed the family. They grew lima beans on the farm, and this soup fed many family members and farm hands cheaply.
In a large soup pot add 6 cups of water, 1 number 10 can whole tomatoes or 1 quart jar of home canned tomatoes, 1 piece of salt pork or ham, 3-4 cups green lima beans (fresh or frozen), 1 can yellow or white corn, 3-4 white potatoes (peeled and cubed), and 1 tbsp sugar. Cover and simmer until all ingredients are tender. During the first 30 minutes of cooking, taste soup for seasonings. Serve hot with fresh baked biscuits.
COLLINS FAMILY BISCUITS
My elementary school friend Fay makes some great homemade biscuits to go with the bean soup. Fay grew up in the country and had a large family also.
Preheat the oven to 450 degrees. Cut one cup shortening or lard into 6 cups flour, 1 tbsp salt and 3 tbsps baking powder. Then add 2 cups of milk. Mix well and knead at least eight times. Form biscuits by rolling the desired amounts of dough with your hands and place them on a floured baking sheet. Bake for about 10-12 minutes. Serve warm.
PECAN PIE
My friend Joy's mom, the late Mrs. Eva Dixon of Greensboro, was well known by family and friends for her delicious pecan pie. This fresh baked pie appeared at all family functions.
Prepare or purchase an eight-inch pie shell, unbaked. Preheat the oven to 400 degrees. Beat 3 eggs until frothy and add 1 cup white or brown sugar, 1/2 cup light corn syrup, a dash of salt, 1 tsp vanilla and 1 cup chopped pecans. Mix well and pour into the pie shell. Place some halved pecans on top for decorative purposes. Bake for 10 minutes, then lower the temperature to 350 degrees and bake another 30 minutes. Cool before serving.
PEPPER RELISH
My niece, Jamie, often talks about her relative who makes pepper relish throughout the year and about how delicious it is. After convincing her to share this recipe for my special column today, let's make this relish.
Prepare 12 green sweet peppers and 12 sweet red peppers (remove the seeds and chop up fine). Clean and chop 12 onions, mix peppers and onions together and pour boiling water over this mixture and let it stand for 5 minutes. Drain well. In a small pot, add 3 cups vinegar, 1 tbsp salt, 2 cups sugar, 2 tbsps celery seed and 2 tbsps mustard seeds. Let stand for five minutes. Cook gently for 10 minutes. When mixture comes to boiling point, remove from heat and pack in pint jars. Makes 6 pints. Instead of hand chopping, you can use a blender to chop peppers and onions.
FRESH CATFISH
Let's go fishing together with Donna and her husband for some fresh catfish. Most weekends, weather permitting, this couple fish and share in the cleaning and cooking.
Combine 2/3 cup yellow cornmeal with 1/4 cup all-purpose flour, 2 tsps salt and 1/2 tsp paprika. Dry the fresh fillets thoroughly and coat each side with cornmeal mixture. Fry in 1/2 cup vegetable oil for about 4 minutes on each side. Drain well on paper towels. This coating mixture can be used on any type of fish.
FRIED GREEN TOMATOES
These were submitted to me by three different ladies in honor of their mothers. So, since their recipes were almost identical, let's call this Rose, Marilyn and Edna's fried green tomatoes.
Use 3 large tomatoes (about 2 1/2 pounds), sliced crosswise about 1/3 inch thick. Arrange the tomatoes on paper towels and sprinkle with 1 tsp salt. Set aside for 30 minutes to draw out the moisture. In the meantime, make a dredging mixture consisting of 2 cups of yellow cornmeal and 1/4 tsp cayenne pepper. When tomatoes are ready to fry — place 1/4 cup solid vegetable oil in a fry pan. When the oil is hot, place a single layer of tomato slices in the pan and fry until golden on each side, turning once. Remove to paper towels for draining. serve immediately.
One note to be added — you can use green tomatoes, red tomatoes or pink tomatoes (partially green but not ripe yet). The green tomato may need a sprinkle of sugar on top at serving time.
SOUTHERN CORNBREAD
How about some Southern cornbread from a true Southern lady and mother — Ms. Bea? She's been living down in Tennessee for the past 15 years.
Preheat the oven to 450 degrees. Sift together 1 cup white or yellow cornmeal with 1/2 tsp baking soda and 1/2 tsp salt. In another bowl, mix one beaten egg with 1 cup buttermilk and 1 tbsp melted shortening. Add wet and dry ingredients together, mix well and pour into a shallow greased pan. Bake for 18 minutes.
BISHOPVILLE BANANA PUDDING
Let's close with a few deserts for that special day, because one thing I know… Moms love desert.
This was always a favorite no matter what time of year in our house. Gather ⅓ cup all-purpose flour, a dash of salt, 2 ½ cups 1% low-fat milk, 1 (14-oz.) can fat-free sweetened condensed milk, 2 egg yolks (lightly beaten), 2 tsps vanilla extract, 3 cups sliced ripe bananas, 48 vanilla wafers, 4 egg whites and ¼ cup sugar. Preheat the oven to 325 degrees. Combine flour and salt in a medium saucepan. Gradually stir in 1% milk, sweetened condensed milk and yolks, and cook over medium heat, stirring constantly, for 8 to 10 minutes or until thickened. Remove from heat, stir in vanilla. Layer 3 banana slices, 3½ tbsp. pudding and 3 vanilla wafers in each of 8 (1-cup) ramekins or ovenproof glass dishes. Top each with 6 banana slices, 3½ tbsp. pudding, and 3 vanilla wafers. Beat egg whites at high speed with an electric mixer until foamy. Add sugar, 1 tbsp. at a time, beating until stiff peaks form and sugar dissolves (2 to 4 minutes). Spread about ½ cup meringue over each pudding. Bake for 15 to 20 minutes or until golden. Let cool for 30 minutes.
EASY PINEAPPLE UPSIDE DOWN CAKE
Gather 3 tbsps butter melted, 1/3 cup packed brown sugar, 9 canned unsweetened pineapple slices, 9 Maraschino cherry halves, 2/3 cup sugar, 2/3 cup fat-free milk and 3 tbsps canola oil. Pour butter into a nine-inch square baking pan; sprinkle with brown sugar. Arrange pineapple slices in a single layer in the pan; place cherry halves in the center of pineapple slices; set aside. In a large bowl, beat the sugar, milk, oil, egg and extracts until well blended. Combine the flour, baking powder and salt; gradually beat into sugar mixture until blended. Pour into the prepared pan. Bake at 350 degrees for 35-40 minutes or until a toothpick comes out clean. Immediately invert onto a serving plate. Serve warm.

title: Seniors show unbridled joy in Kentucky Derby-themed party
author: WILL BONTRAGER wbontrager@chespub.com
content:
Seniors show unbridled joy in Kentucky Derby-themed party

 May 8, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: WILL BONTRAGER wbontrager@chespub.com | Section: News 
 
 770
 Words 

 Read News Document

 CHESTERTOWN — Last Friday, the horse races came a day early when the Amy Lynn Ferris Adult Activity Center was transformed into Churchill Downs for its very first Kentucky Derby Party."There are some amazing artwork and displays," said Susan Higgs the Kent County Project director for the Retired and Senior Volunteer Program of Upper Shore Aging Inc.
Around 50, maybe more, came out to partake in the festivities, wearing giant, elaborate hats, jamming out to a variety music from DJ Pres Jacobs — sharing laughs with friends.
From 10:30 a.m. to 1 p.m. they had finger foods, snacks, cookies and sipped non-alcoholic mint juleps. Each table was adorned with a wooden centerpiece representing the race complete with turf, jockey silks, helmet and stirrups.
But nobody sat at the table for long.
There were exciting things to do, ideas thought up by Activity Coordinator Colleen Upp. Since she has been in her role, many can attest she has breathed new life into the center with creative activities planned daily.
The origin of this idea, she exclaimed, stemmed from her love of horses. Thinking of a horse-themed event, she saw the costumes and pageantry behind the biggest national races as inspiring.
"It was a fun idea and so original," Higgs pointed out.
And like all of Upp's ideas, her enthusiasm in the project was contagious. Soon it was all hands-on-deck to transform the center into a racing hub. In every corner there is something created that adds authenticity to the event and fun.
Starting on the outside of the building, styrofoam containers once used for storing chemicals were airbrushed and made into a brick wall. Wildlife artist John Elburn used his creativity to fashion a unique gateway into the party, complete with plywood horse and jockeys.
His innovation did not stop there. In the doorway, greeting party-goers, was a five-foot, 350 lb. horse head he sculpted from a chainsaw, rotary and chisel tools. The maple sculpture took him 350 hours and was glad to do it for the center.
"Colleen had the idea, and we ran with it," Elburn said.
Past the horse head, going into the dining area, the red rosed archway was designed with the idea of the flower blankets draped over the horses at the competition.
Inside the dining area, every inch seemed decorated...including the party goers, who donned hats of ribbons, feathers and flowers. There was a display of red roses symbolic of the Kentucky Derby, Upp's daughter's exercise saddle, horse figurines arranged in orderly fashion, and of course, the winner's circle perfect for photo ops after the competitions.
Because what's a party without party games, Upp said, including toilet paper horse races.
A total of eight participants (jockeys) held a roll of slightly unrolled toilet paper. At the end of the table, setting on the toilet paper strip was a plastic horse, ready for the race. At the mark, set, go, the jockeys had to roll up the toilet paper keeping the horse on the strip while moving it towards the finish line.
Carol Elburn and Marie Spray had a heated competition in the finals. Elburn edged her out, and both received award winning plates.
In the morning, they held their hat competition, many wearing their creations from the hat-making class held by Brenda Foehrkolb on April 29 with over 20 in attendance.
DJ Pres Jacobs put on a huge Smirnoff Ice Vodka hat and went home the winner of three of the six categories: most comical, most eventful and most outrageous, Upp said laughing.
As they were cleaning up, they had line dancing headed by the boundless activity coordinator. Upp likes to put her own spin on the line dancing, making it adaptable for seniors. She said that dancing promotes coordination, balance, memory and it is just plain fun.
She's named her group of dancers the Vintage Vibes. They dance two times a week, learning different genres and styles from Mark Rice's 1965 song "Ride Around Sally" to hits by American rapper and singer, Pitbull.
"Their grandkids would be amazed to see grandma dancing to Pitbull," said Pam Holland, a friend of Upp.
The horse race parties will continue for two more big races, the Preakness and then the Belmont Stakes. With each change of race, comes new decorations added on to the centerpiece and the wreath; for Preakness, Black-eyed Susans, and for Belmont, white carnations.
It is these little details to add to the experience.
For a list of activities at the center, contact the front desk at 410-778-2564 or stop in at 200 Schauber Rd. Monday through Friday from 8 a.m. to 3 p.m.
"We're having so much fun here! You never know what to expect from our members," Upp said with a "winning" smile... pun intended.

title: 100 years and counting: Talbot County Free Library endures as community linchpin
author: Konner Metz
content:
100 years and counting: Talbot County Free Library endures as community linchpin

 May 14, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Konner Metz | Section: Local News 
 
 664
 Words 

 Read News Document

 EASTON — Over the last 100 years, the Talbot County Free Library has adapted to societal changes such as the creation of the Internet, economic downturns like the Great Depression and, most recently, a global pandemic.As the world changes around it, the organization's staff and volunteers are ensuring sure the library keeps up. Executive Director Dana Newman believes the library is well-positioned to serve the community's needs for years to come.
"I do think the library will continue to move with the future, and it will continue to be here," Newman said.
Serving residents across the entire county, the Talbot County Free Library has oriented itself as a hub for the county. Between a physical collection of over 130,000 books and other items, computer and technology access, and hundreds of free programs, Newman says the library has more resources available than most people would think.
This October, the library will host a centennial gala, an opportunity for many to celebrate the library's history and its impact on residents in the 100 years since its inception.
Emma Poole, TCFL's communications manager, was born in Easton and still has her original library card from when she was 3.
"This has always been such a safe space for me," Poole said. "My parents brought me here all the time. I begged my mom to bring me to the library. I'd drag her out of the house."
During college, Poole used the library's expansive Maryland Room collection in writing her historical thesis. And now as a staff member, Poole recognizes the institution's purpose in Talbot County extends far past books and research.
"It's so much more than books," she said.
ADAPTING OVER TIME
On Oct. 15, 1925, Talbot County Free Library opened in two rooms in the Tred Avon Building on South Washington Street. Caroline Burnite Walker founded the library, which began with an 800-book collection.
She was a longtime children's librarian, and the early days of Talbot's library focused on serving the youth. Scotti Oliver, current assistant director, says the organization's "emphasis has always been on children's services."
The library offers many early literacy programs, partners with local schools and will host the 10th annual Chesapeake Children's Book Festival this June.
TCFL moved inside the courthouse in the 1940s and soon became one of Maryland's first county-wide public library systems. Around three decades later, it moved to West Dover Street, where it sits today.
Ever since its founding, the nonprofit has constantly adapted, library leaders say.
"I think we demonstrated over time that when people think, 'Well maybe the library's a thing of the past,' it's not," Newman said. "Because there's a new need, and there's a need for instruction. We are a learning institution."
Among the many offerings are book clubs, community meeting rooms, a free collection of seeds, tax assistance aid and social services programs.
Following the pandemic, Newman says the organization reinvented itself in a way, focusing much more on digital literacy classes, availability of computers and devices, and internet access.
Newman noted the library has demonstrated an ability to pivot when needed, a skill that'll help tackle future challenges — one being the rise of AI.
COMMUNITY LINCHPIN
While the library's main branch is in well-populated Easton, TCFL is undergoing renovations to its branch site in St. Michaels. The building will expand and add children's spaces.
One of Newman's hopes is that the Bookmobile service can return. Ending in the 1990s due to a lack of funding, the Bookmobile made trips to remote parts of the county such as Tilghman Island, Cordova and Trappe. Newman said the library understands the importance of reaching these communities, and is looking to secure funding for the venture in the near future.
Around 20,000 county residents hold a library card, over 7,000 of them children. Like Poole, many of those cardholders consider the library a safe place. Newman emphasized that unhoused individuals often rely on that "safe space."
"Libraries exist because people have a need, and we're serving that need as much as we can," Newman says. "And that need continues and has continued for many, many years."

title: Star Democrat's newest reporter wants to tell untold stories
author: AHMAD GARNETT agarnett@chespub.com
content:
Star Democrat's newest reporter wants to tell untold stories

 May 15, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: AHMAD GARNETT agarnett@chespub.com | Section: Dorchester 
 
 354
 Words 

 Read News Document

 EASTON — Lily Tierney, a Louisville, Kentucky native recently hired as a reporter at the Star Democrat, is looking forward to telling many different stories on the Eastern Shore.Tierney will be covering Dorchester County and is excited to learn more about Dorchester's ins and outs.
She attended Eckerd College in St. Petersburg, Florida for a few years, then decided to transfer to American University in Washington, D.C., where she graduated in 2024.
Tierney credits getting over her childhood dyslexia as her path to finding journalism.
"I am very dyslexic, and so it took me a while to read," Tierney said. "I finally did learn how to read. I was like, 'Oh, this is sick, this is a cool world,' and being able to just kind of escape into fiction I always loved.
"Then when I went into high school, I started writing poetry, loved poetry. For one of my first gifts when I was 14, I got a typewriter, and I was like, 'Alright, I'm going to be a writer. That's what I'm going to do. I'm going to be a writer.'"
Tragedy in 2020 gave Tierney her drive to tell people's stories.
"2020 hit, and that's when Breonna Taylor was shot and killed in her house. For me that was a really pivotal moment because it was insane to be from Louisville then, and it felt like I was getting a lot of that coverage just because I was from Louisville, but it took a long time for her story to get told," Tierney said. "I wanted to be someone who could tell people's stories who couldn't tell their own anymore."
While at American University, Tierney covered immigration, which she enjoyed because it gave her a chance to tell stories that might have otherwise gone untold.
Tierney wants community members to know she is very friendly and excited to get to know her community.
"I'm just excited to be here," Tierney said. "I'm excited to cover locally because, I mean, as they say in comedy, local jokes get local laughs, but I think it's the same thing in news — local reporting gets local attention, and I think that's really exciting."

title: A better life: Local kids on why America is beautiful
author: WILL BONTRAGER wbontrager@chespub.com
content:
A better life: Local kids on why America is beautiful

 May 16, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: WILL BONTRAGER wbontrager@chespub.com | Section: Life 
 
 540
 Words 

 Read News Document

 Galena Elementary School third grader, Helena Sanchez had no idea she came in first place for the speech she wrote in class.At the C. Henry Price II, American Legion Post 246, earlier this month when President of the Auxiliary Patti Bone announced it, Sanchez was so excited she put her hands to her mouth, glancing around the room in amazement. Her family kept it a secret on purpose to make the moment extra special.
Overcoming stage fright, without a hint of waver in her voice, Sanchez read her essay to 30 people in the room.
This was the first speech of the afternoon for the Legion Auxiliary's annual Americanism Essay Contest, created to teach students the value of patriotism.
Thousands of students from grades three to 12 around the nation participate, each year having a different theme.
This year's topic: "What does 'America the Beautiful' mean to me (regarding veterans and our military).
In her essay, Sanchez thanked our military who fight for our country to protect us from enemies.
"Many people have lost their life for us so we can have a better one," she recited.
She added these soldiers are role models and expressed her love for America to a hearty applause.
Like all six speakers that night, she received a cash prize, (first place $50, second $20, third $10) a certificate, congratulations from Betterton Mayor Donald Sutton and a goody bag of patriotic items like comic books, rulers, flags and candy to sweeten the deal.
Winners receive $50 and a $50 donation in the student's name is made to the Children of Warriors National Presidents' Scholarship fund.
Coming in second among third graders, was Chloe Cummings, who talked about the American flag being the symbol of freedom, pride and unity. In third place, Annistyn Clayton explained America brings unity to the world; America is a special place with beautiful landscapes she wants to visit and is home to great friends.
Coming in first for fifth graders was Liam Miller, detailing what makes our military so special, from the oldest branch, the Army, to the newest, the Space Force. He urged the audience to remember why America is a blessed nation.
"America is beautiful because of the things the soldiers did that would not be forgotten. We as Americans celebrate and remember our soldiers. God bless America," he read.
Amelia Rigby, in second, focused in on the lyrics of "America the Beautiful" calling veterans heroes. She was proud of one hero particularly, her mother, an Air Force veteran. Third place Samantha Carroll also talked about the lyrics of "America the Beautiful" providing an in-depth look at some poignant lines which inspire unity in the world.
Bone said the Betterton auxiliary has been having the essay contest for over 15 years and thanked all members of the Legion and the families for their attendance. She said they are always glad to see the community show up and support the students and socialize with refreshments and cookies.
With free family-focused entertainment in mind, she announced they will hold a Community Day on Flag Day, June 14. Bone encouraged the public to check them out and grab a free hotdog. There will be a bouncy house, petting zoo and some other activities planned for that day.
"We love doing these things for our families," Bone said.

title: Country Cooking: The kitchen catch-all drawer
author: MARIE SAVAGE Country Cooking
content:
Country Cooking: The kitchen catch-all drawer

 May 20, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: MARIE SAVAGE Country Cooking | Section: Life 
 
 1212
 Words 

 Read News Document

 Before I begin my weekly column, I need to recognize a holiday that is dear to me — Memorial Day will be May 26. Fly those American flags in honor of our fallen heroes. Attend the many services held at your local VFW or American Legion.Many other organizations hold events to honor our fellow Americans. One of the many breathtaking sights here on the Eastern Shore is the Veterans Cemetery at the Buelah location outside Hurlock. Each grave is marked with a small individual American flag, astonishing to see in the breeze.
I just automatically place my right hand over my heart and remember the words of our 35th President, the late John Fitzgerald Kennedy — "My fellow Americans, ask not what your country can do for you but what can you do for your country."
Now for this week's column.
Every kitchen has one, but maybe they different names for it — the catch-all drawer, the what you call it drawer, the thing-a-bob drawer or gadget drawer. But once you struggle to get it open, oh my.
It is loaded with a little bit of everything and even though it is in the kitchen it has "stuff" for everything and everywhere. Let me pull my drawer open and see what I find. It is a wooden spring type clothespin I use to close bags with when I can't find the little plastic closure. Here is the old, handheld can opener along with the opener that punches in the top or you can "stab" a hole in a can. Now this is cool — the old handheld potato masher next to the beaters that fit on my electric beater. I have at least five paring knives in here next to the hand peeler and the core remover.
I must add this one — I just saw my modern iced tea maker, but folks, nothing tastes like the ice tea made with tea bags in the saucepan cooking over the flame, removing from heat, squeezing out bags and pouring in the big glass pitcher, adding sugar and squeezing lemon juice and serving in a real glass with ice cubes.
I will finish this inventory another day — let's use modern utensils that have replaced the above and explore the recipes.
A few weeks ago, I visited a store in Salisbury that had a whole wall of tools and modern gadgets. A few things I stopped and looked at, thinking to myself, "Wow, if only I would've had one of these 50 years ago."
In El Paso, Texas back in the '60s, when I was exposed to some many new foods, I remember the Jalapeno pepper being one I was told to stay away from. Those West Texans would eat jalapenos the way we eat apples.
I came across a jalapeno corer in this store and instantly remembered the stories of those older ladies cutting jalapenos until their fingers were numb from the oil of those peppers.
JALAPENO CORN SALAD
1 medium onion (quartered), 2 jalapeno peppers, 1 cup sour cream, 1 cup mayonnaise, 2 ounces cream cheese (softened), 2 tsps ground cumin, 1 tsp garlic powder, 1 tsp chili powder, 1 tsp smoked paprika, 1/4 tsp salt, 1/4 tsp pepper, 4 cups fresh corn (about 8 ears) (cooked and cooled), 1 cup shredded sharp cheddar cheese, 1 cup shredded pepper jack cheese, 1/2 cup crumbled cooked bacon.
Grill onion and jalapenos, covered, over medium-high heat or broil 4 inches from heat for 3-5 minutes on each side or until lightly charred. Cool completely; chop into 1/2-inch pieces. Combine the next nine ingredients. Stir in corn, cheese, half the bacon and the grilled vegetables. Top with remaining bacon to serve.
QUICK DUMPLINGS
Two staples in our kitchen growing up were Flour and a rolling pin. I feel like 90% of our meals used both. Whether it was biscuits for breakfast, dumplings at every meal, or those amazing pies and many, many others. A good rolling pin is almost like your right hand when it comes to the kitchen.
While in this store, I saw one of the best inventions ever — rolling pin that had a hollow core to store flour in. As you are rolling out your dough, it can get dry. Instead of making a mess with moist dough, dry flour and getting it all over the counter, you can just shake a little out of the end of the pin as you roll.
2 cups all-purpose flour, 1/2 tsp baking powder, 1 tsp salt, 1/3 cup shortening (cold), 3/4 to 1 cup buttermilk.
Heat a large Dutch oven over medium high heat. Mix flour, baking powder and salt in a mixing bowl. Cut in the cold shortening using a pastry cutter or food processor. Gradually pour in the buttermilk, stirring until the dough comes together. Turn the dough out on a floured surface and work it just until everything is combined. The dough should not be sticky. Roll the dough out about 1/4-inch thick with your rolling pin to keep it from getting too dry. Cut into 1-inch strips. Cut each of those strips into pieces that are approximately 2 inches in length. Add the milk to the Dutch oven and bring to a simmer. Drop dumplings strips into soup and simmer for 15-20 minutes until cooked through.
That was the "quick" dumpling recipe. Soon I'll post the recipe that I have cooked probably over 10,000 times in the last 50 plus years.
SPICY SAUSAGE PASTA
This next gadget is one that my daughter-in-law Shannon uses at least three or four times a week — a garlic press. Garlic in their household is like salt and pepper in most others. It's always being used in dishes to add flavor.
I don't think my son makes anything that doesn't have fresh chopped or minced garlic in it. If you use minced, chopped or crushed garlic, you can save time by not having to peel or dice with a garlic press. Shannon also told me she uses it to crush nuts for other recipes.
8 ounces uncooked penne, 10.6 ounces hot Italian sausages (sliced and crumbled), 3 cloves garlic (minced), 1/2 cup chicken broth, 1/2 tbsp flour, 1 (14 fluid ounce) can diced tomatoes with juices, 1/2 cup heavy whipping cream, salt and pepper to taste, 6 large leaves basil (sliced/torn into small pieces), freshly grated parmesan cheese to taste.
Bring a large pot of salted water to a boil. Cook pasta al dente according to package directions. Take the sausage meat out of the casings and crumble it into a deep skillet. Cook it for about 5 minutes, stirring occasionally, over medium-high heat until browned. Once the sausage is browned, take it out of the pan and set it aside. Drain the fat. Add the garlic, followed by the chicken broth to the skillet. Sprinkle the flour in. Whisk it until the flour has dissolved and scrape any browned bits from the bottom of the pan. Cook this mixture until it's significantly reduced (should only take a minute or two in total).Add in the tomatoes, cream, and the sausage meat. Cook the sauce for a few more minutes until it's thickened to your liking. Season with salt & pepper as needed. Just prior to serving, add in the torn basil leaves and then toss with the drained pasta. Serve with freshly grated parmesan cheese.

title: The Arc Central Chesapeake Region rebrands to Fello
author: Konner Metz
content:
The Arc Central Chesapeake Region rebrands to Fello

 May 21, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Konner Metz | Section: Local News 
 
 412
 Words 

 Read News Document

 EASTON — The Arc Central Chesapeake Region announced Wednesday it is rebranding to Fello, a name the organization hopes to build a distinct identity under.As part of the change, Fello will no longer be affiliated with The Arc Maryland or the nonprofit's national arm.
President and CEO Jonathon Rondeau said in an interview Tuesday that the name change aims to reflect the organization's "evolution of growth." Rondeau said the nonprofit is serving people all across Maryland and that the brand shift will best reflect that.
"The idea of Fello is that we are fellow citizens, we're fellow neighbors," Rondeau said. "We connect with each other. … We're about lifting up the communities we're in."
The nonprofit serves people with intellectual and developmental disabilities across the majority of the Eastern Shore and in Anne Arundel County. It was founded in 1961.
In Easton, a number of affordable housing projects had been pursued under The Arc Central Chesapeake Region name, some of which are still in the works. Last year, the organization opened the Port Street Commons, a mixed-use building with nine apartment units and office headquarters.
The Arc Central Chesapeake Region previously had two subsidiaries for housing management and community development: Chesapeake Neighbors and Chesapeake Community Development. Under Fello, those subsidiaries will remain. For brand purposes, they'll be jointly presented as Fello Communities.
Rondeau said Fello's history as a longtime chapter of The Arc isn't taken for granted.
The Arc's national organization dates back to the 1950s when it was first organized by parent groups in Minneapolis. It has chapters across the country, including Maryland's chapter and many local chapters within the state.
"Being part of The Arc and a national movement is a really important part of our history, and we would've never gotten here without that," Rondeau said. "But at some point, we all grow up."
In a press release, Fello stated it serves over 4,000 Marylanders in Anne Arundel County and the Eastern Shore. There are over 650 employees, nearly 100 housing units and 43 properties, the release stated.
Those services won't go away due to the name change, Rondeau said.
The Fello president noted the nonprofit's Board of Directors and top executives had been discussing the name change for a couple years. Once they began transitioning in recent months, the excitement has been "contagious," Rondeau said.
"I think there's also excitement of really being able to have our own brand that feels like us, it feels connected to our values, it feels connected to our vision and mission," he said.

title: 400 flags placed to honor heroes this Memorial Day weekend
author: Konner Metz
content:
400 flags placed to honor heroes this Memorial Day weekend

 May 23, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Konner Metz | Section: Local News 
 
 210
 Words 

 Read News Document

 EASTON — Rainy and windy conditions Wednesday didn't stop Civil Air Patrol cadets and Easton Rotary Club members from placing over 400 flags in front of the Talbot County Community Center in advance of Memorial Day weekend.1st. Lt. Richard Mellinger, commander of the Easton Composite Squadron, Civil Air Patrol, led a group of young cadets and senior members in arranging the flags, which are easily spotted by drivers on U.S. Route 50. Mellinger said recognizing fallen heroes with the patriotic display is extremely meaningful.
The flag display is part of the Rotary Club's Flags for Heroes initiative, which honors veterans, law enforcement officers, first responders, teachers, health care workers and more. It was started in 2012, and every May since, flags have been erected throughout Easton.
This year, in addition to the community center, flags were placed at Idlewild Park, Aqua Pools & Spas and Londonderry on the Tred Avon.
Rotary Club Secretary George Hatcher said the tradition "has never failed to be something that brings people together."
The Easton Rotary Club has raised nearly $600,000 since 2012 through donations from those who sponsor a flag for their heroes. The proceeds go to local organizations such as the Talbot County Sheriff's Office, Easton Police Department, Civil Air Patrol, local fire departments and more.

title: Mid-Shore Memorial Day ceremonies and events
author: STAFF REPORT
content:
Mid-Shore Memorial Day ceremonies and events

 May 23, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: STAFF REPORT | Section: News 
 
 464
 Words 

 Read News Document

 In the coming days, Mid-Shore communities and organizations will hold several ceremonies and events in observation of Memorial Day.Denton Memorial Day parade
A parade honoring those who dies in service will take place on Friday, May 23, in downtown Denton.
The parade will make its way down Market Street starting at 6 p.m.
The event is sponsored by American Legion Post 29.
Classic Motor Museum Memorial Day Parade
On Saturday, May 24, from 10:30 to 11:30 a.m., a parade featuring over 50 exhibits will make its way down Talbot Street in St. Michaels.
The parade will include military and veteran groups, classic cars and community groups. Spectators are encouraged to wear patriotic outfits.
An event will be held at the Classic Car Museum on E. Marengo Street following the parade.
Eastern Shore Veterans Cemetery flag placement
Community members are invited to help place flags on 7,000 veteran graves at the cemetery, located at 6827 E. New Market Ellwood Rd. in Hurlock.
Volunteers are encouraged to wear gloves to prevent blisters.
The event begins at 8 a.m. on Saturday, May 24.
Chestertown Memorial Day programming
hestertown celebrates Memorial Day with a parade and remembrance on May 26.
The Memorial Day Committee is inviting community members to participate in the parade by creating floats or showcasing vehicles of interest. Walking groups with patriotic themes are also welcome. No pre-registration is required. Participants will gather at 9 a.m. at Dixon Drive. The parade will start at 10 a.m. and proceed down High Street to Memorial Park.
In advance of the parade, from 9 to 10 a.m., entertainment will be provided by Chester River Voices and the Ukulele Club. Chestertown River Arts will be on hand to distribute "thank you cards" to be sent to veterans. The community arts organization will also sell tissue paper poppies.
Following the parade, keynote speaker Aubrey Sarvis, an Army veteran, will give a short presentation on the Korean War, which claimed the lives of more than 50,000 Americans.
Dorchester American Legion ceremony
The Dorchester American Legion Post 91 will hold its annual Memorial Day Service Monday, May 26, from 11 a.m. to noon at Long Wharf Park in Cambridge.
The flag will be raised and cannon will go off to begin the Service at 11 a.m.
The park will be closed to vehicle traffic at 10 a.m.
Chairs will be limited. Attendees are encourages to consider bringing their own.
At the conclusion of the event, the American Legion will host the community for finger foods and light refreshments.
Eastern Shore Veterans Cemetery Memorial Day service
A ceremony will be held at 1:30 p.m. on Friday, May 30, at the cemetery, located at 6827 E. New Market Ellwood Rd. in Hurlock.
The event will last between 15 and 20 minutes and will feature a keynote speaker and a performance by the Easton Middle School band.
Following the ceremony, a meal will be provided at the Hurlock American Legion.

The Star Democrat's top 10 online stories this week

 May 24, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: STAFF REPORT | Section: Local News

 Here are the 10 stories that attracted the most page views on The Star Democrat's website this week. The stories are ranked in order of number of page views as of Wednesday evening.1. ICE detains 2 longtime Caroline County residents in Preston
Longtime Caroline County residents Olga Velazquez and Frutalco Ramírez were detained by U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement on Saturday, May 10, in Preston.
According to a GoFundMe started by their daughter, Lili Ramirez, the couple are agricultural workers who have been in the United States for more than 20 years with no criminal record.
2. Federal lawsuit fights striped bass restrictions
Striped bass season began on the Chesapeake Bay May 16 amid mounting tensions between fishing industry groups and regulatory agencies. A federal lawsuit has been filed by fishing industry organizations bordering the Atlantic Ocean and its inland waterways.
3. Waterfowl Festival concerned about losing funding
After President Donald Trump proposed eliminating the National Endowment for the Arts, the Waterfowl Festival began to worry about its future.
4. Route 662 reopened, permit approved for next phase of hospital construction
University of Maryland Shore Regional Health and key partners celebrated the reopening of Maryland Route 662 between Airport Road and Hiners Lane with a ribbon cutting ceremony May 15.
5. Anton Black's cause of death should be ruled homicide, audit finds
In 2018, the state medical examiner ruled that Anton Black's death at the hands of police in Greensboro was an accident. An audit report released by the state attorney general's office says the cause of death should have been ruled a homicide.
6. Planning Commission recommends against seafood odor amendment
The Planning Commission provided an unfavorable recommendation on a recently proposed amendment to a seafood odor ordinance.
7. Cambridge nursing facility faces complaints about care
From a lack of care for residents to staffing problems, residents, their family members and former staff members say they have tried to advocate for the residents of a Cambridge nursing home but have not seen change. It has been 2½ years since the last federal inspection of the facility, and the state agency responsible for overseeing nursing homes faces a lawsuit alleging it has failed to inspect nursing facilities and allowed complaints against facilities to pile up.
8. Easton woman charged with placing swastikas on political signs
Police charged an Easton woman for allegedly placing swastika stickers on political signs ahead of Easton's recent election.

According to the National Weather Service, an EF-1 tornado originated in Dorchester County at 6:52 p.m. on Friday, May 16.

The St. Michaels High School baseball team made it to the state semifinal.

title: Community rallies around retired teacher after tornado
author: Lily Tierney
content:
Community rallies around retired teacher after tornado

 May 27, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Lily Tierney | Section: Dorchester 
 
 363
 Words 

 Read News Document

 GALESTOWN — After former North Dorchester High School baseball coach Dan Hortert's home was severely damaged by an EF-1 tornado, the community rallied around him to help pick up the pieces.Members of the baseball and softball teams, teachers, parents and former students responded to a Facebook post encouraging them to come out and help. The response was overwhelming.
People showed up with tractors, cranes, homemade cookies, pizza and determination to Hortert's Galestown, Delaware home Saturday morning.
"It's just unbelievable," the coach said through tears as he looked around at the support. "The Dorchester community as a whole is a whole lot closer than people can even describe," he said.
Hortert officially retired from North Dorchester High School last year. He was a beloved science teacher and baseball coach.
He has lived with his wife Kathy in their Galestown home for the past 50 years, and their daughter Angela lives in the home next door.
The damage to Hortert's home was mainly caused by two trees in the front yard. One of the trees snapped at the base, breaking through the house's roof, and the other was completely uprooted, destroying a shed in the backyard.
The family and one of their cats were in Hortert's home during the tornado, sheltering under the staircase. They got through the storm unharmed.
The cat had delivered a litter of kittens a few weeks prior, and the young cats were living in the garage. As soon as the tornado passed, Angela ran out to check on them, and they were also unscathed. "It all happened so fast," she said.
Hortert said the day after the tornado hit, community members began coming by asking how they could help.
"You know, Hortert's a great guy. He'll probably do anything for anyone. He's very willing to help, especially the youth," said North Dorchester High School senior TJ Leonard. This sentiment was echoed by several of the other volunteers gathered Saturday morning.
Hortert said that 50 years of teaching showed him how good the kids are at heart.
"The public schools are getting a bad rap, and North Dorchester in particular gets that from time to time, but its a wonderful school with wonderful kids that are a wonderful community," Hortert said.

title: Eastern Shore Veterans Cemetery decked out with flag display to honor soldiers
author: Konner Metz
content:
Eastern Shore Veterans Cemetery decked out with flag display to honor soldiers

 May 27, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Konner Metz | Section: Local News 
 
 414
 Words 

 Read News Document

 HURLOCK — Around 100 volunteers placed thousands of flags on graves at the Eastern Shore Veterans Cemetery Saturday morning just outside Hurlock.When the gates opened at 8 a.m., volunteers made quick work of the flag display, cemetery Superintendent Dean Arcoraci said. American flags whipped in the wind along with many Military Order of the Purple Heart flags honoring those killed or wounded in action.
"There's a lot of tradition here," Arcoraci said of the annual flag display.
The Eastern Shore Veterans Cemetery is one of five official veterans cemeteries in the state and the only one on the Eastern Shore. Arcoraci noted it was the first ever Maryland Department of Veterans and Military Families cemetery, opening in 1976.
Civil War veteran John Henry Blades was the first person to be buried at the cemetery. Today, there are around 8,000 burials and there's room for thousands more, Arcoraci said. He said the state also recently relaxed its residency requirements, allowing some families from nearby Delaware to place veterans at the Hurlock cemetery.
The cemetery features a unique design, with the burial sites forming curves facing the American flag in the middle of the cemetery.
Once the flags were placed, Mary Alice Jones and her son Bill Jones took some time to visit the graves of relatives, including Korean War U.S. Army veteran Joseph Horenstein.
Mary Alice Jones said it's important to remember and honor veterans no matter the time of year.
While Memorial Day was widely celebrated Monday, the Eastern Shore Veterans Cemetery commemorates Memorial Day later this week with an annual program.
At 1:30 p.m. Friday, the cemetery will host a Memorial Day program open to the public. It will include remarks from American Legion members and guest speaker Ross Cohen, acting secretary of the Maryland Department of Veterans and Military Families.
Memorial Day was originally observed on May 30 in the years after the Civil War. That tradition continued through much of the 20th century before a federal act moved it to the last Monday in May.
Arcoraci said the cemetery and its committee continues the May 30 program because of tradition. "I'm expecting quite a crowd," he added.
The Eastern Shore Veterans Cemetery partners with a number of local veteran groups and organizations, including local American Legions.
"This cemetery's about community involvement," he said.
The Eastern Shore Veterans Cemetery is located at 6827 E New Market Ellwood Road, Hurlock, MD, 21643.
This article has been updated to correct the name of Friday's guest speaker, Maryland Department of Veterans and Military Families acting Secretary Ross Cohen.

title: Historical society aims to highlight the overlooked history of Delaware town and its founder
author: Josh Shannon jshannon@chespub.com
content:
Historical society aims to highlight the overlooked history of Delaware town and its founder

 May 29, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Josh Shannon jshannon@chespub.com | Section: News 
 
 839
 Words 

 Read News Document

 Few people would recognize the name Matthew Aiken, save for a few local history buffs.But a new effort by the Pencader Heritage Area Association aims to raise awareness of Aiken and the history of the village he founded, Aiken Town, or as it's known today, Glasgow.
On May 17, Pencader hosted the first Matthew Aiken Day, inviting visitors to its museum near the intersection of Old Baltimore Pike and Del. 72 for music, demonstrations, vendors and more. The organization hopes to grow the event into an annual festival.
Pencader president Keith Jackson said his goal is to highlight the history of Glasgow, which tends to get less attention than the history of incorporated towns like Newark.
"I have a fascination with Glasgow. It's the Charlie Brown of towns," Jackson said. "To me, the fascination in the story is the fact that there is no story. But within that no story, there actually is a story. You just have to find it."
Aiken's Tavern dates back to colonial times and was located at a crossroads approximately 1,200 feet north of the present intersection of Del. 896 and U.S. 40. During the Revolutionary War, British troops were quartered there prior to the Battle of Cooch's Bridge.
After the war, Matthew Aiken bought the tavern from his brother John and laid out plans to create a town surrounding the tavern. However, the construction of what is now U.S. Route 40 realigned the road and established a new crossroads, diminishing the tavern's prominence.
The area was later renamed Glasgow by Scottish settlers in the area.
Though Aiken Town never came to fruition as its namesake envisioned, the Glasgow area obviously continued to grow and is now one of the fastest growing areas of New Castle County, Jackson said.
Worried that the few remaining historic buildings in Glasgow will be lost, Pencader is working on an ambitious plan to restore two historic houses and create an event space that will host educational programming and events, like an expanded Matthew Aiken Day festival.
The proposal revolves around a 48-acre property, known both as La Grange and the Barczewski Farm, that is located at the corner of Glasgow Avenue and U.S. 40. It is one of the last remaining undeveloped properties in the area, which is dominated by Peoples Plaza, other shopping centers and housing developments.
There have been several attempts to develop the La Grange property, and the latest comes from developer Steve Nichols. He is proposing to use part of the property to build 98 homes and an assisted living facility.
Nichols would use some of the profits of the development to restore the historic La Grange house as well as purchase and restore the Brooks house on an adjacent property.
Those houses, and the surrounding 10 or 11 acres, would be donated to Pencader, which would use them for historical and educational programming and also turn part of the property into an event venue.
The La Grange house, which is on the National Register of Historic Places, was built in 1815.
It was given its name by Marquis de Lafayette, the French military officer who helped the colonists win the Revolutionary War. Lafayette visited the house during his 1824 tour of the United States and remarked that it reminded him of his home in France, which was called La Grange. The name stuck, Jackson said.
In the early 1800s, the house was owned by prominent Glasgow citizen Dr. Samuel Black, who lived there and also had his doctor's office in the back of the building. Black was an early promoter of vaccines, researched soil depletion to develop more responsible farming practices and served in public office and as a trustee of what became the University of Delaware.
Black was renowned for having one of the finest libraries in the state and for his writing and lectures on both agricultural and medical subjects, according to Jackson.
The property was purchased by the Barczewski family in the 1940s and continued to function as a farm and dairy for many years. The house has been vacant for two decades.
The Brooks house, meanwhile, is located on 1.3 acres directly next to the Barczewski farm and fronts onto Glasgow Avenue.
Jackson said less is known about the Brooks house, though it was built in 1787 and was once owned by relatives of Samuel Black.
The development plan is working its way through New Castle County's development approval process. Jackson has argued that developing part of the property is the only way to save the two historic structures.
The idea got a major boost when, at Jackson's urging, the county added the La Grange site to the list of properties being considered for the new Glasgow Library. Jackson said building the library on the part of the property that is being preserved would complement Pencader's plans for the site and make it an even more important resource for the community.
"The cherry on top is one of the things Dr. Black was known for was he had the finest library in the entire state," Jackson said. "How amazing would it be to put the Glasgow Library on his property?"

title: Mt. Aviat alumnae gather for first reunion in 40 years
author: Jane Bellmyer jbellmyer@cecilwlhig.com
content:
Mt. Aviat alumnae gather for first reunion in 40 years

 May 30, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Jane Bellmyer jbellmyer@cecilwlhig.com | Section: News 
 
 620
 Words 

 Read News Document

 It's been 40 years since these ladies gathered around to reminisce about their halcyon days at Mount Aviat Academy.They met at Schaefer's Canal House in Chesapeake City last month. Their last reunion was 40 years ago at The Swiss Inn in Elkton. (Now Mick's Crab House)
From 1960 until 1972 the school in the Childs area of Elkton was the only Catholic High School in Cecil County and it was a girls-only school for boarding and day students.
"I was in the first graduating class," said Barbara Ashton Johnson. "My last name started with an 'A' so I had to be first."
Having to be the first in line made the Philadelphia native nervous.
"I had to be the first to kneel before the bishop and kiss his ring," Johnson said of the long-ago experience.
Mount Aviat began with a group of Swiss nuns, in a program organized by local parents. The nuns came to the convent and organized the high school, which was led by Sister Francis Marguerite.
"She was idolized," said Eileen Stubbs Viars.
Sister Francis Marguerite was the stuff of legend, according to Alva Eldridge Dopp, who was a boarding student from Fredericktown, Md.
"When she was 19 she lived in Germany. She joined the Oblates and learned to be a nun in Italy," Dopp said of the revered nun. This was during the height of World War II. "The Germans invaded their convent and lined them all up and shot them. The bullets grazed her head and her knee. She fell and played dead."
Elizabeth "Betsy" Patterson Patterson referred to Sister Francis Marguerite as "the heart of the school."
Judy Schamme Hart meanwhile, remembered Father Naulty fondly.
"We give credit for our musical training to Father Naulty. He was our Glee Club director," Hart said, adding that now, 47 years later she continues to use those singing skills in the choir at Immaculate Conception Church in Elkton.
There was a lot of fun to be had, Alva Eldridge Dopp recalled, telling the story of a fellow classmate with a gift for elopement.
"Jewel DiDomenica planned an escape with sheets out the window," Dopp said. "Since I was the littlest they made me go down first. They figured they could hold the sheet."
Sister Mary Beth was waiting at the bottom.
"She said I was a girl once," Viars said. Although guilty as charged the sister meted out their payment less harshly.
For their punishment the young ladies had to clean all the floors at the school. In those days the uniform included clunky black shoes with heavy rubber soles that left a trail all over the floors.
"We were given little scraps of steel wool and we had to remove all the scuff marks off of the floor," Dopp said.
Those uniforms included long dark skirts below the knee, which flew in the face of the 1960s fashion trend of mini skirts. Judy Schamme Hart said she was not alone in fixing that when getting on the bus to go home each afternoon.
"As soon as we got off of school property the top of the skirt got rolled up," she said. In spite of the uniform and the rules, she said: "It was the best time of our lives."
By 1972, Mount Aviat was transitioning to a day school for children from kindergarten through 8th grade. Only nine classes graduated from Mount Aviat Academy's girls high school.
Whether the students lived on campus or went home each evening, all agreed they formed a camaraderie that lasts to this day.
"We came together for Catholic education," Patterson said. "But it wasn't just a Catholic education. It was an education in appreciating each other."
"But the camaraderie we had; relationships with girls not from your home town," Hart said. "We built this community. We had a lot of fun."

title: Memorial Day parade remembers vets, America's 'forgotten war'
author: WILL BONTRAGER
content:
Memorial Day parade remembers vets, America's 'forgotten war'

 May 30, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: WILL BONTRAGER | Section: Life 
 
 560
 Words 

 Read News Document

 High Street in Chestertown was clear Memorial Day of many tourists following a successful Tea Party weekend, but the streets remained filled with locals honoring veterans during an annual parade, a longstanding tradition in the area.First responders from all Kent municipalities, local businesses, organizations, vintage vehicles and marching bands, symbolized the community's appreciation to the fallen. A crowd of approximately 500 lined the sunny streets, shouting well-wishes and flag waving.
After the festive Memorial Day parade, keynote speaker, veteran and board member of Sumner Hall, Aubrey Sarvis, spoke about his time serving during the Korean War, a conflict that started on June 25, 1950 — July 27, 1953.
Sarvis' message was simple yet strong — to never forget.
As a member of the U.S. Army 32nd Infantry Regiment, 7th Infantry Division from 1961-1962, he talked about that war, dubbed the "forgotten war" because it was overshadowed from World War II and Vietnam.
But for those who experienced the conflict, there was no way of forgetting it.
Sarvis said while on guard duty in the 38th parallel, separating North Korea and South Korea, he knew two things about his fellow soldiers: they were afraid and they did not want to die.
Surrounded by veterans, he provided sobering statistics of those who were killed in action or severely wounded, starting from World War I to the wars in the Middle East following Sept. 11, 2001.
He talked about those who died on the Western Front, France and Belgium, buried under poppy fields. He spoke of those 23,613 killed in action in Korea and the 58,220 who deployed in Vietnam and came home in a fresh casket with brand new American flags.
Thinking about his fallen comrades in every conflict, he recited the poem: "In Flanders Fields," by John McCrae, written in World War I. The poem beckons the hearers to remember the dead buried under poppy fields or those living would never be free.
President of Sumner Hall, Vanessa Isaacs Ringgold also remembers the sacrifices of these soldiers and stated how Sumner Hall is one of two existing African American Grand Army of the Republic (GAR) buildings still standing in the country.
She said that in 1868, founder of the Grand Army of the Republic Colonel John A. Logan issued a general order to 7,000 post members to decorate the graves of fallen comrades.
Sumner Hall aims to carry on that tradition of honoring and remembering. She said fraternity, charity and loyalty, is what they strive for, and will continue the legacy of the Parker White American Legion #143, formerly led by by the late Calvin Frasier. It was founded in 1919 and was the first Post in Kent County Maryland started by African Americans.
After the speakers, veterans gathered around the memorial and held a moment of silence for the lost, followed by "Taps" played by trumpeter Brad Holloman.
Ringgold said she was honored to be a part of this ceremony. She added whereas in former years, Sumner Hall has done something separate for Memorial Day, this year, two groups came together, and she hopes they will continue planning the Memorial Day Parade together.
She thanked Katy Weddell, Ellen Uzelac and everyone on the planning commission for their hard work, starting around February.
Sumner Hall encourages veterans to reach out to them, young and old. They hosts monthly events and meetings and is open to the community as an event venue. For information, visit sumnerhall.org.

title: Cambridge's Cannery Park prepares to renovate

Cambridge's Cannery Park prepares to renovate

 Author/Byline: Lily Tierney | Section: Dorchester

 CAMBRIDGE — Cannery Park is getting a makeover this summer, according to a City of Cambridge press release.Phase 1B of the park's design is expected to be complete in late August, according to City Manager Glenn Steckman.
New features will include park benches and a lawn swing surrounding the perimeter; an enclosed dog run and agility features like tunnels, steppers and bridges for dogs; and adirondack chairs for dog owners to lounge on.
"It's going to create a new recreational area that I think will be for people from all age brackets," Steckman said.
The park project is being funded by a $145,000 grant from the Community Development Block Grant of Maryland's Department of Housing and Community Development.
Phase 2B of the park's design will begin in the fall and will hopefully be completed by summer of 2026.
The second phase of the plan includes a splash park, skate and bike park and extended event space.
"I hope the residents are very pleased with the different activities planned down there," Steckman said. "There's even going to be bird watching."
Residents will still be able to access areas of the park that are not under construction.

title: Baywater Animal Rescue needs foster placements
author: Lily Tierney
content:
Baywater Animal Rescue needs foster placements

 June 2, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Lily Tierney | Section: Dorchester 
 
 346
 Words 

 Read News Document

 CAMBRIDGE — Ahead of an expected influx of animals in the coming months, Baywater Animal Rescue is on a mission to find the shelter's residents forever homes.Historically, summer is the busiest season for animal rescue organizations due to an increase in kitten and puppy litters, a rise in lost and stray animals as outdoor activity increases, and a decline in volunteers.
But even as demand increases, Baywater Animal Rescue manages to shelter as many animals as possible. "We will never move an animal out of our facility through euthanasia to make room for another," said Executive Director Steffanie Malkus.
Malkus and her staff have made the facility as much of a home as possible for the animals residing there. The cats and kittens have their own space with three rooms, cat trees galore and a "catio" so the more adventurous felines can roam inside and outside.
The dogs and puppies have the other side of the facility, where they have individual kennels, multiple outdoor play areas with balls and agility courses, and once it's hot enough, kiddie pools to cool off.
Fostering is near and dear to Malkus, who is a self-proclaimed foster failure. "The first night we brought them home, we all piled on the couch, and it was just one big love fest from then on out," she said. Four years later, she couldn't imagine life without her rescue cat Sydney and dog Lucas.
Baywater makes fostering easy. Staff sends their animals to their foster homes with all the necessities and helps train foster volunteers who are new to pets.
"There are certain requirements as to what your knowledge is with caring for an animal or your willingness to be taught on certain care for animals," said former Executive Director Carly Stockus. "There's always different types of fosters that are needed," she said.
Baywater Animal Rescue also encourages community members to come by and volunteer. "If you're not quite ready to foster, you can always come down and volunteer and get to know some of the animals," Malkus said.
Volunteers of all ages are welcomed. Minors must be with a guardian.

title: The Star Democrat's top 10 online stories this week
author: STAFF REPORT
content:
The Star Democrat's top 10 online stories this week

 June 7, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: STAFF REPORT | Section: Local News 
 
 411
 Words 

 Read News Document

 Here are the 10 stories that attracted the most page views on The Star Democrat's website this week. The stories are ranked in order of number of page views as of Wednesday evening.1. Police ask for assistance identifying suspect in bank robbery
Police are asking for the community's assistance identifying a man suspected of robbing a bank in Easton Monday afternoon.
2. Human remains found on farm during Cherrywood Solar construction
On May 20, while Cherrywood Solar workers were at Ronald Spearing Farm, human remains were found.
3. 4 injured in serious crash on Route 50 in Easton
A serious crash on Route 50 last week injured four people, according to the Maryland State Police.
4. HOMICIDE: Fatal shooting under investigation in Queen Anne's
At approximately 1:15 a.m. on June 1, deputies from the Queen Anne's County Office of the Sheriff responded to reports of gunfire in the 1500 block of Centreville Road. Prior to law enforcement arrival, a large party had been held at a residence in the area.
5. Talbot, Queen Anne's counties included on Trump's list of 'sanctuary jurisdictions'
Last week, Talbot and Queen Anne's counties were listed as "sanctuary jurisdictions" by the Trump administration, a label disputed by officials from both counties.
The list was removed from the Department of Homeland Security's website a few days later.
6. Easton, St. Michaels high schools celebrate graduates
Seniors at Easton High School and St. Michaels High School marked the end of a four-year chapter with graduation this week, celebrating accomplishments and looking forward to the future.
7. Middle-schooler is youngest to ever publish a fantasy novel
On Monday afternoon, 12-year-old Evelyn Klotz finished her middle school finals. The previous day, Klotz spoke to a sold-out audience at the Flying Cloud Bookstore about her newly published fantasy novel "Hero of Draconis."
8. Idlewild Park tile wall comes down
After months of delay, the tile wall at Idlewild Park has been taken down. The beloved wall has been covered with hundreds of hand-painted tiles since the park's construction in 2007.
9. Transcript reveals final words from Dali crew before Key Bridge collapse
A transcript released by the National Transportation Safety Board in April, which was first reported by The Baltimore Banner on Monday, details the moments aboard the Dali before the ship struck the Key Bridge.
10. Community rallies around retired teacher after tornado
After former North Dorchester High School baseball coach Dan Hortert's home was severely damaged by an EF-1 tornado, the community rallied around him to help pick up the pieces.
To read these stories and more, visit stardem.com.
