title: Kayak group offers law enforcement, firefighters, vets a chance to relax
author: Michael Reid mreid@somdnews.com
content:
Kayak group offers law enforcement, firefighters, vets a chance to relax

 June 9, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Michael Reid mreid@somdnews.com | Section: News 
 
 734
 Words 

 Read News Document

 Sure, dropping his fishing rod overboard while his son Shane fought to land a chain pickerel during the Heroes on the Water event Saturday at St. Mary's River State Park could have been an embarrassing moment, but Thornton Jackson was just planning ahead.Kayaks can be very temperamental when it comes to balance, so the Waldorf resident was just jettisoning weight in anticipation of the weight of the fish being added to the tandem kayak. Or that one excuse, anyways.
"I did do that," he said happily — and somewhat relieved — when it was suggested to him.
The event was held to allow first responders, law enforcement, firefighters and military veterans a chance to relax and and take a few casts if they so desired.
"It's not serious fishing. We're just out to have a good time, relaxing time on the water," said Maryland Chapter Coordinator Chris Vassallo, who spent 21 years as a senior chief in the U.S. Navy on submarines and recently retired following a career with the Office of Naval Intelligence. "You're maneuvering the kayak, you're using your fishing tackle to try and outsmart [the fish] and it takes your mind off everything else. It shuts that noise off and gives your brain some peace and for me that's what this is all about."
Thornton Jackson spent 13 years as a Yeoman in the U.S. Navy and was deployed "multiple times" and even missed the birth of Shane, "but it was also nice getting back and meeting him at the pier."
And Thornton Jackson certainly appreciated the father-son bonding time.
"It's definitely nice to get away from everything and just being out here spending time with him and just be a dad," said Jackson, who has worked in naval intelligence for the past two years. "Right now I'm here for a bit, but with deployments you never know when they're going to pop up. Just getting some time out on a Saturday and putting the work away to focus on him is great."
"It was fun to spend time with him," said 8-year-old Shane, who reeled in several fish. "I miss him a lot [when he's gone]."
Vassallo found out about the organization while listening to a podcast and attended an event in Montgomery County.
"That was something that I wanted, something that I wanted to establish here in Southern Maryland," he said. "To me this is what it's all about; having the camaraderie and being out on the water and enjoying the time on the water."
He co-coordinated two events and coordinated previous events this year in Laytonsville and Salisbury. The next event will be held July 26 at Mallows Bay in Charles County.
One of the volunteers at the event was Wayne Stinchcomb, a retired U.S. Army chaplain.
"Some of these guys are going through trials and tribulations for what they're going through. They're going through counseling. But when you do something like this it gets them back into real life," he said. "[They think] I can do this, I can be around my guys and I don't have to worry about something or what somebody might think because we're all going through it or been through it. One guy was here just to float in the sun. He didn't even take his pole out. He said the whole idea was to be and relax. If you've been in combat or anything you've been around, and you're around like-minded folks, there's an ease in that."
Mark Anderson of Kent Island drove about two hours to volunteer for the event.
"I didn't serve but I've shot [guns and rifles] competitively with a lot of people who are veterans," said Anderson, who is works in information technology and captured the event with his drone. "I just got to know a lot of them and really appreciate what they do for this country and the sacrifices they've made."
"I just love the military and fishing so that's how I figured I could at least give back," said Nathan Miller, who drove down from Westminster to assist at the event. "My friend brought me out once [to a Heroes on the Water event] and I've been hooked ever since. If there's an event and I know about it ahead of time, I'll figure out a way to help. It's good to see [them relax]. It's worth the drive."
For more information on how to participate or to volunteer at the Mallows Bay event on July 26, email maryland@heroesonthewater.org.

title: More than a house, it's a home: Chesterwye Center welcomes Ewing House completion
author: ANDREA GRABENSTEIN agrabenstein@chespub.com
content:
More than a house, it's a home: Chesterwye Center welcomes Ewing House completion

 June 10, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: ANDREA GRABENSTEIN agrabenstein@chespub.com | Section: News 
 
 551
 Words 

 Read News Document

 GRASONSVILLE — During a tour of the fully renovated, roughly 2,000-square-foot home, Katie Clendaniel, development and grants manager for the Chesterwye Center, explained the Ewing House will serve as a group home and provide supported independent living for up to four adults with developmental or intellectual disabilities.They will receive around the clock care and partake in Chesterwye services.
The newly renovated space, part of the Chesterwye Center, was celebrated with a ribbon-cutting ceremony to celebrate the completion of the home in Grasonville June 5.
Clendaniel and Cathy Frey, chief financial officer, were recognized for their efforts in acquiring funding as the complete rehabilitation of the home was funded by a capital grant from the Maryland Department of Health and a match by the Queen Anne's County commissioners.
Breaking ground in fall 2024, contractor John W. Coursey and his wife, Missy, of Ray's Painting LLC were credited with more than just establishing a house for adults with developmental disabilities to live in but creating a home in which to thrive.
Coursey said with the state the house was in before the project began, it should have been torn down, but instead was gutted and renovated completely to stand as something completely new.
"It can be done," he said, noting it was rewarding to see the finished project and the impact it has to those who truly need it.
"It takes a village," Chesterwye CEO Micheal Yates said. He noted projects such as this one are made possible with local support, and Queen Anne's County stands above any other community he's seen before.
The county was happy to provide the help, County Administrator Todd Mohn said.
While the project saw its share of challenges along the way, according to Yates, the Chesterwye Center will be able to apply aspects learned to support future endeavors.
According to Chesterwye board member Diane McComb, when developing new client homes, an important ask for Chesterwye is, "Would I live here?" and looking over the newly refurbished home, she said, "This certainly meets it."
Chesterwye is committed to improving the lives of individuals and making homes more inviting as well as the environment of its homes and is continually updating, growing and expanding, Yates said.
"You don't receive more referrals without a good reputation," McComb noted.
The work that Chesterwye does is imperative, former Chesterwye Foundation Chair Wheeler Baker noted, as services for adults with developmental disabilities, otherwise end after the age of 21.
Through the Chesterwye programs, clients are busy with activities, field trips and connections for happy, productive lives.
Family member Jeannie Jordan, of Centreville, marveled as she looked over the new home for her nephew Micheal Huddleston, 40.
"It's such a blessing," she said, "Chesterwye provides anything and everything they need."
Through Chesterwye, Jordan said she knows Huddleston is always safe and engaging in activities he wouldn't otherwise.
"Micheal is the happiest child filled with joy, and part of that is his surroundings," she said.
Congratulating Chesterwye on the completion of the home to provide supportive independent living, an official citation from the Maryland General Assembly was presented by Del. Steve Arentz (R-Caroline, Cecil, Kent, Queen Anne's). Renovation of the Chesterwye Center's second residential group home, the Nash House, is expected to begin by July.
The Chesterwye Center has been supporting the Queen Anne's County community since 1967 through day and residential programs.
More information about The Chesterwye Center can be found at chesterwye.org.

title: Chestertown veterans Honor D-Day soldiers at historic armory
author: WILL BONTRAGER wbontrager@chespub.com
content:
Chestertown veterans Honor D-Day soldiers at historic armory

 June 11, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: WILL BONTRAGER wbontrager@chespub.com | Section: News 
 
 267
 Words 

 Read News Document

 CHESTERTOWN — On the 81st anniversary of D-Day, local veterans gathered at the historic John H. Newnam Armory to honor the soldiers who helped turn the tide of World War II — some of whom trained on that very ground.On June 6, 1944, more than 150,000 American, British, Canadian and Free French troops stormed 50 miles of coastline in Normandy, France, launching the largest amphibious assault in military history and opening a critical Western front against Nazi Germany.
The battle came at a steep cost. More than 4,400 Allied troops were killed that day, including 2,501 Americans.
Some of the American soldiers who fought in that campaign trained at the Newnam Armory, built in 1931. To honor their memory, members of Frank M. Jarman American Legion Post 36 held a solemn remembrance ceremony Friday at the armory.
On a quiet afternoon, Post Commander Tim Lloyd placed flowers at the foot of the armory's monument as Captain Paul Showalter, Vice President Lennell Copper and sergeant-at-arms Jim Douglas looked on in reverence.
The monument reads: "In grateful tribute to the men of the medical detachment of the 115th Infantry Regiment Maryland National Guard, both living and dead, this shrine is dedicated. Their valiant efforts helped preserve freedom in America, 1941–1945."
Showalter, who also serves as post chaplain, led a moment of silence and offered a prayer.
He thanked God for the freedoms Americans enjoy and for the victory granted on that pivotal day in 1944.
"A lot of members didn't make it back, but through their sacrifice they helped us become better citizens," Showalter said. "We do this to let them know Chestertown values them."

title: 25-year-old set to bike from Easton to Canada
author: AHMAD GARNETT agarnett@chespub.com
content:
25-year-old set to bike from Easton to Canada

 June 14, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: AHMAD GARNETT agarnett@chespub.com | Section: News 
 
 482
 Words 

 Read News Document

 EASTON — Hayden Kessinger, 25, is set to bike from Easton to Canada beginning Saturday. It isn't his first cross-country bike ride.In 2023, Kessinger biked from Baltimore to San Francisco in 70 days.
Kessinger's motivation for biking across the country came from a book called "The Happiness of Pursuit" by Chris Guillebeau.
"I kind of initially had an idea to do some sort of long-distance bike ride and specifically bike across the country after reading a book," Kessinger said. "... It just sort of inspired me to think about doing something kind of crazy in the eyes of the most people or embarking on some sort of adventure or just exploring more."
Shortly after reading the book, Kessinger learned about the Ulman Foundation, a company the specializes in supporting young adults with cancer. The foundation participates in holds a bike-riding fundraiser, and Kessinger signed up.
The group raised $161,828 during their 2023 ride to San Francisco. Kessigner raised $7,431.
With new hopes on the horizon and used biking gear, Kessinger's sets his eyes on biking from Easton to Montreal, Canada this summer.
Although Kessinger will not be raising funds during this ride, his friend Keisuke "Jima" Nakajima, who will be joining Kessinger from Baltimore to Montreal, is raising funds for the Ulman Foundation.
Nakajima then will take transportation back to Baltimore from Montreal, leaving Kessinger by himself for the grueling bike home.
"The decision to go from my home in Easton to Canada is sort of born out of like being able to go somewhere that I've never been and do it all under my own power," Kessinger said.
During Kessinger's trip in 2023, the other bikers on the trip had built relationships in the past to find places for the group to stay the night. They also had help from the foundation.
But for his trip this summer, Kessinger plans to coordinate sleeping arrangements, showering and food through meeting new people and an app called Warm Showers.
"It's specifically for cycle tourists, so people doing long-distance bike rides, and you can make an account, and you can be a host on there. And so you can connect with these hosts who are all over all over the world," Kessinger said.
Kessinger's job as a dog sitter, gave him opportunity to train for the grueling bike ride. He biked from client to client. Kessinger established a savings with money from high school work and an internship after he graduated from the University of Maryland.
Kessinger's message to anyone scared of taking on new opportunities or trying something different is to just "give it a go."
"Try it," Kessinger said. "Say say when all of those reasons come up of why you know this can't work or you shouldn't do it. Just see what it feels like to ignore those and what it feels like to to say yes, because you'll figure out the rest later."
To follow along with Kessinger, follow is his blog at teamtahoe.substack.com/.

title: New exhibit documents and honors Talbot County's U.S. Colored Troops
author: Konner Metz
content:
New exhibit documents and honors Talbot County's U.S. Colored Troops

 June 19, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Konner Metz | Section: Local News 
 
 712
 Words 

 Read News Document

 EASTON — A new exhibit is documenting the often untold stories of hundreds of African American men from Talbot County who fought for their freedom in the Civil War.And while the project put on by the Talbot Historical Society aims to tell the history of free and enslaved Black men in the Civil War, it doesn't stop there. Extensive research dating back months has helped uncover the names and details of more than 500 Black soldiers from Talbot County.
Before the exhibit's soft opening to the public Tuesday, retired Salisbury University professor and historian Clara Small delivered a moving lecture to a packed room in the Talbot County Free Library.
"This exhibit will help to put flesh on those names," Small said. "The goal is that it's not just a name anymore, but a human being. One of your ancestors."
The exhibit — "Talbot County's United States Colored Troops: A Story of Valor and Honor" — is located on South Washington Street in downtown Easton. The list of names hangs on one end of the exhibit, though that catalog is continuously being updated as historians learn more about the local soldiers.
During the Civil War, as Small noted, the border state of Maryland did not meet its quota for Union Army soldiers. Many white soldiers avoided fighting through fees or purchasing substitutes, she said.
"The solution was to use free Blacks and slaves because they provided an unlimited reservoir of manpower," Small said, noting how many Marylanders and slaveholders rejected the idea of using Black troops, fearing a loss of labor.
Abolitionist and Talbot County native Frederick Douglass advocated for the inclusion of Black soldiers in the Union Army. His work, along with Abraham Lincoln's authorization for the recruitment of slaves, made the United States Colored Troops possible.
Small noted around 180,000 Black men served in the Union Army, with more than 8,000 from Maryland and around 600 or 700 from Talbot County.
Research conducted by the Talbot Historical Society and partnering groups sheds light on the many free and enslaved Black men from Talbot County who answered the call but never received the same recognition white soldiers were granted.
Historical Society member Paul Callahan said it took hours of research, collaboration with local organizations like Easton's American Legion Post 77 and consultation with Small to prepare the list of names.
"I saw so many family names, friends that I grew up with in Oxford," Callahan said. " ... I don't even think they knew that their ancestors were American heroes who fought in the war so valiantly."
The exhibit has records and an electronic database where people can learn specifics about the soldiers: birthplace, date of death, height, eye color, regiment, rank and more. Callahan says it's a tool to empower Talbot County residents to learn more about history and their ancestries.
Historians relied on the online military record database Fold3, as well as records in the library's Maryland Room and from local families or veteran groups.
"It was very tedious," Callahan said.
Some of the artifacts and items on display in the exhibit come from a Civil War reenactment group in Philadelphia. Project leaders also consulted descendants of the 18 U.S. Colored Troops who founded the Unionville community after the war.
During her lecture, Small said the research makes the Civil War more "personable" for local residents. She emphasized that Black families will be better able to trace their heritage.
"There should be very few people in this county that are not connected to some of these men in some way, whether it is by marriage, as cousins or as cousins of cousins," Small said.
The renowned professor highlighted the unfair and discriminatory treatment Black soldiers received even after the Union's victory in the war. She encouraged attendees to tell the accounts of the free and enslaved Black soldiers, stories that aren't told nearly enough.
"That is a legacy that is often forgotten, neglected or is purposely left out of our history books," Small said. "It is way past the time to correct those myths, perceptions and erroneous beliefs."
"This is just the tip of the iceberg," Small added. "We have a lot of work to do."
The Talbot County United States Colored Troops exhibit is located at the Talbot Historical Society at 25 S Washington St. It is open Wednesdays through Saturdays from 10 a.m. to 3 p.m.

title: Thanks for 1,000 American flags
author: Staff Writer
content:
Thanks for 1,000 American flags

 June 21, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Staff Writer | Section: Editors Inbox 
 
 292
 Words 

 Read News Document

 American flags decorate Easton and other area locations this Memorial Day weekend.It started in 2012 with the idea of placing a few American flags around our community during the Memorial Day weekend. This year over 1,000 American flags were displayed in 14 different locations.
Did you ever wonder who did it and why?
The Rotary Club of Easton started what has become a tradition not only in our small town but to other Rotary Clubs across the Delmarva area and in many other states. Those flags represent the visual part of our annual Flags for Heroes program. It was meant to help all of us remember what Memorial Day was really all about.
Businesses, families and individuals sponsor every one of those flags to honor the heroes whether they have fallen in battle, veterans, first responder, etc. Because of the overwhelming support we have received, our club has used those funds locally by supporting deserving community organizations such as, Talbot Hospice, For All Seasons, the Talbot Paramedics Foundation, the Talbot Sheriff's Office, Easton and all area volunteer fire departments, Easton Police Department, local cemeteries that are the final resting place for veterans and many other amazing initiatives.
This would not have been possible if it wasn't for the Town of Easton and the Talbot County Council which allows us to display the flags throughout the area. We must also recognize the Easton Utilities for all their support, The Star Democrat and our local radio stations (WCEI and WINK). Lastly to the wonderful people and businesses of our community, who contribute so generously.
The Rotary Club of Easton would like to say thank you. Memorial Day reminds us of those who gave the ultimate sacrifice for freedom.
To learn more go to: flagsforheroes.org.
JOHN FLOHR
JACKIE WILSON
Rotary Club of Easton

title: Community responds to restock upgraded food pantry
author: HANNAH COMBS hcombs@chespub.com
content:
Community responds to restock upgraded food pantry

 June 23, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: HANNAH COMBS hcombs@chespub.com | Section: News 
 
 240
 Words 

 Read News Document

 ROCK HALL — The Little Free Pantry on Main Street in Rock Hall was replaced this month with a new, upgraded structure purchased by No Child Goes Hungry, a nonprofit organization dedicated to eliminating childhood hunger.Located in the driveway at 5764 N. Main St., behind the spiral staircase and Little Free Library, the pantry operates on a "take what you need, give what you can" basis and is open 24/7. It provides nonperishable food, dry goods, feminine care products and diapers for Kent County residents and visitors.
Originally installed in 2021, the pantry was inspired by the grassroots "Blessing Box" movement that began in Arkansas in 2016 to help combat food insecurity without barriers or judgment.
Ashleigh Rogers, who installed the original pantry at her home, said the concept was also inspired by the philanthropy of chef José Andrés and the World Central Kitchen following the Jan. 6 Capitol attack.
"Sadly, the elements took their toll, and it was falling apart, so I applied for the grant from No Child Goes Hungry, and she had it on the way here within a day," Rogers said. "I don't monitor it, so I'm not sure if needs have increased, but I do know it is used several times a day. The community has been so generous and has kept it stocked."
Community members responded with donations during the "Pack the Pantry" drive held June 19–22 to help restock the upgraded pantry.
For more information, visit facebook.com/littlefreelibraryandpantryonmainstreet.

title: Betterton Legion welcomes families for day of fun
author: WILL BONTRAGER wbontrager@chespub.com
content:
Betterton Legion welcomes families for day of fun

 June 24, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: WILL BONTRAGER wbontrager@chespub.com | Section: Local News 
 
 286
 Words 

 Read News Document

 BETTERTON — An overcast morning did not prevent families from experiencing the fun on June 14 at the C. Henry Price Betterton American Legion during their second annual American Legion Family Day.From 11 a.m. until 3 p.m. they held face painting, a moon bounce house, corn hole games, a petting zoo with goats, donkeys and cows, with popcorn, drinks and hotdogs.
Marcellus Black Jr. organized the music and each Legion station offered smiles and camaraderie.
For some added excitement, kids got to experience what it's like behind the wheel of Engine 4 courtesy of the Kennedyville Volunteer Fire House.
This event was part of the national American Legion Family Day, which is held on the last Saturday of April to recognize and celebrate the accomplishments of Legionnaires, Sons of The American Legion members, Legion Riders and American Legion Auxiliary, and to bring awareness to the organization's "Be the One" initiative to reduce the rate of veteran suicide.
Betterton held its pool tournament on that date, so the family fun event was pushed back to Saturday, said Legion Auxiliary President Patti Bone.
Since it was also Flag Day, the Legion retired many old American Flags, holding a ceremony then burning them to dispose of them — the proper way to do it.
Post Cmdr. Jacob Matthews said since there was a lot going on Saturday, especially in Chestertown, he was pleased with the turnout, and looks forward as the post plans more events that bring the community together.
Every Thursday at 7 p.m., open mic night is hosted by Gerry Werner featuring a 50-50 drawing, music, comedy and trivia. The post meal will be pulled pork barbecue with drinks served by your favorite bartender. Come out and play or sing your favorite tunes.

title: Repairs to damaged Delaware church reveal historical treasures
author: Josh Shannon jshannon@chespub.com
content:
Repairs to damaged Delaware church reveal historical treasures

 June 26, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Josh Shannon jshannon@chespub.com | Section: News 
 
 727
 Words 

 Read News Document

 When construction workers began tearing away a damaged portion of St. John AM Church in Newark on June 23, they unearthed historical artifacts that had been hidden for decades."We were jumping for joy in here because it's part of our history. This is the oldest Black church in this city," Pastor Blaine Hackett said. "It was a very significant part of this community for a long time, and we still are."
The workers found an old wooden sign from the Delaware church's early days that was installed above the original entrance to the building, which was constructed in 1867. The sign was covered up with bricks when the church was renovated in 1960.
Also discovered was a time capsule that was hidden behind a cornerstone during the 1960 renovation. Inside was an old bible, a Book of Discipline dating back to 1907, minutes from a 1960 church trustees meeting and other old documents.
Church leaders plan to display the items inside the church and are planning to include a new time capsule in the renovated portion of the church.
The church, located at the corner of New London Road and Cleveland Avenue, sustained significant damage when it was struck by speeding vehicles twice in a six-month period, once in August and again in January.
After the church spent several months negotiating with the insurance company, hiring a construction company and obtaining city permits, work finally began this week.
"The people in the congregation are really excited about it happening because they've been asking every Sunday for months and months when it's going to start," said Bob Anderson, president of the St. John AM Church trustees.
Since the first crash, the church has been holding services in its fellowship hall, which is in an undamaged portion of the building. Hackett said he hopes the repairs to the sanctuary are complete by September.
"All I can say is, praise God, from whom all blessings flow," he said. "We're finally getting there. We've still got a ways to go, but we're just elated right now to get started."
The renovations will restore the front portion of the church, which sustained heavy damage. The stained glass windows, one of which is being professionally repaired after being damaged, will be reinstalled.
Workers will also slightly expand the footprint of the church in the front.
Currently, the brick church has a small entry vestibule that juts out from the front of the building. That vestibule was heavily damaged in the two crashes.
When it is rebuilt, the vestibule will extend across the entire length of the front of the church.
The left side, the area most likely to be hit by a vehicle, will be used as a cloakroom. The cloakroom will provide a buffer in case the building is struck again. Instead of hitting the sanctuary wall and the last row of pews, a vehicle would hit the cloakroom instead.
On the left side, the church will build a handicapped accessible bathroom.
Currently, the church's only bathrooms are located in the newer portion of the building, behind the sanctuary. If congregants need to use the bathroom during a service, they either have to walk behind the pastor to access the other part of the building, or go outside and enter through a back door. Disabled congregants have no choice but to use a wheelchair ramp outside.
The church also plans to strengthen the bollards in the front yard that are intended to protect the building from vehicles. The two vehicles that hit the building were going so fast, they pulled the bollards out of the ground.
The new bollards will be reinforced, deeper and connected underground for additional strength.
Hackett said the renovations are expected to cost upward of $300,000. Much of the cost will be paid through insurance money and donations the church has received, but Hackett said additional donations are needed, especially for items not covered by insurance, such as new carpet and repairs to pews.
Donations can be made online at paypal.com/fundraiser/charity/1500432. Checks and money orders can be mailed to or dropped off at St. John AM Church, 77 New London Road, Newark DE, 19711.
"We appreciate all the people that helped us thus far. We still have a journey to go, but we trust in God to restore us and make us whole," Hackett said. "It's unfortunate we've had these incidents, but we're here to stay. We've here to still serve this community and share the Gospel."

title: Guidebook aims to 'get people out there'
author: BROOKE ENSMINGER
content:
Guidebook aims to 'get people out there'

 June 27, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: BROOKE ENSMINGER | Section: Business 
 
 560
 Words 

 Read News Document

 A second edition of an Eastern Shore guidebook connects locals and visitors to places and activities they might not have known were just a short drive away.Writer Susan Moynihan, who grew up in Annapolis, decided to create an updated version of her guidebook titled "100 Things to Do in Annapolis and the Eastern Shore Before You Die" to accommodate changes after COVID-19. The book highlights beloved Eastern Shore destinations.
"The fact that we have this beautifully preserved and cared for expanse of land and culture that still stays so close to its roots, I find fascinating," Moynihan said. "I find it to be a really unique part of the world."
In compiling her list, Moynihan began with the things she loved to do in Annapolis and the surrounding areas. She then asked friends and other locals for recommendations, considering whether each item was worth recommending in the book. She said she wanted to put a focus on activities and locations that "wouldn't exist anywhere else."
"Going out on the Skipjack or going to a seafood festival and trying all the food. There's so much," Moynihan said.
Amy Kreiner, the president of the Talbot County Chamber of Commerce, said guidebooks can help visitors find more affordable activities when they have to be financially careful in what they're choosing to do.
"They give an idea of what can be experienced in the different areas," Kreiner said. "There's just so many more things to do that can be explained in a guidebook than a lot of other places."
The list kicks off with food and drink, and includes Rise Up Coffee Roasters and Bas Rouge in Easton and Booze in St. Michaels. Moynihan describes Rise Up as having a distinctive style with its black-and-white graphics and an "indie-inclusive sensibility."
"We have really amazing restaurants and places to stay with really, really outstanding chefs and dining experiences," Kreiner said.
Oysterfest is an annual seafood festival in St. Michaels hosted by the Chesapeake Bay Maritime Museum. The festival kicks off oyster season in October with a day full of oyster-themed events.
While the diverse dining options can be an attraction of their own, Kreiner said the biggest draws to the area are the history and the waterfront.
Moynihan's book highlights waterfront gems like the Skipjack Nathan in Cambridge, where guests can take private sails, and the Oxford-Bellevue Ferry in Oxford, the oldest private ferry in the United States.
Building on the history of the Eastern Shore, the Chesapeake Bay Maritime Museum in St. Michaels showcases the largest collection of Chesapeake boats. Other featured museums include the Water's Edge Museum in Oxford, the Museum of Rural Life in Denton and the Tilghman Watermen's Museum on Tilghman Island.
Entertainment is another unique experience on the Eastern Shore. Many locals have attended a show at the Avalon Theatre, a must-visit entertainment venue on Moynihan's list. Lesser-known, however, is Chesapeake Ghost Tours, where guests can take a haunted walking tour in towns around the Eastern Shore and beyond. Each location offers its own unique tale, but Moynihan recommends the Cambridge tour.
While guidebooks are often seen as tools for tourists to effectively navigate an unfamiliar area, Moynihan wants her book to be a guide for Eastern Shore residents and visitors alike.
She said her goal is "just to get people out there." Locals don't have to travel far to find unique places and activities that are rich in history, culture and entertainment.

title: Fourth of July picnics
author: MARIE SAVAGE Country Cooking
content:
Fourth of July picnics

 July 2, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: MARIE SAVAGE Country Cooking | Section: News 
 
 1563
 Words 

 Read News Document

 My memories of celebrating the Fourth of July holiday go back to my early childhood, since my mom was born on July 4, 1911, in the small town of Selbyville, Delaware. Mom would be celebrating her 112th birthday this year — she left us at age 86 almost 27 years ago.In my early memories, the family packed picnic foods and traveled to visit various sites such as the Philadelphia Zoo, Virginia resort areas, state parks and sites of historic events. We visited historic military sites nearby. Eventually as my parents grew older, the celebrations came back home where we gathered at local swimming areas, campgrounds, parks and, finally, at the site of our small schoolhouse, now a small park, in our town of Bishopville.
One of my favorite memories of those Fourth of July trips would be going to visit my late Aunt Irene and Uncle Fred in Chester, Pennsylvania. Early that morning, my mom got up and started making fried chicken, biscuits, potato salad, cucumbers and onions, corn-on-the-cob, sliced tomatoes, fresh beets, and fresh baked cupcakes. Finally, she made two big jugs of homemade iced tea and a large jug of fresh water.
Daddy backed the big four-door Oldsmobile 98 to the back door and start loading the food. In go the boxes of food, coolers of iced tea and water, coolers of side food and the big roaster pan of fried chicken, finally the picnic tablecloths, wet and dry hand cloths, and plastic ware with plastic cups. The kids load up, and off we go to Pennsylvania.
The ride was wonderful, especially along the C & O Canal and Delaware & Pa. Canal areas. Eventually everyone is hungry, and my father pulls off at a rest area campground. How amazingly beautiful — railroad with a train passing, ships in the ocean, tugs in the canal and a plane overhead.
Mom would also include some of the large dill pickles that we could snack on while riding in the car. I remember the big thick glass gallon jars that were filled with the whole dill, sour or sweet pickles you bought at the store. The lid was a wide-mouth metal lid. The jar was to be saved, washed really well, used to make jugs of tea, lemonade and water. I remember packing one of these pickles, wrapped in saran wrap or foil, in my lunch box, something my grandkids still do.
You know how it is loading kids up in a vehicle to travel. Just before you leave, you line them up to "go to the bathroom" one last time. Well, 20 miles down the road somebody has to go and then all the others start with "I'm thirsty," or "I'm hungry" or "are we there yet?" To stop this, Mom made us all get out, walk around the car, and handed us some pretzels to munch on — Mom thought of it all.
We usually ate before we got to my relatives' house because they enjoyed making a freezer of homemade ice cream and a fresh banana cake or strawberry cake. My favorite part of the trip was just "being in a small city with sidewalks" and "city talking folks." The last thing mom would say as we pulled up in front of the house was "act like you got some raising" and "behave." Remember those words my friends because we were told this wherever we went.
Our last family gathering with our mother was held in Bishopville at the site of our local elementary school park on July 4, 1997 — the day mom turned 86 years old. Mom died four months later. Our father had died 23 years earlier.
Gatherings changed through the years, but those memories have not.
Celebrate the Fourth anywhere or however you want, but have plenty of delicious food, much laughter and fun and games — the day will arrive that you have those memories to cling to.
Happy birthday, America.
COUNTRY FRIED CHICKEN
2 cups buttermilk, 1 tbsp Dijon mustard, 1 tsp salt, 1 tsp ground black pepper, 1 tsp cayenne pepper, 1 whole chicken (cut into pieces), 2 cups all-purpose flour, 1 tbsp baking powder, 1 tbsp garlic powder, 1 tbsp onion powder, 5 cups vegetable oil for frying.
Whisk together buttermilk, mustard, salt, pepper and cayenne in a bowl. Pour buttermilk marinade into a resealable plastic bag. Add chicken pieces, coat with marinade, squeeze out excess air, and seal the bag. Marinate in the refrigerator for two to eight hours. Combine flour, baking powder, garlic powder and onion powder in another resealable plastic bag; shake to mix thoroughly. Working with one piece at a time, transfer marinated chicken to the dry ingredient bag, seal the bag, and shake well to coat. After all chicken pieces are coated, repeat the process by dipping them in buttermilk marinade and shaking in the dry coating again. Then heat oil in a large frying pan over medium-high heat. Place chicken in the pan. Fry chicken in batches in hot oil, turning chicken occasionally, until golden brown and juices run clear. An instant-read thermometer inserted into the meat should read at least 165 degrees.
OIL AND VINEGAR POTATO SALAD
1 1/2 lbs. potatoes (red-skinned or Yukon gold), 1/2 medium red onion (chopped), 2 tbsp chopped fresh parsley, 1/2 tsp granulated sugar, 2 tbsp Dijon mustard, 1/4 cup cooking vinegar, 1/3 cup extra virgin olive oil, 1/2 tsp salt, 1/2 tsp freshly ground black pepper.
Place potatoes in a large pot and fill with water. Place the lid on the pot and bring to a boil over high heat. Continue to cook until potatoes are tender, about 10 minutes. Remove from heat, drain and rinse with cold water until they are cool enough to handle. Chop into 1-inch chunks and place them in a large mixing bowl. Add onion, herbs, sugar, mustard, vinegar and oil, and toss until well coated. Stir to mash the potatoes slightly until they reach your desired texture. Add salt and pepper, and stir to combine. Season with additional salt and pepper to taste, if desired. The ingredients in this recipe don't require refrigeration and make for a perfect road trip side dish.
NO MAYO COLESLAW
1 head of green cabbage (finely shredded), 1 large carrot (grated), 1/2 yellow or red onion (finely sliced), 1/3 cup apple cider vinegar, 3 tbsp olive oil, 1 tbsp honey, 1/2 tbsp Dijon mustard, 1 tsp celery seed, 1/4 tsp salt, 1/4 tsp black pepper.
Add the shredded green cabbage, carrot and onion to a large bowl. In a smaller bowl, whisk together the apple cider vinegar, Dijon mustard, honey, olive oil, celery seed, salt and pepper to create the dressing. Taste the dressing and decide if you'd like to add more honey. Add about half of the dressing to the cabbage, onions and carrots and gently toss. Slowly add more dressing until you've reached your desired consistency.
PUFF PASTRY STAR COOKIES
All-purpose flour for work surface, 2 sheets puff pastry (thawed), 1 large egg beaten, 1/4 cup jam, sanding sugar for sprinkling.
Preheat the oven to 400 degrees. Line two baking sheets with parchment paper. On a lightly floured work surface, roll each sheet of puff pastry into a 10- by 12-inch rectangle. Using a 3 1/2-inch star-shaped cookie cutter, cut out 12 stars from each sheet. Transfer to prepared baking sheets. Brush the points of half the stars with egg; carefully spoon jam (about 1 teaspoon) onto the center of each star. Using a 1 3/4-inch star-shaped cookie cutter, cut out smaller star shapes from the centers of the remaining 12 larger stars. Place stars with the holes over the jam, doing your best to line up the points. Press edges gently to seal. Brush the tops with egg and sprinkle with sugar. Bake, rotating halfway through, until golden brown, 10 to 12 minutes. Cool slightly before serving. Cookies can be made 2 days ahead. Store, tightly covered, at room temperature.
NO MAYO DEVILED EGGS
6 large or extra-large eggs (hard-boiled, peeled and chilled), 1/4 cup sour cream, 1/2 tsp yellow mustard, 2 tsp sweet pickle relish, 1/4 tsp salt, 2 tsp chopped fresh chives or dill plus more for garnish.
Slice each egg in half lengthwise. Remove the yolks and place in a separate bowl. Set the egg halves aside. Add the sour cream, yellow mustard, pickle relish, salt and herbs to the bowl with the yolks. Using a fork, mash everything together until all the ingredients are combined and the mixture is smooth. Using a spoon or a piping bag fitted with a star tip, fill the empty egg whites with the mixture. Garnish with a dash of paprika and more chopped herbs. Serve cold. Use extra paprika for garnish.
STATE FAIR LEMONADE
6 lemons, 1 ¼ cups white sugar, 5 cups cold water.
Wash lemons and peel off all the zest using a vegetable peeler; set peeled lemons aside. Add lemon zest to a bowl and cover with sugar; toss to combine. Cover and let sit for a minimum of 2 hours, or up to overnight. Bring water to a boil in a pot over high heat; turn off heat and pour in lemon-sugar mixture. Stir and let sit until sugar is completely dissolved, about 5 minutes. Pour through a mesh strainer back into the same bowl and discard the zest. Let cool to room temperature, 20 to 30 minutes. Cut lemons in half and squeeze juice into the bowl. Pour lemonade into a serving pitcher and use when needed.

title: Indy celebrates 10th birthday on July 4th
author: Michael Reid mreid@somdnews.com
content:
Indy celebrates 10th birthday on July 4th

 July 2, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Michael Reid mreid@somdnews.com | Section: News 
 
 739
 Words 

 Read News Document

 What do you get a 10-year for their birthday?There are many options. Cellphone? Nah. Concert tickets? Nope. Baseball glove? Waste of money. Gift card? Try again.
What Indy — short for Independence — really wants for the birthday party on July 4 is a bunch of bread, apples and carrots. Besides, the bison might just eat all of the above mentioned gifts.
"He'll be getting plenty of that," said Indy's owner, 83-year-old Dick Wildes of Hollywood, on the birthday treats the bison will receive.
Indy declined to be interviewed for this story, instead choosing to munch corn.
Indy was born July 4, 2015, at Summerseat Farm in Mechanicsville and was just three days old when its mother died.
"I'd never had that happen before," Wildes said, adding he never figured out why the mother died.
Then there was the question about what to do with the newborn.
"I'd heard horror stories from people out west who had raised them [from birth]," he said, "They said, 'You never want to do that,' but when that baby came to me for help, what was I going to do? It was either put it down so it wouldn't suffer or try, and the result was good."
The bison was bottle-fed about four to six times a day by farm staff and Wildes, who had several bison at the farm for pasture management.
"Thankfully, we had the volunteers up there who pitched in to bottle feed as well," he said, adding Indy would follow people around everywhere, even into the feed room.
Summerseat Farm held an open house about a month after Indy was born for the bison and other animals.
"I love animals so I wanted to go out there and see what the farm was about and meet the animals," said Tonya Freed of California, who added that Indy "was adorable."
That same day, Freed inquired about volunteering at the farm and after her training, she helped with one of Indy's bottle feedings.
"Indy is very special," said Freed, who has been volunteering at the farm ever since.
Indy's first birthday was a big event as well with balloons up and down the driveway and a homemade vegetable cake by Wildes.
Indy shares the expansive Hollywood pasture, which includes a forest, pond, fresh water and a daily all-you-can-eat grass buffet, with Dozer, a dominant male.
And the pair are a draw for the Land 'O Lake community walkers, golf carts and passing vehicles, many of whom stop to watch.
Wildes, who said he is "very attached" to Indy, will feed the bison grain and will follow Wildes wherever he goes.
It's an above-humid day and Indy is resting in a small, covered, shaded section of the farm to escape the incessant heat and biting insects, and it looks like the animal is in no mood to move.
But carrying a long loaf of crusty bread — Indy's favorite — Wildes softly repeats "Come on ... come on … come on" and soon enough, Indy trots over to the fence and even gives Wildes a kiss.
Wildes keeps both bison in the pasture, and across the road is another pasture with three cows, two of whom are a cross between bison and Hereford while the third is a cross between a bison and Angus. None of the animals are in danger of being harvested.
"They're just pets," he said of Fuzzy, Toro and Mamma Cow. "But they don't follow me around like Indy does."
Wildes grew up in southern Prince George's County on a farm that produced corn, strawberries and other vegetables as well as tobacco.
After graduating from Surrattsville High School in 1960, he enlisted in the U.S. Navy. Later, he worked for a printing company and, after eight years, he bought a printing company of his own in La Plata that he built into a "good-sized facility" with 30 employees, along with another in White Plains.
He retired after the 2002 tornado ripped through La Plata and destroyed the plant.
Prior to that, he had bought the 20-acre Hollywood farm in 1971.
It was during a trip to Colorado decades ago that he first laid eyes on bison and was smitten instantly.
"They're majestic animals," he said of bison, which can reach speeds of up to 35 miles an hour and, according to an Internet search, typically live 15 to 20 years or even longer when in captivity.
And, as America celebrates its own birthday, Indy will celebrate as well with its favorite foods, although Wildes said the bison will most certainly not wear a birthday hat.

title: Sheeba returns home: Easton community comes together to locate lost pit bull
author: Konner Metz
content:
Sheeba returns home: Easton community comes together to locate lost pit bull

 July 2, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Konner Metz | Section: Local News 
 
 797
 Words 

 Read News Document

 EASTON — When Paul Traynor woke up last Thursday, he noticed a small beige dot on his back deck camera. It took a few moments, but he soon realized it wasn't just a speck. Sheeba was home.It had been eight days since Traynor's tan-and-white pit bull went missing, escaping out the front door on June 18. Traynor was on vacation in Ireland for his 60th birthday at the time — the "last place" he wanted to be when a pet sitter informed him Sheeba was nowhere to be found.
Over the next week, neighbors, residents across Easton and locals with dog-searching expertise endeavored to track Sheeba and bring her back home. It was an overwhelming week for Traynor and his granddaughter, Jocilyn, as they spread the word on social media, kept tabs with family and volunteers, and arranged a flight back to the United States.
Last Thursday morning, Traynor reunited with Sheeba. She found her way back home after an eight-day trek that, in many ways, brought together an entire community.
On Saturday, Traynor sat on his back deck sporting a new faded green baseball cap labeled "Dog Dad." He and his granddaughter recounted the whirlwind of a week while the pit bull walked by intermittently for some love and affection. In some ways, it's still an unbelievably happy ending that his beloved Sheeba returned home.
"I was floored, and still am, that she was out here," Traynor said.
TRACKING SHEEBA
Shy but approachable, Sheeba is around 7 years old and has been with Traynor for four years. He fostered her as an abuse rescue from Talbot Humane after she was found in St. Michaels. He decided to keep her for good.
As word spread on social media that Sheeba went missing, volunteers with experience in tracking lost pets tried to hone in on effective search methods. Local drone photographers chipped in, too, such as Bart Ferguson of Chesapeake Aerial Solutions.
The community's efforts spanned from Facebook posts with hundreds of engagements to posters being placed in the nearby area. When Traynor returned from Ireland, he said it seemed like every other person he encountered knew of Sheeba.
"Half of Easton was looking for this dog," Traynor said.
Inge Peters leads a nonprofit cat rescue shelter in Stevensville and also helps out with lost pet searches in Maryland and surrounding states.
"A lost pet being lost can go wrong so fast," Peters said.
Peters and local searcher Sam Happekotte spent hours tracking Sheeba sightings from residents and the potential paths the dog took, most commonly roads or clearings. Peters advises that owners of lost dogs remain calm if they can locate their furry friend. Yelling their name or chasing them only increases the risk they turn around or dangerously run into a nearby road, she said.
"Talk to them the way you do inside, the way you do every single day," Peters said.
The first sighting of Sheeba came on a Thursday, the day after she went missing from Traynor's home in a neighborhood east of Route 50. Sheeba likely traveled east down Dover Road and was spotted near Dover and Chilcutt Roads.
But it wasn't until the following Sunday that a second sighting was reported — news that Jocilyn Traynor says was energizing after a "really tough" quiet spell.
Sheeba strayed further from home toward North Dover Road, and one resident even noted they potentially heard her barking. Paul Traynor says Sheeba has rarely, if ever, barked in the four years he's had her.
"That just shows that in that mode, in that survival mode, they're different," Peters said of lost dogs.
Sheeba then traveled north to Matthewstown Road, according to multiple sightings, before turning around, potentially crossing Dover Road and making her way home.
Traynor said between the tireless work, heat-sensor drones and other strategies implemented to track Sheeba's whereabouts, he was in shock about how much effort went into bringing her home safely.
Traynor shared many thanks for those who searched far and wide for Sheeba, from the drone photographers, to the everyday residents to his adult daughters, Kellie and Brooke. "You people are amazing," he said.
A video of Sheeba walking up to the back deck, approaching the Blink surveillance camera and then standing at the back door has gained over 400,000 views on Traynor's TikTok. In a way, Traynor said, she's become a local celebrity, bringing together a community in times of division.
By Saturday, Sheeba was healthy and spry, walking inside at times to avoid the midday heat. Despite spending eight days in extreme temperatures, she didn't have too many overwhelming health concerns or weight loss when the vet checked on her, Traynor said — an indication that she found shade, water and food to sustain herself.
"She might be timid, but she's not weak," he said. "She's a tough little girl."
This story has been updated to clarify the date Sheeba returned home.

title: Easton carnival closed Thursday due to stolen equipment
author: Konner Metz
content:
Easton carnival closed Thursday due to stolen equipment

 July 3, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Konner Metz | Section: Local News 
 
 290
 Words 

 Read News Document

 EASTON — The Easton carnival unexpectedly closed Thursday due to stolen amusement ride wires, though organizers said it would be back on Friday for the event's Fourth of July finale.Sponsored by the Easton Knights of Columbus chapter, the carnival is an annual town tradition. It is located behind the Target off of Easton Parkway and Saint Michaels Road, open most nights for two weeks in June and July.
But Thursday it closed, according to the Easton Police Department, and the amusement ride company Shaw and Sons Amusements.
Roy Shaw, owner of the Severn-based amusement ride business, said in a phone interview that six major cables valued at a total of $30,000 were stolen before the carnival opened Thursday. He said the company called Easton police and filed a report.
"Between 11:30 last night and I'm gonna say 3 o'clock this afternoon, some undesirables came in and stole what we call our lead lines, which are wires that go from our generator ... to what we call distribution boxes that power the rides," Shaw said.
Shaw and Sons Amusements provides all the rides for the carnival, Shaw said. He added that he's "never had anything like this ever happen."
Thursday evening, Shaw was driving back to the shop across the Chesapeake Bay to hastily gather what is needed for the final day of the carnival. He said the company just couldn't replace the necessary equipment in time for Thursday.
"We will be ready" for Friday, Shaw said. "It's just a minor setback."
"Somebody stole a night from these kids," the amusement ride company owner said.
The carnival is expected to return Friday, opening at 6 p.m. Opening ceremonies are scheduled for 7 p.m. and fireworks are slated to go off after dusk, weather permitting.

title: He 'loved this town': Easton community remembers Darren Foxwell
author: Konner Metz
content:
He 'loved this town': Easton community remembers Darren Foxwell

 July 3, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Konner Metz | Section: Local News 
 
 720
 Words 

 Read News Document

 EASTON — Inside the Easton High School auditorium on Wednesday, current and former students, teachers and community members gathered. It had barely been a month since seniors walked across the auditorium's stage, received their diplomas and turned their tassels toward the next stage of life. Wednesday's event was a sharp contrast.Family, friends and Easton High students and staff joined together to remember recent graduate Darren Foxwell at a funeral service and, later that day, a celebration of life at the Easton Volunteer Fire Department.
Throughout the day, many remarked how kind, caring and genuine of a person Foxwell was.
Former Principal Sherry Spurry reflected on Foxwell's four years at Easton High while giving a eulogy at the funeral. She commended the honor roll student for his academic talents and especially emphasized his top-notch character.
"He was a beacon of light and joy to everyone who knew him," Spurry said. "He was kind and carried a spirit that was infectious. He brought laughter and warmth to every room that he entered. His kindness had no bounds, and he had this uncanny ability to make everyone feel valued, seen and loved."
On June 17, Foxwell, 18, was a passenger in a single-car crash outside Trappe. He was transported to Shock Trauma in Baltimore for treatment of life-threatening injuries. He died the next day.
In the days since, family, friends and the entire Easton community have grappled with the loss of the recent graduate, also a member of the school's wrestling and lacrosse teams. This fall, Foxwell planned to attend Bethany College in West Virginia to play lacrosse.
Former classmates and teammates say they rarely saw Foxwell sad. He was known for his "signature ear-to-ear grin" — as his older sister, Colleen, said at the funeral Wednesday — and his cheerful greetings in the school hallways.
Wrestling teammate Khadija Popam, a rising sophomore, said Foxwell took time out of a free day earlier this year to watch her compete at a meet in Queen Anne's County. When she won her match, he was "ecstatic" for Popam, telling her to never doubt herself.
Older classmates and teammates were impacted by him, too. Matthew Svehla, a 2024 Easton graduate and former wrestling team captain, said Foxwell, even as a junior, made him a better leader.
"Without him, I wouldn't have been able to work as hard as I did," Svehla said.
At the funeral service, Foxwell's lacrosse teammates sported #17 armbands above their elbows. Hundreds attended, from family and friends to local and state elected officials.
Colleen Foxwell, Spurry and Darren's former Little League assistant coach Wade Dressler delivered speeches. Peter Hyman, rabbi emeritus at Temple B'nai Israel, officiated.
Colleen spoke about her brother's quick-witted humor and how he truly came into himself during his teenage years, growing not just tall, but confident. He was always humble, though, and would treat everyone with kindness, she said.
"Anyone who knows Darren and I knows we were not just brother and sister. We were best friends from the day that he was born," she said.
Darren Foxwell is survived by his parents, Len Foxwell and Kerry Daly; sister, Colleen; maternal grandparents, Jerry and Linda Daly; maternal grandmother, Janice Foxwell; and aunts, uncles and cousins.
Colleen said Wednesday that the family is thankful for the community's overwhelming support.
"Outpour is an absolute understatement for the amount of love and support that we have felt from each and every one of you," she said.
A common theme surfaced during both the funeral and the celebration of life: carrying on Darren's legacy. Spurry and Colleen Foxwell asked the Easton High School community to do just that.
"While we are all mourning this devastating loss of Darren today, and we will continue to for a really long time, let's remember the joy and laughter that he brought into each one of our lives," Spurry said. "Let's remember the memories, appreciate the little moments and embrace life with passion."
"Help us carry on my brother's legacy," Colleen Foxwell said. "Help out your neighbor, smile at a stranger, pick up a piece of trash you see on the ground, play peekaboo with the baby staring at you in the checkout line. As cliche as it sounds, do something nice when nobody's looking.
"My brother loved this town so much. He loved each and every one of you. And we will absolutely never forget the way that you all stood by our side."

title: Celebrating the Fourth
author: JIM JOHNSON jjohnson@chespub.com
content:
Celebrating the Fourth

 July 4, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: JIM JOHNSON jjohnson@chespub.com | Section: Local News 
 
 257
 Words 

 Read News Document

 Three hundred-plus people crowded the streets of St. Michaels on the Fourth of July painting the town red, white and blue.The annual Children's Parade stepped off at 10 a.m. led by Police Chief Jeffrey Oswald, an antique fire engine and the color guard from Scout Troop 741 carrying the flag.
The highlight of the parade was the children — most sporting red, white and blue attire — who marched the parade route that started and ended at the St. Michaels Historical Museum and looped through downtown where the streets were lined with cheering paradegoers. The parade took just over 20 minutes, which seemed like a long time for many of the children as temperatures reached the mid-80s.
Brian Collison and his 14-year-old daughter, Constance, stood on a downtown corner, Brian playing patriotic songs on his trumpet with Constance accompanying him on the drums. The Collisons came from Denver, Colorado, to visit relatives in St. Michaels over the holiday weekend.
Four friends from Crofton came to St. Michaels, the third time they marched in the parade. The four — Megan Elias, Ellie Cockrell, Taylor Sundick and Ella Davis — painted their faces red, white and blue.
"We love being patriotic," Sundick said.
Following the parade a traditional Fourth of July program was held on the museum lawn starting with the Scout troop raising the flag and reciting the Pledge of Allegiance. The program included patriotic and folk songs.
The Fourth of July weekend in St. Michaels concluded Saturday with Big Band Night at the Chesapeake Bay Maritime Museum followed by fireworks at dusk.

title: The Star Democrat's top 10 online stories this week
author: STAFF REPORT
content:
The Star Democrat's top 10 online stories this week

 July 5, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: STAFF REPORT | Section: Local News 
 
 370
 Words

 Here are the 10 stories that attracted the most page views on The Star Democrat's website this week. The stories are ranked in order of number of page views as of Wednesday evening.1. Talbot County woman gives record $25M to new Easton hospital
A Talbot County woman and her family made a record $25 million gift toward Easton's in-construction medical center, University of Maryland Shore Regional Health announced Tuesday.
2. Planners not sold on 365-unit development near new Easton hospital
An application for a 365-unit residential development near the in-construction regional medical center in Easton has been submitted to the town's Planning Commission for review, though it's drawing criticism from some town and county officials.
3. Community rallies around family after drowning death of toddlers
Community members are banding together to support the family of two toddlers who died in Greensboro on Sunday.
4. Toddlers drown in incident in Greensboro on Sunday
Two toddlers drowned in an incident in Greensboro on Sunday, according to the Caroline County Sheriff's Office. Police are actively investigating the incident.
5. An unexpected path ends
Easton High School graduate Darren Foxwell had found an unexpected path to college before he was killed in a car accident last month.
6. Easton High School graduate dies in car crash
The Easton community is mourning the death of recent high school graduate Darren Foxwell.
7. Dorchester County K-9 dies: investigation underway
The Dorchester County Sheriff's Office announced that K-9 Ender, a 5-year-old German Shepherd, died last week.
8. Body sits in Greensboro yard for hours due to traffic delay, town says |
On June 22 at about 1:57 p.m., the Greensboro Police Department were dispatched to an apartment on Maple Avenue in Greensboro in reference to an unattended death. The body of the man who died sat in the yard for upwards of four hours after the medical examiner got stuck in Bay Bridge traffic.
9. Cambridge man killed in shooting
Police are investigating a shooting that killed a Cambridge man last week.
Steven Lee Dennis, 45, was identified as the victim by the Cambridge Police Department on Thursday. Police are actively conducting a homicide investigation.
10. Sheeba returns home: Easton community comes together to locate lost pit bull
The Easton community come together to help locate a missing dog.

title: Welcome to the Star Democrat's new newsletter
author: Staff Writer
content:
Welcome to the Star Democrat's new newsletter

 July 7, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Staff Writer | Section: Headlines 
 
 202
 Words 

 Read News Document

 If you've been reading our newsletters for a while, you've probably noticed that this one looks a little different.We are excited to share our new newsletter, a revamped way to connect with our readers. Five days a week, our newsletter will deliver the most relevant news directly to your inbox. The headlines will be curated to ensure you see what stories matter the most in our community.
This new format gives us an opportunity to offer you a glimpse into our newsroom and introduce you to the people who put together your community news.
The Mid-Shore community is tight-knit, bound together by mutual interests in the area's heritage, culture and potential. We also find topics we are divided on — growth and development, traffic, the best place in town to get a crab cake. And we know that what you value most is transparency and being well informed.
This will be your direct connection to our common interest, Mid-Shore readers, and we hope that by directly talking with our readers, we can continue to foster the strong community bonds we've been forging for more than two centuries.
From the bottom of our hearts, thank you for your sincere interest in supporting local news.
— Wendy Weitzel

title: A sneak peak into the Talbot County Fair
author: Lily Tierney
content:
A sneak peak into the Talbot County Fair

 July 8, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Lily Tierney | Section: News 
 
 234
 Words 

 Read News Document

 The Talbot County Fair is back once again to showcase the county's top animals, cuisine, music and much more.According fair representative Michelle McCully, this year will have more live music than years past "and then every day we're going to have midway games, vendors and inflatables."
Thursday
Thursday evening fairgoers can expect a pork barbecue dinner hosted by Talbot 4-H Shooting Sports. That evening also will feature the market hog show as well as the 4-H fashion show. At night, singers Quinn Parsley and Mike Whiskey will be performing.
Friday
Friday will feature the dog, pygmy goat and dairy show. That dinner is going to be the beef barbecue dinner put on by Fairview Church of the Brethren. For entertainment, Bobby Reed and Pat Donahue will perform that night.
Saturday
"Saturday, we have a whole bunch more shows," McCully said. There will be a rabbit show, poultry show, beef show, goat show, and the sheep show and a chicken dinner hosted by the Future Farmers of America alumni. The big entertainment for Saturday night is the band Black Dog Alley.
Fair information
McCulley said she is excited about having more live music and hopes attendees like it too.
"It's a lot of fun for the whole family," she said. "We have, you know, things for all ages and just enjoying the animals as well."
The Talbot County Fair runs from Thursday, July 10, through Saturday, July 12, and admission is $5 per car.

title: 'A good time with great people' boat docking contest draws crowd
author: Lily Tierney
content:
'A good time with great people' boat docking contest draws crowd

 July 8, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Lily Tierney | Section: Local News 
 
 368
 Words 

 Read News Document

 ROCK HALL — The annual Kent County Watermen's Association Watermen's Day and Boat Docking Contest went off without a hitch on Sunday afternoon at Rock Hall Bulkhead.Watermen raced their boats around the corner of the dock making a sharp right turn, quickly backing into the space between two pilings — one marked with the American flag the other with the Maryland state flag — and swung a rodeo-like rope around the dock to mark their time.
Spectators from down the road to New Jersey came out to celebrate the long withstanding watermen's tradition. Leslie and Chick Graber first came out to the event 30 years ago and still love it to this day.
"It's just a good time with great people and a great atmosphere," Chick said.
Leslie said it's nice to see younger kids doing activities outside of their screens.
"They're not on their phones," she said. "I'm happy."
The Watermen's Day and Boat Docking Contest is a family friendly event with food, vendors and refreshments. The Kent County Watermen's Association sold its annual Waterman's Day T-shirts by shore and water on the Skiff Rowe and sold tickets to their annual crab feast.
Hard to Handle, May Worm, Wild Child, Bri-Steff, No Doubt, Outlaw, and many more fantastically named boats participated in Sunday's event. With Jake Jacobs at the helm, Outlaw made a record breaking run of 17 seconds.
There were several waves of competition starting with the smaller boats and ending with the larger vessels. The smaller boats were generally operated by the younger up-and-coming watermen while the larger boats were generally operated by the more seasoned pros.
That is except for 11-year-old Peyton Reiss who was at the helm of May Worm and came in third place among the 31- to 40-foot boats.
In a Facebook post, Rock Hall Mayor James Cook noted that "Waterman's Day in Rock Hall is the best way to end the 4th of July weekend festivities." He added that the event is a blast, and it supports "one of the most important organizations" in the county, the Kent County Watermen's Association.
Cook went on to thank those that put the event together, Rock Hall Police Department and the Rock Hall Volunteer Fire Company for keeping participants and spectators safe.

title: Washington Street Pub returns to Easton
author: Konner Metz
content:
Washington Street Pub returns to Easton

 July 9, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Konner Metz | Section: Local News 
 
 575
 Words 

 Read News Document

 EASTON — An iconic restaurant in downtown Easton is back — and so are its renowned pub chips.The Washington Street Pub is opening Wednesday under new ownership, a rebirth for the staple dining spot after it closed a few years ago.
Bluepoint Hospitality Group, owned by Paul Prager, has added the Pub to its portfolio of downtown restaurants and businesses such as the fine dining Bas Rouge and pizza service Roma Alla Pala, among other establishments.
Located at 20 N. Washington St., the restaurant has undergone significant renovations from what was a building in rough shape with structural issues, says Holly DeKarske, executive director of the Easton Economic Development Corporation.
"It is really, really satisfying to now see the Pub back open and to be here and bring some vibrancy back to Washington Street," DeKarske said.
Prager and Washington Street Pub Executive Chef Daniel Pochron emphasize that the Pub will be affordable, something many residents have been asking for since plans to reopen it were announced. Almost the entire menu will be under $30, Pochron said.
The two-level dining area seats around 160 people, complete with a sizable bar on the first floor and large TVs visible from both levels.
Employees worked on finishing touches Tuesday. Sitting on the second level, Pochron, a 26-year resident of the Eastern Shore, beamed with excitement when thinking back to how he and his wife often dined at the former Pub.
"We'd come here on a Friday and a Saturday night, and this place was packed," he said. "That's the excitement that I want to bring back. I love it more than anything."
There'll be a raw bar with five types of oysters, Pochron said. Other seafood options include lobster, shrimp (peel-and-eat, cocktail and tacos), fish and chips, crab cakes and cream of crab soup.
Pochron noted additional entrees such as the meatloaf, chicken pot pie and burger are reasonably priced. There are salads under $20 and sandwiches around $15.
Desserts include apple pie, carrot cake, a root beer float, bread pudding and a chocolate chip cookie skillet.
"To make the food comfort food that's good and fair priced. That's what brought me back to the pub," said Pochron, a longtime chef in the area with stops at the Tidewater Inn and the Inn at Perry Cabin in St. Michaels.
Prager said in an interview last month that it was important for the establishment to remain as the Washington Street Pub, a place where he hopes "everybody would feel comfortable in."
And yes, the highly requested pub chips are back. In fact, Pochron said it was a lengthy process to try to source former Pub employees to find where to get the chips.
"Anywhere I go, the first question I have to answer is, 'I got the pub chips back,'" the chef said.
"You wouldn't believe how many people asked about pub chips," Prager said. "So it was like, 'OK, we got to figure that out.'"
The Washington Street Pub will be open Wednesday to Monday from 11 a.m. to midnight and closed on Tuesdays.
DeKarske shared excitement for the boost she believes the restaurant will bring to Easton's downtown, especially during the summer months and the Waterfowl Festival in November.
"To have another dining establishment is huge," DeKarske said. "That's what brings people downtown. That's what gets locals and visitors out and about, and then also helps boost all of our retail.
"It was definitely felt when it closed," she said. "But I think that we are going to feel it when it reopens as well."

title: 'An amazing turnout' — Talbot County Fair back once again
author: Lily Tierney
content:
'An amazing turnout' — Talbot County Fair back once again

 July 14, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Lily Tierney | Section: Local News 
 
 451
 Words 

 Read News Document

 EASTON — The Talbot County Fair came back this past weekend for its 42nd year of showcasing Maryland's state sport of jousting, providing games galore, highlighting many food vendors, and hosting a multitude of animal shows and exhibits.The fair ran from Thursday, July 10, to Saturday, July 12. Each day offered something different and exciting, like the pygmy goat show on Friday and the annual watermelon eating contest on Saturday.
Chairman of the Talbot County Fair Michelle McCulley said the watermelon eating contest was her favorite part of the weekend.
"That was so much fun to watch," McCulley said.
Young farmers from 4-H manned the games booths, sold fair gear and showed off their animals each day, an opportunity for the agriculture students to test their skills.
Former 4-H member and 2025 pygmy goat show winner Stacey Thompson has been showing animals since she was 10 years old. Thompson, now 36, is a mentor to many of the young 4-Hers at the fair.
As the leader of the Just Kidding Around 4-H Club, Thompson said she enjoys returning to her roots and sharing her experiences with the younger generations.
"A lot of these little kids you see running around I've actually trained," Thompson said.
Thompson proudly watched the young farmers show their goats after she won first place in her heat.
McCulley said she was very happy with the weather conditions and turnout of this year's event.
"We really lucked out with the weather. There was no rain, and I don't know if that's the first time, but it's a miracle," she said. "So I think that really helped us. We had a really good turnout, better than we have the past couple years."
The annual watermelon eating contest drew the largest turnout of all the events of the weekend. The competition was divided by age bracket.
Everyone had one minute to eat as much of their watermelon as possible, except for the 21 and older crowd, who had 45 seconds. Juice dripped from the sides of participants' mouths as the judge yelled, "drop your watermelons."
First and second place competitors received prizes, and everyone else received purple ribbons. First time Talbot County Fair goer Gabby Hernandez came out victorious in the 21 and older category but said she was initially super nervous. "I was like, making a whole plan," Hernandez said.
Hernandez, who ate her watermelon slice down to the rind, beat her husband and all the other men at the table. "This is my first time. I've never done anything like that before," she said about the eating contest.
The fair will be back around the same time next year. "It was an amazing turnout, and all the money goes back to the 4-H and supporting youth projects and learning," McCulley said.

title: A tough question: How much watermelon can you eat?
author: Staff Writer
content:
A tough question: How much watermelon can you eat?

 July 14, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Staff Writer | Section: Headlines 
 
 124
 Words 

 Read News Document

 I returned to the newsroom from my vacation to find The Star Democrat's reporters had spent the past week asking tough questions.Among them was this one — how much watermelon can you eat in 45 seconds?
Reporter Lily Tierney found out last weekend while covering the Talbot County Fair, which came back for its 42nd year of showcasing local musicians, fresh culinary offerings and, most importantly, the results of 4-H students' efforts to raise and show farm animals.
The adult winner of this year's watermelon contest beat her husband and all the other men at the table in the competition Saturday, her first ever eating contest.

A century of firefighting fueled by a community's spirit

 Words

 At the top of today's headlines newsletter, readers will find a story that would not exist without a community's resilience.The Tilghman Island Volunteer Fire Department has endured nearly a century of difficulties — from financial hardships and troubles with volunteer retention to several relocations and expansions.
