title: Tilghman Island Volunteer Fire Department marks 100 years with parade Saturday
author: Konner Metz
content:
Tilghman Island Volunteer Fire Department marks 100 years with parade Saturday

 July 16, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Konner Metz | Section: Local News 
 
 619
 Words 

 Read News Document

 TILGHMAN ISLAND — It began in 1925 as a wagon with tanks, and now, the Tilghman Island Volunteer Fire Department is celebrating its centennial.Serving residents in the waterfront village, the fire department has persisted through many ups and downs, president Jesse Gottleib said.
"So many small companies don't see 100 years because of not only funding, but more so because of lack of participation, lack of volunteers for the department," he said.
Such challenges are true in Tilghman Island — there are around 30 volunteers, 12 of them firefighters, the president noted. And while money is always a challenge, Gottleib said the department is extremely active in hosting community fundraisers.
The key cog in the fire department's survival and success has been community support, said Gottleib and his mother Linda, the department's secretary.
"We would've never thought it," he said of reaching the 100-year mark. "And I think the reason is because people in this side of St. Michaels down, they realize that we're gonna be there when they need it."
To celebrate the milestone, Tilghman Island firefighters are hosting a parade on Saturday. It begins at 10 a.m. with a fair atmosphere, including food, live music and games. At 11:30 a.m., kids will hop in fire gear to compete in a junior firefighters competition, spraying hoses at targets.
"It might help them to say, 'I wanna join,'" Linda Gottleib said.
The parade begins near the Knapps Narrows Bridge at 1 p.m. A friendly firefighters' competition will follow, and later that evening, the department plans to host a private ceremony to honor some key life members.
On Wednesday at the fire house, the Gottleibs pointed out some of the unsung heroes of the fire department. Dewayne Stewart, a line officer for 36 years, and Billy Lednum, a line officer for 31 years, have been integral to the company's success.
"You'll see a hurt in the fire department when those two are gone," Jesse Gottleib said.
The Tilghman Island Volunteer Fire Department doesn't go on a ton of calls — sometimes two to 10 per month, Gottleib said. But the department often provides mutual aid or helps with water rescues. Most recently, the Tilghman fire boat assisted state searchers with a rescue in Broad Creek on July 4.
In addition to the fire boat, the fire station houses multiple fire trucks and a Talbot County ambulance. Last year, the station donated a fire engine to a Tennessee fire department dealing with damages from Hurricane Helene.
Jesse Gottleib, 43, is the youngest sitting president and has been a member since he turned 16 in 1997. His mother joined in 1999 and has served a number of roles, including secretary, president and board member.
In recent days, they've been scouring through old newspaper clips and photos to create collages for Saturday's festivities. Some photos show the fire station in its three different buildings, the current one built in 2005.
It's a family affair for Jesse Gottleib, as it is for many of the volunteers. He recalled once ditching a baseball game — while actively manning left field — just to watch the fire trucks pull out of the station when he was about 9 years old.
"First game that we had down here at Tilghman school, the fire siren went off," he said. "And (my mom) and my dad were standing there and were like, 'Is he leaving?' And I ran across the field to go to the fence."
Saturday will be a chance to reflect on some of those fun memories, interact with the community and honor longtime volunteer firefighters and administrators. Gottleib said the dedication of volunteers has been remarkable.
"Their time is appreciated here," Gottleib said. "I feel like they play a key role into getting us to where we are now at 100 years."

title: She's worth it: Bikers raise funds for injured woman
author: MARTY MADDEN mmadden@somdnews.com
content:
She's worth it: Bikers raise funds for injured woman

 July 23, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: MARTY MADDEN mmadden@somdnews.com | Section: News 
 
 245
 Words 

 Read News Document

 The event T-shirts said it all — "I'm worth it."Her family, friends and members of the Southern Maryland region's motorcycle community concur. That's why motorcyclists hopped on their bikes, took off and made a 3.5 mile round trip on July 19 to participate in a charity poker run.
The event raised money to aid Nichole "Cici" Moneymaker, who was seriously injured in a June 3 crash at Route 2/4 and Southern Connector Boulevard in Lusby.
Moneymaker was flown to shock trauma. She still has internal injuries and hasn't been able to go back to work.
The poker run, which started and finished at the Patuxent Moose Lodge in Hollywood, was held to help raise money to help Moneymaker with the costs incurred.
"The biker community is very giving. They have a good heart," Tiffany Gilroy, Moneymaker's sister, told Southern Maryland News. Gilroy organized the event on her sister's behalf.
"It's a family, everybody is involved," Sandie Greene, Nichole's mother, said. As for her daughter's recovery from the serious crash, Greene said, "slowly but surely. We're taking it one day at a time,"
In addition to the entry funds collected from riders, sales from T-shirts designed locally by Kimberly Oliver are also providing revenue to provide aid.
Oliver said she had met Moneymaker at vendor events and wanted to help out. The T-shirts have the words, "I'm Worth It" on the front.
"Sales are going good today," Oliver said at Saturday's event.
Greene said organizers are also hoping "to raise awareness about distracted driving."

 It's been a busy week in the newsroom.I had a moment to reflect on that Friday evening as I waited for Lily Tierney's final assignment of the day — her report on a protest in Easton.
The protest on Route 50 drew a crowd of about 150 Mid-Shore residents, who called for the release of Easton pastor Daniel Fuentes Espinal from U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement custody. Espinal's detainment has drawn national attention in the days since his arrest Monday.

Weeks like this are demanding, but they're also a powerful reminder of why we do what we do: to keep our community informed.

title: Easton Beer Fest canceled after slow ticket sales
author: Konner Metz
content:
Easton Beer Fest canceled after slow ticket sales

 July 25, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Konner Metz | Section: Local News 
 
 403
 Words 

 Read News Document

 EASTON — Slow ticket sales and a lack of vendors led the Easton Volunteer Fire Department to cancel next month's 10th annual Easton Beer Fest.The event, slated for Aug. 16, is known for a wide craft beer selection, bringing together hundreds of people each year since 2016. But forging ahead with this year's festival would've put the fire department at an operating loss for the effort, according to treasurer Chris Hash.
Beer Fest is usually an October event, but a slew of other festivals led organizers to move it up to August in an attempt to attract vendors and festivalgoers. Ticket sales this year, as of Tuesday's cancelation announcement, were 45% of what they normally would be around a month before the event, Hash said.
"Ticket sales were drastically below those benchmarks," he said. "That combined with an overall shift in the craft beer industry with a number of brewers that have closed or other ones that have cut back in their staffing. We were faced with breweries that were not able to attend, which left us below our benchmark to have or produce a successful event."
Typically, around 35 breweries would attend, and sometimes as many as 45, Hash said. Less than 25 were scheduled for this year.
Hash says he's seen a dip in Maryland's craft beer industry recently. Nationwide, the nonprofit Brewers Association tracked nearly 400 closings of breweries in 2024, which outpaced the number of openings.
One less fundraiser
Canceling the fundraiser is a financial strain on the Easton's fire department. Hash said the festival has brought in $250,000 over the last nine years.
Leaders at the Easton Volunteer Fire Department are encouraging residents to give financial support through other upcoming events. The department is hosting a golf tournament in September. Spots are sold out, but sponsorships are still available, Hash said.
And on Feb. 21, the fire department will host Stews & Brews at the fire hall, a fundraising event that coincides with the annual Chesapeake Fire & Ice Festival.
For future events, Hash said he hopes attendees buy tickets early if they're able, as ticket projections play a role in cancelation decisions.
He said the fire department hopes to bring back Easton Beer Fest in the future.
"It's something that, personally, I enjoy doing," Hash said. "I enjoy bringing people in, bringing good beer to them. You feel like you're letting people down when you're not able to provide an event or what they've become accustomed to."

title: Denton holding first ever Restaurant Week
author: AHMAD GARNETT agarnett@chespub.com
content:
Denton holding first ever Restaurant Week

 July 25, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: AHMAD GARNETT agarnett@chespub.com | Section: News 
 
 336
 Words 

 Read News Document

 DENTON — From July 28 to Aug. 2, Downtown Denton Main Street will be celebrating its first Restaurant Week.Restaurant Week is a chance for Denton to highlight its food options and bring new customers to town.
Jessica Willoughby, director of Downtown Denton Main Street, said the thought of doing a Restaurant Week came from research.
"So far, all of the business have been very receptive," Willoughby said. "I think they're excited. I'm just trying to get all the restaurants and all the businesses downtown promoted so people will come to downtown Denton."
The restaurants in downtown Denton participating are Pizza Empire, Caroline's in Denton, El Chupacabra, Craft Bakery & Cafe, Market Street Pub and Shore Gourmet.
"We want to try to get a lot of people off 404 and bring them through town because if we do that, they going take some of this wonderful food that we got going on in here," Market Street Pub, Head Chef, Iris Francis said. "We want people to be able to not just taste the food. We have shops up and down here that could be seen and stuff and they could purchase things from."
All restaurants will be running specials during restaurant week.
"One of the wonderful things in here in Denton, it's all great people, all the restaurant come together," El Chupakabra co-owner, Guadalupe Galindo, said.
Restaurant week will include a game for residents and visitors to play with a chance for a price if the resident visits all restaurants.
"We've made up a stamp card which has all all the restaurants that are participating on that card and when you go there to eat or to dine out you get your card stamped," Willoughby said. "At the end of the week, there will have a box at the visitor center in Denton that you put your card in. It has your name on the back and your telephone number for so we can reach you."
The winner, who will be selected randomly, will win a free customized fire pit from Blue Line Metal Works.

title: Cow chip toss defining moment for reporter
author: Carl Hamilton cahamilton@chespub.com
content:
Cow chip toss defining moment for reporter

 July 25, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Carl Hamilton cahamilton@chespub.com | Section: News 
 
 1056
 Words 

 Read News Document

 FAIR HILL — I never gave a crap about cow chip tosses until I competed in one at the Cecil County Fair on Sunday evening.My editor assigned me the story. And it was consistent with the other George-Plimpton-style assignments he had doled out to me for our fair (the event, not the quality of work) coverage in the past.
He is the reason why I plunged my face into a miniature peach cobbler topped with a cumulus cloud of whipped cream during the annual pie-eating contest two years ago, as one example.
The contest is simple. Contestants competing by gender and in various age brackets attempt to toss a "cow chip" into a metal bucket, which is about 15 feet away. Those who sink the cow chip advance to Round 2, when the toss-line is moved back to approximately 20 feet away from the target, and those who miss are eliminated.
This process is repeated until every competitor is sidelined except for the most accurate tosser, who smiles moments later as a fair representative presents him or her with the 1st Place Ribbon.
Then, that elated cow-chip-toss winner looks straight into the lens and gushes, "I'm going to Disney World," after the off-camera reporter asks what will be the champion's next conquest . . . OK, OK, I made up that last part.
Before I continue with my slightly embellished account, it's important to clear up some misleading cow-chip-toss terms, the first of which is the term "cow chip." For the record, I and my fellow contestants did not toss cow chips.
Instead, we tossed clay pigeons, the kind that hunters use for target practice. Those clay pigeons are normally propelled high into the air by a machine or by a guy with a really, really strong throwing arm to simulate the flight of pheasants, geese, ducks and other winged prey and hunters shoot them down with their shotguns.
I hate to quibble, but the clay pigeons we tossed Sunday evening looked nothing like pigeons — or any other type of bird, reptile or mammal, including humans. What we cow-chip-toss gladiators tossed were orangey, palm-sized discs.
Furthermore, I feel compelled to be a stickler about this: clay pigeons aren't made of clay, but they actually are comprised of limestone and petroleum pitch — based on my extensive AI and Wikipedia research . . . Yeah, it's starting to dawn on me now that I don't hate to quibble after all.
So why is the contest called a cow chip toss?
Well, this is where it gets repulsively interesting. It seems that, up until an estimated two decades ago, according to some unofficial Cecil County Fair historians, cow chip toss competitors tossed actual cow chips.
What is a cow chip, some may ask. Sure, I'll field this one. A cow chip is manure that has been dropped in a field by — you guessed it, a cow — and then has been dried out by the sun into a hardened, disc-like shape.
It should not be confused with the terms "cow patties" or "cow pies," however, if I'm comprehending my AI/Wikipedia research information correctly.
Cow patties and cow pies are fresh (Oxymoron Alert), wet cow dung, before they've been petrified by the sun. Speaking of petrified, the AI Overview included a photo of a fresh, wet cow patty and it scared me to death. Some things in life you truly cannot unsee.
So where was I? Oh yeah, petrified cow crap and how it was once used in the cow chip toss contests.
I assumed, naturally, that Cecil County Fair officials overseeing the cow chip toss competition 20-some years ago pooh-pooh'ed the practice of using real dry dung discs and replaced them with clay pigeons — or discs masquerading as clay and as pigeons — because it would be more sanitary.
But that is not the reason, according to local farmer and fellow contestant Mark Crouse, who chatted with me Sunday evening during the competition. He explained that fair planners in the Cow Chip Toss Department opted for clay pigeons (ahem) at some point because of a supply-and-demand problem encountered when doing things the organic, old-fashioned way.
Turns out, Crouse, who is 48, traipsed through the fields on the Miller Family dairy farm near North East when he was a teenager and gathered cow chips for the annual fair contest. Al Miller, who has served on the Cecil County Fair Board for 47 years, also served on that cow chip collection crew.
"It's harder to collect suitable cow chips than you would think," Crouse emphasized.
Then Crouse outlined, "The cow had to go in the pasture. You couldn't have rain the day before or even two days before, either, because it had to be completely dried out. You hope it's dry before you pick it up, but that isn't always the case."
It's noteworthy here that, according to my AI research, a fresh cow patty consists of approximately 83 percent water. Yes, it actually cited "about" 83 percent. I'm assuming a more precise cow-manure-moisture reading would involve a decimal point followed by lots more numbers, all of which compiled by scientists in white lab coats and buoyed by government grants.
Miller further explained that changes in the dairy farming field (no pun intended) created the supply problem. "The cows used to go out in the pasture, but the cows are more confined now," Miller said, agreeing that the change leading to the paucity of perfect cow poo occurred about 20 to 30 years ago.
So where was I? Oh yeah, Sunday evening's cow chip toss contest and my participation in it.
Well, we're running out of space now because, apparently, I digressed for quite a bit back there. So I'll finally cut to the chase. I competed in the class for men who are 26 and older and sunk my first "cow chip." During Round 2, I missed slightly to the right of the bucket, with my clay pigeon crashing onto the ground and exploding into tiny pieces like it had been shot by a target-practicing hunter.
After Round 3, which I watched from the sidelines, it was determined that I tied for 2nd Place. And I, quite surprised, received a ribbon indicating that feat.
But I must say this: Knowing that I could have been tossing real cow chips if that supply-and-demand problem hadn't happened, I left the fair Sunday evening feeling like I took home a 1st Place Ribbon.

title: Temple B'nai Israel welcomes new permanent rabbi
author: BROOKE ENSMINGER
content:
Temple B'nai Israel welcomes new permanent rabbi

 July 26, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: BROOKE ENSMINGER | Section: Local News 
 
 566
 Words 

 Read News Document

 EASTON — Nearly nine months after the previous rabbi retired, a new permanent rabbi has stepped into the role at Temple B'nai Israel.Rabbi Jordan Goldson assumed the position on July 1, following the retirement of Rabbi Peter Hyman in October.
In the search for a new permanent rabbi, the temple's Board of Trustees created a list of potential candidates for interviews after establishing priorities, according to Barbara Spector, the board president during the selection process. Spector said the board was looking for a Reform rabbi with more experience to fit Temple B'nai Israel's established congregation.
Before coming to Easton, Goldson had extensive experience leading congregations. After being ordained at Hebrew Union College in 1987, Goldson became a full-time Reform rabbi at Temple B'nai Tikvah in Calgary, Alberta, Canada, where he served for 12 years. Upon leaving the temple, Goldson lived in Israel for some time before moving back to the U.S. to lead several congregations around the country. Most recently, Goldson served as the rabbi at Har Sinai Temple in Pennington, New Jersey.
"He has a very calm demeanor and a wonderful background with his experience in being part of an inclusive congregation," David Holtz said. Holtz took over the position of temple executive director after Goldson was selected.
Holtz described him as "one of those very nice people that you're grateful that you've been able to encounter, particularly in a role that will mean so much to the community and to the congregation."
Hyman described Goldson as very bright, engaging, warm, creative and people-focused.
As the former rabbi at the temple, Hyman said maintaining a presence in the community was always his first priority, and he has great confidence in Goldson building on that foundation.
"He's really terrific," Hyman said. "He's going to continue to grow the congregation, and I know he'll be successful."
Hyman's years of dedication and congregation building have not gone unnoticed. Goldson recognized Hyman for his "spectacular job" in expanding the congregation and said he will build on what Hyman has done to increase the temple's reach.
Focused on inclusivity, Goldson said his plans to grow the congregation, creating an environment where "people feel that they matter."
Temple B'nai Israel is the hub for Jewish life on the Eastern Shore and represents a vast community. Goldson said he will reach out to the community and welcome people who may not know about the congregation.
"We'll be doing a lot of different things that I think are going to attract people to the temple," Goldson said.
The temple offers a religious school for students in kindergarten through 12th grade. Spector said she expects Goldson will help attract more young families to the temple and expand the religious school.
"We're just hoping he can help us get ready for the next decade by helping us educate young Jewish children," Spector said.
To support this effort, Goldson plans to expand the temple's programs, including youth, community service and religious education initiatives.
As he becomes more comfortable in his new role, Goldson has enjoyed the positive energy and dynamics of the community, and he recognizes that it will take more than just him to grow the congregation's impact.
"I can see that this is a community that embraces each other," Goldson said. "It's a very tight-knit, religious community and I'm really looking forward to working with the larger community here to see what we can do to make Easton and the surrounding areas the most wonderful place it can be."

title: Fair season is here with affordable fun for the whole family
author: AHMAD GARNETT agarnett@chespub.com
content:
Fair season is here with affordable fun for the whole family

 August 1, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: AHMAD GARNETT agarnett@chespub.com | Section: Headlines 
 
 155
 Words 

 Read News Document

 It's fair season, and there are multiple fairs happening for the next couple of weeks on the Mid-Shore.I personally enjoy fairs for the prizes and the food.
Trappe Volunteer Fire Company is holding its annual Old Tyme Fair this weekend. Unfortunately, the first day of the fair was cancelled due to inclement weather.
I have never seen a fair with as low as prices than the Old Tyme Fair. From $2 games to great prices for food, it is an affordable option for family fun this weekend.
Plus, supporting a local volunteer fire company is always a bonus.
Fair season is the best, and if you're looking for a fair this weekend, the Old Tyme Fair is a perfect option. You can read more about it in my story below.
Also in today's newsletter: protests continue for an Easton pastor detained by ICE, Talbot County's proposed cannabis regulations receive mixed reviews, and more.
Thanks for reading.

title: Shore decor: Coastal Cottage boutique opens in Chester

content:
Shore decor: Coastal Cottage boutique opens in Chester

 August 2, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: ANDREA GRABENSTEIN agrabenstein@chespub.com | Section: News

 Words 

 Read News Document

 CHESTER — With bright pastels and images of Bay life, walking into the Coastal Cottage, one can practically hear the waves lapping with their living room.That was the desire for boutique owner Tara Rose, as the boutique celebrated a grand opening at the Red Apple Promenade in Chester July 26.
Stepping away from corporate America, Rose was inspired to showcase her passion for home design and breathe new life into the boutique.
Offering coastal home decor and gifts, the Coastal Cottage specializes in thoughtfully curated coastal furniture, home decor, and unique gifts to bring the relaxed elegance of seaside living into any space, Rose said.
Bringing a little something to your home to make it more comfortable can make all the difference in how we feel, according to Rose.
"If you have a coastal inspired decor you feel like you're a little bit relaxed and taken back to great memories," she said.
More than generic beach themed goods, the boutique specializes in specific Eastern Shore, Kent Island and Chesapeake Bay themed home decor.
Rose collaborates with surrounding businesses and local artists to carry different product lines not found elsewhere.
"That way we're supporting everybody," she said.
"Decorating and making homes beautiful is a passion of mine," Rose said, and in her designs, she values providing options to beautify the home, but also a variety of price points.
From economic prints, to original art pieces, the boutique carries coastal decor to meet every budget.
"I wanted to make sure there was something here for everybody," she said.
Coastal Cottage looks forward to continually partnering with local businesses and artists and always welcomes recommendations for new items to bring feelings of shore style to any home.
"It's a wonderful community and a very special day," Rose said.
Located at 110 South Piney Rd Chester, Coastal Cottage summer hours are Tuesday and Wednesday from 11 a.m. to 7 p.m., Thursday 10 a.m. to 6 p.m., Friday, Saturday, and Sunday 10 a.m. to 5 p.m. and closed Mondays.

title: 'One for the books' — Betterton Day draws families for a day of suds and fun
author: WILL BONTRAGER wbontrager@chespub.com
content:
'One for the books' — Betterton Day draws families for a day of suds and fun

 August 4, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: WILL BONTRAGER wbontrager@chespub.com | Section: News 
 
 407
 Words 

 Read News Document

 BETTERTON — The weather was gorgeous and the beach was well-attended for Betterton Appreciation Day on Friday night into Saturday afternoon."Betterton Day was perfect with amazing weather, the parade was awesome. The band had people dancing. The magic show had the kids and adults laughing. It was a great time," replied a representative for Betterton Day.
Fireworks on Friday night on the boardwalk bedazzled audiences.
The next morning, Ryann Marchetti sang the "Star Spangled Banner". The parade followed, featuring Kent's first responders, marching bands and fun floats before beachside vendors sold everything from bookmarks to baked goods.
Betterton vendor, Nina's Baked Goods sold great tasting items including their bacon cheddar scones, said Nina and Sienna Fahrman, residents of Betterton.
The Union United Methodist Church in Worton offered savory trout, said volunteer George Johnson.
Jim DeCaro of Still Pond Creations sold paintings of journeys to the Outer Banks in North Carolina, a double rainbow in an azure sky, a sunset on the Sassafras and many other works.
Everyone seemed to participate in the fun. Dave LeClair from his residence on the hill, shot off tiny plastic soldiers on parachutes down to expectant kids. Residents from Rigby Bluff II condominiums threw beachballs down to the kids simultaneously as the Willy Woo Woo Productions float operated a bubble machine spreading suds.
Toys, bubbles and candy surrounded scurrying kids, having fun while their parents froze those fond moments on their cell phones.
New this year was the magic show by magician of 50 years, Michael Cox and family, Jennifer, Hailey and Caidyn Cox of Willy Woo Woo Productions.
The show drew around 150 adults and kids near the pavilion steps such as little Layanna Johnson. Her aunt Akilah Johnson-Downes complimented the show.
"We definitely enjoyed this. This year's Betterton Day was one for the books."
That was followed up by the crowd favorite at the park, Cow Plop Bingo, and while Rosa the cow did not "plop", money went to Fred Zink, noted volunteer for the fire company, as his number was drawn at random from approximately 500 plots.
Representatives for Betterton Day extended their thanks to organizers.
"Thank you so much to the Betterton Community Development Corporation, Betterton American Legion, Betterton Volunteer Fire Company and the Betterton Still Pond Lions Club, especially volunteers, Gerry and Linda Werner for pouring countless hours bringing this event to life."
For more information and pictures of Betterton Day, find them on Facebook and do not forget to attend next year's beach party, Gerry and Linda Werner reminded.

title: Too many stories, not enough space
author: Staff Writer
content:
Too many stories, not enough space

 August 5, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Staff Writer | Section: Headlines 
 
 146
 Words 

 Read News Document

 I've been playing Tetris with Wednesday's newspaper all evening.Actually, that's how I spend most evenings in the newsroom — sifting through the stories of the day, figuring out which are the most pressing or compelling, and fitting them into the print edition around ads, comics and columns.
Tonight, that was a little trickier than normal. A lot of interesting news has broken since our last print edition came out on Saturday. It's a good problem to have.
Among the stories I managed to fit into Wednesday's paper are:
A piece on the Caroline County Sheriff's Office taking over policing in Federalsburg.A piece on Easton Town Council members' reactions to increased ICE arrests in town.A piece on the cultural consequences of a Chesapeake Bay sea monster.
You can read all of them below — or by picking up a copy of The Star Democrat.
Thanks, as always, for reading.
— Wendy Weitzel

title: Man honors the dead, one headstone at a time
author: Aamaly Hossain somdnewsintern@chespub.com
content:
Man honors the dead, one headstone at a time

 August 5, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Aamaly Hossain somdnewsintern@chespub.com | Section: News 
 
 501
 Words 

 Read News Document

 For over two years, Sidney Waugh has been bringing memorial headstones back to life — in a sense.What began as a personal act of love — buying a headstone for his late mother when he was 50-years-old — has grown into a mission to help families honor their deceased loved ones.
In March 2023, Waugh officially launched Memorial Restoration and Engraving Services, located at 5887 Crain Highway in La Plata.
But long before that, the Maryland man was already restoring and engraving headstones across Charles County in the southern part of the state.
"I basically do all my own engravings, all my own installations," Waugh said. "I go into the cemeteries to clean stones, reset 'em, put the color back in them."
His services range from simple cleanings to deep restorations. At 58 years old, Waugh's one-man operation has taken him to cemeteries in White Plains, Brandywine, La Plata and beyond.
"It was difficult getting access to them [cemeteries] or finding out who to properly talk to [for permission]," he said, but that hasn't stopped him from doing the work.
Most of Waugh's projects are deeply personal for the families he helps.
Donna Briscoe, 63, of Waldorf turned to him when two of her relatives' stones became very worn down.
"The stone had gotten so weathered that you can't even read the information on it," Waugh said.
Waugh cleaned and repaired Briscoe's great-great-grandfather's headstone, along with the headstones of his children, all dating back to the 19th century — no charge, at the time.
"That's the type of work he does," Briscoe said, adding that Waugh provides great service.
For Waugh, this was about more than just restoration. It's about honor and connection.
"I never met my grandmother, my great-grandmother or my great-grandfather, but I was able to clean and reset both of their stones," he said. "For me, it helps me stay in contact with the people."
Often, he said, people don't know where their ancestors are buried until they reach out to him for help — to locate and restore long-forgotten headstones.
"It's like bringing a piece of their family's story back to them," Waugh said.
He added that memorial headstones shouldn't be somber, but personalized, bringing back happy memories of a loved one's personality.
With that, Waugh has engraved small details — such as bingo cards, custom cars, travel imagery and even sewing thimbles — for several headstones.
Sometimes, his role goes beyond restoration and engraving.
Grief can be heavy, Waugh said, and when clients come to him, they may just need someone to talk to, so he listens.
"This is something that God planned ahead for me," Waugh said. "This was never something that I saw myself doing," but he did anyway.
Things like brass spinning, stones discoloration from various elements and moss is what lures Waugh into cleaning and restoring these headstones, with the bonus of honoring the dead and God.
"My dream for this business is to be able to help as many people and restore as many stones as I can," he said. "To show my grandchildren that nothing in this world is impossible."

title: Caroline Dorchester County Fair kicks off with ribbon cutting
author: AHMAD GARNETT agarnett@chespub.com
content:
Caroline Dorchester County Fair kicks off with ribbon cutting

 August 7, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: AHMAD GARNETT agarnett@chespub.com | Section: News 
 
 428
 Words 

 Read News Document

 DENTON — On Wednesday, the Caroline Dorchester County Fair begin with a ribbon cutting ceremony.Commonly known as "the fair too big for one county," this annual fair will be hosted at the Caroline County 4-H Park through Saturday. During the ribbon cutting, multiple county officials spoke on how important 4-H Park is to the community and how important the fair is to the park.
"4-H and these county fairs are just such an essential part of keeping our future going," Dorchester County Council member Mike Detmer said.
"...I love coming here with my family. I love coming here and enjoying all the families and kids that are here. I just want them to know we just are cheering for them so much and we're counting on them. We're so appreciative for the the opportunity this gives to 4-H and other students here that are doing such a great job. We're so proud of you."
Sen. Johnny Mautz (R-Caroline, Dorchester, Talbot, Wicomico) spoke on behalf of the Eastern Shore legislative delegation.
"We always look forward to this wonderful tradition," Mautz said. "It is Americana in person right here in Caroline County. It's an honor to be a part of it, and especially we want to salute our 4-H'ers. We always like to come out here seeing everything you guys put into those animals every year. Its a great thing, so God bless the 4-H and God bless the fair."
The fair includes family fun for all ages with different events and themes and attractions each day.
One particular exhibit that drew a crowd at the fair was Lumberjack Ray.
Ray Geist, a Talbot County native, is a former Timber Sports professional. He was able to put his skills on display for Caroline and Dorchester residents at the fair Wednesday.
Geist started Timber Sports, a lumberjack-style sport, in 2011. He participated in all four years of college and then got a job at the Great Alaskan Lumberjack Show in Ketchikan, Alaska.
"I did that for 10 years off and on and then came back here and been back in Maryland, which is home sweet home," he said.
Geist performed axe throwing, log rolling, underhand chop and more on Wednesday. He said it was amazing to perform for his hometown because people don't get a chance to see Timber Sports in person.
"People haven't seen it in real life, TV here and there, but to be able to have the demonstration here and to have my local family and friends here to see it, it's a lot of fun," Geist said.
For more information on the schedule for the fair, visit carolinedorchestercountyfair.com.

title: Hog heaven: Gracie's pigs are top tier at local fair
author: WILL BONTRAGER wbontrager@chespub.com
content:
Hog heaven: Gracie's pigs are top tier at local fair

 August 8, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: WILL BONTRAGER wbontrager@chespub.com | Section: Life 
 
 354
 Words 

 Read News Document

 Congratulations go out to 18-year-old Constance "Gracie" Troyer for a successful performance at the Kent County Fair last month. Her swine Novalee was awarded grand champion among market hogs.Novalee started out winning first among heavyweights. Then Randy, Troyer's other hog, was awarded first among middleweights. At the final showdown, it was between Novalee, Randy, and Laurel Clarke's lightweight champion hog, Diva.
Judge Kelsey Zepp's decision was Novalee, exclaiming one hog stood out among the others throughout the competition.
Troyer's mother, Stacie was among her daughter's cheering campaign and beamed, "Proud momma here! She has worked so hard."
Troyer exclaimed she always did well in past competitions but was shocked that both Randy and Novalee went home winners.
The mixed breed hogs can hold their snouts up high as the best there is in 2025.
Troyer pointed out the judge looks for a specific musculature among heavy weights and for middle weight Randy, the same kind of structure just slightly leaner. Zepp also looks for how clean they are and basically the potential of a quality market pig.
Having prize-winning hogs requires dedication. For Novalee and Randy, training started around January. Troyer walked them every day to build stamina, washed their coats making sure there were no yellow circles and ensured they had clean water.
Recently they have found a quality feed that works for them too — Sunglow — which provides a balance of carbohydrates, amino acids, innovative ingredients, active nutrient supply, and show micronutrients.
All this prepared before under the bright lights of the fair, the swine were led by their handlers around the ring with pig sticks to encourage their utmost cooperation.
The prize was taken back home to Harmony Acres in Kennedyville, where Novalee and Randy and the Troyer family could get a little rest.
Troyer, a graduate of Queen Anne's County High School, enjoys learning, competing and making friends in 4-H. She has one more year at the fair and will be attending Chesapeake College in the fall pursuing an early childhood teaching degree.
"This was a very cool experience," she remarked.
So what rewards do the grand champion hogs get?
"Just some street-cred around here," Stacie joked. "No...correction on that...some fair-cred."

title: Free walking tours capture downtown Easton’s rich history
author: BROOKE ENSMINGER
content:
Free walking tours capture downtown Easton’s rich history

 August 9, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: BROOKE ENSMINGER | Section: Local News 
 
 424
 Words 

 Read News Document

 The Talbot Historical Society strives to keep the 360-year history of Easton alive with free historic walking tours held on the third Saturday of each month. Two tours are offered, one at 11 a.m. and another at noon, each providing a unique perspective on the town's history.The 11 a.m. tour takes participants on a walk through central Easton, highlighting important buildings and sharing stories about the town's rich history. The noon tour focuses on the architecture of the six buildings that make up the historical society's campus.
The historical society began offering these tours around 10 years ago. Archivist Patti Rockwell joined the society around that time and is now one of several tour guides.
"The people that live here are just blown away by the history," Rockwell said. "They said 'I had no idea.'"
The tours attract both tourists and locals, who often bring their visiting guests. They are free and open to the public, but registration is required.
The tours start at 25 South Washington St., in front of the historical society, and continue through downtown Easton, looping back to the starting point. The main tour features about 15 stops.
"I think what's really important is finding out how we've evolved to where we are today," Rockwell said.
The tours focus on the impact of the Revolutionary War and the Civil War on the town, as well as fires that brought destruction to several areas. One surprising fact, Rockwell said, is that the town of Easton took an early stand against British control — something many visitors are unaware of.
"You always hear about Boston, but this community took a stand at one time prior to the war starting too," Rockwell said.
Each tour is unique since tour guides create their own scripts. Rockwell said her favorite story to tell involves a hidden armory that stored weapons during the Revolutionary War. That site is now a parking lot partially used by the Easton Farmers Market.
Along with their information cards, tour guides carry a collection of photographs showing what Easton's buildings looked like a century ago. Some include drawings of Easton from before photography existed.
Rockwell said she hopes participants leave with greater awareness of the town's past.
"This town has done a remarkable job of preserving the past, keeping the same buildings here, if we can, without tearing them down so that people can see what it was like at least 100 years ago," Rockwell said.
"These buildings are still downtown, waiting for people to find out a little clue as to what was going on."
More information can be found at talbothistory.org.

title: Reporting from the splash zone
author: AHMAD GARNETT agarnett@chespub.com
content:
Reporting from the splash zone

 August 11, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: AHMAD GARNETT agarnett@chespub.com | Section: Headlines 
 
 143
 Words 

 Read News Document

 Watermen's Appreciation Day boat docking competition was a huge success on Sunday, but somebody forgot to mention something to me.My editors didn't tell me I would be in the splash zone while taking pictures of the contest.
The great water of the Miles River splashed on me and other photographers as we watched some of the fastest moving boats dock at the Chesapeake Bay Maritime Museum in record time.
It was pretty warm outside, so I didn't mind the water. I'll just make sure to tell my editors to send me with a company-branded towel next year.
The event was fantastic. There's nothing like the smell of Old Bay seasoning on a crab. You can read all about it in my story below.
If you missed out on Watermen's Appreciation Day, you should come next year. Just look for me in the splash zone.
— Ahmad Garnett

title: Country Cooking: Treats from carnivals and fairs
author: MARIE SAVAGE Country Cooking
content:
Country Cooking: Treats from carnivals and fairs

 August 12, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: MARIE SAVAGE Country Cooking | Section: News 
 
 1278
 Words 

 Read News Document

 Carnivals and fairs — what a welcome treat each year for folks of all ages.Growing up on the farm, we always looked forward to traveling to those adventures. Even though we lived just a few miles from the boardwalks in Ocean City and Rehoboth Beach, we always attended the carnivals and the Delaware State Fair in Harrington.
The local carnivals had the usual rides — smaller Ferris wheels, small train rides on short tracks, tilt-a-wheels and swings. The state fair would have much more active rides on a larger scale.
Of course, the boardwalks had the famous bumper cars, a giant Ferris wheel, small boat rides, a merry-go-round and that laughing lady — I was always scared of her.
Let's check out the food at the local carnivals. Most of the carnival foods are cooked on the grounds by the local volunteer firefighters and their families, along with other local volunteers.
Some of the best oyster fritter sandwiches and fried soft crab sandwiches on the Shore can be found here — did I mention clam strips and fries. Some other fair and carnival foods and treats include: corn dogs, deep fried onions, fried pickles, funnel cakes, caramel apples, cotton candy, popcorn balls, hot dogs, hamburgers, fried alligator and snow cones, and the list goes on.
Enjoy all these foods, and try some of them at home.
DEEP FRIED OREO COOKIES
2 quarts vegetable oil for frying, 1 cup milk, 1 large egg, 2 tsps vegetable oil, 1 cup pancake mix, 1 18-oz package cream-filled chocolate sandwich cookies.
Gather all ingredients. Heat oil in a deep fryer or large saucepan to 375 degrees. Whisk milk, egg and 2 tsps of vegetable oil in a large bowl until smooth. Stir in the pancake mix until no dry lumps remain. Dip cookies into batter, one at a time, and carefully place into hot oil. Fry in batches, 4 or 5 at a time, until cookies are golden brown, about 2 minutes. Drain on a paper towel-lined plate before serving.
STATE FAIR CORNDOG
1 cup yellow cornmeal, 1 cup all-purpose flour, ¼ cup white sugar, 4 tsps baking powder, ¼ tsp salt, ⅛ tsp black pepper, 1 cup milk, 1 large egg, 1 quart vegetable oil for frying, 2 16-oz packages beef hot dogs, wooden skewers.
Combine cornmeal, flour, sugar, baking powder, salt, and pepper in a medium bowl; stir in milk and egg to make a batter. Heat oil in a deep fryer or large saucepan to 375 degrees. Meanwhile, pat hot dogs dry and insert a skewer into each one. Roll hot dogs in batter until well coated. Fry 2 or 3 corn dogs at a time in preheated oil until lightly browned, about 3 minutes. Drain on paper towels.
FUNNEL CAKES
3 ⅔ cups all-purpose flour (divided), 2 tsps baking powder, ½ tsp salt, 2 cups milk, 3 large eggs, ¼ cup white sugar, 1 quart vegetable oil for frying, 2 tbsps confectioners' sugar.
Mix together half of the flour, baking powder and salt in a medium bowl. Set aside. Beat together milk, eggs, and sugar in a large bowl. Add flour mixture and beat until smooth. Add remaining flour, using only enough to achieve a runny batter thin enough to flow through a funnel. Heat 1 inch oil in an 8-inch skillet to 375 degrees. Put your finger over the bottom opening of a funnel and fill with a generous 1/2 cup batter. Release batter close to the surface of hot oil while making a circular motion and fry until the bottom is golden brown, 1 to 2 minutes. Use tongs and a wide spatula to carefully turn cake over and fry until the other side is golden brown, about 1 minute more. Drain cake on a paper towel-lined plate and sprinkle with confectioners' sugar. Repeat with remaining batter.
TURKEY LEGS
1 2-liter bottle lemon-lime flavored carbonated beverage, 2 tbsps sugar, 2 tbsps hot sauce, 1 tbsp crushed red pepper flakes, 1 tbsp black pepper, 1 large sweet onion (sliced), 4 turkey legs, 2 tbsps honey, 1 tbsp steak seasoning.
Preheat an outdoor grill for high heat, and lightly oil grate. In a large pot, mix the lemon-lime flavored carbonated beverage, sugar, hot sauce, red pepper, pepper and onion. Place the turkey legs in the mixture and bring to a boil. Cook 30 to 45 minutes until the turkey has reached an internal temperature of 180 degrees. Remove onion slices from the mixture, and arrange on the prepared grill. Place turkey legs over the onions. Drizzle with honey and season with steak seasoning. Cook, tuning once, 20 minutes, or until a crisp browned crust has formed on the turkey legs.
DEEP FRIED PICKLES
2 eggs, 1 cup buttermilk, 1 tbsp Worcestershire sauce, ½ tsp vinegar-based hot pepper sauce, ¾ tsp cayenne pepper, ¼ tsp seasoning salt, ¼ tsp garlic powder, 1 cup cornmeal, 2 ¼ cups all-purpose flour, 1 tsp salt, ¾ tsp ground black pepper, 1 32-oz jar dill pickle slices, 1 cup vegetable oil for deep frying, salt and pepper to taste.
In a large bowl, combine eggs, 1/4 cup of the flour, buttermilk, Worcestershire sauce, hot sauce, cayenne pepper, seasoning salt and garlic powder. In a separate mixing bowl, combine cornmeal, 2 cups flour, salt and 3/4 tsp black pepper. Preheat oil in a deep fryer or pot to 365 degrees. Dip drained pickles into milk mixture and then dredge them in the flour mixture. Deep fry until golden brown. Drain on paper towels. Salt and pepper to taste
STATE FAIR SWEET TEA
2 cups water, 6 black tea bags, 1/8 tsp baking soda, 2/3 cup sugar, 6 cups cold water.
In a small saucepan, bring water to a boil. Remove from the heat; add tea bags. Cover and steep for 10 minutes. Discard tea bags. Sprinkle baking soda into a 2-quart pitcher. Transfer tea to pitcher; stir in sugar. Add cold water. Refrigerate until chilled.
CARNIVAL CHURROS
6 tbsps unsalted butter, 2 tbsps plus 1 cup granulated sugar (divided), 1 tsp pure vanilla extract, 1 cup all-purpose flour, 1 tsp kosher salt, 1/4 cup ground cinnamon, 2 large eggs, vegetable oil for frying.
In a large saucepan over medium heat, bring butter, 2 tbsps sugar and 1 cup water to a boil, then stir in vanilla. Remove from heat and add flour and salt. Stir with a wooden spoon until thickened, about 30 seconds. Let cool 10 minutes. Meanwhile, on a rimmed baking sheet or large plate, mix cinnamon and remaining 1 cup sugar. Using a handheld mixer on medium speed, add eggs one at a time, beating to blend after each addition. Transfer mixture to a piping bag fitted with a large open star tip. Into a large pot fitted with a deep-fry thermometer, pour oil to come halfway up sides. Heat over medium-high heat until the thermometer registers 375 degrees. Holding a piping bag a few inches above oil, carefully pipe churros into 6-inch ropes. Using kitchen scissors, cut off dough from the piping bag. Working in batches, fry churros, turning as needed, until golden brown, 4 to 5 minutes; make sure oil registers 375 degrees between batches. Using a slotted spoon or tongs, immediately roll churros in cinnamon sugar, then transfer to a wire rack.
CARAMEL POPCORN
6 quarts popped popcorn, 2 cups packed brown sugar, 1 cup butter (cubed), 1/2 cup corn syrup, 1 tsp salt, 3 tsps vanilla extract, 1/2 tsp baking soda.
Place popcorn in a large bowl and set aside. In a large saucepan, combine the brown sugar, butter, corn syrup and salt; bring to a boil over medium heat, stirring constantly. Boil for 5 minutes, stirring occasionally. Remove from the heat. Stir in vanilla and baking soda; mix well. Pour over popcorn and stir until well coated. Pour into 2 greased 13-by-9-inch baking pans.

title: Rock Hall Bull Roast returns for 70th season
author: BOB FORD Special contribution to the Star Democrat
content:
Rock Hall Bull Roast returns for 70th season

 August 12, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: BOB FORD Special contribution to the Star Democrat | Section: News 
 
 625
 Words 

 Read News Document

 ROCK HALL — When St. John Catholic Church parish members in Rock Hall first planned a fundraising bull roast to help build a new church for the congregation, they probably couldn't imagine the event would one day be celebrating its 70th renewal.That is the case, however, and the 2025 edition of the event that began in 1954 — missing only two years during the COVID pandemic — will return for the 70th time on Sunday, Aug. 17 from 1 to 5 p.m. at the Rock Hall Volunteer Fire Company.
"This event is kind of the mountaintop for the community every year," said Deacon John L. Davis, who has been with the Sacred Heart/St. John parish for more than 20 years. "It's humbling to see how many people give their time and their talent to always make it a success. There have been times when you are tempted to say, 'Well, this year might not work,' but it always does and it's always great."
The first bull roast and several thereafter were held on the Eastern Neck farm property of Dr. Norbert Nitsch, and was organized by Nitsch, his wife, Ethel Nitsch, and neighbors Ernest "Tot" Willson and his wife, Mary Willson. The groundbreaking for the new church took place soon after and the brick church still in use today was dedicated in November, 1955.
The Bull Roast moved in 1960 to the open lawn between the new church and the original 1890 parish church, before moving one more time to the Rock Hall Volunteer Fire Company building in 2022.
One thing that hasn't changed is the quality of the food served, which starts at 6:30 a.m. behind the firehouse with a roast beef-grilling crew overseen by Ernest "Tot" Strong, the grandson of one of the founders. His wife, Millie Strong, is co-chair of the 2025 Bull Roast, along with Beth Dunn.
"It runs very smoothly. We start having meetings in April and there are probably about 25 people on the committee," Millie Strong said "Last year we served 337 dinners and there were also 85 takeout dinners. This is the most important fundraiser of the year for Sacred Heart and St. John. We're able to maintain the buildings and make improvements. We recently had all the stained glass removed to clean and repair. But the Bull Roast is also a part of our history. When you think of St. John and Rock Hall, you think of the Bull Roast. It's synonymous."
The traditional menu, aside from the sliced beef, includes grilled hot dogs and sausage with peppers and onions, french fries, potato salad, sliced tomatoes, baked beans, corn on the cob, and an extensive dessert table. The food is locally sourced from Redman's Farm and Bayside Market. Included with admission are beer and soft drinks. There is also a silent auction, music, and games.
"We're thrilled to be able to help out a community partner like this," said Andy Glenn, president of the fire company. "I grew up down the street from the church. To me, the Bull Roast is a town institution. We do a little setup to make sure they have what they need, but they do all the work and we're more than happy that we have the space for them."
The indoor event is rain or shine, and tickets can be purchased in advance for $25 for adults, $12 for youngsters 7-12 years old, by visiting sacredparish.org. On the day of the Roast, admission is $30 for adults and remains $12 for the youngsters.
What started out as merely a way to build a new church has become over the years the means to build old traditions and continuing community alliances. That's worth celebrating, and on Sunday, Aug. 17, St. John will do just that for the 70th time.

title: Autumn Block Party in Ridgely approved for second year
author: AHMAD GARNETT agarnett@chespub.com
content:
Autumn Block Party in Ridgely approved for second year

 August 14, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: AHMAD GARNETT agarnett@chespub.com | Section: News 
 
 444
 Words 

 Read News Document

 RIDGELY — The Autumn Block Party in Ridgely is back for another year, and committee members expect it to be better than last year.At their July meeting, the Ridgley Town Commissioners approved the block party for the second year.
The idea of the block party came from a conversation in a Facebook group last year started by committee member Anthony Duckery.
Committee member Holly Justice, commented on Duckery's post and they began conversations about creating an autumn block party for the youth in Caroline County.
After more conversations multiple members of the community Tina Hurley, Erin Wheeler and Chad Leister joined the committee.
At the end of the block party last year, the committee put out a poll to the community to see what could be better about the event. Extending the time was the biggest item the residents raised.
"People said that they would have liked it to be longer and a couple of other things, so we did decide this year to make it from 12 p.m. to 7 p.m. just to give people that weren't able to make it due to sports or whatever they had going on last year, they can maybe attend this year," Justice said.
Other changes include the amount of vendors and the resources those vendors provide for the community.
"We offer nonprofits the opportunity to set up information tables," Justice said. "We do not charge them a vendor fee because we get how difficult it is with for-profit. We wanted to give them a platform to tell people about their services."
Food and family fun will continue to be free at the event. The committee ensured the block party had many free components because they wanted children and families in the community to have something to enjoy without worrying about a price.
"This is something that we want to do, and we really are about trying to keep this a free event. That was key for us is making it free," Justice said. "... I didn't want for the block party to be something that people had to see if they could do. I wanted them to know they could do it and it not be finances that would keep them from it.
"I don't feel that children should be excluded from the fun things, and life in general, just because unfortunately this economy is crazy and everything is astronomically priced. I wanted to just be able to give them a day where no one had to worry."
The block party will include a DJ, bands, dance performances, free games, face paintings, sports tournaments, craft stations and more.
It will be held on Saturday, Sept. 13, from noon to 7 p.m. at Martin Sutton Park in Ridgely.

title: Remembering Sgt. Mowbray: community marks 50 years since officer’s line-of-duty death
author: ANDREA GRABENSTEIN agrabenstein@chespub.com
content:
Remembering Sgt. Mowbray: community marks 50 years since officer’s line-of-duty death

 August 16, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: ANDREA GRABENSTEIN agrabenstein@chespub.com | Section: Local News 
 
 548
 Words 

 Read News Document

 STEVENSVILLE — The community gathered Aug. 9 to mark the 50th anniversary of Mowbray Park's rededication and honor Maryland State Police Sgt. Wallace J. Mowbray, who was killed in the line of duty in 1975.Mowbray, 39, was shot while performing a routine stop on a suspicious vehicle near a liquor store in Chester shortly before midnight on Aug. 9, 1975. Investigators later found that the van had stolen registration plates and that two of its occupants had outstanding warrants.
Mowbray was flown to a Baltimore hospital, where he died shortly after midnight on Aug. 10. He had served 13 years with the Maryland State Police.
"Everybody that I've had conversations with knew exactly where they were and what they were doing," said Parks and Recreation Director Steve Chandlee, reflecting on the close-knit feel of the county and the impact of Mowbray's death.
County Commissioner Chris Corchiarino said Mowbray was a husband, father and natural-born police officer who, on the night he was killed, was doing what he did best: protecting the community.
"The loss of Mowbray does not erase the good he did, the lives he touched, and the safety he ensured," Corchiarino said. "As we rededicate this memorial, we renew our promise to never forget his sacrifice and character and the enduring impact he left on our community."
Mowbray was also an active member of the community, participating regularly in softball and Little League. Mowbray Park, named in his honor, serves as a safe place for children to play.
Deputy Sgt. Ryan Davidson of the Queen Anne's County Office of the Sheriff said the rededication reaffirmed the community's promise to protect first responders and remember that behind every badge is a human being.
"The park will continue to serve as a place of recreation, reflection on bravery, and a reminder of one who represented the best of the community," Davidson said.
Patrick McLaughlin, now a county commissioner, recalled visiting the park with his children before he knew its namesake. "It just meant so much to me," he said.
Gretchen McKethan, of Kent Island, attended the ceremony on behalf of a grateful community. She graduated in 1975 with Rusty, the youngest Mowbray son. "It was devastating to celebrate our senior year one month and lose your father another," she said. "It's a tearful day and a happy day. Everyone knew and loved Trooper Mowbray."
Nancy Davis recalled that her father, Jack Stowe, worked in the Chester liquor store and heard the gunshots that night. She reflected on how close she could have been to losing her own father if not for Mowbray's courageous actions.
Robin Mowbray, the oldest daughter, said it was inspiring to learn how many lives her father touched. "We had each other," she said, noting the family also received strong support from the Maryland State Police. She authored a book, The Ultimate Sacrifice: The Story of Maryland State Policeman Sgt. Wallace J. Mowbray.
On the park's original opening day in the 1970s, Robin's brother Ryan, then 12, hit the first Little League home run out of the field. "This gives me chills to this day. I bet our dad was smiling up in Heaven that day," she said.
Mowbray Park is located at 629 Romancoke Road in Stevensville. More information about Mowbray's story is available at odmp.org, and details about the park can be found at qac.org.

title: Caroline Summerfest 2025 brings large crowd to Denton
author: AHMAD GARNETT agarnett@chespub.com
content:
Caroline Summerfest 2025 brings large crowd to Denton

 August 18, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: AHMAD GARNETT agarnett@chespub.com | Section: News 
 
 302
 Words 

 Read News Document

 DENTON — Last weekend, Caroline Summerfest drew one its biggest Friday night crowds in recent years."I would say this has been a busier Friday night than the past few years," Caroline County Recreations and Parks Executive Director Jamie Beechey said. "The weather's a little less humid than it has been. I think that people have been really excited about coming out."
Attendees visited more than 150 nonprofit organizations' tents and learned new information while enjoying food for sale, proceeds from which benefited the nonprofits.
"It's our biggest event of the year," said Victor Reynolds, a communication representative for CASA of Caroline. "We're very lucky in particular to have our booth directly in front of our office."
Outside CASA's office on Main Street, Reynolds said how important the event was for exposure for all nonprofits in Caroline County.
"It's a vital day for them as well, including just the overall exposure for people that, maybe the resources that are traveling through or that are in the county, that might not be aware of certain resources available to them," Reynolds said.
For entertainment, attendees rode on a fire truck courtesy of the Denton Volunteer Fire Company, enjoyed cars in the car show, listened to singing from multiple artists and groups, and ate food from multiple different vendors.
The "Back to the 80's" theme gave attendees a chance to pull out their 1980s-style outfits.
"It feels really good because this is what I remember in these areas when I was growing up, big festivals, carnivals and stuff like that, so it kind of like brings everybody together," said Alex Green, owner of Harriet Tubman Tours in Cambridge said the '80s theme.
Organizers said this summer's event was a success. Caroline County Recreations and Park said in a Facebook post Sunday, "Thank you all for the love this weekend we had a blast."

title: Easton approves permit for 54th annual Waterfowl Festival
author: Konner Metz
content:
Easton approves permit for 54th annual Waterfowl Festival

 August 19, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Konner Metz | Section: Local News 
 
 451
 Words 

 Read News Document

 EASTON — In less than three months, thousands will take to the streets of downtown Easton for the 54th annual Waterfowl Festival.On Monday, the Town Council unanimously approved the festival's permit, along with its transportation plan and food vendors list. This year's festival is slated for Nov. 13-16. Last year, over 25,000 attended, a record-breaking mark.
Waterfowl Festival Executive Director Deena Kilmon answered questions about the permit request on Monday.
Kilmon said a key change in this year's transportation plan is the addition of two bus stops, one at the festival building on the corner of South Harrison and South streets, and the other at the Framptom Funeral Home on the corner of North Harrison and Goldsborough streets.
The funeral home is a new venue for a festival art gallery, Kilmon noted.
According to the permit application, festival organizers expect there to be five buses on Friday, Nov. 14; 11 on Saturday, Nov. 15; and six on Sunday, Nov. 16.
Attendees will be encouraged to park at the Easton Elementary, Middle and High schools, along with other locations, including The Country School and Easton VFW Post 5118. Organizers reviewed the transportation plan with a bus charter service, police and economic development leaders.
"We have made every effort to minimize impact on local residents," the plan stated.
The approved food vendors list has 14 locations across town with around 22 total vendors. Kilmon said there are three fewer food trucks than last year.
"As our brick-and-mortar people can take over whatever they need to take over, we are backing down because we do not want to be in the food truck business," Kilmon said. " … We do it for the festival, because it's overwhelming for our local restaurants, especially with all our children."
Town Council President Don Abbatiello asked about an open-container alcohol concern that was noted by the Easton Police Department in its permit review.
"I know it was a concern that people would leave establishments with alcohol and walk around the streets," Abbatiello said. "Even though we don't allow that, it was still occurring. Has there been any reaching out to these different businesses to say, 'you need to do a little bit better tightening of that'?"
Kilmon said organizers, including newly appointed Festival Commission members, have been reaching out to businesses.
"We have expressed our concerns, too," Kilmon said. "We want our people, if you're buying our alcohol, to stay on our own property."
She said the Framptom Funeral Home parking lot will host the festival's tasting pavilion. There will be a fence and festival volunteers in the lot, who she hopes will prevent people from leaving the site with open alcohol containers.
"I think we're going to have better luck keeping our people where they're supposed to be," Kilmon said.

title: Federalsburg Activities Center hopes to bring joy to the whole community
author: AHMAD GARNETT agarnett@chespub.com
content:
Federalsburg Activities Center hopes to bring joy to the whole community

 August 26, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: AHMAD GARNETT agarnett@chespub.com | Section: News 
 
 631
 Words 

 Read News Document

 FEDERALSBURG — An idea for a space where children could have fun in Federalsburg turned into a place where everyone could have fun.The Federalsburg Activities Center began with a conversation between the Rev. Pam Bockart and the Rev. Stanford Ricks at a meeting in 2019.
Bockart was the Pastor at Christ Church, and she recalled "kids outside just walking the streets having nowhere to go."
She decided to call a meeting about finding something for the children to do. After the meeting, Bockart and Ricks selected a location for a community center project at the old Dollar General building on Morris Avenue in Federalsburg.
Ricks is the vice president of Men for Change, an organization the specializes in "changing our community through service" by mentoring youth in Federalsburg. The group wanted a central location.
A partnership was formed. For the next five years, Bockart, Ricks and a board of stakeholders overcame financial and logistical obstacles to open the Federalsburg Activities Center.
"We started on a journey. We had nothing, no money, just a vision to open up this building," Ricks said, looking around the center, which opened in the former Dollar General building earlier this year.
The group gained ownership of the building with help from its former owner and a loan. But even after the building's ownership was squared away, multiple renovations needed to be done to make the space functional.
After multiple grants, donations from local businesses and an anonymous $400,000 private donation, the Activities Center was renovated and ready for the community.
"Over the five years, we never got frustrated," Ricks said. "That was the great thing to me. The the board that we had, we met every week, we came here, we enjoyed each other, we talked positive and never got frustrated. I think we kind of knew it was going to be a long journey.
"... So now we went from phase one, which was to get the building open. Now were going into phase two of the project, getting the programs up and running in the building."
The current programs at the Activities Center are Men For Change on Friday, bible study on Saturday, senior lunches on Friday, garden club once a month and Make Federalsburg Beautiful meetings once a month. Men For Change sees 30 to 50 kids on Fridays, and the senior lunches see 20 to 40 seniors.
Part of the next phase for the center will be partnering youth with older community members. Board members said older community members tend to feel left out, with a lack of activities catered toward them. The board hopes this partnership will increase seniors' drive and provide mentorship opportunities for local youth.
"We would like to bring the young ones, who are starting their vision, and the old ones, who have their vision, and we want them to kind of get together so that the seniors can tell the younger ones about their story and how to get there themselves that they may have a good life," Ricks said.
Another part of the next phase is adding new programs within the activities center. The board has plans to add a science, technology, engineering and mathematics program; arts and crafts; a coffee club; and a running club. Board members said negotiations for Boys and Girls Club and 4-H partnerships are ongoing.
The board is most excited about the potential of what the activities center can do for the town of Federalsburg.
"There is something in all of us when we give to others," said Wendy Garner, secretary for the board. "We get back as much if not more, and that's what I think all these skills, all these learning curves, whether it's for the kids, the adults, or the seniors — this is a community center."
The board encourages all community members who want volunteer or who have ideas to email fac2024@aol.com.

title: Lost sign finds its way back to Dorchester's Old Trinity Church
author: Lily Tierney
content:
Lost sign finds its way back to Dorchester's Old Trinity Church

 August 29, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Lily Tierney | Section: Dorchester 
 
 503
 Words 

 Read News Document

 CHURCH CREEK — Members of the small congregation of Old Trinity Church, Maryland's oldest active church, were surprised to see one of Old Trinity's former signs being sold at auction this month.After the sign sold to the highest bidder, the congregation thought it was gone for good.
But the following Sunday, The Rev. Dan Dunlap walked into the vesting room of John's Chapel, the other church he serves, where he was greeted by the sign. A close friend of Dunlap's heard about the auction, tracked the sign down, and bought it for Dunlap.
"I said, 'I'm just overwhelmed, I'm humbled.' I mean, it was such a gift," Dunlap said.
Gage Thomas, a collector of Dorchester County artifacts who sold the sign to Dunlap's friend at the Aug. 23 Foxwell Auction, said he was happy the sign had been returned to Old Trinity. "It's a historical location in Dorchester County. I'm happy that the sign has made its way back to there," Thomas said.
Old Trinity Church predates its relationship with the Anglican Church and the creation of the Episcopal Diocese. It was built through private funds roughly a decade before the establishment of the Episcopal Church, Dunlap said.
The church has undergone multiple iterations and bore several names, initially being called The Church of Dorchester Parish. In 1853, it was renamed Trinity. Community members referred to it as "the old church," and over time, the name "Old Trinity" stuck.
The small, red-brick church building was built around 1670 and was restored to its original colonial style in the 1950s. The restoration was made possible by legacy funds bequeathed to the church, which are now held in accounts to accrue interest.
"I've served at a number of churches, but I've never really been part of a church quite like this that felt that its roots were in this community," Dunlap said.
The sign was not the church's original sign. It came along sometime in the centuries after, though Dunlap did not know exactly when.
Dunlap said it was a strange feeling when he saw how much the sign was sold for. He figured the old piece of painted wood that was likely thrown in the trash would sell for maybe $100.
Thomas said he bought the sign about 15 years ago for $200. This time around, the sign was sold for $400.
"My first thought was, 'I didn't realize we were that important,'" Dunlap said.
After that initial thought passed, a weird feeling sank in. "But not all bad. I mean, I wasn't troubled by it, I was just confused by it," Dunlap said. "And then just to see it the next Sunday, waiting for me at the vesting area of the other church, I was just I, I shed a tear. I just couldn't believe it."
For Dunlap, the sign being sold at auction has highlighted the church's importance to the community.
"The church is here for people to come and to enjoy it, to add their story to our story. That's why you can't say who owns Old Trinity," Dunlap said. "It's the community's church."

title: Talbot County celebrates its most famous native son
author: BILL PEAK Talbot County Free Library
content:
Talbot County celebrates its most famous native son

 September 5, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: BILL PEAK Talbot County Free Library | Section: Life 
 
 857
 Words 

 Read News Document

 Over the years, Edinburgh University's Professor Celeste-Marie Bernier has taught me a great deal about Frederick Douglass, though her most important contribution to the study of the man may be, curiously, the research she has done not on Douglass but on Douglass' wife and children.Bernier's work has revealed just how important his family's support was to the Great Orator's success.
All of which has gotten me thinking about the other people that must have made the road Douglass trod a tad easier. Probably the most important of these would also be the least known: the people that helped him escape slavery.
We know that his wife Anna put the money together and sewed the clothing that would make her husband's flight possible, but we also know there would have been others, perhaps many others, involved as well: conductors on the Underground Railroad, people who took him in for the night along the way, and who knows, perhaps a boat owner or two, or even someone with a wagonload of hay.
We know that these people — however nameless now — existed because they are in Douglass' autobiography, though he alluded to them obscurely. Douglass always carefully avoided providing their names or any particulars that might aid those intent upon derailing their clandestine work. "The peculiar institution" was thriving when Douglass first penned his autobiography, and the last thing he wanted to do was reveal routes, methods and personnel still being used to funnel enslaved African Americans to freedom.
But there would have been others too, perhaps not as dramatic in their assistance, but important to Douglass's eventual success nonetheless.
Some of these are well known: Polly and Nathan Johnson, who sheltered Douglass and Anna in their home when the couple first arrived in New Bedford; William Lloyd Garrison, who brought Douglass to the attention of the abolitionist movement; and Abraham Lincoln, who befriended Douglass and wrote the pass that would allow him to travel unimpeded during the Civil War.
But what about the other people who must have made contributions, perhaps only small contributions, to Douglass's journey from property to prophet? We all depend upon people like this, the childhood friend who stuck up for us when we were bullied, the person who helped us with some difficult task, the passing stranger who gave us a smile when we were feeling down. Life is often obstructed, but then something gives, and, for a moment, there is an intoxicating sense of forward motion. How many now anonymous souls helped remove an obstacle from Douglass' path? Helped send him sailing toward us?
Perhaps more important still, how many would-be, could-be, Douglasses do we unknowingly lend a hand to today?
On Saturday, Sept. 27, the people of Talbot County will come together once again to honor the legacy of Frederick Douglass, their most famous native son. The parade this year will feature, among others, the Easton High School Junior ROTC Color Guard, the Easton Middle School and White Marsh Elementary School marching bands, Randy Welch on bagpipes, the Hispanic Dance Group, and, for the first time, engines from both the Easton and Oxford Volunteer Fire Companies.
At the Welcome Ceremony on the courthouse lawn, 15-year-old Javion Jones, a minister at Union Baptist Church, will give the opening invocation, county and city officials will offer their thoughts, Washington College fellow Darius Johnson will read a portion of a famous Douglass speech, the MidShore Community Band will play two pieces and Dana Bowser will sing a capella.
Afterward, at the Children's Village set up in front of the library, there will be story time with St. Michaels library branch manager Shauna Beulah, face-painting, the ever-popular portrait booth with Frederick Douglass, Frederick Douglass coloring books with sticker insert, a prize wheel with toy giveaways, and the opportunity for youngsters to sign up for the Frederick Douglass Reading Challenge (featuring six $50 Target gift certificates as prizes).
Within the library itself, the National Park Service will have an exhibit of Frederick Douglass artifacts on display, and, at 1 p.m., Nicholas Buccola — the Dr. Jules L. Whitehill Professor of Humanism and Ethics at Claremont-McKenna College — will lecture on his book, "The Essential Frederick Douglass," copies of which will be available for purchase and signing.
From noon to 3 p.m., the festival's entertainment stage will feature performances by the Bay Country Chorus, Sofia Fernandez, the New St. Johns Male Chorus, the St. Michaels Middle School Choir, Friends in Faith, Ruby Fisher, the Allegro Academy, Ayla Dennis and the Asbury United Methodist Church choir, as well as line dancing and block party music provided by Allan Butler.
Oh, and of course, once again, there will be food vendors on hand with delicious food to satisfy the most demanding hunger.
All in all, it's shaping up to be a fun day for people of all ages and interests. Moreover, it's a day where your attendance, your enthusiasm, could end up encouraging some youngster (think the BAAM kids who will be in attendance, or the recipient of one of the Frederick Douglass Honor Society's scholarships) to set his or her eyes on the prize.
Like so many before you, you could be clearing the path for America's next great freedom fighter.
