title: Charles humane society celebrates 50 years
author: Ilana Williams iwilliams@somdnews.com
content:
Charles humane society celebrates 50 years

 September 9, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Ilana Williams iwilliams@somdnews.com | Section: News 
 
 547
 Words 

 Read News Document

 While many things have changed over the last half century, once constant has been the care provided to animals by the Humane Society of Charles County.The nonprofit organization is hosting its Golden Paws Gala on Oct. 10 to celebrate 50 years of taking care of sick, injured and homeless animals.
The event is from 6 p.m. to 10 p.m. at the Waldorf Jaycees at 3090 Crain Highway. Tickets are $75 per person.
Local humane societies are not directly attached to the National Humane Society, making the Humane Society of Charles County 100% reliant on local donations, grants and fundraising, Rayanne Benya, president of the board of directors for the Humane Society of Charles County, said.
In 1975, the humane society did not have a building. Instead, people who found an injured animal had to take them home, Anne Gardiner, founder of the Humane Society of Charles County, said. In 1981, the St. Charles County Association of Realtors gave the humane society the land for a shelter and it opened in 1983.
"It was tough getting started," Gardiner said. "One time I had [animals] in all three bathrooms and we were wondering what we were going to do."
The humane society has three sections: the kennel, which houses animals ranging from dogs and cats to guinea pigs, rabbits, lizards, turtles and snakes; the humane education program, which teaches students about animals and environmental science; and the clinic.
"Fifty years later, we're still here," Benya said. "We're here because we're supported by the residents of the county … and I think that's something to celebrate."
The gala will have a silent auction with dog baskets, Gardiner said. Other baskets will have household items. Wine and alcohol will be raffled, and there will also be gift cards for restaurants and businesses.
Live music will be performed by the "Original" Moonlighters and there will be a lipsologist — a person who "reads" lip prints — and a cash bar. Food is being donated by the Waldorf Jaycees.
"It's just for a great cause," Benya said. "We adopt out anywhere from one to 2,000 animals a year and all those animals need medical care."
Under the shelter's care, the humane society often has about 150 animals, an amount that can go up to 250 animals during the summer, Benya said.
Throughout the year, the shelter has around 200 volunteers who help with adoption events, laundry and being around the animals. They also want to build an animal medical facility for emergencies and a larger surgery wing.
"When [people] come here and they volunteer, they see the connection … between humans and animals," Benya said.
The humane society is holding its annual photo contest until Sept. 27, Benya said. People can send a cute photo of their pet that can be featured in a calendar.
On Sept. 20, they will have an adoption event at the humane society, Benya said.
The nonprofit also has a program called Freedom Friends year round that offers discounts to veterans to adopt animals for animals that have been in the shelter for six months or longer.
"It's important that we receive the funding … so we can continue to be here for the county," Benya said. "If we disappear, that's going to be devastating for the animal population.
For more information about the Oct. 10 gala or to purchase tickets, go to humanesocietycc.org.

title: Taking stories on the road: Brackish Books mobile bookstore opens in QA
author: ANDREA GRABENSTEIN agrabenstein@chespub.com
content:
Taking stories on the road: Brackish Books mobile bookstore opens in QA

 September 9, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: ANDREA GRABENSTEIN agrabenstein@chespub.com | Section: News 
 
 463
 Words 

 Read News Document

 CHESTER — Understanding books can transport us to new worlds, a local business owner is taking that one step further by bringing that experience to the community with the opening of a new mobile bookstore, Brackish Books.Sharing a love of books with the community, former teacher and now Indie business owner Liz Gilbert along with her partner Ken Nyczaj, of Kent Island have converted a horse trailer into a whimsical mobile bookstore filled with a curated collection of new and used books for the community.
Proclaiming "Books, not bots,' Gilbert said, "In a world of algorithms and AI, we want to do things the old fashioned way."
With a new and used book selection spanning from history and biographies to the latest fiction, as well as selections of children's books, readers off all types are encouraged to discover hidden gems to "Treat your shelf for your TBR (to be read) pile.
All of us can be guilty of at least a little too much screen time, Nyczaj said, and the duo seek to foster closer camaraderie and reconnect the community with the joy of a good book.
"Reading to me is like education, meditation and relaxation all at once. We are the best versions of ourselves when reading becomes part of a daily routine," Nyczaj said.
Many of the curated books come from Gilbert's own collection as an avid reader seeking to share her passion with others and inspire a love of reading.
"We believe that humans will always learn more from books, not bots. We are a community focused on knowledge and growth from all genres of literature," she said.
Inviting everyone to pick up their next read, Brackish Books is interested in providing suggestions as well as listening to what the community is reading and catering to local tastes, according to Gilbert.
"We love to talk about books, recommend books and shout out our amazing local authors," Gilbert said, "Let's talk about books, and see if my TBR list matches yours."
Gilbert is immensely proud of her local authors section, highlighting the local talent of the area.
The trailers pop up locations are based on strong connections Gilbert and Nyczaj have made through their time living on Kent Island and the Eastern Shore.
"We improve our lives in more ways than one through reading," she said.
The ultimate goal is to open a Brackish brick and mortar bookstore, but for now the bookworm duo are happy to meet the community where they are.
Because, as the official Brackish Books' t-shirt merchandise proclaims, "Life is short, buy the books."
Beginning this month, Brackish Books is now a regular vendor at the weekly outdoor Kent Island Farmers Market from 3:30 p.m. to 6 p.m. outside Cult Classic Brewery.
More information including upcoming times and pop up locations can be found on the Brackish Books social media pages.

title: Treasures resurface at Foxwell Auction
author: Lily Tierney
content:
Treasures resurface at Foxwell Auction

 September 9, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Lily Tierney | Section: Headlines 
 
 229
 Words 

 Read News Document

 It appears that the Foxwell Auction on Aug. 13 had more valuables than the eye could see. A few weeks ago, I was alerted that a decommissioned Old Trinity Church sign was sold at this auction and returned the rector the following Sunday.Another story came out of this auction. Bernie Dryden perused every item of the large auction until he found an old Bible he described as "tattered" and had fountain ink stains from water damage over the years.
The Bible sat on the final table of the auction hall and he decided to purchase it for $12.50 to give to his grandson, who is studying theology. Upon getting home, he began flipping through the pages of the old text and realized it was a family bible.
Dryden read through the names listed in the birth, marriage and death records held within the religious text and found a familiar name. His grandson decided returning the Bible to the original family was the Christian thing to do.
Once again, a religious relic has gone home. Read this story and more from the day in today's edition. As always, thanks for reading.
Do you love puzzles? The Star Democrat is considering adding a daily puzzles page to stardem.com. We are looking for readers to test it and give us their opinion on the puzzles. Interested? Contact Executive Editor Jim Johnson at jjohnson@chespub.com.

title: Fun for good cause: 5K Color Run benefits Kent Goes Purple for 7th year
author: WILL BONTRAGER wbontrager@chespub.com
content:
Fun for good cause: 5K Color Run benefits Kent Goes Purple for 7th year

 September 10, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: WILL BONTRAGER wbontrager@chespub.com | Section: News 
 
 347
 Words 

 Read News Document

 CHESTERTOWN — Painted sneakers and damp, smiling faces could be spotted on Sunday morning down South Cross Street. The rain did nothing to stop walkers and runners of all ages from participating in the 2025 5K Color Fun Run/Walk, benefiting Kent Goes Purple.Kent Goes Purple is a substance abuse awareness and prevention initiative of the Kent County Sheriff's Office and Chestertown Rotary Club, engaging the community and youth to stand up against substance abuse.
Now into its seventh year, the race began bright and early at Wilmer Park, extended down South Cross Street, turned at John Brown Road then returned to the park for a finish.
It kicked off with purple foam bubbles shooting courtesy of Willy Woo Woo Productions and a burst of blue paint at the finish line coating everybody. People scattered playfully away, ducking under the police tape heading for the road.
Along the route, participants, if they asked for it, were doused in more paint by over-eager students. Roadside, the Chestertown Elks Club provided water and encouragement. Police did a great job ensuring participants were safe from traffic as mothers walked their children in strollers, friends ran beside each other, and dads jogged with their daughters.
After the race, the Purple Jamboree was held at the park. Kids danced and played in the foam machine of Willy Woo Woo, who provided some sports games, popcorn, cotton candy and snow cones.
Paul Gunther's Catering offered cheeseburgers and grilled chicken sandwiches.
Along the walkway towards the water, Shore Community Outreach Team were on-hand to administer health advice and blood pressure checks, the Elks informed people of their kids Drug Awareness Program handing out frisbees, coloring books and other items, (DAR), and Recovery in Motion and the The AF Whitsitt Center gave assistance and information about their programs.
Andy Meehan Chestertown Rotary club member said, "We had a very enthusiastic turnout. Over 130 people signed up and with volunteers and vendors that's another 30. People had a great time."
They all enjoyed themselves but are hoping for a sunny day next year come race time.
For information about Kent Goes Purple check out www.kentgoespurple.org.

title: Family Bible finds its way home to Dorchester County family
author: Lily Tierney
content:
Family Bible finds its way home to Dorchester County family

 September 10, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Lily Tierney | Section: Dorchester 
 
 564
 Words 

 Read News Document

 NECK DISTRICT — Bernie Dryden perused an auction in late August, viewing every item. An old tattered Bible that sat on the very last table caught his eye. Dryden purchased it for $12.50 as the very last item sold at the auction.He figured he would give the Bible to his grandson, who is currently studying theology, but upon thumbing through the pages, he found extensive records from a singular family dating back to the Civil War Era. While analyzing the text, he realized one of the final names listed in the birth records was his friend, Alan Wright.
"This is a family Bible, and I recognized the surname as being prominent down in the Neck District, where I live. So I kept looking, and there was an entry there documenting a birth, and I knew the guy," Dryden said.
Dryden's grandson didn't accept the gift, saying it was more Christian to return it to the original family.
Wright was unaware the family Bible even existed before its return.
"When I got to look at it after Bernie gave it to me, my sister's name was in there, my brother's name was in there, and my father's," Wright said. This is the fourth family Bible in the Wright lineage.
Wright said his sister Ellen Paul is the family's historian, having compiled a detailed family tree and collected all the obituaries she can find.
Paul has spent the past 10 years compiling family records and has found the Historical Society and the Maryland room at the library particularly helpful. She has been able to trace the lineage of her family back to the early 1800s.
For Paul, the Bible was the missing piece of multiple family documents, helping verify important family dates and lineage. It even contained a marriage certificate from six generations back, providing a marriage date previously unknown.
A majority of the surnames in the Bible are Marshall until Paul and Wright's great grandmother, Lydia Marshall, married a Wright. "It's a Marshall Bible. Most of it is Marshalls, but it does have him (their father) and us three kids in there," Paul said.
The return of the Bible comes at an interesting time when another religious relic in Dorchester County that was purchased at the same auction was also returned to its original home.
A decades-old decommissioned sign from Old Trinity Church in Church Creek was sold at the same auction for $400. Members of the congregation were upset that someone was profiting off the church's name and expressed these feelings online.
The following Sunday, the sign showed up in the vesting room of St. John's Chapel, where The Rev. Dan Dunlap, rector of Old Trinity, serves as Vicar. A friend of Dunlap's purchased the sign back and gave it to Dunlap as a personal gift. He said it brought a tear to his eye, and he was deeply touched and humbled.
This time, a religious family relic has found its way home in an extremely similar nature — same auction, same seller, and also returned by a friend.
Wright said it felt fantastic to get the Bible, which was auctioned by Gage Thomas, a relative of Wright and Paul's, and to have it returned by a friend.
The religious relics finding their way back home are seen as somewhat of a parable to the Old Trinity Church congregation and to Wright and Paul.
"I mean, it's come full circle, right back to us, you know?" Paul said.

title: Leaders emphasize need for unity during 9/11 Remembrance Ceremony
author: Konner Metz
content:
Leaders emphasize need for unity during 9/11 Remembrance Ceremony

 September 11, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Konner Metz | Section: Local News 
 
 450
 Words 

 Read News Document

 EASTON — On the 24th anniversary of the 9/11 attacks, Talbot County and Easton officials gathered to pay tribute to first responders who put their lives on the line on Sept. 11, 2001, and honor those who continue to serve today.The annual 9/11 Remembrance Ceremony brought first responders and residents to the corner of Dover and West streets for a solemn display of remembrance for those who lost their lives in the attacks.
Speakers at the ceremony emphasized a theme of unity. Talbot County Council Vice President Pete Lesher delivered opening remarks.
"We come together today with unity of purpose," Lesher said. "It is a unity we recall we had in those days and weeks following the tragic events those 24 years ago. When attacked, Americans pulled together. We gathered together in our churches. We gathered with our friends, with our colleagues at work."
Lesher recalled how the nation showed immense gratitude toward police officers, firefighters, medical personnel and others in the days and weeks after 9/11. That display of gratitude has continued, he said.
"Today, as we gather, we continue to salute those first responders in our own community," he said. "Thank you to all of you, our first responders, for your service."
Easton Mayor Megan Cook said the "importance of 9/11 cannot be understated." She encouraged residents to lift each other up as people around the nation did in the days following the terror attacks in New York.
"Every day offers us the chance to support, encourage and serve one another, making our towns, our communities and a country a better place," Cook said. "Our greatness as a nation has always come from unity, our ability to come together as a sum greater than our parts."
Thursday's ceremony included a presentation of a wreath honoring the victims of the 9/11 attacks. During a moment of silence, members of the Easton Volunteer Fire Department participated in the tolling of the bells.
St. Michaels High School senior Thalia Turner sang the national anthem and "This Is My Country." Sean Guschke of the St. Michaels Fire Department performed "Amazing Grace," and Talbot County Sheriff's Office Deputy John Coleman belted "God Bless America."
The Easton Middle School band performed as people filtered in and out of the ceremony.
Talbot County Council Member Dave Stepp reflected on the kindness that spread throughout the nation on Sept. 12, 2001, a day Americans were forced to come to grips with the reality of the tragic events the day prior.
He asked those in the crowd to carry that same kindness and unity as they go about their everyday lives.
"There's a lot of lessons we can take from that day," Stepp said.
"As we move forward, let's not only remember 9/11," he added. "Let's also remember 9/12."

title: '“We are praying we can rebuild': Crash causes extensive damage to historic Jeffers Chapel
author: ANDREA GRABENSTEIN agrabenstein@chespub.com
content:
'“We are praying we can rebuild': Crash causes extensive damage to historic Jeffers Chapel

 September 12, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: ANDREA GRABENSTEIN agrabenstein@chespub.com | Section: Local News 
 
 393
 Words 

 Read News Document

 SUDLERSVILLE — Shortly before 5:30 p.m. Sept. 3, Maryland State Police Centreville Barrack troopers responded to Route 300 at Benton Corner Road for reports of a two-vehicle crash, according to police.A Ford F-350 with an attached trailer was traveling east on Route 300 when a Nissan NV failed to stop at a stop sign on Benton Corner Road and struck the side of the Ford, a preliminary investigation found.
The impact caused the trailer to uncouple from the Ford and come to rest in a grassy area along Route 300. The Ford spun and went rear-first into the building at Jeffers Chapel, police said.
The Nissan overturned onto its driver's side, and the driver was taken by ambulance to Christiana Hospital. No other injuries were reported, according to police.
"A truck took out the whole front side of the building," Jeffers Chapel trustee Lisa Kennedy said, calling the incident "devastating for my whole family."
"We are praying we can rebuild and fix it," Kennedy said.
The one-room historic Black church was built around 1894 by her ancestors, she said. Jeffers Chapel was established in 1894 by local families, and the church and surrounding grounds are still cared for and maintained by descendants of the original founding families, according to Kennedy.
The church was originally affiliated with the United Methodist denomination but closed for regular services due to low membership. In 1995, it was incorporated as a non-denominational house of worship, she said.
The church now opens about once a year or for special occasions, and the fellowship was preparing to celebrate the 103rd homecoming, she said.
Kennedy credited first responders, including the Sudlersville Volunteer Fire Company, for swiftly stabilizing the building to prevent collapse and moving church items — including pews and bibles — into storage.
"It has just been an outpouring of help and we really, really appreciate it," she said.
Homecoming celebrations are still planned, with neighboring churches offering space for services or with outdoor tents, according to Kennedy.
The church is awaiting insurance and structural engineering reports to determine repair costs, she said.
"We are confident that our little chapel can be restored and we welcome prayers and monetary donations to ensure we are able to reopen for our Annual Homecoming in the near future," Kennedy said.
Support can be made via GoFundMe under the title "Support Jeffers Chapel's Restoration After Accident."
For more information about Jeffers Chapel, contact Lisa Kennedy at lisak2595@gmail.com

title: New plaques at Harmony Community Park honor Roger Layton, Sarah Mueller
author: Konner Metz
content:
New plaques at Harmony Community Park honor Roger Layton, Sarah Mueller

 September 23, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Konner Metz | Section: Caroline 
 
 548
 Words 

 Read News Document

 HARMONY — Caroline County honored two respected leaders Saturday by unveiling plaques in their names at the Harmony Community Park.Families and friends of Roger Layton and Sarah Mueller gathered for a joint dedication at the park, which is on Route 16 north of Preston and south of Denton.
A fence for the park's ball field got a new addition: a plaque cementing it as Roger Layton Memorial Field, named after the former Caroline County commissioner and longtime youth softball and baseball coach.
In front of the park's pavilion, a large plaque set on brick dedicated the park to Sarah Mueller, a well-known community volunteer and former Character Counts coach at Preston Elementary School. Character Counts coaches teach trustworthiness, respect and fairness to school-age kids.
Current Caroline County commissioners and other officials attended and spoke to the expansive impacts both Layton and Mueller had on the local community.
Stacy Seward, one many local softball players coached by Layton, recalled fond memories of her former mentor.
"He created lasting memories for so many young athletes," said Seward, the county's grants coordinator. "For example, teaching us how to slide in the playground sand at Denton Elementary School, saying 'If I can get my old body down here, you girls can too.'"
Steward said he was key to creating the county's first ever softball travel team.
"He was the true backbone to girls' softball, not only in Caroline County, but to the entire Eastern Shore," Seward said.
Commission Vice President Larry Porter said Layton, a commissioner of eight years and former investigator for the State's Attorney's Office, always put Caroline County first.
Daughter Jaclyn Crawford said her father's "real gift was his deep commitment to young people."
"In each role, he was known for his competitive spirit, but above all, his determination to make life safer and better for the community," Crawford said.
In addition to Crawford, other family members of Roger Layton who attended Saturday's dedication included: wife Faye Layton, sister Rena Callahan, stepfather Ronald Sard, granddaughter Madison Weston, cousin Rick Davis and more.
After Layton's sign was unveiled, the curtain was removed off of a large plaque dedicated to Mueller. Husband John Mueller then reflected on his wife's knack for helping people.
"If she heard that you needed something, she'd be the one to offer," her husband said. " ... She was always there first."
He recalled not just her volunteer efforts as a character coach for elementary school kids, but also her assistance in collecting dog and cat food for the local Humane Society.
In addition to John Mueller, his four kids and six grandchildren attended Saturday's dedication, as well as Sarah's mom, Jessie Browne.
Around four years ago, the Mueller family donated $20,000 to the county for upkeep and improvements at Harmony Community Park, including to the pavilion, walking trails and playground.
County commissioners thanked the Mueller family for their donation to the park and spoke about Sarah Mueller's lasting legacy.
"Sarah was more than a neighbor," Porter said. "She was a friend, volunteer, mother and a mentor who gave so much of herself to this community, from her time as a Character Counts coach to her years with the Girl Scouts, where she poured her love into children and back.
"By placing her name here at Harmony Park, we make sure her kindness, spirit and her legacy will always be a part of this place."

title: Elliott Road apartments to begin move-in this weekend
author: Konner Metz
content:
Elliott Road apartments to begin move-in this weekend

 September 25, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Konner Metz | Section: Local News 
 
 347
 Words 

 Read News Document

 EASTON — Town officials and project leaders cut the ribbon on a 136-apartment complex on Elliott Road on Wednesday.The Promenade at Easton is made up of four buildings, each with at least 30 apartment units. It will begin to welcome new residents this weekend.
The project, which sits right off of Matthewstown Road, was led by Mallard Construction Group.
Easton Mayor Megan Cook, Ward 2 Councilmember Robert Rankin and other town officials toured the apartments on Wednesday, getting a look at the first of four buildings at the site.
Jim DiDonato, president of Mallard Construction Group, thanked town officials and his team for making the project possible.
"We're glad that we can deliver a product that I think the town can be really happy with," DiDonato said.
Units include one-, two- and three-bedroom apartments. Amenities offered are a bike storage room, pickleball court, dog wash station, patio and more. The one-bedroom units start at just under $1,800 a month, while larger apartments range from $2,000 to $2,300, according to the complex's website.
Stephen Margerum, principal with Cove Property Management, said five people will move in this weekend, which will kick off a "consistent flow of move-ins" through November.
"We have a lot of demand, a lot of people wanting to move in as quickly as possible," Margerum said. "The response from the prospective residents have been really great."
He said the two 38-unit buildings will be filled out by the end of the year. The other two buildings, both 30 units and still under construction, will be delivered next spring, Margerum said.
Property management has been busy with tours and applications, he said. Before the leasing office was set up, more than 400 people signed up or went into the The Promenade's applicant database, Margerum said.
The Elliott Road project is one of Easton's larger housing developments, by units, currently in the pipeline. More than 1,000 units have recently opened, are under construction or have received town approval.
Earlier this month, developers for a downtown apartment complex on Brookletts Avenue cut the ribbon on a new leasing office. Construction on that 116-unit project begins later this fall.

author: STAFF REPORT
content:
The Star Democrat's top 10 online stories this week

 September 27, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: STAFF REPORT | Section: Local News

 Read News Document

 Here are the 10 stories that attracted the most page views on The Star Democrat's website this week. The stories are ranked in order of number of page views as of Wednesday evening.1. Maryland State Police investigating two late-night fatal crashes in Queen Anne's, Kent
Maryland State Police are investigating two fatal crashes that occurred late last Saturday in Queen Anne's and Kent counties, police said.
2. Trial begins for Cambridge man accused of murder, kidnapping of woman
Witness testimony began Sept. 16 in the jury trial for a Cambridge man charged with murdering and kidnapping a woman last year.
Kenneth Bradley, 43, was found guilty of first-degree murder and kidnapping later that week.
3. Queen Anne's denies charter school application
In a 3-2 vote, the Queen Anne's County Public Schools Board of Education voted to uphold the superintendent's recommendation and deny application for what would have been the first classical charter school in Queen Anne's County Sept. 10.
4. George Walish announces campaign for Maryland's 1st District
On Sept. 10, George Walish Jr. launched his campaign as a Democratic candidate for Maryland's 1st Congressional District.
5. Easton, other Eastern Shore towns host vigils for Charlie Kirk
Communities on the Eastern Shore have been hosting vigils for political activist Charlie Kirk after last week's shooting, including in Easton, where Republican officials organized a gathering in front of the Talbot County Courthouse.
6. Warriors rally to edge Bucs
Jordan Horsey's three touchdowns and Luke Stanco's three points after touchdown helped Easton rally from 17-point second-half deficit.
7. Caroline County officials learn about Early Head Start cut
On Tuesday, Charles Huester, executive director for Maryland Rural Development Cooperation, discussed Early Head Start funding cuts with the Caroline County Commissioners.
8. Easton business leaders reflect on summer, look ahead to fall
After an up-and-down summer with mixed results for local shops and restaurants, Easton business owners and leaders are keen for the fall season to start.
9. Crowds fuel Cambridge's 11th annual Maryland Ironman
The 11th annual Maryland Ironman was held on Saturday, Sept. 20. Thousands of people came out to support the athletes participating in the grueling events.
10. Delaware man convicted of sexual assault, burglary
In 2005, a match of fingerprints and DNA led to the arrest and now the conviction of a Delaware man for the sexual assault of a Cambridge woman in October 2002.

title: Chefs showcase local flavors at 17th annual Taste of Cambridge
author: Lily Tierney
content:
Chefs showcase local flavors at 17th annual Taste of Cambridge

 September 29, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Lily Tierney | Section: Dorchester 
 
 418
 Words 

 Read News Document

 CAMBRIDGE — Residents came out to support the sold-out 17th annual Taste of Cambridge on Saturday, Sept. 27, donned in rain jackets and ponchos and clutching their umbrellas alongside the delicious dishes given out by vendors.The event featured 20 dishes across five categories made by 10 local chefs.
"We were very happy with today's turnout, despite the overcast weather," Executive Director of Cambridge Main Street Christina Wingate-Spence said.
Crab cakes, hush puppies, tacos and seafood soup were among some of the dishes available Saturday.
GMK Catering Company won first place for the people's choice award this year, with participants commenting that the stew dish was "fantastic." The vote was incredibly close with GMK Catering Co winning by just four votes.
Head Chef and Owner of GMK Catering Company Christopher Branch brought his predecessors, who also happen to be brothers, Ramello and Cordell Whittaker, to compete in the seafood stew category. The stew included blackened rockfish, lump crab, black-eyed peas and a tomato-based curry sauce with mirepoix and chickpeas.
The event also had four guest judges who picked the 2025 best of dishes in five categories: best seafood soup or stew, best crab cake, best crab specialty, best Eastern Shore fare and best dessert.
Guest judges included radio host Jessica Dutra from Mix 106.5 Baltimore, Chef and Owner of Hamilton House Events and Catering and Executive Chef of Great Oak Manor Jordan Lloyd, Cambridge Mayor Lajan Cephas and Andrea Elgin with Coastal Style Magazine.
"I was invited to be on the panel of this amazing event. I'm honored to be here, and it's so fun to watch all these brilliant chefs really put their whole heart on the plate," Lloyd said.
"Some of these dishes, I can't put them down. I feel like it's not a taste of Cambridge. I feel like this is a meal of Cambridge, so I'm trying to be conservative, save some room," Cephas said after tasting eight of the 20 dishes.
The judges' picks for the 2025 awards were:
For best seafood soup or stew, the award went to Blue Ruin.For best crab cake, the award went to Blue Ruin.For best crab specialty, the award went to RaR Brewing.For best Eastern Shore fare, the award went to the Hyatt Regency Chesapeake Bay.For best dessert, the award went to Black Water Bakery.
"We could not be happier for the turnout. It's a great opportunity for literally hundreds of people to come to downtown Cambridge and support our restaurants and our shops and just kind of see the revitalization that's going on down here," Wingate-Spence said.

title: 'Hashtag Oxford scarecrows' are coming to town
author: Lily Tierney
content:
'Hashtag Oxford scarecrows' are coming to town

 October 2, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Lily Tierney | Section: Local News 
 
 351
 Words 

 Read News Document

 OXFORD — The Oxford Community Center hosted its first ever scarecrow building event on Wednesday. The scarecrows will be placed around town, and one fear-inducing, straw-filled figure will take home the grand prize.The town-wide scarecrow contest is a newly added element that aims to encourage residents and visitors to explore Oxford. The scarecrows will be placed on front porches, business and perhaps even on the beach.
"It'll just be really fun. And we wanted to create a space where when you're visiting Oxford, you can sit next to the scarecrow and take your selfies and be like, 'hashtag Oxford scarecrows,' and just make it a whole reason to come and explore during the holidays," said Oxford Community Center Executive Director Liza Ledford.
The idea to have the scarecrow building contest came about through a collaborative committee including members of the Oxford Fire Company Auxiliary, Oxford Community Center, Parks and Recreation, and Oxford Business Association.
Ledford said by combining forces, the group is able to reach a broader audience within the town.
The contest echoes a past town scavenger hunt that encouraged residents and visitors to find picket fences placed around in town.
"We used to do a thing where there were picket fences all over Oxford, and people would go and look and try to find them," Ledford said. "So we're like, well, if people put a scarecrow on their front porch, people will wander through town, they'll enjoy Oxford."
Ledford hopes the scarecrows are a particular hit on Oxford's upcoming Community Day on Oct. 18. The event kicks off at 9 a.m. with a 5k walk/run and beer truck to really tie in the Oktoberfest vibes.
From then until 2 p.m., there will be bouncy houses, food and a live band.
Community Day originally featured around 17 tables for nonprofits and Oxford associations, but Ledford said foot traffic was limited, which prompted the shift to an Oktoberfest/fall fun theme.
"So it just rolled all together where there would be great foot traffic, a beer truck, Bratwurst and community," Ledford said. "And then a whole month where you can check out Oxford and see the scarecrows all over town."

 GREENSBORO — The Town of Greensboro is currently accepting donations of new or clean, gently used winter clothes items for its annual winter clothes drive.Town resident Cathy Spencer said the event started because she hates to see people cold.
"As a child I never liked being cold, and as I got older, I saw other people, and I hate to think of children being cold," Spencer said. "So, people are always willing to give things, and I figure a winter clothes drive would be the perfect way to get clothes that people donated out of the public so no one's cold this winter."
The town is accepting winter clothes such as coats, hoodies, sweatshirts, heavy sweaters, gloves, scarfs, winter hats, ski pants and snow boots in all sizes, but mainly children's sizes.
The distribution event is scheduled for Nov. 21 at the Greensboro Community Hall at 13781 Greensboro Road. The drive begins at 10 a.m. to 1 p.m. and then 4 p.m. until 7 p.m.
The town emphasizes that everyone is welcome to attend, no matter their address or income.
Donated items can be dropped of at Greensboro Town Hall during normal business hours or at 509 N. Academy Street in Greensboro.
"I'm a giver, so I love doing this," Spencer said. "It just makes me feel good to see them come in there. eEverybody's laughing, everybody's smiling."
In addition to donations, the town is looking for a Spanish-speaking translator to help attendees who do not speak English.
Any person interested in being a translator for the drive should call the town at 410-482-6222 and ask to speak to Julie.

title: Country Cooking: Fall for these apple recipes
author: MARIE SAVAGE Country Cooking
content:
Country Cooking: Fall for these apple recipes

 October 3, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: MARIE SAVAGE Country Cooking | Section: Food 
 
 1473
 Words 

 Read News Document

 We all love the fall season and the farm products that are freshly grown and available — turnips, pumpkins, apples, late cabbage, and more.My friend Joy said they had picked two baskets of lima beans from their garden recently.
One of my favorite fall delicacies happens to be the apple. Before it was a multibillion-dollar communications or computer company, it was just a plain old fruit with many uses.
This week, we are doing the annual apple recipes — from simply washing the apples and eating them to making fresh pies, apple dumplings, apple crisp and more.
We never had apple trees on the farm growing up, but there were many local apple orchards nearby. Check your local newspaper or roadside stands for locations near you.
Once the two storage sheds were filled with potatoes, sweet potatoes, turnips and other fall vegetables, there would be a small spot set aside for storing some apples.
Different varieties of apples found on the Eastern Shore include Gala, Fuji, Honey Crisp, Golden Delicious, Red Delicious, McIntosh and Stayman. Everybody has their favorite.
With my favorite cook's (Mom's) influence, I use the following guide for cooking with apples:
The best apples for apple pies and apple crisp are Honeycrisp apples. They are known for their sweetness and crisp snap.Fuji apples are known for their largeness, crispness and sweetness and are popular for eating raw — perfect for lunch boxes or a snack any time of the day.Granny Smith is my favorite to use in apple dumplings due to their firmness.
Remember growing up with our parents saying, "An apple a day keeps the doctor away." It isn't true, folks.
We ate lots of apples but still had to go to town and get those "torpedo size needles." But there are health benefits.
Apples contain pectin, which help lower cholesterol and reduce the risk of heart disease. And the fruit is rich in antioxidants.
Before we begin exploring this week's apple recipes, I need to remind you of the upcoming Apple-Scrapple Festival being held in Bridgeville, Delaware. This year is the 33rd year Bridgeville has held this Festival. The celebration begins Friday evening, Oct. 10, at 4 p.m. with the opening ceremony and on Saturday, Oct. 11, from 9 a.m. to 6 p.m.
There is something for all ages to enjoy — including those delicious scrapple sandwiches, apple pies, apple dumplings, candy apples and more.
Now, let's cook with apples.
APPLE CRUMB PIE
7 1/2 cups apples (peeled, cored and sliced), 1 1/2 cups sugar, 2 tsps cinnamon, nutmeg to tase, unbaked pie shell, butter, 3/4 cup flour, 1/2 cup margarine.
Toss apples with 1 cup sugar, cinnamon and nutmeg . Put this mixture in an unbaked pie shell and dot it with butter. Make a topping consisting of 1/2 cup sugar, flour and margarine. Mix well and top the apples in a pie shell with this mixture. Bake at 350 degrees for one hour or until the apples are tender.
APPLE PIE COOKIES
3 tbsps salted butter, 2 apples (peeled and diced), 1/2 cup packed light brown sugar, juice of 1/2 lemon, 2 tbsps apple juice or cider, 1 tbsp cornstarch, 1 (14-oz) package refrigerated pie dough (2 crusts), 1/2 cup powdered sugar, 2 to 3 tsps heavy cream.
In a medium saucepan, melt the butter over medium-high heat. Add the apples and cook until they start to soften, 3 to 4 minutes. Stir in the brown sugar and lemon juice, bring to a simmer and cook until the apples are soft and the liquid is starting to reduce, 3 to 4 more minutes. In a small bowl, whisk together the apple juice and cornstarch and add it to the pan. Cook, stirring, until the mixture thickens, about 1 more minute. Remove from the heat and let cool. Preheat the oven to 350 degrees. Line a baking sheet with parchment paper. Roll out one piece of pie dough into a 12-inch round. Using a 3-inch cutter, cut out 12 small rounds and arrange on the baking sheet. Re-roll the scraps and cut out two more rounds. Roll the other piece of dough into a 12-inch round. Cut into 1/2-inch-wide strips. Cut the strips into shorter 3 1/2- to 4-inch pieces (you should have about 56 pieces). Arrange the dough rounds on the baking sheet. Place 1 tbsp of the apple mixture in the center of each. Lay 2 parallel strips of dough on top, then lay 2 more strips perpendicular to the first to look like a lattice. (Alternatively, weave the strips into a lattice.) Trim the edges of the strips, then press around the edges with a fork to seal. Bake until golden, 18 to 20 minutes. Remove to a rack to cool. For the glaze: In a small bowl, whisk together the powdered sugar, heavy cream, and cardamom. Drizzle over the cookies. If you are a diabetic like myself, instead of 2 tbsps of apple juice you can use water.
SOUR CREAM APPLE PIE
2 beaten eggs, 3/4 cup sugar, 1 cup sour cream, 1/3 cup + 2 tbsps flour, 1 tsp vanilla, apple pie spice, pinch of salt, 2 apples (peeled, cored and sliced), 1/3 cup brown sugar, 1/4 cup butter.
Preheat the oven to 350 degrees. Combine eggs, sugar, sour cream, 2 tbsps flour, vanilla, 1 tsp apple pie spice, pinch of salt and apples. Mix well and place in a baking dish. In another bowl mix brown sugar, 1/3 cup flour, 1 tsp apple pie spice and butter. Mix until crumbly and place on top of the apple mixture. Bake for 30 to 40 minutes.
APPLESAUCE
Here is one you can make with your kids.
4 sweet apples, 1/2 cup water, 1/2 tsp cinnamon.
Wash apples, cut into quarter pieces and place in a saucepan. Add water and cinnamon on top. Simmer with a cover on top until just tender — about 20 minutes. Let the children mash the cooked apples with a handheld potato masher.
HOMEMADE APPLE BUTTER
2 quarts apple cider, 4 quarts apples (thinly sliced), 2 cups sugar, 2 cups dark corn syrup, 1 tsp cinnamon.
Boil apple cider until reduced to only one quart. Put the apples into the cider and cook slowly, stirring frequently, until it begins to thicken. Add sugar, corn syrup and cinnamon and continue to cook until thick enough to spread when cool. Seal in sterilized jars. Makes 5 to 6 pints.
COUNTRY APPLE DUMPLINGS
2 large Granny Smith apples, 2 10-oz. cans refrigerated crescent rolls, 1 cup butter, 1 1/2 cups sugar, 1 tsp cinnamon, 12-oz can Mountain Dew or Diet Mountain Dew.
Preheat the oven to 350 degrees. Grease a 9-by-13-inch baking dish. Cut apples into eight triangles and set aside. Unroll crescent rolls into eight triangles. Roll each apple wedge in the, starting at the smallest end. Pinch to seal so the dough is fully closed around the apple wedge and place in the baking dish. Melt butter in a small pan and stir in sugar and cinnamon. Pour this mixture over the apple dumplings. Next pour Mountain Dew or Diet Mountain Dew, if you are a diabetic like myself, over the apple dumplings. Bake for 35 to 45 minutes until golden brown.
SOUTHERN FRIED APPLES
½ cup butter, ½ cup white sugar, 2 tbsps ground cinnamon (or to taste), 4 Granny Smith apples (peeled, cored and sliced).
Melt butter in a large skillet over medium heat. Add sugar and cinnamon; stir until sugar dissolves. Add apples and cook until softened, 5 to 8 minutes. At this point you can let them cool a little or dig right in.
DEEP FRIED APPLE RINGS
The best options are Granny Smith or Pink Lady for this recipe.
½ cup all-purpose flour, 3 tbsps milk, 1 tsp rum, 1 large egg, 1 tbsp granulated sugar or vanilla flavored sugar, 2 apples (large), 1 1/4 cups vegetable, ¼ cup granulated sugar or powdered sugar, 1 tsp ground cinnamon.
In a small bowl, mix flour, milk, rum, egg and 1 tbsp of sugar until you get a nice smooth batter. Wash and peel the apples. Slice them into thin slices (you should get 5-6 slices out of each apple). Remove the core using a small round cookie cutter. Or use apple corer, if you have one. Heat up the oil in a frying pan/skillet or deep fryer. Dip each ring in the batter and fry until both sides are golden brown. Place each apple ring onto a paper kitchen towel to get rid of the excess oil. While it is still warm, coat them in cinnamon sugar (mix sugar and cinnamon together).
Wait a minute. No Apple Pie recipe, Marie?
Not this time. I'll save that for my yearly pie column around Thanksgiving.
Also, as I put in the diabetic substitutes for some of the recipes. I'm working on a few columns for certain diets such as diabetic, fatty liver, heart healthy etc. If you have a certain diet, you'd like me to throw it in here, I'd be glad to do it. Reach me at mmsavage21145@gmail.com.

Mid-Shore Calendar

 October 4, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Staff Writer | Section: Calendar 
 
 2349
 Words 

 Read News Document

 Those seeking to have an event published in the Star Democrat's calendar are asked to email details to community@stardem.com.CARS AND COFFEE, 8:30 to 10:30 a.m., Oxford Community Center, 200 Oxford Road, Oxford. Free. Exotics, classics, muscle cars, imports all welcome. Sponsored by Prestige Auto Vault, Eat Sprout & Doc's Sunset Grille.
EASTON FALL KICKOFF, 10 a.m. to 7 p.m., downtown Easton. Pumpkin trail. live music, art shows, live pumpkin carving, free pumpkin painting, movie night and more. Info: discovereaston.com/fallkickoff/.
YOGA CLASS, 9:30 a.m., Oxford Community Center, 200 Oxford Road, Oxford. Intermediate yoga with Suzie Hurley. $20 per class. $150 for 10 classes. Info: 410-226-5904 or oxfordcc.org.
EASTON FARMERS MARKET, 8 a.m. to noon, 114 N. Harrison Street, Easton. Open rain or shine. Live music. Info: avalonfoundation.org.
ST. MICHAELS FARMERS MARKET, 8:30 to 11 a.m., 206 S. Talbot Street, St. Michaels. Open rain or shine.
YOGA WITH PATTY, 8 to 9 a.m., Dorchester Chamber of Commerce, second floor conference room, 306 High St., Cambridge. Designed for all skill levels, this class offers a harmonious blend of postures and breathing techniques to rejuvenate both mind and body. Call/text 410-463-8393 for reservations.
HURLOCK FALL FESTIVAL, 9 to 4 p.m., downtown Hurlock. Family Friendly event featuring arts and crafts show, parade down Main Street, music, food, train rides and more. Parade will begin at 10 a.m.
FALL RABIES CLINIC, 9 to 10 a.m., East New Market Volunteer Fire Department, 4020 E.New Market Bypass, East New Market. Vaccinate dogs, cats and ferrets. $5 per animal. Dogs must be leashed. Cats and ferrets must be in carriers. Cash or checks only. Call Kimberly Keene at 443-521-4996 with any questions.
BOATYARD BASH, 1 to 5 p.m., Richardson Maritime Museum, 103 Hayward Street, Cambridge. Oysters on the half shell, live music, food/beverage trucks, silent auction, vendors, boats, free parking, more. Adults $26, ages 13-20 $10, under 12 free. Rain date Oct. 5. richardsonmuseum.org.
TALBOT BIRD CLUB, Pickering Creek. Waterfowl, shorebirds, passerines. All welcome. Bring binoculars. Meet at Pickering Creek Audubon Center parking area at 7 a.m. (GPS 38.86 N, 76.124 W). Leaders: Lisa Sargeant (978-697-0135 or sargeant76@gmail.com).
GFNY BICYCLE RACE, Race Street in Cambridge and throughout Dorchester County. The full course is 92 miles with a medium course of 48 miles available. The race starts and finishes on Race Street. Info: maryland.gfny.com/.
HARVEST FESTIVAL, noon to 4 p.m., Layton's Chance Vineyard & Winery, 4225 New Bridge Road, Vienna. Craft vendors, grape stomping, Cascading Carlos, food trucks, live music, more. Tickets: laytonschance.orderport.net/wines/Event-Tickets
GIFT CARD BINGO, noon to 5 p.m., Cambridge Elks Lodge 1272, 5464 Elks Lodge Road, Cambridge. 20 regular games will win a $50 gift card. Special games will be available at the door and will have $100+ prizes. Elks Lodge will be selling food and drinks. $25 in advance, $30 at the door.
GROCERY BINGO, Doors open at 5:45 p.m., games begin at 6:30 p.m., Cordova Firehouse. Refreshments will be available for purchase. Info: 410-924-6535.
YOGA CLASS, Oxford Community Center, 200 Oxford Road. 1 p.m. Yoga for advanced beginners with Suzie Hurley. $20 per class. $150 for 10 classes. Info: 410-226-5904 or oxfordcc.org.
INTRO TO IMPROV, 7:30 to 9 p.m. Six-week beginner workshop with Improv Easton. No experience required. Advance registration required: https://tinyurl.com/Intro2ImprovSept2025. Info: ImprovEaston@gmail.com.
INTRODUCTION TO SQUARE DANCE, 5:30 to 7:30 p.m., Maple Elementary School, 5225 Egypt Road, Cambridge. Free introductory lessons. Come as a single or bring a partner. Beginners from middle schoolers through senior adults welcome. Experienced dancers are invited to join.
STRONG AND STEADY, 10 a.m., Oxford Community Center, 200 Oxford Road, OxfoRoad Workout class for adults seeking to improve muscle strength with Janet Pfeffer. $10 per class. $80 for 10 classes. Info: 410-226-5904 or oxfordcc.org.

GRIEF SUPPORT GROUP, 9 to 10:30 a.m., Coastal Hospice Dorchester Office, 316 Dorchester Ave., Cambridge. Free.
YARN AND NEEDLE GROUP, 12:30 to 3 p.m., Brookletts Place Talbot County Senior Center, Easton. Every Tuesday. Some help may be available for knitting and crocheting. Open to anyone 60 years of age or older at no cost. Info: 410-822-2869.
BINGO, 7:30 p.m., American Legion Post 29, 9238 Legion Road, Denton. 5 p.m. doors open, 7:30 p.m. games start. Info:410-479-2708.

title: Easton's Fall Kickoff adorns downtown with pumpkins
author: Konner Metz
content:
Easton's Fall Kickoff adorns downtown with pumpkins

 October 7, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Konner Metz | Section: Local News 
 
 252
 Words 

 Read News Document

 EASTON — Downtown Easton is beginning to look a lot more festive.As warm summer-like weather persists, the town continued its tradition of hosting a two-day Fall Kickoff event during the opening weekend of October. Families walked downtown streets for live music, pumpkin painting and more on Friday and Saturday.
Easton Economic Development Corporation Executive Director Holly DeKarske said the event went well, especially compared to past iterations.
"This is probably one of the best years that we had it," DeKarske said.
On streets like Harrison and Washington, many businesses placed carved pumpkins outside their doors, making a decorative walk for residents and visitors. A contest for the best decorations is being held, with voting open on the Discover Easton Facebook page until Oct. 13.
A giant crab made out of pumpkins was placed in front of Thompson Park on the corner of Washington and Dover streets — a display that took professionals about eight or nine hours to create, DeKarske said.
Live music and performances entertained residents and passersby at Thompson Park, while many stopped in the Waterfowl Festival building for a Breast Cancer Awareness month fundraiser by the Working Artists Forum.
The Academy Art Museum hosted a pumpkin-painting event for kids. DeKarske said around 150 children participated, maybe twice as many as last year.
DeKarske noted she saw families walking around even after storefronts closed to enjoy the decorated downtown.
"We want people to hopefully dine and stop into the stores," DeKarske said. "But at the same time, getting people out and offering something that's free and family-friendly."

title: 'Out here in God's country': Molly's Maryland Outdoor Festival draws 3,000
author: WILL BONTRAGER wbontrager@chespub.com
content:
'Out here in God's country': Molly's Maryland Outdoor Festival draws 3,000

 October 9, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: WILL BONTRAGER wbontrager@chespub.com | Section: Life 
 
 519
 Words 

 Read News Document

 Molly's Place 15th annual fall tent sale returned late last month, rebranded last year as the Maryland Outdoor Festival.The three-day event in Kennedyville, held Sept. 26-28, featured a tent filled with deals on hunting, fishing and outdoor gear. Major sponsors included Benelli USA, Hevi-Shot, Banded and Vortex Optics.
Sales representatives answered questions while food vendors, live music and children's activities kept crowds entertained.
"We're out here in God's country, the Eastern Shore, surrounded by like-minded people. It doesn't get better than that," said world champion duck caller Sean Mann, who offered a calling clinic Sunday, teaching mallard calls.
"Most ducks respond to mallard calls. That's always the first thing we teach on the Shore," he said.
Nearby, Jimmy Wren, owner of United Call Works, led Saturday clinics and gave away merchandise. A Maryland native, Wren said he was glad to be home and reported selling more than 40 calls during the festival.
Decoy artists Jeff Coates and Nick Castiglione demonstrated their painting techniques, with Coates applying a natural-looking feathered texture to cork wood.
Firearm retailers and representatives such as Retay from Easton, shotgun manufacturers and LWRCI discussed trends in gun ownership. A hot topic this year was silencers and short barrels, with attendees asking questions following the decision to reduce the National Firearms Act tax on suppressors from $200 to $0 beginning Jan. 1.
"Using silencers is all about hearing protection," said sales representative Liam Parker, who praised lawmakers' move to eliminate the fee.
"This will open up a section of new buyers," said Scott Tull, account manager for LWRCI.
Other vendors also had strong sales. Under Armour sold out of many items, while Banded Hunting Gear reported hip waders, panel blinds and Phantom Tech soft shell hoodies as top sellers.
Outside the tent, Chestertown Lions Club members directed parking while families enjoyed children's activities. Shore Party Rentals provided a bounce house, Kent 4-H Triple Shots offered a BB gun and archery range, and Beth Hill, principal agent associate for 4-H Youth Development in Kent County, demonstrated leaf-pattern tracing. Face painter Ashley Burl kept a steady line of children waiting for designs.
Food vendors drew crowds as well. The Robinson family's Madhouse Oysters sold 300 oysters by Saturday afternoon. The Farmers Daughter BBQ served pulled pork, Jimmy's Fat Rolls offered lobster rolls, and Get the Scoop dished out hand-dipped ice cream, milkshakes and sundaes.
Music filled the festival grounds with Friday performances by Gunner's Rest, Nicholas Ray — playing one of his last local shows before moving to Nashville — and Ashley Vagnoni Chapa. Saturday featured singer-songwriter Joe Bryan, playing alt-country, classic rock and indie covers, followed by the Old School Duo from Galena. Easton country artist Justin Ryan closed out the weekend Sunday.
Chestertown Lions Club member Michael Moore estimated 300 vehicles were parked on-site around noon Saturday.
Marketing coordinator Justin Ly said more than 3,300 people attended the three-day event.
"Another one in the books! Thank you to everyone who came out, to our vendors, brand partners, sponsors, nonprofits and every member of the Molly's family. It was a great weekend," Ly said.
Molly's Place operates in Kennedyville and recently opened a second location, Molly's Easton. More information is available at mollys.com.

A day full of Mid-Shore stories worth reading

 October 10, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Staff Writer | Section: Headlines 
 
 104
 Words 

 Read News Document

 Sometimes it's difficult to figure out what to write in these newsletter introductions.They're supposed to point to the most impactful, most interesting, most creative story of the day. But some evenings, I struggle to pick out just one to highlight for our readers.
Tonight is one of those nights.
We have produced a lot of meaningful content, from a breaking story about a sewer line break to a feature about a new radio station broadcasting local history and an informational piece about an upcoming storm and its potential impacts.
You can find all of those stories and more at the links below.
Thanks, as always, for reading.

title: Mid-Shore Community Foundation welcomes eight new members
author: SUBMITTED NEWS
content:
Mid-Shore Community Foundation welcomes eight new members

 October 14, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: SUBMITTED NEWS | Section: News 
 
 665
 Words 

 Read News Document

 EASTON — Mid-Shore Community Foundation welcomes eight new members to its board of directors: Leslie Bishop, Suze Chaffinch, LaMonte Cooke, Kathleen Deoudes, Rabbi Peter E. Hyman, Richard "Rich" Loeffler, Margaret "Peggy" Rennels and Arraminta Ware.The Foundation works with donors to establish funds for the region — funds that are distributed as grants and scholarships, provides training programs and endowment management services to area nonprofits, and supports start‐up charities and local charitable projects through fiscal sponsorship.
"As one of the founding board members, I am always pleased to welcome a new slate of directors to this outstanding organization," said Moorhead Vermilye, president of the board of directors. "With Buck Duncan at the helm and a robust, working board of directors, MSCF does exponential good on the Mid-Shore. We love to see more people energized and inspired by the work."
Vermilye said he was grateful for the 2025 board of directors and thanked outgoing board members Bill Christopher, Joe Holt, John Lewis, Becky Loukides, Jenny Rhodes and Tracy Tyler for their service to the Mid-Shore.
In 2016, after raising two sons and having a career as a residential interior designer, Leslie Bishop and her husband retired to Cambridge from Washington, D.C., and soon after, she founded MidShore Meals til Monday, a supplemental food program for children and families facing food insecurity in Dorchester County.
Suze Chaffinch of Denton was born and raised on the Eastern Shore and has lived most of her life in Caroline County. As an elementary school teacher, she taught for many years at Greensboro Elementary School. Since retirement, she has enjoyed volunteering with various organizations. Chaffinch previously served on the Foundation board from 2018 to 2024.
LaMonte Cooke of Chestertown is the director of the Queen Anne's County Department of Corrections, a position he has held since 1987. He has more than 40 years of criminal justice and government service experience, including serving as the first African American Kent County Deputy Sheriff.
Kathleen "Kathy" Deoudes currently serves as chair of the UMMS Shore Regional Health Board of Directors. Before retirement, she worked in the Maryland State Senate as a legislative aide to state Sen. E.J. Pipkin. She lives in Queen Anne's County with her husband Nick. Deoudes served on the Foundation board from 2017 to 2023.
Rabbi Peter E. Hyman of Easton recently retired after serving 18 years as the first full-time rabbi at Easton's Temple B'nai Israel. Hyman is very active in the community, and he has a long history of promoting greater understanding and respect for individuals with different religious beliefs.
Richard "Rich" Loeffler has worked as a business consultant for the Maryland Small Business Development Center (SBDC). Before working for the SBDC, Loeffler was part owner of a small manufacturing company located in Dorchester County, where he served as president of the Dorchester YMCA and on the board of directors for Dorchester General Hospital.
Margaret "Peggy" Rennels was born and raised in Talbot County. After graduating from Easton High School and Skidmore College, she received her M.D. at the University of Maryland School of Medicine. Rennels cared for patients, taught, and was involved with clinical evaluations of vaccines for the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention, part of the U.S. Department of Health and Human Services, and the Food and Drug Administration. Since retirement, she has devoted her energies to the wellbeing of children through her work on the board of directors of the Critchlow Adkins Children's Center. Rennels served on the Foundation board 2018 to 2024.
Arraminta Ware grew up on a farm near Sudlersville. After graduating from Lynchburg College with an accounting degree, Ware began working in Chestertown, where she is a principal with Anthony, Judge and Ware LLC. Ware lives near Chestertown with her husband Eric Schrader, a self-employed farmer. She serves on the board of directors of Chesapeake Bank and Trust and served on the Foundation board from 2016 to 2022.
Officers for the 2026 board of directors are Vermilye, chair; Alice Ryan, vice chair; Carrie Manuel, treasurer; David Nagel, assistant treasurer and Andy Meehan, secretary.

title: 'The end of an era': St. Paul's Church gets deconsecrated
author: Lily Tierney
content:
'The end of an era': St. Paul's Church gets deconsecrated

 October 15, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Lily Tierney | Section: News 
 
 515
 Words 

 Read News Document

 VIENNA — On Sundays, when the pews should have been packed, the Rev. Dennis Morgan would walk into St. Paul's Episcopal Church in Vienna and, at most, see two parishioners prepared for sermon.That is until Sept. 21, when the parish had its final service and St. Paul's closed its doors for good. The church's closure was not the town's first this year.
St. Paul's was deconsecrated just months after Vienna United Methodist Church, located directly across the street, stopped its services, Morgan said.
"It's a very, very bittersweet time," he said. "You know, realizing that it must be done, but, at the same time, you know, it's heartbreaking."
The church closures are the consequence of attendance trends seen in Vienna and across the country.
About 33% of adults in the United States attend religious services in person as of February 2025. This is a dramatic decline from 2007, when 50% of adults attended religious services in person, according to a recent Pew Research Center study.
"There have been really low numbers at St. Paul's for several years, and it just wasn't sustainable," said Administrative Assistant to the Bishop of the Episcopal Diocese of Easton Lynn Anstatt.
In 2020, there were 18 parishioners on the books at St. Paul's, with roughly eight members attending services weekly. This dropped to 11 members on the books with around two attending weekly services by 2025, Morgan said.
He said the pandemic and static population of Vienna largely contributed to decreased attendance of all the churches in the area. Only a handful still hold weekly services.
Keeping St. Paul's open and active had become an existential question for Morgan.
"We could have kept the property going probably for quite a while, but we had no mission, no outreach and we questioned the 'why' of it more than the 'how' of it," the pastor said.
Morgan was in conversation with the Bishop of the Episcopal Diocese of Easton for around three years in an attempt to keep the church open. But after seeing minimal improvement, he could no longer justify keeping the parish going.
"The church is still available to use although it has been deconsecrated, so we do have access to the church. But in terms of services and everything, that does come to an end," Morgan said.
The decommissioning of St. Paul's comes after more than 300 years of active service in Vienna.
There are now no Episcopal Churches in Vienna, but because attendance was so low and the church was not involved in the community, Morgan doesn't think the deconsecration will have much negative impact on the larger Vienna community.
Many community members have family buried in the cemetery on the property and have inquired with Morgan about the cemetery's future.
"The difficult decision to close the church, despite such a vast legacy, was driven by factors such as declining membership and the increasing costs of maintaining historic structures," former parishioner of St. Paul's and Vienna resident Susan Donaghue wrote in an email to the Star Democrat. "The conclusion of ministry at St. Paul's marks the end of an era for the town of Vienna and the community it so faithfully served."

title: 42nd annual Easton Prayer Breakfast honors the founder
author: Lily Tierney
content:
42nd annual Easton Prayer Breakfast honors the founder

 October 16, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Lily Tierney | Section: Local News 
 
 221
 Words 

 Read News Document

 EASTON — The 42nd annual Easton Prayer Breakfast was held Oct. 16 at the Easton Volunteer Fire Department with Talbot County Sheriff Joe Gamble presiding as the master of ceremonies.The breakfast included full programming with prayers and speeches from Easton residents. Prayers covered government, those who protect and serve, educators, churches, families, businesses and Thanksgiving.
The event was dedicated to longtime Easton resident Bob Dunsmoor, who died in April while praying by his bedside. A tribute to Dunsmoor and his late wife, Liz, acknowledged their work in ministry and in starting the Easton Prayer Breakfast.
Daron Miller was the keynote speaker of the event. Miller discovered the gospel during his 13 years as a Navy SEAL. He said he successfully completed the basic underwater Navy SEAL training with "supernatural assistance" rather than with natural aptitude, even if he didn't know it at the time.
Upon moving to Easton, Miller discipled at Talbot Bible Church and followed successive steps to biblical studies, seminary and chaplaincy.
Sts. Peter and Paul High School sophomore Chase Olavsrud presented his essay "More Than a Fisherman, The Making of a Saint." The work detailed Saint Peter's journey, emphasizing faith, failure, repentance, leadership and sacrifice as the path to holiness.
Deputy John Coleman belted the hymn "How Great Thou Art" from Psalms 150 before Gamble closed the breakfast with a final prayer.

title: As it has for generations before, Rocky Horror still astounds
author: Lily Tierney
content:
As it has for generations before, Rocky Horror still astounds

 October 17, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Lily Tierney | Section: Local News 
 
 315
 Words 

 Read News Document

 EASTON — Inside the Waterfowl building on Thursday evening, Janet, Brad, Riff Raff, Eddie Ex and Magenta could be found doing the time warp again.Woohoo Productions put on its first-ever Rocky Horror Picture Show with bags of props for each attendee, a buffet themed alongside the film and games galore before the show began.
The games included a costume contest, a raunchy fill-in-the-blank game for first timers and a chaotic "find the item" game where guests scrambled to find items ranging from red lipstick to a high heel.
The master of ceremonies sprayed water guns at guests to mimic the rain scene, encouraged audience participation with cues from the film that have endured for decades and by the end of the night, no one was a stranger.
"It brings people together who are so similar and you can just sit together and you see them dancing together and throwing all the ridiculous stuff around. It's so fun," said Woohoo Productions founder Angel Perez. "And at the end of the day, that's what really matters, is just bring the community together in some way to have a good time and Who knows? Some people may leave the building today and create some new friendships."
Perez founded Woohoo Productions three months ago, and this was the company's first major event.
For Perez who has been doing community and family events in Caroline County as CEO of Caroline Pride, program manager at Chesapeake Culinary Center, board member of Shore Legal and more, he's excited to pivot to adult-focused events.
"I thought now it's time for me to try to make some money out of here and do the fun stuff, something I've been doing for free for the last 10 years," Perez said.
He was happy with the turnout of the event considering it was a Thursday evening and the first time they've hosted this event, but he hopes to grow attendance next year.

title: Circle of giving expands impact: Community backs programs focused on recovery, rescue and feeding families
author: ANDREA GRABENSTEIN agrabenstein@chespub.com
content:
Circle of giving expands impact: Community backs programs focused on recovery, rescue and feeding families

 October 17, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: ANDREA GRABENSTEIN agrabenstein@chespub.com | Section: Life 
 
 700
 Words 

 Read News Document

 As part of its mission to understand community needs and leverage collective resources in support, the Kent Island Giving Circle awarded funding to several organizations across Queen Anne's County.Those recognized during the group's biannual meeting Oct. 6 at the Chesapeake Bay Environmental Center in Grasonville are dedicated to substance abuse recovery, controlling feral cat populations and feeding local families.
Not My Child
After the heart-wrenching loss of her husband's son, Anthony Reno Jr., to fentanyl poisoning at age 21, Not My Child Inc. was founded to fight the heroin and opioid epidemic, said Executive Director Laura Reno.
"Growing from a need to do more with grief, Not My Child seeks to provide access and unwavering support for individuals in recovery and their families," Reno said.
The organization's name comes from a common misconception — that addiction "won't affect my family." Reno said Not My Child works to build inclusive communities where individuals in recovery can thrive without stigma or barriers.
"Addiction is not a choice, and when one person struggles with substance use disorder, the entire family struggles," she said.
With community support, including from the Giving Circle, Not My Child has launched its Project Restart program, which connects individuals in recovery with potential employers, job training and education.
Recognizing that those in recovery often face limited opportunities, Reno said the program aims to "break the cycle and develop meaningful success stories instead."
Beginning in November, Not My Child will offer a series of licensed-therapist and peer-led support groups, including Choose Hope, dedicated to loved ones of individuals struggling with substance use disorder.
Awareness campaigns and events also partner with local organizations such as Celebrate Recovery, Queen Anne's County Goes Purple, the Giving the Edge Foundation, Compass Hospice and the Jacob Sloan Foundation.
"While we can't undo tragedies, by reducing stigma and providing resources, together we can choose how we respond," Reno said.
Saving Future Feral Cats Inc.
When it comes to community cats, Inge Peters' phone is always buzzing.
As founder of Saving Future Feral Cats Inc., Peters is dedicated to reducing overpopulation and easing the suffering of abandoned cats in Queen Anne's County.
To humanely rescue and rehabilitate abandoned cats, the organization operates a trap-neuter-vaccinate-return program to help maintain healthy feral cat populations.
"We believe it is our responsibility as a community to care for the cats that we as humans have abandoned, failed to spay or neuter, or forced to live outdoors," Peters said.
For cats that cannot be adopted, Saving Future Feral Cats places them as barn cats.
The group also partners with other animal welfare organizations for education, fundraising and outreach.
Peters said she has transformed her home into "a rescued cat oasis."
"It is their home now," she said.
The nonprofit relies on a core group of volunteers and is always seeking more — even those who simply want to stop by and socialize with the cats.
"There is nothing more decompressing than petting a cat," Peters said.
Feed A Family
As a community-based food program, Feed A Family demonstrates that even once-a-year actions can make a big impact.
Sponsored by local churches and supported by community donations, Feed A Family provides door-to-door delivery and pickup of Thanksgiving food boxes filled with all the essentials and trimmings for a memorable holiday meal, said representative Bobbie Bell.
A key part of the program is its support for local food pantries, helping relieve their workload during the holiday season.
"Through our collections, food banks can supplement food for other weeks of the year and give their volunteers a much-needed break," Bell said.
While Feed A Family does not yet have official 501©(3) status, it partners with local organizations and serves as a drop-off site for communitywide food efforts to ensure no family goes hungry during the holidays.
"We are blessed with such a bounty," Bell said.
The organization is always seeking volunteers to sort, package and deliver donations. Leading up to Thanksgiving, "Turkey Tags" can be picked up at local churches, businesses and schools to help provide food for families in need.
Currently serving residents from Kent Island to Centreville, Feed A Family hopes to expand north into Sudlersville with additional support, Bell said.
The Kent Island Giving Circle, established in 2022, meets twice a year to support local organizations that serve community needs. The group recently celebrated its 50th member.
More information is available at kentislandgivingcircle.org

title: Spooktacular Fest in Denton brings family fun energy to start spooky season
author: AHMAD GARNETT agarnett@chespub.com
content:
Spooktacular Fest in Denton brings family fun energy to start spooky season

 October 21, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: AHMAD GARNETT agarnett@chespub.com | Section: News 
 
 256
 Words 

 Read News Document

 DENTON — On Friday evening, hundreds of Caroline County residents attend Spooktacular Fest in Denton, hosted by the Chesapeake Culinary Center.According to project manager Angel Perez, the major Halloween event is one of the biggest in Caroline County because the preparation starts in the summer to come up with new ideas to improve from the previous year's event.
"It takes a couple months to plan this this event, you always trying to show or provide something different than the previous year," Perez said.
Perez also mentioned new this year were more vendors and community resources.
According to Perez, the event saw more than 750 people this year with the new and improved haunted house inside the Chesapeake Culinary Center being the main attraction.
"We have a different haunted house this year, it's a little more like spooky than friendly," Perez said about new things at Spooktacular Fest this year. "We had venders this year, we had a DJ, we had an MC, we had a trivia game."
With vendors at the Spooktacular Fest, the hope was to give families an opportunity to have fun but also learn about community resources.
For growing and new families in Caroline County, the Spooktacular Fest allows for a fun place to enjoy the town besides the normal trick or treat day.
"We've lived in Denton for like five or six years, and I think it's just nice to have other than trick or treating like a party that our family can get dressed up and go to, and it has everything," said Denton resident Jennifer Reilby.

title: Historic Wye Church hosts 60th annual bazaar
author: Staff Writer
content:
Historic Wye Church hosts 60th annual bazaar

 October 22, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Staff Writer | Section: Life 
 
 242
 Words 

 Read News Document

 The Wye Parish Bazaar will mark its 60th anniversary on Saturday, Nov. 1, from 9 a.m. to 2 p.m. at the Parish Hall and on the grounds of Old Wye Church on Route 662 in Wye Mills.The Christmas Shoppe will feature decorations, many handmade by the church ladies. Winter blooming plants including amaryllis, Christmas cactus and paper whites will be available. Trinkets and Treasures will offer jewelry and other items, while Handmades will include mittens.
The Sweet and Savory Shoppe will sell homemade cakes, cookies and pies, as well as brandied cranberries, fruitcake, jams and jellies, bread-and-butter pickles, basil paste and herbed olive oil.
New this year is the Emporium, located under a tent by the church, offering bargain-priced items. The Christmas Book Cottage in the Vestry House will sell books at 80 percent off, including adult and children's titles, holiday-themed books, cookbooks, puzzles and stocking-stuffers.
The Bazaar Cafe will serve vegetable crab soup, sausage and potato soup, Italian wedding soup, country ham biscuits and Smith Island cake.
At 11 a.m., the Wye Parish town crier will announce a performance by the Queen Anne's Chorale of Christmas music in Old Wye Church. Church tours will be offered throughout the morning. The church has been restored to its original 1721 condition.
The bazaar is a fundraising activity of the Episcopal Church Women of Wye Parish. Proceeds will be donated to Haven Ministries, Compass Regional Hospice and Tides of Grace.
For more information, call the church office at 410-827-8484.

title: Sons and Daughters of American Revolution hold membership workshop
author: Staff Writer
content:
Sons and Daughters of American Revolution hold membership workshop

 October 22, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Staff Writer | Section: Life 
 
 168
 Words 

 Read News Document

 On Oct. 25 from 2-4 p.m., the Colonel Tench Tilghman Chapter of the Maryland Society Sons of the American Revolution and the General Perry Benson Chapter of the Daughters of the American Revolution will sponsor a workshop hosted by the Talbot County Free Library in Easton.The workshop is titled "How to Join the SAR or DAR." Both organizations will have representatives present who will provide a brief overview about the founding and mission of both organizations as well as the activities they provide for members and services they provide to residents of the Mid-Shore community.
Afterward, members of the organizations will help those interested in joining either organization perform online family history research to create a family tree diagram and begin to prepare a membership application that traces an individual's lineage back to one of their patriot ancestors.
The event is free and open to the public. Seating is limited. If interested in participating in this workshop, please reply by sending an email to WesleyOHagood@gmail.com.
Light refreshments will be served.
